title: Group appeals Maine’s decision to give education contracts to AI-powered firm
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Last month, an out-of-state firm backed by private equity and venture capital beat a Maine-based early childhood education organization for a pair of state contracts.
Now, advocates are sounding the alarm over what the decision could mean for Maine children and raising concerns about how the Maine Department of Health and Human Services evaluated the proposals.
Shine Early Learning, a New York organization backed by the private equity behemoth BlackRock, won two multimillion-dollar contracts to provide training and assistance to Maine’s early childhood educators through 2028.
The firm underbid Maine Roads to Quality, a group created in 1999 by the Catherine Cutler Institute at the University of Southern Maine, by about $2 million. Shine Early Learning said it will achieve lower costs by using artificial intelligence to do much of the work Maine Roads’ 30-odd employees currently perform.
Those employees are now bracing for layoffs as Maine Roads might be forced to shut down. The University of Maine System appealed the contract decisions last week.
Ending a decades-long partnership in favor of an out-of-state tech company could have drastic effects on the state’s early childhood education system, said Lauren Stark, an analyst with the progressive Maine Center for Economic Policy.
“There is not necessarily an incentive for the company to improve early learning or to increase access to affordable childcare. There’s not a public good motivation for them as a for-profit venture capitalist company,” Stark said. “The motivation is to have a greater profit.”
“Lower cost is not the same as a better value,” she added.
Maine Roads provides training and assistance to about 10,000 Maine childcare providers each year. It’s cultivated relationships with schools, educators, students and regulators alike over the last 27 years, said University of Maine System spokesperson Samantha Warren.
Work that was historically housed under a single contract was instead split into two earlier this year: One for coaching, credentialing and training educators, and another for providing a DHHS-approved plan “designed to improve (the) quality” of child care services.
Kimberlee Belcher-Badal is the executive director of the National Workforce Registry Alliance, a group that supports early childhood workforce registry systems across the country. The alliance has worked with Maine Roads for decades, Belcher-Badal said.
In a letter to DHHS’ appeals committee, Belcher-Badal said “Maine’s registry and its team are among the strongest in the nation” and questioned whether Shine Early Learning’s plans to implement AI chatbots would really benefit Maine educators.
In Missouri, Montana and many other states where Shine Early Learning operates, established early childcare providers have seen similar outcomes after losing contracts to the firm: Sweeping layoffs, worse services and less person-to-person connection in a field heavily reliant upon it.
DHHS graded Maine Roads’ and Shine Early Learning’s proposals on a scale from 0 to 100, as it does all submissions. Shine Early Learning’s bid for the coaching contract received a 97 and its proposal for the training plan got a perfect 100, public records show. Maine Roads received about 73 points on each.
In a pair of letters sent to the state, the university system questioned how DHHS graded each proposal and asked regulators to invalidate the contract decisions over irregularities in the scoring process. Maine Roads lost points “for no stated reason,” the appeal alleges.
“(DHHS) gave Shine near-perfect technical scores without resolving questions the evaluators themselves raised,” the appeal reads. “The award is arbitrary and capricious, and the evaluation contains irregularities creating fundamental unfairness.”
A DHHS spokesperson said the scores were issued in accordance with the processes laid out in its requests for proposals but did not specify how Shine Early Learning received such high marks.
Shine Early Learning’s website says the company uses “data-driven services and solutions” to “accelerate child and family outcomes.” The company has not responded to requests for comment on its expansion into Maine.
The company’s proposals state they plan to use AI agents and chatbots to screen prospective teachers’ applications, power a “family navigation assistant” and manage the state’s early childcare provider registry.
Stark, with the Maine Center for Economic Policy, is skeptical that AI will be an adequate replacement for Maine Roads’ human staff.
“You need people with expertise to set up the systems, you need mentors who have experience in the field working with early childhood educators. And a chatbot is not a mentor,” she said.
Shine Early Learning is owned by Acelero Inc., a company backed by some of the world’s largest private equity and venture capital companies. The senior portfolio manager for BlackRock, which manages some $11 trillion in assets globally, said the firm was investing in Acelero to widen its reach across the country.
A report published in February by the National Women’s Law Center, a nonprofit advocacy organization, found private equity groups are increasingly acquiring vital community services, from childcare to housing.
“Private equity investors face more structural incentives to prioritize short-term profits than any other form of corporate ownership or investment,” the report states. “This makes them the quickest and most likely to identify and exploit opportunities to extract wealth from any market.”
It is unclear when the appeal will be resolved. The state’s contracts with the firm have not yet been finalized, a DHHS spokesperson said, and won’t be until the appeals process is complete.

title: Community rallies to save historic Bath clock tower after rot is found
text:
Community rallies to save historic Bath clock tower after rot is discovered
People in Bath are seeking help in their effort to save the historic clock tower at First Baptist Church.
The clock tower has stood watch over the Maine community for more than 170 years, but recent renovation work on the church's clock and steeple uncovered severe rot damage, likely doubling the cost of the renovation project.
Bath residents are now rallying to save the piece of history.
"Because of funds, we are stuck," said Fred Bogue, a First Baptist Church trustee. "It's our bell tower, but it's also the city's clock. The bell rings, and it has been ringing since 1855. We would like to see it continue."
A GoFundMe page has been set up in an effort to raise money to help fund the project, which is expected to cost about $150,000.

title: Maine’s candidate for U.S. Senate answer your questions
text:
To put the focus on the topics and concerns that matter most to you, the BDN opinion section asked subscribers for their questions for the candidates for governor, U.S. Senate and U.S. House. In coming days, we’ll share their answers. Today, we have the answers from Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who is seeking a sixth term in the U.S. Senate, and her Democratic challenger Troy Jackson, former president of the Maine Senate.
What measures would you vote for to ensure that all Mainers have access to affordable healthcare? Should all Americans have access to the same coverage, at the same cost, as members of Congress? Do you support Medicare-for-all or another form of universal health care? If so, how would you pay for it? If not, why not.
Susan Collins
Increasing health care access and affordability remains a top priority. I worked to lower prescription drug costs, expand rural health care, advance diabetes and Alzheimer’s research and treatment, and strengthen the health care workforce. I voted against President Donald Trump’s Medicaid cuts, and instead pushed to create the $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Fund, which has brought $190 million to Maine. I’ve secured nearly $300 million in funds directly for Maine hospitals, health and dental clinics, recovery centers, emergency services, and health care workforce training programs across Maine since 2021. I supported bipartisan bills to promote lower-cost generics, end surprise billing, and outlaw pharmacy “gag clauses” that prevented patients from paying the lowest price for medicine. I’m leading bipartisan legislation to cap the out-of-pocket cost of insulin at $35 per month.
Members of Congress obtain their health insurance through the Affordable Care Act exchanges. I support this requirement.
We should expand access to high-quality and affordable health care, not create government-run monopolies. A government-run plan would cost a staggering $30 trillion, require massive tax increases on middle- and low-income Americans, force 165 million Americans off their current insurance, threaten access to health care in rural America, and leave us without the funds we need to protect Social Security. Government-run plans in other countries have led to long wait times for care, excess deaths, and a two-tiered system that favors the rich. We don’t need that in America.
Troy Jackson
Health care is a human right. No Mainer should avoid the doctor, ration their medicine, or face bankruptcy because they got sick. I support Medicare for All because it would guarantee every American comprehensive care without premiums, deductibles, or massive medical debt — and finally stop insurance companies from profiting by denying people the care they need. Sen. Susan Collins has spent years siding with drug companies, insurance companies, and Donald Trump’s efforts to gut Mainers’ health care; I’ll always stand with Maine families.
And while the federal government says there’s no money for health care or Social Security, it’s spending billions of dollars funding endless wars abroad and giving a $70 billion blank check to ICE while giving tax cuts for the wealthy. We have the money — we’re just spending it the wrong way.
What specific steps do you support to preserve the financial stability of Social Security? Would you support raising the payroll tax on higher incomes? Raising the full retirement age? Reducing benefits, particularly to those with high incomes? Should government spending be reduced in other areas?
Jackson
People who work hard their entire lives should be able to retire with dignity. They should be able to afford food, medicine, and a roof over their heads without wondering whether the benefits they spent decades earning will be there. Social Security is a promise. I intend to keep it.
While Susan Collins has repeatedly voted to weaken Social Security, I have always been clear about where I stand: In the Senate, I’ll work to scrap the cap and require millionaires to pay Social Security taxes on their income, allow Medicare to negotiate the price of every drug, eliminate profiteering and waste, and expand benefits — not raise the retirement age. Elon Musk and the other billionaires spending millions to support Collins can afford to pay more to make sure that Social Security keeps its promises to seniors.
Collins
Social Security is one of the most effective lifesaving programs in our nation’s history. It
provides a vital safety net so Americans can live with dignity after a lifetime of work. In any discussions on reform, I will be guided by the principle that all Americans who have earned Social Security benefits should receive the full benefits they are owed; we should not solve Social Security’s financial problems by denying people benefits they have earned.
That is exactly why I authored the Social Security Fairness Act. Since it became law, benefits have increased for 2.8 million Americans — many of whom are retired public servants like teachers, firefighters, and police officers. This bill restored earned benefits for more than 25,000 Mainers and provided nearly $185 million in retroactive payments last year.
One idea worth considering is to extend Social Security taxes on the very wealthy. I believe these wealthier Americans can contribute more as part of a responsible solution. At the same time, we must ensure that taxes intended for the wealthy be carefully designed to avoid unintentionally harming our nation’s small businesses. I oppose raising the retirement age.
I believe a lasting Social Security solution must be bipartisan. I support an independent
commission of experts and lawmakers appointed by House and Senate leaders from both parties that could work in a truly nonpartisan manner to develop thoughtful and actionable recommendations for Congress. A similar bipartisan commission helped reform Social Security in the early 1980s, strengthening it for decades.
Do you believe that climate change is real and made worse by burning fossil fuels? If not, why not? If so, what specific actions would you support to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and to ensure the U.S. reengages with international partners to address climate change? How would you support the transition to cleaner energy sources? How would you stand up to the president to move a climate-focused agenda forward?
Collins
I have long been a supporter of taking action to address climate change and continue to advocate for commonsense policies to reduce harmful pollution. Climate change is a significant environmental challenge that requires global solutions to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. From tourism and recreation to working forests, fishing, and agriculture, Maine’s economy is inextricably linked to the environment.
As chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, I have worked to secure key funding priorities for clean energy at the Department of Energy and other agencies. I also partnered with my Senate colleagues to co-author bipartisan solutions such as the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act and the Better Energy Storage Technology (BEST) Act. These laws made substantial investments in clean energy generation and energy storage technologies, which hold great promise in the fight against climate change and will help shape our clean energy future.
I have also not hesitated to oppose the administration when it has made decisions that I disagreed with. For example, I joined my Senate colleagues in November 2025 in voting in favor of a resolution to overturn an EPA rule that delayed requirements for oil and natural gas facilities to install pollution-control equipment. I also support climate diplomacy and would encourage the State Department to continue its engagement on this important issue. For international climate efforts to advance, it is essential that the United States keep a seat at the table.
Jackson
It’s up to all of us to ensure that Maine’s natural resources and natural spaces are here for our kids and our grandkids to enjoy. In the state Senate, I fought to invest in clean energy and grow Maine’s clean energy economy. I know that protecting our environment and protecting working people have always gone hand in hand. Our forests, waters, and working lands aren’t just part of who we are — they support thousands of jobs and communities across our state. I’ve spent my life working in the Maine woods, and I know we don’t have to choose between protecting the places we love and creating good-paying jobs.
I’ll bring that same approach to the U.S. Senate where I’ll fight for investments in clean energy that lower costs, create union jobs here at home, and preserve Maine’s natural resources for generations to come.
How will you make sure our laws, including the Constitution, are enforced equally for everyone, including members of Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the president? What laws should be enforced or changed to hold the president accountable and to ensure the survival of our democracy? Is this a top priority for you? What steps will you take to protect mail-in voting?
Jackson
Right now, we’re watching our government be sold to the highest bidder. Susan Collins and Donald Trump rake in campaign contributions, then do the bidding of billionaires. We need a government that works for everyday working people where the rule of law is equally enforced for everyone and applied to everyone — and that includes the president and ICE agents.
I will support strong enforcement of our anti-corruption and civil rights laws and congressional oversight that holds the president accountable. Congress is supposed to be a check on the president, not a rubber stamp. But Susan Collins has voted with Trump 96% of the time. She has repeatedly failed to hold this administration accountable and instead helped to advance Trump’s policies that gut health care and Trump’s nominees who have ripped away reproductive rights. I’ll fight to restore congressional oversight and make sure no president can put themselves above the law. Mainers deserve a government that works for them and answers to them — not the highest bidder, corporation, or lobbyist. I’m running for U.S. Senate to put power back in the hands of the people.
It is a high priority of mine to ensure that we have a president who is held to real ethics standards. For now, our best method of accountability is the ballot box, and I am dedicated to protecting our right to vote by mail. I will oppose any effort to make voting harder for eligible Americans, and I will fight to get our election officials the resources they need to administer our elections securely.
Collins
No one is above the law, including the president and members of federal law enforcement. I support measures to ensure accountability for immigration enforcement officers in the performance of their work and interactions with the American people. For example, I helped secure $20 million for body-worn cameras for ICE officers, and worked with the Department of Homeland Security secretary to ensure these body-worn cameras were deployed quickly and officers were trained in their use. I support further accountability measures, including requiring ICE officers to wear and display numerical and agency identifiers and prohibiting officers from wearing masks with reasonable exceptions.
The Constitution is the foundation of our American democracy, and nothing is more essential to the survival of democracy than an orderly transfer of power. Following the dangerous and shameful attack on the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, I led a group of my colleagues to write and pass the Electoral Count Reform and Presidential Transition Improvement Act to remedy the deep structural problems with our system of certifying and counting the electoral votes for president and vice president. I voted to convict President Donald Trump for his actions leading up to the attack on Jan. 6, and I supported an independent, bipartisan commission to investigate the events of that day.
I strongly support mail-in voting. Mail-in and absentee voting is especially critical for Maine’s rural communities. I have opposed legislative efforts that would restrict mail-in and absentee voting, and would continue to oppose such efforts if re-elected.
What are your top 3 accomplishments as a lawmaker?
Collins
Paycheck Protection Act. When the COVID-19 crisis struck our nation, I worked across party lines to create the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP). The PPP became a critical lifeline, providing forgivable loans to help employers stay afloat and keep their workers on the payroll. In Maine, our small businesses received more than 47,000 forgivable loans totaling $3.2 billion, supporting hundreds of thousands of Maine jobs.
Expanding Social Security benefits. I led the effort to pass the Social Security Fairness Act, restoring full Social Security benefits for millions of public servants, including teachers, school custodians, police officers, and firefighters. For some retirees, the law will more than triple the Social Security benefits they had been receiving. These workers earned these benefits through decades of service, and I was proud to help correct an unfairness that had reduced their retirement income.
Delivering results for Maine. As chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, I have authored appropriations bills that have brought nearly $1.5 billion to Maine for 672 projects in all 16 counties. These investments are addressing critical needs in communities across the state, including funding for 45 fire stations, roads and bridges, child care centers, and workforce training programs at community colleges and the University of Maine. By directing federal resources to projects identified by communities themselves, these investments are helping improve public safety, strengthen infrastructure, expand economic opportunity, and give Maine workers and families the tools they need to succeed.
Jackson
I served as Maine Senate president for six years, during which I delivered historic wins for working Mainers. I’m proud of the work I did to improve health care outcomes in the state; I stood up to big pharma to lower prescription drug prices, passed legislation to fund rural hospital and ambulance services, and enshrined patient protections into law to ensure that insurance companies cover essential health benefits and patients with pre-existing conditions.
During my time in the Legislature, I also stood strongly to advance reproductive rights. When Roe v. Wade was overturned, I immediately condemned the ruling and pledged that Maine Senate Democrats would fight attempts to undermine abortion rights. As Senate president, I sponsored and secured one of the strongest abortion laws in the country. I have helped make Maine one of the most progressive states in the nation fighting to protect reproductive care. I have expanded access to abortion and contraception, removed penalties for abortion, countered attempts to create waiting periods and forced ultrasounds, and protected both patients and providers from hostile actions initiated by other states.
More than anything, I’m proud to have a record of standing up for Maine families. When I was Senate president, I brought together Republicans and Democrats to pass legislation to deliver universal school meals for public school students. I also secured paid family leave to help Maine families navigate supporting a family member, managing their health, or caring for a new child. In 2023, I led a bill to secure a historic $60 million investment to support the child care industry, increasing financial assistance to working families to help cover child care costs and increase wages for workers.
Why should we trust you?
Jackson
Mainers can look at my record of voting on the side of working families for the last decade-plus while serving in the Maine state Legislature, and though I’m running for a different office this time, I’ll carry over my commitment to make lives better for the working-class people in our state every chance I get while I’m your senator.
Susan Collins has had 30 years in office to prove she’s on the side of working Mainers, and instead, she’s sided with Donald Trump and his cronies 96% of the time, to advance bills that have squeezed people dry. And now, ProPublica is reporting on FBI scrutiny of her campaign’s dealings with a major donor while she secured them taxpayer-funded contracts. Mainers deserve answers — and a senator whose first loyalty is to them.
Don’t just take my word for it: a grassroots army of volunteers, progressive organizations, small business owners, and union members have all backed my campaign for Senate. You can trust that I’ll be among the most labor-friendly senators in office, and that I mean it when I say that I’ll work hard every day to put you first.
Collins
Trust is something you earn. The people of Maine know me and know that I always do what I believe is best for our state and for America.
My first job was picking potatoes in Caribou at age 10. That experience taught me the value of hard work, responsibility, integrity, and keeping your commitments. I bring those same values to the Senate every day. I represent all Mainers, whether they voted for me or not. I show up, listen, and work hard, casting more than 10,000 consecutive votes without missing one. I meet with thousands of Mainers every year and work to address their concerns through constituent services at my six state offices.
I also have the knowledge, seniority, and experience to deliver for Maine. As the first Mainer in 92 years to chair the Senate Appropriations Committee, I have used this once-in-a-century opportunity to secure funding for projects in all 16 counties. As a result, Maine is the second-highest recipient of congressionally directed spending per capita in the country.
These investments are helping hospitals, strengthening workforce programs, repairing roads and bridges, improving airports, supporting child care and community centers, upgrading fire stations, and funding clean drinking water and wastewater projects. They help communities address critical needs without using property tax hikes.
I care deeply about Maine and our country. I know the importance of strong, effective leadership. Maine deserves a senator who will continue to serve with integrity, work across party lines, and deliver results.

title: There’s a Maine Lake That Looks Exactly Like a Lobster Claw
text:
Maine Has a Hidden Lake That’s Literally Shaped Like a Lobster Claw
I think I've found the most remote hike in Maine you'll experience this fall.
Sitting pretty all hidden way out in the northern Maine woods is a place called Lobster Lake and yes, it is as remote as it sounds.
We’re talking about a destination where getting there is part of the adventure.
The lake sits east of Moosehead Lake and south of the Golden Road, more than 100 miles from the coast.
And there’s a pretty funny reason it’s called Lobster Lake, just look at it on Google Maps and you’ll see the lake is literally shaped like a lobster claw and only reachable by canoe! Because apparently Maine names its lakes based on what they actually look like.
But the real reason to put this one on your radar is Lobster Mountain.
The hike to the mountain’s outlook is only about 1.5 miles from Lobster Lake, making it a manageable hike once you’ve made the journey into this remote corner of the state.
Carter Coy shared these gorgeous photos from his visit to Lobster Lake on Facebook.
At the top, you’re rewarded with sweeping views of the surrounding mountains and lakes, including Moosehead Lake and Big Moose Mountain.
And on a clear day? You can even see Katahdin!
The catch is that this isn’t exactly a “park the SUV and start walking” kind of hike. Getting to Lobster Lake involves paddling in, which means this is much more of an adventure than a quick afternoon trail.
Honestly, that might be the best part.
No crowded parking lot. No traffic noise. Just a canoe, a remote Maine lake, a mountain trail and one heck of a view.
And now I really want to go.

title: President Trump promotes strong dollar
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The economic reports from the Trump administration point to a solid economy. But poll after poll finds Americans do not think the economy is in good shape.
As the 2026 midterm elections approach, the Trump administration keeps insisting the economy is doing great.
The polls keep showing that Americans think the economy is doing badly.
Gray Media’s White House correspondent Jon Decker asked President Donald Trump on Tuesday about a key economic indicator, the strength of the US dollar, and whether the dollar has strengthened too much against the euro.
President Trump answered, “Much more a dollar versus the euro right now. No, we have a very strong dollar. That’s because we’re doing well. You know, a strong dollar is good in many ways. In certain ways you could make a case that it slows things down, but a strong dollar gives you a lot of life. And by the way, you know, what a strong dollar does gives you no inflation.”
President Trump’s message is that things are coming together for a golden age of America; even as Americans worry about rising prices at the pump and the grocery store.

title: Maine needs to ban fluoride in drinking water
text:
On Sept. 25, my family and thousands of other residents of Anson, Madison and Embden were told not to drink our tap water.
The Anson & Madison Water District had detected elevated fluoride levels. The fluoride feed was shut down, the system was flushed and a Do Not Drink order went out to roughly 2,100 service connections. The order was lifted the next day, but the fluoride feed system is still offline while the cause is investigated.
A system meant to add a measured dose of fluoride malfunctioned, and three towns could not drink from their taps. We were lucky the monitoring caught it — what if it doesn’t next time?
Last year, Rep. Jennifer Poirier’s LD 1570 would have prohibited fluoridation statewide. The Legislature did not advance it. The September incident is why it should come back — and I have asked her to reintroduce it.
No Maine family should have to wonder if their tap water is safe because of an additive the water system chose to add. Fluoride is available at the dentist, the pharmacy, in toothpaste — it doesn’t need to be in the water supply, where a malfunction can put entire towns under a Do Not Drink order.
I urge my neighbors to ask our legislators — Rep. Ducharme, Sen. Farrin, Rep. Poirier — to support a statewide ban, and I urge the Water District to release the full incident record.
Anthony Salisbury
Madison

title: Merton Wesley “Bud” Farley
text:
Merton Wesley “Bud” Farley, 88, died on September 7, 2026 at his home. Bud was the oldest of seven children born to the late Merton and Bertha (Strang) Farley. He grew up in Brewer and learned early on the importance of hard work and family. While still in high school, he worked at Herrick’s grocery and general store in South Brewer to help support his family. He graduated from Brewer High School in 1956 and went on to serve three years in the U.S. Army, including two years at Fort Leonard Wood, Missouri.
After his military service, Bud made his home on Mount Desert Island, where he spent more than 40 years working at Don’s Shop ’N Save in Bar Harbor. As Meat Department Manager, he became a familiar face to generations of customers and coworkers. He took pride in his work and was known for being honest, dependable, hardworking, and kind. He had a wonderful and unmistakable laugh that those who knew him will remember.

title: Troy Jackson needs to start running like there’s nothing to lose
text:
Lorenzo Krakowsky of Owls Head is a former teacher and high school principal.
This is a message for Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson.
There is less than a month left to win this election, and it is time for you to make your case urgently and directly to the people of Maine. Enough with the endless fundraising, TV ads, limited community events and outside consultants. Stop listening to the DSCC and the Democratic Party establishment politicos — they’re not Mainers, and they don’t know what we need.
Your personal story and your vision for how to truly serve working Mainers is what will win this thing, and it’s what people will rally around. Folks want to hear from you in person, in their towns and in their counties. They want to be inspired and fired up directly by you. You know Maine and you’ve been fighting for us for years.
Here’s what it will take:
- Use your current funds to go on a 40-day town hall barnstormer through all of Maine, north to south and east to west. Open those town halls to everyone who wants to come. Answer every question that is asked. Stay as long as is needed to hear and connect to everyone.
- Use your volunteers to generate enthusiasm and boost attendance at those town halls. Rally them to phonebank, canvass, go to demonstrations, connect socially and get out the vote now. Get as many folks as possible out to your town halls in October.
- At those town halls, let loose: call Sen. Collins a corrupt politician, call what’s going on in Gaza a genocide, tell your personal story, tell us exactly what you’ve done and what you’re going to do to make life for working Mainers fair and equitable. Run as the fighting progressive that you are. Don’t hold anything back!
- Hold a press conference ASAP to call on Sen. Collins to resign immediately and drop out of the race because of the allegations of corruption against her. Bring this up every single day from now until Election Day.
- Relentlessly pressure Sen. Collins to justify her vote to confirm Brett Kavanaugh and end the right to have abortions, and her votes to fund ICE and support its authoritarian, illegal actions.
- Use the October debates to hammer Sen. Collins about her corruption, her elite insiderism and her incompetence as the Appropriations Committee chair. Label her a corrupt politician, an elitist, a hypocrite, a Trump puppet and an AIPAC tool. Let everyone know she’s in the pocket of special interests and the rich oligarchs outside of Maine who want to crush us. Don’t be deferential.
So many of us are rooting for you, and we are 100% behind you, but we need this campaign to be ferociously urgent, completely open, genuinely grassroots and unrelentingly aggressive.
You need to run like you have nothing to lose — it’s the only way we will win.

title: Letter: Madison Cook has earned our trust
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
I am proud to support Madison Cook for state representative in House District 39.
As a longtime Belmont resident, volunteer firefighter, small-business owner, healthcare industry professional, mother of two, and someone who has worked on campaigns before, I have been impressed by Madison’s focus throughout this race.
A great candidate does more than attend events and put up yard signs; they offer a clear vision for helping their district thrive today and for generations to come. I believe Madison’s work in Augusta will improve my life, my neighbors’ lives, and create real opportunity for our children’s futures.
Families across Waldo County are struggling with rising costs. Property taxes have increased, and childcare can now cost as much as a mortgage payment. Several friends have left the area because it has become too expensive to stay. If we want young families to grow here, we need a representative who understands the real impact policy decisions have on working people.
Madison has already proven her commitment to public service. In 2025, she won a seat on the RSU 71 school board as a write-in candidate. She is always willing to step up, do the hard work, and earn the trust of our community.
Madison understands our challenges and our hopes for the future. I believe she will make thoughtful decisions for District 39 and Maine, with working families, local businesses, schools, and our environment in mind. That is why I am volunteering for her campaign and voting for Madison Cook on Nov. 3.
Quincy Hamilton
Belmont

title: Thomas College gets $3M federal grant to integrate AI across curriculum, support new positions
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WATERVILLE — Thomas College announced Tuesday that it accepted a $3 million federal grant to build artificial intelligence into all academic programs.
The Title III Strengthening Institutions Grant signals the start of a multi-year project to teach practical, critical and ethical artificial intelligence literacy, according to a news release. The grant will fund multiple full-time positions, including an AI specialist in residence, and support professional development for faculty.
College President Jeannine Diddle Uzzi said the project is a key component of Thomas College’s strategic plan, which aims to make Thomas the “college of the future.”
Uzzi said Thomas will begin integrating AI across every program by preparing faculty to use the new technology effectively and ethically.
“AI is disrupting every field. So our accounting faculty have to be experts in how AI is being used in accounting … but the same thing is true for our English faculty, and for our political science faculty, and for our biology faculty,” Uzzi said. “Every faculty member in every field has a different challenge with AI.”
Uzzi said she knows students and faculty may be resistant to the idea of using AI. Maine’s public university system recently awarded a $1.39 million contract to OpenAI to get optional ChatGPT access for its students, staff and faculty, and colleges across the country are embracing the technology, although the response from students has been mixed.
“Student concerns about AI, whether they’re ethical, whether they’re environmental, they are to my mind valid,” Uzzi said. “The beauty of having an AI expert on campus is because that person will help us move from the fear and the myth to the reality. As in all things, knowledge is power.”
Thomas is hiring for three new positions. The specialist in residence will teach, run workshops and work with individual faculty members to help them learn and incorporate AI. That position will be paid up to $120,000 a year. A project manager will oversee the application of the grant, and will earn $65,000 a year.
The college will also hire an administrative specialist, but Uzzi said she doesn’t yet know whether that position will be full time or include student internships.
Garvan Donegan, president and CEO of the Central Maine Growth Council, said a major competitive federal grant like this will have a direct impact on central Maine businesses. Even one employee who knows how to use AI can change what a company can do, he said in the news release.
Uzzi said everyone has fears about AI, but she doesn’t want to let that stop Thomas College from embracing it.
“Unfortunately, AI is not going to stop developing just because we’re afraid,” she said. “What we have to do at Thomas College is put our students first. Someone my age has the luxury maybe of not using AI, but our students who have 30 and 40 year careers ahead of them will not.”
Uzzi said she hopes the grant will help distinguish Thomas College as an institution preparing its students for rapid technological development. The college is exploring the idea of a future AI management major to prepare students to manage the technology in future roles.
“We want to be on the cutting ede of preparing students to really thrive with AI,” Uzzi said. “Thomas College is thinking about the long future that our students will have long after many of us who are teaching and working at the college won’t be around.”

title: What Trump said about Iran taking out Los Angeles, San Diego
text:
In Context: What Trump said about gas prices, Iran and taking out Los Angeles and San Diego
Critics took issue with President Donald Trump’s comments at an Oct. 5 Nebraska campaign rally, saying Trump had called for an attack on two American cities.
This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.
“Trump says Iran bombing Los Angeles, San Diego would be a ‘very small price to pay,’” read the headline on a TikTok video by the Courier Newsroom, a left-leaning outlet. Others on TikTok shared that headline.
On MS Now’s “Morning Joe,” co-host Mika Brzezinski shared the clip of Trump’s speech and said the president was “casually calling for Iran to attack two of the most populous cities in the United States.”
California Gov. Gavin Newsom wrote on X, “After sending the National Guard and Marines to occupy California, Donald Trump is now saying our foreign enemies should ‘take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego,” calling Trump “deranged and dangerous.”
The White House said Democrats misrepresented Trump’s comments.
Steven Cheung, White House communications director, reshared an X post of Trump’s comments by Headquarters, a progressive media outlet started by former Vice President Kamala Harris, and wrote, “He was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped.”
PolitiFact contacted the White House press office for additional comment and a spokesperson referred us to Cheung’s X post. The Rapid Response 47 X account, an official White House account, also disputed a Los Angeles Times headline about Trump’s comments.
Earlier in his somewhat meandering speech, Trump cited Iran’s nuclear ambitions as a reason for the war, and said the war’s end would bring down the higher gasoline prices that have resulted from it.
“You know, by the way, we’re kicking Iran’s ass. You do know that, right? And that’ll end soon. It’s gonna end one way or the other. It’s gonna end very soon and your prices are gonna come tumbling. All your prices have been tumbling down. In fact, oil is less than it was under Biden, just so you understand. And we are saving this country from a problem, and the Middle East and Israel and everybody. We’re saving the world from what could be one of the worst tragedies ever.”
Trump then touched on a number of topics over the next seven minutes: He boasted about the military’s work in Iran, complained about the news media, joked about running for a third term and bragged about a long line to get into the rally. Then he stressed the importance of Republicans winning the midterm elections. “You wanna see a tremendous victory, because it verifies all the things we did,” he said.
Here’s the video and a transcript of Trump’s comments that followed, including his mention of the two California cities:
“And again, remember with the war, it’s just artificial. It’s a little bit high. It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe. They can take out a city. Let them take, let it, let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego. That’s, this is a very small price to pay, and it’s gonna be over very soon. It’s essentially almost over with.
“And they might keep going a little long, you know? They always say they have a big threshold for pain. They need it, let me tell you. They need it. But it’s gonna end very soon, and it’ll end one way or the other, and your gas and your gasoline and all of the things. And don’t forget, we also took on a country known as Venezuela. They never talk about that. They never talk about Venezuela. And we’re taking in hundreds of millions of barrels of oil every week.”
This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.
It is republished here as part of a reporting and fact-checking partnership between PolitiFact and Hearst Television.

title: give IT. get IT. wants to increase technology access for Mainers and beyond
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WATERVILLE, Maine (WABI) - give IT. get IT wants to increase technology access for Mainers and beyond. Workers at the nonprofit’s Waterville warehouse process nearly a million pounds of devices every year.
A nonprofit built on recycled tech
“It’s a lot of controlled chaos,” said Chris Martin, co-founder and operations director of give IT. get IT. “It’s moving all the time.”
TVs, medical equipment and microwaves are among the items the team at give IT. get IT. handles.
The nonprofit was founded in 2002. It trains people, offers free tech support and gives quality computers to those who need them most.
“We go as far as Connecticut. Most of work is in Maine and New Hampshire,” Martin said.
give IT. get IT. currently employs 26 people. Nineteen of them work in the warehouse refurbishing technology.
Businesses supply used equipment
More than 400 businesses trust the nonprofit with their old technology. give IT. get IT.is NAID certified, meaning it meets global standards for securely destroying electronic media.
“That’s the lifeblood of our operation here – all the banks, hospitals, manufacturers and agencies that let us literally intercept their entire pile of what’s to them used equipment. To us, it’s a gem because then we just refurbish it and get it to people who need it,” Martin said.
“This is where the magic happens as far as getting computers ready to go to somebody who needs it,” Martin said.
Martin said give IT. get IT. is the only nonprofit recycler that reuses or recovers value from tech to directly benefit the community.
“We’re helping folks who can’t afford to just replace their technology every two years. This isn’t an offering of you’ve got to accept what we have, this is an offering of what are your goals and how do we best meet that with the right technology?” Martin said.
Free tech support and community recycling
“Whatever we provide for a device to a family that needs it, we’re also providing equal to if not ten times the value of that in just a free number to call, literally right to your Wi-Fi. We don’t provide your Wi-Fi, but if it’s inhibiting your ability to use your technology to your goal, we will help. At least the best we can,” Martin said.
give IT. get IT. also offers community recycling. Any Maine household can drop off items such as flat screen monitors, computers and printers for free, seven days a week. The goal is to keep these electronics out of landfills.
“That’s been a free service to the community since 2012,” Martin said.
Items can be dropped off outside the facility at 60 Industrial Street in Waterville.
While the facility is not currently open to the public, Martin said he hopes to grow into a larger space and change that.
Martin said people facing technology hurdles should reach out.
“When it comes to the stuff folks need to go to school, to access resources, to build up their career skills, stay connected with family – we’ve mastered that. We’ve got that,” Martin said.
For more information, visit the organization’s website or call 338-4233.

title: Maine regulators deny CMP’s $7 rate hike as utility weighs potential layoffs
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine utility regulators denied Central Maine Power Co.’s request for almost $70 million in increased rates on Tuesday, a major win for advocacy groups that means bills will not increase this fall.
The Maine Public Utilities Commission’s unanimous denial of CMP’s bid to increase the average household’s bill by about $7 per month comes with potentially serious financial consequences for the utility, company representatives said in filings before Tuesday’s hearing. A CMP executive told employees last week that the company would reconsider workforce levels if the PUC denied its request.
Current distribution rates are likely to remain in place until the spring, when regulators are expected to decide on the merits of the utility’s full $189 million rate case.
State law allows utilities to recoup “temporary rates” during a longer case, as long as the amount they’re seeking to raise is agreed upon. That’s what CMP was seeking here: the first step of a two-part rate increase, intended to help pay for infrastructure CMP has built in recent years.
The PUC had recommended this approach last year when it dismissed CMP’s five-year plan, which would have raised the average household’s bill by about $35.
But the three members of the Maine Public Utilities Commission agreed Tuesday that intervening groups — from the Office of the Public Advocate to the Department of Energy Resources to consumer advocates — had disputed all $69.3 million of CMP’s ask, and that they therefore could not allow the utility to raise rates.
The commission’s decision aligned with the recommendation of its staff last month.
Much of the dispute was based on return on equity — the return CMP’s shareholders can make on the company’s capital projects. Return on equity is the only way a utility monopoly can make profit under Maine’s regulatory structure, and it’s become a focal point in the rate case.
About two-thirds of CMP’s temporary rate ask was to right-size its return on equity, which the company said was necessary to attract investment and maintain its credit ratings.
“I simply could not pinpoint a number that I would feel comfortable saying was not in dispute in this matter,” PUC Chair Philip Bartlett said during deliberations Tuesday.
Bartlett also said that, since the utility has exceeded its capital spending forecast by about 50% from 2022 to 2025, “to some extent, this is a problem of CMP’s own making.”
In the eight days since PUC staff recommended the commissioners reject CMP’s increase, the utility has removed 70 job postings for line workers and customer service positions, paused plans to improve 19 transformers servicing thousands of customers from York to Rangeley, and halted several other infrastructure projects.
A spokesperson for CMP did not respond Tuesday to a request for comment, but in a filing before the hearing Tuesday, the company said it would be hit hard by a denial.
In addition to deferring upgrades to its grid infrastructure and pausing hiring, CMP said it would be forced to “consider workforce reductions.” The company’s financial outlook was downgraded this summer by S&P Global Ratings to “negative” because of lag in this rate case and a $100 million cash flow deficit.
“Customers do not experience regulatory delay in the abstract,” attorneys for CMP wrote to regulators last week. “They experience it through aging transformers, deferred maintenance, postponed reliability projects, and infrastructure that continues operating long after it should have been replaced.”
Linda Ball, the president and CEO of CMP, said in a Sept. 28 email to employees that it would be irresponsible for the utility not “to carefully evaluate current workforce levels, hiring plans and apprenticeship programs” given the “regulatory challenges we face.”
“I recognize that news like this creates uncertainty and concern,” Ball said in the email. “Please know that our leadership team takes these challenges seriously and remains focused on supporting our employees, maintaining safe and reliable service for our customers, and advocating for the investments necessary to sustain Maine’s electric system for the long term, while balancing the impacts this situation has on the business.”
No decisions about workforce levels have been made, Ball wrote. CMP employs almost 1,000 people, the company’s website says.
Meanwhile, the PUC decision marks a substantial win for advocacy groups, which have fought CMP’s rate increase at each step.
Fight the Hike, a coalition of advocacy groups opposed to CMP’s increase, celebrated the PUC’s decision in a news release and said it would continue to oppose the utility’s efforts to raise rates in the next several months.
“(Delaying grid projects is) an attempt at blackmail,” Seth Berry, the executive director of coalition member Our Power, said in the release. “Unlike any other business, CMP has a monopoly. This is a privilege granted to them by the people of Maine. It’s time for CMP shareholders to start funding grid maintenance from their $160 million in annual profits — not squeezing still more from struggling families.”
Heather Sanborn, the state’s public advocate, said she applauded the PUC’s decision to wait to increase rates until the end of the yearlong proceeding. Any increase should be decided on its merits, she said, and should take into account affordability concerns.
Rebecca Schultz, the clean energy expert for the Natural Resources Council of Maine, one of the intervening parties in the case, applauded the PUC’s decision, especially in the face of rising costs in other areas.
Schultz also criticized CMP’s response.
“In the past few weeks, facing reasonable and completely foreseeable pushback to their request, the company chose to threaten Mainers with cutting union jobs and delaying important safety and reliability upgrades that were already underway,” she said in a statement. “This is unacceptable behavior for any company granted a monopoly business opportunity in Maine.”
The ruling Tuesday is likely to be the final major decision during Bartlett’s tenure as the PUC’s chair. After seven years leading the commission, Bartlett announced last month that he’d be stepping down Friday to move into the private sector.

title: Cross Country Wins Maine State Title Meet for Third Year In a Row
text:
Bowdoin hosted the annual Maine State Title Meet for cross country on Sept. 19. Both the men’s and women’s teams, led by Coach Danny Feldman, came out to compete.
The men’s cross country team placed first out of 12 teams at Bowdoin College, outrunning Division I University of Maine. This marks the third year straight that the Bates men have won the Maine State Title Meet at Bowdoin’s Pickard XC course, and the ninth state championship in the last twelve years.
The women’s cross country team finished first out of the Division III teams and second of the eleven teams competing. This is the highest they have placed in the last two years.
Charlotte Crum ‘30 won All-State honors with a fourth-place finish in the women’s 6Kand a race time of 21:39.6. Not far behind was Zoe McCullough ‘30, who clinched the top ten with a 10th place finish and a time of 21:57.4.
In the men’s race, Bates’ Nathaniel Aronson ‘27 placed first with a time of 25:09.3, surpassing UMaine’s top runners.
“[I] was pretty shocked after crossing the line,” Aronson said. “I had considered the possibility of being able to win the race beforehand, but I knew it was going to be very challenging,”
Along with Aronson, Bobcats Nick Walker ‘29, Jack Crum ‘27 and Max Hoffman ‘28 all secured top ten spots in the men’s 8k. Walker came in 7th with a time of 25:28.1, with Crum and Hoffman coming in eighth and tenth with times of 25:34.8 and 25:41.0.
“The results of this race proved we are all in the best shape of our lives,” Aronson said. “None of us are planning on taking our feet off the gas until we can finally achieve our goals and compete at the national meet our team missed by one spot last year.”
Aronson credits the team’s success to Feldman, who has been coaching both men’s and women’s cross country since 2022. Feldman “served as such an amazing coach and mentor throughout my entire career,” Aronson said. “We all made a big jump in our training volume over the summer” and that hard work ended up paying off.

title: NH firefighter engulfed in flames while running out of burning home
text:
Video shows New Hampshire firefighter engulfed in flames while running out of burning Londonderry home
The New Hampshire firefighter who caught fire during a call is now recovering at home.
Londonderry Fire Lt. Mike England was responding to a house fire Friday night when a flashover broke out in the house. A flashover is when a room fills with hot air and smoke, then the entire room catches fire.
England said he was inside because he thought there could still be people there. Video shows England engulfed in flames while running out of the burning home. WMTW sister station WMUR did not air the video of England's escape until speaking with him.
"Other firefighters that were there put him out by patting him down to put the fire out," said Battalion Chief Bruce Hallowell.
Hallowell said England, who has been with the Londonderry Fire Department for 11 years, did not realize he was injured at first and went back to continue firefighting.
England sustained minor burns but fractured his leg after jumping off the porch. He told WMUR that he is out of the hospital, and that he considers himself the "luckiest unlucky guy" when considering his injuries in the context of what happened.
Every member at the Londonderry Fire Department recently received two brand new sets of personal protective equipment.
"This is the happy result that, you know, the lieutenant was able to sustain a significant thermal assault and get out with very limited injuries," Hallowell said.
There were five people inside the home when the fire started in the kitchen. They were all able to evacuate themselves and refused medical treatment.
Emergency crews from Derry, Salem, Litchfield, Bedford, Windham and Manchester responded to the scene.

title: Controversial televangelist Jim Bakker dies at 86
text:
(Gray News) - Televangelist Jim Bakker has died at 86.
“It is with a broken heart that I share that my beloved husband, Jim Bakker, went home to be with the Lord this evening,” his wife, Lori Bakker, wrote in an Instagram post on Oct. 5.
Bakker was known for hosting “The PTL Club” and developing the PTL Satellite Network, as well as developing the defunct Christian theme park Heritage USA.
He resigned from the ministry in 1987 after paying hush money to a church secretary who said she had been sexually assaulted by Bakker.
The next year, he was indicted on several counts of mail fraud, wire fraud, and one count of conspiracy, related to PTL’s finances. He was sentenced to 45 years in prison, but was paroled in 1994.
Since then, he began hosting “The Jim Bakker Show” and selling survivalist products.
“Jim loved people deeply. He loved this ministry, and he loved the friends and partners who stood with him throughout the years,” Lori wrote.

title: Out-of-state lawmakers join Maine leaders at Ellsworth High to learn student support model
text:
ELLSWORTH, Maine (WABI) - Education leaders and lawmakers from out of state visited Ellsworth High School Tuesday for an inside look at how the school’s bar was raised for student support.
Ellsworth High adopted the Building Assets, Reducing Risks model in 2024. The school saw its graduation rate increase from 73% to 90%.
State policy leaders, BARR center members from Minnesota, and legislators from Oklahoma visited the school today to learn more about how the school implemented the BARR model.
School academic leaders say the model has helped to build better relationships between students and teachers.
“You get to know little, tiny things about them, what their interests are, what life is like at home, what they did last summer, all those things matter to kids, and they matter to teachers, and it just gives us a jumping board to get to know them quickly,” said Ellsworth High Principial Dan Clifford.
Ellsworth High School staff also emphasize the importance of creating a support system for students, especially for newer freshmen adjusting to high school academics.
Since adopting the BARR model, ninth-grade course failure rates fell to 10%.

title: 'The silence was deafening': Entourage actress Constance Zimmer reveals cancer diagnosis
text:
'The silence was deafening': Entourage actress Constance Zimmer reveals cancer diagnosis
Actress Constance Zimmer revealed in a post on social media that she was diagnosed with breast cancer.
The "Love Story" and "Entourage" actress said she received the news of her diagnosis in March from her doctor via a Zoom call.
Related video: Bruce Springsteen says wife, Patti Scialfa, in remission after cancer diagnosis
“On March 13th when I was away from home– I heard these words from my doctor over zoom: 'You have DCIS, also refereed to as Stage 0 breast cancer.' the silence was deafening," Zimmer said in a post on Instagram.
Zimmer kept her health development a secret while promoting the FX drama, "Love Story," inspired by the relationship of John F. Kennedy Jr. and Carolyn Bessette.
“October is #breastcancerawarenessmonth and I never thought I’d be honoring it with my own story,” Zimmer wrote in the post’s caption, alongside images and videos of herself in the hospital undergoing treatment.
Zimmer said she weighed whether or not to have a lumpectomy, which she said she decided to do after her doctor said: "I feel confident I can get it (cancer) out."
"It did take 3 surgeries - 3 weeks in a row, but she did it, she saved my breast and it looks good too," Zimmer said.
She now says she is cancer-free.
"From hospital gowns, to Emmy glamour, this was one hell of a ride," Zimmer said.
Zimmer was nominated for Outstanding Supporting Actress in a Limited or Anthology Series or Movie for her "Love Story" performance as Ann Messina Freeman, the late Bessette’s mother.

title: Man admitted to stabbing woman 15 times in random hiking trail attack, police say
text:
PHOENIX (AZFamily/Gray News) - A man in Arizona accused of murdering a woman on a a hiking trail more than three years ago will likely avoid the death penalty through a plea deal.
Court records said that Zion Teasley pleaded guilty to first-degree murder in court Friday in connection with the death of Lauren Heike.
Heike’s murder gained international attention after she was found stabbed more than a dozen times not far from her apartment, on April 28, 2023.
Days later, police arrested Teasley. Investigators said they linked Teasley to her death through DNA on Heike’s shoe, along with other forensic evidence, including cellphone location data.
Police believed Heike fought off her attacker and escaped but that her injuries were too severe.
Teasley was indicted on 10 counts after investigators said he had sexually explicit images involving a child under 15 years old and possibly shared them.
Authorities said they believe at this time that the attack was random, but added that they “have not concluded our investigation into that.”
He pleaded guilty to one count of sexual exploitation of a minor in that case.
Sentencing in that case is scheduled for Dec. 4.

title: Tennessee Republicans consider more execution options after Christa Pike lethal injection fails
text:
Tennessee Republicans consider more execution options after Christa Pike lethal injection fails
Some of Tennessee's top Republicans said Monday they want to explore alternative ways of executing condemned prisoners after the failed execution of Christa Pike, which relied on a large dose of pentobarbital.
U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the state's Republican candidate for governor, said Pike's unsuccessful execution last week "should not be grounds to halt carrying out the death penalty." Rather, she said, Tennessee needs to reevaluate the way it does executions.
"If it's lethal injection, if it is electric chair, what we do know is we have to find a way to do this — and do it successfully," Blackburn told The Associated Press.
Top legislative leaders have already spoken with Blackburn about potential changes to state execution laws during their 2027 session.
"We want to broaden it, include more methods," House Speaker Cameron Sexton said. "What those are as of today, I'm not sure. But I don't think there's any method that's off the table at this point."
Hear from the Tennessee House speaker in the video player at the top
Most U.S. states that allow executions use lethal injection as their primary means, though South Carolina sets its default as electrocution and Idaho the firing squad, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. Some states give prisoners a choice of execution methods. Death by electricity or gas is authorized in nine states, including five that specify nitrogen gas, the center said. Five states authorize a firing squad.
Florida, which leads the nation in executions this year, uses a three-drug lethal injection that includes a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart.
Tennessee's execution procedures have been in the national spotlight since Wednesday, when prison officials gave Pike two doses of a barbiturate that were supposed to be lethal but didn't ultimately kill her. Pike has remained hospitalized under guard, left unconscious and on a ventilator with blisters and burns on her arms from the drug, her lawyers have said.
Pike, now 50, was sentenced to death for the 1995 torture and slaying of a classmate, Colleen Slemmer. Pike was age 18 at the time and became one of the youngest women sent to death row.
Republican Gov. Bill Lee, whose term ends in January, halted the one remaining execution scheduled for this year and ordered an independent investigation into the state's capital punishment system after Pike's failed execution. He said Saturday the commissioner of the Department of Correction will step down.
Blackburn said comprehensive change is needed — "it is personnel, processes, procedures, protocols that are all going to need to be addressed."
Tennessee law already allows electrocution if the department is unable to carry out a lethal injection despite reasonable efforts to do so. State law also gives people who committed crimes before 1999 the option of choosing electrocution.
Between 2018 and 2020, five Tennessee prisoners chose electrocution. That could remain an option for about two dozen of the 40 people on death row.
Sexton said the legislature could consider amending the law to give the state a choice of execution methods.
House Majority Leader William Lamberth said he is open to making electrocution the state's primary means of execution. But no matter the method, Lamberth said he doesn't want any changes to take too long to implement.
"We want these sentences to be carried out effectively, efficiently and humanely," he said, adding: "Whatever we do, I do not want it to delay justice for these victims' families."
Republican state Sen. Todd Gardenhire, chair of the Senate Judiciary Committee, said he expects a deliberate review of what went wrong and what can be done to improve the execution process.
"I think the electric chair is the quickest and simplest way to do it," he said.

title: Popular social media star arrested near college bar over the weekend, police say
text:
COLLEGE STATION, Texas. (KBTX/Gray News) - A popular social media star was arrested in Texas near a college bar over the weekend, according to authorities.
Benjamin Beard, 34, known as BenDaDonnn online, was charged Sunday with evading arrest.
Another man, 29-year-old Kenny Carter, was charged with interference with public duties.
Police said they were attempting to clear people from the roadway in front of a bar when a group refused to listen to the officers.
As the incident became physical, police said one of their officers was shoved to the ground by Carter, who identified himself as Beard’s security guard.
Police said an officer used a taser on Beard, who was attempting to get away.
Police said as officers moved the two to a staging area to wait to be taken to jail, a large “entourage” crowded around them before being told several times to move back.
Earlier that evening, Beard appeared on Texas A&M football’s official X account, showing him on the sidelines during the game near the rest of the team.
Another X account showed Beard attempting to enter the locker room during halftime with cameras rolling, only to be kicked out by coach Elko.
Beard is better known on social media platforms as a live streamer and social media influencer who often collaborates with other well-known entertainers, including Drake, and athletes on comedy skits, social media content and music.
He has a combined social media following of over 3.7 million followers across his platforms.

title: Obituary: Diana M. Markos
text:
OLD ORCHARD BEACH – It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of our beloved Mom, Nana, sister, aunt, and friend, who died peacefully on Sept. 28, 2026, surrounded by her loving family, after a brief illness.
The daughter of the late Alson “Ike” and Edna Soule, she was predeceased by her beloved husband, Arthur “Tom” Markos, in 2018.
She leaves behind her daughter, Carol Sinclair, and her husband Robert of Farmingdale, her son, Christopher and his partner Mary Hoffmann of Rockport, and her son, Stephen and his wife Katie of Winchester, Mass. She was the cherished Nana of Nicholas Sinclair and his wife, Lauren, of Boston, Ryan Sinclair and his wife Ellen of Boston, Avery and Arianna Markos of Gardiner, and Quinn and Hayden Markos of Winchester. She is also survived by her sister, Jane Serwacki,, and her husband,, Larry,, of North Berwick, as well as many other family members and dear friends.
She grew up in Auburn, Maine, and graduated from Edward Little High School, Class of 1967. The friendships she made there remained an important part of her life. She especially treasured her longtime group of high school friends, who continued to gather for monthly lunches—a tradition that brought her great joy over the years.
After many years working for the Paper Industry Information Office, she made the decision to retire early and devote herself to what mattered most to her: her family. Family truly was the center of her world, and there was nothing she enjoyed more than having the people she loved gathered together.
She was, quite simply, the strongest person we knew. That strength was matched by an extraordinary capacity to care for others. She lovingly cared for our father through his final days, just as she had cared for her parents and her beloved aunts, whom she looked after with the same unwavering devotion. When someone she loved needed her, she was there—steadfast, selfless, and strong.
Her generosity and devotion to others extended well beyond her family. She was a longtime member of Beta Sigma Phi, a sorority devoted to service, and her church was an important part of her life. For many years, she was a member of Holy Trinity Greek Orthodox Church in Lewiston and, more recently, Holy Trinity Greek Orthodox Church in Portland. She served as Treasurer of Philoptochos and formed many cherished friendships through her years of involvement with the church.
She gave generously of her time and talents to her church community, spending countless hours in the church kitchen baking Greek breads and pastries for functions and celebrations. For her, cooking and baking were acts of love, whether she was doing so for her church community or for the family she adored.
She enjoyed an active lifestyle right up until her illness, rising at the crack of dawn each morning to join her exercise buddies—first at Curves and later at Planet Fitness—often followed by a stop at Panera, where their circle of friends grew to include other regulars who remained in touch throughout her illness. We often joked that she could run circles around all of us.
Her home in Old Orchard Beach became a special gathering place for her extended family and the setting for countless happy memories. She was a phenomenal cook and baker, and the family feasts she lovingly prepared were nothing short of amazing. No gathering was ever small or quiet—they were large, loud, filled with wonderful food, plenty of laughter, and, most of all, love. She delighted in bringing everyone together and creating the traditions and memories her family will carry with them always.
More than anything, she loved being a mother and Nana. Her children and grandchildren were her greatest joy, and she took tremendous pride in each of them. The love she gave so freely will remain at the heart of the family she cherished so deeply.
Our family would like to extend our heartfelt gratitude to the wonderful hospice nurses and caregivers who helped us care for our Mom and made it possible for her to remain peacefully at home, surrounded by the people she loved. We are especially grateful to Betsy, Charlotte, Tabby, and her team for the kindness, compassion, and loving care they provided to her and to our entire family during her final days.
The family will hold a private ceremony at a later date.
In lieu of flowers,
donations in her memory may be made to:
Holy Trinity Greek
Orthodox Church
133 Pleasant St.

text:
