Coldest night yet
Freeze warnings and frost advisories issued for Tuesday night into Wednesday morning
High pressure controls Maine's weather on Tuesday, keeping storms away and skies clear. Blustery northwest winds gust to 20 to 30 mph Tuesday afternoon but will ease up after dark.
Tuesday night will then be the coldest of the season so far, with lows in the 20s to mid-30s. Frost advisories and freeze warnings have been issued for areas where the growing season is still ongoing.
Frost and freeze conditions could kill crops and other sensitive vegetation and possibly damage unprotected outdoor plumbing.
After a cold start, Wednesday is a nice fall day with mostly sunny skies and highs in the 60s. It won't be as windy, but still breezy at times, with gusts to around 25 mph possible. A stray shower can't be ruled out.
A passing shower is possible on Thursday as a cold front crosses Maine. A nice, mild day otherwise, with highs in the 60s and low 70s. Quiet weather is expected for Friday and the weekend, with only an isolated shower possible, mainly in the mountains.

title: On the same misguided mission, Bernie returns to Maine
text:
I understand why Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders is preparing for a weekend of rallying across Maine beside Senate contender Troy Jackson. I can even allow that it might boost the Democrat’s campaign.
But I wish Sen. Sanders wasn’t coming here.
Sanders has always struck me as a crabby old man who has spent his lifetime griping about nearly every colleague and issue on the national stage — without racking up any serious legislative accomplishments.
Everyone I knew who had spent time around him, mostly staffers on Capitol Hill, had little good to say about him. In person, they told me, he was often a jerk.
Somehow, Sanders became a hero to young people when he began running for president in 2015. They bought his mistaken portrait of former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, the Democratic presidential frontrunner, as a corrupt warmonger.
These idealistic voters wanted change — and believed the crotchety Vermonter could bring it about.
Not me. I worried then, as I still do, that extremists on the left and right will squeeze the political middle into extinction, leaving our leaders unable to compromise and letting major issue linger unsolved.
In the spring of 2016, I was interested to watch Sanders speak to a huge crowd of young people on town green beside Yale University. Those gathered to cheer him on were eager for a more progressive government after two terms with President Barack Obama at the helm.
The lead singer of R.E.M., Michael Stipe, introduced Sanders with a complaint about the “grotesque level of wealth and inequality in America.” He told the crowd, “Brothers and sisters, instead of giving tax breaks to billionaires, we are going to rebuild inner cities.”
Sanders came on and thundered in the same vein, eventually taking a shot at Yale for having such a large endowment while people in neighborhoods next door struggled to survive.
During his address, Sanders told his backers, “Don’t believe what anyone tells you, that we cannot change the status quo.”
While I didn’t really disagree with much of what he had to say, I feared that in knocking Clinton, who was clearly going to be the Democratic nominee, the only thing Sanders was accomplishing was to help elevate Republican Donald Trump.
We know now how it all turned out. And, rest assured, billionaires are doing well while those on the flip side of economic inequality are not. It’s also clear to us now who the real corrupt warmonger in that race was.
The status quo from a decade ago, before the White House became a gilded playhouse for the ultra-rich to stomp on those who are struggling, now seems like something magical.
I know Bernie Sanders isn’t solely responsible for the revolutionary changes of the Trump era. That shame can be traced back to many, including Hillary Clinton and, sadly, to a majority of Americans who bought into the Trumpian agenda of greed and hate.
Sanders will tell Mainers this weekend that it doesn’t have to be this way, that we can throw out Trump’s enablers in Congress, including Sen. Susan Collins, and pursue the America so many have fought to create during the past 250 years.
Maybe so, but I’m tired of big promises and broken government. Castigating the establishment isn’t the way to a better America. Working together is.

title: Fire at Ambition Brewing in Wilton ruled accidental
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The origin of a fire that gutted Ambition Brewing in Wilton on Monday afternoon has been determined accidental and caused by ongoing renovation work.
The fire began beneath the rear section of the building at 295 Main St. where old flooring was being cut and removed, according to a release from the Office of State Fire Marshal.
The fire was discovered about 3 p.m. by the property owner after old flooring had been cut and was in the process of being removed.
The business was founded by Jeff Chaisson and Josh Michaud in 2018.
The underside of the building was partially open to the elements, allowing leaves and other organic debris to accumulate beneath the structure over time. The material had become dry and readily combustible and most likely ignited during the flooring removal process, according to investigators.
Firefighters from multiple departments were able to contain the fire to one of the two buildings occupied by the business. The second building received smoke and water damage. No injuries were reported.
“Today has been a tough day for Ambition Brewing,” according to a post on the pub’s Facebook page. “We experienced a major fire, and while we’re still taking it all in, the most important thing is that everyone is safe.”
The post continued: “To the Wilton Fire & Rescue, Jay, Farmington, Rumford, Temple, and East Dixfield fire departments, Wilton Police, emergency medical services, and the investigators at Office of State Fire Marshal: ‘thank you for your tireless work, dedication, and care. We are deeply grateful for everything you’ve done today.'”
The owners couldn’t be immediately reached for comment Tuesday.

title: Despite Mullin’s comment, President Trump has grown wealthier while in office
text:
Fact check: Has President Trump lost money by being in office, as Markwayne Mullin suggested?
In a warm-up speech before President Donald Trump addressed Oklahoma rally-goers, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told the crowd in his home state that Trump took a financial hit to serve as president.
This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.
“He doesn’t have to do this,” Mullin, a former U.S. senator, said at the Oct. 1 rally in Durant. “There’s no financial gain like the past presidents have had. It’s cost him to be in office.”
That’s not what Trump told the federal government.
His 927-page financial disclosure form for 2025 shows at least $1.4 billion in cryptocurrency revenue alone.
A New York Times analysis estimated that overall, Trump “pulled in at least $2.2 billion” in 2025. That was up from $622 million in 2024, which was before he began his second term.
And a September analysis by Forbes — which has been tracking the holdings of the super-wealthy for decades — found that Trump “is an estimated $2.7 billion richer than when he won the 2024 election.” The Forbes analysis runs through 2026.
“2025 was the most lucrative year of Trump’s life, by far,” said Robert Maguire, vice president of research and data at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, an advocacy group that has sued Trump and his administration over such issues as foreign emoluments and a proposed fund to compensate people who experienced what Trump called “government weaponization.”
“There is essentially no scenario, based on public information, where the presidency hasn’t made Donald Trump far richer than he’s ever been,” Maguire said.
White House says to look at Trump’s first term
Mullin’s department did not respond to our questions about his remarks, but the White House did.
In a statement to PolitiFact, the White House cited Forbes data showing Trump’s net worth fell from $3.7 billion in 2016 — the year before his first term — to $2.5 billion in 2021, the year after he left the White House. That’s a 32% decline in net worth during his first term. (For comparison, the median U.S. household net worth with members at least 75 years old — which is close to Trump’s age — is $335,600.)
Mullin’s statement would have been accurate if he’d said it in 2021. But Trump’s financial picture is vastly different in 2026.
Forbes currently calculates Trump’s net worth at $7 billion. That’s almost double the $3.7 billion Trump held before he became president the first time, and it’s also far above his pre-presidential high of $4.5 billion in 2015.
The White House also said Trump has not taken a salary. The White House hasn’t always provided documentation of this, but even if it’s correct, that’s only $400,000 a year foregone — a tiny fraction of Trump’s $2.2 billion in 2025 revenues.
Cryptocurrency accounts for a clear majority of Trump’s 2025 revenue, bringing in $1.4 billion. His 2025 disclosure showed another $400 million from sources such as real estate, legal settlements, overseas licensing agreements and branded merchandise such as watches and footwear.
Could Trump’s added expenses have canceled out his gains?
Experts said it was unlikely that the $2.2 billion or more that Trump has taken in would have been gobbled up by added expenses from being president.
“The only extra expenses I think he could possibly have incurred as president would come from things like extra security costs or travel, but the taxpayers have footed the bill to increase security at the president’s private properties,” said Danielle Caputo, senior legal counsel for ethics with the Campaign Legal Center, which tracks campaign finance and ethics issues.
MAGA Inc., a Trump-aligned super PAC, has reported paying for some of Trump’s travel, but that’s not considered Trump’s own money, Caputo said. “I don’t think that either could account for $1.6 billion in expenses,” Caputo said.
As for traditional overhead expenses that might stem from Trump’s businesses, Maguire said that the biggest sources of revenue disclosed in Trump’s 2025 form are from enterprises that are relatively free of overhead, such as cryptocurrency and licensing deals. These are “about as close to pure income that you can get,” Maguire said.
How do previous presidents compare?
Trump entered office both times with the highest net worth of any recent president — $3.7 billion the first time and $3.9 billion the second time. The next closest was John F. Kennedy, who had family wealth; pre-presidency, Kennedy is estimated to have been worth $100 million in inflation-adjusted dollars.
Two recent Democratic presidents — Bill Clinton and Barack Obama — saw their net worth skyrocket after leaving office. They both entered office with an estimated $1.3 million and finished up their tenures with $120 million and $70 million, respectively.
Those are significant increases, but Trump’s wealth has grown by far more.
Our ruling
Mullin said that for Trump, “There’s no financial gain like the past presidents have had. It’s cost him to be in office.”
Trump’s own financial disclosure form shows he made at least $2.2 billion in revenues in 2025, up from $622 million in 2024, before he began his second term. A Forbes analysis estimated that Trump is $2.7 billion richer than in 2024.
It’s not plausible that overhead or added expenses could have consumed all that extra income, experts said. And the scale of Trump’s presidential wealth gains dwarf those of recent presidents.
From the best information we have, Mullin’s comment is off by more than $1 billion. We rate the statement False.
This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.
It is republished here as part of a reporting and fact-checking partnership between PolitiFact and Hearst Television.

title: 'Financial pressure' may force CMP to delay construction
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Financial pressure on Central Maine Power could force it to delay construction projects aimed at improving reliable electric service and upgrading aging infrastructure, according to the company.
The utility’s warning comes ahead of a Maine Public Utilities Commission decision on whether to grant CMP’s request to temporarily increase customer prices to raise about $70 million.
CMP CEO Linda Ball said rising inflation, construction prices and borrowing costs make it increasingly difficult to continue investing in the electric grid. The company said most of the rate increase it wants will pay off projects already started and completed.
“For more than a year, we have continued investing in reliability and system improvements while managing rising costs and awaiting the necessary regulatory approval to align rates with the cost of providing service,” Ball said in a statement.
Projects in South Portland, Biddeford and Saco, Lewiston and Auburn, and Bridgton that benefit thousands of customers could be delayed, according to CMP.
The utility also has suspended hiring for 70 open positions and pulled out of a University of Southern Maine job fair.
The austerity moves started shortly after the commission’s staff recommended that commissioners reject CMP’s temporary rate hike. The company wants to impose higher costs now while it negotiates long-term prices for electric transmission and distribution.
But commission staff said that there was no “undisputed” amount of near-term rates that could be imposed amid widespread public concern about rising energy prices and vigorous opposition from organizations that include the Maine Office of Public Advocate.
Some opposing groups, including the Natural Resources Council of Maine and Acadia Center, have criticized CMP’s hiring and investment pause and urged the company to meet its obligations to customers.
Noah Berman, a utility advocate with Acadia Center, said in an interview that he doubted the company’s claim of financial strain.
“I do not believe CMP is accurately portraying its capability in ensuring that Mainers have safe and reliable and adequate service which is its obligation under the law,” Berman said.
The utilities commission will deliberate whether to permit temporary rates at its meeting Tuesday.
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.

title: Fifty Years After Brian De Palma's Film, Amazon Prime Brings Ewen High School Back To Screens
text:
From Trash To Treasure, Stephen King’s ‘Carrie’ Gets Another Screen Reimagining
For many readers, "Carrie" was their introduction to Stephen King, who has since gone on to pen more than 60 novels since that 1974 debut.
Now -- more than five decades later, on Oct. 7, 2026 -- King's first novel will get a new treatment on Amazon Prime courtesy of Mike Flanagan's TV series.
King, who's never been shy about sharing his feelings (good or bad) about interpretations of his work, has already weighed in on the latest adaptation of young Carrie White's harrowing high school experience.
Indeed, King makes this reader wonder what Flanagan -- who also adapted King's "Gerald's Game" and "Doctor Sleep" -- brings to the story of the telekinetic teen who's bullied to disastrous effect for everyone in the small town of Chamberlain, Maine.
Famously, King's wife and fellow novelist, Tabitha King, rescued "Carrie" from the trash while the couple and their two children lived in a double-wide trailer in Hermon, just outside Bangor.
It's a good thing she did.
Related: Stephen King’s College Columns Shed Light On His Early Thoughts
When Signet later bought the paperback rights to the novel for $400,000 -- half of which went to King -- it allowed the then-English teacher at Hampden Academy to focus exclusively on writing.
So, in short, "Carrie" was a big deal in King's career.
Two years later in 1976, director Brian De Palma first brought the story to the big screen. Sissy Spacek, then 26 years old, starred as the innocent but tormented teen and earned herself an Academy Award nomination in the process.
A hard act to follow
In 1999, "The Rage: Carrie 2" hit he big screen. The sequel to the 1976 film starred Emily Bergl as Rachel Lang, the younger half-sister of Carrie White. Rachel shares Carrie's telekinetic abilities, as well as her penchant for revenge against bullies.
Critics didn't like it that much. Personally, I watched this movie not long ago, and didn't think it was that bad.
In 2002, "Carrie" hit the small screen for the first time, with Angela Bettis portraying the title character. Critics were not kind, though, saying the adaptation didn't match the intensity of the original and the run-time was just too long.
It wasn't until 2013, when Chloë Grace Moretz reprised the role on the big screen in an updated telling of the story. This is the first time social media enters the chat -- as it does in Flanagan's series -- and much like its actual effect on society, it amplifies the harassment and the resulting destruction.
Related: 14 Places Every Stephen King Fan Must Stop While in Bangor, Maine
The 2013 remake, while pretty true to the story, also didn't get the accolades of the original, with critics nonplussed by the heavy use of CGI in the film. But let me say, I thought the performances -- including Julianne Moore as Carrie's paranoid and domineering mother -- were pretty good in this one.
Thirteen years later, King fans now eagerly await this 8-episode series starring Canadian-born actress Summer H. Howell.
Personally, I wondered how Flanagan would spread the novel over eight episodes, but a recent Instagram post (below) answered that question. (Note: You have to appreciate the nod to King's novel, which took place at Ewen High School. The 1976 film later changed the name to Bates High School.)
I think we all know what "AP Physics" means. 🔥🔥🔥
Now that you've watched the trailer, what do you think? Is it possible ot live up to the original?
Whether the series compares with de Palma's film is really irrelevant, I suppose. The fact that King's nearly-trashed story has survived to be adapted so often is a testament to its continued relevance.

title: How Trump's red-dyed diesel order could impact fuel affordability for drivers and farmers
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
How Trump's red-dyed diesel order could impact fuel affordability for drivers and farmers
President Donald Trump temporarily expanded access to tax-free fuel in an executive order ahead of midterm elections.
How Trump's red-dyed diesel order could impact fuel affordability for drivers and farmers
President Donald Trump temporarily expanded access to tax-free fuel in an executive order ahead of midterm elections.
A new executive order signed by President Donald Trump this week will temporarily expand access to tax-free fuel called red-dyed diesel.
It's the latest step that Trump has taken to offer relief in the lead-up to midterm elections, at a time when consumers and farmers are being squeezed by steep diesel prices driven higher by overseas conflicts, including his war with Iran.
"Today, I'm announcing another unprecedented step to bring down costs," Trump declared at a campaign stop in Nebraska on Monday.
But one Nebraska farmer that we spoke to isn't buying it.
What is red-dyed diesel?
Red-dyed diesel is typically reserved for off-road vehicles, like farm equipment, but Trump's executive order temporarily authorizes highway use and defers the federal diesel excise tax through the end of the year while the administration considers ways to potentially forgive those duties.
How much could drivers save?
Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis for Gas Buddy, said consumers could see a difference of up to 60 cents per gallon between dyed diesel and traditional on-road diesel, but that will vary depending on state taxes.
De Haan said Americans with diesel-powered cars and trucks can generally fill up their tanks with dyed diesel, but availability is limited in some areas. He said drivers should also be wary of potential fines if they're crossing state lines.
"States can still enforce their own rules and regulations, and some states have not waived diesel requirements, meaning that in some states, it's still illegal to use off-road dye diesel on a road or on a highway," De Haan said.
Will trucker savings lead to lower food prices?
De Haan said the patchwork of state rules may prevent some long-haul truckers from taking advantage of the executive order, potentially limiting its impact.
Yet Trump has argued that the order will save truckers as much as $100 per fill, noting that lower transportation costs could be passed down to consumers in the form of lower food prices at the grocery store.
What does this mean for farmers?
Trump also claimed that his order would save farmers "millions."
Dr. Faith Parum, an economist with the American Farm Bureau Federation, said the order will offer some relief during harvest season.
"It's a great first step. Hopefully, we can get removal of the full tax," Parum said.
Parum also stressed that farmers will still be paying much more for red-dyed diesel than usual.
"Last year, around this time of year, it was only $3 a gallon. This year, it's about $5.61 a gallon on average. So that's a pretty large jump for farmers and ranchers," Parum said.
Scott Thomsen, a fourth-generation farmer in Nebraska who previously supported Trump, said he's considering staying home this election season due to frustration over rising costs and the war with Iran. He said the executive order isn't going to sway his vote.
"President Trump ran on lowering fuel prices, lowering overall expenses, and so far everything's inflated in price," Thomsen said.
Thomsen also raised concerns that the president's order could lead to shortages of red-dyed diesel. A White House fact sheet notes that the Secretary of Agriculture should "ensure farmers’ access to dyed diesel in high-demand areas."

title: Portland trade show and media company promotes development officer
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Diversified, a Portland-based trade show and media company, has promoted Oakley Dyer to a newly created chief corporate development officer role as the company continues to expand through acquisitions and new product launches.
In his new role, Dyer will continue to lead Diversified‘s strategy and corporate development team, working with brand managers to identify, evaluate and integrate acquisitions and new product opportunities.
Dyer joined Diversified in 2013 and has led more than 30 acquisitions, expanding the company into new markets and growing its presence in existing ones. His team has also supported dozens of new product launches.
“Diversified‘s growth has come from strong organic performance across our portfolio, supplemented by strategic acquisitions and new product launches,” said Dyer.
“What sets us apart from private equity-backed organizers is patience. We’re focused on the long-term success of the products and people who join us, not a short-term exit. As a family-owned business, we intend to stay that way, and we’ll keep pursuing acquisitions that fit both our strategy and our values.”
Before joining Diversified, Dyer held roles at IDEXX Laboratories and North Atlantic Capital. He holds a bachelor’s degree in economics and political science from Colgate University and an MBA from Babson College.
About Diversified
Diversified is a media company with a portfolio of exhibitions and conferences, online communities and digital and print publications. Its goal is to connect, educate and strengthen business communities in a range of industries, including food and beverage, health care, natural and organic, business management and technology. Established in 1949 and headquartered in Portland, it is a privately held, family-owned business now in its third generation.

title: Whatever method you use, hunting for grouse something to be thankful for
text:
There’s a running quip among Maine hunters regarding the difference between grouse and partridge. When you approach a gallinaceous game bird , if it flies away, it’s a grouse. If it walks away, it’s a partridge.
In truth, our most abundant upland bird is a grouse, a ruffed grouse to be more precise. That’s an important distinction, because in higher elevations and northern areas of Maine, you might also come across a spruce grouse, which is not legal game. The only true partridges in the U.S. have been imported or raised in captivity for hunting preserves.
Still, that tongue-in-cheek distinction has a lot to do with how folks go about hunting the species. In southern and cental Maine, where people are more abundant, the birds are less abundant and considered “wilder” by bird hunters. By that, they mean the birds are more inclined to flush, often long before offering a shot opportunity. Most hunters in these areas employ one of two methods. One is to simply stroll along in hopes of flushing a bird within range. The other is to enlist the aid of dogs.
Dog hunters are a different breed, no pun intended. Regardless of the game, be it birds, bear or hare, the hunt is more about the dogs than the quarry. Watching a well-trained pointer or setter work a scent is a thing of beauty. If they can hold a bird in position until hunters arrive, it’s a win, whether the shot is a hit or a miss.
In the north woods, grouse (or partridge) could be considered a pedestrian bird. One reason is because you’ll often find them walking along the side of the road, or in the middle of it. Another is because their propensity to do so might make them seem a bit dull and uninspiring. Either way, you can’t help but to stop for them.
Some folks are concerned that this method of hunting “easy targets” could be detrimental to grouse populations. One only need look at satellite imagery of the landscape to see the fallacy in that argument. Roads are few and far between, and for every bird you encounter along them, there are just as many where the roads and most hunters don’t go.
Someone once asked me what grouse tastes like. I said, “like turkey, with a hint of cranberry sauce.” Regardless of how they’re harvested, whether randomly, over a stoic setter or on the roadside, we should give thanks for the opportunity.
Bob Humphrey is a freelance writer and Registered Maine Guide who lives in Pownal. He can be reached at: [email protected]

title: Letter: Vote for Democrats to improve healthcare
text:
I think I speak for many as I continue to age, necessarily requiring more encounters with our healthcare system. It has become more than academic for me now.
Yes, I used to speak of our need for a single-payer healthcare system plan in the U.S. I reminded people I knew about the fact that we are the only industrialized nation in the world that doesn’t provide healthcare for its citizens. And I participated in organizations and committees volunteering to encourage my political representatives to make the changes needed to bring about that end. Was it all for nothing? Now that I truly need healthcare where am I?
Our Maine hospitals are cutting departments or even closing down for various reasons — Medicaid cuts, nurse shortages. Nursing homes, birthing centers and even local medical practices, especially in our more rural areas, are suffering as well. And we hear many explanations. OK so now what?
I have friends who have looked for solutions — everything from alternative medicine locally to traveling to specialized treatment centers in other states and even to using eye surgeries, dental care and joint replacement in other countries. I’m not likely to do any of these things. I’m simply hoping for my government to provide the healthcare we all need.
One thing I do know: The government we have now won’t come to my aid. I hope my fellow citizens will come to the polls in November and vote to make the necessary changes in governmental leadership. I believe the only hope for the changes we need will come under a government led by Democrats.
Betsy Braunhut
Deer Isle

title: ABC and Trump's FCC battle in federal court over issues of free speech and jurisdiction
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A lawyer for ABC on Tuesday asked a federal judge to prevent the Trump administration from conducting an unusual, early review of its broadcast licenses, likening it to a looming execution by guillotine that was already chilling the network’s editorial decisions just weeks before the U.S. midterm elections.
U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan did not immediately rule on ABC’s request for a preliminary injunction prohibiting the Federal Communications Commission from conducting its early review, which it said was unconstitutional, a violation of free speech and a retaliation for content President Donald Trump dislikes.
A government attorney argued that, as a procedural matter, the court doesn’t have jurisdiction over ABC’s case because it belongs in a different venue. The government also challenged the network’s First Amendment arguments, and said ABC had failed to show it suffered irreparable harm.
A ruling was not expected until at least mid-October. The judge asked the two sides to submit brief additional arguments by Oct. 9, for the government, and Oct. 14, for ABC.
ABC and its parent company, Disney, sued the FCC and FCC Commissioner Brendan Carr in August, several months after the commission ordered eight ABC-owned stations to submit renewal applications for their broadcast licenses years ahead of schedule.
The case is one of several ongoing legal battles between Trump’s administration and news outlets — including The Associated Press — over their coverage and access to the executive branch since Trump returned to the White House for a second term.
ABC had asked the judge to temporarily prohibit the FCC from taking any further action related to its license renewal proceedings. ABC also sought to prohibit the commission from trying to coerce or threaten the network to alter its “exercise of editorial discretion.”
“The First Amendment demands an immediate end to the Commission’s retaliatory campaign,” ABC attorneys wrote.
Carr, a Trump ally, ordered the early review of the stations’ licenses in April — just after a joke by ABC’s late-night host Jimmy Kimmel infuriated Trump, who called for the comedian’s firing.
ABC also had been fighting Carr’s efforts to make the morning talk show “The View” subject to equal-time rules. Carr defended his agency’s actions against ABC by saying broadcasters have a duty to “operate in the public interest.”
Government attorneys urged the court to dismiss ABC’s lawsuit, accusing the network of trying to prematurely ward off scrutiny by federal regulators.
“To foreclose the Commission from using all the tools at its disposal to investigate whether Plaintiffs are meeting their statutory and regulatory duties would seriously harm both the government and the public,” Justice Department lawyers wrote.
AliKhan was nominated to the bench by President Joe Biden, a Democrat.
___
Noveck reported from New York, and Boone from Boise, Idaho.

title: Troy Jackson needs to start running like there’s nothing to lose
text:
Lorenzo Krakowsky of Owls Head is a former teacher and high school principal.
This is a message for Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson.
There is less than a month left to win this election, and it is time for you to make your case urgently and directly to the people of Maine. Enough with the endless fundraising, TV ads, limited community events and outside consultants. Stop listening to the DSCC and the Democratic Party establishment politicos — they’re not Mainers, and they don’t know what we need.
Your personal story and your vision for how to truly serve working Mainers is what will win this thing, and it’s what people will rally around. Folks want to hear from you in person, in their towns and in their counties. They want to be inspired and fired up directly by you. You know Maine and you’ve been fighting for us for years.
Here’s what it will take:
- Use your current funds to go on a 40-day town hall barnstormer through all of Maine, north to south and east to west. Open those town halls to everyone who wants to come. Answer every question that is asked. Stay as long as is needed to hear and connect to everyone.
- Use your volunteers to generate enthusiasm and boost attendance at those town halls. Rally them to phonebank, canvass, go to demonstrations, connect socially and get out the vote now. Get as many folks as possible out to your town halls in October.
- At those town halls, let loose: call Sen. Collins a corrupt politician, call what’s going on in Gaza a genocide, tell your personal story, tell us exactly what you’ve done and what you’re going to do to make life for working Mainers fair and equitable. Run as the fighting progressive that you are. Don’t hold anything back!
- Hold a press conference ASAP to call on Sen. Collins to resign immediately and drop out of the race because of the allegations of corruption against her. Bring this up every single day from now until Election Day.
- Relentlessly pressure Sen. Collins to justify her vote to confirm Brett Kavanaugh and end the right to have abortions, and her votes to fund ICE and support its authoritarian, illegal actions.
- Use the October debates to hammer Sen. Collins about her corruption, her elite insiderism and her incompetence as the Appropriations Committee chair. Label her a corrupt politician, an elitist, a hypocrite, a Trump puppet and an AIPAC tool. Let everyone know she’s in the pocket of special interests and the rich oligarchs outside of Maine who want to crush us. Don’t be deferential.
So many of us are rooting for you, and we are 100% behind you, but we need this campaign to be ferociously urgent, completely open, genuinely grassroots and unrelentingly aggressive.
You need to run like you have nothing to lose — it’s the only way we will win.

title: Tennessee Republicans consider more execution options after Christa Pike lethal injection fails
text:
(AP) - Some of Tennessee’s top Republicans said Monday they want to explore alternative ways of executing condemned prisoners after the failed execution of Christa Pike, which relied on a large dose of pentobarbital.
U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the state’s Republican candidate for governor, said Pike’s unsuccessful execution last week “should not be grounds to halt carrying out the death penalty.” Rather, she said, Tennessee needs to reevaluate the way it does executions.
“If it’s lethal injection, if it is electric chair, what we do know is we have to find a way to do this — and do it successfully,” Blackburn told The Associated Press.
Top legislative leaders have already spoken with Blackburn about potential changes to state execution laws during their 2027 session.
“We want to broaden it, include more methods,” House Speaker Cameron Sexton said. ”What those are as of today, I’m not sure. But I don’t think there’s any method that’s off the table at this point.”
Most U.S. states that allow executions use lethal injection as their primary means, though South Carolina sets its default as electrocution and Idaho the firing squad, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. Some states give prisoners a choice of execution methods. Death by electricity or gas is authorized in nine states, including five that specify nitrogen gas, the center said. Five states authorize a firing squad.
Florida, which leads the nation in executions this year, uses a three-drug lethal injection that includes a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart.
Tennessee’s execution procedures have been in the national spotlight since Wednesday, when prison officials gave Pike two doses of a barbiturate that were supposed to be lethal but didn’t ultimately kill her. Pike has remained hospitalized under guard, left unconscious and on a ventilator with blisters and burns on her arms from the drug, her lawyers have said.
Pike, now 50, was sentenced to death for the 1995 torture and slaying of a classmate, Colleen Slemmer. Pike was age 18 at the time and became one of the youngest women sent to death row.
Republican Gov. Bill Lee, whose term ends in January, halted the one remaining execution scheduled for this year and ordered an independent investigation into the state’s capital punishment system after Pike’s failed execution. He said Saturday the commissioner of the Department of Correction will step down.
Blackburn said comprehensive change is needed — “it is personnel, processes, procedures, protocols that are all going to need to be addressed.”
Tennessee law already allows electrocution if the department is unable to carry out a lethal injection despite reasonable efforts to do so. State law also gives people who committed crimes before 1999 the option of choosing electrocution.
Between 2018 and 2020, five Tennessee prisoners chose electrocution. That could remain an option for about two dozen of the 40 people on death row.
Sexton said the legislature could consider amending the law to give the state a choice of execution methods.
House Majority Leader William Lamberth said he is open to making electrocution the state’s primary means of execution. But no matter the method, Lamberth said he doesn’t want any changes to take too long to implement.
“We want these sentences to be carried out effectively, efficiently and humanely,” he said, adding: ”Whatever we do, I do not want it to delay justice for these victims’ families.”
Republican state Sen. Todd Gardenhire, chair of the Senate Judiciary Committee, said he expects a deliberate review of what went wrong and what can be done to improve the execution process.
“I think the electric chair is the quickest and simplest way to do it,” he said.

title: Reverse mentoring: How generations can beat workplace ageism together
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Aging Untold) — Ageism at work isn’t always obvious. It can hide in quiet assumptions — about who understands technology, who communicates well or who has something valuable to contribute.
The Aging Untold hosts are digging into reverse mentoring, a strategy that flips the traditional mentor-mentee relationship so every generation in the office has something to teach and something to learn.
What is reverse mentoring?
The idea isn’t new. Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, traced it back to corporate history.
“Jack Welch, former CEO of General Electric, started an official reverse mentoring program at his company,” O’Rourke said. “He could see that the younger people had all this technology knowledge, and he could see that the older adults had some institutional memory and some people skills that could be passed on.”
O’Rourke said Welch’s program was formal and structured, built so older and younger employees could learn from each other.
Older generations weren’t raised with the technology — and that’s OK
Gerontologist Sam Cradduck said that older employees may feel behind simply because of when they grew up.
“Maybe our older generation wasn’t raised with technology,” Cradduck said. “I was a senior when we got our computers in high school. So our older generation wasn’t raised with a smartphone in their hand and a computer. The mainframes took up great big rooms back then.”
Cradduck added that while younger coworkers have a lot to offer older generations, she sometimes sees resistance to that exchange.
The antidote to ageism: belief in yourself
Not everyone agreed that resistance is the full picture.
Katherine Ambrose, an aging-well coach, argued that longevity in the workforce is an advantage, not a liability.
“What I think is that makes us perfectly equipped because we invented this stuff,” Ambrose said. “We were here as every new thing came along — that perfectly positions us to lead.”
Ambrose said the real defense against age bias isn’t avoiding new tools — it’s having the right attitude.
“The antidote to ageism is belief in yourself, and staying on top of trends and helping to lead the way,” Ambrose said. “Your personal energy, your personal capacity really matters. If you don’t want to get left behind and you want to be competitive, compete.”
Moving past an “all-or-none” mindset
The conversation turned to how generations can stop viewing each other in extremes.
“I think we have to get away from this all-or-none mentality,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
She said there is an opportunity for generations to integrate rather than compete, since older workers bring experience while younger workers bring technology fluency — and both groups can benefit from each other.
“The younger people look up to the older people for the wisdom,” Rogers said.
Practical tips for bridging the generational gap
O’Rourke offered direct advice for older workers looking to engage younger colleagues.
“If I’m an older person in the workforce, here’s some tips that I would give: Learn how to ask open-ended questions of the younger person,” O’Rourke said. “What are the trends you’re seeing? ... What do you not know, and be humble enough to ask a question.”
She also had advice for younger employees who may feel hesitant to approach older coworkers.
“If you’re younger, you’re insecure, you might be more fearful,” O’Rourke said. “But go ahead and ask an older adult: Do you see me doing anything that I could get better at? Do you see anything that I should know that I don’t even know that I should know?”
Key takeaways
- Competition can silo generations, but collaboration wins. Ditching the “all-or-none” mentality helps coworkers of every age connect.
- Be humble across generations. Ask older coworkers what you might be missing, and ask younger coworkers what trends or tech you may not know.
- Staying valuable is the antidote to ageism. Keep your attitude, energy, and contribution strong to stay competitive at any age.

Troy Jackson rallies for reproductive rights, explains change in abortion stance
Jackson said he "listened to Maine women" as he explained what he called an evolution in his opinion on abortion rights.
Senate candidate Troy Jackson sat down with Planned Parenthood Maine on Monday in Bath and touched on how his opinions on abortion rights have changed over the years. Jackson once held anti-abortion views, but said he has gone through an "evolution."
"It just became clear to me that I was wrong and that reproductive rights is healthcare and I always have thought that people should have healthcare," Jackson said.
Jackson told Nicole Clegg, president and CEO of Planned Parenthood Maine Action Fund, that his change of heart on abortion came after he spoke with Maine women, and said that led him to push for expanded abortion access in the state. Jackson was in favor of 2023 legislation that allowed for later-in-pregnancy abortions. Planned Parenthood previously threw support behind Janet Mills during her senate bid, and later Graham Platner before endorsing Troy Jackson once Platner dropped out.
"I was not supposed to be blocking it for people who needed that decision," Jackson said.
He once again criticized Sen. Susan Collins for voting to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, saying her vote impacted women far beyond Maine after the Dobbs decision.
"When she came out and said she was going to vote for him, to me it was clear that she knew what was going to happen, too," Jackson said.
While talking about Collins' vote for Kavanaugh, Jackson called Collins "stupid."
"She thinks we are stupid that is what it comes down to. She thinks people don't understand the process that she did not know what he was going to do. Everyone in the country knew what she was going to do. It is not us that are stupid, it's her," Jackson said.
Jackson later said he wanted to clarify his statement at the end of the night.
"I should clarify that Sen. Collins would be stupid if she did not think we could see what's going on. Not that she is stupid," Jackson said.

title: Group appeals Maine’s decision to give education contracts to AI-powered firm
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Last month, an out-of-state firm backed by private equity and venture capital beat a Maine-based early childhood education organization for a pair of state contracts.
Now, advocates are sounding the alarm over what the decision could mean for Maine children and raising concerns about how the Maine Department of Health and Human Services evaluated the proposals.
Shine Early Learning, a New York organization backed by the private equity behemoth BlackRock, won two multimillion-dollar contracts to provide training and assistance to Maine’s early childhood educators through 2028.
The firm underbid Maine Roads to Quality, a group created in 1999 by the Catherine Cutler Institute at the University of Southern Maine, by about $2 million. Shine Early Learning said it will achieve lower costs by using artificial intelligence to do much of the work Maine Roads’ 30-odd employees currently perform.
Those employees are now bracing for layoffs as Maine Roads might be forced to shut down. The University of Maine System appealed the contract decisions last week.
Ending a decades-long partnership in favor of an out-of-state tech company could have drastic effects on the state’s early childhood education system, said Lauren Stark, an analyst with the progressive Maine Center for Economic Policy.
“There is not necessarily an incentive for the company to improve early learning or to increase access to affordable childcare. There’s not a public good motivation for them as a for-profit venture capitalist company,” Stark said. “The motivation is to have a greater profit.”
“Lower cost is not the same as a better value,” she added.
Maine Roads provides training and assistance to about 10,000 Maine childcare providers each year. It’s cultivated relationships with schools, educators, students and regulators alike over the last 27 years, said University of Maine System spokesperson Samantha Warren.
Work that was historically housed under a single contract was instead split into two earlier this year: One for coaching, credentialing and training educators, and another for providing a DHHS-approved plan “designed to improve (the) quality” of child care services.
Kimberlee Belcher-Badal is the executive director of the National Workforce Registry Alliance, a group that supports early childhood workforce registry systems across the country. The alliance has worked with Maine Roads for decades, Belcher-Badal said.
In a letter to DHHS’ appeals committee, Belcher-Badal said “Maine’s registry and its team are among the strongest in the nation” and questioned whether Shine Early Learning’s plans to implement AI chatbots would really benefit Maine educators.
In Missouri, Montana and many other states where Shine Early Learning operates, established early childcare providers have seen similar outcomes after losing contracts to the firm: Sweeping layoffs, worse services and less person-to-person connection in a field heavily reliant upon it.
DHHS graded Maine Roads’ and Shine Early Learning’s proposals on a scale from 0 to 100, as it does all submissions. Shine Early Learning’s bid for the coaching contract received a 97 and its proposal for the training plan got a perfect 100, public records show. Maine Roads received about 73 points on each.
In a pair of letters sent to the state, the university system questioned how DHHS graded each proposal and asked regulators to invalidate the contract decisions over irregularities in the scoring process. Maine Roads lost points “for no stated reason,” the appeal alleges.
“(DHHS) gave Shine near-perfect technical scores without resolving questions the evaluators themselves raised,” the appeal reads. “The award is arbitrary and capricious, and the evaluation contains irregularities creating fundamental unfairness.”
A DHHS spokesperson said the scores were issued in accordance with the processes laid out in its requests for proposals but did not specify how Shine Early Learning received such high marks.
Shine Early Learning’s website says the company uses “data-driven services and solutions” to “accelerate child and family outcomes.” The company has not responded to requests for comment on its expansion into Maine.
The company’s proposals state they plan to use AI agents and chatbots to screen prospective teachers’ applications, power a “family navigation assistant” and manage the state’s early childcare provider registry.
Stark, with the Maine Center for Economic Policy, is skeptical that AI will be an adequate replacement for Maine Roads’ human staff.
“You need people with expertise to set up the systems, you need mentors who have experience in the field working with early childhood educators. And a chatbot is not a mentor,” she said.
Shine Early Learning is owned by Acelero Inc., a company backed by some of the world’s largest private equity and venture capital companies. The senior portfolio manager for BlackRock, which manages some $11 trillion in assets globally, said the firm was investing in Acelero to widen its reach across the country.
A report published in February by the National Women’s Law Center, a nonprofit advocacy organization, found private equity groups are increasingly acquiring vital community services, from childcare to housing.
“Private equity investors face more structural incentives to prioritize short-term profits than any other form of corporate ownership or investment,” the report states. “This makes them the quickest and most likely to identify and exploit opportunities to extract wealth from any market.”
It is unclear when the appeal will be resolved. The state’s contracts with the firm have not yet been finalized, a DHHS spokesperson said, and won’t be until the appeals process is complete.

Football fans are cutting back on spending this season, survey finds
text:
(InvestigateTV) — More than a third of Americans plan to cut back on football-related spending this season because of the economy, according to a new LendingTree survey, even though many fans could still end up taking on hundreds of dollars in football-related debt.
LendingTree found almost half of Americans plan to spend money on their football fandom this year, down more than 10 percentage points from 65% last year. The survey covered a wide range of football-related costs, including game tickets, team merchandise, streaming subscriptions, and food and drinks for watch parties and tailgates.
Matt Schulz, with LendingTree, said football fans are feeling the same economic pressure affecting other areas of spending.
“As much as Americans love football, even football isn’t immune to the effects of inflation,” Schulz said. “We are seeing an awful lot of Americans who say that they’re going to spend at least a little bit less on football fandom this fall, and a big part of it is just because of the economy.”
For fans who still plan to spend on the season, Schulz recommends building football into the household budget as its own line item.
“It may seem a little silly to some to have a line item in your budget that says ‘football,’ but we don’t think anything of that when it comes to passions like travel and things like that,” Schulz said. “So if football is something that’s meaningful to you, that you spend an awful lot of money on and an awful lot of time on, you should have a line item for it.”
Schulz said budgeting specifically for football gives fans more control over their spending and allows them to pursue the hobby without creating larger financial problems.

title: Trump approves firing squad execution for Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan
text:
(AP) - President Donald Trump has approved the execution by firing squad of Army Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan for the 2009 shooting rampage at Fort Hood, Texas.
The U.S. military has not carried out the death penalty since 1961. The Army secretary will decide a time and place for the execution, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell wrote in a post on X.
“Judgement day for Hasan has finally come,” Parnell wrote.
Hasan, an Army psychiatrist, walked into a medical building where soldiers were getting medical checkups, shouted “Allahu akbar” — Arabic for “God is great!” — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun. Thirteen people were killed and more than 30 injured.
He said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims and made almost no effort to defend himself at trial. He told jurors that evidence would show he was the shooter and described himself as a soldier who had “switched sides.”
Trump’s approval triggers a series of procedural steps toward carrying out the execution, but Hasan could put them on hold — potentially for years — with a habeas corpus appeal in the civilian federal court system, according to an article published in May in the magazine Army Lawyer.
Death sentences are extremely rare in the military justice system, and executions even rarer. Four men, including Hasan, are currently on the military’s death row at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. President George W. Bush approved the execution Army Spc. Ronald Gray in 2008 but it was put on hold by a judge and he remains at Leavenworth.
The last man executed in the military system was Pvt. John Bennett, hanged in 1961 for raping an 11-year-old girl.
Trump approved the firing squad execution days after a failed attempt to execute Christa Pike by lethal injection pushed Tennessee’s governor to halt further executions this year and order an independent review.
Trump resumed the federal death penalty after an informal moratorium during previous administrations. The federal government executed 13 people between 2020 and early 2021, contributing to making Trump the most prolific execution president in over 130 years.
Asked whether the botched execution in Tennessee would lead him to seek changes to capital punishment, Trump said it was “an interesting situation.”
“It shouldn’t be very difficult,” Trump said of carrying out lethal injections.

title: Aging Untold: How having babies later alters roles for parents, grandparents
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, explore the realities of having babies later in life and how those pregnancies alter roles for both parents and grandparents.
Plus, find out how reverse mentoring can bridge generational divides on the job to break down workplace stereotypes.
We also meet a father and son in Wisconsin crafting a musical legacy one handmade guitar at a time.
More women over 40 are having children.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said many women now have more wisdom, resources and financial stability by the time they decide to have children.
But pregnancy after 40 is classified as advanced maternal age, and it can carry a higher risk for high blood pressure, preeclampsia, gestational diabetes and chromosomal abnormalities, Rogers said. Physicians who specialize in high-risk pregnancies are available to help manage those risks.
Find the full conversation, including the impact parenthood later in life has on the role of grandparents here.
Reverse mentoring is a strategy that flips the traditional mentor-mentee relationship so every generation in the office has something to teach and something to learn.
Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said these programs are built so older and younger employees can learn from each other.
The Aging Untold experts are providing tips on how different generations can speak to each other and work in collaboration and explaining how longevity in the workforce can be an advantage, not a liability.
Nicole Parmelee is a mom of two and found there was little support for new moms who were dealing with a lack of sleep and breastfeeding challenges while healing after giving birth.
“They prepare you for how to swaddle a baby, how to change a diaper, you know, how to respond to your baby’s cries, but they don’t prepare the mother for how they might feel,” Parmelee said.
So, she decided to do something about it. She started the New Moms School.
Bruce Petros was working as a tour guide in a town in Colorado when he found the $15 guitar kit that would change his life.
He took the kit he found in a shop back to the resort where he was living and put it together.
“And I looked at it and I went, ‘Wow, this is really cool. I could do this,’” Petros said.
He started building guitars in the basement until he built a shop.
His company, Petros Guitars, now supplies guitars and ukuleles to musicians around the world, including collectors, working musicians and hobbyists. He plans to hand the company down to his son, Matt.

title: Auburn residents to vote on Flock camera ban in March
text:
AUBURN — Voters will be able to choose whether to ban automatic license plate reader systems in the city on March 2, 2027.
City councilors voted Monday to set a vote for the measure, which comes after residents spent months pursuing a citizens initiative to put the issue before the City Council.
The proposed ordinance prohibits Auburn from using automatic license plate recognition systems, which includes the use of computer algorithms that make images of license plates searchable, and restricts the city from accessing information generated through other automatic license plate recognition systems.
Absentee voting and in-person early voting will begin 30 days before March 2, 2027.
Republican state Reps. Laurel Libby and Quentin Chapman of Auburn and Rep. David Boyer of Poland initiated the petition drive after residents became aware city police installed Flock Safety cameras without public input or a council vote.
The petition, which gathered over 200 signatures more than the required 1,568, was handed in to the city July 30 and verified by the city clerk.
The measure came before councilors on Sept. 21 and was rejected, which automatically sent it to voters.
Councilors opted in May while building the 2026-27 city budget not to fund further use of Flock Safety’s system and terminated the city’s agreement in August.
After weeks of silence following a request by the city to have the cameras and equipment removed, Flock Safety recently notified city officials that removal is being scheduled. No timeline was set by the company.
According to the agreement between the city and Flock Safety, equipment will be removed within a “commercially reasonable” period of time, which the city interprets as six to eight weeks. If the cameras and equipment have not been removed by the end of that period, the city will remove them, city officials said.

title: Mother and son from Bermuda named as passengers on missing medical flight from Bermuda to Boston
text:
(AP) - The two passengers aboard an air ambulance that crashed in the waters off Massachusetts over the weekend while flying from Bermuda to Boston were identified Monday as a mother from Bermuda and her son.
Bermuda police said Marilyn Lavonne Bean, 66, and Sergio Wayne Lottimore, 41, both Bermudian nationals, were aboard a Gulfstream G100 along with four crew members when it went missing off Nantucket around 1 a.m. Saturday. Bermuda is about 750 to 780 miles (roughly 1,200 to 1,250 kilometers) southeast of Boston.
Searchers later found a “debris field” off the coast of the island, but with no sign of the six people on board after a 66-hour search that spanned more than 4,400 miles (7,081 kilometers), the U.S. Coast Guard suspended rescue efforts Sunday.
“While we held out hope for the best, the worst fears have been realized,” Bermuda Premier David Burt said in a statement. “Let us open our hearts to the families in the hope that our expressions of love, support and compassion will bring some comfort as they attempt to deal with this terrible loss.”
Warwick Academy, the school Lottimore attended in Bermuda, remembered him as a school prefect and an “ outstanding person.” Hamilton Re, the Bermuda insurance firm where he served as a senior vice president, said it had lost a “ respected leader, colleague and friend.”
The names of the plane’s crew have not been released, but Latitude Air Ambulance, the Ontario-based company that owned the plane, said Sunday that its staff faces the “heartbreaking reality” that all aboard the plane are now presumed dead, even if they have not been officially declared dead.
“Our four crew members were valued members of the Latitude family,” the company said in a statement. “They dedicated themselves to providing care to people at some of the most difficult moments in their lives, and they were carrying out that mission when this tragedy occurred. We are grieving their loss deeply.”
Peter Byl, president of Latitude Air Ambulance, said Monday the company’s immediate focus was on supporting the victims’ families and cooperating fully with authorities.
“We will not speculate about the circumstances or cause of the accident while that work is underway,” he wrote in an email.
The Canadian-registered jet had departed Bermuda’s L.F. Wade International Airport on a nighttime flight to Massachusetts. Air traffic audio indicates that the plane may have been “coming in blind” as a storm loomed. The pilot reported electrical problems and declared an emergency as the jet approached the coast.
Canada’s Transportation Safety Board said it will send investigators in the coming days to assist in the search for and recovery of the aircraft. The agency said it is leading the investigation into the crash with assistance from its U.S. counterpart, the National Transportation Safety Board.

title: UMaine football makes a rare move with rare midseason firing. Is it the right one?
text:
ORONO — Jordan Stevens answered the questions, one day after making the most consequential decision of his time as head coach of the University of Maine football team. Stevens was resolute.
Mikahael Waters, Maine’s offensive coordinator and quarterbacks coach since 2024, is out. Sean Green, in his first season on Stevens’ staff as the running backs coach, is now the interim offensive coordinator.
When you fire your offensive coordinator in the middle of the season, you’d better be absolutely sure it’s the right move. It’s not a move you can make emotionally or haphazardly.
“We have a very talented roster, and we’ve done a lot of good things this season. We’ve got to be more consistent. We’ve got to score points,” Stevens said following Tuesday morning’s practice.
The Black Bears are 1-5. Since winning the season opener at Towson, Maine has lost five games in a row. You don’t have to break down the statistics too deeply to see that the team’s offense has been the major contributing factor to the weak start.
Averaging just 270.2 yards per game, Maine ranks 115 of 124 teams in the Football Championship Subdivision, and last in the Coastal Athletic Association. Scoring an average of 14.5 point per game, Maine is 118th nationally and, again, last in the league.
Rushing offense? Ranked 110th at 96 yards per game. Passing offense? Ranked 93th, just over 174 yards per game. Third-down conversions? Ranked 90th with a 33% success rate. The Black Bears’ best national ranking is in first downs, in which they’re tied for 85th.
All that said, firing an assistant coach in the middle of the season is a rare move. It happens, but usually for off-the-field reasons. Conversations with two Maine football alumni whose relationships with the program go back decades said they’ve never heard of a Black Bears coach losing his job midseason.
Stevens noted that the slow start doesn’t all fall on Waters. But he determined that enough of it does to warrant the rare midseason change. Waiting until the end of the season wasn’t going to work.
Stevens sees the situation as one that needs immediate attention, one that can set the tone for the remaining five games.
“When you look at our team, I believe we are a team that can win football games,” Stevens said. “I’m not sitting here just throwing in the towel on the season. I’m not willing to do that.”
Green is no stranger to football fans in Maine. He coached Portland to the Class A state title in 2024. In 2021, Green coached Cape Elizabeth to the Class C championship. Two of the players who were pivotal in those title runs are now among the weapons Green has in the Black Bears’ offense. Running back Nick Laughlin of Cape Elizabeth is a key contributor whose four touchdowns lead the team. Freshman wide receiver Cordell Jones of Portland has yet to see game action.
Green was not made available for comment Tuesday.
College football is a production business, Stevens said. You judge production in wins. Every coach has to do a better job, he said. If players aren’t playing with confidence, coaches need to instill it. If players aren’t executing on the field, coaches need to develop ways to find success. Stevens said he’s not pointing the finger, he’s pointing the thumb, back at himself and the rest of the staff.
“It’s really about us recommitting ourselves to the season,” Stevens said. “I don’t need to make a narrative over scoring more points. You can see that. We need to score more points so we can win football games. … Winning is the expectation, and not winning is never OK. We grow from those experiences, but we do need to compete and win football games. I refuse to hold us to a standard that’s anything less than that. That’s not who I am. That’s not who we’re going to be as a team.”
Since being named head coach prior to the 2022, Stevens’ teams are 16-36, the high point being a 6-6 mark last season. Asked if he felt any other assistant coaches, or even himself, were on the hot seat, Stevens was curt.
“No,” he said.
Is replacing the offensive coordinator exactly what the Black Bears need, or is it a last-ditch effort to keep a season from completely slipping away? Starting with the home game against Bryant on Oct. 17, they’ll have five games to find out.

title: President Trump promotes strong dollar
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The economic reports from the Trump administration point to a solid economy. But poll after poll finds Americans do not think the economy is in good shape.
As the 2026 midterm elections approach, the Trump administration keeps insisting the economy is doing great.
The polls keep showing that Americans think the economy is doing badly.
Gray Media’s White House correspondent Jon Decker asked President Donald Trump on Tuesday about a key economic indicator, the strength of the US dollar, and whether the dollar has strengthened too much against the euro.
President Trump answered, “Much more a dollar versus the euro right now. No, we have a very strong dollar. That’s because we’re doing well. You know, a strong dollar is good in many ways. In certain ways you could make a case that it slows things down, but a strong dollar gives you a lot of life. And by the way, you know, what a strong dollar does gives you no inflation.”
President Trump’s message is that things are coming together for a golden age of America; even as Americans worry about rising prices at the pump and the grocery store.
