title: Man arrested in UK on suspicion of terror offense over incident at US-run air base
text:
Man arrested in UK on suspicion of terror offense over incident at US-run air base
British police said on Tuesday that they arrested a 22-year-old man in London on suspicion of a terror offense over a security incident at a U.S.-run military air base in England that authorities have linked to Iran.
Related video: Trump criticizes UK days after releasing suspects in alleged terror plot targeting base used by US
Counter Terrorism Policing said the man, a British national, was detained in the Westminster area of central London on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts.
The arrest is the seventh in connection with a suspected plot against RAF Fairford in western England, which has been used by American bombers to strike Iran.
Six other men have been released on bail under investigation.
Scores of residents were evacuated from their homes near the base early on Sept. 27 as armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts swooped on the rural area. Police later said they had found a quantity of an accelerant – gasoline – in three vans linked to the five suspects, but no explosives.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the U.K. sees "strong indications" that Iran played a part in the incident.
Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for counterterrorism policing, said detectives "continue to pursue multiple lines of enquiry" and "remain committed to investigating all possible angles."

title: 'Live in the moment': College student recalls rare cancer diagnosis
text:
'Live in the moment': College student recalls rare cancer diagnosis
"It's kind of a funny story," 24-year-old Minnesota native Abbie Whittemore says while reflecting on how she never expected to attend Drake University in Des Moines, Iowa.
"I was Big Ten schools. Big sports."
Her mother, Melissa Carstens, had a different perspective.
"She's like you're somebody that asks a bunch of questions in class and is super engaged and likes to be involved and likes to lead. I think you might like a small private school, and I was like, no, no way," Whittemore said.
A detour to Des Moines during a trip to a high school soccer tournament in Coralville led to a pivotal moment.
"And I was like, no, I've heard a lot about this campus. I think it's beautiful and we need to check it out," Carstens said.
After visiting, Whittemore admitted her mom was right.
"And it was really personal right away. I was like, oh wait, my mom might be right," she said.
Years later, walking through campus on a fall Friday night brings back memories for Whittemore.
Both good...
"It's so pretty when the leaves start to change," she said.
And challenging.
"She was healthy the last time I saw her. And then I got a phone call, and it all changed," Carstens remembers.
Whittemore was a sophomore when she began experiencing abdominal pain.
"They gave me a CAT scan of my abdomen and found a spot there. Just a small one. They told me to keep an eye on it," she said.
While studying abroad during her junior year, the pain returned.
"When I came back in March, I went to the doctor for the first time," Whittemore said.
She says a subsequent scan revealed worrisome changes.
"Came back that it was bigger than it had been the last time. So that was an area for concern," Whittemore said.
After multiple tests, doctors diagnosed her with Solitary Plasmacytoma of the rib, a rare cancer typically seen in people over 55.
"It was shocking, very hard, very stressful not having her near me," Carstens said.
Before her diagnosis, Whittemore felt on top of the world.
"Classes were hard but manageable. I was living in a sorority house with 50 of my best friends," Whittemore said.
But says life changed quickly.
"I still tried to go to classes every day for a while, but I was having a lot of appointments and testing, and I just wasn't doing very well mentally," Whittemore said.
Her cancer carried a high risk of progressing to multiple myeloma, which has no cure.
"The anxiety it can bring on is a lot," Carstens said.
Whittemore said the rarity of her specific cancer meant she would likely notice pain before scans or tests could detect its spread.
"So, every time I have some sort of headache, or I have something, my knee hurts or my back hurts or my hip hurts," she said. "The uncertainty part is so challenging."
Throughout her journey, Whittemore found unwavering support from the Drake community.
"Everybody here. My faculty professors, staff that I was working with and organizations were so supportive," she said.
Carstens echoed the sentiment.
"People really made the time to make it work for her and that was huge. That is a huge thing for me to have seen her still be able to live out and stay on track with what she had hoped to get from the experience," Carstens said.
Whittemore says her friends also rallied around her.
"I was actually in the hospital for a week that summer and there was never a time that I was alone in that room, which was so cool," Whittemore said.
Whittemore has been in remission since July 2023.
She graduated a year later and now works as a clinical research associate in Des Moines.
"I love what I do," she said.
Reflecting on her journey, Whittemore said, "Taught me a lot a lot a lot. Just like how grateful to be and how in the moment to be and how to really say yes to everything."
Life's path may have obstacles, but Whittemore has learned it can also lead to special places.

title: Patience Woolman Durand Willner
text:
Patience Woolman Durand Willner set off on her next adventure on Sept. 12, 2026, getting an alpine start. She was born in West Chester, Penn., on Oct. 7, 1928, and moved with her family to Cambridge and then Lincoln, Mass., where she met her life-long best friend Tilly Snider Keevil. She returned every summer to the family farm in Embreeville, Penn., where multiple generations of the Hayes family would put on plays, canoe and swim in the Brandywine, climb trees, and attend Romansville Friends Meeting. She grew up using "thee" and "thy" with her Quaker family and continued until her sister passed in 2012. She was a member of Swarthmore Friends Meeting and attended Acadia Friends Meeting.
Mom started college at the University of Geneva in Switzerland when her father was the OSS Chief of Station in Berlin at the end of World War II. She studied Russian at Georgetown University and graduated with a Liberal Studies degree from Lewis and Clark College. She spoke and sang multiple languages. She and her husband Don settled in Portland, Ore., where she raised their four daughters. She was an avid horsewoman, made beautiful pottery and always had flowers on her table. Later in life she became a physical therapist assistant and enjoyed helping others with recovery.

title: Paramount and Warner Bros are now one Hollywood giant: Skydance. Here’s how we got here
text:
CHICAGO (AP) — It’s official: Skydance-owned Paramount closed its $81 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery on Tuesday, ushering in a new Hollywood behemoth.
The merger brings two of America’s oldest moviemaking studios together under a new name: Skydance.
HBO Max, titles ranging from “Harry Potter” to “Sinners” and networks such as CNN now also find themselves under the same roof as Paramount+, CBS and the likes of “Top Gun” and “The Godfather.” All are under the helm of billionaire David Ellison and his new co-CEO Ynon Kreiz.
“Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry,” Ellison said. “We couldn’t be more excited to get to work.”
Ellison’s Skydance bought Paramount for $8 billion last year before setting its sights on Warner. What followed erupted into a tumultuous, roughly yearlong fight over the storied Hollywood giant. Including billions of dollars in debt, the acquisition amounts to nearly $111 billion.
The now-combined Skydance marks one of the biggest tie-ups in media and entertainment history, further concentrating power in an industry already run by just a handful of big players. Politics also loomed over much of the process. The Ellison family has notably held a long relationship with Republican President Donald Trump, who said Tuesday that Skydance is “going to be a great company.”
Netflix gets into a bidding war with Paramount for Warner
The early days of Paramount’s quest for Warner turned into a messy bidding war.
Months after disclosing it was open to selling all or part of its business, Warner initially struck a studio and streaming deal with Netflix in December.
But Paramount said it also had made offers that Warner management “never engaged meaningfully” with. It soon launched a hostile counterbid.
The Hollywood giants spent much of early 2026 in a heated back-and-forth over who had a stronger offer, with Warner leadership repeatedly backing Netflix as its preferred suitor. But Netflix bowed out after Paramount eventually upped its offer to buy all of Warner for $31 per share.
Warner and Paramount inked a mutual merger agreement in late February.
Hollywood stars made their thoughts known
Hollywood was closely watching the fight over Warner’s future. From awards shows to online petitions, A-list celebrities and other creatives made their voices known.
In April, thousands of movie stars, writers, directors and other professionals announced their “unequivocal opposition” to the Paramount-Warner merger. An open letter — which was signed by long-outspoken critics of the deal like Jane Fonda and Mark Ruffalo, as well as Hollywood heavyweights from Denis Villeneuve to J.J. Abrams — warned of fewer jobs and “less choice for audiences in the United States and around the world.”
Others lined up to back Paramount as Ellison reiterated his commitments to the movies. At CinemaCon, the company debuted a glossy mini movie about the studio directed by Jon M. Chu and narrated by Tom Cruise — who ended the spot atop the iconic Paramount water tower, with the words “the future is paramount and the future looks pretty great from here.” Director James Cameron also doubled down on his support of Ellison.
The prospect of a new Warner owner also loomed over awards season, from #BlockTheMerger pins to more subtle nods in acceptance speeches. When accepting her Emmy last month, “Remarkably Bright Creatures” actor Sally Field — who also signed the open letter in opposition to the Paramount-Warner deal — stressed that “unique storytelling matters” and “we can’t let those voices be silenced, or compromised or merged.”
Many industry critics were also outspoken when Netflix’s studio and streaming deal was on the table, with a particular focus on the future of movies staying in theaters.
Trump has attacked CNN
Critics are also watching what happens with CNN under Skydance.
Trump has regularly attacked reporting he deems unfavorable at CNN (most recently attempting to bar the outlet from the White House altogether). And over the course of the Warner buyout, his administration also chimed in about hopes for a new owner.
Days after Paramount launched its hostile bid for Warner, Trump said CNN spread “poison and lies” and that it was “imperative” the network be sold. The White House took aim again at CNN in March, over the network’s coverage of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth told reporters that “the sooner David Ellison takes over that network, the better.”
Ellison has said editorial independence will be maintained at CNN. On Tuesday, he told reporters that the company had “not talked to any political leader of any party about news — other than to say that we want to be in the truth business and we want be in the trust business.”
Skydance is retaining Mark Thompson as CNN’s editor-in-chief. And under a settlement finalized last month with states that had sued over the takeover, the company agreed to form a “News Editorial Independence Board.”
Still, critics point to turmoil already seen at CBS under Skydance ownership and aren’t convinced this new body will be able to do much. The company’s corporate board will oversee appointments.
Ellison has maintained a close relationship with Trump overall. He reportedly hosted a dinner in Washington in Trump’s honor in April, on the same day Warner shareholders gave their green light for the merger. In June, just two days after the Justice Department said it wouldn’t intervene in the deal, Ellison attended an Ultimate Fighting Championship match on the White House lawn for Trump’s 80th birthday (streamed by Paramount+).
“We have a good relationship with this administration,” Ellison noted Tuesday. But he said he “also had a really good relationship” with Democratic President Joe Biden, among other politicians.
3 Gulf countries helped back the deal
To help fund its Warner buyout, Paramount racked up billions of dollars in financial backing from three Gulf countries: Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. The Federal Communications Commission approved the company’s request for sizable indirect ownership from those foreign investors.
Paramount previously disclosed it expected those funds to indirectly own nearly 50% of equity interests — but no voting rights — of Skydance. But the company asked for clearance of up to 100% to account for potential future investments, which the FCC granted, citing in part that access to more capital would strengthen the broadcast industry and was therefore “in the public interest.”
The FCC’s sole Democratic commissioner, Anna Gomez, and other critics have called the move alarming and unprecedented. They argue that amount of money opens the door to behind-the-scenes influence.
Legal fights stalled the deal
Paramount cleared antitrust hurdles for its Warner acquisition from the Justice Department and regulators worldwide over the summer.
But in July, Democratic attorneys general from 12 states — led by California’s Rob Bonta — sued to block the merger, alleging the combined company would “extinguish competition” and lead to fewer choices for consumers, particularly movie theatergoers and cable customers.
The Writers Guild of America followed suit.
Settlements emerged in September. The states’ terms, approved by a judge, include pledges from the company to increase film production in the U.S. over the next five years, commit millions of dollars to a fund aimed at supporting workers displaced by the merger and establish new editorial monitoring of CNN and CBS.
Critics said the remedies were too weak, but the settlements cleared the way for the deal to close.

title: Washington man conspired with Canadian school shooter before attack, officials say
text:
SEATTLE (AP) — Federal authorities have arrested and charged a 30-year-old man from Washington state in connection with a February school shooting in British Columbia.
The U.S. attorney’s office in Seattle says James Cody Bryant of Bellingham, Washington, communicated with the 18-year-old shooter for six months ahead of time. He did not report her plans to authorities and conspired with her to broadcast the attacks, authorities allege.
Authorities say Jesse Van Rootselaar killed eight people and wounded 25 others. She first killed her mother and stepbrother at home before attacking a nearby school in the mountain community of Tumbler Ridge, officials said.
It was Canada’s deadliest mass shooting in years.
Van Rootselaar was later found dead from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound.

title: Suspect arrested after pregnant woman killed, unborn child removed from her womb
text:
CLARKSVILLE, Tenn. (WYMT/WSMV/Gray News) - Authorities say a man accused of killing a pregnant woman in Kentucky was arrested in Tennessee following a weeklong investigation.
April Barlow Celio, 41, was found dead Sept. 23 at a home in Pineville, Kentucky. The Pineville Police and the Bell County Coroner’s Office determined she was the victim of a homicide.
The next day, investigators learned Celio was pregnant at the time of her death, but the State Medical Examiner’s Office found no fetus in her womb. While processing the crime scene, investigators later found what are believed to be fetal remains.
The investigation identified DeMarcus Kenneth Johnson-Wright as a suspect in the case. He had an extensive violent criminal history and several outstanding violent felony warrants out of Tennessee.
The Bell County District Court issued a warrant for Johnson-Wright on Sep. 25 for first-degree robbery and kidnapping — adult. Additional warrants for him for murder — domestic violence and tampering with physical evidence were issued last Wednesday.
That same day, the U.S. Marshals Service learned Johnson-Wright was living in Clarksville, Tennessee, where he was arrested at a home later that night. A subsequent search warrant was applied for and granted for the home, and marshals say materials relating to the case were recovered.
Johnson-Wright was booked into the Montgomery County Detention Center in Tennessee, where he is awaiting extradition back to Kentucky.
The investigation is ongoing.

title: Frost likely tonight

We will be having cooler conditions today and overnight across Maine

Temperatures will be below average Tuesday afternoon, with high temperatures in the mid to upper 50s. Gusty winds will be noticeable, with gusts potentially reaching 20 to 30 mph. Sunshine will last all day Tuesday, and winds will diminish as we head into the evening.
The calmer winds and clear skies tonight will actually contribute to the formation of frost early Wednesday morning. Tuesday night will be the coldest night of the season so far. A Frost Advisory is in place from midnight Tuesday to 8 a.m. on Wednesday. Temperatures will dip into the 30s and even upper 20s in mountain areas.
Despite the chilly morning on Wednesday, afternoon temperatures will be near normal in the mid to upper 60s. Thursday will be even warmer, with some areas reaching 70 degrees. Scattered showers are possible on Thursday with a cold front moving through, but the weekend is looking dry.

title: The New County Jail Won’t Be Constructed in P.I.
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - One Central Aroostook community is already out of the race for the county’s new jail.
Presque Isle says it decided not to bid to host the facility. The County Commissioners’ Office says it’s searching for a new jail site because the current one is overcrowded and no longer meets the county’s needs. We reached out to the City of Presque Isle about its decision not to host the new jail.
Presque Isle City Manager Sonja Eyler said, quote: “The City Council unanimously determined that Presque Isle does not have a suitable site to offer. At the same time, we strongly believe the facility should be located in Central Aroostook, where its location can help limit transportation costs and maintain reasonable access to the courts and other services. Presque Isle is prepared to support another community that has an appropriate location and is interested in pursuing the project.”
Proposals for the project were due to the County Commissioners by September 28th. Other communities in the county have already submitted bids. Loring, in Limestone, is one of them. We reached out to the LDA about their proposal. We’ll have more on their bid tomorrow on NewsSource8 at 6.

"The typical trucker will save over $100 every time they fill up. So, it's more than $100 each time and farmers will also save millions and millions of dollars," Trump said.

title: 2 young children found starved to death in home were dead for several days, authorities say
text:
LADSON, S.C. (WCSC/Gray News) — South Carolina authorities say two children who were found inside a Ladson-area home late last month had been dead for several days before they were discovered.
Charleston County authorities identified the children as Emory Deacon, 2, and Harlow Deacon, 15 months old. Charleston County coroner Bobbi Jo O’Neal said they died of starvation and dehydration due to neglect.
Justine May, the children’s mother and described as their primary caregiver, was charged in the case with two counts of homicide by child abuse.
According to the Charleston County Sheriff’s Office, deputies had responded to numerous calls at the Pinewood Drive residence before ultimately finding the two children dead during a welfare check at the home.
The previous calls to the home were said to have included welfare checks and visits coordinated with the South Carolina Department of Social Services and the South Carolina Department of Mental Health Mobile Crisis Unit.
Authorities said deputies made contact with May and the children in August and again several more times in September, noting they observed no signs of concern during those visits.
Last Tuesday, authorities said they were called back to the home after a 911 call came through that morning asking deputies to conduct a welfare check on the two young girls after they had not been seen, with their mother acting differently while walking around the neighborhood by herself.
“I’m just concerned because she didn’t have her kids, and nobody has seen her kids,” the caller told the Charleston County 911 dispatcher. “She was walking down the road today, and she didn’t have her babies, and that’s not like her.”
When deputies arrived at the home that afternoon, they said May exited the house and was crying and speaking incoherently. Upon entering, that’s when they saw the two children dead.
May was taken into custody.
According to affidavits, after being read her Miranda rights, May told detectives that she had spent the previous two weeks in a “blur,” saying she could not remember the last time she fed Emory and Harlow or gave them anything to drink.
Authorities said May told detectives that she believed her children were dead because they did not eat. She reportedly told deputies that she knew that not feeding her children was neglectful and confirmed she had been the only one present at home and was the sole caregiver for the girls over the last few weeks.
May remained jailed at the Al Cannon Detention Center.

title: Maine Law Doesn't Ban Front-seat Dogs, But Sudden Stops And Airbags Pose Real Risks
text:
Can You Legally Drive With Your Dog in the Front Seat in Maine?
If your dog loves riding shotgun, you might be wondering whether it's actually legal to have your furry co-pilot in the front seat while driving in Maine.
Since getting Moondog, I've learned that he would happily go just about anywhere with us. The only problem? He'd prefer to be sitting as close to me as possible, which isn't exactly ideal when I'm behind the wheel.
So, what does Maine law say?
Can your dog legally ride in the front seat?
There is no specific Maine law that outright prohibits dogs from riding in the front passenger seat. Maine does have laws about transporting dogs in the open beds of vehicles, but those rules don't specifically ban dogs from riding inside the car.
However, there's a catch.
Maine's distracted-driving law could come into play if your dog interferes with your ability to drive safely.
That means if your pup is climbing into your lap, blocking your view, or getting in the way of the steering wheel, you could potentially get into trouble.
And even if it's legal, that doesn't necessarily make it safe.
Think about what could happen if you suddenly had to slam on the brakes or were involved in an accident. An unrestrained dog can be seriously injured, and airbags can pose additional dangers to pets riding in the front seat.
Read More: Can I Legally Drive With My Dog on My Lap in Maine?
My advice? Let your dog enjoy the ride, but keep them safely secured with a crash-tested harness or in an appropriate carrier.
Because as much as we love bringing our dogs everywhere, we'd all prefer to arrive with our four-legged passengers safe and sound.

Since getting Moondog, I've learned that he would happily go just about anywhere with us. The only problem? He'd prefer to be sitting as close to me as possible, which isn't exactly ideal when I'm behind the wheel.
So, what does Maine law say?
Can your dog legally ride in the front seat?
There is no specific Maine law that outright prohibits dogs from riding in the front passenger seat. Maine does have laws about transporting dogs in the open beds of vehicles, but those rules don't specifically ban dogs from riding inside the car.
However, there's a catch.
Maine's distracted-driving law could come into play if your dog interferes with your ability to drive safely.
That means if your pup is climbing into your lap, blocking your view, or getting in the way of the steering wheel, you could potentially get into trouble.
And even if it's legal, that doesn't necessarily make it safe.
Think about what could happen if you suddenly had to slam on the brakes or were involved in an accident. An unrestrained dog can be seriously injured, and airbags can pose additional dangers to pets riding in the front seat.
Read More: Can I Legally Drive With My Dog on My Lap in Maine?
My advice? Let your dog enjoy the ride, but keep them safely secured with a crash-tested harness or in an appropriate carrier.
Because as much as we love bringing our dogs everywhere, we'd all prefer to arrive with our four-legged passengers safe and sound.

title: Fryeburg Solar fined $204K for damaging environment
text:
An out-of-state energy developer is facing a civil fine of more than $200,000 after regulators found that heavy runoff generated during the construction of a solar farm in Fryeburg polluted nearby streams and wetlands.
According to its proposed agreement with the state, New Jersey-based Fryeburg Solar jumped the gun in 2021 by starting work at the 45-acre site before it got final approvals and demonstrated that it could afford to decommission the facility if needed.
State inspectors found construction crews exposed more land at one time than allowed, failed to maintain erosion controls and winter construction standards and let sediment and soil runoff pollute wetlands, streams, properties and nearby Lovewell Pond.
The runoff problems began in 2021 and, despite repeated state inspections, violations persisted. The Maine Department of Environmental Protection cited Fryeburg Solar in October 2022 and the underlying landowners in August 2023.
As solar farms spread across rural Maine, the proposed settlement highlights the ecological risks of the burgeoning market. It is also a warning for rural landowners that they may be on the hook if their solar tenants breach environmental laws.
Following legislative changes encouraging community solar, dozens of 5-megawatt arrays were fast-tracked across rural Maine. The land clearing has often collided with the steep topography and long mud seasons, making erosion control a recurring friction point.
Under Maine law, soil discharged into state waters is deemed a pollutant, and inspectors tracked mud plumes flowing toward Lovewell Pond, which is a key recreational, fishing and boating hub in Oxford County.
In late 2022, DEP ordered Fryeburg Solar to implement a state-approved plan to remove the soil and replant wetland vegetation. The developer used a special vacuum system to extract sediment from the 1,717 linear feet of streams and just under an acre of impaired wetlands.
In December 2025, DEP declared the restoration a success and began drawing up a civil penalty of $204,499. Because the amount exceeds $50,000, DEP must report the fine to the IRS, which means Fryeburg Solar won’t be able to write the payment off as a business expense on its taxes.
If approved, the Fryeburg Solar deal will be the sixth consent agreement of 2026, records show.
Fines for the other five range from as low as $1,654 for a homeowner who used driveway gravel to maintain his China Lake boat launch to more than $284,000 for a Milford homeowner who built a driveway over a stream that provided high-value habitat for waterfowl and wading birds.
Procedurally, violators entering an consent agreement must send their penalty payment to DEP before a proposed deal can be considered by the Board of Environmental Protection, said agency spokesman Dave Madore. That won’t happen until after a public comment period ends Nov. 2.
A spokesman for Nautilus Solar, Fryeburg parent company, said a check was mailed on Sept. 26.
“We took those matters seriously and worked closely with the (state), environmental consultants and contractors to address the concerns and implement corrective actions,” the spokesman said in an emailed statement.
The state is not requiring the five individual landowners to pay a civil penalty, but being cited in the settlement can create disclosure requirements during property sales and complicate refinancing.

title: Obituary: Milton Ber
text:
PORTLAND – Milton Ber, 91, a lifelong resident of Portland’s Munjoy Hill neighborhood, passed away on Oct. 2, 2026, at The Cedars. He was the eldest son of Sara Rebecca (née Levi) and Isaac Ber.
Milton graduated from Portland High School in 1953, a time in his life he remembered with great fondness. Following graduation, he worked for Ballard Oil Company on Commercial Street in Portland. In May of 1956, he enlisted in the United States Army and was stationed in Japan. He served as Specialist 4th Class and was honorably discharged in May of 1959.
After completing his military service, Milton began a career in public service with the U.S. Treasury Department, serving as a Taxpayer Assistor with the Internal Revenue Service. He later worked for the Federal Government with the Social Security Administration. In May 1966, he received a letter of commendation recognizing his courtesy, tact, and polite firmness – qualities that reflected both his professionalism and his character.
Milton was deeply devoted to his mother, Becky, and shared a close and enduring bond with his brothers, Davey and Stanley. He found happiness in life’s simple pleasures, particularly his daily crossword puzzle and conversations with Stan. Selfless and kind, Milton never asked for much. His greatest wish was simply to be remembered as a good person.
Those who knew Milton will remember his wonderful sense of humor, quick wit, and giving nature. He was especially beloved by the staff at the Osher Inn, who came to consider him family, providing extraordinary care and compassion in his later years.
Milton is survived by his younger brother, Stanley, of Silver Spring, Md., and Bradenton, Fla. He was predeceased by his brother, David R. Ber, of Portland.
Milton lived a quiet and unassuming life, but his kindness and the warmth he brought to those around him will not be forgotten. He will be remembered just as he had hoped – as truly, a good person.
Arrangements are entrusted to Portland Jewish Funeral Home.

title: Eagles All-Pro offensive lineman Lane Johnson retires after 14 seasons
text:
Eagles All-Pro offensive lineman Lane Johnson retires after 14 seasons
Philadelphia Eagles All-Pro offensive lineman Lane Johnson has announced his retirement from the NFL after 14 seasons.
"I have given it my all for 14 years," Johnson said Tuesday in a statement, "season after season pushing my body to the max and tirelessly working my craft to not only live up to the legacy of the guys that came before me, but to set a new standard of success for the best franchise in all of sports."
Johnson had been a late scratch for last week's game against the Los Angeles Rams for personal reasons. He said Tuesday despite wanting to finish the season, his "personal and family priorities in my life have changed."
Johnson missed time in training camp for personal reasons before saying that this season would probably be his last.
The 36-year-old Johnson was a first-round pick in 2013 and was a first-team All-Pro in 2017 and 2022. He earned second-team honors in 2021, 2023 and 2024. Johnson has been a pillar at right tackle and won a pair of Super Bowls with the Eagles.
Johnson took a leave of absence during the 2021 season as he battled anxiety and depression and has since shared his story at mental health clinics in the area.
Johnson, a six-time Pro Bowl selection, said earlier this year his potential retirement came into focus last season after conversations with his family and an injury-filled season. He missed Philadelphia's final seven regular-season games and the wild-card playoff loss to the San Francisco 49ers.
"Right now, it is critical that I focus on my mental health," Johnson said. "I owe it to my teammates, coaches, the organization and the fans to have my head and heart 100 percent in the game. And right now my heart is telling me that it's time to say goodbye to football."

title: Fire breaks out at Wilton brewery, deemed accidental
text:
WILTON, Maine (WABI) - A fire broke out Monday afternoon at Ambition Brewing in downtown Wilton.
The fire was contained to one of the two buildings being used by the business, according to the State Fire Marshal’s Office, though the second building did sustain some smoke and water damage. No one was injured.
Officials say the fire was found by the property owner in an area where flooring was in the process of being removed.
Investigators say the underside of the building is partially open to the elements, allowing leaves and other debris to accumulate. They believe that the debris had grown dry and readily combustible, ultimately igniting during the renovation work.
The Fire Marshal’s Office has deemed the fire accidental.
Crews from Wilton, Jay, Farmington, Rumford, Temple and East Dixfield responded. The brewery thanked first responders and neighboring Main Street businesses for their support.

title: Video shows school bus crash that killed student on her first day of cheerleading practice
text:
WINTER HAVEN, Fla. (WESH) - A multi-vehicle crash involving a school bus in Winter Haven, Florida, Monday morning left two people dead.
The Polk County Sheriff’s Office said a white Chevy Malibu clipped the back of the school bus, causing it to swerve into another lane.
The bus struck an oncoming Jeep head-on.
WARNING: Some viewers may find this video disturbing.
“You see how quickly death occurs in a vehicle crash, a horrible, horrible, horrible vehicle crash. At that instant, two people lost their life, but there was a lot of emotional pain and injury that occurred in that crash. When this crash happened, it happened in the blink of an eye,” Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said. “So, it was absolutely impossible for that driver to get any kind of control over that bus because it immediately crashed into this Jeep.”
A person in the Jeep was killed. The identity of that person has not been released.
Student identified
A 10th grade student on the bus was also killed. Polk County Public Schools identified her as Adinaluz Guadalupe Prieto Oyola, a student at Winter Haven High School.
“An amazing young lady in every account. Teachers loved her, friends loved her,” Polk County Public Schools Superintendent Frederick Heid said.
Heid said Monday was to be Prieto Oyola’s first day of cheerleading practice.
“As you can imagine, it’s been a very difficult 24 hours,” Heid said.

title: Weather Discussion 10/6/26
Suspect in Portland killing dies days after police shot him
text:
The suspect in a Portland killing who was shot by police has died.
Brian Oliver, 41, of Portland succumbed to his wounds at Maine Medical Center on Thursday, according to Brad Nadeau, a spokesperson for the Portland Police Department.
Officers Joseph Lowe and David Moore went to a Colonial Road residence about 8:16 p.m. on Sept. 21 after getting a call about a disturbance there.
A tenant met the officers and escorted them inside, but then the tenant, who was ahead of Lowe and Moore, ran back toward them, screaming, Nadeau said at the time.
Inside Lowe and Moore found Oliver allegedly assaulting 69-year-old Mark Tschamler, according to Nadeau.
Oliver allegedly didn’t obey commands to drop his weapon, and the officers shot him.
Oliver was taken to Maine Medical Center, while Tschamler died at the scene.
Oliver was poised to face a murder charge, but no charge had been filed because of his injuries and condition.
Lowe and Moore were placed on administrative leave, as is standard procedure. The Maine attorney general’s office is investigating, as is standard procedure whenever law enforcement officers use deadly force in the state.
It was the second police shooting in the Forest City in less than a month. On Aug. 27, Portland police shot and killed 37-year-old Jacob Hastings at the Casco Bay Lines ferry terminal on Commercial Street after a string of armed carjackings.

title: In grief, good memories can be comforting
text:
I, like Professor Barbara Held in the case of her sister, don’t deny that my beloved husband died (“Grief is not a problem to be solved,” Opinion, Sept. 29).
We seem to agree there is no one to be angry with — neither one of us believes in God — but, unlike her, I am depressed even though I have accepted my husband’s death. If I am wrong, and my husband is under God’s watch, I appreciate people who are believers praying for him. Yet, I think heaven is not better than being alive and by my side.
Unlike Professor Held, my good memories are comforting. I think of his laughing at my silly jokes; of being able to see his handsome face; of his listening when I needed him to calm or reassure me; and of his undying affection.
I respect Professor Held’s feeling that good memories don’t help. I feel differently. But I was happy that her last memory of her sister was “… a gift from the gods.” I wish my last recollection of my husband was as consoling. He died in agony saying, “Just kill me.”
But as Professor Held states, with a quote from Dr. Colin Murray Parkes: “The pain of grief is just as much a part of life as the joy of love.” I will endure the loneliness because of the loving memories of 51 years of marriage, and I will try to ignore the disturbing remembrances that are painful.
B. Ann Levine, Ph.D.
Kennebunk

title: Trump administration to assign government lawyers to migrant kids’ cases, worrying advocates
text:
MIAMI (AP) — The Trump administration is creating a team of attorneys to represent children who traveled alone to the United States in immigration proceedings, which critics say would deprive them of having lawyers who aren’t employed by the government and could put them at greater risk of deportation.
The U.S. Health and Human Services Department lawyers will “provide direct legal advice and counsel” to unaccompanied migrant children, according to an announcement in the Federal Register signed by Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The decision, announced last week without fanfare, offered no details beyond that broad mandate.
Health and Human Services said in a statement that its Unaccompanied Alien Children Legal Representation Division will work under its general counsel’s direction toward “safely reuniting these children with their families and ensuring they have the legal support they need.”
“This new division will give the Department an additional mechanism to provide these children direct legal support while dedicated public servants work around the clock to safely reunify them with their families,” the department told The Associated Press in a brief statement. It didn’t answer additional questions, including whether it would continue to contract with nongovernmental groups for legal representation or when its new legal division is expected to be fully operational.
The move appears to lay the groundwork for one of the biggest changes since guaranteed free legal representation for unaccompanied migrant children was introduced in 2008. It comes after the administration cut ties with the Acacia Center for Justice, a nongovernmental organization that managed 24,000 cases and held a contract to provide representation through a vast network of legal service providers.
The change means migrant children will not have an independent representative to advocate for them who doesn’t have a conflict of interest, said Shaina Aber, the Acacia Center’s executive director.
“Placing children’s legal representation and services inside of the same agency that holds children in federal immigration custody is an unprecedented step that does not meet basic standards of independence of counsel,” Aber said. It “will only give HHS new opportunities to forsake children’s rights and well-being.”
Wendy Young, president of Kids in Need of Defense, a nonprofit that provides free legal representation and social services to unaccompanied children, called the creation of the new in-house HHS legal team “part of a pattern of attacks that this administration has engaged in, in terms of undermining zealous representation of unaccompanied children in their immigration proceedings.”
The new division will work independently from other government agencies that deal with the minors, including the HHS Office of Refugee Resettlement, which is responsible for the custody and care of the children who arrive in the U.S. without a parent or legal guardian.
There is some precedent for government-paid attorneys defending clients against government prosecutors in civilian and military courts, but as criminal defense lawyers and not in immigration court.
But Young noted that the child’s lawyer, the judge, and government attorneys seeking deportation will all be federal employees. Judges are appointed by the Justice Department and prosecutors work at the Department of Homeland Security.
“A government attorney who’s employed by the government most likely would be coached and encouraged to take the position of encouraging the child to agree to voluntary departure and to leave the United States rather than to present a full representation of the facts of their case,” Young said.
Amid the uncertainty, children have been going to their court hearings without legal representation lately, according to advocates.
Americans for Immigrant Justice, another nonprofit that provides free legal representation to unaccompanied immigrant children, said it has been challenging to secure lawyers for the minors since the government suspended funding to legal aid organizations on July 31 through Acacia.
Sui Chung, the group’s executive director, said the need for legal representation exceeds the available resources.
“To deny legal counsel to the most vulnerable among us — children who have already fled trauma — is a fundamental breakdown of the fairness our Constitution promises,” Chung said. “Children deserve our strongest protection.”
The government recently awarded a contract to another organization, Our Rescue, with a potential value of up to $244 million. The transition to Our Rescue, which has been challenged by Acacia, has led to short-term arrangements, including a temporary contract with the U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants.

title: Maine football relieves offensive coordinator and quarterbacks coach Mikahael Waters of his duties
text:
ORONO, Maine (WABI) - The Maine football team will look to end its five-game losing streak after its bye week with a new offensive coordinator.
Head coach Jordan Stevens spoke about firing offensive coordinator and quarterbacks coach Mikahael Waters.
“Sean Green will be our interim offensive coordinator right now and coach our quarterbacks. Cooper Heisey will help with coaching the running backs. Those decisions that are really hard. They affect everyone involved. They affect our team, our players, our coaches, families, so there’s a lot that goes into that. It’s just trying to do what’s best for the football team and objectively put us in a better position to win,” said Stevens.
Stevens spoke about the mid-season timing of the move, Green stepping into the role, and how the Maine coaches need to help the players reach a high level.
“We have a very talented roster. We’ve done a lot of good things this season, but we’ve got to be more consistent, and we’ve got to be able to score points. (Green’s) an experienced coach, and it’s not just one person, I would say too. I’ve got to do a better job, and it starts with me. We have to coach better. We have to put our players in a better position to make plays. That’s from a confidence standpoint. That’s from an execution standpoint. When we talk execution, that’s not on the players. That’s on us to make sure they’re in a position to execute. I’m not pointing the finger, I’m pointing the thumb. We’ve got to make sure our guys can execute at a high level,” said Stevens.
Stevens explained the standard that’s in place.
“This is a production business. We’ve got to win football games. We need to score more points so we can win football games. Our team, I believe that we are a team that can win football games. So, I’m not sitting here just throwing in the towel on the season. I’m not willing to do that. Winning is the expectation, and not winning is never okay. I refuse to hold us in a standard that is anything less than that,” said Stevens.
Stevens had a simple response when asked if he thought anyone else, including himself, was on the hot seat.
“No. No,” said Stevens.
Maine is on a bye week before hosting Bryant on Sat. Oct. 17 at 1 p.m.

text:
WATERBORO, Maine (WABI) - A man was taken into custody Monday after officials say he ran off after crashing into multiple vehicles and a home in Waterboro.
The York County Sheriff’s Office says Zackery Lacourse, 21, of Shapleigh is facing charges of OUI, failure to stop, and leaving the scene of a crash.

title: Archaeologists find 7 coffins with human remains at governor’s residence
text:
BISMARCK, N.D. (KFYR/Gray News) - Officials in North Dakota say several coffins with human remains have been found at the governor’s residence.
State officials said archaeologists located seven coffins holding human remains, plus another wooden box, at the North Dakota Governor’s Residence after a monthslong investigation.
According to OMB Facilities Management Director Brandon Solberg, crews inspected more than 80 spots flagged during the investigation before concluding fieldwork on Sept. 14.
Investigators said the discovery dates back to May 19, when contractors excavating at the southwest corner of the property first uncovered remains, coffin hardware and fragments.
Construction work was paused, and the State Historical Society conducted a radar scan, followed by a dig that started Sept. 1.
Archaeologists said they would review and catalog all remains and recovered items in a process expected to run into early next year. They added the team has also contracted a local funeral home, with Crisis Care Chaplaincy volunteering to help ensure that the relocation was handled with care and reverence.
Reburial is expected in spring 2027 at an area cemetery.
The governor’s residence property was Bismarck’s first community cemetery from 1873 to 1877. Most graves were thought to have been moved to St. Mary’s and Fairview cemeteries in the 1880s, but past projects, including 13 burials found in 1903 and five more in 1959, have shown that some have been left behind.

title: Deaf cheer team competes in its first hearing competition
text:
FARIBAULT, Minn. (InvestigateTV) – Minnesota’s only all-deaf high school cheerleading team became the first in its school history to perform in a hearing competition.
In January, the Minnesota State Academy for the Deaf (MSAD) Trojan cheer team competed in their first cheerleading competition of 2026.
MSAD cheerleaders have been tumbling out of Faribault since the 1940’s and have opened the door for 18-year-old Mya Palmer and 16-year-old Sophia Nelson to try something new.
“I like doing the stunts. I’m a base, and I love getting ready and lifting our cheerleader,” Palmer said.
“Cheerleading is kind of random for me, but I like it so far,” Nelson added.
The team is often cheering in the National Deaf Cheer Competition or the Great Plains Schools for the Deaf competitions.
Going into their first hearing competition, coach Marika Ulrich said the Trojans will sign throughout cheer routines.
“We actually rely heavily on visual cues and the drum, which cues us in. It tells us the rhythm of the cheer,” Ulrich said. “We’ll move to the rhythm, like clap our hands, do the jive, that kind of thing, and do our school mascot, the Trojan sign.”
Coach Ulrich is deaf and Coach Miller has a deaf daughter but is hearing. They say having both leading the squad is an advantage.
“It really helps having two coaches because she’s able to instruct, so they’re understanding what I’m saying and then they’re also able to see me do the cheers, so then they can see the visual,” Miller explained.
The Trojans have no doubt they can get the job done together.
The team was the only group registered in their division, therefore they did not place in the competition.
In February 2026, the team earned third place in the Greater Plains Schools for the Deaf cheerleading competition.

title: Tennessee Republicans consider more execution options after Christa Pike lethal injection fails
text:
(AP) - Some of Tennessee’s top Republicans said Monday they want to explore alternative ways of executing condemned prisoners after the failed execution of Christa Pike, which relied on a large dose of pentobarbital.
U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the state’s Republican candidate for governor, said Pike’s unsuccessful execution last week “should not be grounds to halt carrying out the death penalty.” Rather, she said, Tennessee needs to reevaluate the way it does executions.
“If it’s lethal injection, if it is electric chair, what we do know is we have to find a way to do this — and do it successfully,” Blackburn told The Associated Press.
Top legislative leaders have already spoken with Blackburn about potential changes to state execution laws during their 2027 session.
“We want to broaden it, include more methods,” House Speaker Cameron Sexton said. ”What those are as of today, I’m not sure. But I don’t think there’s any method that’s off the table at this point.”
Most U.S. states that allow executions use lethal injection as their primary means, though South Carolina sets its default as electrocution and Idaho the firing squad, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. Some states give prisoners a choice of execution methods. Death by electricity or gas is authorized in nine states, including five that specify nitrogen gas, the center said. Five states authorize a firing squad.
Florida, which leads the nation in executions this year, uses a three-drug lethal injection that includes a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart.
Tennessee’s execution procedures have been in the national spotlight since Wednesday, when prison officials gave Pike two doses of a barbiturate that were supposed to be lethal but didn’t ultimately kill her. Pike has remained hospitalized under guard, left unconscious and on a ventilator with blisters and burns on her arms from the drug, her lawyers have said.
Pike, now 50, was sentenced to death for the 1995 torture and slaying of a classmate, Colleen Slemmer. Pike was age 18 at the time and became one of the youngest women sent to death row.
Republican Gov. Bill Lee, whose term ends in January, halted the one remaining execution scheduled for this year and ordered an independent investigation into the state’s capital punishment system after Pike’s failed execution. He said Saturday the commissioner of the Department of Correction will step down.
Blackburn said comprehensive change is needed — “it is personnel, processes, procedures, protocols that are all going to need to be addressed.”
Tennessee law already allows electrocution if the department is unable to carry out a lethal injection despite reasonable efforts to do so. State law also gives people who committed crimes before 1999 the option of choosing electrocution.
Between 2018 and 2020, five Tennessee prisoners chose electrocution. That could remain an option for about two dozen of the 40 people on death row.
Sexton said the legislature could consider amending the law to give the state a choice of execution methods.
House Majority Leader William Lamberth said he is open to making electrocution the state’s primary means of execution. But no matter the method, Lamberth said he doesn’t want any changes to take too long to implement.
“We want these sentences to be carried out effectively, efficiently and humanely,” he said, adding: ”Whatever we do, I do not want it to delay justice for these victims’ families.”
Republican state Sen. Todd Gardenhire, chair of the Senate Judiciary Committee, said he expects a deliberate review of what went wrong and what can be done to improve the execution process.
“I think the electric chair is the quickest and simplest way to do it,” he said.

title: French riot police fire tear gas as more than 250,000 rally nationwide for school funding
text:
PARIS (AP) — Police fired tear gas to control crowds in Paris and elsewhere in France on Tuesday as more than a quarter of a million people rallied nationwide to support high school students demanding more education funding, according to government figures. The protests increased pressure on the administration of outgoing President Emmanuel Macron.
As pupils blockaded high schools, large crowds waving flags and placards gathered in Marseille, Strasbourg and other cities. The demonstrations showed how protests that began at a high school in the Paris region in mid-September have grown into a nationwide movement — the latest of many that have marked Macron’s nearly decade-long tenure.
“We need to listen to them,” said Léa Monimart, an adult demonstrator in the northern city of Lille. “They are 17 years old; they are not completely clueless, and they know what they are talking about. It’s important to show that there are adults who support them.”
The Interior Ministry estimated that 266,000 people took part in demonstrations across the country on Tuesday, including 56,000 in Paris, where small groups of protesters clashed with riot officers at a city square at the end of a largely peaceful march.
Nearly 500 people were detained Tuesday, the ministry said. The widespread use of arrests, tear gas and riot-control weapons against teenagers is fueling defiance and angering some parents and teachers. Some student groups called for new protests Thursday.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the police response had been proportionate in “almost all cases” and that the protests had at times turned into riots, requiring police intervention.
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the government and school leaders must listen to students’ concerns and find solutions.
Questioned in parliament on Tuesday about the protest movement, Lecornu denounced “ultra violence” threatening schools. Responding to criticism of police tactics, he pledged that any “accidents” would be investigated and described allegations that the police are racist as a “lie.”
Class boycotts with police making thousands of arrests
More than two weeks of class boycotts and school blockades, and policing that has led to more than 6,500 arrests, mostly of minors, have become a flashpoint in the early days of the presidential election campaign.
Felix Barney, a university student, described the police response as disproportionate, saying it doesn’t make “any sense to hit minors.”
“Riot police, batons, rubber bullets, tear gas,” said Aurélien Le Coq, a lawmaker with the far-left France Unbowed party. Its presidential candidate is strongly backing the protests.
The violence is “absolutely unbearable,” Le Coq said.
Nuñez defended police tactics despite a growing number of severe injuries blamed on officers’ riot-control weapons. In the latest case, a 15-year-old boy lost a hand Monday in an incident involving a police stun grenade. He said 715 officers had been injured.
The teenage protesters have struck a chord amid widespread discontent in France. Frustrations extend beyond immediate difficulties, such as fuel prices that have soared because of the Iran war, to broader concerns about constraints on public spending, rising poverty and wealth inequality under Macron, who can’t run for a third consecutive term.
Against that backdrop, pupils’ complaints that education funding shortfalls are endangering their futures have found a sympathetic audience.
“You say ‘young people are the future,’ so listen to them,” read a handwritten placard attached to a metal barrier outside a Paris school.
Ministry offers online portal for complaints
At the Hélène Boucher lycée, or high school, in Paris’ 20th district, protesters tipped over trash cans and bicycles onto their sides to create a makeshift barricade.
Like hundreds of others around the country, the school was closed. Authorities began shutting schools last week to take some steam out of the demonstrations after widespread damage to schools and mounting injuries among staff, students and police. Classes were totally or partially suspended on Tuesday at 891 schools, according to the Education Ministry.
Facing accusations that it was ignoring protesters, the ministry launched an online portal inviting high school students to anonymously describe the difficulties they face at school and the changes they want to see.
Student protests have drawn attention to rundown classrooms
At Hélène Boucher, parents and other adults positioned themselves on Tuesday between protesters and police keeping watch.
“They are our children. Teachers, parents, federations, we all share the same goal: the protection of children’s rights, and it is a legitimate right to demonstrate and to make demands,” said Emilia Sichili Suriam, who is a member of an association of parents.
Demonstrators have voiced a range of grievances, often centering on a lack of resources and opportunities for students in disadvantaged schools, despite the promise of France’s national motto: “Liberty, Equality, Fraternity.”
Students have drawn attention to rundown classrooms that lack basics such as desks and chairs, become sweltering in summer without air conditioning and, in some cases, are infested with rats. Other common complaints include staff shortages and exhausting workloads. French high school students’ compulsory classroom hours are among the highest in Europe.
Suzanne Nijdam, president of the federation of student associations, vowed that demonstrations would continue until authorities address the complaints.
“So, we really need to act now, and it’s in the government’s hands, to see these demands through to the end,” she said. “It’s a matter of political priority, a matter of prioritizing the youth and the future of our country.”
Neighboring Belgium is also seeing student protests. More than 30 were arrested Tuesday and several police injured in the eastern city of Liege, and smaller protests were held in Brussels and other cities.
___
John Leicester, Mark Carlson and Sylvain Plazy in Lille, Jeffrey Schaeffer, Masha Macpherson and Catherine Gaschka in Paris, Mike Corder in The Hague, Netherlands, and Lorne Cook in Brussels contributed to this report.

title: Whatever method you use, hunting for grouse something to be thankful for
text:
There’s a running quip among Maine hunters regarding the difference between grouse and partridge. When you approach a gallinaceous game bird , if it flies away, it’s a grouse. If it walks away, it’s a partridge.
In truth, our most abundant upland bird is a grouse, a ruffed grouse to be more precise. That’s an important distinction, because in higher elevations and northern areas of Maine, you might also come across a spruce grouse, which is not legal game. The only true partridges in the U.S. have been imported or raised in captivity for hunting preserves.
Still, that tongue-in-cheek distinction has a lot to do with how folks go about hunting the species. In southern and cental Maine, where people are more abundant, the birds are less abundant and considered “wilder” by bird hunters. By that, they mean the birds are more inclined to flush, often long before offering a shot opportunity. Most hunters in these areas employ one of two methods. One is to simply stroll along in hopes of flushing a bird within range. The other is to enlist the aid of dogs.
Dog hunters are a different breed, no pun intended. Regardless of the game, be it birds, bear or hare, the hunt is more about the dogs than the quarry. Watching a well-trained pointer or setter work a scent is a thing of beauty. If they can hold a bird in position until hunters arrive, it’s a win, whether the shot is a hit or a miss.
In the north woods, grouse (or partridge) could be considered a pedestrian bird. One reason is because you’ll often find them walking along the side of the road, or in the middle of it. Another is because their propensity to do so might make them seem a bit dull and uninspiring. Either way, you can’t help but to stop for them.
Some folks are concerned that this method of hunting “easy targets” could be detrimental to grouse populations. One only need look at satellite imagery of the landscape to see the fallacy in that argument. Roads are few and far between, and for every bird you encounter along them, there are just as many where the roads and most hunters don’t go.
Someone once asked me what grouse tastes like. I said, “like turkey, with a hint of cranberry sauce.” Regardless of how they’re harvested, whether randomly, over a stoic setter or on the roadside, we should give thanks for the opportunity.
Bob Humphrey is a freelance writer and Registered Maine Guide who lives in Pownal. He can be reached at: [email protected]

title: What Maine’s next generation of farms needs to succeed
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Ryan Douglas is a Maine-based strategic advisor to cultivation businesses and the
author of “Presence is a Strategy: The Competitive Advantage You Can’t Automate.”
Last week, a news report announced that the Lisbon greenhouse facility operated
by Springworks Farm is headed to auction.
Roughly 40 miles away, Vertical Harvest, a high-tech producer of indoor leafy greens in Westbrook, has faced significant delays and has yet to reach the commercial scale it originally envisioned.
If Maine is going to support innovative agriculture with public resources, it should ask one question before a project moves forward: Is the operation ready to run?
Early in my career, I worked for an ornamental flower grower in Mississippi who operated on five acres of patched-up, run-down greenhouses. The facility wasn’t impressive, but the crops were consistently exceptional.
Years later, I consulted for a publicly traded cannabis company in Colombia. It had sophisticated facilities, a ton of cash and a board with impressive credentials. But when I stepped into the company’s greenhouse, I was speechless. Every plant was dead.
How could an operation with every advantage fail at the most basic task, while the unimpressive greenhouse produced exceptional crops?
Those two experiences reinforced a lesson I’ve learned throughout my career: operational readiness is fundamental to success.
As a lifelong Mainer, I’ve spent three decades in commercial horticulture throughout the U.S., Canada and South America. Most of my career has been under glass as a grower, manager and consultant, and I previously served as general manager for Backyard Farms, the 40-acre tomato greenhouse range in Madison.
Operational readiness is having the people, systems and discipline to run a facility reliably from day one. In this business, margins are made or lost in the consistent execution of mundane but essential work.
Skipping a crop walk on Friday could mean missing signs that insect pressure has increased due to warmer weather. By Monday, that small oversight can mean unsaleable product, additional labor and lost revenue.
In a small greenhouse, that mistake may have a limited impact. But at a commercial scale, small mistakes compounded over time can quickly turn into major losses. No amount of money can replace the need for operational experience, seasoned judgment and common sense. Operational readiness must be built into a cultivation project from day one, not treated as a problem to solve once construction is complete.
Springworks Farm received meaningful public support, including a $300,000 Maine Technology Institute award for greenhouse expansion. The Finance Authority of Maine insured a $5 million loan and a $1 million working-capital loan in partnership with Farm
Credit East.
Vertical Harvest received nearly $49 million in USDA-guaranteed loans, approximately $8 million in financing facilitated through Efficiency Maine and $1 million in direct loans from the Finance Authority of Maine.
When public resources support private projects at this scale, Mainers have a legitimate stake in whether those projects are built and managed to succeed. Operational readiness should be scrutinized as closely as technology, job creation, capital investment and economic impact.
I am 100% in favor of continued investment in Maine’s ability to feed itself. Considering our short outdoor growing season, innovative cultivation projects like these will be a key part of the solution. But these latest developments are a reminder that impressive facilities alone aren’t enough.
Public funding shouldn’t just help ambitious agricultural ventures get off the ground. It should increase their chances of actually sticking around.

title: Russia says nearly 900 Ukrainian drones downed and Moscow region fuel depot reportedly burns
text:
Russia says nearly 900 Ukrainian drones downed and Moscow region fuel depot reportedly burns
Russian air defenses intercepted nearly 900 Ukrainian drones overnight over multiple regions of the country, as well as the occupied Crimean Peninsula and the Sea of Azov, the Defense Ministry in Moscow said Tuesday.
Related video: Could the executive order signed by President Trump Monday lower diesel costs ahead of midterms?
Unconfirmed media reports said a major fuel depot in the Moscow region was on fire after the attack that killed two people.
Ukraine’s domestically developed long-range drones and, increasingly, missiles have allowed Kyiv to hit Russian soil during the more than 4 ½ years since Moscow’s forces launched a full-scale invasion.
The bigger Russian military’s air superiority during the war has made aerial attacks on civilian areas of Ukraine routine.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 650 drones flew toward the Moscow region between Monday evening and Tuesday morning. Most were destroyed far away, and 105 were downed as they approached the city, he said.
Sobyanin later reported 68 more drones targeting Moscow were downed during daylight on Tuesday morning.
Ukraine has regularly targeted Russian oil refineries and storage depots, claiming last weekend that it had disabled 51% of Russia’s oil refining capacity. The claim could not be independently verified. Russian President Vladimir Putin said last week that the attacks had cost Russia roughly 1% of its gross domestic product.
Russia has traditionally been the world’s third-largest producer of refined fuel products from crude, after the U.S. and China. The Kremlin has banned diesel exports due to the Ukrainian strikes, pushing global prices higher. That prompted U.S. President Donald Trump last month to urge Ukraine to stop hitting Russia’s refineries.
After several days of targeting bridges in the Ukrainian capital Kyiv, as part of a campaign to make civilian life difficult, Russia attacked one of the bridges over the Dnipro River in the southern city of Zaporizhzhia, according to Mykhailo Semikin, the regional military administration chief.
Traffic across the bridge was temporarily suspended as a result of the attack, he said.
A nighttime Russian attack on a Zaporizhzhia residential building wounded five people and a daylight strike on a warehouse in the city caused a large fire, regional head Mikhail Semikin said.
Russian forces are also trying to choke shipping in Ukrainian ports in the Black Sea, denying Kyiv vital grain export revenue.
The Russian Defense Ministry said its forces overnight struck targets in Ukraine's southern Odesa region on the Black Sea coast with drones. An ammunition depot was hit, as were a bulk carrier in the Chornomorsk port carrying dual-use goods and port infrastructure in Izmail, the ministry said.

title: Historic connection to Boston Tea Party recognized in Lamoine
text:
LAMOINE, Maine (WABI) - As part of America’s 250th anniversary, historians are making five stops across Maine this week to recognize people from the past who have direct connections to the Boston Tea Party. One commemorative marker ceremony Tuesday afternoon was held at Forest Hill Cemetery in Lamoine.
“We are recognizing Elkanah Young as an eyewitness to history, someone connected to the Boston Tea Party of December 16, 1773,” said Evan O’Brien, Creative Manager at the Boston Tea Party Ships and Museum.
Elkanah Young was born in 1745 in Eastham, Massachusetts. When Young died in 1832, he was buried at the Lamoine cemetery.
“We know that he was intimately involved in Boston at the time. He had moved to Maine, and we’re not entirely certain, though, why in 1773 he returned. More than likely, he would have been on board one of his ships, and he was in port in Boston at the time and got caught up in the fervor,” said O’Brien.
Attending the ceremony were many historians, as well as descendants of Young. One descendant was Keith Young of Massachusetts, who says he had researched Elkanah for many years.
“I didn’t realize growing up that the rest of my ancestors are all here in this little, tiny cemetery,” said Young, “I am just very, very pleased that the Boston Tea Party and Ships Museum has made an official recognition on him.”
Since 2018, The Boston Tea Party Ships and Museum, in partnership with Revolution 250, have traveled around the U.S. to recognize those with connections to the Boston Tea Party, bringing attention to stories that have been passed down for generations
“We want to talk about the Boston Tea Party. We’re going to talk about Hancock and Adams, both Samuel and John. We’re going to talk about William Mullineaux, all the names that people should know, but we’re also here to talk about people like Elkanah Young, who is not known to many except his family,” said Jonathan Lane, Executive Director of Revolution 250.
“This whole idea of story and sharing family story over the years is critical to our American experience and our American history,” said O’Brien.
“We ought to be proud of our heritage,” said Young, ”History is alive, and you are part of it.”
On Monday, Lemuel Trescott was honored with a plaque in Lubec. Wednesday, a ceremony on Islesboro will honor Joseph Boardman. Two other ceremonies will take place this week in Bowdoin and Portland.

title: Disney is raising some ticket prices at its theme parks again
text:
Disney is raising some ticket prices at its theme parks again
Disney is raising prices on some theme park tickets and services in California and Florida, CNN reports.
At Walt Disney World in Florida, some multi-day ticket options and skip-the-line services are becoming more expensive. Annual pass prices are also increasing.
The highest-priced one-day ticket at Disney World will rise to $229, plus tax, during part of 2027, according to CNN.
At Disneyland in California, several mid-tier ticket options and add-ons will cost more. The park’s least expensive one-day ticket will remain $104, a price in place since 2019.
Annual passes, parking and multi-day tickets at Disneyland will also remain at their current prices.
Disney said the pricing strategy allows the company to increase prices on premium options while keeping lower-cost entry points available to visitors.

title: Live updates: Susan Collins and Troy Jackson face off in 1st Senate debate
text:
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic opponent Troy Jackson meet at 7 p.m. Tuesday for their first debate of Maine’s U.S. Senate race, hosted by CBS News 13 at its Portland studio.
Jackson, a former Maine Senate president from Allagash, is the slightest of favorites. Decision Desk HQ, the BDN’s election results partner, gives him a 53% chance of winning. A Marist poll released this week had him up 51-47, while a CBS News/YouGov poll had the race tied.

Maine is central to control of the Senate as the only top battleground won by Kamala Harris in 2024. title: Day two of testimony held in 1984 Calais murder trial
text:
MACHIAS, Maine (WABI) - Jurors heard testimony Tuesday from the medical examiner, DNA analysts, family members and a friend of Linda Maxwell in the murder trial of Raymond Brown.
Brown, 67, of Bangor, is accused of killing Maxwell, 18, of Calais, in 1984.
Body found in river
Prosecutors say Maxwell’s nude body was found at the Robbinston boat landing, floating face-up in the St. Croix River. Investigators say no clothing was ever found.
Jurors heard from first responders, including former Calais patrolman William Cody, and from Maxwell’s brother, Franklin, who said she couldn’t swim and was dating another man at the time.
Boyfriend testifies
That man, Ronald Todd Miller, took the stand and described their relationship as a good relationship.
Miller said he knew Brown through another friend but didn’t have a close relationship with him.
Miller testified about their last outing at Round Pond, saying he, Maxwell and their friends discussed who would drive.
He said Maxwell drove when they left, but Brown took over driving once they got back to Calais. Miller said he went home once they got back.
Defense questions prior statements
The defense questioned Miller about previous statements on the night they were out.
The defense asked Miller to confirm if he was upset with Maxwell for drinking too much and questioned why he let her get behind the wheel anyway.
Miller answered that he didn’t stop her.
The defense also questioned Miller about a statement to police saying he was jealous because Maxwell was speaking to others, but Miller said he did not recall saying that.
When the state questioned Miller again, he clarified he was not jealous but was bothered by the situation at the end of the night, leading him to hop off Brown’s truck and go home.
Miller said he left town in September 1984 after Maxwell’s death.
Testimony in the trial will continue Wednesday.

title: There’s a Maine Lake That Looks Exactly Like a Lobster Claw
text:
Maine Has a Hidden Lake That’s Literally Shaped Like a Lobster Claw
I think I've found the most remote hike in Maine you'll experience this fall.
Sitting pretty all hidden way out in the northern Maine woods is a place called Lobster Lake and yes, it is as remote as it sounds.
We’re talking about a destination where getting there is part of the adventure.
The lake sits east of Moosehead Lake and south of the Golden Road, more than 100 miles from the coast.
And there’s a pretty funny reason it’s called Lobster Lake, just look at it on Google Maps and you’ll see the lake is literally shaped like a lobster claw and only reachable by canoe! Because apparently Maine names its lakes based on what they actually look like.
But the real reason to put this one on your radar is Lobster Mountain.
The hike to the mountain’s outlook is only about 1.5 miles from Lobster Lake, making it a manageable hike once you’ve made the journey into this remote corner of the state.
Carter Coy shared these gorgeous photos from his visit to Lobster Lake on Facebook.
At the top, you’re rewarded with sweeping views of the surrounding mountains and lakes, including Moosehead Lake and Big Moose Mountain.
And on a clear day? You can even see Katahdin!
The catch is that this isn’t exactly a “park the SUV and start walking” kind of hike. Getting to Lobster Lake involves paddling in, which means this is much more of an adventure than a quick afternoon trail.
Honestly, that might be the best part.
No crowded parking lot. No traffic noise. Just a canoe, a remote Maine lake, a mountain trail and one heck of a view.
And now I really want to go.
