title: Susan Collins camp releases new info disputing alleged pay-to-play scheme
text:
Sen. Susan Collins’ reelection campaign released new information on Tuesday that it says absolves the Republican incumbent of the recent pay-to-play allegations currently being seized on by Democrats.
Campaign Manager Steve Abbott took aim at a story published by ProPublica on Sept. 22 that, among other things, reported that former Navatek CEO Martin Kao told the FBI that Collins required political contributions before meeting with donors.
Abbott said the outlet’s reporting failed to acknowledge Collins’ full history with Navatek, the company at the center of the scandal. Collins started working with Navatek only after a local university requested defense funding, Abbott contended.
On a video call with reporters, Abbott showed a 2017 letter from the University of Maine seeking $5 million in federal funding for a project in partnership with Navatek “to launch a collaborative research program to address the U.S. Navy’s pressing need to enhance the mobility of future marine vehicles.” Collins ultimately secured the funding in the fiscal year 2018 budget.
Abbott also showed a photo of Collins meeting with Kao in her office with other officials in February of 2018. Kao later told federal investigators that Collins refused to meet that year with him unless he made a donation to her 2020 reelection campaign.
But Kao did not make his first donation to Collins until June 27, 2018, federal records show.
“ProPublica has the theory that Martin Kao, based on Martin Kao’s word, had to make a donation before he could get in to see Susan Collins,” Abbott said. “As you can see from that picture, it’s not true.”
The photo was taken by a Senate photographer on Feb. 15, 2018, embedded data showed, according to a screenshot released by the campaign.
The campaign’s media call was another example of how Collins is aggressively responding to allegations that could undercut her work as the top senate appropriator. The money she brings home to Maine is a key theme of her reelection campaign against Democrat Troy Jackson, a former logger and state Senate president.
It also comes ahead of Collins’ first televised debate against Troy Jackson, who is likely to raise the issue of ProPublica’s reporting. Jackson has maintained a narrow lead in the Maine’s closely watched Senate race, according to most polls.
Kao pleaded guilty to charges involving money laundering and bank fraud in 2022, and is currently in federal prison. He had been cooperating with federal investigators in an effort to get his sentence reduced.
ProPublica reported that the FBI was gearing up for a widespread corruption probe of Collins and other members of Congress based on statements Kao made to investigators between 2022 and 2024. The outlet reported that the investigation was abandoned when Trump returned to office in 2025 and disbanded anti-corruption units.
After her campaign’s initial response to the ProPublica story, the outlet fact-checked statements made by Collins’ team, finding some of their claims to be false. For example, a Collins spokesperson claimed that the outlet “took the word of” Kao in their story, “someone who pled guilty to five counts of money laundering.”
ProPublica reporters contend that they independently corroborated much of his account, reviewing “a trove of evidence gathered by the FBI,” examining “thousands of pages of legal records” and interviewing “dozens of people familiar with Navatek, its Washington operations and the FBI inquiry.”
The news site reported that Kao gave $150,000 to a super PAC supporting Collins, who in turn promised to steer $32 million in additional contracts to Navatek. Kao made the illegal donation through a shell company because federal contractors are prohibited from donating to political campaigns.
But Abbott said neither Collins, nor anybody else on her staff, would have promised a specific level of funding.
“We would never say that because there is no way we would know that we could get that done,” Abbott said. “No chance that that is true. Absolutely false.”
State and national Democrats are now using the ProPublica report to push an anti-corruption message in the final month of the election.
“The facts are clear — as recently as 2025, the FBI was circling Susan Collins for her involvement in a pay-to-play scheme until the Trump administration killed the unit that was looking into her,” Misha Linnehan, spokesperson for the Maine Democratic Party, said in a statement. “No amount of bluster from Collins’ team can distract Mainers from the fact that she sold them out for campaign cash.”
WinSenate, a super PAC aligned with Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer of New York, launched a $3.4 million ad campaign last week in Maine highlighting the ProPublica story.

title: Winthrop, Monmouth move toward merging police forces
text:
The towns of Monmouth and Winthrop are moving forward with consolidating their police departments after the Winthrop Town Council supported the move at a meeting Sept. 21.
In June, Monmouth residents voted in favor of a proposal to merge the departments.
The consolidation process began in the summer of 2024, according to Paul Ferland, police chief for both communities since 2023. Ferland was Monmouth chief and became the chief for both towns after former Winthrop Chief Ryan Frost retired in 2023.
At the Sept. 21 meeting, Ferland made a presentation on the proposed merger to the Winthrop Council saying it would make official an already well-established working relationship between the two forces, attract better-trained officers to the force, enhance the chance for promotions, and allow for better coverage of shifts for sick, vacation and training time.
Ferland wasn’t able to answer the question of whether consolidation would save the towns money.
“When we make an investment, I’m looking at if it’s still going to be viable 10 years down the road, or are we going to have to replace it five or 10 years down the road?” Ferland told councilors. “Let’s spend a little bit more money up front right now for the longevity of that service down the road.”
Ferland’s plan suggests a “transitional approach” that would merge the two police departments over a period of time.
In the first year of consolidation, which would start at the beginning of the 2028 fiscal year on July 1, 2027, each community would continue to fund its own department at the necessary rate. Monmouth would give Winthrop that amount to administer both departments.
Over the next 12 to 24 months, the towns would analyze a variety of department areas, including staffing, calls for service and need for coverage. The data would form the basis of a merged budget the following year, Ferland said.
With Winthrop’s approval last month, the town will now name three residents to the Joint Police Commission. Monmouth has already appointed two members and an alternate.
The commission will assist in the consolidation, including creating the legal framework for the merger, establishing the interlocal agreement, ironing out the budgeting details, and helping develop the new department’s policies.
There is no set timeline for the merger. The two councils must approve the specifics of the consolidation before it is official.

title: Firefighter catches on fire while responding to burning home
text:
LONDONDERRY, N.H. (WMUR) - A firefighter is recovering after he was engulfed in flames while responding to a house fire.
The incident was captured on video.
The video shows fire bursting from a home as Lt. Mike England rushes out. England thought someone was still inside and was trying to use his thermal imaging camera when a flashover broke out, according to Londonderry Fire Department Battalion Chief Bruce Hallowell.
“So the temperature within the room has risen to a point where the products within the room start to off gas. That off gassing is a combustible gas, and eventually the temperature within the room gets to the point where all of the contents and the gases ignite,” Hallowell said.
The flashover sent England out of the house and off the porch, which is how he fractured his leg.
Other firefighters put out the flames
Hallowell was on the scene Friday night.
“Other firefighters that were there put him out by patting him down to put the fire out, but yeah he was on fire,” Hallowell said.
News Nine spoke to England Sunday morning before he shared the video. He called himself the luckiest unlucky guy when considering his injuries in the context of what happened.
Hallowell pointed to discoloring on England’s gear.
“This discoloring is basically where the thermal assault was taken,” Hallowell said.
Gear credited with saving his life
England’s gear is credited with saving his life. Every member of the Londonderry Fire Department recently received two brand new sets of personal protective equipment, which Hallowell said he is grateful for.
“This is the result. This is the happy result that, you know, the lieutenant was was able to sustain a significant thermal assault, and get out, with very limited injuries,” Hallowell said.
Besides the broken leg, England also suffered minor burns. He was released from the hospital and is recovering at home.

title: Belgrade man indicted on charges related to shots fired incident near a summer camp
text:
A Kennebec County grand jury indicted the 36-year-old man accused of firing about 20 shots near a summer camp Aug. 7.
Nathan Hewett was indicted in late September on charges of reckless conduct with a firearm, criminal threatening with a dangerous weapon and terrorizing with a dangerous weapon, which are felony charges, and discharging firearm near a dwelling, which is a misdemeanor-level charge.
An indictment is not a determination of guilt but indicates enough evidence exists for a case to move forward to trial.
Hewett allegedly fired the shots following an altercation with security guards at Camp Modin, a jewish summer camp. There were about 400 campers and staff members at the camp at the time. No one was injured.
Camp Modin was granted a protection order against Hewett on Sept. 28 after a complaint citing years of problems with Hewett, a neighbor of the camp.
Hewett was released from custody on $50,000 bail, and is barred from accessing dangerous weapons and using alcohol as conditions of his bail. He’s also barred from having contact with his father, Raymond Hewett, who is also a neighbor of the camp and was present for the interaction that preceded the shots being fired.
Hewett petitioned the court to modify this condition of his release, and his petition was denied.
Hewett’s dispositional conference — a nontestimonial hearing where the involved parties discuss the merits of the evidence, defense and motions with a judge — is scheduled for Nov. 10. at the Capital Judicial Center in Augusta.

title: Trump to speak with Putin soon about possible pneumonic plague case in Siberia
text:
President Trump says a call is scheduled with Putin to discuss possible case of pneumonic plague in Russia
President Donald Trump on Tuesday said he has a call scheduled with Russian President Vladimir Putin to discuss a possible case of plague at a Siberian research institute.
Speaking to reporters at the White House, Trump said he would be talking with Putin about the case “very soon.” Health authorities are investigating after the death of an employee at an anti-plague institute, which authorities attributed to pneumonia with an unknown cause.
Asked what the U.S. intelligence community was saying about the case, Trump said the U.S. is in “very deep discussions” on the topic. “We’ll be able to report about it, probably tomorrow,” Trump said.
Related video below: Secretary of State Marco Rubio urges Russia to share more information about the death of a lab worker in Siberia
The World Health Organization on Tuesday said the case presents a “very low” risk outside Russia. The United Nations agency said it was in contact with Russian authorities following reports of the death last week of a woman who worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East.
On Monday, Trump said the U.S. would be willing to help Russia with the situation. “It’s a rough disease. You know, that’s a disease we used to be able to control, but somehow those microbes have gotten stronger and smarter. They’re like an army,” Trump told reporters at the White House.
The call also comes as the Trump administration faces an Oct. 18 deadline to decide which Russian entities, if any, it will sanction under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which Trump signed into law on Sept. 18.
Ukraine has given the administration and Congress a wish list of Russian companies, vessels and individuals it would like to see hit with U.S. sanctions under that law.
__
AP writer Collin Binkley contributed to this report.

title: UMaine, Thomas College announce scholarships for Alfond Grant recipients
text:
AUGUSTA — Paige McNef, Samantha Hamilton and Ethan LeHay weren’t fully aware that they were some of the first babies in Maine to receive a $500 Alfond Grant growing up. But when it came time to think about college, those grants came as a big relief.
McNef, Hamilton and LeHay, who grew up in central Maine, all started their first semesters at college this fall, thanks in part to that early investment in their futures.
“I had no clue how I was going to pay for college,” said LeHay, who now goes to Central Maine Community College in Auburn. “Then my grandmother had told me about the Alfond Grant, and that took a huge weight off my shoulders.”
Now LeHay, who is going to come out of his first year of college debt-free, can focus on enjoying the beginning of his college experience.
The Alfond Grant Program, started by Maine businessman and philanthropist Harold Alfond shortly before he died in 2007, has granted $500 to every child born in Maine since 2013, totaling over 184,000 recipients, to use for education after high school. The program was first launched in 2008 and was awarded to 650 children born in Waterville and Augusta before later becoming available to all Maine children.
At an event celebrating this milestone Tuesday on the University of Maine at Augusta campus, the Alfond Scholarship Foundation announced new partnerships with the University of Maine System and Thomas College, which will now offer additional scholarships to eligible Alfond Grant recipients who attend those schools. The scholarships include $250 from the University of Maine system and $500 from Thomas College in Waterville.
“It is our way of saying, ‘Hey, this is one heck of an idea. It is blooming, and we want to make it bloom even bigger,'” Dannel P. Malloy, chancellor of the University of Maine System, said. “And we want to be a part of the effort to make sure that more families, at the birth of a child, are participating in this investment, not just investments in money, investment in the child.”
Eighteen years after the first 650 children received those $500 grants, the value of the grants now total around $2,500 or more depending on additional parental contributions.
The Alfond Scholarship Foundation invests the funds until a child is ready to use them, allowing them to grow over time. Families are also encouraged to open a NextGen 529 account, a state-sponsored investment account for higher education, alongside the grant to add their own contributions and receive matching grants from the Finance Authority of Maine, allowing the accounts to grow even more.
“It (has) that practical benefit of being real money in a real account,” Colleen Quint, president and CEO of the Alfond Scholarship Foundation, said. “It has that aspirational benefit of not just kind of encouraging kids to think about their futures, but also, and we hear this a lot from kids and from parents, is that someone else believes in my child, someone sees my child as having value. And that’s a really powerful thing.”
Early investments in education often have a positive impact on children’s aspirations, development and outcomes in school, Quint said, as well as increasing parents’ aspirations for their children’s futures.
The grant can be used for a wide array of higher education opportunities like college, vocational school, certificate programs, apprenticeships or graduate school and is not limited just to institutions in Maine.
“That’s money all to power the higher education opportunities for Maine kids, and then for those Maine kids to have a better life because of it,” Greg Powell, CEO and president of the Harold Alfond Foundation, said. “I like to think the state is better off too, because it’s really allowed our workforce now to have a leg up, and we will see that in the years ahead.”
Hamilton is using her grant to study civil engineering at University of Maine in Orono, McNef is studying radiology at Kennebec Valley Community College and LeHay is pursuing accounting at Central Maine Community College.
When asked what they would tell younger students preparing for their futures, all three grant recipients said to dream big and invest early.
“Just taking it day by day, going, ‘What can I do today to make my future better?'” Hamilton advised younger students. “And I think the Alfond Grant is incredible in that financially.”

title: Steve Gleason reflects on 20 years since iconic punt block and life with ALS
text:
Steve Gleason reflects on 20 years since iconic punt block and life with ALS
Former Saints player Steve Gleason reflects on the 20th anniversary of his legendary punt block, his battle with ALS, and the enduring connection between his life and the city of New Orleans.
Steve Gleason reflects on 20 years since iconic punt block and life with ALS
Former Saints player Steve Gleason reflects on the 20th anniversary of his legendary punt block, his battle with ALS, and the enduring connection between his life and the city of New Orleans.
Twenty years after his iconic punt block during the New Orleans Saints' "Domecoming" game, Steve Gleason reflects on the moment that became a symbol of hope for a city recovering from Hurricane Katrina.
Inside his lakefront home, Gleason, who is wheelchair-bound due to ALS, continues to fight the disease daily.
He has no movement in his arms or legs and uses his eyes and a computer to communicate.
“I know what it feels like to have your body taken away the ways you expect it to live,” Gleason said.
His wife, Michel, helps him manage the disease, even using tape to hold his eyelids open. She inscribed a special message, writing sister station's WDSU call letters, for this interview.
“I was just a little white dude lucky enough to find the place on this team and in New Orleans,” Gleason said. “The people here welcomed me, celebrated with me, and when my life changed, stayed with me.”
The punt block, which occurred just minutes into the September 2006 game against the Atlanta Falcons, led to a Saints touchdown and is now memorialized outside the Superdome as "Rebirth."
The play spurred the Saints to a decade of success and gave hope to fans still rebuilding their lives after Hurricane Katrina.
“That Monday night was about so much more than football,” Gleason said.
Reflecting on the time that has passed, Gleason said, “Twenty years? Yeah. You all may find this crazy, but given all I’ve been through, it feels more like twenty lifetimes. In some ways, I’ve already died to the life I thought I wanted and the life I thought I could control. And I’ve been reborn into a life of acceptance, gratitude, and miraculous beauty. When I blocked that punt, I could never have imagined the lives that would follow. ALS has changed my body, my plan, and my understanding of what it means to live. But I’m still here.”
Gleason acknowledged the significance of that moment for the city and its people.
“More than a scoreboard can measure,” he said. “People have endured so much loss. That night gave us somewhere to bring the grief, the fury, and the love all at once. I have lived through those thirteen months too. Even in the seconds after the block, I sensed this was bigger than a football play. The sound in the dome, the people around me. I felt like I was in every inch of the place.”
He added, “There was this incredible energy. People had chosen to come home and rebuild. I don’t think we were bringing New Orleans back—New Orleans had already determined it was coming back. We were fortunate to represent that spirit on the field and to the rest of the world. That’s what that moment means to me. We were part of something much bigger than football.”
Five years after the punt block, Gleason was diagnosed with ALS.
Since then, Team Gleason has raised more than $65 million over the past 15 years to raise awareness and search for a cure.
His efforts earned him the Congressional Gold Medal.
Gleason has also embraced fatherhood, raising two children, Rivers and Gray, with his wife, Michel.
“So much has changed,” Gleason said. “The man who blocked the punt could never have imagined this body or this life. My arms and legs are still. I cannot breathe, brother. I’m breathed. I have never hugged Rivers or Gray. That heartbreak is real for all of us. And so is the beauty. Michel, Rivers, Gray, our family, our friends, our caregivers, this city—they are my life.”
Reflecting on his journey, Gleason said;
"For me, it is a reminder that I am still here with them, still a father, still loving and being loved. I say this in my book, *A Life Impossible*, that if I don’t block that punt, I’d be dead. That moment connected my life to New Orleans in a way I never could have planned. When the ALS came, this community showed up for us. Twenty years later, I feel that love, and I’m grateful to be here for whatever comes next.”

title: Chicago woman sues U.S. government, saying Maine Border Patrol agent shot her
text:
A Chicago woman who says she was shot by a U.S. Customs and Border Protection agent from Maine is now suing the federal government.
Marimar Martinez was driving the morning of Oct. 4, 2025, when she observed three federal agents who appeared to be surveilling a Chicago neighborhood during an immigration enforcement surge last fall, according to her complaint. The lawsuit says she began following the agents through her neighborhood, honking her horn and calling out to alert residents “of the danger she believed the approaching agents posed to them.”
The lawsuit alleges that agent Charles Exum swerved his vehicle into her lane before firing his handgun, shooting Martinez five times. Both the vehicle and gun were government issued, according to the complaint.
Exum never turned on his body camera, according to the complaint, in violation of CBP directive. Martinez alleged that body cameras from two other agents in Exum’s vehicle captured him driving into her lane. Their cameras also recorded an agent saying “do something, (expletive)” as Martinez honked at them, according to the complaint. About four seconds before Exum allegedly drove into Martinez’s lane, the lawsuit says, the videos also recorded an agent saying “it’s time to get aggressive.”
On Tuesday, a spokesperson for CBP said Exum is being investigated for the use of force incident by a board of officials from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice. Exum was placed on administrative leave after the shooting, the spokesperson said. It’s unclear what the agent’s employment status is now.
Exum could not be immediately reached on Tuesday by phone or through either federal agency. He’s not a named defendant in the lawsuit.
Christopher Parente, Martinez’s attorney, said that Chicago police are also conducting a criminal investigation. A spokesperson for Chicago police said that the case remains active and open.
Martinez was charged in October 2025 with assaulting an officer after the other two agents accused her of ramming into their vehicle first. That charge was dismissed in late November.
In Martinez’s complaint, which was filed in the U.S. District Court of Northern Illinois on Monday, she is pursuing claims of negligence, battery, assault, infliction of emotional distress, false imprisonment and false prosecution.
Martinez is a 30-year-old Montessori school teaching aide and a U.S. citizen, according to her complaint. Her lawsuit alleges that during the Department of Homeland Security’s “Operation Midway Blitz” in Chicago last year, agents were “targeting brown people … with little regard for their citizenship.”
Martinez told reporters during a press conference on Monday that she’s suing because “I want to spread awareness because what’s happening is not normal,” according to reporting from ABC7 Chicago.
“We shouldn’t sit here and normalize what’s happening,” Martinez said.
Exum’s name was revealed during Martinez’s criminal case last year, after her defense attorneys complained that he had driven the government vehicle to Maine before they could inspect it. According to documents obtained through a public records request, Exum is certified by the Maine Criminal Justice Academy to enforce Maine law as a federal officer.
Martinez’s attorneys also shared copies of texts that Exum allegedly sent other federal agents after the shooting, in which he appeared to brag about his shooting skills.
“Cool. I’m up for another round of (expletive) around and find out,” Exum allegedly wrote in one text.
Martinez’s attorneys stated in court records that they filed a notice of their claim with the government six months ago.

title: Mother and son from Bermuda named as passengers on missing medical flight from Bermuda to Boston
text:
(AP) - The two passengers aboard an air ambulance that crashed in the waters off Massachusetts over the weekend while flying from Bermuda to Boston were identified Monday as a mother from Bermuda and her son.
Bermuda police said Marilyn Lavonne Bean, 66, and Sergio Wayne Lottimore, 41, both Bermudian nationals, were aboard a Gulfstream G100 along with four crew members when it went missing off Nantucket around 1 a.m. Saturday. Bermuda is about 750 to 780 miles (roughly 1,200 to 1,250 kilometers) southeast of Boston.
Searchers later found a “debris field” off the coast of the island, but with no sign of the six people on board after a 66-hour search that spanned more than 4,400 miles (7,081 kilometers), the U.S. Coast Guard suspended rescue efforts Sunday.
“While we held out hope for the best, the worst fears have been realized,” Bermuda Premier David Burt said in a statement. “Let us open our hearts to the families in the hope that our expressions of love, support and compassion will bring some comfort as they attempt to deal with this terrible loss.”
Warwick Academy, the school Lottimore attended in Bermuda, remembered him as a school prefect and an “ outstanding person.” Hamilton Re, the Bermuda insurance firm where he served as a senior vice president, said it had lost a “ respected leader, colleague and friend.”
The names of the plane’s crew have not been released, but Latitude Air Ambulance, the Ontario-based company that owned the plane, said Sunday that its staff faces the “heartbreaking reality” that all aboard the plane are now presumed dead, even if they have not been officially declared dead.
“Our four crew members were valued members of the Latitude family,” the company said in a statement. “They dedicated themselves to providing care to people at some of the most difficult moments in their lives, and they were carrying out that mission when this tragedy occurred. We are grieving their loss deeply.”
Peter Byl, president of Latitude Air Ambulance, said Monday the company’s immediate focus was on supporting the victims’ families and cooperating fully with authorities.
“We will not speculate about the circumstances or cause of the accident while that work is underway,” he wrote in an email.
The Canadian-registered jet had departed Bermuda’s L.F. Wade International Airport on a nighttime flight to Massachusetts. Air traffic audio indicates that the plane may have been “coming in blind” as a storm loomed. The pilot reported electrical problems and declared an emergency as the jet approached the coast.
Canada’s Transportation Safety Board said it will send investigators in the coming days to assist in the search for and recovery of the aircraft. The agency said it is leading the investigation into the crash with assistance from its U.S. counterpart, the National Transportation Safety Board.

title: Voters reject Turner land purchase for school district for second time in 5 months
text:
For the second time in five months, Maine School District 52 voters Tuesday rejected buying land in Turner for a transportation facility and fuel tanks, and potentially athletic fields.
The combined vote for Greene, Leeds and Turner was 835-353.
Each town opposed what some called “a once in a lifetime opportunity.”
The tallies were: Greene, 306 nos, 82 yeses; Leeds, 165-71; and Turner, 364-200.
The district has an option to buy 18.8 acres on Cobb Road from the Ralph Caldwell Living Trust through Dec. 31. The district has allocated $500,000 in a reserve account for the property.
District representatives had hoped to buy the land to install new diesel fuel and gas tanks, build a small transportation facility and add athletic fields when the funds are available.
“The school board will continue to look for solutions to the pressing problems the district has related to the transportation department, fuel supplies and safety issues related to parking at the high school,” MSAD 52 Superintendent Cari Medd wrote in email.
A snowmobile trail on the property and access to fishing at the Nezinscot River would have remained open to the public.
Turner voters approved the purchase in May while Greene and Leeds opposed it in a combined vote of 322-242.
The site is centrally located between the Leavitt Area High School at 21 Matthews Way, Tripp Middle School at 65 Matthews Way and Turner Primary School at 59 Cobb Road.
District officials say they need to relocate diesel fuel tanks because their use is expiring. The tanks are in the midst of a crowded parking area on school property. The site does not meet Maine Department of Environmental Protection requirements because it is too close to water sources, Medd previously said.
The district would also have added gas tanks to save money; it is currently purchasing gas off site.
There is no transportation facility for the district, and parking spots need to be saved routinely for buses during busy athletic programs and school activities. Medd said the district’s 30 buses and 25 vans no longer fit in the Leavitt Area High School parking lot and the crowded campus has no practical on-site solution.
Woods behind the high school and the middle school are all considered wetlands and the land next to Turner Primary School is too close to the public water supply at Jimmy’s General Store, Medd said. The small field next to the Central Office at 486 Turner Center Road is too close to private wells and the office well, and too small for the transportation fleet.
Another of the priorities was to keep the transportation fleet near the Turner campus because 1,500 students are transported to the campus each day. There are also 256 middle and high school sports trips each year.
The land would have also allowed the district to create two more sports fields since there is no room for more fields on existing property and more students are participating each year.

title: These Winter Storms Could Bury New England This Winter
text:
The staff at The Weather Channel has released their list of names that could be used for severe winter storms over the winter of 2026/2027.
A total of 21 names have been selected for the upcoming winter. They are in alphabetical order, with the exception of the letters that were skipped, of course.
Why Do We Name Winter Storms?
The practice of naming severe winter storms first started in 2012. Believe it or not, the National Weather Service has nothing to do with naming winter storms. While the National Weather Service names tropical storms and hurricanes, it is actually the Weather Channel that started naming winter storms.
Obviously, not every storm gets a name. If they named every storm, we’d go through the list of names in about a month. In order for a storm to get a name, it must bring widespread, high-impact snow or ice that prompts National Weather Service winter storm, blizzard, or ice storm warnings to qualify for a name. Naming lists also avoid current Atlantic and eastern Pacific hurricane names for the next six years, along with retired names tied to especially historic or destructive storms.
According to the Weather Channel there are some good reasons why they do this. You can read more about it on the website.

title: Obituary: Patricia “Pat” Helm Lyford
text:
WATERVILLE – Patricia “Pat” Helm Lyford, 88, passed away Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026, at 12:15 p.m. at Bedside Manor in Oakland, Maine, with family present.
Pat was born in Woonsocket, RI, on Nov. 21, 1937. Her parents were George Theodore Helm and Marjory (Ward) Helm. She graduated as valedictorian of Burrillville High School in Harrisville, RI in June 1955. She attended the University of Rhode Island (URI) and graduated Bachelor of Arts with “highest scholastic honors” in June 1959.
While at URI, Pat met Gordon G. Lyford from Dover-Foxcroft, Maine. They married on July 25, 1959, in Slatersville, RI. Their first home together was in Chepachet, RI, and Pat was a first grade teacher for two years at the local elementary school. In 1961, Pat and Gordon moved to Maine. Their first child, Peter, was born in March 1962 in Portland, Maine. Moving to Waterville later in 1962, Pat became a lifelong homemaker. Their second child, Kimberly, was born in August 1963 in Waterville, followed by Nancy (December, 1966) and Christopher (October, 1968).
Pat and Gordon joined the First Congregational Church of Waterville in 1962, and she continued as an active member until her passing. She served the church in many capacities: Sunday School Teacher, Sunday School Superintendent, President of Evening Fellowship, President of Women’s Fellowship, Member of the Board of Deacons (three terms), and 16 years as Clerk. She was a member of the Evening Sandwich Program for 30 years. Pat was a faithful blood donor at Red Cross Blood Drives throughout her life. She volunteered as a Girl Scout leader, a Cub Scout den mother, a Member of Thayer Hospital Auxiliary, a Member of Board of Directors of Sunset Home, and a Member of Waterville AAUW. Pat received the Micah Award from the Kennebec Valley Organization in 2014 for her many services to her church and her community.
Pat was predeceased by her husband Gordon on May 3, 1983. Her parents, George and Marjory Helm, predeceased her in 2003 and 2007 respectively.
Family was central to Pat’s life, and she hosted many family events here in Waterville, on Cape Cod, and at the family camp in Sebec, Maine. Pat’s cookies, bars, brownies and rum cakes are remembered fondly and will be greatly missed by all.
She is survived by her children, Peter Lyford and wife Lee Kimberly Lyford, Nancy (Lyford) Hale and husband Steve, Christopher Lyford and wife Cari; her six grandchildren, Zachary Hale and wife Katelynn, Helm Toler, Seamus Toler, Noah Lyford, Caleb Lyford, and Harper Lyford); and three great-grandchildren, Grayson, Delaney, and Elijah Hale were especially precious to her and brought her immense joy.
Her siblings, Ted Helm and wife Judy, Jeffrey Helm and wife Kathy, Jennifer (Helm) Geurtsen and husband John, also survive her; along with eight nephews and nieces, John Helm, Michael Helm, Kelly Helm-Pullar, Brent Helm, Kala Helm Campbell, Melissa Geurtsen Norwood, Kerry Geurtsen Jerin, and Andrew Geurtsen.
A memorial service and celebration of life will take place on Saturday, Oct. 31, 2026, at 1 p.m. at St Marks Episcopal Church, 60 Eustis Parkway, in Waterville. The service will be followed by a reception/collation at the same location. Pat specified there be no visiting hours and a private committal service.
The family would like to thank the caregivers who provided 24-hour in-home support to Pat in 2023. We are also grateful for the loving care Pat received from the staff at Bedside Manor East in Oakland from October 2023 to her passing, and for the care and comfort provided by MaineGeneral Homecare and Hospice in her final days.
In lieu of flowers,
memorial gifts may be made to:
First Congregational Church of Waterville, United Church of Christ
21 College Ave.
Waterville, ME 04901

title: South Portland to replace ballots after printing error on public safety bond question
text:
South Portland to replace ballots after printing error on public safety bond question
South Portland is replacing its November municipal ballots after a printer mistakenly listed the wrong total cost for a proposed public safety bond.
South Portland to replace ballots after printing error on public safety bond question
South Portland is replacing its November municipal ballots after a printer mistakenly listed the wrong total cost for a proposed public safety bond.
City officials notified voters via Facebook Tuesday night that the error appears on side two of the ballot, which includes the Public Safety Bond Question. The ballot correctly lists the bond principal as $88.6 million and the estimated interest cost as $61,798,500.
However, instead of the correct combined total of $150,398,500, the ballot lists $105,398,500.
The city said the $88.6 million principal and $61,798,500 interest figures were the amounts presented to and approved by the South Portland City Council and provided to the ballot printer.
The printer is reprinting the ballots at no cost to the city. The corrected ballots will also fix a minor typo in the bond question's description.
The City Clerk's Office expects to receive the replacement ballots later this week. Once they arrive, the city said it will immediately stop using the ballots containing the errors and begin using the corrected ones.
City officials emphasized that votes cast on ballots containing the error are valid and will be counted.
Voters who cast an absentee ballot at South Portland City Hall on Monday, Oct. 5, or who were mailed an absentee ballot containing the error will receive a notice in the mail.
People who vote absentee at City Hall before the corrected ballots arrive also will receive a ballot with the error. A staff member will inform voters about the issue, and a notice explaining the correct figures will be posted in the voting booths.
Voters who cast an absentee ballot after the corrected ballots arrive, as well as those who vote on Election Day, will receive ballots without the error.
Anyone who has already voted and wants to change their vote because of the printing error can contact the City Clerk's Office. Staff will mark the original ballot as spoiled and issue a new ballot. The city said it tracks spoiled ballots and ballot errors to account for every ballot issued.
The City Clerk's Office has also posted a notice about the issue at City Hall, as required under Maine law.

title: A combination bookstore and bar is coming to downtown Bangor
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Bangor’s reading enthusiasts will soon have a dedicated nightlife spot downtown.
Britney Ellis said she wants to build on untapped potential in the reading community and add a “completely different” type of space to the city with her business, the Fireheart Tavern at 105 Main St.
“It’ll be a mix between a brewery feeling, but also a cozy cafe feeling,” Ellis said when describing what visitors should expect when they walk in.
The tavern will be unique in Bangor and one of few in the state after Portland’s book-themed bar, Novel, closed earlier this year. The Happy Crow also recently opened in Gardiner.
The Fireheart Tavern’s name alludes to characters many fantasy fans will be familiar with — think the “Fireheart” nickname from Sarah J. Maas’ “Throne of Glass” or the protagonist in the children’s book series “Warriors.”
Customers will be able to browse both used and new books, and the bar serving cocktails, mocktails, wine and beer will double as a cafe counter with specialty coffee, matcha and chai. The store will offer books and events for a wide variety of genres, with a particular emphasis on fantasy.
“I’m hoping to bring something completely different to Maine,” Ellis said, noting the already-strong book community in the Bangor area, especially given the tourism to the city as Stephen King’s hometown. She also pointed to the variety of book clubs and events already in the area, like the annual Bangor Authors’ Book Fair and Literary Festival.
She wants the space to offer more of a relaxed atmosphere than a typical bar and host affordable events like author readings, slam poetry events, Dungeons and Dragons nights and craft events. The space will have a community room that people will also be able to rent out for their own clubs.
The store will host several in-house book clubs too, starting with one for fantasy and another for horror and thriller books, Ellis said. Those clubs will meet at least monthly, and members will be able to vote on the book selections.
For now though, the Main Street space is undergoing a complete renovation, including taking down interior walls, removing carpet and adding new lighting. Ellis plans to add two bathrooms, a six-seat bar, a reading nook area and cozy seating like couches and cushioned chairs.
Ellis said she chose the space, which sits between Portland Pie Co. and Bangor Window Shade and Drapery Co., for its interior brick wall and large windows after searching for eight months for the right space. She signed the lease in May and hopes to finish the renovations by early December, she said.
Although there’s still work to be done, Ellis said she’s already collected hundreds of used books for the store.
Once it’s ready to open, she plans to start with a Tuesday through Saturday schedule, with afternoon hours during the week and longer days on Friday and Saturday. She hopes to expand to seven days per week later on.
She also wants to eventually add a kitchen so visitors can access a cafe-style menu with charcuterie, paninis and salads, as well as baked goods from other local businesses.
Until the kitchen is added, anyone under 21 will need parental supervision to visit, but the store will host children’s programs and accept donations for a library-style collection that kids can borrow from for free, Ellis said.
A Bangor-area resident for about three years, the owner also works at the Animal Orphanage in Old Town and wants to use her business to help the shelter and the community more broadly. She wrote a children’s book that she plans to publish, with all proceeds going to the shelter.
Correction: The story has been updated to include a recently opened book bar in Gardiner, the Happy Crow.

title: A child rape suspect is expected to become a community’s next police chief. Here’s why
text:
ELIZABETH, La. (KPLC/Gray News) — Leaders in a Louisiana community are responding to the likelihood that a candidate accused of raping two children is set to become their next police chief.
Elizabeth, a village in Allen Parish with around 400 residents, is scheduled to elect its next police chief in November. One of the candidates was recently arrested on rape charges, and now the other has announced that he is stepping down from the race.
Christopher Paul, 48, was arrested in early September after he was accused of raping two 13-year-old girls 20 years ago. He faces two counts of second-degree rape.
Elizabeth Mayor Mandy Green reminded residents in a Facebook post that Paul has not been convicted of a crime, and he is presumed innocent until proven guilty. She also said she and the village’s Board of Aldermen have no authority to change the ballot under state law.
But a big change could also be coming to how Elizabeth chooses its police chief.
During a special-called meeting Friday afternoon, the village’s Board of Aldermen approved an ordinance to put an item on the Dec. 12 ballot that would change the police chief position from an elected position to an appointed position, if voted in.
It is unclear whether the proposition stemmed from the current situation and when it would go into effect. KPLC reached out to village officials, but they declined to comment or did not return our phone calls.
In her post, Green invited residents to attend the village’s next monthly meeting on Oct. 12 to voice their concerns.
“Moving forward, my administration will always act in the best interests of our community. Together with the Board of Aldermen, we remain committed to total transparency, maintaining an open-door policy, and navigating these circumstances together with you,” she wrote.
Paul’s opponent, Zachary LaCaze, said he withdrew after learning that his candidacy violated the Hatch Act because he works for the federal government. LaCaze was running as a nonpartisan candidate, while Paul is running as a Republican. LaCaze said that when asked to choose between his job and the race, he decided to keep his job to continue supporting his family.
The Secretary of State’s Office said Tuesday it has not yet received LaCaze’s withdrawal notice, but when it does, Paul will be elected to the position since he is running unopposed. He is eligible to hold office unless convicted of a felony.
The Youth Peace & Justice Foundation, a national nonprofit that aims to prevent violence against children, called for Paul to voluntarily step aside from the race while the case against him is pending.
The new chief is set to take office on Jan. 1.

title: US citizen who was shot by immigration agent from Maine in Chicago files lawsuit alleging he fired from behind
text:
(AP) - An American citizen shot by a Customs and Border Protection agent one year ago during a sweeping immigration crackdown in Chicago filed a lawsuit against the federal government on Monday, alleging the agent lied about the shooting and fired into her vehicle from behind.
Federal prosecutors initially accused Marimar Martinez, then 30, of using her vehicle to strike and box in agent Charles Exum’s SUV on Chicago’s southwest side on Oct. 4, 2025, during “Operation Midway Blitz.” Exum then exited his car and opened fire, leaving Martinez with seven gunshot wounds.
In the month after the shooting, prosecutors filed to dismiss the charges in a dramatic reversal of the closely watched case in the nation’s third-largest city.
Agent fired into rear of car, attorneys say
Her lawyers said Monday that they commissioned an expert to analyze bullet trajectories and her injuries and determined Exum wasn’t in the path of her car when he opened fire. They said he had walked several feet toward her car, contrary to statements he made to the FBI, and fired off five shots in less than a second, the last from the rear side of her vehicle.
“Charles Exum told the FBI agent on that day, within hours of the shooting, that Marimar was driving her car directly at him, that he shot her five times through the windshield, and that he ceased firing once he was no longer in the path of the vehicle. Those are three objective lies that you’ll see here today,” said one of her attorneys, Chris Parente.
Parente said there were only three bullet holes in Martinez’ windshield on the right passenger side, which indicated Martinez wasn’t driving toward the agent. He said the fourth shot was fired through the front passenger side window, adding another bullet hole in the back of Martinez’ car seat showed the agent fired the fifth shot from behind her.
“In what world can a U.S. law enforcement officer stand behind a car and fire his Glock service weapon through the rear passenger window at a young woman who’s crouched over the steering wheel?” Parente said.
CBP said in a statement to The Associated Press in response to the suit that Exum had been placed on administrative leave. Use-of-force incidents are “thoroughly investigated, reviewed, and presented” to an independent board, it added.
Exum is not a defendant in the lawsuit against the federal government, which was filed under the Federal Tort Claims Act and does not allow for lawsuits against individual agents. It was not known where Exum could be reached.
Body-worn camera footage from another agent in Exum’s vehicle before the shooting captured the agents saying it was “time to get aggressive” and making other profanity-laced comments encouraging violence, according to the complaint.
Martinez taken from hospital with bullet holes ‘leaking blood,’ suit says
The FBI arrested Martinez, taking her out of the hospital just hours after the shooting when she was “wheelchair bound and her bullet holes were leaking blood through her bandages,” according to the lawsuit. A judge ordered her release two days after her arrest.
Messages released by Martinez’ attorneys in February showed that former head of Border Patrol Greg Bovino had praised Exum for his “excellent service in Chicago” after the shooting. Other messages they released showed agents in a group chat congratulating Exum and calling him a “legend.”
Martinez was one several people shot in their cars by federal agents during President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown. An immigration agent shot a Venezuelan delivery driver in his car in Austin, Texas, last month, and another shot a Colombian driver in Biddeford, Maine, in July. The Trump administration has at times justified such shootings as self-defense against people allegedly weaponizing their vehicles.
Martinez appeared with her attorneys at a news conference Monday, saying the various shootings spurred her to file suit.
“If I don’t, then who else, you know? Look at what happened to Renee and all these victims,” she said, referring to Renee Good, a woman shot dead in her vehicle by a federal agent in Minneapolis in January.
“What’s happening is not normal. We shouldn’t stay here and normalize what’s happening,” she said.

title: I’m one of the few old men who still hunt deer. I asked a psychologist why.
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
As an aging hunter and outdoor writer, I have begun to look inward. Since I was a kid, I have always been drawn to the hunt. Truth be known, I have never taken the time to ponder why. I just know that it is apparently the way I am wired, perhaps some mysterious connection with my primitive ancestry.
A psychologist might conclude that I have an addiction to deer hunting in particular. So be it.
I have been hunting big game for more than 60 years, and most of my contemporaries were once die-hard deer hunters. But many have found their enthusiasm cooling, either because of health or because they have simply lost their appetite for the hunt. My knees are not what they used to be, and I tend to be clumsy in the woods, walking on uneven ground or stepping over blowdowns.
Because I have plenty of free time now, I deer hunted this past fall to my heart’s delight, from September through December. I did it all — bow, rifle and black powder. The deer were exceptionally plentiful. As I told my son, “Darned if this wasn’t one of the best deer seasons ever, in spite of my age and sore joints.”
The downside is that my physical capabilities are fading at a time when I still enjoy the hunt so much. It might be easier if my enthusiasm were cooling like that of so many of my aging buddies, who once enjoyed the hunt as much as I still do.
To gain some perspective on all of this, I ran it by an acquaintance who happens to be very knowledgeable about psychology and human behavior. He asked for anonymity, so we will call him Dr. Insight.
I asked him if it was normal for me to remain so enthusiastic about deer hunting after all these years.
He said there was nothing wrong with me. Enjoyment doesn’t necessarily fade with age. For some people, it can actually become more meaningful over time.
After 60 years of deer hunting, he said, my enjoyment probably isn’t just about venison or antlers. It is also tied to memories, experience, familiarity and a sense of belonging. He didn’t see that as addiction, but as part of who I am.
I also asked him if it was unusual that I seem to be in the minority of older men who still deer hunt.
“Psychologically, these are two equally valid strategies for aging. One reduces desire to match declining ability. The other preserves desire and renegotiates risk, discomfort and expectation.”
“Neither is healthier in the abstract. They’re simply different ways of staying whole.”
As I told Dr. Insight, the hard truth is that my physical capabilities are fading at a time when I still enjoy the hunt so much. His response was that the real tension is not desire versus decline. It’s honesty versus nostalgia.
He said, “That’s the true conflict — and it’s an ancient one. The risk isn’t that your ardor remains high. It’s that nostalgia may quietly edit out the present-day costs. Clumsiness, falls, exhaustion, recovery time — these aren’t moral failings, but they do require honest reckoning. Cooling ardor would make things easier. But easier isn’t the same as truer.”
Am I fooling myself? Just chasing youth? Or am I just plain stubborn, trying to maintain the best years of my life as long as I am blessed to do so?
What do you think?

title: Couple arrested on child abuse charges in surrogacy investigation involving more than 20 children, police say
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — An extremely wealthy Chinese immigrant and his wife amassed a brood of 21 children through a surrogacy scheme and raised them in a “house of horrors,” prosecutors alleged Tuesday.
Guojun Xuan, 66, and Silvia Zhang, 39, were arrested at their sprawling mansion in Arcadia, a city about 13 miles (20 kilometers) northeast of downtown Los Angeles.
The children suffered daily beatings from cruel nannies as the couple watched over a network of surveillance cameras and laughed, according to prosecutors. The couple allegedly recruited women across the country to serve as surrogates, promising them that they were just looking for another child to grow their family.
The couple face several counts of child abuse as well as conspiracy to commit child abuse, accessory after the fact and dissuading a witness, according to Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman.
“This case is unprecedented. It is horrific,” he said during a morning news conference. “The physical abuse, beating and punishment that these very young children received is despicable.”
In an afternoon court appearance in nearby Pasadena, the couple pleaded not guilty and denied all allegations with a Mandarin interpreter. Prosecutors sought $100 million bail per person because of the serious nature of the charges and because they are flight risks.
The couple have over 200 personal and 70 corporate bank accounts with annual transfers of $250 million, Deputy District Attorney MacKenzie Teymouri said.
Both were said to have U.S., Mexican and Chinese passports, though investigators have not determined if they are all legitimate; prosecutors said they used fake passports to create some of the bank accounts.
Inside the couple’s home, investigators found a bank statement showing more than $70 million in one account along with assets such as antique sculptures and specialty alcohol that added up to nearly $10 million, according to Teymouri.
LA County Superior Court Judge Kerry White set bail at $20 million each with home detention and a protective order against visiting their children.
Mitchell Krems, the couple’s attorney, called the bail amount “absurd” for the type of charges his clients face and said Zhang’s health should be taken into consideration.
Zhang, who appeared in court in a wheelchair, has a rare form of leukemia and is recovering from a bone marrow transplant, Krems said.
Fifteen children were removed from the opulent home last year after an allegation of abuse, and another six living elsewhere were also located. They ranged in age from 2 months to 13 years, with most between 1 and 3. Police believe Zhang gave birth to one or two of the children, while the rest were carried and delivered by surrogates.
Hochman said the couple set up an agency, Mark Surrogacy, that they operated from home and used to hire surrogates throughout the U.S. But prosecutors said the couple misled the women, telling some that they could not conceive and others that they only had one child and wanted one more to complete their family.
“The house could only be described as a house of horrors for these incredible young children,” Hochman said.
Prosecutor says videos show nannies and Xuan abusing children
Zhang and Xuan were first arrested in May 2025 after a hospital reported that their 2-month-old infant had a traumatic head injury, the result of being violently shaken by a nanny, according to Arcadia police.
Police did not file charges at the time, saying they needed to complete the investigation.
Hochman said the couple set up three rooms they called learning centers, where the children spent several hours a day sitting at desks under the supervision of nannies.
Through an extensive surveillance system including motion-activated cameras, the couple watched and at times laughed as the nannies physically abused the children, including daily beatings, he said.
In one video, Xuan is shown entering a room and telling a nanny to strike a child harder, Hochman said, and in another he joins the nanny in hitting the child.
The nannies were allegedly told “not to leave any physical marks on the children,” and when police arrived to investigate in May 2025, the children were told to deny they had been beaten.
After examining the surveillance video, police issued an arrest warrant for Chunmei Li, the nanny seen hurting the 2-month-old infant. However she fled to Tijuana, Mexico, and then China.
After the children were taken into state custody, Xuan and Zhang were allowed supervised visits. During one such visit, Zhang read to a child and wrote in the book, “Tell them you’re happy with me, tell them you want to come home,” lead prosecutor Teymouri said.
Krems said it was “patently false” that Xuan was involved in beating any of the children and blamed all the abuse on the nannies.
“My client, Mr. Xuan, intervened swiftly,” Krems said. “He fired the nanny, excised her from the house.”
Prosecutor says motive for discipline remains under investigation
When asked about the couple’s motivation, Hochman said that was part of the investigation, as was the parentage of each child.
Krems, Xuan’s attorney, previously told ABC7 that Xuan’s goal was to raise children who become productive adults.
“The reason he has all these children is because he wants them to contribute to society. He is not a man who is self-indulgent,” Krems said. “Some who are wealthy might spend on jewelry or cars, but he is actually spending his resources to help his children become educated.”
After Tuesday’s court hearing, he said Xuan and Zhang immigrated from China to exercise their freedom and have as many children as they want.
“If they were white, if they were Elon Musk, and they weren’t Chinese, they wouldn’t experience this level of scrutiny,” Krems said.
Surrogates say they were misled
Surrogacy is an arrangement in which a woman agrees to carry and deliver a child for another person or couple, often after an embryo transfer.
There is no comprehensive federal law regulating surrogacy, leaving most rules to the states.
California is considered to be surrogacy-friendly because it has clear laws governing the process. Both sides are required to have lawyers, and there must be a written, notarized contract before an embryo transfer takes place.
At least eight women came forward to say they were aggressively pursued to serve as surrogates. The women, many of them first-time surrogates, said they were given misleading or incomplete information about the couple’s family situation and intentions.
Krems denied that the couple lied to surrogates about their intentions.
The district attorney’s office said a federal investigation was ongoing.
___
Marcelo reported from New York.

title: Madawaska and MSAD33 Schools Plan Consolidation
text:
AROOSTOOK COUNTY, Maine (WAGM) - Three Aroostook County communities could soon share a brand-new school and tonight, the committee overseeing that project meets the architects designing it.
Madawaska and MSAD33 are working on a plan for a shared, state-funded PreK-12 school. They applied for Maine’s Integrated, Consolidated 9-16 Educational Facility program. A committee made up of community members and school staff from Frenchville, Madawaska, and St. Agatha is overseeing the project. That committee meets tonight and members will meet the engineers and architects designing the project.
Superintendent Benjamin Sirois oversees MSAD33 and the Madawaska School Department. He said, quote: “Tonight’s meeting is for the full school construction committee to meet the engineering/architectural firm. The Harriman team has been working with sub-committees over the past several months. Specifically, they have worked with the site-selection sub-committee and the educational visioning sub-committee.”
Sirois says the meeting will cover the state’s school construction process and preliminary timelines. It will also cover site selection, educational planning, and ways the community can stay involved. The meeting begins at 6 p.m. at the Madawaska Middle/High School library. All residents of Frenchville, Madawaska, and St. Agatha are encouraged to attend.

title: Chicago woman sues U.S. government, saying Maine Border Patrol agent shot her
text:
A Chicago woman who says she was shot by a U.S. Customs and Border Protection agent from Maine is now suing the federal government.
Marimar Martinez was driving the morning of Oct. 4, 2025, when she observed three federal agents who appeared to be surveilling a Chicago neighborhood during an immigration enforcement surge last fall, according to her complaint. The lawsuit says she began following the agents through her neighborhood, honking her horn and calling out to alert residents “of the danger she believed the approaching agents posed to them.”
The lawsuit alleges that agent Charles Exum swerved his vehicle into her lane before firing his handgun, shooting Martinez five times. Both the vehicle and gun were government issued, according to the complaint.
Exum never turned on his body camera, according to the complaint, in violation of CBP directive. Martinez alleged that body cameras from two other agents in Exum’s vehicle captured him driving into her lane. Their cameras also recorded an agent saying “do something, (expletive)” as Martinez honked at them, according to the complaint. About four seconds before Exum allegedly drove into Martinez’s lane, the lawsuit says, the videos also recorded an agent saying “it’s time to get aggressive.”
On Tuesday, a spokesperson for CBP said Exum is being investigated for the use of force incident by a board of officials from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice. Exum was placed on administrative leave after the shooting, the spokesperson said. It’s unclear what the agent’s employment status is now.
Exum could not be immediately reached on Tuesday by phone or through either federal agency. He’s not a named defendant in the lawsuit.
Christopher Parente, Martinez’s attorney, said that Chicago police are also conducting a criminal investigation. A spokesperson for Chicago police said that the case remains active and open.
Martinez was charged in October 2025 with assaulting an officer after the other two agents accused her of ramming into their vehicle first. That charge was dismissed in late November.
In Martinez’s complaint, which was filed in the U.S. District Court of Northern Illinois on Monday, she is pursuing claims of negligence, battery, assault, infliction of emotional distress, false imprisonment and false prosecution.
Martinez is a 30-year-old Montessori school teaching aide and a U.S. citizen, according to her complaint. Her lawsuit alleges that during the Department of Homeland Security’s “Operation Midway Blitz” in Chicago last year, agents were “targeting brown people … with little regard for their citizenship.”
Martinez told reporters during a press conference on Monday that she’s suing because “I want to spread awareness because what’s happening is not normal,” according to reporting from ABC7 Chicago.
“We shouldn’t sit here and normalize what’s happening,” Martinez said.
Exum’s name was revealed during Martinez’s criminal case last year, after her defense attorneys complained that he had driven the government vehicle to Maine before they could inspect it. According to documents obtained through a public records request, Exum is certified by the Maine Criminal Justice Academy to enforce Maine law as a federal officer.
Martinez’s attorneys also shared copies of texts that Exum allegedly sent other federal agents after the shooting, in which he appeared to brag about his shooting skills.
“Cool. I’m up for another round of (expletive) around and find out,” Exum allegedly wrote in one text.
Martinez’s attorneys stated in court records that they filed a notice of their claim with the government six months ago.

title: Fire at Ambition Brewing in Wilton ruled accidental
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The origin of a fire that gutted Ambition Brewing in Wilton on Monday afternoon has been determined accidental and caused by ongoing renovation work.
The fire began beneath the rear section of the building at 295 Main St. where old flooring was being cut and removed, according to a release from the Office of State Fire Marshal.
The fire was discovered about 3 p.m. by the property owner after old flooring had been cut and was in the process of being removed.
The business was founded by Jeff Chaisson and Josh Michaud in 2018.
The underside of the building was partially open to the elements, allowing leaves and other organic debris to accumulate beneath the structure over time. The material had become dry and readily combustible and most likely ignited during the flooring removal process, according to investigators.
Firefighters from multiple departments were able to contain the fire to one of the two buildings occupied by the business. The second building received smoke and water damage. No injuries were reported.
“Today has been a tough day for Ambition Brewing,” according to a post on the pub’s Facebook page. “We experienced a major fire, and while we’re still taking it all in, the most important thing is that everyone is safe.”
The post continued: “To the Wilton Fire & Rescue, Jay, Farmington, Rumford, Temple, and East Dixfield fire departments, Wilton Police, emergency medical services, and the investigators at Office of State Fire Marshal: ‘thank you for your tireless work, dedication, and care. We are deeply grateful for everything you’ve done today.'”
The owners couldn’t be immediately reached for comment Tuesday.

title: To tackle nicotine addiction, we need federal resources
text:
I agree with the concern expressed about protecting Maine youth from nicotine addiction (“Susan Collins questions Trump’s FDA nominee about vapes, drugs for rare diseases,” Sept. 24). But if we are going to talk about protecting children, we should also talk about what has happened to the federal infrastructure responsible for tobacco prevention.
On April 1, 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Office on Smoking and Health — the nation’s primary federal tobacco-prevention office — was essentially dismantled. Approximately 200 staff and contractors were terminated. The Tips From Former Smokers campaign was ended, and surveillance systems used to track tobacco use and cessation trends have been degraded.
That matters because the statistics we rely on to understand youth vaping, nicotine-pouch use and other tobacco trends don’t simply appear. They require ongoing federal surveillance and scientific expertise.
Congress ultimately preserved tobacco-control funding for FY2026, yet the Office on Smoking and Health had not been restored.
Sen. Susan Collins deserves credit for questioning a nominee about youth vaping. But as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, she also has an important responsibility to protect the federal tobacco-prevention infrastructure that Maine and other states depend upon.
If we truly want to protect Maine children, we need more than hearings about nicotine. We need the data, science and public health programs to prevent addiction.
Mary Lou Warn
Winslow

title: Student protests are rocking France as more than 250,000 rally
text:
Student protests are rocking France as more than 250,000 rally for school funding
Police fired tear gas to control crowds in Paris and elsewhere in France on Tuesday as more than a quarter of a million people rallied nationwide to support school pupils demanding more education funding, according to government figures. The protests increased pressure on the administration of outgoing President Emmanuel Macron.
As pupils blockaded high schools, large crowds waving flags and placards gathered in Marseille, Strasbourg and other cities. The demonstrations showed how protests that began at a high school in the Paris region in mid-September have grown into a nationwide movement — the latest of many that have marked Macron’s nearly decade-long tenure.
“We need to listen to them,” said Léa Monimart, an adult demonstrator in the northern city of Lille. “They are 17 years old; they are not completely clueless, and they know what they are talking about. It’s important to show that there are adults who support them.”
The Interior Ministry estimated that 266,000 people took part in demonstrations across the country on Tuesday, including 56,000 in Paris, where small groups of protesters clashed with riot officers at a city square at the end of a largely peaceful march.
Nearly 500 people were detained Tuesday, the ministry said. The widespread use of arrests, tear gas and riot-control weapons against teenagers is fueling defiance and angering some parents and teachers. Some student groups called for new protests Thursday.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the police response had been proportionate in “almost all cases” and that the protests had at times turned into riots, requiring police intervention.
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the government and school leaders must listen to students’ concerns and find solutions.
Questioned in parliament on Tuesday about the protest movement, Lecornu denounced “ultra violence” threatening schools. Responding to criticism of police tactics, he pledged that any “accidents” would be investigated and described allegations that the police are racist as a “lie.”
Class boycotts with police making thousands of arrests
More than two weeks of class boycotts and school blockades, and policing that has led to more than 6,500 arrests, mostly of minors, have become a flashpoint in the early days of the presidential election campaign.
Felix Barney, a university student, described the police response as disproportionate, saying it doesn't make “any sense to hit minors.”
“Riot police, batons, rubber bullets, tear gas,” said Aurélien Le Coq, a lawmaker with the far-left France Unbowed party. Its presidential candidate is strongly backing the protests.
The violence is “absolutely unbearable,” Le Coq said.
Nuñez defended police tactics despite a growing number of severe injuries blamed on officers’ riot-control weapons. In the latest case, a 15-year-old boy lost a hand Monday in an incident involving a police stun grenade. He said 715 officers had been injured.
The teenage protesters have struck a chord amid widespread discontent in France. Frustrations extend beyond immediate difficulties, such as fuel prices that have soared because of the Iran war, to broader concerns about constraints on public spending, rising poverty and wealth inequality under Macron, who can't run for a third consecutive term.
Against that backdrop, pupils’ complaints that education funding shortfalls are endangering their futures have found a sympathetic audience.
“You say ‘young people are the future,’ so listen to them,” read a handwritten placard attached to a metal barrier outside a Paris school.
Ministry offers online portal for complaints
At the Hélène Boucher lycée, or high school, in Paris' 20th district, protesters tipped over trash cans and bicycles onto their sides to create a makeshift barricade.
Like hundreds of others around the country, the school was closed. Authorities began shutting schools last week to take some steam out of the demonstrations after widespread damage to schools and mounting injuries among staff, students and police. Classes were totally or partially suspended on Tuesday at 891 schools, according to the Education Ministry.
Facing accusations that it was ignoring protesters, the ministry launched an online portal inviting high school students to anonymously describe the difficulties they face at school and the changes they want to see.
Student protests have drawn attention to rundown classrooms
At Hélène Boucher, parents and other adults positioned themselves on Tuesday between protesters and police keeping watch.
“They are our children. Teachers, parents, federations, we all share the same goal: the protection of children’s rights, and it is a legitimate right to demonstrate and to make demands,” said Emilia Sichili Suriam, who is a member of an association of parents.
Demonstrators have voiced a range of grievances, often centering on a lack of resources and opportunities for students in disadvantaged schools, despite the promise of France’s national motto: “Liberty, Equality, Fraternity.”
Students have drawn attention to rundown classrooms that lack basics such as desks and chairs, become sweltering in summer without air conditioning and, in some cases, are infested with rats. Other common complaints include staff shortages and exhausting workloads. French high school students’ compulsory classroom hours are among the highest in Europe.
Suzanne Nijdam, president of the federation of student associations, vowed that demonstrations would continue until authorities address the complaints.
“So, we really need to act now, and it’s in the government’s hands, to see these demands through to the end,” she said. “It’s a matter of political priority, a matter of prioritizing the youth and the future of our country.”
Neighboring Belgium is also seeing student protests. More than 30 were arrested Tuesday, and several police were injured in the eastern city of Liege, and smaller protests were held in Brussels and other cities.
John Leicester, Mark Carlson and Sylvain Plazy in Lille, Jeffrey Schaeffer, Masha Macpherson and Catherine Gaschka in Paris, Mike Corder in The Hague, Netherlands, and Lorne Cook in Brussels contributed to this report.

title: Painting bought for $30 at estate sale sells for more than $1.3 million at auction
text:
(CNN) — A $30 find at an estate sale has turned into a million-dollar jackpot.
The small oil painting was discovered in a dark corner of a Michigan home this summer.
The buyer spotted a faint signature reading “Abercrombie, 51” and decided to take a chance.
Experts later confirmed it was Gertrude Abercrombie’s “Alderman Merriam’s Shells,” a 1951 work that had not been seen publicly in nearly 75 years.
The painting was expected to fetch up to $250,000. Instead, it sold at auction for more than $1.35 million, setting a new record for Abercrombie’s work.

title: give IT. get IT. wants to increase technology access for Mainers and beyond
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WATERVILLE, Maine (WABI) - give IT. get IT wants to increase technology access for Mainers and beyond. Workers at the nonprofit’s Waterville warehouse process nearly a million pounds of devices every year.
A nonprofit built on recycled tech
“It’s a lot of controlled chaos,” said Chris Martin, co-founder and operations director of give IT. get IT. “It’s moving all the time.”
TVs, medical equipment and microwaves are among the items the team at give IT. get IT. handles.
The nonprofit was founded in 2002. It trains people, offers free tech support and gives quality computers to those who need them most.
“We go as far as Connecticut. Most of work is in Maine and New Hampshire,” Martin said.
give IT. get IT. currently employs 26 people. Nineteen of them work in the warehouse refurbishing technology.
Businesses supply used equipment
More than 400 businesses trust the nonprofit with their old technology. give IT. get IT.is NAID certified, meaning it meets global standards for securely destroying electronic media.
“That’s the lifeblood of our operation here – all the banks, hospitals, manufacturers and agencies that let us literally intercept their entire pile of what’s to them used equipment. To us, it’s a gem because then we just refurbish it and get it to people who need it,” Martin said.
“This is where the magic happens as far as getting computers ready to go to somebody who needs it,” Martin said.
Martin said give IT. get IT. is the only nonprofit recycler that reuses or recovers value from tech to directly benefit the community.
“We’re helping folks who can’t afford to just replace their technology every two years. This isn’t an offering of you’ve got to accept what we have, this is an offering of what are your goals and how do we best meet that with the right technology?” Martin said.
Free tech support and community recycling
“Whatever we provide for a device to a family that needs it, we’re also providing equal to if not ten times the value of that in just a free number to call, literally right to your Wi-Fi. We don’t provide your Wi-Fi, but if it’s inhibiting your ability to use your technology to your goal, we will help. At least the best we can,” Martin said.
give IT. get IT. also offers community recycling. Any Maine household can drop off items such as flat screen monitors, computers and printers for free, seven days a week. The goal is to keep these electronics out of landfills.
“That’s been a free service to the community since 2012,” Martin said.
Items can be dropped off outside the facility at 60 Industrial Street in Waterville.
While the facility is not currently open to the public, Martin said he hopes to grow into a larger space and change that.
Martin said people facing technology hurdles should reach out.
“When it comes to the stuff folks need to go to school, to access resources, to build up their career skills, stay connected with family – we’ve mastered that. We’ve got that,” Martin said.
For more information, visit the organization’s website or call 338-4233.
