title: Former CIA official accused of stealing $40M in gold bars pleads guilty
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A former senior CIA official pleaded guilty on Tuesday in Virginia to a charge that he abused his position and government funds to enrich himself by acquiring Florida real estate and hundreds of gold bars worth over $40 million, according to court records.
David J. Rush fabricated a “highly classified” government program to justify the acquisition of luxury property in south Florida that he intended to resell for personal profit, according to a court filing. Rush separately concocted a bogus “sensitive government activity” to obtain the gold bars, the filing says.
Rush’s fraudulent conduct cost the federal government approximately $194 million in total losses, according to the Justice Department.
Prosecutors also accuse Rush of lying to colleagues and government contractors about his military and academic credentials and the fake program that he invented, falsely claiming it was authorized by high-ranking U.S. officials.
“Rush used his legitimate government authority and manufactured personal bona fides to create confidence in his directions,” the court filing says.
Rush, 49, of Ashburn, Virginia, pleaded guilty to one count of wire fraud, which carries a maximum prison sentence of 20 years, court records show. District Judge Michael Nachmanoff is scheduled to sentence Rush on Jan. 28 in Alexandria, Virginia.
Several months ago, Rush tried to fraudulently authorize the release of $100 million from a government contract, according to Tuesday’s filing. He directed somebody else to transfer approximately $145 million to a holding company formed at his direction, then used those funds to acquire four “luxury” properties in Palm Beach and Hobe Sound, Florida, the filing says.
In previous court filings, prosecutors said Rush stashed roughly $46 million worth of gold bars from the federal government at his Virginia home. They also accused him of fraudulently claiming tens of thousands of dollars in compensation for military leave after he was honorably discharged from the U.S. Navy in 2015.
“Federal employees are entrusted with serving the American people, not themselves,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement.
CIA Director John Ratcliffe said the agency immediately referred the matter to the FBI after an internal investigation turned up evidence of Rush’s crimes.
“David Rush abused his position and betrayed the public trust and should be held fully accountable for his actions,” Ratcliffe said in a statement.
Rush was arrested after investigators searched his home and seized approximately 300 gold bars, roughly $2 million in U.S. currency and about 35 luxury watches, according to an FBI agent’s affidavit. A judge ordered Rush to be held without bond after his initial court appearance earlier this year.
During a hearing in June, defense attorney Jessica Carmichael said Rush wasn’t charged initially with any crimes related to the discovery of the gold bars, which she referred to as “basically a nonissue” and “nothing more than a sensational tidbit.” She said her client properly obtained the gold bars and kept them locked in a safe in his basement.
“Mr. Rush never claimed they were his,” Carmichael said.
Carmichael declined to comment on Rush’s guilty plea after Tuesday’s hearing.
Authorities say Rush lied about his education and military background on job applications, falsely claiming to be a former Navy pilot who graduated with a bachelor’s degree from Clemson University in South Carolina and a master’s degree from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute in New York.
Investigators determined that he didn’t serve as a Navy pilot and didn’t attend either school. Rush enlisted in the Navy in 1997 and was honorably discharged from the U.S. Navy Reserve as a lieutenant in 2015, according to the FBI affidavit.

title: 71-year-old man thrown from bike, killed after hitting dog in Central Park
text:
NEW YORK (WABC) - A 71-year-old man cycling in New York’s Central Park was thrown from his bike and killed after he hit a dog that wasn’t on a leash.
The incident happened just before 8:30 a.m. Monday in the park.
The 71-year-old cyclist, who was wearing a helmet, was riding a trek racing pedal bike when he hit a golden retriever that wasn’t on a leash. He was thrown from his bike and struck the pavement, suffering injuries to his head and body. First responders rushed the victim to the hospital, where he was pronounced dead.
The dog’s owner was on the scene, and police say the dog was not injured.
There is no word yet if anyone will face charges in the deadly incident.
Dogs are permitted to be off leash in Central Park from 6 a.m. to 9 a.m., but they must be on a short leash on park drives at all times.
The Central Park Conservancy released a statement Monday, calling on all New Yorkers to follow the rules of the park.
“We are heartbroken to hear of the fatal incident that occurred in Central Park this morning involving a cyclist and an off-leash dog. Our thoughts are with the family, friends, and loved ones of the cyclist who lost his life,” the statement read. “Central Park was created more than 150 years ago to provide a peaceful, joyful respite for all from the intense pace and pressures of the surrounding city. The Park cannot continue to serve that purpose unless all New Yorkers hold to the essential agreement of public space: know and follow the rules, and respect your fellow visitors.”

title: Winthrop, Monmouth move toward merging police forces
text:
The towns of Monmouth and Winthrop are moving forward with consolidating their police departments after the Winthrop Town Council supported the move at a meeting Sept. 21.
In June, Monmouth residents voted in favor of a proposal to merge the departments.
The consolidation process began in the summer of 2024, according to Paul Ferland, police chief for both communities since 2023. Ferland was Monmouth chief and became the chief for both towns after former Winthrop Chief Ryan Frost retired in 2023.
At the Sept. 21 meeting, Ferland made a presentation on the proposed merger to the Winthrop Council saying it would make official an already well-established working relationship between the two forces, attract better-trained officers to the force, enhance the chance for promotions, and allow for better coverage of shifts for sick, vacation and training time.
Ferland wasn’t able to answer the question of whether consolidation would save the towns money.
“When we make an investment, I’m looking at if it’s still going to be viable 10 years down the road, or are we going to have to replace it five or 10 years down the road?” Ferland told councilors. “Let’s spend a little bit more money up front right now for the longevity of that service down the road.”
Ferland’s plan suggests a “transitional approach” that would merge the two police departments over a period of time.
In the first year of consolidation, which would start at the beginning of the 2028 fiscal year on July 1, 2027, each community would continue to fund its own department at the necessary rate. Monmouth would give Winthrop that amount to administer both departments.
Over the next 12 to 24 months, the towns would analyze a variety of department areas, including staffing, calls for service and need for coverage. The data would form the basis of a merged budget the following year, Ferland said.
With Winthrop’s approval last month, the town will now name three residents to the Joint Police Commission. Monmouth has already appointed two members and an alternate.
The commission will assist in the consolidation, including creating the legal framework for the merger, establishing the interlocal agreement, ironing out the budgeting details, and helping develop the new department’s policies.
There is no set timeline for the merger. The two councils must approve the specifics of the consolidation before it is official.

title: Woman suddenly fighting for her life after feeling pain on family hiking trip, receiving rare diagnosis
text:
OSHKOSH, Wis. (WBAY/Gray News) - A Wisconsin family says they are working to get their beloved family member home after she suddenly became hospitalized during a family hiking trip in Utah.
Chris Kamke beat breast cancer over the summer and last month left for Utah with her husband, Kendall, and son, Kyle, to visit national parks.
On Sept. 19, the family said they hiked the Narrows in Zion National Park.
However, the next day at Emerald Pools, Kamke said her hips and legs hurt badly. The pain got worse. By the time they drove to Bryce Canyon, she couldn’t sit, stand or lie down.
“So, Kendall and Kyle decided that they should take her in to be seen. So, they drove about 30 minutes to a hospital in Panguitch, Utah,” Tammy Thomas, Kamke’s sister, said.
Doctors first thought it was the heat. When Kamke struggled to breathe, they discovered bacterial pneumonia, according to the family.
Kamke was airlifted to another Utah hospital on Sept. 20, where her condition has since worsened.
“By the time I got there on Friday, she was completely non-responsive, and has been since then. So, since Sept. 25, she has been comatose,” Thomas said.
Kamke has since been diagnosed with neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, a rare autoimmune disease impacting one in 250,000 people.
Loved ones said she is currently paralyzed, in a coma and on a ventilator.
Thomas added that the family could never have seen something like this coming.
“That’s the really strange thing because Chris was extremely active. She walked, they kayaked, they biked, they golfed. I mean, Chris is 65, and she still plays softball with her softball team,” Thomas said.
The family said they want Kamke back to Wisconsin so she can be surrounded by loved ones. But a hospital transport costs $50,000, and insurance won’t cover it.
So, the family is working with the nonprofit Grace on Wings, where crews volunteer and the family pays for jet fuel, estimated at $27,000 to $28,000.
The family has started a GoFundMe to hope to fly her back within the next week, which has helped raise more than $25,000.

title: What Maine’s next generation of farms needs to succeed
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Ryan Douglas is a Maine-based strategic advisor to cultivation businesses and the
author of “Presence is a Strategy: The Competitive Advantage You Can’t Automate.”
Last week, a news report announced that the Lisbon greenhouse facility operated
by Springworks Farm is headed to auction.
Roughly 40 miles away, Vertical Harvest, a high-tech producer of indoor leafy greens in Westbrook, has faced significant delays and has yet to reach the commercial scale it originally envisioned.
If Maine is going to support innovative agriculture with public resources, it should ask one question before a project moves forward: Is the operation ready to run?
Early in my career, I worked for an ornamental flower grower in Mississippi who operated on five acres of patched-up, run-down greenhouses. The facility wasn’t impressive, but the crops were consistently exceptional.
Years later, I consulted for a publicly traded cannabis company in Colombia. It had sophisticated facilities, a ton of cash and a board with impressive credentials. But when I stepped into the company’s greenhouse, I was speechless. Every plant was dead.
How could an operation with every advantage fail at the most basic task, while the unimpressive greenhouse produced exceptional crops?
Those two experiences reinforced a lesson I’ve learned throughout my career: operational readiness is fundamental to success.
As a lifelong Mainer, I’ve spent three decades in commercial horticulture throughout the U.S., Canada and South America. Most of my career has been under glass as a grower, manager and consultant, and I previously served as general manager for Backyard Farms, the 40-acre tomato greenhouse range in Madison.
Operational readiness is having the people, systems and discipline to run a facility reliably from day one. In this business, margins are made or lost in the consistent execution of mundane but essential work.
Skipping a crop walk on Friday could mean missing signs that insect pressure has increased due to warmer weather. By Monday, that small oversight can mean unsaleable product, additional labor and lost revenue.
In a small greenhouse, that mistake may have a limited impact. But at a commercial scale, small mistakes compounded over time can quickly turn into major losses. No amount of money can replace the need for operational experience, seasoned judgment and common sense. Operational readiness must be built into a cultivation project from day one, not treated as a problem to solve once construction is complete.
Springworks Farm received meaningful public support, including a $300,000 Maine Technology Institute award for greenhouse expansion. The Finance Authority of Maine insured a $5 million loan and a $1 million working-capital loan in partnership with Farm
Credit East.
Vertical Harvest received nearly $49 million in USDA-guaranteed loans, approximately $8 million in financing facilitated through Efficiency Maine and $1 million in direct loans from the Finance Authority of Maine.
When public resources support private projects at this scale, Mainers have a legitimate stake in whether those projects are built and managed to succeed. Operational readiness should be scrutinized as closely as technology, job creation, capital investment and economic impact.
I am 100% in favor of continued investment in Maine’s ability to feed itself. Considering our short outdoor growing season, innovative cultivation projects like these will be a key part of the solution. But these latest developments are a reminder that impressive facilities alone aren’t enough.
Public funding shouldn’t just help ambitious agricultural ventures get off the ground. It should increase their chances of actually sticking around.

title: Accused Lewiston shooter indicted by grand jury
text:
LEWISTON — A 20-year-old local man accused of opening fire on Walnut Street in late July was indicted this week on charges of attempted murder, aggravated assault and reckless conduct.
Ethan Nazir Parrilla, of Lewiston, is accused of shooting a 21-year-old in the leg as he fired a half dozen shots on the afternoon of July 27.
Police said Parrilla was planning to shoot three people near the corner of Walnut and Bartlett streets when his handgun jammed.
Witnesses said at least six shots were fired. Struck in the leg was 21-year-old Abdirkrim Abukar, a man with whom Parrilla had fought with the day before, according to court documents.
Just before 6 p.m. the day of the shooting, Parrilla left his girlfriend’s apartment and appeared to be “on a mission,” according to the girlfriend and one other witness.
Armed with a handgun, witnesses said, Parrilla made his way to the intersection of Walnut and Bartlett streets, where he had words with three people, including Abukar, a teenage boy and a third young man who has not yet been identified.
Moments later, Parrilla brandished the pistol and started shooting. One witness said it appeared he was trying to shoot all three of the people he had previously fought with.
Abukar, the lone victim of the shooting, was treated at Central Maine Medical Center in Lewiston for a gunshot to the leg. He was later released.
At least one other person was injured as they fled the sounds of gunfire, witnesses said.
Parrilla fled the area on foot, but was soon contacted by police who convinced the suspect to come to the police station.
Parrilla has remained at the Androscoggin County Jail in Auburn on $100,000 cash bail since his arrest. However, because of an alleged bail violation stemming from an earlier charge of domestic assault, he will not be allowed bail pending his next court appearance scheduled in December.

title: Live updates: Susan Collins and Troy Jackson debate for the first time
text:
Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson are set to debate Tuesday, the first time voters will see them share a stage.
Democrats have long coveted Collins’ seat, which she has held since 1996. But she’s never faced a reelection battle quite like this. The opponent Democratic voters nominated in June, Graham Platner, abruptly withdrew from the race after a woman credibly accused him of sexual assault. (Platner has denied the allegation.) Jackson was nominated to replace Platner at a convention later that month.
Most polls show Jackson ahead of Collins, but the incumbent is outspending him on the airwaves. Tonight’s debate is certain to feature talk about the cost of living, the Iran War, President Donald Trump and Collins’ recent spate of negative national press. Follow along with us live here.
That’s a wrap!
Thanks for following along with us. Until next time.
-Kirby Wilson and Billy Kobin
But I didn’t see anything game changing. Three more debates to go!
-Kirby Wilson
“To be effective in the Senate, you need knowledge, experience, seniority and relationships. That combination has allowed me to pass bipartisan legislation,” Collins said.
Jackson said that “I don’t owe Donald Trump and the billionaires anything. You know, I owe the people of the state everything.” He brought up again how Collins voted with Trump around 96% of the time and that she’s been fighting for “the billionaire class.”
“Tonight, Sen. Collins has told us how powerful she is, but power means nothing if you won’t use it when the people in Maine need it,” Jackson said, adding he passed legislation at the State House to lower prescription drug costs, support childcare and provide universal school meals along with sponsoring abortion access legislation.
“I’m never going to forget where I came from. I’m an everyday person that is so indebted to people who put me in this position to fight for them,” Jackson said.
The two shared a laugh when moderator Gregg Lagerquist of WGME said at the end he was going to ask both of them during the lightning round if the New England Patriots will make the playoffs.
Collins said they absolutely will, and razzed Jackson for being a Steelers fan.
Each candidate left the stage smiling.
-Kirby Wilson
-There should be more restrictions on data centers
-Mifepristone, which is a medication used for abortions, should be available.
But the candidates disagreed over:
-Whether Americans should have to show ID at the polls. (Collins: Yes. Jackson: No.)
-Whether Israel should have the same level of support from the U.S. government, less support, or more support. (Collins: the same. Jackson: less, but there was more nuance to this answer.)
-Kirby Wilson
A note on the style of the candidates
To touch on the optics of the debate or the tone so far, Collins has repeatedly gotten defensive when Jackson has criticized her. It feels safe to say Jackson has been more on offense rather than defense. Not an entirely surprising thing given the incumbent often faces plenty of attacks.
-Billy Kobin
Jackson criticized Collins for voting for Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who Jackson said was clearly going to push for tariffs, long one of Trump’s signature policy aims.
“I’m not going to give her credit for getting one thing back,” Jackson said, when thousands of other items are more expensive under Trump.
-Kirby Wilson
Collins reiterated that “you cannot abolish ICE” while saying it needs reforms. She argued the $70 billion figure that Jackson cited was not really all for ICE but rather split between ICE and Customs and Border Protection.
“You don’t (pour) more money into an agency that is killing people across the country,” Jackson said.
-Billy Kobin
Jackson promises to not be a “blank check” for any president, Republican or Democrat.
-Kirby Wilson
Jackson said he supports Medicare for All and wants to help Mainers get covered.
While Collins points to her 2017 vote to block a Republican attempt to repeal the Affordable Care Act, Jackson noted she and Republicans let ACA tax credits expire at the end of 2025.
-Billy Kobin
Collins responds by noting that she’s always been pro-choice, and that Jackson hasn’t.
“I clearly don’t agree with how Brett Kavanaugh voted on Roe v. Wade,” Collins said.
-Kirby Wilson
Collins referred to Navatek and its former CEO Martin Kao, calling him a “crook.” She mentioned the University of Maine project that Navatek was involved in and a photo of the two of them together, saying that photo was taken months before there was “ever a contribution” from Kao.
Jackson wouldn’t let her get off easy on this, and he brought up how Trump ended the FBI probe that was continuing into Kao and the pro-Collins super PAC. Collins kept criticizing all of this as false.
Collins then brought up Jackson’s past case in which a Republican lawmaker filed an ethics complaint against him for using an Augusta home when serving in the Legislature.
The Maine Ethics Commission voted unanimously against investigating Jackson in 2023, and commissioners noted they could only weigh in on whether Jackson violated any campaign finance rules through the Augusta residence and not on the additional claims that he committed crimes such as mortgage fraud.
-Billy Kobin
In January, Trump said Collins “should never be elected to office again,” though relations between the two seem to have improved since then.
-Billy Kobin and Kirby Wilson
“Whatever,” Jackson said of her rate of voting for the president’s priorities. “It’s far too often.”
-Billy Kobin
“Sen. Collins is like an arsonist who helps set the fire and then she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out,” Jackson said, emphasizing she advanced the bill and that GOP colleagues have “called her a team player.”
-Billy Kobin
Jackson fired back by saying Mainers are struggling because Collins has failed to stand up for Donald Trump as he wages war in Iran.
-Kirby Wilson
It was a more aggressive opening statement than Collins’.
-Kirby Wilson
It will be interesting to see how aggressive Jackson is with his attacks and whether he can land a few blows. He’s not the most gifted speaker, so how he delivers his attacks and responds to Collins’ rebuttals will be important to watch.
Meanwhile, Collins, 73, will have to parry those attacks from Jackson and try to land a few rhetorical punches of her own. Her campaign spoke with reporters earlier today about how they plan to push back on pay-to-play allegations made in a ProPublica story two weeks ago. And she and her Republican allies have been mining Jackson’s legislative record for problematic votes.
This will be Collins’ first televised debate in roughly six years. Her energy and sharpness will likely be scrutinized.
Collins, who has been in office for nearly 30 years, clearly has an advantage when it comes to in-depth knowledge about national policy and international affairs. Jackson has to hold his own without making any gaffes that could live on in social media posts or advertisements.
-Randy Billings

title: Costs will skyrocket for many in Maine if ban on prescription drug imports takes effect
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND — Maida Uhlig said she’s been purchasing anxiety medication from Canada for about 20 years, and would have to pay thousands more per year if a new U.S. Customs and Border Protection rule goes into effect later this month that would ban people from buying medicines internationally by mail.
Uhlig, 81, of Portland, said she takes Lexapro, which her insurance doesn’t cover because there’s a generic equivalent available. Uhlig said she’s tried the generics, but for her they’re not effective. She said only the brand name medication alleviates her anxiety.
She pays about $675 per year out-of-pocket for the brand name medication, purchasing by mail through Canadian pharmacies. If she had to purchase that same drug in the U.S., Uhlig estimates the cost would be about $6,300.
“I couldn’t do it. I don’t have that money,” said Uhlig, a retired administrative assistant. “It would be debilitating if I couldn’t take this medication.”
The rule is set to go into effect Oct. 22, eliminating an exemption that previously allowed importation of prescription drugs through the international postal system.
U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, D-1st District, said in an interview last week that she signed onto a letter from dozens of House members asking the Trump administration to abandon the rule.
“People have been doing this for a long time, and it shouldn’t be taken away from them,” Pingree said. “We need to make sure people who are getting their prescriptions this way don’t get caught in this trap.”
A 2020 University of Florida study found that about 2 million Americans purchase prescriptions from international pharmacies.
Ken Hunter, executive director of the Campaign for Personal Prescription Importation, a New Jersey-based advocacy group, said in an interview Friday that many countries, including Canada, regulate drug prices more than the U.S., which leads to many prescription medications being cheaper when imported.
Hunter said for decades, the federal government has allowed drugs for individual prescriptions to be imported through the U.S. mail, through the Medicare Modernization Act of 2003. In the era before drugs could be purchased internationally over the internet, the federal government allowed people to drive over the Canadian border to purchase personal prescriptions.
“Drug prices, when buying internationally, are much less than what they are in the U.S., typically half the price to one-fifth the price,” Hunter said. “This is going to price people out of the ability to use these drugs. We are heading toward a significant healthcare crisis.”
Hunter pointed to Eliquis, a blood thinner often prescribed to prevent strokes, as a commonly imported medication. When purchased from Canada, it costs about $550 for a three-month supply, but in the U.S. it’s priced at over $1,000, he said. Hunter said while generic drugs are often inexpensive in the U.S., it can sometimes take years for a new medication to have a generic equivalent. Or, he said, there may be generics available in other countries, but not the United States.
CBP said on Friday that it would respond to questions about the new rule. The agency had not responded by Tuesday.
According to the published rule, CBP cited the potential of “illicit-drug importations” as one of the reasons.
Hunter said banning the importation of personal prescription medications is not going to be effective in reducing the flow of illicit drugs into the U.S., which occur in much larger volumes.
Ann Woloson, executive director of the Maine-based nonprofit Consumers for Affordable Health Care, said in an interview Friday that the impacts of the new rule would be devastating for many who already have difficulty affording their medications.
Many people have high-deductible insurance plans or those where the patient has to pay a certain percentage of drug costs. In those cases, insurance would not protect people from paying thousands in out-of-pocket costs, Woloson said.
“It’s another sad example of how our current administration is going to make it harder for people to afford the healthcare they need,” she said.
Thirty-two percent of Maine residents surveyed this year by Consumers for Affordable Health Care reported that they took fewer pills than prescribed to save money.
Uhlig said she has a supply of anxiety pills that will last about a year, but after that she would have to take a 10-hour, round-trip bus to Montreal to purchase the medications directly from Canadian pharmacies. Hunter said the new rule doesn’t prohibit people from personally crossing the border to buy drugs from Canadian pharmacies, but making people travel long distances to get medications they need would be a hardship for many.
Uhlig said people shouldn’t be forced to pay exorbitant costs for medicine they need.
“It’s so unfair, because people rely on these drugs to live,” she said.

title: Trump approves firing squad execution for Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan
text:
(AP) - President Donald Trump has approved the execution by firing squad of Army Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan for the 2009 shooting rampage at Fort Hood, Texas.
The U.S. military has not carried out the death penalty since 1961. The Army secretary will decide a time and place for the execution, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell wrote in a post on X.
“Judgement day for Hasan has finally come,” Parnell wrote.
Hasan, an Army psychiatrist, walked into a medical building where soldiers were getting medical checkups, shouted “Allahu akbar” — Arabic for “God is great!” — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun. Thirteen people were killed and more than 30 injured.
He said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims and made almost no effort to defend himself at trial. He told jurors that evidence would show he was the shooter and described himself as a soldier who had “switched sides.”
Trump’s approval triggers a series of procedural steps toward carrying out the execution, but Hasan could put them on hold — potentially for years — with a habeas corpus appeal in the civilian federal court system, according to an article published in May in the magazine Army Lawyer.
Death sentences are extremely rare in the military justice system, and executions even rarer. Four men, including Hasan, are currently on the military’s death row at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. President George W. Bush approved the execution Army Spc. Ronald Gray in 2008 but it was put on hold by a judge and he remains at Leavenworth.
The last man executed in the military system was Pvt. John Bennett, hanged in 1961 for raping an 11-year-old girl.
Trump approved the firing squad execution days after a failed attempt to execute Christa Pike by lethal injection pushed Tennessee’s governor to halt further executions this year and order an independent review.
Trump resumed the federal death penalty after an informal moratorium during previous administrations. The federal government executed 13 people between 2020 and early 2021, contributing to making Trump the most prolific execution president in over 130 years.
Asked whether the botched execution in Tennessee would lead him to seek changes to capital punishment, Trump said it was “an interesting situation.”
“It shouldn’t be very difficult,” Trump said of carrying out lethal injections.

title: Friends mourn 16-year-old killed after being hit by deputy’s car: ‘She was a great person’
text:
ST. FRANCOIS COUNTY, Mo. (KMOV/Gray News) - An investigation is underway in Missouri as loved ones mourn a 16-year-old girl who died after she was hit by a deputy’s car while lying on the road.
The community held a candlelight vigil Monday night for 16-year-old Persephone Berger, a student at West County High School. She was killed early Saturday after being hit by a St. Francois County Sheriff’s deputy’s car.
“She was just a really lively, understanding person. She never judged a soul. She was just a really sweet person,” said Persephone’s friend, Emma Houser.
Houser, along with Persephone’s friends Riley Skaggs and Isaac Madden, say the 16-year-old’s death weighed on the entire student body Monday as everyone wanted to make sure she was remembered and honored.
“You go to school. You see the photos. You see decorations and talking about it, and you can’t help but cry. It’s very sad,” Madden said.
“Everybody was wearing pink today in honor of her. We hung up pictures, laughed, talked about stories of her, but the halls were extremely quiet. There was a big change,” Skaggs said.
What deputies say happened
St. Francois County Sheriff Jeffrey Crites said deputies responded to a call about 3:43 a.m. Saturday for an unresponsive person lying on the road – later identified as Persephone. The person who made the call stayed at the scene.
As a deputy was approaching the scene, he saw the caller’s car with its hazards on but did not see Persephone on the road and struck her, Crites says. The deputy stayed at the scene and notified their supervisor.
Investigators says it’s unknown why Persephone was on the road.
St. Francois County Coroner Jason Coplin was called to the scene around 4 a.m. He said Persephone had suffered blunt trauma injuries, but an official cause of death cannot be confirmed until further tests are done.
Investigators say a preliminary autopsy conducted Monday did not show any injuries aside from those that involved the crash with the deputy’s car.
The Missouri State Highway Patrol has been asked to conduct an independent crash investigation.
Crites says the crash was not due to a police chase and no deputies left the scene, as some have claimed on social media.
Friends mourn as questions remain
While many questions remain in the community about what happened, Monday night’s vigil was a chance to focus on Persephone.
“She felt kind of like an older sister and like someone you can lean on and talk to about anything,” Houser said. “I relied on her as a person to be there for me, talk to me when I needed to talk to her, just a bunch of stuff.”
Madden said Persephone was one of the first people he met when he moved to the district, and that memory stands out.
“She was very, very kind, cared about everybody, super funny, probably one of the best people that I’ve ever met in my life,” he said. “She was really smart. She had a bright future ahead of her.”
Skaggs said she had known Persephone since middle school, and they became really close in high school.
“Big fan of Harry Potter, brought in some Harry Potter stuff. Her Alanis, her gummy clusters, we brought. But we’ll always remember Persephone as fun-loving, very smart,” she said. “Her loss has made a huge impact on the West County family.”
The three friends are working on a T-shirt fundraiser to support Persephone’s parents and three siblings, so the family knows they’re thinking of them.
“I just want the family to know that she was a great person and made the community come together... She’s very deeply missed,” Madden said.
A GoFundMe has also been set up to support Persephone’s family.

title: All fraternities suspended at university amid wave of misconduct reports
text:
TUCSON, Ariz. (KPHO/Gray News) — The University of Arizona has hit pause on all fraternity activities amid a wave of misconduct investigations.
In an internal university memo, Chrissy Lieberman, the dean of students, said her office is investigating multiple reports of misconduct involving nearly half of the 21 fraternities on campus.
The violations range from physical assault, hazing and drug and alcohol violations to creating unsafe environments for students, according to Lieberman.
Effective immediately, all fraternity chapters have been placed on an interim activities suspension until all chapter advisors have met with the dean.
Six fraternities — Zeta Beta Tau, Sigma Phi Epsilon, Phi Delta Theta, Sigma Chi, Theta Xi and Phi Gamma Delta — were suspended immediately.
Swallowing live goldfish, hazing, blackout allegations
Several chapters were deemed responsible for code of conduct violations this spring and remain on disciplinary status, according to the Dean of Students Office.
According to officials, chapters are on active suspension, while others have been banned from working with their new member classes, with severe cases under criminal investigation.
Last month, Sigma Tau Gamma was placed on activities suspension after being accused of forcing members to drink large amounts of alcohol and swallowing live goldfish.
In April, six fraternities were under investigation by the school. Three of them, Sigma Alpha Mu, Sigma Chi and Phi Delta Theta, faced serious allegations.
The allegations against Sigma Alpha Mu include burns from hot liquids, forced alcohol consumption, alcohol poisoning, blackouts and hospitalizations.
Sigma Chi allegedly hosted a party that was alcohol-free, but alcohol was consumed, drugs were knowingly and unknowingly given to members, and multiple people were hospitalized.
Phi Delta Theta was placed on suspension for hazing, where members were allegedly subjected to forced alcohol consumption, degradation, humiliation and other threatening and endangering behaviors.
Another fraternity, Sigma Phi Epsilon, was placed on probation until May 31, 2027, and must pay a fine of nearly $4,000. The accusations against the fraternity included sleep deprivation, forced alcohol consumption, kidnapping and forced calisthenics. Members were also accused of illegal drug use.
The last time the university cut ties with a fraternity was in 2024, when Pi Kappa Phi was found guilty of hazing and violating the school’s code of conduct.
Mandatory meetings with chapter advisers
An activities suspension prohibits the fraternities from hosting, attending, sponsoring and participating in any organizational activities. Only business meetings are allowed during the suspension.
Once a chapter adviser has attended one of the three mandatory meetings, chapters that were in good standing will resume activities as normal.
Chapters with upcoming events must ensure that their adviser attends a mandatory meeting. The chapter must return to good standing before any event can be hosted.
Adviser meetings are said to continue quarterly, and advisers must be in attendance at each meeting. If an adviser doesn’t attend, the chapter will be removed from good standing, and its continuation could be jeopardized.
University president met with fraternities
University President Suresh Garimella met with all fraternity presidents on Aug. 27, where he said that the university would not “tolerate further violations that put our students in harm’s way.”
University leadership told fraternity leadership to “step up and be accountable for the men in their chapters” and stop behaviors that violated the school’s code of conduct.
“It was made clear that if the chapters did not meet this expectation, the university would be forced to act,” Lieberman wrote in the memo, dated Monday.
Cases at capacity
Lieberman said that reports are continuing to pour in about concerns within the fraternities, including from parents, students and the community.
The Dean of Students Office is at capacity for the number of cases its staff can investigate at one time, and every case involved a fraternity chapter, according to Lieberman.
“As you know, the value of the Greek experience is under scrutiny nationwide. It is time for the University of Arizona Greek community to step up and set an example for good. It is time to have difficult conversations with each other and the members of the community,” a portion of the memo stated.
The Dean of Students Office noted it would investigate the allegations alongside the University of Arizona Police Department.

title: 5 children found alone in boarded-up house without food or power, police say
text:
DAYTON, Ohio (WHIO) - Police in Ohio are investigating after five children were found living inside a boarded-up house without food or electricity.
Dayton Police responded to a boarded-up, abandoned property around 12:30 p.m. last Thursday for a welfare check. Officers found five children, ranging in age from 4 to 12, living inside the house.
Police say it appears there was no food or power in the house, and no adults were present. Body camera footage shows flies in the house, and in one bedroom, there is a mattress on the floor along with piles of clothes and trash.
The children were taken to the hospital for evaluations. They were then placed in the custody of Montgomery County Children’s Services.
The Dayton Police Department’s Care House Unit is investigating the incident.

title: Man admitted to stabbing woman 15 times in random hiking trail attack, police say
text:
PHOENIX (AZFamily/Gray News) - A man in Arizona accused of murdering a woman on a a hiking trail more than three years ago will likely avoid the death penalty through a plea deal.
Court records said that Zion Teasley pleaded guilty to first-degree murder in court Friday in connection with the death of Lauren Heike.
Heike’s murder gained international attention after she was found stabbed more than a dozen times not far from her apartment, on April 28, 2023.
Days later, police arrested Teasley. Investigators said they linked Teasley to her death through DNA on Heike’s shoe, along with other forensic evidence, including cellphone location data.
Police believed Heike fought off her attacker and escaped but that her injuries were too severe.
Teasley was indicted on 10 counts after investigators said he had sexually explicit images involving a child under 15 years old and possibly shared them.
Authorities said they believe at this time that the attack was random, but added that they “have not concluded our investigation into that.”
He pleaded guilty to one count of sexual exploitation of a minor in that case.
Sentencing in that case is scheduled for Dec. 4.

title: Out-of-state lawmakers join Maine leaders at Ellsworth High to learn student support model
text:
ELLSWORTH, Maine (WABI) - Education leaders and lawmakers from out of state visited Ellsworth High School Tuesday for an inside look at how the school’s bar was raised for student support.
Ellsworth High adopted the Building Assets, Reducing Risks model in 2024. The school saw its graduation rate increase from 73% to 90%.
State policy leaders, BARR center members from Minnesota, and legislators from Oklahoma visited the school today to learn more about how the school implemented the BARR model.
School academic leaders say the model has helped to build better relationships between students and teachers.
“You get to know little, tiny things about them, what their interests are, what life is like at home, what they did last summer, all those things matter to kids, and they matter to teachers, and it just gives us a jumping board to get to know them quickly,” said Ellsworth High Principial Dan Clifford.
Ellsworth High School staff also emphasize the importance of creating a support system for students, especially for newer freshmen adjusting to high school academics.
Since adopting the BARR model, ninth-grade course failure rates fell to 10%.

title: Susan Collins gets more national scrutiny for campaign donations
text:
Donations to Sen. Susan Collins were the subject of another story from a national news outlet Tuesday.
Executives at a company that produces an armored vehicle for the Army donated to political committees supporting Collins, R-Maine, and other appropriators this year after they approved funding for the vehicle — despite Army leaders saying they did not need it, according to a new report from The Intercept.
Monday’s story comes after ProPublica published an investigation in September that focused on how the FBI was probing allegations of a “pay-to-play” scheme involving a convicted former defense contractor and a pro-Collins super PAC before President Donald Trump’s administration ended the investigation in 2025.
The Republican senator and her staff have bashed the recent reporting and have never been charged in connection with any of the allegations. However, the stories have become the source of fresh campaign fodder for former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson and Collins critics amid the high-profile Senate reelection battle between Jackson and Collins.
In February, Congress approved a defense spending bill that included $345 million for the Army to acquire more deliveries of what is known as a Joint Light Tactical Vehicle. Within the next few weeks of that bill’s passage, employees with the vehicle’s maker, AM General, and the company’s PAC gave at least a combined $50,000 to committees supporting Collins, The Intercept reported.
Last year, AM General was ramping up its production line in Indiana when then-Army Secretary Dan Driscoll announced he would cancel its order, saying the additional deliveries of the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle would result in an “excess.” The Intercept noted another appropriator, Rep. Ken Calvert, R-Calif., also received five-figure donations from employees with AM General and the private equity firm that owns it.
Collins’ office said in response to The Intercept’s reporting that Collins did not make the decision to appropriate funds for the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle. It was instead the defense subcommittee chair, Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and vice chair Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del.
Lawmakers in both parties supported the revival of the Army’s order, including the top House Democrat for defense appropriations, Rep. Betty McCollum of Minnesota.
“Sen. Collins was not involved in this decision,” Collins spokesperson Phoebe Keller told The Intercept.
McConnell did not receive donations from employees at AM General or its parent group this election cycle, while the company’s employee PAC gave $2,500 to Coons, The Intercept noted. FEC records show McCollum’s leadership PAC received $5,000 from AM General’s employee PAC last year.
AM General CEO John Chadbourne told the news outlet in an email that the company does not comment on campaign donations, “all of which fully comply with FEC rules and regulations.”
In response to Driscoll’s comment on not needing additional vehicles, a joint statement from the House and Senate, which Collins’ office said was produced by the defense subcommittees, said that the Army had provided “inadequate supporting analysis.”
One concern was that without the efficiencies from a larger order that included the Army, the cost-per-unit price of vehicles that the Marines still wanted would rise, as The Intercept noted.

title: New moms school offers postpartum support
text:
GREENVILLE, S.C. (Aging Untold) — A new program in South Carolina is offering support to women during the postpartum period, connecting them with experts and other mothers navigating early motherhood.
Nicole Parmelee, who has two children, started the New Moms School after her own experience with the fourth trimester, the time after a woman gives birth.
“They prepare you for how to swaddle a baby, how to change a diaper, you know, how to respond to your baby’s cries, but they don’t prepare the mother for how they might feel,” Parmelee said.
A difficult transition
Parmelee said new mothers deal with a lack of sleep, breastfeeding challenges and post-delivery healing.
“It was very isolating,” Parmelee said. “You’re constantly questioning yourself, wondering if you’re doing things the right way, wondering if this is normal.”
Parmelee said she felt there was a lack of support for women during the postpartum period.
“I never knew there was a pelvic floor physical therapist,” Parmelee said. “Everyone tells you when you go to the doctor, if you, ‘Oh, I’m peeing when I sneeze’, or ‘I’m peeing when I laugh or jump’ and they’re like, ‘That’s normal. That happens.’”
Parmelee said she learned that was not normal and that there are ways to help the body heal.
An eight-week program
The New Moms School is an eight-week program that includes support sessions with experts such as a relationship counselor, positive parent coach, therapist, lactation consultant and speech-language pathologist.
“It’s really an investment in the mother because studies have shown that if mom is happy, baby’s happy, family’s happy,” Parmelee said.
The program also connects mothers with each other outside of class through a Facebook group and group chat.
“So not only are we providing them with the experts from the community, but we’re also helping them build their own community,” Parmelee said. “We encourage the moms to get together outside of class. We will put them in a Facebook group so they have contact with each other, we’ll, you know, get a group chat going.”
“That’s just women supporting other women, and we really need more of that,” Parmelee said.

title: ‘He had a big heart’: Family mourns 15-year-old killed in downtown Las Vegas shooting
text:
LAS VEGAS (KVVU/Gray News) — A family is mourning the loss of their 15-year-old son who was killed in a shooting in a downtown Las Vegas arts district.
The family of the teen killed in Friday night’s shooting identified him as 15-year-old Carth Onasi Jacobs-Rodgers. The teen’s stepmother said he was a sophomore at Desert Pines High School.
She described him as smart, brave and strong-willed, the oldest of nine siblings, who loved his sisters and little brother, making people laugh, boxing, basketball and video games.
“He had a big heart... He was goofy — when he laughed you couldn’t help but laugh too... He is loved by many and will be missed by all of us,” she said in a statement to KVVU.
The family has set up an online fundraiser to help with funeral costs.
Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department said officers were near South Main Street and West Charleston Boulevard around 10:17 p.m. Friday during a community First Friday event when they heard shots in the area. Officers found two gunshot victims in a crowd, then a third. All three were taken to a hospital. Jacobs-Rodgers later died from his injuries.
Homicide Lt. Robert Price said the two survivors have non-life-threatening injuries.
Detectives determined a fight occurred between several individuals. At some point, an unknown male produced a firearm and began shooting, striking multiple people, police said. The suspect fled prior to officers arriving.
Mayor Pro Tem Olivia Diaz expressed her sympathy with the victims and attendees from the First Friday shooting.
“My heart is with the victims, victims’ families, and First Friday attendees affected by last night’s shooting in the Arts District,” she said. “Thank you to all the LVMPD officers, first responders, First Friday staff, community partners and volunteers who jumped into action to help guide people to safety.”
The First Friday Foundation said it is “heartbroken” and “grateful” for the law enforcement’s swift response. The Arts District Neighborhood Association, which works closely with the foundation, also expressed sadness and pledged to help make First Friday safer moving forward.
“We hold the victims, their loved ones, and all those affected close to our hearts,” the association said.

title: Cornell brings in ex-DOJ official Sally Yates to review school’s handling of sex assault claims
text:
Cornell brings in ex-DOJ official Sally Yates to review school’s handling of sex assault claims
A former high-ranking Department of Justice official will look at how Cornell handles sexual misconduct complaints, university trustees announced Tuesday as they tried to address an outpouring of anger over allegations of a 2024 gang rape at a fraternity house.
Sally Yates, who was a deputy attorney general in the Obama administration, will spearhead the review, the trustees said in an announcement. The assessment is to include how the Ivy League university investigates reports of sexual assault and sexual harassment, what support students get, how the disciplinary process works, campus police responses and oversight of fraternities, sororities and other student organizations.
The announcement comes after days of outrage and demonstrations over Cornell’s response to a complaint from a woman known publicly only as Jane Doe, who told campus police in November 2024 that she had been sexually assaulted by multiple Chi Phi fraternity brothers the month before after being pressured into drinking and taking drugs.
No criminal charges have been filed. The Chi Phi chapter at Cornell was shut down, and the Ivy League university has said it expelled some students and suspended others.
She sued the university, seven former students, the fraternity and others last month. The suit put a new, nationwide spotlight on the allegations and how the campus police, university and local prosecutor had reacted.
New York’s attorney general is now conducting a criminal investigation, and the state’s governor called for an independent review of Cornell’s handling of the matter — the review that Yates now will lead.
Cornell students, professors and others thronged a campus plaza Monday to protest the university’s response to the matter.
Yates had a decades-long career at the Justice Department, serving for years as the top federal prosecutor in Atlanta and later as a deputy attorney general.
She achieved particular prominence in January 2017 when, as acting attorney general in the early days of the Trump administration, she directed Justice Department attorneys to not defend the constitutionality of President Donald Trump’s refugee and immigration ban. She was swiftly fired, with Trump accusing her of betrayal and insubordination.
Yates also generated headlines when it emerged that, in a conversation days before her departure, she had expressed alarm to the Trump White House about contacts that Trump’s new national security adviser, Michael Flynn, had had with the Russian ambassador during the presidential transition period. Flynn was later fired.
Yates has been in private practice since her departure from the Justice Department. Her practice at the King & Spalding law firm includes conducting independent investigations for outside organizations and companies.
Among her investigations was a high-profile inquiry into alleged abuse and misconduct, including claims of harassment and coercion, at the National Women’s Soccer League. The investigation concluded in 2022 with a finding of systemic abuse.

title: Chicago-bound British Airways flight makes emergency landing after dropping 27,000 feet
text:
Chicago-bound British Airways flight makes emergency landing after dropping 27,000 feet
A British Airways flight bound for Chicago from London, England, made an emergency landing nearly five hours after it descended 27,000 feet in minutes due to a technical issue, according to several reports.
Related video: AUDIO: 2 planes with the same flight number avoid possible disaster thanks to quick-thinking controller
Flight BA2PD departed the London airport at 11:50 a.m. local time Monday and dropped 27,000 feet roughly a half hour into the flight, People Magazine reported. Officials said the plane dropped thousands of feet in minutes.
Once the plane was over Ireland, it quickly descended 9,000 feet before turning back and returning to Heathrow.
According to a FlightAware map, the plane did not immediately land. It instead "zig-zagged over England and St. George's Canal before safely landing at Heathrow." The plane remained in the air for nearly five hours.
"The aircraft landed safely after our highly-trained pilots returned to Heathrow following a technical issue," the New York Post said in reference to a statement reportedly issued by British Airways. "Customers disembarked the aircraft normally and our teams are working to get their travel plans back on track as quickly as possible."
No injuries have been reported.

title: Heartbreak for Bates Football: 22-21 Loss to Tufts on Parents’ Weekend
text:
Bates led Tufts after three quarters on Parents’ Weekend, but the Bobcats fell short in the 4th quarter, losing 22-21 on the back of a last-minute blocked field goal. The defeat drops Bates to 0-3 on the season after a 43-0 loss last week against Trinity.
The first quarter offered an early warning as the Bobcats fumbled early off a designed QB run to Zachary Hurd ’30 at the 5:15 mark. A face mask later extended the Jumbos drive leading to an opening touchdown, as they cashed in off a run play resulting in a lead at the end of the second quarter.
The second quarter brought one. Tufts went for it on fourth down at 13:27 and converted, then scored a touchdown off a halfback slip screen. The Bobcats responded with a drive built on a quarterback sneak, a designed run for a first down, a 20-yard throw to Jeff Vidou’28 and a back-shoulder catch by Riley Provencher’29 that put them in the red zone.
A substitution penalty pushed the Bobcats back to the nine , but a trick play moved them to the four, and they got within a foot of the end zone off a quarterback draw. A turnover on downs at 3:30 stopped the drive. The Bobcats defense got the ball back with an interception at 1:50, and Jack Gilmore’29 punched in a quarterback draw at 1:36 to cut the deficit. Tufts intercepted a Bates pass at 0:43 to end the half, leaving the Bobcats down 14-7.
At halftime, reactions in the stands ranged from frustration to optimism. Noah Barrett ’30 pointed to the Bobcats’ late defensive push in the second quarter as a reason for hope.
“Bates picked up later on in the second as we got two interceptions and we also got in the red zone once, but I think overall it’s been a pretty good game,” Barrett said. He added that improving the passing game could make the difference. “I think we can improve more on our throwing game, we can win this game easily.”
Miles Lesser ’30 said mental mistakes were costing the Bobcats. “It’s been a close game. They’ve looked okay. The mental mistakes are what’s been costing the Bates team,” Lesser said. “It feels like they should be up or at least tied 14-14.”
He said the defense needed to tighten up. “They have to stop letting number one just run through them constantly. And instead, like, wrap them up.”
The Bobcats opened the second half with a 40-yard strike to Provencher. Bates pounded it in for its second score at 10:33 of the third quarter. The defense held after a Tufts drive stalled at the 50 on a sack by Camden Zambrowicz ’27 at 6:31.
After that Gilmore connected to Vidou on a 25-yard strike to keep the Bobcats driving at 4:47, and Bates took the lead at 3:01 in the third quarter on a 25-yard touchdown pass to Cole Piaseczynski ’29 putting the Bobcats up 21-14.
Fourth-quarter drives would decide the game. The Bobcats turned the ball over on downs at the 45 after the end of the third quarter. Tufts drove, but a sack by Liam Keaney’29 stalled the series, and a second sack by Shawn Bauman’30 pushed the Jumbos into a third and long. Facing a critical fourth and seven, Tufts turned the ball over on downs. But a quarterback injury led to a punt for the Bobcats.
Tufts then got a break when a miracle throw-away pass resulted in a 30-yard gain. The Jumbos kept driving, and a touchdown with a two-point conversion put Tufts ahead 22-21.
Bates had one more chance. A broken play turned into a 30-yard reception for Ryan Gleason ’27, and another strike moved the Bobcats to the Tufts 25 with 33 seconds left. A game-winning field goal attempt was blocked.
After the game, Luke Hart ’30 praised the effort. “I was really proud of the Bobcats’ fight. You know, the ending was a little disappointing, but, you know, I can’t do much about a blocked field goal. ”
Student spectator Simon Murphy ‘30 said the loss was particularly frustrating after Bates remained competitive for most of the game. “That was heartbreaking, honestly. I don’t know how that even happened, but next time we got him,” Murphy said. He added that the positive was that the team was doing okay for most of the night. The negative was “the entire fourth quarter.”
Head coach Matt Coyne said the program has been dealing with injuries but lots of young players have stepped up. He said the team “competed very well” against Tufts. And highlighted the performance of Gilmore, who he noted is essentially a freshman after losing last season to injury.
Coyne added that this week they “weren’t happy with our performance in week two.” He added that there are “things we can get better at,” and said the focus is on “how do you just keep getting better.” He wants the team to carry the great preparation and focus against Tufts into the lead up versus Williams.
The loss extends the Bobcats’ winless start to 0-3, but the performance against Tufts showed heart after last week’s shutout. Penalties and fourth-quarter execution will be points of emphasis as the team regroups in practice this week.

title: US citizen who was shot by immigration agent from Maine in Chicago files lawsuit alleging he fired from behind
text:
(AP) - An American citizen shot by a Customs and Border Protection agent one year ago during a sweeping immigration crackdown in Chicago filed a lawsuit against the federal government on Monday, alleging the agent lied about the shooting and fired into her vehicle from behind.
Federal prosecutors initially accused Marimar Martinez, then 30, of using her vehicle to strike and box in agent Charles Exum’s SUV on Chicago’s southwest side on Oct. 4, 2025, during “Operation Midway Blitz.” Exum then exited his car and opened fire, leaving Martinez with seven gunshot wounds.
In the month after the shooting, prosecutors filed to dismiss the charges in a dramatic reversal of the closely watched case in the nation’s third-largest city.
Agent fired into rear of car, attorneys say
Her lawyers said Monday that they commissioned an expert to analyze bullet trajectories and her injuries and determined Exum wasn’t in the path of her car when he opened fire. They said he had walked several feet toward her car, contrary to statements he made to the FBI, and fired off five shots in less than a second, the last from the rear side of her vehicle.
“Charles Exum told the FBI agent on that day, within hours of the shooting, that Marimar was driving her car directly at him, that he shot her five times through the windshield, and that he ceased firing once he was no longer in the path of the vehicle. Those are three objective lies that you’ll see here today,” said one of her attorneys, Chris Parente.
Parente said there were only three bullet holes in Martinez’ windshield on the right passenger side, which indicated Martinez wasn’t driving toward the agent. He said the fourth shot was fired through the front passenger side window, adding another bullet hole in the back of Martinez’ car seat showed the agent fired the fifth shot from behind her.
“In what world can a U.S. law enforcement officer stand behind a car and fire his Glock service weapon through the rear passenger window at a young woman who’s crouched over the steering wheel?” Parente said.
CBP said in a statement to The Associated Press in response to the suit that Exum had been placed on administrative leave. Use-of-force incidents are “thoroughly investigated, reviewed, and presented” to an independent board, it added.
Exum is not a defendant in the lawsuit against the federal government, which was filed under the Federal Tort Claims Act and does not allow for lawsuits against individual agents. It was not known where Exum could be reached.
Body-worn camera footage from another agent in Exum’s vehicle before the shooting captured the agents saying it was “time to get aggressive” and making other profanity-laced comments encouraging violence, according to the complaint.
Martinez taken from hospital with bullet holes ‘leaking blood,’ suit says
The FBI arrested Martinez, taking her out of the hospital just hours after the shooting when she was “wheelchair bound and her bullet holes were leaking blood through her bandages,” according to the lawsuit. A judge ordered her release two days after her arrest.
Messages released by Martinez’ attorneys in February showed that former head of Border Patrol Greg Bovino had praised Exum for his “excellent service in Chicago” after the shooting. Other messages they released showed agents in a group chat congratulating Exum and calling him a “legend.”
Martinez was one several people shot in their cars by federal agents during President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown. An immigration agent shot a Venezuelan delivery driver in his car in Austin, Texas, last month, and another shot a Colombian driver in Biddeford, Maine, in July. The Trump administration has at times justified such shootings as self-defense against people allegedly weaponizing their vehicles.
Martinez appeared with her attorneys at a news conference Monday, saying the various shootings spurred her to file suit.
“If I don’t, then who else, you know? Look at what happened to Renee and all these victims,” she said, referring to Renee Good, a woman shot dead in her vehicle by a federal agent in Minneapolis in January.
“What’s happening is not normal. We shouldn’t stay here and normalize what’s happening,” she said.

title: Frost and freeze advisories issued for coastal Maine; more seasonable conditions expected to end the week
text:
Sub-freezing temperatures Tuesday night into Wednesday are expected to give way to a more seasonable end to the first full week of October in Maine.
The National Weather Service placed all of coastal Maine under a frost advisory from midnight until 8 a.m. Wednesday, with expected lows between 30 and 35 degrees. Meanwhile, interior Cumberland and Androscoggin counties were placed under a freeze warning, with temperatures as low as 25 degrees expected in the same timeframe.
Areas further inland, including Fryeburg, Rumford, Rangeley and Jackman, were also expected to see temperatures fall to between 25 and 30 degrees overnight, according to the weather service.
Despite the equally cold temperatures elsewhere in the state, Hunter Tubbs, a meteorologist at the weather service’s Gray office, explained that the advisories are limited to coastal regions as the growing season remains active there until Oct. 11.
“Some areas are already past the growing season, so we don’t have (advisories) out for those areas,” he said in a phone call Tuesday.
He said this is around the time when meteorologists would expect the region to begin experiencing frosty overnight temperatures. The weather service advises residents to cover or bring inside any sensitive outdoor plants.
Tubbs said Tuesday night into Wednesday would likely see the coldest temperatures of the week, with the remainder of the week looking more seasonable.
“That’s just because we had a strong cold front that came through, and that allowed for strong northwesterly winds to bring down colder air from Canada,” Tubbs explained.
Wednesday’s highs are expected to be in the high 50s and low 60s across southern and central Maine, according to the weather service.
But temperatures are expected to rise Thursday, with some areas, including Portland and Lewiston, slated to be as warm as 70 degrees. Tubbs said the projected uptick in temperatures is thanks to warmer air pushing in from the southwest.
Then, the weather service forecasts high temperatures will dip back down to the low 60s — and even to the low 50s in some western Maine communities — Friday and Saturday. Things are expected to begin warming up again on Sunday, with highs potentially reaching 70 degrees once more on Monday.
Meanwhile, low temperatures are expected to remain fairly steady: Southeastern regions, including Greater Portland, can expect lows in the mid-to-low 40s Thursday through the beginning of next week, while areas farther north and west can expect lows in the mid-to-high 30s.
Some showers could be in the mix across the western mountains late this week, according to the weather service, but Tubbs said it isn’t expected to amount to much.
“As of right now, it doesn’t look like anything significant in terms of rainfall,” he said Tuesday.
On Tuesday morning, the Mount Washington Observatory reported the first measurable snowfall of the season atop New Hampshire’s tallest peak, with just over a half-inch of snow accumulating in a 24-hour period. It noted that a wind gust of 110 miles per hour was recorded.

title: Woman suddenly fighting for her life after feeling pain on family hiking trip, receiving rare diagnosis
text:
OSHKOSH, Wis. (WBAY/Gray News) - A Wisconsin family says they are working to get their beloved family member home after she suddenly became hospitalized during a family hiking trip in Utah.
Chris Kamke beat breast cancer over the summer and last month left for Utah with her husband, Kendall, and son, Kyle, to visit national parks.
On Sept. 19, the family said they hiked the Narrows in Zion National Park.
However, the next day at Emerald Pools, Kamke said her hips and legs hurt badly. The pain got worse. By the time they drove to Bryce Canyon, she couldn’t sit, stand or lie down.
“So, Kendall and Kyle decided that they should take her in to be seen. So, they drove about 30 minutes to a hospital in Panguitch, Utah,” Tammy Thomas, Kamke’s sister, said.
Doctors first thought it was the heat. When Kamke struggled to breathe, they discovered bacterial pneumonia, according to the family.
Kamke was airlifted to another Utah hospital on Sept. 20, where her condition has since worsened.
“By the time I got there on Friday, she was completely non-responsive, and has been since then. So, since Sept. 25, she has been comatose,” Thomas said.
Kamke has since been diagnosed with neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, a rare autoimmune disease impacting one in 250,000 people.
Loved ones said she is currently paralyzed, in a coma and on a ventilator.
Thomas added that the family could never have seen something like this coming.
“That’s the really strange thing because Chris was extremely active. She walked, they kayaked, they biked, they golfed. I mean, Chris is 65, and she still plays softball with her softball team,” Thomas said.
The family said they want Kamke back to Wisconsin so she can be surrounded by loved ones. But a hospital transport costs $50,000, and insurance won’t cover it.
So, the family is working with the nonprofit Grace on Wings, where crews volunteer and the family pays for jet fuel, estimated at $27,000 to $28,000.
The family has started a GoFundMe to hope to fly her back within the next week, which has helped raise more than $25,000.

title: Dunkin’ Announces ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Drinks and Snacks
text:
Dunkin’ Announces Massive Lineup of ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Drinks and Donuts
We’re in the endgame now all right ...
You would expect nothing less than an all-out marketing and promotional tie-in onslaught for a film as massive (and expensive) as Avengers: Doomsday. And sure enough, with the film still more than two months away, the deluge has begun with Dunkin’ announcing an Avengers-sized lineup of beverages and donuts tied to the film.
First let’s look at the treats. They are...
- Doomsday Donut: The fan-favorite Brownie Batter Donut returns with chocolate icing and green and chocolate sprinkles inspired by Doctor Doom.
- Avenging Donut: A cotton candy-filled donut topped with vanilla-flavored icing and red, yellow and blue sprinkles representing the Avengers, X-Men and Fantastic Four.
Cotton candy filled donut ... wow. That does sound like some sort of diabolical invention of a mad super-villain. There are also Munchkin versions of both of these. (Doctor Doom famously loves Munchkins.)
READ MORE: I Ate the Weirdest Food Inspired By Movies in History
There are only two donuts — but there are six different drinks. Start prepping your bladder now. They are...
- Iced Captain’ccino: Espresso, caramel flavor and coffee milk, lightly blended and served over ice for a bold, frothy sip worthy of any hero.
- Clobbered Cloud Latte: Espresso, whole milk and toasted white chocolate flavor topped with Cookie Butter Cold Foam and crumbles inspired by The Thing’s rocky exterior.
- Wakandan Daydream Refresher: Berry Clementine Refresher, raspberry flavor and oatmilk topped with Purple Marshmallow Cold Foam for a bright, creamy sip inspired by Black Panther.
- Optic Blast Lemonade: Sweet-tart lemonade charged with blue raspberry flavor and inspired by Cyclops.
- Doom’s Orders Energy: Green Apple Dunkin' Zero, sparkling water and Purple Marshmallow Cold Foam create a sweet, tart and fizzy sip inspired by Doctor Doom.
- Doom Cloud Latte: Espresso, whole milk, mocha swirl and vanilla flavors topped with Sweet Cold Foam and cocoa powder. Dark, velvety and Doom-worthy.
Okay first of all: The Captain’ccino is a good name. Good job, Dunkin’. That made me laugh.
Second of all: It is extremely funny to imagine Doctor Doom ordering a cloud latte. “YOU THERE! INSOLENT WELP! MAKE DOOM HIS CLOUD LATTE! Oh, and can Doom get a double shot of that Sweet Cold Foam? OF COURSE HE CAN! HE IS DOOM! ALL KNEEL BEFORE HIM!”
Dunkin’ will also have a bunch of Avengers merch as well, like a Doctor Doom-shaped Munchkin tin. (I told you Doctor Doom loves Munchkins.)
Dunkin will also be selling “Avengers: Doomsday-Themed Glove Cup Sleeves” which ... appear to be a drink sleeve with a built-in superhero glove, based on Doctor Doom, Black Panther, Mister Fantastic and Captain America? You think Doctor Doom would allow a cold drink to make his hand uncomfortable? Never!
This is a lot of stuff. And it’s all just from one restaurant. And we don’t think this is the only one of these tie-in menus coming for Doomsday, do we? I sure don’t.
Dunkin’s Avengers: Doomsday food, drinks, and gloves will go on sale on November 4. Truly, that will be doomsday for my blood sugar levels.

title: Maine should vote against Trump
text:
As we cast votes in Maine’s U.S. Senate race this year, we should remember that President Trump has asked voters to pretend that he’s on the ballot.
For once, I agree with him. Trump’s domestic and foreign policies have been disastrous, with tariffs, rising inflation and and war in Iran at the top of a long list. He has indicated that he wants to lead like a dictator, focused on relentless attacks on voting and election results and expressing admiration for Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Kim Jong Un.
Although Sen. Susan Collins holds a position of influence in the Senate, she has not provided a meaningful check on Trump’s power. She voted to advance the “big, beautiful bill” then voted against it. She voted in support of the war in Iran then voted against it. She has also voted for the vast majority of Trump’s dismal administration and judicial nominations.
Donald Trump is on the ballot. Let’s vote against him and Collins, and for Troy Jackson.
Daniel Hildreth
Falmouth

title: Historic connection to Boston Tea Party recognized in Lamoine
text:
LAMOINE, Maine (WABI) - As part of America’s 250th anniversary, historians are making five stops across Maine this week to recognize people from the past who have direct connections to the Boston Tea Party. One commemorative marker ceremony Tuesday afternoon was held at Forest Hill Cemetery in Lamoine.
“We are recognizing Elkanah Young as an eyewitness to history, someone connected to the Boston Tea Party of December 16, 1773,” said Evan O’Brien, Creative Manager at the Boston Tea Party Ships and Museum.
Elkanah Young was born in 1745 in Eastham, Massachusetts. When Young died in 1832, he was buried at the Lamoine cemetery.
“We know that he was intimately involved in Boston at the time. He had moved to Maine, and we’re not entirely certain, though, why in 1773 he returned. More than likely, he would have been on board one of his ships, and he was in port in Boston at the time and got caught up in the fervor,” said O’Brien.
Attending the ceremony were many historians, as well as descendants of Young. One descendant was Keith Young of Massachusetts, who says he had researched Elkanah for many years.
“I didn’t realize growing up that the rest of my ancestors are all here in this little, tiny cemetery,” said Young, “I am just very, very pleased that the Boston Tea Party and Ships Museum has made an official recognition on him.”
Since 2018, The Boston Tea Party Ships and Museum, in partnership with Revolution 250, have traveled around the U.S. to recognize those with connections to the Boston Tea Party, bringing attention to stories that have been passed down for generations
“We want to talk about the Boston Tea Party. We’re going to talk about Hancock and Adams, both Samuel and John. We’re going to talk about William Mullineaux, all the names that people should know, but we’re also here to talk about people like Elkanah Young, who is not known to many except his family,” said Jonathan Lane, Executive Director of Revolution 250.
“This whole idea of story and sharing family story over the years is critical to our American experience and our American history,” said O’Brien.
“We ought to be proud of our heritage,” said Young, ”History is alive, and you are part of it.”
On Monday, Lemuel Trescott was honored with a plaque in Lubec. Wednesday, a ceremony on Islesboro will honor Joseph Boardman. Two other ceremonies will take place this week in Bowdoin and Portland.
