title: 40 miles for 40 acres: Maryland minister walks from Brunswick to Augusta for reparations
text:
RICHMOND —A little more than halfway through his trek in Maine on Tuesday, the Rev. Dr. Robert Turner already knew the walk would be physically and mentally taxing.
“The walks are always long. It’s never a walk where I’m just at the end doing cartwheels. My body is sore. But it’s also a spiritual moment for me. I reflect, I meditate. It’s like a pilgrimage. But it’s also a call to action,” Turner explained.
Turner, who is the pastor at the Empowerment Temple AME Church in Baltimore, was walking about 38 miles from Brunswick to Augusta to advocate for reparations to the descendants of enslaved Africans, a continuation of his previous initiative 40 Miles for 40 Acres, where he walked from Baltimore to Washington, D.C., each month to highlight the broken promise of Union Gen. William T. Sherman’s 40 acres and a mule.
Turner started out at the John Brown Russworm African American Center in Brunswick at 5 a.m., traveling north through Topsham along the Kennebec River, and he expected to reach the State Capitol in Augusta around 5:40 p.m. Outside of Richmond, he walked under a cloudless sky with wind blowing off the river through the rolling roads, holding a sign that read “REPARATIONS NOW” and sporting a reflective orange-and-yellow jacket.
Tuesday’s walk held additional significance. It falls on the 185th anniversary of Maine’s first Colored Convention, the 1841 gathering where African Americans met in Portland to discuss abolition and racial equality across Maine. Turner dedicated his walk to the late Gerald E. Talbot, Maine’s first Black legislator and a civil rights advocate.
“You have so much that has happened here that needs repair from, and the evidence of the suffering is still being felt on Oct. 6, 2026,” Turner said.
Turner cited historical events of oppression and racism in Maine, such as the state’s involvement with the slave trade and the history of Malaga Island. He spoke about continued racial disparities in the state, where Black people are more likely to be incarcerated, underhoused and under the poverty line.
After moving from Tulsa, Oklahoma, to Baltimore in 2021, he decided to walk the 42.9 miles to Washington, D.C., to call for reparations. Since then, he has done that walk 40 times, once every month, and then expanded the cause to a national level with walks in Alabama, North Carolina and Virginia. Maine is his ninth state and he plans to walk in all 50.
“I’ve walked in the ice, the snow, the rain, the thunderstorms, you name it, I’ve walked. I’ve never postponed a walk due to weather,” he said. “So I’ve walked in snowstorms, I’ve walked in weather advisories … I’ve walked when cities were closed down. God has kept me these 49 times. I’ve slipped, but I’ve never fallen.”
Turner’s choice to start his walk in Brunswick holds additional historical significance, being the place where Harriet Beecher Stowe wrote “Uncle Tom’s Cabin,” the anti-slavery novel. John Brown Russwurm was one of the first Black college graduates in the United States, graduating from Bowdoin College in 1826; he eventually helped found the nation’s first Black newspaper.
Walking up Route 24 outside of Richmond, Turner said he’d received both positive and negative reactions. Some responded enthusiastically to the cause. One woman stopped him alongside the road to question why he is not fighting for other groups such as Irish Americans.
“I’m not against anybody who is suffering from getting reparations,” he said.
Turner said his plan, when he reached Augusta, was to lay a wreath of 400 roses down on the state capital to represent 400 years of oppression. He planned to pray at the State Capitol, and read Chapter 61 from the Book of Isaiah in the Bible, which he reads at the end of every walk.
“Then I leave. I leave physically, but spiritually praying and politically advocating through petitions, through emails, through phone calls for repair being done in Maine,” he said.
His next state to walk is South Carolina. He plans to organize his future walks by finding historical dates in the state he will be walking in, hopefully doing the northern states in the summer and the southern states in the winter. He urges each state he walks through to repair the damage that has been done in history.
“I think Maine, by doing reparations, which is the truest form of justice that America has never seen, can help lead the nation. … Maine was one of the first states to abolish slavery,” Turner said. “Maine could also lead the nation as one of the first states to issue reparations.”

title: Woman Fears Boyfriend Wants to Marry Her for Her Money
text:
A woman on Reddit is worried her boyfriend may want to marry her for more than love — and money could be playing a bigger role than she realized.
The 26-year-old said she and her 29-year-old boyfriend have been together for about a year and a half and are discussing marriage and eventually living together.
They're also in couples counseling, where a recent conversation about finances left her questioning his motives.
Uncomfortable Questions About Money
During the session, her boyfriend said living alone was becoming "financially difficult" and "progressively difficult" on his current income. He explained that living together would allow them to "share the burden together."
READ MORE: 'Fed-Up' Woman Gives Boyfriend of Seven Years Deadline to Propose
That prompted their therapist to ask whether he was saying there was a financial benefit to him from living with his girlfriend. She said yes, that's how it sounded to her.
Her boyfriend clarified that he meant combining their households would be financially beneficial for both of them.
Her Boyfriend Has Made Jokes About Her Money Before
The explanation might have been enough — except she said there had been other comments that made her suspicious.
Her boyfriend has jokingly called her the "breadwinner" since she got a promotion, joked about her pulling up in a future Lexus to pick him up and once joked about wanting an older woman to take care of him.
She stressed that she doesn't think he's planning to quit his job or have her support him.
READ MORE: Chelsea Handler Calls Out ‘Cheap’ Celebrity Chef After Bad Date
Instead, she's wondering whether her higher income is simply part of the appeal of marrying her.
He knows she makes more money than he does, although he doesn't know her exact salary. She also lives in a wealthy town more than an hour away from him, while currently living with her family.
She pointed out that when she told him she wouldn't live with him unless they were married, he brought up proposing and asked what kind of ring she wanted.
Now she's wondering whether she's seeing a genuine red flag or reading too much into a perfectly normal conversation about combining finances.
Reddit Has Some Advice About His Motives
One user suggested a prenup and a clear agreement about how much each person would contribute to their household, arguing that his reaction would tell her plenty.
Another commenter offered a less suspicious take: Living together is more economical than maintaining two separate households, and recognizing that doesn't automatically mean he sees her as a financial resource.
READ MORE: Man Breaks $400 Worth of Wife’s Treasures Thanks to ‘Booby Traps'
"If he cannot live within his means at his current income," the commenter wrote, "there is a decent chance he cannot within yours (jointly) either."
Their advice? Have the uncomfortable conversation now — with actual numbers, a budget and clear expectations — before making the relationship legally and financially permanent.

title: 2 young children found starved to death in home were dead for several days, authorities say
text:
LADSON, S.C. (WCSC/Gray News) — South Carolina authorities say two children who were found inside a Ladson-area home late last month had been dead for several days before they were discovered.
Charleston County authorities identified the children as Emory Deacon, 2, and Harlow Deacon, 15 months old. Charleston County coroner Bobbi Jo O’Neal said they died of starvation and dehydration due to neglect.
Justine May, the children’s mother and described as their primary caregiver, was charged in the case with two counts of homicide by child abuse.
According to the Charleston County Sheriff’s Office, deputies had responded to numerous calls at the Pinewood Drive residence before ultimately finding the two children dead during a welfare check at the home.
The previous calls to the home were said to have included welfare checks and visits coordinated with the South Carolina Department of Social Services and the South Carolina Department of Mental Health Mobile Crisis Unit.
Authorities said deputies made contact with May and the children in August and again several more times in September, noting they observed no signs of concern during those visits.
Last Tuesday, authorities said they were called back to the home after a 911 call came through that morning asking deputies to conduct a welfare check on the two young girls after they had not been seen, with their mother acting differently while walking around the neighborhood by herself.
“I’m just concerned because she didn’t have her kids, and nobody has seen her kids,” the caller told the Charleston County 911 dispatcher. “She was walking down the road today, and she didn’t have her babies, and that’s not like her.”
When deputies arrived at the home that afternoon, they said May exited the house and was crying and speaking incoherently. Upon entering, that’s when they saw the two children dead.
May was taken into custody.
According to affidavits, after being read her Miranda rights, May told detectives that she had spent the previous two weeks in a “blur,” saying she could not remember the last time she fed Emory and Harlow or gave them anything to drink.
Authorities said May told detectives that she believed her children were dead because they did not eat. She reportedly told deputies that she knew that not feeding her children was neglectful and confirmed she had been the only one present at home and was the sole caregiver for the girls over the last few weeks.
May remained jailed at the Al Cannon Detention Center.

title: Remembering a beloved family farm dog
text:
In 1948, my maternal grandparents, Florian and Lucille Yeaton, brought home Bonnie, the runt of a border collie litter purchased in Farmington. This scrappy pup caught Grampa’s attention by fearlessly wrestling with littermates twice her size.
They took her to their Mercer farmhouse, where she slept on a horsehair blanket behind the wood cookstove. However, their hopes for a collie to herd sheep and dairy cows dimmed as Bonnie’s weight plummeted.
As a last resort, Grammy Lue wrapped Bonnie in the blanket and, in a gamble, placed her in the pigpen with a 250-pound sow nursing six piglets.
“We’ll know by day’s end whether the sow takes to her,” Grammy said to Grampa.
For 10 days, Bonnie nursed alongside the pink piglets, thriving under her unlikely foster mother’s warmth and care. Her weight — scarcely three pounds — more than doubled. Within two months, she was racing between the farmhouse and the barn.
My grandparents initially wondered if such an unusual start would leave a lasting mark. It did, but not the one they feared. Bonnie matured into an extraordinarily intelligent working dog, consistently proving her capabilities in protecting her family and livestock.
One summer afternoon in 1953, my 5-year-old brother, Robert, came face-to-face with a rabid fox behind the barn. Bonnie didn’t attack. Instead, she steadily nipped at Robert’s heels, driving him back toward the farmhouse while keeping her body between him and the fox. Grampa killed the fox with his shotgun.
A year later, Robert and our cousin, Cheryl, accidentally started a barn fire while playing with matches. Bonnie’s frantic barking alerted the family before anyone smelled smoke. Grampa fought the flames with pails of rainwater from the cistern, Mother smothered them with wet blankets, and Grammy herded the frightened livestock into the pasture. Together, they saved the barn.
But Bonnie’s greatest feat occurred on a sweltering August day in 1958.
While wading in the Sandy River to cool off, my 6-year-old twin brother, Don, was swept into the deep channel. Mother dove in after him but couldn’t dog-paddle fast enough to close the gap as he drifted downstream.
Bonnie understood the river’s currents better than either of them. Instead of immediately jumping in, she sprinted along the high bank, tracking Don as he fought to keep his head above water. Nearly 300 feet downriver, she launched off the bank, entered the current just ahead of the hairpin rapids, clamped onto his shirt collar, and hauled him onto a gravel bar.
The next morning, Don, still shaken, sat beside Grampa in the milking parlor. From his three-legged stool, Grampa squirted warm milk to the waiting barn cats and Bonnie, as he did every morning. Watching Bonnie lick her whiskers, my twin laughed through his tears and pulled her close.
The day before, she had saved his life — that morning, she helped restore his spirit.
Age never dulled her instincts. Shortly after midnight in October 1961, Don and I woke to growls rising from the pumpkin pine floorboards at the foot of our bed.
“Why’s Bonnie growling?” we yelled into the dark.
“Might be a bear in the barnyard,” Grampa answered from the adjacent bedroom. “She found fresh tracks in the orchard yesterday.”
He lit a kerosene lantern and retrieved the 12-gauge from above the kitchen door. Bonnie paced and whined at the latch. The second it lifted, she shot through the doorway and bolted toward the pigpen, her dark silhouette framed by a huge harvest moon.
“You boys go back to bed,” Grammy barked.
We obeyed but opened our bedroom window to listen. The hogs were squealing, Bonnie was barking, and a single shotgun blast cracked across the farm. Then everything went deadly quiet.
The next 10 minutes felt like an hour before Grampa and Bonnie returned to the kitchen.
“She chased a bear clean out of the pigpen,” he said, still catching his breath. “The pen door’s stove to hell, but the hogs are fine.”
Two nights later, a few miles from our farm, Ralph True shot the same bear after it killed one of his sheep. The boar weighed 490 pounds.
“Its front paws,” he told Grampa, “were the size of dinner plates.”
When cancer took Bonnie in April 1962, Grampa wrapped her one last time in the ratty horsehair blanket she’d slept on her entire life and carried her up the knoll to the apple orchard — her favorite spot on the farm. He dug her grave that night by moonlight, working past the frost line with a pickaxe and shovel. The next afternoon, my three siblings and I picked yellow daffodils from the south side of the farmhouse and planted them on her grave.
That evening, my heartbroken 5-year-old sister, Gale, barely ate her supper. When the meal was over, she quietly walked behind the cookstove and scraped her plate into Bonnie’s enamel bowl.
In the morning, her eyes lit up at the sight of an empty bowl.
Years later, E.B. White gave me the words for what Bonnie meant to our family: “A really companionable and indispensable dog is an accident of nature. You can’t get it by breeding for it, and you can’t buy it with money.”
Ron Joseph of Sidney is the author of “Bald Eagles, Bear Cubs, and Hermit Bill: Memories of a Maine Wildlife Biologist,” published by Islandport Press.

Windy & Cool Day Ahead; Much Calmer Wednesday
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Windy conditions will be the main focus for the day today as strong low pressure spins to our northeast and high pressure builds in from the west. The pressure gradient over the state will remain tight resulting in a strong northwest wind gusting to 40-50 MPH for areas from Greenville to Millinocket northward and 30-40 MPH gusts possible elsewhere throughout the day. Isolated power outages will be possible. It’ll be a very fall-like day with a very dry, crisp feeling air mass in place. We’ll see a partly to mostly sunny sky for the day with high temperatures in the mid-40s to low 50s north and low to mid-50s elsewhere. The strong winds will diminish tonight... becoming light and variable as the night progresses. With light winds and clear to partly cloudy skies expected... temperatures will be colder tonight with lows in the low to mid-30s for most locales. As a result... we’ll likely see widespread frost... especially away from the coast.
Wednesday will be a much quieter day as high pressure builds in... allowing the pressure gradient to relax... resulting in a much lighter wind. A warm front approaching the state will bring us more clouds and a slight chance for a few isolated showers... mainly across the north. Expect a partly to mostly cloudy sky and more seasonable temperatures with highs in the mid-50s to low 60s. A cold front is forecast to move through during the day Thursday. The front doesn’t have a whole lot of moisture with it so at this point... just expecting a slight chance for a few showers Thursday as the front moves through. Otherwise expect a decent day with partly to mostly sunny skies and high temperatures in the 60s to near 70°. Cooler air will move in behind the front for the end of the week. We’ll see a nice day Friday under partly to mostly sunny skies. High temperatures on Friday will be in the 50s to near 60°. High pressure will build in to bring us a nice weekend. Saturday will feature sunshine and highs in the 50s. Sunday is looking good too with temperatures reaching the mid-50s to mid-60s.
Rest of Today: Partly to mostly sunny. Windy and cooler. Highs in the mid-40s to low 50s north and low to mid-50s elsewhere. Northwest wind 15-25 MPH with gusts to 40-50 MPH possible north and 30-40 MPH possible closer to the coast.
Tonight: Clear to partly cloudy and cold. Areas of frost. Diminishing wind. Lows in the 30s. Wind will become light and variable.
Wednesday: Partly to mostly cloudy. An isolated shower possible across the north. Highs in the mid-50s to low 60s. South/southwest wind 5-15 MPH.
Thursday: Partly to mostly sunny with a few showers possible. Highs in the 60s to near 70°.
Friday: Partly to mostly sunny and cooler. Highs in the 50s to around 60°.
Saturday: Partly to mostly sunny. Highs in the 50s.

title: This teen turned a bus into a mobile clothing store
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BATON ROUGE, La. (InvestigateTV) - A New Orleans teenager has converted a used bus into a traveling clothing boutique, taking his business on the road across the Gulf South.
Valen Purvis, a student at Rummel High School in New Orleans, operates a mobile clothing store called Transit. The concept began during a family vacation in Point Clear, Alabama.
“Me and my dad, and my mom were on vacation in Point Clear, Alabama, just trying to enjoy the beach because they have a good beach out there,” Purvis said. “And we saw the bus on the side of the road for sale. So we’re curious people. Of course, we stopped, and we checked it out.”
Purvis said he saw a $3,000 price tag on the bus and pitched the owner his idea for a mobile streetwear store. The owner reduced the price.
“He actually notched it down to [$2,000],” Purvis said. “So we got a steal, AC, bus running. We drove it all the way back from Point Clear to New Orleans.”
Purvis then removed the transit seats, installed clothing racks, and added a custom ceiling design inspired by the New Orleans downtown scene.
“Put some wood in it and we kept the lights in here, took the covers off of it, having more of like a futuristic vibe,” Purvis said. “And of course the clothes, the addition of clothes — it’s a store now.”
In less than a year, Transit has appeared at 20 to 30 events from Baton Rouge to Houston. Purvis said the inventory is intentionally curated.
“I don’t just buy bulk, and like, I’m gonna just see what happens,” Purvis said. “But like, it’s handpicked. It’s kind of luxurious, a little bit.”
Purvis said future stops include Florida, Alabama, and Oklahoma. He also said the business has offered lessons beyond retail.
“Just like lighten people’s day and just help people find like specific personality traits that they can express through clothing,” he said. “And really like learn from myself too. Like this bus is a representation of myself. So I’m learning myself, and I’m learning others too while I’m doing this business.”
Purvis said he plans to attend college and pursue a career in a corporate setting while maintaining the independence Transit currently provides.
“See where it takes me,” Purvis said. “It’s a bus. I mean, it’s going to take me somewhere, right?”

title: Longtime college football head coach Dennis Franchione dies at 75
text:
BIRMINGHAM, Ala. (WBRC/Gray News) - Former college football head coach Dennis Franchione has died. He was 75.
Franchione’s head coaching career spanned more than 30 years, with over 200 victories and major stints at colleges that included the University of Alabama, Texas A&M and TCU.
TCU Athletic Director Mike Buddie said Tuesday that the Horned Frogs’ program would not be where it is without the coach.
“Beyond his talent as a football coach, he was a beloved father, mentor, and friend to so many,” Buddie said. “Our thoughts and prayers are with his wife, Kim, and the entire Franchione family.”
Franchione was known as being an offensive innovator, leading multiple teams to conference championships and bowl games, including turning TCU from a 1-10 team to an upset bowl victory the following season over USC.
He retired from coaching in 2015 after stepping down at Texas State.
Franchione’s cause of death was not immediately shared, but ESPN reported that he had been diagnosed with cancer in 2016 and again in 2021.
His cancer was said to have gone into remission before returning this year, according to family members. Franchione had recently been put in hospice, the Fort Worth Star-Telegram reported.

title: Archaeologists find 7 coffins with human remains at governor’s residence
text:
BISMARCK, N.D. (KFYR/Gray News) - Officials in North Dakota say several coffins with human remains have been found at the governor’s residence.
State officials said archaeologists located seven coffins holding human remains, plus another wooden box, at the North Dakota Governor’s Residence after a monthslong investigation.
According to OMB Facilities Management Director Brandon Solberg, crews inspected more than 80 spots flagged during the investigation before concluding fieldwork on Sept. 14.
Investigators said the discovery dates back to May 19, when contractors excavating at the southwest corner of the property first uncovered remains, coffin hardware and fragments.
Construction work was paused, and the State Historical Society conducted a radar scan, followed by a dig that started Sept. 1.
Archaeologists said they would review and catalog all remains and recovered items in a process expected to run into early next year. They added the team has also contracted a local funeral home, with Crisis Care Chaplaincy volunteering to help ensure that the relocation was handled with care and reverence.
Reburial is expected in spring 2027 at an area cemetery.
The governor’s residence property was Bismarck’s first community cemetery from 1873 to 1877. Most graves were thought to have been moved to St. Mary’s and Fairview cemeteries in the 1880s, but past projects, including 13 burials found in 1903 and five more in 1959, have shown that some have been left behind.

title: Belfast may condemn former church
text:
Belfast’s city council is set to decide Tuesday whether to designate a deteriorating downtown building as a dangerous structure, which would clear the way for the city to potentially abate or demolish it at the owner’s expense.
The large white building at 333 High St. was an active Apostolic church for about eight years until shortly before James Constable bought it in 2011. Since then, it has been mostly vacant and generally unmaintained, according to the city, which took Constable to court over land use violations there last year.
A settlement agreement reached this summer requires the city to impose a dangerous building order in order to demolish it and cover the costs through a special tax if the owner doesn’t make improvements. But Constable said he plans to appeal any such vote.
Four years ago, the city’s code enforcement officer, Steve Wilson, sent a violation notice about outside property maintenance, he said in a memo. Wilson received a letter from Constable’s attorney that outlined unpermitted electrical work, window and door replacements there, which Wilson then added to the violations and sent as an updated violation letter, according to his memo.
Wilson fully inspected the inside with Constable’s engineer in 2024, he said, and two engineering reports found “significant structural failures.”
A 2024 report identified issues with the building’s foundation, supports, exterior surface drainage, ventilation, along with dry rot in timbers and mold, City Manager Erin Herbig said in a memo to councilors.
The council then authorized taking court action over the violations in February 2025 that went to civil trial.
Constable appealed a judgment against him to Maine’s Supreme Court, and the city then reached a settlement agreement this July.
He’s violating the court order and the settlement agreement by not having gotten necessary permits for making the building safe by the end of August, the city said.
Constable started some repairs, including a $45,000 new foundation, but it only addressed a “limited portion” of safety issues, according to court documents.
A court order on the property maintenance portion of the violations also noted Constable did not dispute many of the city’s claims.
That order also said that, while the building didn’t appear to be occupied, concerns about squatters contributed to the finding that the building was dangerous and a public risk.
It also found him responsible for $144,000 in fines and the city’s legal costs.
In a Sept. 30 email to the city included in Tuesday’s council packet, Constable said he objected to any motion to declare the building dangerous or demolish it, arguing it has been remediated and the city doesn’t have legal standing to find it dangerous.
More than $100,000 has been spent to remediate the building, he said, and he intends to appeal any finding against him to the Maine Supreme Judicial Court. Wilson’s memo said the city’s attorney advised that Constable couldn’t challenge the process or findings of the order because of the settlement agreement.
City officials and Belfast’s attorney are scheduled to discuss the proposed order at Tuesday’s meeting, followed by a public hearing and a council vote.
“The house is not dangerous. The city gave permission for people to work in it,” Constable said as part of a response to a request from the BDN for further comment Monday, referencing state building and energy codes that he believes prevent the city from moving ahead on the order.

title: The Latest: Trump agrees to have his super PAC, not taxpayers, pay for his ads
text:
In response to a major backlash, President Donald Trump says he will stop using taxpayer funds for television advertisements glorifying himself and instead tap his super PAC to cover such costs going forward. Trump defended the use of at least $1.5 million in federal funds to pay for the ads, saying Monday that they were “positive promotion for our Great U.S.A.”
Trump on Monday criticized election officials in Arizona’s Maricopa County after about 3,000 ballots were mistakenly mailed six days early to voters. The vendor error will have no effect on the ballots or the process, the recorder’s office said. Maricopa County has about 2.5 million registered voters.
Trump has approved the execution by firing squad of Army Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan for a 2009 shooting rampage at Fort Hood, Texas. The U.S. military has not carried out the death penalty since 1961. The Army secretary will decide its time and place, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell wrote in a post on X.
The Latest:
Trump draws cheers, then criticism for musing about Iran taking out US cities
During his rally Monday night in Nebraska, Trump was going through his usual insistence that gas prices are only temporarily high and worth it as part of his war on Iran.
Then he added a new wrinkle, floating the idea that Tehran could “take out” two major American cities.
“They could take out a city,” he said. “Let ‘em take out Los Angeles. Let ’em take out San Diego.”
He continued as the crowd laughed and cheered: “This is a very small price to pay, and it’s going to be over with very soon.”
California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat who may run for president in 2028, answered on X, calling Trump “deranged and dangerous.”
Trump has a history of denigrating U.S. cities, especially the largest ones that lean heavily Democratic. Los Angeles was among the cities where Trump deployed federal military personnel for what he said was a crackdown on crime, despite local authorities not wanting the troops.
At a recent North Carolina campaign rally, Trump said the state’s cities are “blood-soaked killing fields.” North Carolina’s violent crime rate ranks in the middle third of states, according to FBI statistics.
Cold War memories stir Rubio in Iceland as he hails diplomacy for conflict resolution
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio hailed the role of diplomacy in resolving conflicts as he began a three-nation tour of NATO allies in Iceland, where concerns over the Trump administration’s often brusque approach to traditional friends and partners have stirred unease.
Rubio met Tuesday with Icelandic Foreign Secretary Thorgerdur Katrín Gunnarsdóttir at Reykjavik’s Hofdi House, the site of the 1986 summit between former U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev that is widely regarded as the beginning of the end of the Cold War.
“The house symbolizes diplomacy’s role in ending the Cold War and defeating communism,” Rubio posted on social media after the talks that took place just days before the 40th anniversary of the landmark Oct 11-12 meeting.
Despite an agreement signed last month between the U.S., Denmark and Greenland that eased fears of Trump taking over Greenland. Iceland has been uneasy about Trump’s intentions toward it after posting a map showing the colors of the U.S. flag sprawling across all of North America and including Iceland and Greenland.
Republicans return to tough-on-crime message ahead of difficult midterm elections
Political advertising warns about Democratic plots to defund the police. Campaign events feature law enforcement unions and tough talk about law and order. Stump speeches boast about record low levels of violent crime.
From coast to coast, Republicans are focusing on public disorder, illegal immigration and violent crime in midterm campaigns as voters sour on their party’s handling of the cost of living and the war with Iran.
The messaging reflects a belief that lawlessness is safer political ground in the midterms despite Donald Trump’s own criminal record for paying hush money to a porn star, making him the only president to be convicted of a felony. Democrats have tried to counter the attacks by recruiting candidates with law enforcement backgrounds and emphasizing their own anti-crime plans, but Republicans believe it’s a rare opportunity to go on the offensive in an otherwise challenging year.
Trump returned to the topic on Monday night in Nebraska, warning about how the country used to be before he returned to the White House.
“We had a border with people pouring in, crime like nobody’s ever seen,” he said.
Trump approves firing squad execution for Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan
Trump has approved the execution by firing squad of Army Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan for the 2009 shooting rampage at Fort Hood, Texas.
The U.S. military has not carried out the death penalty since 1961. The Army secretary will decide a time and place for the execution, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell wrote in a post on X.
Hasan, an Army psychiatrist, walked into a medical building where soldiers were getting medical checkups, shouted “Allahu akbar” — Arabic for “God is great!” — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun. Thirteen people were killed and more than 30 injured.
He said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims and made almost no effort to defend himself at trial. He told jurors that evidence would show he was the shooter and described himself as a soldier who had “switched sides.”
Trump’s approval triggers a series of procedural steps toward carrying out the execution, but Hasan could put them on hold — potentially for years — with a habeas corpus appeal in the civilian federal court system, according to an article published in May in the magazine Army Lawyer.
Trump criticizes election officials in Arizona’s Maricopa County over error affecting 3,000 ballots
Trump on Monday criticized election officials in Arizona’s Maricopa County after about 3,000 ballots were mistakenly mailed early to voters.
The miscue, blamed on a vendor error, would have no effect on the voters who received the ballots, the county recorder’s office said. Maricopa County has about 2.5 million registered voters.
The president, as he typically does ahead of an election, has been ramping up his rhetoric around voting as Election Day draws near in this year’s midterm elections, with control of Congress at stake.
His latest comments referred to a vendor error that came to light over the weekend. The Maricopa County Recorder’s Office, which is run by Republican Recorder Justin Heap, said Sunday that Runbeck Election Services told the office that it “mistakenly mailed 3,126 early ballots the previous day,” six days before they were scheduled to be sent to voters for this year’s midterm elections.
The ballots were mailed to the correct voters, are still valid and can be completed and returned normally by those voters, the recorder’s office said in a statement.
Jeff Ellington, president and CEO of Runbeck Election Services, said Monday that Maricopa County was not at fault in the snafu.
Trump says his super PAC will pay for taxpayer-funded ads that sparked backlash for glorifying him
President Donald Trump said Monday that he will stop using taxpayer funds for television advertisements glorifying himself, which sparked a major backlash, and instead tap his super PAC to cover costs going forward.
In a post on his social media site, Trump defended the ads, which cost at least $1.5 million in federal funds and have drawn intense criticism. Trump said they were “positive promotion for our Great U.S.A.”
“This is a rather standard thing to do,” the president wrote, while blaming intense criticism for using taxpayer funds on the ads on the “Radical Left.” But the president added that he’d “decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.”
That is Trump’s political war chest, which had amassed more than $400 million by the end of July. Trump has begun to tap it to boost Republican candidates around the country ahead of midterm elections.
Trump provided no details on reimbursing taxpayers for ads that already aired, nor how he would go about having his political organization pay for such future advertising.

title: Former Bangor Tire Garage On Market Street Becomes Music Studio This December
text:
For over 50 years, the family-run business of Bangor Tire operated out of a garage on Market Street in Bangor. While the business originally started on Franklin Street, it spent a decade on Market Street before ultimately moving to its current location, Coldbrook Road in Hermon, back in 2021.
Following Bangor Tire's exit, Bob Briggs and his family moved their business, Center Line Utility Service, to the location, but it only utilizes a few of the garage bays. Briggs's wife, Jori-Lynn, played with a small group of musicians called the Bangor Ensemble, so he offered to let the group set up in some of the office space to practice.
A little over a year ago, Jori-Lynn passed away suddenly, and the Bangor Ensemble became the Jori-Lynn Ensemble in her honor.
The group wanted to create a musical scholarship to honor her as well, and when they were talking about it, inspiration hit, and the idea to create a musical studio space and name it after her came about.
All of a sudden, this unused space, that was just kind of sitting there, had a new life and purpose.
Read More: After Decades In The City, Bangor Tire Moving To Hermon
Two local musicians have been spearheading the effort, ensuring that the building will soon be filled with tunes instead of tires!
Lisa Cooley and Claude Junkins are working to turn this former automotive garage into a future space for musicians to practice or perform: The Jori-Lynn Studios.
Junkins recently began to spread.
"We are in the process of creating new music instruction, rehearsal, and recital space.
Very reasonable rates, excellent parking, and accessible. Teach instrument or voice?
Looking for a practice location - we may be able to help. Staffed always."
Cooley, who will serve as the organization's Music Director, says the vision is to provide not only the space, but possibly storage down the road for folks to bring in their instruments and gear to make music.
"We are thinking of it as a multi-use studio space. The large space will be available first, and smaller spaces for lessons or practice will be available further on...We will be available for all kinds of rehearsals, but we don't have equipment that other rehearsal studios have. I believe that we will have storage space."
Junkins, a retired project manager from the University of Maine system who also teaches trumpet, says the goal is to make the space feel less like a garage and more like a music space, and that could take a couple of months.
"The family is letting us use the space. I'm doing some work in here...and it's getting there...getting the place softened up and making the place less hollow, from a tire room with a concrete floor to a place with some rugs. We've gotten quite a few people who have responded to the notice...We had one lady who has about 45 piano students, and she wants to be able to move the lessons out of her house, so we hope to be able to accommodate her. "

"We have a couple of pianos, one electric and one upright."
Junkins says he hopes to be able to take some donations of instruments, in the future, that could be refurbished and loaned out to students.
"Hopefully students who are not getting the music lessons they want and can't find them will look at this place as a nice place to come, easy parking, wide-open, well lit and secured and monitored, that they would be more apt to spend more time practicing."
He says there's a lot of potential in the space that could be helpful to young musicians and music instructors alike. He sees a future with some great after-school access to musical programs and a space for newly formed bands or groups to gather.

title: Football fans are cutting back on spending this season, survey finds
text:
(InvestigateTV) — More than a third of Americans plan to cut back on football-related spending this season because of the economy, according to a new LendingTree survey, even though many fans could still end up taking on hundreds of dollars in football-related debt.
LendingTree found almost half of Americans plan to spend money on their football fandom this year, down more than 10 percentage points from 65% last year. The survey covered a wide range of football-related costs, including game tickets, team merchandise, streaming subscriptions, and food and drinks for watch parties and tailgates.
Matt Schulz, with LendingTree, said football fans are feeling the same economic pressure affecting other areas of spending.
“As much as Americans love football, even football isn’t immune to the effects of inflation,” Schulz said. “We are seeing an awful lot of Americans who say that they’re going to spend at least a little bit less on football fandom this fall, and a big part of it is just because of the economy.”
For fans who still plan to spend on the season, Schulz recommends building football into the household budget as its own line item.
“It may seem a little silly to some to have a line item in your budget that says ‘football,’ but we don’t think anything of that when it comes to passions like travel and things like that,” Schulz said. “So if football is something that’s meaningful to you, that you spend an awful lot of money on and an awful lot of time on, you should have a line item for it.”
Schulz said budgeting specifically for football gives fans more control over their spending and allows them to pursue the hobby without creating larger financial problems.

title: Death Notice: Danal A. Gerrard
Flock cameras have no business in Lewiston
text:
During the last Supreme Court term, the Court in the case of Chatrie v. United States ruled 6-3 to invalidate a police tactic called a “geofence warrant.”
A geofence warrant is a mass surveillance tool which a law enforcement agency demands from a tech company (like Google) location data from every mobile device within a defined geographic area with a certain timeframe, without specifying a suspect or suspects. It is clear that this constitutes a Fourth Amendment violation; geofencing is a mass, dragnet search of innocent people guilty of no crime.
In June 2025, the Lewiston City Council approved and accepted as part of the U.S. DOJ’s Byrne Community Grant, which was intended for surveillance camera technology. This grant funding then gets us to October 2025, when the Lewiston Police Department entered into a 60-day trial with Flock Safety. Without a City Council vote, the city went on to acquire and implement a 13-camera system.
According to one report, 82 Flock contracts nationwide have been canceled. Unlike Auburn, Lewiston has not decided to end funding. We the people of Lewiston should follow Auburn’s lead in ending Flock’s contract and removing this mass surveillance network. While the Chatrie decision is new, time will show that automated license plate readers are like a geofence warrant, a mass surveillance tactic and a clear violation of the Fourth Amendment.
Matthew Roy
Lewiston

title: Brewer, Lincoln Academy set the pace at KVAC golf qualifier
text:
VASSALBORO — How do you follow up winning a conference championship despite thunder, lightning and hail that forced delays?
If you’re Bangor’s Jacoby Harvey, you turn around less than 16 hours later and shoot a 79 while dealing with windy conditions.
“You just have to be the most mental (tough),” said Harvey. “Just kind of grind through every shot, take one shot at a time, don’t move past the next one.”
Harvey was one of 33 golfers to shoot a qualifying score for the individual state championship during the Kennebec Valley Athletic Conference qualifier Tuesday at Natanis Golf Course. He tied with Liam Greenlaw of Brewer for the second-best score in Class A behind Greyson Dooley of Messalonskee.
Bangor (349), having already won the KVAC Class A championship Monday, also qualified for the team state championship. Brewer (330), Messalonskee (331) and Camden Hills (336) were the other three Class A teams to qualify.
“I had a good front, shot minus-1, was trying to keep doing what I was doing, obviously,” Harvey said. “Things on the back (nine) didn’t go as planned, but at the end of the day, 79, can’t be complaining.”
Lincoln Academy (343) led the pack in Class B on Tuesday. Leavitt (358), Belfast (362) and Nokomis (364) rounded out the team qualifiers.
“They’re a great bunch of young athletes and they’re a joy to coach,” Lincoln coach Todd Brackett said. “They jell really well. And today, what you don’t know behind the scenes is my No. 3 guy isn’t here. He’s sick. So my No. 7 guy stepped up and actually shot 90, which we used as part of the team score today. So I think that’s the advantage that they have, is we’ve got some depth. One through seven, any given time, they’re going to be competitive.”
Colin Mitchell shot an 80 to anchor Lincoln, tying with Leavitt’s James Brisson for the lowest score in Class B. Caden Chretien (81) of Nokomis placed third.
Mitchell made par on the sixth hole and chipped in for birdie on the seventh after starting the round with a bogey and a double bogey. On the back nine, he started with two double bogeys but was able to string together some pars across the rest of the round.
“I was trying to keep it low under the wind for the most part, just being happy with par, not trying to get too greedy,” Mitchell said.
Like Bangor, Lincoln Academy had already qualified for the state championship. The Eagles won the KVAC Class B championship on Oct. 1, and they excelled again Tuesday on the Tomahawk course.
“I said, ‘You know, guys, let’s treat it more like a practice round,’” Brackett said. “‘Go out. It’s you against the golf course. It doesn’t matter who you’re playing with, just do the best you can. We’re already qualified.’ But they’re like, ‘Geez coach, I want to qualify as an individual.’ So their mindset is to be competitive, I think, anyway. So I’m not sure that (already having qualified) eased their minds as much as I’d hoped it would.”
The Class A team and individual state championships will take place Friday, while the Class B championships are scheduled for Saturday, both on the Tomahawk course at Natanis.

title: ‘We refuse to close the chapter’: Leaders, Nolan Wells’ parents renew push for federal investigation into his death
text:
INGLEWOOD, Calif. (WLOX/Gray News) — Civil rights attorney Ben Crump and the parents of 18-year-old Nolan Wells, along with other community leaders, held a press conference to call for a federal investigation into Wells’ death.
California Congresswoman Maxine Waters, Florida Congresswoman Frederica Wilson and others sent a letter to Jessica Bowron, acting director of the U.S. National Park Service, asking the agency’s Investigative Services Branch to open a “prompt and exhaustive investigation” into Wells’ death.
The letter read, in part, “Nolan’s family deserves answers, and this matter demands and deserves your immediate attention.”
The letter pointed out that most of Horn Island is federally designated land and asked the park service to “examine every circumstance surrounding Nolan’s death and pursue every available lead.”
“We have not closed our case, and we refuse to close the chapter of Nolan Xavier Wells,” Crump said.
Wells’ body was found in the water just off Horn Island on the morning of July 6. He was reported missing the night of July 4 after he didn’t return from a boating trip with friends.
Two and a half months later, a Jackson County grand jury returned a “no true bill,” meaning no criminal charges or indictments will be issued at this time.
Jackson County District Attorney Angel Meyers McIlrath has repeatedly said that her office has taken the investigation seriously and turned over all available evidence to the grand jury.
Stop AAPI Hate Executive Director Cynthia Choi spoke at the press conference, saying the organization stands with Wells’ family, “for as long as it takes.”
“When a family is denied truth, and when anyone seeking justice is met with closed doors — intimidation instead of answers — this fight belongs to us,” Choi said.
Choi also condemned those attempting to harass or threaten Wells’ family, referencing those who targeted his mother, Christine Wells Wonsley, and her job as a nurse practitioner.
At the National Asian Pacific American Women’s Forum on Saturday, Wonsley was given the organization’s “Voice of Courage” award for “standing in the gap and fighting for the truth of Nolan Wells,” according to Crump.
At Monday’s press conference, Wonsley said she “never thought [she] would be in this position.”
“I never thought I would be someone who was giving a voice to so many who feel like they have none because our justice system told us to take the answer you’ve been given,” Wonsley said. “We have been left with more questions and heartbreak than any answers. As a matter of fact, no one has given us any answers, other than, ‘consistent with accidentally drowning.’ That’s all our Black child, our Black and Asian child, has received, is ‘accidental drowning.’”
Both the state and independent autopsies ruled Wells’ cause and manner of death undetermined. According to the independent autopsy, blunt-force injuries were found on the back of his head and other areas of his back.
The grand jury report noted that accidental drowning is consistent with the evidence and that the evidence does not rule it out.
“Today, I am asking the people whose job it is to serve and protect to keep their word to our family,” Elmore Wonsley, Wells’ dad, said at the press conference. “Our son was found on federal land, and we are asking the FBI to step in and do a full investigation. We’re not asking for special treatment. We’re asking for what any father would do for his child, and that’s to find the truth about what happened to his child.”

title: Damariscotta Pumpkinfest Spans Early October With Pumpkin Pancakes, Pie Eating Contests, And Pumpkin Regatta Races
text:
According to Merriam-Webster, a pumpkin is "a large, round, orange-skinned fruit of a trailing vine belonging to the gourd family (Cucurbitaceae)."
While most people use this winter squash as a source of food, with it's flesh and seeds both edible and delicious roasted, pureed or baked into pies or breads, folks in Damariscotta have come to celebrate their pumpkins for all the other things you can do with them.
Read More: Protecting Pumpkins From Wildlife In Your Garden
They revere this glorious gourds to such a degree, they've dedicated an entire weekend's festivities to the giant orange orb, in a way only Mainers could come up with.
How did all of this start?
For almost 20 years (their first big foray into promoting pumpkins was in 2007) the Damariscotta Pumpkinfest and Regatta has been all about educating folks about just how great the pumpkin really is.
"Damariscotta Pumpkinfest & Regatta™ is an innovative program that promotes horticultural education to gardeners of all ages regarding the specific agricultural science required to grow Atlantic Giant Pumpkins."
"This program culminates in a family-oriented festival, held for ten days in early October thorough Indigenous Peoples’ Day weekend each year to showcase the pumpkin growers results in a number of creative ways. "
Read More: 7 Pumpkin Color Meanings You Should Know Before Halloween
What impact has the pumpkin had on this region?
The quiet little community in Lincoln County becomes a hustling and bustling haven for tourists and pumpkin-enthusiast for a short while in fall, as roughly 60,000 visitors make their way to the mid-coast region for the celebrations.
What can visitors expect?
The weekend's festivities include (just to name a few activities) a pumpkin pancake breakfast, pumpkin art, a dessert contest full of pumpkin goodies, a giant pumpkin parade, a kids zone with Mr. Drew and his animals, too!
There's also a pumpkin pie eating contest, a Tour de Gourd 5k & Walk, a pumpkin hunt, a pumpkin drop, a free kids' movie, a pumpkin derby, a whole bunch of pumpkin art and of course the famous Pumpkin Regatta where folks dry to stay afloat in their pumpkin boat!
"The Pumpkinboat Regatta, featuring numerous 400-700 pound, hollowed-out pumpkins with motors attached or paddled, piloted by volunteer captains, racing one another in the Damariscotta Harbor. This event is live-fed into the local theater."
The official Damariscotta Pumpkinfest & Regatta website says the event is completely free to attend and also 100% run by volunteers!
Where do the pumpkins come from?
Well, according to organizers, it all starts in the spring of each year, when "50 third-grade students at local Great Salt Bay School volunteer their time to fill 600 pots with soil and amendments for each year’s seeds."
Those seeds are then distributed to a network of around 400 growers who then, under the advice and tutelage of experts, nurture the plants, to see just how big they can get them to grow.
They take notes and keep logs going, recording what works and what doesn't. Then in October, they bring those pumpkins for an official "weigh off" the weekend before the Pumpkinfest and Regatta, to see who has grown the biggest plant.
How big do these giant pumpkins get?
The pumpkins usually weigh in in the range of 200 lbs to 1,400 lbs. This year's winner was whopping 1847 lbs, grown by a repeat champion grower, Elroy Morgan.
Read More: Maine's Biggest Pumpkin for 2026 Weighs 1847 Pounds
"Seeds from the largest, hardiest pumpkins are dried & planted in the subsequent year, for the purpose of high grading the overall stock."
For a complete list of the weekend's events, you can find that on the Damariscotta Pumpkinfest & Regatta Facebook Page or their website, by clicking here.

title: Suspect, 35, arrested nearly 20 years after 10-year-old boy, stepmother were stabbed to death
text:
FRANKLIN, Ind. (KLTV/Gray News) - Authorities in Indiana believe they have identified a suspect in the deaths of a boy and his stepmother from two decades ago.
A grand jury has returned an indictment against 35-year-old Michael Jerome James in the 2006 murders of Blake and Chynna Dickus.
On July 24, 2006, Blake Dickus, 10 and his stepmother Chynna Dickus, 26, were found stabbed to death.
Newly unsealed indictments suggest the killings may have happened during an attempted burglary.
James would have been about 14 at the time of the killings.
In the years since, the Franklin Police Department has continued to search for their killer, using billboards, a $25,000 reward and “tens of thousands of man-hours” without identifying a suspect until now.
Grand jury members reviewed the evidence for three weeks before delivering the indictment.
James has his first court appearance Thursday morning in Johnson County.

title: Controversial televangelist Jim Bakker dies at 86
text:
(Gray News) - Televangelist Jim Bakker has died at 86.
“It is with a broken heart that I share that my beloved husband, Jim Bakker, went home to be with the Lord this evening,” his wife, Lori Bakker, wrote in an Instagram post on Oct. 5.
Bakker was known for hosting “The PTL Club” and developing the PTL Satellite Network, as well as developing the defunct Christian theme park Heritage USA.
He resigned from the ministry in 1987 after paying hush money to a church secretary who said she had been sexually assaulted by Bakker.
The next year, he was indicted on several counts of mail fraud, wire fraud, and one count of conspiracy, related to PTL’s finances. He was sentenced to 45 years in prison, but was paroled in 1994.
Since then, he began hosting “The Jim Bakker Show” and selling survivalist products.
“Jim loved people deeply. He loved this ministry, and he loved the friends and partners who stood with him throughout the years,” Lori wrote.

title: Remembering a beloved family farm dog
text:
In 1948, my maternal grandparents, Florian and Lucille Yeaton, brought home Bonnie, the runt of a border collie litter purchased in Farmington. This scrappy pup caught Grampa’s attention by fearlessly wrestling with littermates twice her size.
They took her to their Mercer farmhouse, where she slept on a horsehair blanket behind the wood cookstove. However, their hopes for a collie to herd sheep and dairy cows dimmed as Bonnie’s weight plummeted.
As a last resort, Grammy Lue wrapped Bonnie in the blanket and, in a gamble, placed her in the pigpen with a 250-pound sow nursing six piglets.
“We’ll know by day’s end whether the sow takes to her,” Grammy said to Grampa.
For 10 days, Bonnie nursed alongside the pink piglets, thriving under her unlikely foster mother’s warmth and care. Her weight — scarcely three pounds — more than doubled. Within two months, she was racing between the farmhouse and the barn.
My grandparents initially wondered if such an unusual start would leave a lasting mark. It did, but not the one they feared. Bonnie matured into an extraordinarily intelligent working dog, consistently proving her capabilities in protecting her family and livestock.
One summer afternoon in 1953, my 5-year-old brother, Robert, came face-to-face with a rabid fox behind the barn. Bonnie didn’t attack. Instead, she steadily nipped at Robert’s heels, driving him back toward the farmhouse while keeping her body between him and the fox. Grampa killed the fox with his shotgun.
A year later, Robert and our cousin, Cheryl, accidentally started a barn fire while playing with matches. Bonnie’s frantic barking alerted the family before anyone smelled smoke. Grampa fought the flames with pails of rainwater from the cistern, Mother smothered them with wet blankets, and Grammy herded the frightened livestock into the pasture. Together, they saved the barn.
But Bonnie’s greatest feat occurred on a sweltering August day in 1958.
While wading in the Sandy River to cool off, my 6-year-old twin brother, Don, was swept into the deep channel. Mother dove in after him but couldn’t dog-paddle fast enough to close the gap as he drifted downstream.
Bonnie understood the river’s currents better than either of them. Instead of immediately jumping in, she sprinted along the high bank, tracking Don as he fought to keep his head above water. Nearly 300 feet downriver, she launched off the bank, entered the current just ahead of the hairpin rapids, clamped onto his shirt collar, and hauled him onto a gravel bar.
The next morning, Don, still shaken, sat beside Grampa in the milking parlor. From his three-legged stool, Grampa squirted warm milk to the waiting barn cats and Bonnie, as he did every morning. Watching Bonnie lick her whiskers, my twin laughed through his tears and pulled her close.
The day before, she had saved his life — that morning, she helped restore his spirit.
Age never dulled her instincts. Shortly after midnight in October 1961, Don and I woke to growls rising from the pumpkin pine floorboards at the foot of our bed.
“Why’s Bonnie growling?” we yelled into the dark.
“Might be a bear in the barnyard,” Grampa answered from the adjacent bedroom. “She found fresh tracks in the orchard yesterday.”
He lit a kerosene lantern and retrieved the 12-gauge from above the kitchen door. Bonnie paced and whined at the latch. The second it lifted, she shot through the doorway and bolted toward the pigpen, her dark silhouette framed by a huge harvest moon.
“You boys go back to bed,” Grammy barked.
We obeyed but opened our bedroom window to listen. The hogs were squealing, Bonnie was barking, and a single shotgun blast cracked across the farm. Then everything went deadly quiet.
The next 10 minutes felt like an hour before Grampa and Bonnie returned to the kitchen.
“She chased a bear clean out of the pigpen,” he said, still catching his breath. “The pen door’s stove to hell, but the hogs are fine.”
Two nights later, a few miles from our farm, Ralph True shot the same bear after it killed one of his sheep. The boar weighed 490 pounds.
“Its front paws,” he told Grampa, “were the size of dinner plates.”
When cancer took Bonnie in April 1962, Grampa wrapped her one last time in the ratty horsehair blanket she’d slept on her entire life and carried her up the knoll to the apple orchard — her favorite spot on the farm. He dug her grave that night by moonlight, working past the frost line with a pickaxe and shovel. The next afternoon, my three siblings and I picked yellow daffodils from the south side of the farmhouse and planted them on her grave.
That evening, my heartbroken 5-year-old sister, Gale, barely ate her supper. When the meal was over, she quietly walked behind the cookstove and scraped her plate into Bonnie’s enamel bowl.
In the morning, her eyes lit up at the sight of an empty bowl.
Years later, E.B. White gave me the words for what Bonnie meant to our family: “A really companionable and indispensable dog is an accident of nature. You can’t get it by breeding for it, and you can’t buy it with money.”
Ron Joseph of Sidney is the author of “Bald Eagles, Bear Cubs, and Hermit Bill: Memories of a Maine Wildlife Biologist,” published by Islandport Press.

title: Trump signs order extending tax-free use of red-dyed diesel, saying it will save farmers ‘millions’
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
GRAND ISLAND, Neb. (AP) — President Donald Trump on Monday took his Republican midterm rescue mission to Nebraska, where he signed an executive order to ease limits on the tax-free use of red-dyed diesel, a decision he said would save “millions” for farmers and drive down the cost of all goods with just four weeks to go until the elections.
“Pete and Jim, this should absolutely ensure your election, I guarantee you that,” Trump said, addressing GOP Sen. Pete Ricketts, who is running against an independent candidate backed by national Democrats, and Gov. Jim Pillen, who is seeking a second term.
Diesel fuel prices have spiked in the aftermath of the Iran war, rattling voters and putting pressure on Republicans. Diesel fuel that is intended for off-road uses such as agriculture is exempt from federal and state excise taxes, and it is dyed for law enforcement purposes, the White House explained in a fact sheet. Temporarily removing the limits would reduce cost pressures on the businesses that rely on diesel.
“The typical trucker will save more than $100 every time they fill up,” Trump said, signing the executive order onstage before a crowd in Grand Island, Nebraska, in the solidly conservative south-central part of the state. He said the order will save farmers millions of dollars and drive down the cost of goods.
Patrick De Haan of GasBuddy, a platform that monitors national gasoline and diesel prices, noted last week, when news of the possible action began to surface, that such an order could save money for on-road users but not farmers, who already use red-dyed diesel.
“Taxes aren’t the problem, supply is,” De Haan wrote on X.
Trump’s trip is part of what the Republican president says is a 32-day blitz of rallies ahead of Nov. 3 that so far has taken him to ruby-red territory such as Oklahoma and Alabama. On Wednesday, he’ll make his second stop in two weeks in Texas with a rally in San Antonio.
Ricketts, a former governor of the state, was appointed then later elected to fill Sen. Ben Sasse’s seat when he left to run the University of Florida in 2023. Now Ricketts is running for his first full six-year term against independent Dan Osborn — a race that initially was not expected to be competitive but is now being watched by the national parties.
Republicans facing headwinds amid voter discontent
Voters across the country are frustrated with Trump’s handling of the economy, including persistently high costs for fuel and groceries. It’s a major issue for rural voters who have backed the president and his party in recent elections.
The administration’s plan to allow more imports of foreign beef has particularly roiled the agriculture-rich state of Nebraska. Trump wants to lower beef prices for consumers, but ranchers have rebelled against the import proposal, arguing it would undercut them.
“The plan to import low-quality foreign beef is not helping Nebraska ranchers,” Ricketts told the AP. “I would advise the White House to change that policy and look for longer-term things that will help us build the size of the herd and ultimately bring the price of beef down for consumers.”
In Grand Island, rally-goers said they they trusted Trump to solve the high cost of living.
“I feel like if we get our reserves built back up, get this situation in Iran taken care of, our gas prices will go down. The economy as far as groceries and stuff like that, it’s going to go down too. It’ll stabilize. I have faith in him. More faith in him than I ever had in any other president,” said Marlene Abel from Garfield, Kansas.
David Kuncl, who grew up on a farm, expressed confidence things would improve in the long run. But the Lincoln, Nebraska, resident insisted Trump wasn’t to blame, pointing instead to what he believes is “a coup, a plot to try to hurt Trump” and the Republicans in the midterms.
“It’s hurting us. Gas prices. Diesel prices. Beef prices,” he said. “I don’t know why they’re high. But it’s not that Trump’s got anything to do with that. He’ll do what he can. But of course he can’t wave a magic wand and make it go lower.”
Democrats are aiming to flip a House seat in Nebraska
In the House of Representatives, the Grand Island area is represented by Republican Rep. Adrian Smith, whose race is not expected to be close.
But Nebraska has a competitive House race farther east in Omaha, in the 2nd District — considered the “blue dot” of the state because the area’s electoral vote in presidential elections often goes to Democrats. The district is in the midst of a competitive race between Republican Brinker Harding and Democrat Denise Powell to fill retiring Rep. Don Bacon ’s open seat.
Monday’s rally came as the Congressional Leadership Fund, a super PAC dedicated to electing Republicans to the House, cancelled $1.1 million in planned broadcast spending on behalf of the Republican candidate in the race, according to AdImpact, which tracks campaign media spending. It was a possible sign that GOP leaders feel the money could be put to better use elsewhere. The group did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
There are tentative plans for Trump to travel to other election battlegrounds, including Michigan, North Carolina, Georgia, Ohio, Kansas, Montana, Pennsylvania, Alaska, Nevada and Arizona before November’s Election Day. That’s according to a person familiar with the plans who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly and cautioned the plans could shift.
There are a few Senate races where independents are the challengers
Osborn, a former labor union chief, ran against Republican Sen. Deb Fischer in 2024 and lost by 7 percentage points. Though national Democrats support him, he has refused to say what party he would caucus with should he be elected in November.
Other independents in the Senate, including Maine’s Angus King on the moderate end and Vermont’s Bernie Sanders on the left, caucus with Democrats for organizational purposes and committee assignments.
With the Democratic brand remaining deeply unpopular in conservative states, Osborn isn’t the only declared independent running for the Senate against Republicans this year. In South Dakota, Brian Bengs is campaigning as an independent against Republican Sen. Mike Rounds. Bengs ran as a Democrat for the Senate four years ago and was handily defeated by now-Senate Majority Leader John Thune. It’s a similar dynamic in Idaho, where independent Todd Achilles is challenging GOP Sen. Jim Risch.
Democratic voters in Nebraska chose Cindy Burbank as their party nominee, but Burbank campaigned on ensuring that no votes would be siphoned from Osborn in the general election, and she has since dropped out of the race.
Osborn has been traveling across Nebraska to hold meetings in all 93 counties, and has repeatedly criticized Ricketts for not holding town halls to meet with constituents.
Ricketts, whose family founded TD Ameritrade and owns Major League Baseball’s Chicago Cubs, served as governor from 2015 to 2023.
Vance stumps in Alaska
As Trump traveled to Nebraska, Vice President JD Vance headed to Fairbanks to rally with Republican candidates, including Sen. Dan Sullivan, who is locked in a contest with Democrat Mary Peltola that’s one of a handful expected to determine control of the chamber in the November elections.
Vance praised Sullivan before a crowd gathered at the airport, saying the two-term senator is known for texting Cabinet members in the middle of the night to make the case for Alaska interests.
He cast Peltola, who served in the House from late 2022 and lost reelection in 2024, as ineffective during her time in Congress and called her a “servant of the far left.” Peltola has sought to distance herself from national Democrats and emphasize that she is doing what she thinks is best for the state. Alaska Democrats described Vance’s visit to help Sullivan as an act of desperation.
Sullivan was in the Oval Office last week as Trump announced that South Korea planned to invest about $54 billion in a natural gas project in Alaska, but South Korean officials were more cautious, saying they needed to assess the project’s commercial viability before committing to the investment.
Vance also expressed support for Rep. Nick Begich, whom he called a “machine” and a hard worker. Begich, first elected in 2024, is facing independent Bill Hill, a commercial fisherman and former educator, as his main competitor.

title: UMaine football makes a rare move with rare midseason firing. Is it the right one?
text:
ORONO — Jordan Stevens answered the questions, one day after making the most consequential decision of his time as head coach of the University of Maine football team. Stevens was resolute.
Mikahael Waters, Maine’s offensive coordinator and quarterbacks coach since 2024, is out. Sean Green, in his first season on Stevens’ staff as the running backs coach, is now the interim offensive coordinator.
When you fire your offensive coordinator in the middle of the season, you’d better be absolutely sure it’s the right move. It’s not a move you can make emotionally or haphazardly.
“We have a very talented roster, and we’ve done a lot of good things this season. We’ve got to be more consistent. We’ve got to score points,” Stevens said following Tuesday morning’s practice.
The Black Bears are 1-5. Since winning the season opener at Towson, Maine has lost five games in a row. You don’t have to break down the statistics too deeply to see that the team’s offense has been the major contributing factor to the weak start.
Averaging just 270.2 yards per game, Maine ranks 115 of 124 teams in the Football Championship Subdivision, and last in the Coastal Athletic Association. Scoring an average of 14.5 point per game, Maine is 118th nationally and, again, last in the league.
Rushing offense? Ranked 110th at 96 yards per game. Passing offense? Ranked 93th, just over 174 yards per game. Third-down conversions? Ranked 90th with a 33% success rate. The Black Bears’ best national ranking is in first downs, in which they’re tied for 85th.
All that said, firing an assistant coach in the middle of the season is a rare move. It happens, but usually for off-the-field reasons. Conversations with two Maine football alumni whose relationships with the program go back decades said they’ve never heard of a Black Bears coach losing his job midseason.
Stevens noted that the slow start doesn’t all fall on Waters. But he determined that enough of it does to warrant the rare midseason change. Waiting until the end of the season wasn’t going to work.
Stevens sees the situation as one that needs immediate attention, one that can set the tone for the remaining five games.
“When you look at our team, I believe we are a team that can win football games,” Stevens said. “I’m not sitting here just throwing in the towel on the season. I’m not willing to do that.”
Green is no stranger to football fans in Maine. He coached Portland to the Class A state title in 2024. In 2021, Green coached Cape Elizabeth to the Class C championship. Two of the players who were pivotal in those title runs are now among the weapons Green has in the Black Bears’ offense. Running back Nick Laughlin of Cape Elizabeth is a key contributor whose four touchdowns lead the team. Freshman wide receiver Cordell Jones of Portland has yet to see game action.
Green was not made available for comment Tuesday.
College football is a production business, Stevens said. You judge production in wins. Every coach has to do a better job, he said. If players aren’t playing with confidence, coaches need to instill it. If players aren’t executing on the field, coaches need to develop ways to find success. Stevens said he’s not pointing the finger, he’s pointing the thumb, back at himself and the rest of the staff.
“It’s really about us recommitting ourselves to the season,” Stevens said. “I don’t need to make a narrative over scoring more points. You can see that. We need to score more points so we can win football games. … Winning is the expectation, and not winning is never OK. We grow from those experiences, but we do need to compete and win football games. I refuse to hold us to a standard that’s anything less than that. That’s not who I am. That’s not who we’re going to be as a team.”
Since being named head coach prior to the 2022, Stevens’ teams are 16-36, the high point being a 6-6 mark last season. Asked if he felt any other assistant coaches, or even himself, were on the hot seat, Stevens was curt.
“No,” he said.
Is replacing the offensive coordinator exactly what the Black Bears need, or is it a last-ditch effort to keep a season from completely slipping away? Starting with the home game against Bryant on Oct. 17, they’ll have five games to find out.

title: ‘Why can’t you?’: Woman, 80, hosts her own funeral, celebrates life with her loved ones
text:
MACON, Ga. (WMAZ) - An 80-year-old Georgia woman had a front-row seat to her own funeral.
Shelvy Neal hosted her own funeral Sunday, even though she has a lot more living left to do. She called it a “FOMO funeral” for fear of missing out. It was a celebration of Shelvy’s life, the relationships she’s made and her 80th birthday.
“It’s gonna be about celebrating Christ and my life, 80 years of my life,” Shelvy said before the event. “It’s been a good one.”
The FOMO funeral was held at the Macon property Shelvy and her husband owned for about 25 years before they sold it to a funeral home in 2020. The sale came with a catch: two funerals, one for each of them.
Her husband’s funeral was in March, and it got Shelvy thinking about her own.
“I said, ‘You know, I’d love to be at my own funeral,’” Shelvy said. “My daughter said, ‘Well, why can’t you?’”
So, Shelvy and her family set about planning. Guests were invited to speak at an open microphone, and before the event, Shelvy said she was ready for whatever they might say.
“If they want to, they can say bad things, but I’m gonna be there, and I might cut the mic,” she said. “I’m gonna control my own funeral.”
Around 100 people showed up to Shelvy’s FOMO funeral, which featured a coffin with a cardboard printout of Shelvy lying inside. The real Shelvy wore a sash that read “Back by popular demand,” and her family celebrated with a cake that read, “She refuses to miss anything… especially her own funeral.”
Shelvy herself made the flowers for her funeral, and she was the guest speaker.
“I think it will be easier on my family to do something like this, but also, you know, funeral is F-U-N. And I like fun,” she said.
When the real goodbye comes, Shelvy says it will be a simple graveside service instead of a traditional funeral.

title: Brewer, Lincoln Academy set the pace at KVAC golf qualifier
text:
VASSALBORO — How do you follow up winning a conference championship despite thunder, lightning and hail that forced delays?
If you’re Bangor’s Jacoby Harvey, you turn around less than 16 hours later and shoot a 79 while dealing with windy conditions.
“You just have to be the most mental (tough),” said Harvey. “Just kind of grind through every shot, take one shot at a time, don’t move past the next one.”
Harvey was one of 33 golfers to shoot a qualifying score for the individual state championship during the Kennebec Valley Athletic Conference qualifier Tuesday at Natanis Golf Course. He tied with Liam Greenlaw of Brewer for the second-best score in Class A behind Greyson Dooley of Messalonskee.
Bangor (349), having already won the KVAC Class A championship Monday, also qualified for the team state championship. Brewer (330), Messalonskee (331) and Camden Hills (336) were the other three Class A teams to qualify.
“I had a good front, shot minus-1, was trying to keep doing what I was doing, obviously,” Harvey said. “Things on the back (nine) didn’t go as planned, but at the end of the day, 79, can’t be complaining.”
Lincoln Academy (343) led the pack in Class B on Tuesday. Leavitt (358), Belfast (362) and Nokomis (364) rounded out the team qualifiers.
“They’re a great bunch of young athletes and they’re a joy to coach,” Lincoln coach Todd Brackett said. “They jell really well. And today, what you don’t know behind the scenes is my No. 3 guy isn’t here. He’s sick. So my No. 7 guy stepped up and actually shot 90, which we used as part of the team score today. So I think that’s the advantage that they have, is we’ve got some depth. One through seven, any given time, they’re going to be competitive.”
Colin Mitchell shot an 80 to anchor Lincoln, tying with Leavitt’s James Brisson for the lowest score in Class B. Caden Chretien (81) of Nokomis placed third.
Mitchell made par on the sixth hole and chipped in for birdie on the seventh after starting the round with a bogey and a double bogey. On the back nine, he started with two double bogeys but was able to string together some pars across the rest of the round.
“I was trying to keep it low under the wind for the most part, just being happy with par, not trying to get too greedy,” Mitchell said.
Like Bangor, Lincoln Academy had already qualified for the state championship. The Eagles won the KVAC Class B championship on Oct. 1, and they excelled again Tuesday on the Tomahawk course.
“I said, ‘You know, guys, let’s treat it more like a practice round,’” Brackett said. “‘Go out. It’s you against the golf course. It doesn’t matter who you’re playing with, just do the best you can. We’re already qualified.’ But they’re like, ‘Geez coach, I want to qualify as an individual.’ So their mindset is to be competitive, I think, anyway. So I’m not sure that (already having qualified) eased their minds as much as I’d hoped it would.”
The Class A team and individual state championships will take place Friday, while the Class B championships are scheduled for Saturday, both on the Tomahawk course at Natanis.
