title: Group blew up a vehicle with Tannerite in a small Maine town
text:
A group blew up a vehicle with Tannerite in Readfield late last month.
The group was shooting at Tannerite placed inside a vehicle off Main Street on Sept. 27, according to Maj. Aaron Turcotte, a spokesperson for the Maine Department of Public Safety.
Under Maine law, it is legal to possess up to five pounds of binary target material, such as Tannerite, for sport shooting. Turcotte said Monday that it is illegal to explode anything other than the material Tannerite is mixed in.
The investigation is ongoing, including whether any charges are warranted.

title: Six Emergency Department Nurses Leave N.M.M.C.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
FORT KENT, Maine (WAGM) - Six nurses in the Emergency Department at Northen Maine Medical Center have left and several others have given notice.
According to the Maine Nurses Association, there are several reasons for the nurses’ departure including: staff not feeling valued or respected, high turnover, lack of communication with management, a high number of hired traveling nurses rather than skilled and experienced nurses, pressure of shift rotations and changing schedules, and continued short staff during the hospital’s busiest times.
Northern Maine Medical Center’s press release on the issue states: “Northern Maine Medical Center maintains a staffing model designed to provide safe, continuous emergency care 24 hours a day, seven days a week, ensuring patients have access to care at all times…In the event of an unexpected staff departure, Northern Maine Medical Center utilizes highly experienced travel Registered Nurses to maintain coverage while recruiting qualified staff… We have expanded the specialty services available to support emergency patients. Recent additions and growth in trauma surgery, orthopedics, cardiology, urology, pain management and rehabilitation and therapy services have strengthened the hospital’s ability to evaluate, treat, and manage patients locally.”
We will have more on this issue with one of the nurses at NMMC on a future NewsSource8 at 6.

title: Susan Collins camp releases new info disputing alleged pay-to-play scheme
text:
Sen. Susan Collins’ reelection campaign released new information on Tuesday that it says absolves the Republican incumbent of the recent pay-to-play allegations currently being seized on by Democrats.
Campaign Manager Steve Abbott took aim at a story published by ProPublica on Sept. 22 that, among other things, reported that former Navatek CEO Martin Kao told the FBI that Collins required political contributions before meeting with donors.
Abbott said the outlet’s reporting failed to acknowledge Collins’ full history with Navatek, the company at the center of the scandal. Collins started working with Navatek only after a local university requested defense funding, Abbott contended.
On a video call with reporters, Abbott showed a 2017 letter from the University of Maine seeking $5 million in federal funding for a project in partnership with Navatek “to launch a collaborative research program to address the U.S. Navy’s pressing need to enhance the mobility of future marine vehicles.” Collins ultimately secured the funding in the fiscal year 2018 budget.
Abbott also showed a photo of Collins meeting with Kao in her office with other officials in February of 2018. Kao later told federal investigators that Collins refused to meet that year with him unless he made a donation to her 2020 reelection campaign.
But Kao did not make his first donation to Collins until June 27, 2018, federal records show.
“ProPublica has the theory that Martin Kao, based on Martin Kao’s word, had to make a donation before he could get in to see Susan Collins,” Abbott said. “As you can see from that picture, it’s not true.”
The photo was taken by a Senate photographer on Feb. 15, 2018, embedded data showed, according to a screenshot released by the campaign.
The campaign’s media call was another example of how Collins is aggressively responding to allegations that could undercut her work as the top senate appropriator. The money she brings home to Maine is a key theme of her reelection campaign against Democrat Troy Jackson, a former logger and state Senate president.
It also comes ahead of Collins’ first televised debate against Troy Jackson, who is likely to raise the issue of ProPublica’s reporting. Jackson has maintained a narrow lead in the Maine’s closely watched Senate race, according to most polls.
Kao pleaded guilty to charges involving money laundering and bank fraud in 2022, and is currently in federal prison. He had been cooperating with federal investigators in an effort to get his sentence reduced.
ProPublica reported that the FBI was gearing up for a widespread corruption probe of Collins and other members of Congress based on statements Kao made to investigators between 2022 and 2024. The outlet reported that the investigation was abandoned when Trump returned to office in 2025 and disbanded anti-corruption units.
After her campaign’s initial response to the ProPublica story, the outlet fact-checked statements made by Collins’ team, finding some of their claims to be false. For example, a Collins spokesperson claimed that the outlet “took the word of” Kao in their story, “someone who pled guilty to five counts of money laundering.”
ProPublica reporters contend that they independently corroborated much of his account, reviewing “a trove of evidence gathered by the FBI,” examining “thousands of pages of legal records” and interviewing “dozens of people familiar with Navatek, its Washington operations and the FBI inquiry.”
The news site reported that Kao gave $150,000 to a super PAC supporting Collins, who in turn promised to steer $32 million in additional contracts to Navatek. Kao made the illegal donation through a shell company because federal contractors are prohibited from donating to political campaigns.
But Abbott said neither Collins, nor anybody else on her staff, would have promised a specific level of funding.
“We would never say that because there is no way we would know that we could get that done,” Abbott said. “No chance that that is true. Absolutely false.”
State and national Democrats are now using the ProPublica report to push an anti-corruption message in the final month of the election.
“The facts are clear — as recently as 2025, the FBI was circling Susan Collins for her involvement in a pay-to-play scheme until the Trump administration killed the unit that was looking into her,” Misha Linnehan, spokesperson for the Maine Democratic Party, said in a statement. “No amount of bluster from Collins’ team can distract Mainers from the fact that she sold them out for campaign cash.”
WinSenate, a super PAC aligned with Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer of New York, launched a $3.4 million ad campaign last week in Maine highlighting the ProPublica story.

title: The enduring popularity of Elvis Presley's Graceland is a monument to his legacy
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Elvis Presley’s Graceland.
Paul Simon sang about going there to ease an aching heart in 1986 on a Grammy-winning album titled, well, “Graceland.” A year later, Philadelphia punk band The Dead Milkmen wrote their own song about a trip to Graceland that was decidedly less reverent, with lyrics like, “Goin’ to Graceland/It’s gonna be fun/We’ll get to see all Elvis’s guns.”
Maybe Graceland is all things to all people.
Elvis bought the large Classical revival home on about 14 acres of farmland in 1957, moving in with his mother, father and grandmother. Later came his wife Priscilla and then daughter Lisa Marie. From the beginning, the home was accessible to the public, right there on Highway 51 South, now known as Elvis Presley Boulevard. The distinctive wrought-iron gates decorated with musical notes and guitar players resembling Elvis are pretty much a giveaway.
Bruce Springsteen tells a story of jumping over the wall in the 1970s in hopes of meeting Elvis. He wasn’t home at the time, but if he had been, he might have allowed the visit. Elvis was known to watch for fans on the security cameras and go down to the gates to sign autographs.
When Elvis died at Graceland in 1977, mourners lined up outside the walls in a spontaneous vigil. They came back the next year and the next. After the home was opened to tours in 1982, they were finally able to enter the gates and file past Elvis’ grave.
Yes, Elvis is buried at Graceland — right in the yard — along with his parents, grandmother, daughter and grandson.
Today we take Graceland as a pilgrimage site for granted, but stepping back for a second it seems rather odd. The homes of most other celebrities aren’t thronged by adoring fans, certainly not half a century after their deaths. Maybe it’s the way Elvis’ mythology is so entwined with his Memphis house?
“Such a strong association between a man and his home is unique and unprecedented in the 20th century” is the way a 2006 application for National Historic Landmark status put it. (Spoiler alert: They got it.)
Then there’s the name: Graceland.
Although Elvis didn’t name the house himself, it’s hard to imagine his legacy would be the same if he had lived at “Presleyland,” or that Paul Simon would have waxed poetic about going to “The Elvis Mansion.”
As Simon so aptly put it: ”I’ve reason to believe we all will be received in Graceland.”

title: Fire burns Maine brewery
text:
A fire burned a Wilton brewery Monday afternoon.
The fire broke out at Ambition Brewing on Main Street, according to Shannon Moss, a spokesperson for the Maine Department of Public Safety.
Firefighters contained the blaze to one of the two buildings used by the brewery, though the second sustained smoke and water damage, Moss said Tuesday morning.
Investigators determined that the fire started under the rear portion of the building, where renovations were underway. Combustible organic material had accumulated under the floor; a portion of the rear of the building was partially exposed to the elements.
That material became dry enough to combust.
The fire was ruled accidental.

title: Longtime college football head coach Dennis Franchione dies at 75
text:
BIRMINGHAM, Ala. (WBRC/Gray News) - Former college football head coach Dennis Franchione has died. He was 75.
Franchione’s head coaching career spanned more than 30 years, with over 200 victories and major stints at colleges that included the University of Alabama, Texas A&M and TCU.
TCU Athletic Director Mike Buddie said Tuesday that the Horned Frogs’ program would not be where it is without the coach.
“Beyond his talent as a football coach, he was a beloved father, mentor, and friend to so many,” Buddie said. “Our thoughts and prayers are with his wife, Kim, and the entire Franchione family.”
Franchione was known as being an offensive innovator, leading multiple teams to conference championships and bowl games, including turning TCU from a 1-10 team to an upset bowl victory the following season over USC.
He retired from coaching in 2015 after stepping down at Texas State.
Franchione’s cause of death was not immediately shared, but ESPN reported that he had been diagnosed with cancer in 2016 and again in 2021.
His cancer was said to have gone into remission before returning this year, according to family members. Franchione had recently been put in hospice, the Fort Worth Star-Telegram reported.

title: Trump draws backlash after he suggests Iran could 'take out' Los Angeles or San Diego
text:
Trump draws backlash after he suggests Iran could 'take out' Los Angeles or San Diego
Officials in California denounced comments made by President Donald Trump as “dangerous” on Monday after he appeared to suggest Iran could “take out” Los Angeles or San Diego – major cities in a state he has often criticized.
Speaking at a rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, ahead of the midterm elections, Trump once again called the consequences of the war with Iran a “small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe,” adding that Iran could potentially take out an American city.
“Let, let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego,” Trump said in comments that drew swift backlash from California’s leaders.
“This is a very small price to pay and it’s gonna be over with very soon,” he said of the war.
Trump has repeatedly made the argument that high gas prices are a small price to pay for the war in Iran and in his Nebraska comments, he appeared to contrast that with a dramatically higher price to pay – an attack on a U.S. city.
White House Communications Director Steven Cheung said on X that Trump was “clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped.”
“America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money,” Cheung said.
Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom said he will have officials monitoring the situation.
"Donald Trump’s remarks were dangerous — if not treasonous — putting a target on two of our biggest cities and one of America’s largest naval hubs," Newsom wrote on X Tuesday morning. "I am directing the State Threat Assessment Center to actively monitor the situation in the event that foreign actors interpret the President’s remarks as an invitation to target California."
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said the statements about the city “could potentially compromise our safety.”
“The role of a president is to protect the country, not to actively threaten it and encourage attacks on American lives,” said Bass, also a Democrat.
The Democratic mayor of San Diego, Todd Gloria, said the city “is not collateral damage. We are not expendable. And we are never a ‘small price to pay.’ Keep our city out of your reckless war talk.”
Trump’s comments also drew criticism from Republican congressional candidate Jim Desmond, who said he “vehemently” disagreed with the president.
“America must stand up to Iran and defend our interests, but the first responsibility of our Commander in Chief is to protect the American people and our homeland,” said Desmond, who is running in California’s 48th Congressional district. He added, “No American city is expendable, and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage.”
Trump’s highlighting of cities in California that could be targeted by Iran comes as he has frequently criticized the state and its leaders over immigration, state elections and wildfires.
The president also repeated during his speech in Nebraska that the war is “going to end very soon.”
At the onset of the war, Trump had vowed that the conflict would only last a few weeks, but it has since gone on seven months.
The president made the new argument last week that his initial four- to six-week timeline had just been about the time it would take to eradicate the nuclear threat from Iran and not the time it would take to conclude the entire war.

title: 77-year-old woman kills man who attacked her in parking lot, authorities say
text:
BAKER COUNTY, Fla. (Gray News) - A 77-year-old woman shot and killed a man who attacked her Monday in Florida, according to authorities.
Baker County Sheriff’s Office deputies responded to the parking lot of Macclenny Veterinary Hospital around 4:30 a.m. Monday after the woman called to report that she had shot a man who attacked her.
Alvin Tyrone Tisdale, 57, was taken to the hospital where he died from his injuries, WJXT reported.

title: CNN now has a new owner. What will the future of the network be under Skydance?
text:
CNN has a new owner: Skydance.
After a tumultuous, roughly yearlong process, Skydance-owned Paramount closed its $81 billion buyout of Warner Bros. Discovery on Tuesday. And beyond Hollywood, the mega merger brings two titans of the American TV news landscape — CBS and CNN — under the same roof.
On the eve of the deal’s completion, Skydance confirmed that CNN’s Mark Thompson will stay on as editor-in-chief of the network — separate from CBS, where Bari Weiss remains at the helm. But how the combined company’s news operations will look farther down the road are yet to be seen.
Politics are also top of mind. The billionaire family of Skydance CEO David Ellison has a cozy relationship with President Donald Trump — who has been far from shy about targeting coverage he deems unfavorable from both CNN and CBS. Last month, his administration moved to bar CNN from the White House. And the network’s new ownership arrives as coverage ramps up less than a month ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.
Ellison has pledged to maintain editorial independence. Under a recent settlement with states that challenged the merger, the company agreed to establish new monitoring of CBS and CNN by forming a “News Editorial Independence Board” within 180 days of completing its Warner acquisition.
Still, Skydance’s corporate leaders are to choose who sits on this board. And critics are bracing for potentially deepening editorial turmoil.
CNN’s editor-in-chief remains in top spot
Skydance announced on Monday that Thompson — who has been CNN’s chair and CEO since 2023 — would continue to lead the network. In a memo to staff published by Business Insider and other outlets, Thompson said he had “real confidence” Ellison and other Skydance leaders “will fully support the principle and practice of the kind of independent news that CNN has always stood for.”
Thompson acknowledged that all the specifics of how CNN would operate have yet to be finalized — but said he planned to lead the network “as an independent Editor-in-Chief with the same responsibilities and prerogatives that I have now.”
Paramount-owned CBS News and its hallmark “60 Minutes” program have already seen editorial turmoil since coming under Skydance ownership last year. For critics of those changes, news of Thompson staying at CNN marked a meaningful safeguard — but some experts cautioned that time will tell.
“Both CNN and CBS News will ultimately sit under the same corporate ownership, and ownership can exert influence in ways that are much more subtle than directly telling an editor what stories to cover,” said J. Christopher Hamilton, an associate professor at Syracuse University. Decisions about everything from budgets to personnel “can gradually affect the editorial character of a news organization.”
The long-term question “is whether that independence remains intact when it becomes costly or uncomfortable for the parent company,” he said.
New editorial monitoring
According to court documents, the new editorial independence body will include five “active or retired” journalists with at least 10 years of experience.
Still, those members will be appointed by and report to the combined company’s board of directors. Ellison is remaining chairman of what is now the combined Skydance.
“This board, while it is termed independent, it is going to be filled with members appointed by Paramount,” said Megan Duncan, an associate professor of journalism at Virginia Tech’s School of Communication. She predicts that will “lessen the teeth of this board.”
The settlement outlines some additional criteria for board members, including that no more than two members be affiliated with the same political party, and that no government employees be appointed to the board or have oversight over who is on it.
According to court documents, the responsibilities of the board include establishing a set of “guiding editorial principles” based on CBS and CNN’s standards and practices, resolving “any disputes” between both employees at the two networks and corporate management and “monitoring adherence to ethical journalism” overall for coverage across the U.S. specifically.
Members are to serve for terms of three years, although the board of the combined Paramount-Warner can still remove them for cause.
‘Disappointed that we could not do more’
Top state prosecutors like California Attorney General Rob Bonta — who led the coalition of 12 states that initially sought to block the Paramount-Warner merger — said when announcing the deal on Sept. 21 that the board will help “ensure independent, objective, fact-based reporting at CBS News and CNN.”
Still, others wished the settlement could’ve gone further, including Connecticut Attorney General William Tong, who wanted a full divestiture of CNN and CBS and said he was “deeply disappointed that we could not do more.”
Meanwhile, while joining the rest of the states in the wider settlement, Colorado and Washington notably declined to sign off on the proposed editorial board terms.
As part of a separate settlement with Hollywood writers, the Writers Guild of America said that Paramount had also agreed to prohibit writer layoffs at CBS News Broadcast for the next five years.
Ellison, meanwhile, previously promised that editorial independence “will absolutely be maintained” under Paramount ownership.
“It’s maintained at CBS. It’ll be maintained at CNN,” Ellison told CNBC’s “Squawk on the Street” in March, while noting that his company wants to speak to “the 70%” of viewers who he said identify as center-left or center-right. And in an August opt-ed published by the New York Times amid the height of Paramount’s antitrust battle with 12 states, he reiterated that “our journalists will continue to answer to the facts and to all the people they serve — not to any party or cause.”
Trump and CNN
Last month, Trump barred CNN — as well as Politico and MS NOW — from the White House due to what he called unfavorable coverage and “fake news.” All three outlets have since filed a joint lawsuit, and are continuing to fight their case in court.
CNN has long attracted ire from the Republican president, and members of his administration have also made their opinions clear about the network’s future ownership. Shortly after Trump joined Israel to launch the war against Iran earlier this year, for example, the White House attacked CNN for its coverage — and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth told reporters that “the sooner David Ellison takes over that network, the better.”
CBS has faced its own attacks from Trump. Skydance’s 2025 acquisition of Paramount was approved by the Federal Communications Commission just weeks after the company agreed to pay Trump $16 million to settle a lawsuit over editing at the network’s “60 Minutes” program.

title: 5-year-old dead, 16-year-old charged after UTV crash
text:
LITTLE COMPTON, R.I. (WJAR) — A 16-year-old is facing charges after a utility terrain vehicle crash that killed a 5-year-old girl, police in Rhode Island said.
Police said the teen was driving a John Deere UTV in a field Sunday afternoon when the driver lost control and the vehicle tipped over. All seven passengers and the driver were ejected from the Gator.
Two children hospitalized
When police arrived, they found two 5-year-old girls seriously hurt, one of whom was unresponsive. Both were taken to the hospital, and one did not survive.
School sends note to parents
The principal of the kindergarten-through-8th grade Wilbur and McMahon School in Little Compton sent a note to parents Sunday night acknowledging the loss in the community. The note said that while the child did not attend WMS, she participated in school activities.
Mental health counselors were available at the school all day Monday.
Charges filed
The teenage driver has been charged with two felonies: driving to endanger resulting in death and driving to endanger resulting in serious bodily injury.
Location
Police said the crash happened at 530 Long Highway. State records show that address is Maurolou Family Farm, a local campground and event venue.

title: Bangor leaders address homelessness through winter shelter funding, downtown safety
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Bangor leaders are addressing homelessness, from winter shelter beds to safety downtown.
Warming shelters took center stage at Monday’s Government Operations Committee meeting.
Shelter funding
MaineHousing awarded funds to expand the Bangor Area Homeless Shelter by five beds and the Brick Church by 65 beds. The Mansion Church and Together Place were not funded.
Officials said an average of 85 people used warming shelter beds each night last winter, topping 100 on 11 nights. They are now planning for the coldest nights ahead.
Police response
Homeless policy was another issue discussed at length. Bangor Chief of Police Mark Hathaway said mental health is just as big of an issue as the addiction crisis in the city.
He said the police department has been overwhelmed, and that it’s hard to keep up with a systemic issue specific to Bangor.
“We have more of a problem here because we literally, and I think everybody understands it, we’re caring for a large chunk of the state’s most vulnerable people. We’re just overwhelmed with it. And I don’t think it’s fair to classify one community as doing a better job, when really, we all know that most communities point their most vulnerable to the community with all the services, and that’s Bangor. We expect the street police officer to solve all of society’s failures, but we don’t give them the tools to do that job,” Hathaway said.
He went on to say that they are doing everything possible to make sure that Bangor’s residents feel comfortable walking around downtown, and that their safety is a top priority.
Copyright 2026 WABI. All rights reserved.

title: 40 miles for 40 acres: Maryland minister walks from Brunswick to Augusta for reparations
text:
RICHMOND —A little more than halfway through his trek in Maine on Tuesday, the Rev. Dr. Robert Turner already knew the walk would be physically and mentally taxing.
“The walks are always long. It’s never a walk where I’m just at the end doing cartwheels. My body is sore. But it’s also a spiritual moment for me. I reflect, I meditate. It’s like a pilgrimage. But it’s also a call to action,” Turner explained.
Turner, who is the pastor at the Empowerment Temple AME Church in Baltimore, was walking about 38 miles from Brunswick to Augusta to advocate for reparations to the descendants of enslaved Africans, a continuation of his previous initiative 40 Miles for 40 Acres, where he walked from Baltimore to Washington, D.C., each month to highlight the broken promise of Union Gen. William T. Sherman’s 40 acres and a mule.
Turner started out at the John Brown Russworm African American Center in Brunswick at 5 a.m., traveling north through Topsham along the Kennebec River, and he expected to reach the State Capitol in Augusta around 5:40 p.m. Outside of Richmond, he walked under a cloudless sky with wind blowing off the river through the rolling roads, holding a sign that read “REPARATIONS NOW” and sporting a reflective orange-and-yellow jacket.
Tuesday’s walk held additional significance. It falls on the 185th anniversary of Maine’s first Colored Convention, the 1841 gathering where African Americans met in Portland to discuss abolition and racial equality across Maine. Turner dedicated his walk to the late Gerald E. Talbot, Maine’s first Black legislator and a civil rights advocate.
“You have so much that has happened here that needs repair from, and the evidence of the suffering is still being felt on Oct. 6, 2026,” Turner said.
Turner cited historical events of oppression and racism in Maine, such as the state’s involvement with the slave trade and the history of Malaga Island. He spoke about continued racial disparities in the state, where Black people are more likely to be incarcerated, underhoused and under the poverty line.
After moving from Tulsa, Oklahoma, to Baltimore in 2021, he decided to walk the 42.9 miles to Washington, D.C., to call for reparations. Since then, he has done that walk 40 times, once every month, and then expanded the cause to a national level with walks in Alabama, North Carolina and Virginia. Maine is his ninth state and he plans to walk in all 50.
“I’ve walked in the ice, the snow, the rain, the thunderstorms, you name it, I’ve walked. I’ve never postponed a walk due to weather,” he said. “So I’ve walked in snowstorms, I’ve walked in weather advisories … I’ve walked when cities were closed down. God has kept me these 49 times. I’ve slipped, but I’ve never fallen.”
Turner’s choice to start his walk in Brunswick holds additional historical significance, being the place where Harriet Beecher Stowe wrote “Uncle Tom’s Cabin,” the anti-slavery novel. John Brown Russwurm was one of the first Black college graduates in the United States, graduating from Bowdoin College in 1826; he eventually helped found the nation’s first Black newspaper.
Walking up Route 24 outside of Richmond, Turner said he’d received both positive and negative reactions. Some responded enthusiastically to the cause. One woman stopped him alongside the road to question why he is not fighting for other groups such as Irish Americans.
“I’m not against anybody who is suffering from getting reparations,” he said.
Turner said his plan, when he reached Augusta, was to lay a wreath of 400 roses down on the state capital to represent 400 years of oppression. He planned to pray at the State Capitol, and read Chapter 61 from the Book of Isaiah in the Bible, which he reads at the end of every walk.
“Then I leave. I leave physically, but spiritually praying and politically advocating through petitions, through emails, through phone calls for repair being done in Maine,” he said.
His next state to walk is South Carolina. He plans to organize his future walks by finding historical dates in the state he will be walking in, hopefully doing the northern states in the summer and the southern states in the winter. He urges each state he walks through to repair the damage that has been done in history.
“I think Maine, by doing reparations, which is the truest form of justice that America has never seen, can help lead the nation. … Maine was one of the first states to abolish slavery,” Turner said. “Maine could also lead the nation as one of the first states to issue reparations.”

title: Scarborough Town Council candidate had extensive disciplinary history as sheriff’s deputy
text:
A Scarborough Town Council candidate has an extensive history of discipline from his 28 years as a Cumberland County sheriff’s deputy, culminating in a recommendation in 2021 that he be fired.
Disciplinary records for Samuel Cofone span 65 pages and show numerous suspensions, reprimands and warnings from 1995 to 2021. The offenses vary from missing work, to car accidents and making inappropriate sexual comments.
Cofone is one of seven candidates running for three seats on Scarborough’s Town Council. This is his first time running for public office. Cofone said in a brief interview Monday that his disciplinary record is just “small stuff.” He said his work history is irrelevant to his council candidacy, and it is unfair that his employment at the sheriff’s office was being put in the public eye.
In a survey response for the Portland Press Herald’s Voter Guide, Cofone said one of his top priorities is making the town government more transparent and holding employees and officials accountable for their actions.
According to the disciplinary records, Cofone was suspended seven times and received at least 19 written reprimands or warnings over 26 years. The suspensions ranged from one to eight days.
“The totality of your disciplinary records demonstrates a consistent pattern of policy violations and job performance that has not met expectations,” reads a document from Capt. Kerry Joyce to Cofone dated Nov. 5, 2021, in which Kerry recommended that Cofone be terminated effective immediately.
On Nov. 9, 2021, the sheriff’s office sent a memo to all law enforcement stating that Cofone was no longer employed by the Cumberland County Sheriff’s Office. Cofone said he retired. The sheriff’s office did not respond to questions about how Cofone’s employment ended.
Cofone was suspended for the first time after he was found to be involved in an avoidable two-vehicle crash on May 8, 1995. He was suspended for a day and enrolled in a defensive driving course.
In 1998, Cofone was involved in two more crashes and was suspended for four days. He also received a written reprimand for a preventable accident in 2010, and rear-ended another vehicle, causing $13,500 in total damage in 2018.
Twice, he was disciplined for erratic or unsafe driving — for one of those incidents, he received an eight-day suspension, the records show.
Cofone’s disciplinary file also includes numerous writeups for failing to report for duty, often attributed to “oversleeping.” He was once suspended for eight days after a lieutenant called him when they noticed Cofone was not on duty. Cofone’s alarm clock hadn’t gone off, he said, and the phone call woke him up, according to the documents.
Cofone said Monday that he was experiencing adverse effects to medication, and he attributed his failure to report for duty and his car crashes to that.
In 2016, Cofone was removed from the department’s marine patrol after his superiors determined he made inappropriate sexual comments to a Department of Marine Resources instructor during training. The instructor told another deputy that she felt uncomfortable being around Cofone.
“That was blown way out of proportion,” Cofone said. “I wasn’t even talking to her.”
In 2021, he was suspended for six days after throwing away a Black Lives Matter sign that had been spray-painted with racist language, when he should have placed it into evidence and processed it for fingerprints, according to the documents.
“This was not done intentionally; I have no malice toward a group of people,” Cofone said during the pre-determination hearing, the documents state. Cofone said Monday that the person who reported the incident didn’t want to write a statement, so there was no case, and therefore, no evidence.
Cofone was also disciplined for not wearing a face mask when directed, clearing himself from a call without permission because he thought his presence wasn’t necessary because other deputies were also sent to respond, not completing a proper preliminary investigation, not wearing the correct uniform, and disseminating investigative information to a suspect, among other incidents.

title: Susan Collins gets more national scrutiny for campaign donations
text:
Donations to Sen. Susan Collins were the subject of another story from a national news outlet Tuesday.
Executives at a company that produces an armored vehicle for the Army donated to political committees supporting Collins, R-Maine, and other appropriators this year after they approved funding for the vehicle — despite Army leaders saying they did not need it, according to a new report from The Intercept.
Monday’s story comes after ProPublica published an investigation in September that focused on how the FBI was probing allegations of a “pay-to-play” scheme involving a convicted former defense contractor and a pro-Collins super PAC before President Donald Trump’s administration ended the investigation in 2025.
The Republican senator and her staff have bashed the recent reporting and have never been charged in connection with any of the allegations. However, the stories have become the source of fresh campaign fodder for former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson and Collins critics amid the high-profile Senate reelection battle between Jackson and Collins.
In February, Congress approved a defense spending bill that included $345 million for the Army to acquire more deliveries of what is known as a Joint Light Tactical Vehicle. Within the next few weeks of that bill’s passage, employees with the vehicle’s maker, AM General, and the company’s PAC gave at least a combined $50,000 to committees supporting Collins, The Intercept reported.
Last year, AM General was ramping up its production line in Indiana when then-Army Secretary Dan Driscoll announced he would cancel its order, saying the additional deliveries of the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle would result in an “excess.” The Intercept noted another appropriator, Rep. Ken Calvert, R-Calif., also received five-figure donations from employees with AM General and the private equity firm that owns it.
Collins’ office said in response to The Intercept’s reporting that Collins did not make the decision to appropriate funds for the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle. It was instead the defense subcommittee chair, Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and vice chair Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del.
Lawmakers in both parties supported the revival of the Army’s order, including the top House Democrat for defense appropriations, Rep. Betty McCollum of Minnesota.
“Sen. Collins was not involved in this decision,” Collins spokesperson Phoebe Keller told The Intercept.
McConnell did not receive donations from employees at AM General or its parent group this election cycle, while the company’s employee PAC gave $2,500 to Coons, The Intercept noted. FEC records show McCollum’s leadership PAC received $5,000 from AM General’s employee PAC last year.
AM General CEO John Chadbourne told the news outlet in an email that the company does not comment on campaign donations, “all of which fully comply with FEC rules and regulations.”
In response to Driscoll’s comment on not needing additional vehicles, a joint statement from the House and Senate, which Collins’ office said was produced by the defense subcommittees, said that the Army had provided “inadequate supporting analysis.”
One concern was that without the efficiencies from a larger order that included the Army, the cost-per-unit price of vehicles that the Marines still wanted would rise, as The Intercept noted.

title: Nonprofit law firm weighs in on 'Roosters of Ogunquit' debate
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Nonprofit law firm Institute for Justice weighs in on 'Roosters of Ogunquit' debate
A national nonprofit, public interest law firm is asking a Maine town to rescind the fine it levied against a family over decorative roosters.
The town of Ogunquit has fined Dave and Sara LeBlanc because it says the roosters are illegal signage for their restaurant, The Omelette Factory, which is attached to their home.
The couple argues, however, that they only put the roosters up because their 6-year-old autistic daughter, Pyper, loves roosters.
The LeBlancs have moved the roosters away from the roadside to just in front of their home, but they said that is when their fine from the town doubled.
Daniel Woislaw, an attorney from the Institute for Justice, recently sent a letter to Ogunquit Town Manager Matthew Buttrick and Code Enforcement Officer Tyler McOsker. In the letter, Woislaw said the town is violating the First Amendment and risking "costly litigation" by fining the LeBlancs.
"Don't be bullied. Don't be bullied," said Dave LeBlanc. "If we just back down and go away, then bullies win. Bullies suck."
"So this is about supporting (Pyper) and her needs," said Sara LeBlanc. "A couple of times Dave was like, 'God, it's going to be...,' and I'm like, 'I'm not stopping.' It's hard, yes, but we're doing this for her, and we're doing this because we need to for all the other people out there, too, to show that we have rights."
Maine's Total Coverage has contacted McOsker and Ogunquit Town Clerk Christine Murphy for comment on the letter from the Institute for Justice, but had not received a reply as of Tuesday evening.

title: ‘Beatles’ in Lewiston, ‘Dead’ in Bath, wife carrying in Newry, THE fair in Fryeburg, and more
text:
Head to Fryeburg for Maine’s last agricultural fair of the season
FRYEBURG — The 176th Fryeburg Fair is taking place all this week through Sunday.
The annual tradition, which is always the final licensed agricultural fair of the Maine season, ends on a high note, with a weeklong program stuffed with events, shows, races, demonstrations, competitions, animals, exhibitions, food, live entertainment and more.
For a complete list of all the fair’s many offerings, tickets and more information, go to fryeburgfair.org. Tickets are $5 general admission, $15 premium, children under 12 are free.
The fairgrounds is at 1154 Main St.
Catch the early Beatles’ tribute Studio Tour in Lewiston
LEWISTON — On Saturday, Oct. 10, at 7:30 p.m., Studio Two will bring their early Beatles tribute music to the Franco Center stage.
The band is comprised of experienced musicians of today’s generation “dedicated to preserving the memory and fan culture of The Beatles generation. By recreating the Fab Four’s music, appearance, instruments, and onstage banter, Studio Two performs favorite Beatles hits that will bring people to the dance floor,” say organizers.
Doors and cash bar open at 6 p.m. Concert starts at 7 p.m. Tickets are $35 in advance and $40 at the door day of the show and can be purchased online at francocenter.org, by phone at 207-689-2000 or in person at the box office between 11 a.m. and 4 p.m. Tuesdays and Wednesdays.
Join in Apple Pumpkin Scarecrow Day in Rumford
RUMFORD — Apple Pumpkin Scarecrow Day will take place Saturday, Oct. 10, from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. at Rumford Center Meeting House.
The free event will feature a fall family day with scarecrow making, pumpkin carving or painting, cider pressing, a colonial photo booth, and an exhibit on Frances Perkins.
All proceeds benefit the restoration of the Meeting House, overseen by the Rumford Center Village Improvement Society.
The Meeting House is at 1352 Route 2 in Rumford Center.
Listen to ‘Stories Through Music’ in Farmington
FARMINGTON — ArtsFarmington will present Portland Piano Trio’s “Stories Through Music” on Friday, Oct. 9, from 7-9 p.m. at the University of Farmington’s Nordica Auditorium.
The event will feature a classical concert from members of the Portland Piano Trio with guest flutist Nicole Rabata of Colby College in Waterville, telling musical stories by composers including Clara and Robert Schumann.
The concert is free for UMF students and for youths 18 and younger. Adult admission is $25 and $20 for ArtsFarmington members. “Pay as you can” is accepted and no one is turned away.
For more information and for tickets, go to artsfarmington.org or at the door. Nordica Auditorium is on the second floor of Merrill Hall on the UMF campus at 224 Main St.
Carry your wife around in Newry
NEWRY — The North American Wife Carrying Championship will take place Saturday and Sunday, Oct. 10-11, at Sunday River Resort.
In the self-described “quirky championship event,” paired contestants race while carrying one another through a course.
Entry is $50 for those competing, while the free spectacle draws spectators from far and wide.
Sunday River Resort is at 15 South Ridge Road.
Take in Kouchera, Dead to the Core in Bath
BATH — The Chocolate Church Performing Arts Center will host two shows in the next week bringing both the energy and the Dead to the stage.
On Thursday, Oct. 8, at 7:30 p.m. Kouchera will deliver a “high-energy live performance rooted in Haitian Konpa, Soul and R&B. Their sets are designed to engage audiences and create a welcoming, feel-good atmosphere,” organizers say of the all-ages show.
Tickets are $15 in advance, $20 day of the show.
Then on Saturday, Oct. 10, at 7:30 p.m. Dead to the Core will bring its love of the Grateful Dead to the stage.
The collective of singer-songwriters and acoustic musicians “celebrate the band’s music not through note-for-note re-creations but by playing the songs their own way — letting them grow and evolve collaboratively in the true spirit of the Dead,” say organizers.
Tickets are $18-$20.
Saturday at 4 p.m before the evening concert the band will host a Grateful Dead Hootenanny with Dead to the Core. It will be a pre-concert workshop singing and playing classic Grateful Dead songs. Attendees are encouraged to “bring any acoustic instrument, or just your voice. The band will supply lyric and chord charts and go through the basic form and rhythm of each song,” say organizers. Tickets are $15.
For more information for either show and for tickets, go to chocolatechurcharts.org, phone 207-442-8455 or email [email protected].
The center is at 804 Washington St.
Spend an evening with ‘Walt Whitman’ in Lewiston
LEWISTON — Cambridge actor, educator, lecturer and historian Stephen Collins will perform a one-man show as one of America’s greatest poets when he presents “Unlaunch’d Voices: an Evening with Walt Whitman” on Wednesday, Oct. 7, from 5-7 p.m. in Callahan Hall at the Lewiston Public Library.
As Whitman, Collins explores the “Leaves of Grass” poet’s young life and then his maturing and later years, including “… the most important work of my life …” nursing the wounded soldiers in the hospitals during the Civil War.
“Through poetry and readings of actual letters, we experience Whitman’s movement from selfishness and selflessness and his growth into a mature artist who is at peace about ‘himself, God and death,'” say organizers.
This event is free and open to the public. No reservations or tickets are required. The performance lasts about an hour and will be followed by a Q&A.
The Lewiston Public Library is at 200 Lisbon St. For more info call 207-513-3134 or email [email protected].
Hear the Vanessa Jones Duo play at Oasis of Music in Lewiston
LEWISTON — On Wednesday, Oct. 7, the Vanessa Jones Duo will bring an afternoon of original folk/Americana music to the Oasis of Music beginning at 12:30 p.m. Accompanying Jones will be Jerry Adams on bass.
The Maine-based multi-instrumentalist has performed with a wide variety of bands, from jazz, to punk, country, Celtic, rock, classical, Americana/folk, choral, theater, blues, alternative, and beyond.
“(Jones) enjoys bringing sparkle to the human experience through the sharing of songs based in honesty, imagery, truth, pain and love,” say organizers.
On Wednesday, Oct. 14, “Keith Prairie will bring his voice and hammer dulcimer to share his special approach to folk music at the Oasis of Music,” say organizers. The program will begin at 12:30 p.m.
The Oasis of Music is at Trinity Commons, 247 Bates St. Admission is free, with donations accepted. Free parking is available in the Agora parking lot. For more information call 207-344-3106.
Have an event you’d like to get in? Email details to [email protected] to be considered for inclusion in the weekly listing. And add your event to the Sun Journal calendar here: www.sunjournal.com/events-calendar/.

title: High schools Tuesday: Winslow field hockey vanquishes Lawrence
text:
Adrianna Lombardi scored in the first and third quarters as Winslow earned a 2-0 win over Lawrence in a Kennebec Valley Athletic Conference field hockey game Tuesday in Winslow.
Emma Fales notched an assist on the first goal, helping Winslow improve to 5-4.
Silver Picard and Emma McCaslin combined on the shutout, making a total of eight saves. Anna Rogers stopped 11 shots for Lawrence (2-8).
BOYS SOCCER
BUCKFIELD 4, OAK HILL 3: Krosby Harvey’s two goals paced the Bucks (5-4-2) to victory over the Raiders (2-5-2) in Buckfield.
Harvey had a goal in each half. Aidan Stoodley scored in the first half, and Brayden Monto added a goal for Buckfield in the second half.
Kieran Stanley and Rocco Mastrianno netted first-half goals to send the game to halftime with the scored tied 2-2. The Bucks limited Oak Hill to a penalty kick goal by Cayden Fyfe in the second half.
Buckfield keeper Nathan Thomas stopped nine shots, while Oak Hill’s Logan Richardson made eight saves.
MORSE 5, CONY 0: Joao Menakuanzambi finished with two goals and an assist, leading the Shipbuilders (3-5-2) over the Rams (0-10) in Augusta.
Milton Paulo, Payton Price and Declan Riley also scored.
MOUNTAIN VALLEY 2, RICHMOND 1: Landon Canwell and Ryder Harding scored to help the Falcons (5-2-2) outlast the Bobcats (1-8-1) in Rumford.
Canwell’s goal came late in the first half, moments after Gavin Lincoln gave Richmond a 1-0 lead. Canwell booted the ball from outside Mountain Valley’s offensive third, and it got caught in the strong winds at the Hosmer Field Complex and snuck into the back of the net.
Harding scored an opportunistic goal in the second half, taking advantage when a through ball from teammate Jack Glover was misplayed by a Richmond defender.
Falcons keeper Gabe Hall made eight saves, while Richmond’s Sullivan McDaniel had four saves.
Zaden Steele assisted on Lincoln’s goal.
MT. ABRAM 2, MARANACOOK 1: Brennan Mitchell’s goal and an assist helped the Roadrunners (5-2-2) get past the Black Bears (6-4) in Salem Township.
Will Swain also scored for Mt. Abram.
Max Caban potted Maranacook’s goal.
Ben Beaulier earned the victory by making four saves for the Roadrunners. Grady Hreben stopped seven shots in the loss.
PINE TREE ACADEMY 8, RANGELEY 0: Lucky Kabeya and Fitzroy Hakizimana each tallied two goals and an assist as the Breakers (8-0) beat the Lakers (3-2-1) in Rangeley.
Rhett Tyson and Collin Verrill both chipped in with goal and two assists. Dante Lopez had a goal and an assist, and Rio Soram also scored.
SKOWHEGAN 1, LAWRENCE 0: Eben LaCasse knocked in a header early in the first half, lifting the River Hawks (6-3-1) to a win over the Bulldogs (2-7-1) in Skowhegan.
Conner Noyes preserved the shutout with a key save in the second half.
GIRLS SOCCER
MOUNTAIN VALLEY 3, CARRABEC 0: Ella Aasen netted a pair of goals and Violet Simmons made 13 saves as the Falcons (3-5-1) shut out the Cobras (1-9) in North Anson.
Mackenzie Gammon was the other goal scorer. Annabel Taylor was credited with an assist.
Carrabec keeper Lydia Dixon had 10 saves.
MESSALONSKEE 3, OXFORD HILLS 1: Two Lauren Wolfe corner kicks led to goals by the Eagles (3-8) in their victory over the Vikings (0-8-1) in Oakland.
First, a corner kick by Wolfe ended up with Caraline Lee, who passed to Lydia Parent for a goal with 11:30 left in the first half. Ten minutes later, Wolfe had another corner kick that turned into an Elsie Spear goal, with the assist going to Nora Kalback.
Madelyn Gagnon scored Messalonskee’s third goal, burying a deflection of teammate Grace McKay’s shot. Eagles keeper Ember Fitcher stopped two of the three shots she faced.
Nyrobie Cox scored for Oxford Hills on a scramble in the box. Adeline Heaward made eight saves.
SKOWHEGAN 7, LAWRENCE 0: Lydia Herrick notched two goals and added three assists for the River Hawks (8-1-1) in a win over the Bulldogs (2-6-3) in Fairfield.
Mae Dubois scored twice, while Vivian Hart and McKaela McLaughlin contributed a goal and an assist each. Madi Flannery also scored for Skowhegan.
Lawrence goalie Riley Soucy turned aside 30 shots.

title: Couple arrested on child abuse charges in surrogacy investigation involving more than 20 children, police say
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — An extremely wealthy Chinese immigrant and his wife amassed a brood of 21 children through a surrogacy scheme and raised them in a “house of horrors,” prosecutors alleged Tuesday.
Guojun Xuan, 66, and Silvia Zhang, 39, were arrested at their sprawling mansion in Arcadia, a city about 13 miles (20 kilometers) northeast of downtown Los Angeles.
The children suffered daily beatings from cruel nannies as the couple watched over a network of surveillance cameras and laughed, according to prosecutors. The couple allegedly recruited women across the country to serve as surrogates, promising them that they were just looking for another child to grow their family.
The couple face several counts of child abuse as well as conspiracy to commit child abuse, accessory after the fact and dissuading a witness, according to Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman.
“This case is unprecedented. It is horrific,” he said during a morning news conference. “The physical abuse, beating and punishment that these very young children received is despicable.”
In an afternoon court appearance in nearby Pasadena, the couple pleaded not guilty and denied all allegations with a Mandarin interpreter. Prosecutors sought $100 million bail per person because of the serious nature of the charges and because they are flight risks.
The couple have over 200 personal and 70 corporate bank accounts with annual transfers of $250 million, Deputy District Attorney MacKenzie Teymouri said.
Both were said to have U.S., Mexican and Chinese passports, though investigators have not determined if they are all legitimate; prosecutors said they used fake passports to create some of the bank accounts.
Inside the couple’s home, investigators found a bank statement showing more than $70 million in one account along with assets such as antique sculptures and specialty alcohol that added up to nearly $10 million, according to Teymouri.
LA County Superior Court Judge Kerry White set bail at $20 million each with home detention and a protective order against visiting their children.
Mitchell Krems, the couple’s attorney, called the bail amount “absurd” for the type of charges his clients face and said Zhang’s health should be taken into consideration.
Zhang, who appeared in court in a wheelchair, has a rare form of leukemia and is recovering from a bone marrow transplant, Krems said.
Fifteen children were removed from the opulent home last year after an allegation of abuse, and another six living elsewhere were also located. They ranged in age from 2 months to 13 years, with most between 1 and 3. Police believe Zhang gave birth to one or two of the children, while the rest were carried and delivered by surrogates.
Hochman said the couple set up an agency, Mark Surrogacy, that they operated from home and used to hire surrogates throughout the U.S. But prosecutors said the couple misled the women, telling some that they could not conceive and others that they only had one child and wanted one more to complete their family.
“The house could only be described as a house of horrors for these incredible young children,” Hochman said.
Prosecutor says videos show nannies and Xuan abusing children
Zhang and Xuan were first arrested in May 2025 after a hospital reported that their 2-month-old infant had a traumatic head injury, the result of being violently shaken by a nanny, according to Arcadia police.
Police did not file charges at the time, saying they needed to complete the investigation.
Hochman said the couple set up three rooms they called learning centers, where the children spent several hours a day sitting at desks under the supervision of nannies.
Through an extensive surveillance system including motion-activated cameras, the couple watched and at times laughed as the nannies physically abused the children, including daily beatings, he said.
In one video, Xuan is shown entering a room and telling a nanny to strike a child harder, Hochman said, and in another he joins the nanny in hitting the child.
The nannies were allegedly told “not to leave any physical marks on the children,” and when police arrived to investigate in May 2025, the children were told to deny they had been beaten.
After examining the surveillance video, police issued an arrest warrant for Chunmei Li, the nanny seen hurting the 2-month-old infant. However she fled to Tijuana, Mexico, and then China.
After the children were taken into state custody, Xuan and Zhang were allowed supervised visits. During one such visit, Zhang read to a child and wrote in the book, “Tell them you’re happy with me, tell them you want to come home,” lead prosecutor Teymouri said.
Krems said it was “patently false” that Xuan was involved in beating any of the children and blamed all the abuse on the nannies.
“My client, Mr. Xuan, intervened swiftly,” Krems said. “He fired the nanny, excised her from the house.”
Prosecutor says motive for discipline remains under investigation
When asked about the couple’s motivation, Hochman said that was part of the investigation, as was the parentage of each child.
Krems, Xuan’s attorney, previously told ABC7 that Xuan’s goal was to raise children who become productive adults.
“The reason he has all these children is because he wants them to contribute to society. He is not a man who is self-indulgent,” Krems said. “Some who are wealthy might spend on jewelry or cars, but he is actually spending his resources to help his children become educated.”
After Tuesday’s court hearing, he said Xuan and Zhang immigrated from China to exercise their freedom and have as many children as they want.
“If they were white, if they were Elon Musk, and they weren’t Chinese, they wouldn’t experience this level of scrutiny,” Krems said.
Surrogates say they were misled
Surrogacy is an arrangement in which a woman agrees to carry and deliver a child for another person or couple, often after an embryo transfer.
There is no comprehensive federal law regulating surrogacy, leaving most rules to the states.
California is considered to be surrogacy-friendly because it has clear laws governing the process. Both sides are required to have lawyers, and there must be a written, notarized contract before an embryo transfer takes place.
At least eight women came forward to say they were aggressively pursued to serve as surrogates. The women, many of them first-time surrogates, said they were given misleading or incomplete information about the couple’s family situation and intentions.
Krems denied that the couple lied to surrogates about their intentions.
The district attorney’s office said a federal investigation was ongoing.
___
Marcelo reported from New York.

title: How the world is responding to possible case of pneumonic plague after lab worker dies
text:
GENEVA (AP) — The World Health Organization says a possible case of pneumonic plague in Russia presents a “very low” risk outside the country as investigators look into what caused the death of a lab employee there last week.
The U.N. health agency said Tuesday that it has been in contact with Russian authorities following reports of the death last week of a woman who worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East.
The case and the investigation, led by Russian officials, have revived memories of the COVID-19 pandemic and allegations the coronavirus may have emerged at a Chinese lab. WHO has not provided a definitive answer to how the pandemic began.
“There is currently no indication that we are dealing with anything similar to the pandemic,” WHO spokesman Christian Lindmeier told The Associated Press, referring to the woman’s illness.
Here’s what to know about the case and how experts are mobilizing after her death:
Pneumonic plague is a form of the disease that affects the lungs
The incubation period for pneumonic plague — which means lung-based, and is the most virulent form of the disease — can be as short as 24 hours, according to WHO. It’s a less common but severe form that can spread between people through respiratory particles.
If untreated, the illness can be fatal, but recovery rates are high if detected and treated in time, WHO says.
Symptoms include shortness of breath and coughing, often involving the coughing up of blood.
The more common form of plague — bubonic plague — is caused by the bite of an infected flea, and can develop into open sores filled with pus.
Pneumonia is a form of acute respiratory infection that is mostly caused by viruses or bacteria, and is spread generally through contact with infected people or from airborne droplets. WHO says pneumonia is the single largest infectious cause of death in children worldwide.
What Russian officials are saying about the case
Through an international health alert system, Russian health officials on Tuesday said a full range of preventive measures had been carried out — including tracing of the deceased woman’s contacts, medical monitoring and lab tests.
“Test results showed no presence of dangerous infectious disease pathogens in any of the contacts,” said the note from Russian authorities, which was relayed to The Associated Press by WHO.
“Based on available data, laboratory test results, and health status, medical monitoring for 100% of the contacts has now been concluded,” it said. “The epidemiological situation is stable and remains under monitoring.”
The woman died at a hospital in Shelekhov, a town just outside the city of Irkutsk, and its mayor said the hospital was placed under quarantine. The top officials from Russia’s national public health watchdog traveled to the region Friday.
On Monday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov advised the public to follow official statements from the watchdog agency, Rospotrebnadzor, rather than “rumors or speculation.”
WHO has mobilized its own experts to look into the case
Lindmeier, the WHO spokesman, told a U.N. briefing Tuesday that the institute where the woman worked “studies dangerous pathogens,” including plague in a part of Siberia where the disease “occurs naturally in wild animals.”
He said Russian officials have not yet asked for WHO experts to deploy to Russia, where authorities are “looking into whether pneumonic plague caused her death.”
Russian authorities later told WHO that no case of plague has been recorded in Irkutsk, Lindmeier said.
“According to the authorities, the woman’s illness initially presented as a typical acute respiratory viral infection,” he said. “No case of plague or other high threat pathogen has been found.”
Trump and Rubio comment on the case
U.S. President Donald Trump said Monday that he was watching the situation with concern and that the United States would be willing to help, though he said he had not spoken to Russian President Vladimir Putin about the case.
Asked about Trump’s remarks, Kremlin spokesman Peskov said Tuesday that “it is always very good when mutual assistance is offered.” He wouldn’t elaborate further, deferring to Rospotrebnadzor.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged Russian authorities to share more information.
“Maybe there’s nothing there. Maybe it’s bigger than we thought. We don’t know,” he said at a news conference in Iceland.
“We encourage Russia to be more transparent and share more information with the world,” Rubio said, adding this has so far been “quite limited, but hopefully that will change in the next few hours and days.”
Ian Jones, professor of virology at the University of Reading, said that “plague carries a huge history and is still present in many parts of the world, including Russia,” although because of modern living conditions and antibiotics, its potential was limited.
Dr. Glenn Wortmann, at the MedStar Washington Hospital Center, said the bacteria that cause plague don’t “travel very far” and a person would “really need to be face-to-face” with an infected person to get pneumonic plague.
“The chance of this spreading widely in Russia and then extending here to the U.S. will not happen, not with this type of bacteria, because it’s not spread easily and we have antibiotics to stop it from spreading,” he added.
___
Associated Press writers Dasha Litvinova in Tallinn, Estonia, and Matthew Lee in Reykjavik, Iceland, contributed to this report.

title: Cape Elizabeth moves up in Varsity Maine girls soccer poll
text:
Camden Hills remains at the top of the Varsity Maine girls soccer poll, the third week in a row at No. 1 for the Windjammers. Scarborough is second for the third straight week, after being No. 1 in the first two polls. The Windjammers (9-0) and the Red Storm (9-0-1) are the only remaining Class A teams without a loss.

Bonny Eagle (6-1-2) joins the rankings at seventh. Only Windham has defeated the Scots, who also have played Scarborough and No. 6 South Portland to scoreless draws.

title: This teen turned a bus into a mobile clothing store
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BATON ROUGE, La. (InvestigateTV) - A New Orleans teenager has converted a used bus into a traveling clothing boutique, taking his business on the road across the Gulf South.
Valen Purvis, a student at Rummel High School in New Orleans, operates a mobile clothing store called Transit. The concept began during a family vacation in Point Clear, Alabama.
“Me and my dad, and my mom were on vacation in Point Clear, Alabama, just trying to enjoy the beach because they have a good beach out there,” Purvis said. “And we saw the bus on the side of the road for sale. So we’re curious people. Of course, we stopped, and we checked it out.”
Purvis said he saw a $3,000 price tag on the bus and pitched the owner his idea for a mobile streetwear store. The owner reduced the price.
“He actually notched it down to [$2,000],” Purvis said. “So we got a steal, AC, bus running. We drove it all the way back from Point Clear to New Orleans.”
Purvis then removed the transit seats, installed clothing racks, and added a custom ceiling design inspired by the New Orleans downtown scene.
“Put some wood in it and we kept the lights in here, took the covers off of it, having more of like a futuristic vibe,” Purvis said. “And of course the clothes, the addition of clothes — it’s a store now.”
In less than a year, Transit has appeared at 20 to 30 events from Baton Rouge to Houston. Purvis said the inventory is intentionally curated.
“I don’t just buy bulk, and like, I’m gonna just see what happens,” Purvis said. “But like, it’s handpicked. It’s kind of luxurious, a little bit.”
Purvis said future stops include Florida, Alabama, and Oklahoma. He also said the business has offered lessons beyond retail.
“Just like lighten people’s day and just help people find like specific personality traits that they can express through clothing,” he said. “And really like learn from myself too. Like this bus is a representation of myself. So I’m learning myself, and I’m learning others too while I’m doing this business.”
Purvis said he plans to attend college and pursue a career in a corporate setting while maintaining the independence Transit currently provides.
“See where it takes me,” Purvis said. “It’s a bus. I mean, it’s going to take me somewhere, right?”

title: Gardiner field hockey ends Belfast’s 40-game winning streak
text:
GARDINER — The Gardiner field hockey team has been in search of its first signature win of the 2026 season.
The Tigers found it Tuesday night.
A goal by sophomore Anna Griffiths broke a tie with 7:19 remaining and gave Gardiner a 3-2 victory over two-time defending Class B champion Belfast at Hoch Field. The result snapped the Lions’ 40-game winning streak that dated back to 2024. It just so happens that Gardiner delivered that previous loss.
“It’s really awesome to see. They deserve (the win),” Gardiner coach Jess Merrill said. “It’s nice to see the hard work showing off tonight.”
Gardiner (8-3) broke the tie by dominating possession in the fourth quarter, setting up Griffiths’ deflection into the cage. Cora Pare, a freshman, was credited with the assist.
The win bumped Gardiner up to fourth place in the tightly contested Class B North Heal point standings, which currently are led by Nokomis (9-1), Cony (7-2-1) and Belfast (7-1).
Tigers finally break through
Through its first 10 games, Gardiner’s only losses were against three of the state’s top teams — rival Cony (1-0), perennial Class A North champion Skowhegan (2-0) and Nokomis (2-0).
“We graduated so many girls (from last season), it was just trying to figure out who’s going to be our goal scorers (early in the season),” Merrill said. “I think they’re starting to figure that out. It’s nice to see us finally finish today. We’ve had so many opportunities in all of our games so far. But to finally finish, it’s really good to see and good momentum going forward.”
Multiple scorers stepped up for the Tigers, including senior captain Zoey Sullivan-Brennan and junior Izzy Stone.
“Our team chemistry (is key),” Sullivan-Brennan said. “We all trust each other on the field. Obviously, we’re very young. Our younger players are really stepping up this year. I think we’ve just found the connections on the field and have been working really well together.”
Reloaded Lions chugging along
Belfast graduated a large chunk of a group that led the program to its eighth and ninth state championships. This season, the Lions don’t have a single senior on the roster, and the only juniors are Jordan Wight, goaltender Opal Woodbury and captain Hope Reynolds. There are 10 sophomores.
“We do play very well as a team,” Belfast coach Jan Jackson said. “They’re young, and we have a lot of different people who can score goals, which is nice. We’ll learn from our mistakes and move on.”
Still, the Lions outscored opponents by a 38-7 margin in their first seven games. Reynolds and sophomore Charley Miles were the goal scorers on Tuesday.
Unsung hero
Belfast sophomore Morgan Shorey, who is usually a goalie, made one of the best saves of the season as a defender against the Tigers.
Leading 2-1 with 3:39 left in the third quarter, Gardiner got the ball past Woodbury, who was trying to make an aggressive stop on the ball. That gave the Tigers a shot on an open cage, but Shorey dove and saved the ball with her stick. The Lions then tied the game early in the fourth quarter.
Statistical leaders
• Gardiner: Zoey Sullivan-Brennan (1 goal, 1 assist), Izzy Stone (1 goal), Anna Griffiths (1 goal), Emma Jean (8 saves)
• Belfast: Charley Miles (1 goal), Hope Reynolds (1 goal), Opal Woodbury (18 saves)

title: Frost and freeze advisories issued for coastal Maine; more seasonable conditions expected to end the week
text:
Sub-freezing temperatures Tuesday night into Wednesday are expected to give way to a more seasonable end to the first full week of October in Maine.
The National Weather Service placed all of coastal Maine under a frost advisory from midnight until 8 a.m. Wednesday, with expected lows between 30 and 35 degrees. Meanwhile, interior Cumberland and Androscoggin counties were placed under a freeze warning, with temperatures as low as 25 degrees expected in the same timeframe.
Areas further inland, including Fryeburg, Rumford, Rangeley and Jackman, were also expected to see temperatures fall to between 25 and 30 degrees overnight, according to the weather service.
Despite the equally cold temperatures elsewhere in the state, Hunter Tubbs, a meteorologist at the weather service’s Gray office, explained that the advisories are limited to coastal regions as the growing season remains active there until Oct. 11.
“Some areas are already past the growing season, so we don’t have (advisories) out for those areas,” he said in a phone call Tuesday.
He said this is around the time when meteorologists would expect the region to begin experiencing frosty overnight temperatures. The weather service advises residents to cover or bring inside any sensitive outdoor plants.
Tubbs said Tuesday night into Wednesday would likely see the coldest temperatures of the week, with the remainder of the week looking more seasonable.
“That’s just because we had a strong cold front that came through, and that allowed for strong northwesterly winds to bring down colder air from Canada,” Tubbs explained.
Wednesday’s highs are expected to be in the high 50s and low 60s across southern and central Maine, according to the weather service.
But temperatures are expected to rise Thursday, with some areas, including Portland and Lewiston, slated to be as warm as 70 degrees. Tubbs said the projected uptick in temperatures is thanks to warmer air pushing in from the southwest.
Then, the weather service forecasts high temperatures will dip back down to the low 60s — and even to the low 50s in some western Maine communities — Friday and Saturday. Things are expected to begin warming up again on Sunday, with highs potentially reaching 70 degrees once more on Monday.
Meanwhile, low temperatures are expected to remain fairly steady: Southeastern regions, including Greater Portland, can expect lows in the mid-to-low 40s Thursday through the beginning of next week, while areas farther north and west can expect lows in the mid-to-high 30s.
Some showers could be in the mix across the western mountains late this week, according to the weather service, but Tubbs said it isn’t expected to amount to much.
“As of right now, it doesn’t look like anything significant in terms of rainfall,” he said Tuesday.
On Tuesday morning, the Mount Washington Observatory reported the first measurable snowfall of the season atop New Hampshire’s tallest peak, with just over a half-inch of snow accumulating in a 24-hour period. It noted that a wind gust of 110 miles per hour was recorded.

title: Billion Dollar Blitz: Business of College Sports bankrolled by taxpayers and students
text:
Are non-athlete students unknowingly bankrolling massive college athletics programs?
In this episode of Following Leads: The Podcast, InvestigateTV national reporter Chris Nakamoto breaks down a nationwide investigation into the explosive financial reality of college sports.
Out of 109 public FBS universities analyzed, only 10 generate enough revenue to cover their own athletic costs. The rest pulled in over $2.1 billion in mandatory student fees and university general funds—meaning regular students taking out loans may end up paying off sports department deficits for decades.
