title: Maine’s top court rejects eviction appeal by midcoast farmers
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The couple who managed Harpswell’s last sizable farm have moved themselves and their livestock off the property and lost their latest appeal to Maine’s highest court.
The Maine Supreme Judicial Court rejected the appeal of Joseph and Laura Grady, who ran Two Coves Farm for more than 16 years but were ousted because, according to an arbitrator, they failed to pay roughly $124,000 in rent and grow crops as they had once agreed.
The Aug. 19 ruling capped a protracted legal fight that had the Gradys claiming they were being forced out of their home and stripped of their livelihood in spite of their good faith efforts and in contravention of Maine’s protections for home renters.
Opposing them was Helen Norton, who — with her late husband — bought the 100-acre tract in hopes of preserving a vestige of Harpswell Neck’s agrarian history. Norton’s lawyers alleged that the Gradys had taken advantage of an ailing 94-year-old woman and were “squatting” on the land while dragging out the process with a series of “11th hour arguments.”
The Supreme Judicial Court ruling rejected the latest of those appeals. It affirmed a longer order dated July 28 in which the court upheld the arbitrator’s decision and spurned the couple’s contention that the arbitrator had exceeded his authority in treating the lease as a strictly commercial contract rather than one that also provided the Gradys with a place to live and raise their children.
Norton said she was pleased by the ruling and is working to make repairs to the property that will allow her to “find a good, responsible farmer and his family and make it a viable working farm” as soon as next spring.
Of the legal fight, she said, “It has cost me a lot of money, it has cost me a lot of time and effort, and it has made us quite unhappy.”
The Gradys declined to participate in an interview for this article. Joe Grady requested questions in writing, then declined to answer them. However, court filings from their legal team lay out their position in detail. In a brief statement emailed to the Anchor, they said they are disappointed but determined.
“The last two years of defending ourselves from the claims made against us have been exhausting; losing our home where we planned to spend the rest of our lives, as well as the business we built from scratch, was devastating and is still fresh for us,” they said in the statement.
Partners in protection
The legal battle brought a bitter closing chapter to what began as a pastoral partnership.
Two decades ago, in 2006, Norton and her late husband, Walter, bought a 100-acre saltwater farm near their home on Harpswell Neck. The entity they formed, Neils Point LLC, in 2008 granted an agriculture conservation easement to the Maine Farmland Trust, with the Harpswell Heritage Land Trust overseeing the easement.
The purpose of the arrangement was to protect the farm “from encroaching suburban sprawl so that it will always be available for its traditional use as a productive cropland, open fields and forest,” according to the arbitrator’s findings.
In 2009, a young farming couple — the Gradys — signed on as stewards of the property, an agreement renewed in 2017 for an additional 25 years. In exchange for the right to live and farm there, the couple agreed to keep the farm in productive operation and to pay rent equal to 10% of their “annual net proceeds” — their farming revenue minus legitimate operating expenses.
For many years, all seemed to be going smoothly at Two Coves Farm. Drivers passing the property on Harpswell Neck Road saw signs advertising a farm stand along a tree-lined lane that sold, among other things, eggs, lamb, tomatoes, cucumbers, yarn and sheepskins.
A ‘stark injustice’ or an end to a ‘free ride’?
But trouble arrived last year, when relations between Norton and the Gradys took a sharp downward turn. In July 2025, an arbitrator presided over a hearing to examine Norton’s allegations that the couple had failed to live up to their end of the deal.
After examining evidence and hearing from both sides, arbitrator and Portland lawyer Timothy J. Bryant concluded that the Gradys had not made rent payments on time and “failed to pay any rent whatsoever for the years of 2023 and 2024.” In a decision dated Oct. 24, 2025, the arbitrator concluded that the Gradys had understated their revenues and “knowingly inflated their operational expenses by treating household and personal expenses as business expenses.”
The arbitrator also agreed with Norton that the Gradys had failed to “use the farm to actively plant and grow productive crops,” as required by the 2017 lease.
He ordered the Gradys to pay Norton’s Neils Point LLC $124,175 and to vacate the farm no later than Dec. 31, 2025.
The Gradys did not move out, instead filing a Dec. 30 appeal asking a Maine Superior Court justice to vacate the decision and allow them to continue working and living at Two Coves. Because the farm was also their home, they argued that state law prohibited them from being evicted without the formal court process guaranteed to residential tenants.
Norton’s legal team countered by saying that the arbitrator’s ruling was sound, and that the Gradys had voluntarily agreed to arbitration as the method for resolving disputes. In a Feb. 4 ruling, Superior Court Justice Darcie N. McElwee sided with Norton and agreed that the Gradys must vacate.
In late February, the Gradys took their appeal to the Supreme Judicial Court.
“This case presents a stark injustice,” wrote the Gradys’ lawyers, Regan A. Sweeney and J. Spencer Hoffman. “A wealthy landowner has utilized commercial arbitration to dispossess a tenant farming family from the property they have called home and worked for over sixteen years.”
The lawyers stated that the Gradys had been served a “writ of possession” on Feb. 25, giving them 48 hours to vacate. “The Gradys were afforded no meaningful opportunity to seek appellate relief before the coercive machinery of eviction was set in motion,” they wrote.
The court’s ruling would affect not just the Gradys, their lawyers wrote, but also other farmers.
“Farmers are the backbone of Maine’s communities. They feed their neighbors, steward the land, and embody the independence and self-reliance that define this State’s character,” they said. “Yet the (ruling) treats farmers as something less than every other resident of Maine. The Gradys are people who work the land they live on. They are not commercial tenants operating a warehouse or retail establishment. … Their home is their farm, and their farm is their home. The two are inseparable.”
Norton’s lawyers countered with strong words of their own in a Feb. 27 pleading. Noting that the Gradys had already relocated their livestock and “never grew any crops in the first place,” they said the couple faced no real hardship.
“For the last decade, the (Gradys) have had possession of the farm under false pretenses. For the last two months, they have trespassed on the property unlawfully,” said attorneys Thimi R. Mina and Alfred C. Frawley IV. “Meanwhile, Mrs. Norton is 94 years old and recently suffered a significant injury. Put simply, time is of the essence, and the balance of the equities lies in favor of ending the (Gradys’) decade-long free ride while Mrs. Norton still has the opportunity to put the property to productive use.”
The legal point and counterpoint continued through the spring and summer. Following the adverse July 28 Supreme Judicial Court ruling, the Gradys again appealed and — in August — lost again.
The court rejected the Gradys’ argument that they were entitled to the same channels of legal appeal available to a tenant facing eviction from a rental home. Instead, the Gradys had to abide by the arbitrator’s decision after earlier agreeing on that course of conflict resolution.
As their legal battle wound down, both the Gradys and Norton expressed gratitude for the support they had received from neighbors.
“I am very happy for the support that I’ve received from the community,” said Norton, who, along with her husband, has invested in conserving a large amount of open land in Harpswell and neighboring communities.
“To all those in Harpswell who have supported us and Two Coves Farm, we want to pass on our thanks and let you all know that we are doing well and have transitioned to a new home,” the Grady family said in their statement emailed to the Anchor.
“We do not know what the future holds at the moment,” they added, “but we will certainly be finding our way back to farming in the months and years ahead.”

title: Reverse mentoring: How generations can beat workplace ageism together
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Aging Untold) — Ageism at work isn’t always obvious. It can hide in quiet assumptions — about who understands technology, who communicates well or who has something valuable to contribute.
The Aging Untold hosts are digging into reverse mentoring, a strategy that flips the traditional mentor-mentee relationship so every generation in the office has something to teach and something to learn.
What is reverse mentoring?
The idea isn’t new. Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, traced it back to corporate history.
“Jack Welch, former CEO of General Electric, started an official reverse mentoring program at his company,” O’Rourke said. “He could see that the younger people had all this technology knowledge, and he could see that the older adults had some institutional memory and some people skills that could be passed on.”
O’Rourke said Welch’s program was formal and structured, built so older and younger employees could learn from each other.
Older generations weren’t raised with the technology — and that’s OK
Gerontologist Sam Cradduck said that older employees may feel behind simply because of when they grew up.
“Maybe our older generation wasn’t raised with technology,” Cradduck said. “I was a senior when we got our computers in high school. So our older generation wasn’t raised with a smartphone in their hand and a computer. The mainframes took up great big rooms back then.”
Cradduck added that while younger coworkers have a lot to offer older generations, she sometimes sees resistance to that exchange.
The antidote to ageism: belief in yourself
Not everyone agreed that resistance is the full picture.
Katherine Ambrose, an aging-well coach, argued that longevity in the workforce is an advantage, not a liability.
“What I think is that makes us perfectly equipped because we invented this stuff,” Ambrose said. “We were here as every new thing came along — that perfectly positions us to lead.”
Ambrose said the real defense against age bias isn’t avoiding new tools — it’s having the right attitude.
“The antidote to ageism is belief in yourself, and staying on top of trends and helping to lead the way,” Ambrose said. “Your personal energy, your personal capacity really matters. If you don’t want to get left behind and you want to be competitive, compete.”
Moving past an “all-or-none” mindset
The conversation turned to how generations can stop viewing each other in extremes.
“I think we have to get away from this all-or-none mentality,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
She said there is an opportunity for generations to integrate rather than compete, since older workers bring experience while younger workers bring technology fluency — and both groups can benefit from each other.
“The younger people look up to the older people for the wisdom,” Rogers said.
Practical tips for bridging the generational gap
O’Rourke offered direct advice for older workers looking to engage younger colleagues.
“If I’m an older person in the workforce, here’s some tips that I would give: Learn how to ask open-ended questions of the younger person,” O’Rourke said. “What are the trends you’re seeing? ... What do you not know, and be humble enough to ask a question.”
She also had advice for younger employees who may feel hesitant to approach older coworkers.
“If you’re younger, you’re insecure, you might be more fearful,” O’Rourke said. “But go ahead and ask an older adult: Do you see me doing anything that I could get better at? Do you see anything that I should know that I don’t even know that I should know?”
Key takeaways
- Competition can silo generations, but collaboration wins. Ditching the “all-or-none” mentality helps coworkers of every age connect.
- Be humble across generations. Ask older coworkers what you might be missing, and ask younger coworkers what trends or tech you may not know.
- Staying valuable is the antidote to ageism. Keep your attitude, energy, and contribution strong to stay competitive at any age.

title: Cape Elizabeth moves up in Varsity Maine girls soccer poll

title: UMaine football fires offensive coordinator Mikahael Waters
text:
The slumping University of Maine football team has fired offensive coordinator Mikahael Waters.
Head coach Jordan Stevens confirmed the move Tuesday. Waters had been offensive coordinator for the Black Bears since 2024.
The move comes as a sputtering Maine offense is ranked 118th out of 124 Football Championship Subdivision teams in points per game (14.5). The Black Bears have lost five consecutive games, most recently a 24-16 home defeat Saturday against Sacred Heart.
Waters was in his eighth season with the Black Bears, having joined the staff in 2019 under then-first-year head coach Nick Charlton. He served as Maine’s tight ends coach from 2019-22 and as special teams coordinator in 2023 prior to his promotion to offensive coordinator.
Maine’s offensive struggles have been a theme all season. In addition to their paltry points-per-game ranking, the Black Bears rank 93rd in passing yards per game and 110th in rushing yards per game. The team has just 66 points in 22 quarters since scoring 21 in the first half of the season opener at Towson.
“We have to coach better, and we have to put our players in a better position to make plays, and that’s from a confidence standpoint and from an execution standpoint,” Stevens told the media Tuesday. “When we talk execution, that’s not on the players; that’s on us to make sure they’re in a position to execute.”
Maine’s output in 2026 is a significant drop-off from the previous two seasons under Waters. The Black Bears averaged 24.2 points per game (67th) last year, and 23.2 points per game (74th) in Waters’ first season as offensive coordinator in 2024.
Sean Green, Maine’s running backs coach and a former state title-winning head coach at Portland and Cape Elizabeth high schools, will take over play-calling duties. Offensive analyst Cooper Heisey will take over for Green as running backs coach.
Maine is on a bye this week. The Black Bears will be back in action at 1 p.m. on Oct. 17 when they host Bryant (4-1 overall, 2-0 Coastal Athletic Association).

title: Construction worker dies after excavator overturns at Gray site
text:
Maine construction worker dies after excavator overturns at Gray site
A Maine man has died after the excavator he was operating at a work site in Gray overturned, according to authorities.
John Woodman, 61, of Standish, was identified as the victim of Monday's accident off of Bull Run Road.
The Cumberland County Sheriff's Office said deputies and members of the Gray Fire & Rescue Department and New Gloucester Fire & Rescue Department responded to the scene shortly before 2:10 p.m.
Officials said crews from Shaw Brothers Construction and Unitil were performing work on a petroleum pipeline in a wooded area behind a Bull Run Road property when the excavator Woodman was operating overturned while going up a steep grade.
Woodman, a longtime employee of Shaw Brothers Construction, suffered fatal injuries from the accident, according to officials.
The Cumberland County Sheriff's Office said it does not appear that alcohol is a factor in the incident, which is being investigated by the agency's Criminal Investigation Division, the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner and the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA).

title: Tropical disturbance in the Gulf could become a storm by Friday. Here’s what forecasters say
text:
BATON ROUGE, La. (WAFB/Gray News) - A tropical disturbance in the Gulf is getting better organized as forecasters say they are watching for possible tropical storm or hurricane development.
Morning satellite imagery Tuesday showed a noticeable increase in thunderstorm activity around the system compared with Monday as it continues organizing over the southwestern Gulf.
The National Hurricane Center said early Tuesday that Invest 92L has an 80% chance of developing within the next 48 hours and an 80% chance of development over the next seven days.
If the system strengthens into a tropical storm, it would be named Isaias.
The system is expected to drift east-northeast through the middle of the week before turning north toward the northern Gulf Coast.
Some early tracks show the storm possibly heading toward Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama and Florida.
The National Hurricane Center said it currently remains too early to determine specific impacts, but people along the northern Gulf Coast should closely monitor the system.
Forecasters in Louisiana said impacts could begin as early as Friday night and continue into Saturday, depending on how quickly the system develops and where it ultimately tracks.
But what those impacts could include remains uncertain.
The risks of rain, wind, storm surge and coastal flooding will become clearer once the system develops and forecasters have a better understanding of its track and strength.

title: 71-year-old man thrown from bike, killed after hitting dog in Central Park
text:
NEW YORK (WABC) - A 71-year-old man cycling in New York’s Central Park was thrown from his bike and killed after he hit a dog that wasn’t on a leash.
The incident happened just before 8:30 a.m. Monday in the park.
The 71-year-old cyclist, who was wearing a helmet, was riding a trek racing pedal bike when he hit a golden retriever that wasn’t on a leash. He was thrown from his bike and struck the pavement, suffering injuries to his head and body. First responders rushed the victim to the hospital, where he was pronounced dead.
The dog’s owner was on the scene, and police say the dog was not injured.
There is no word yet if anyone will face charges in the deadly incident.
Dogs are permitted to be off leash in Central Park from 6 a.m. to 9 a.m., but they must be on a short leash on park drives at all times.
The Central Park Conservancy released a statement Monday, calling on all New Yorkers to follow the rules of the park.
“We are heartbroken to hear of the fatal incident that occurred in Central Park this morning involving a cyclist and an off-leash dog. Our thoughts are with the family, friends, and loved ones of the cyclist who lost his life,” the statement read. “Central Park was created more than 150 years ago to provide a peaceful, joyful respite for all from the intense pace and pressures of the surrounding city. The Park cannot continue to serve that purpose unless all New Yorkers hold to the essential agreement of public space: know and follow the rules, and respect your fellow visitors.”

title: Hit or miss, The Biergarten in Skowhegan earns 3 stars
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Biergarten is a casual restaurant, so homey and unpretentious that our server briefly plunked down at the table to chat. I hadn’t experienced this since eating 12 years ago at a place called — not even kidding — It Don’t Matter Family Restaurant, in Highland Home, Alabama. (With a name that nihilistic, you just have to stop in, if only to find out exactly what don’t matter.)
There, as here, the cozy chumminess is all part of the charm.
Located inside a stylishly renovated former wool mill, The Biergarten is an airy, tasteful loft space that applies German aesthetics sparingly. Small deer antlers adorn the communal pine tables; antique beer steins from “mug club” members flank the rough-hewn wood frame of the mirror behind the bar. More Oktoberfest-style tables and benches are available on the back patio alongside the Kennebec River on weekend evenings.
A local brewery had originally planned to open a brewpub in the space before backing out. When Biergarten Managing Owner Amber Lambke and and her son, General Manager Miles Lambke, stepped in, they stuck with the beer theme, since many of the state’s breweries use grains sourced from Skowhegan’s Maine Grains. (Amber Lambke is co-founder and CEO of Maine Grains, and also owns The Miller’s Table, the excellent cafe, bakery and pizzeria in its same building.)
But the Lambkes didn’t want to serve run-of-the-wool-mill pub fare. They’d get a certain amount of out-of-town customers, particularly since The Biergarten is the restaurant for the adjoining boutique hotel, The Skowhegan by Kasa. But they still wanted it to be affordable and family-friendly for locals, the bulk of their clientele.
“There’s a void of German food in Central Maine, so it made sense to fill that gap,” Miles said. “And when it comes down to it, German food is basic meat-and-potatoes most of the time. So even though it comes with an unfamiliar name like schnitzel, it’s easy to explain to people and get them on board with fried chicken.”
A pork version is an occasional weekly special, but Chicken Schnitzel ($29) is a staple. Their deep-fried version was well seasoned, with raucously crunchy panko coating, though we found the thin-pounded meat a touch dry. A side of pleasantly soft braised red cabbage offers balanced, straightforward flavors of brown sugar, apples and cider vinegar; a little warm spice might lend fetching depth. Even better were the buttery, squishy squiggles of spaetzle — made from nutty Maine Grains spelt flour, a Biergarten workhorse — with their crisped brown edges.
You have to admire how the Lambkes’ concept provides such a fitting home for Maine-made products like sausage from The Sausage Kitchen in Lisbon Falls, Morse’s sauerkraut and Raye’s Old World brown mustard, all of which are showcased on their Bratwurst ($18). A scrumptious griddled bun from The Good Crust in Canaan cradles the long, juicy link, and might even be the best part of the tasty dish.
The Sausage Kitchen also supplies links for The Wurst Plate ($18), portions of knackwurst, mettwurst and whiskey-peppercorn bratwurst with a trio of mustards. Though fine, the flavor differences among the meats were vanishingly subtle, perhaps defeating the purpose of a sampler.
Our very first taste of The Biergarten was… odd. Their filtered tap water tasted earthy, like fresh-dug beetroot. Miles said while he doesn’t personally notice anything off in the taste, other out-of-town customers have commented about the water. Seems like a new filter is in order.
Then we tried the aptly named Forest Fire ($15), a smoked riff on an Old Fashioned. It looked like a short pour, not quite reaching halfway up its small rocks glass. But the real problem was how the acrid, ashy smoke from dried rosemary (which should be delightfully woodsy) laid waste to an otherwise good cocktail. The cocktail smoker may be also be overdue for maintenance.
We course-corrected with a splendid, malty Ayinger Celebrator Doppelbock ($8.50) and crisp, fruity Raimund Prüm Essence Riesling ($14) from Germany’s Mosel region. The Biergarten stocks 16 beers and ciders on tap, most local, with a few German imports custom-built for the cuisine. They also sell eight wines by the glass ($9-$15), and 16 by the bottle ($32-$78), an approachably priced and unclichéd selection of Old and New World options.
My dining partner grew up in Alsace, France, and flammkuchen (or tarte flambée, as she knew it) is her soul food. She rhapsodizes about thin, cracker-crisp crust smeared with rich crème fraîche and scattered with thin slices of onion and plump lardons. When our Flammkuchen Tavern Pizza ($23) hit the table, she was aghast.
Crunchy bacon bits stand in for lardons, Jackson Pollock-like squirts of crème fraîche are cut with mustard, and — most appalling to her — the crust (from The Good Crust) was far too soft, and actually seemed more like pita bread.
Sure, it’s not authentic, but I won’t fault them for that. It also fails as “tavern pizza,” though. It’s the kind of pizza your mom might try to slip by you on scrounge night.
“Mom, what is this?”
“I told you, it’s pizza. Eat your pizza, dear.”
Our starters and entrées arrived basically at once, though we’d asked for separation. Our server was apologetic, even as she made room on the table for more dishes, glancing helplessly toward the kitchen on that quiet Tuesday night. “They’re just kicking (the dishes) out,” she shrugged.
The Biergarten doesn’t have a head chef, just a kitchen crew that works off recipes and standard operating procedures. Miles explained that the local culinary talent pool has fewer professionally trained cooks than more densely populated areas, so they made sure their menu was uncomplicated and could be pulled off by “people with a variety of skill sets.”
We eventually cleared the decks for dessert, their popular Black Forest Brownie Sundae ($10). The spectacular warm spelt brownie from The Miller’s Table was gooey and intensely fudgy, but buried under too much whipped cream and cherry compote, itself overwhelmed by almond extract.
When I come back to The Biergarten, hopefully to enjoy some lovely fall weather at one of their outdoor tables, I’ll again order the Giant Soft Spelt Pretzel ($13). Its well-calibrated trio of Maine Grains flours make for a tender, chewy belly and crispy inner spindles. Dip a piece into the accompanying Bavarian beer cheese, featuring brie from Haymay Creamery in Farmington, for a touch of funk. I’d like to catch the pork schnitzel special, and I also want to try their Rueben, served on a rye English muffin from Portland chef Ilma Lopez.
The Biertgarten marks its one-year anniversary this month. The missteps in our meal mostly seem like quick and easy fixes, and I’d bet it won’t be long before they’re levelled up. Amber Lambke cares deeply about Maine-made food. She’s helped shape the local and state food economy on a literally granular level. She knows — it all matters.
RATING: ***
WHERE: 7 Island Ave., Skowhegan, skowheganbiergarten.com
SERVING: Noon-8 p.m., Sunday through Thursday; Noon-9 p.m., Friday and Saturday; outdoor seating 4-8 p.m., Friday through Sunday
PRICE RANGE: Starters $8-$23, mains $15-$29
NOISE LEVEL: Medium-low on an early weeknight
VEGETARIAN: Some dishes
GLUTEN-FREE: Some dishes
RESERVATIONS: Yes
BAR: Cocktails, wine, beer, cider 
WHEELCHAIR ACCESS: Yes
BOTTOM LINE: When Maine Grains co-founder Amber Lambke and her son Miles launched The Biergarten in The Spinning Mill last October, they aimed to offer family-friendly German beer hall food and beverages at accessible price points. They’ve succeeded in parts, though some dishes and drinks need more attention to detail. Maine Grains spelt flour is the common thread in some of the best items, like a nutty and faintly sweet giant soft pretzel, pillowy buttered spaetzle, and a killer brownie (that gets unfortunately lost in a pile of whipped cream and cherry compote). Sausage, sauerkraut, mustard and buns from Maine partner producers come together in a tasty bratwurst dish, while the flammkuchen was a miss. We had issues with a smoky cocktail, but the local and German beer selection is robust, and the accommodating wine list likely has something that suits both your food and personal preferences. Tables on the back riverside patio seem like a great place to hunker down for fall festivities. 
Ratings follow this scale and take into consideration food, atmosphere, service and value and type of restaurant (a casual bistro will be judged as a casual bistro, an expensive upscale restaurant as such):
* Poor 
** Fair
*** Good
**** Excellent
***** Extraordinary
The Maine Sunday Telegram visits each restaurant once; if the first meal was unsatisfactory, the reviewer returns for a second. The reviewer never accepts free food or drink.

title: Bangor leaders address homelessness, winter shelter capacity
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Bangor leaders are addressing homelessness, from winter shelter beds to safety downtown.
Warming shelters took center stage at Monday’s Government Operations Committee meeting.
Shelter funding
MaineHousing awarded funds to expand the Bangor Area Homeless Shelter by five beds and the Brick Church by 65 beds. The Mansion Church and Together Place were not funded.
Officials said an average of 85 people used warming shelter beds each night last winter, topping 100 on 11 nights. They are now planning for the coldest nights ahead.
Police response
Homeless policy was another issue discussed at length. Bangor Chief of Police Mark Hathaway said mental health is just as big of an issue as the addiction crisis in the city.
He said the police department has been overwhelmed, and that it’s hard to keep up with a systemic issue specific to Bangor.
“We have more of a problem here because we literally, and I think everybody understands it, we’re caring for a large chunk of the state’s most vulnerable people. We’re just overwhelmed with it. And I don’t think it’s fair to classify one community as doing a better job, when really, we all know that most communities point their most vulnerable to the community with all the services, and that’s Bangor. We expect the street police officer to solve all of society’s failures, but we don’t give them the tools to do that job,” Hathaway said.
He went on to say that they are doing everything possible to make sure that Bangor’s residents feel comfortable walking around downtown, and that their safety is a top priority.

title: Portland could be the next Maine city to regulate data centers
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Portland City Council could soon ask city staff to draft new regulations on data centers as Greater Portland sees increasing development interest.
The Housing & Economic Development Committee is slated to discuss the issue Tuesday and could forward a resolution to the council that would begin a planning board review.
According to a committee memo, existing ordinances in Portland “do not adequately address” the infrastructure demands and environmental and neighborhood impacts of data centers.
Councilor Pious Ali, who chairs the committee, asked that the committee review and possibly vote on the draft resolution, which states that “there is increasing interest within or surrounding the city of Portland in the siting and development of large-scale data center facilities.”
The memo says both city councilors and Portland residents have raised concerns about data centers typically using large amounts of land, electricity and water and generating air, water and noise pollution.
Ali said Tuesday that he supports an outright ban on such facilities in Portland because of such concerns.
“Before we commit our city to that kind of development, we need to consider the impact on residents, our environment and our ability to meet Portland’s needs,” he said. “My responsibility is to put our community and people first.”
Data centers are facilities that house computers and other digital infrastructure to store data and run online applications and services. While the centers have existed for decades, new developments in artificial intelligence technology have increased demand for the sites, as well as public concern about their development.
If ultimately approved, Maine’s largest city would join several other municipalities that have either regulated or passed moratoriums regarding data centers this year after Gov. Janet Mills vetoed a bill to temporarily restrict permitting new data centers statewide.
Bangor, Brunswick, Gorham, Gray, Saco, Sanford, Scarborough and Westbrook, among other communities, have approved temporary bans since May, intended to give them time to address concerns and potentially adjust their zoning ordinances.
In Portland, city planning staff recently began considering changes to zoning ordinances because of the lack of regulations on the books, the committee memo says.
Other neighboring municipalities, including Falmouth, South Portland and Yarmouth, are not seeing regulations as immediately necessary and believe that the Legislature’s support for a statewide ban means the issue will be brought back.

title: Maine's September bull moose season success up from last year
text:
Outdoors
The BDN outdoors section brings readers into the woods, waters and wild places of Maine. It features stories on hunting, fishing, wildlife, conservation and recreation, told by people who live these experiences. This section emphasizes hands-on knowledge, field reports, issues, trends and the traditions that define life outside in Maine. Read more Outdoors stories here. 
Maine’s September bull moose season ended with a 71% success rate, with hunters filling 818 of the 1,150 permits, a significant increase from last year’s 57% success rate.
The table below summarizes results for each zone. There were 100 additional permits allocated this year — 65 in WMD 7, 10 in WMD 13, 15 in WMD 12 and 10 in WMD 10. Hunters drawn for WMDs 7 or 13, 12 or 15, 14 or 17, or 27 or 28 were permitted to hunt in either district. Permit allocations remained unchanged for all other WMDs. No bull tags were issued for WMDs 8, 9, 14 or 17.
MDIFW said it will review anomalous records before the results are considered official.
So why was success higher this year?
Maine moose biologist Lee Kantar said several factors can affect the outcome of a moose hunt, including drought, weather, hunter effort and experience.
“Consider the deer rifle season — four weeks of hunting results in 20% success,” he said. “If the weather is not great one week, you have three other weeks.”
A six-day moose hunt is more compressed, he said, leaving hunters with little leeway when conditions do not work in their favor.
Despite rain during the first two days of the season, hunters continued filling permits throughout the week.
Jaxen Wiegand of Skowhegan, who entered his name in the moose lottery for the first time, harvested a 50-inch bull in WMD 12 at 6:36 a.m. on opening day.
Kassidy Noem Peters, daughter of former South Dakota Gov. Kristi Noem, filled her permit on opening day, harvesting an 829-pound bull with a 44-inch antler spread in WMD 5. Peters hunted as part of a relationship-building trip with supporters and friends of Pheasants Forever and Quail Forever.
“It was an amazing experience,” Peters said, describing the hunt as an opportunity to spend time with local Maine residents and connect over a shared love of hunting, conservation and the outdoors.
John and Joy Thompson of Purcellville, Virginia, also filled their permit on opening day, with John shooting a 770-pound bull with a 50.5-inch antler spread at 35 yards in WMD 1. The couple had been putting in for a moose permit for 35 years.
Later in the week, Kayden Richard of Belfast harvested a 46-inch bull in WMD 1 after cow calling and raking brought the animal into range in a black spruce swamp. The moose was about a half-mile from the road and was quartered and packed out after dark.
On Thursday morning, Devin Benner harvested a 741-pound bull in WMD 2 with a roughly 360-yard shot. The Benner family spent the week camping in the North Maine Woods with 10 children, nine of whom were 5 or younger. The family has collectively harvested 12 moose since 2012.
Zach Potvin of Shapleigh harvested an 863-pound bull with a 59-inch antler spread at 2:45 p.m. Saturday. “Down to the wire,” Tobey Brook Guide Service said. “Was a fun week and persistence paid off.”
MDIFW will run its annual winter tick transects on moose at multiple stations across the state next week, Kantar said. The department has conducted the index since 2006, when the October bull season was the latest moose season. After the data are returned, biologists will summarize the findings and determine where this year fits within the long-term data set and what it might mean for winter tick infestations and overwintering calf mortality and survival.

title: Thomas College awarded $3 million grant to build artificial intelligence integration across curriculum
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WATERVILLE — Thomas College has been awarded a $3 million Title III Strengthening Institutions Grant “Building the College of the Future: Integrating Artificial Intelligence Across the Curriculum” to build appropriate artificial intelligence proficiency into all academic programs.
This multi-year project will support an institution-wide effort to ensure that every Thomas College graduate develops practical, critical and ethical AI literacy. The grant supports hiring several full-time positions including an AI specialist in residence to support professional development for faculty; ensure AI is embedded across curricula; expand applied learning through AI access; bring awareness to the resource needs and sustainability aspects to having AI; and develop a design space with equipment specialized for fabrication, testing, robotics, automation, data acquisition and computer-aided design.
“This Title III grant aligns seamlessly with who Thomas College is and where we are headed,” Provost Jeremy Qualls said. “Thomas College is committed to and excels at providing a career-driven education, and this grant will allow us to provide the most cutting-edge curriculum to make sure our graduates are ready to use technology in their future careers.”
This project will impact all students and allow the College to create new majors to be competitive in a rapidly evolving AI market.
“Bringing a major competitive federal grant like this to Maine is a big deal, and it will be felt directly by the businesses that make up our economy. For a small business or early-stage startup in Central Maine, a single employee who knows how to use AI well can change what the entire company is able to do. Thomas College’s Title III award means that talent will be developed right here, with AI literacy and hands-on proficiency built into every program,” Central Maine Growth Council President & CEO, Garvan Donegan said. “This is exactly how we deepen technical expertise in computational sciences and AI across Central Maine and beyond: by securing national resources and putting them to work for the people and businesses already here.”

title: Top Democrat is investigating Jared Kushner’s financial investments after recent report
text:
Top Democrat is investigating Jared Kushner’s financial investments after recent report
A top Democratic lawmaker is seeking information on Jared Kushner’s financial investments following a CNN investigation last week that found his private equity firm is the largest shareholder in an Israeli company backing businesses involved in Israel’s military campaigns.
Rep. Robert Garcia, the ranking member on the House Oversight Committee, sent Kushner’s investment firm, Affinity Partners, a letter on Monday saying Democrats on the committee were “investigating the unprecedented and dangerous ways in which President Trump and his family have profited directly from their access to power.
“…I request detailed information about your business dealings in the Middle East to understand whether your significant financial gains have come at the cost of Americans’ safety and security,” the California representative wrote.
The letter is yet another sign that House Democrats are poised to investigate President Donald Trump’s family members’ business dealings overseas and in the U.S., should they retake the majority in the midterm elections this fall.
An attorney for Kushner dismissed Garcia’s criticisms and sought to draw attention to the congressman’s own holdings in investments scrutinized in CNN’s report on Kushner – Phoenix Financial, an Israeli financial services firm which counts Affinity Partners as its biggest investor, and Elbit Systems, Israel’s largest arms manufacturer.
“Rep. Garcia’s letter is a masterclass in irony: A member of Congress questioning a private citizen for having an interest in the same stock in which the member also holds an interest,” the attorney said in a statement to CNN. “Jared has no role in deciding what Phoenix buys or sells. But if that doesn’t matter to Rep. Garcia, he should begin by investigating himself.”
Garcia’s most recent disclosure forms indicate that his pension plans are managed through the California Public Employees’ Retirement System and the California State Teachers Retirement System. Both plans hold stock in Phoenix Financials or Elbit Systems.
A spokesperson for Garcia said Kushner’s attorney was trying to “deflect” from his client’s own conduct, adding the congressman does not trade stocks and, like the millions of other public employees in the pension plan, does not have any control over the fund and cannot opt out.
Kushner “makes millions with no accountability all while he travels the Middle East on behalf of his father in law,” said Sara Guerrero, Garcia’s spokesperson.
“The apparent conflict of interest between Affinity Partners’ investments and your work in the Middle East, and in particular the potential for corrupt dealmaking given those competing interests, demands congressional oversight and accountability,” Garcia’s letter stated.
CNN’s investigation raised questions about potential conflicts of interest between Kushner’s volunteer role as a peace envoy to the Middle East, and his firm’s financial investments. Kushner’s attorney did not address his client’s role as a negotiator on behalf of the Trump administration.
As part of the review into Kushner’s financial holdings, CNN used Israeli financial transparency laws to trace investments made by Phoenix Financial, a Tel Aviv-based firm that Kushner’s Affinity Partners doubled its stake in last year, shortly before Trump returned to the Oval Office. CNN’s reporting specifically excluded Phoenix’s investments through retirement accounts and focused on insurance holdings instead.
Those records, which include only some of Phoenix’s holdings, show Phoenix has invested hundreds of millions of dollars into Elbit Systems. Phoenix also holds stakes in at least eight other companies providing equipment for the Israeli military ranging from drones and warships to demolition machinery, CNN found.
All nine companies identified by CNN saw their stock value climb last year, with many stating the war in Gaza had driven demand for their businesses.
Affinity doesn’t directly hold a stake in the nine companies CNN identified – but it does stand to reap rewards when Phoenix makes a profit. Kushner described Phoenix as Affinity’s “best investment” in September 2025.
CNN found no indication that Kushner’s actions as a diplomat directly affected the investments reviewed. Kushner’s attorney told CNN his client has “never participated in or directed Phoenix’s decisions” on where to invest.
A day after CNN’s reporting, Kushner posted a rare response on X, calling CNN’s story “deeply misleading.” Kushner did not point to any inaccuracies in the piece in his post.
“Misleading stories will not distract me from the work President Trump asked me to do: help end wars, bring people together and pursue peace. That work is too important,” Kushner wrote on X.
Garcia referenced Kushner’s social media post, writing “despite your denial of improper behavior, the fact remains that you have been allowed to hold a position of enormous power and responsibility, exempt from financial disclosure requirements and outside oversight.”
In addition to CNN’s report, the New York Times published a story detailing additional “intermingling” between Kushner’s volunteer diplomatic role and his businesses, as it related to the war in Ukraine.
US talks with Russia to end that war have expanded to include a multibillion-dollar deal selling oil assets from one of Russia’s biggest energy companies to a group of investors with ties to Steve Witkoff and Kushner, the two main negotiators for the Trump administration, according to the Times.
A spokeswoman for Witkoff told the Times he “has no conflict of interest or financial stake in this matter” and said his work for the US administration is undertaken “at his own expense.”
Kushner’s attorney did not respond to CNN’s inquiry about this reporting.
Garcia and other Democrats have for years demanded answers from the White House and Trump’s family about concerns over “apparent influence peddling and quid pro quo deals” and whether foreign money is being used “to buy access to the President and influence American policy.”
In March, Garcia and Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden specifically requested information from the White House about Affinity Partners’ fundraising in the Middle East – Kushner secured a $2 billion investment for his firm from Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund in 2021— in light of Kushner’s government work.
Neither Kushner nor Affinity Partners responded to the congressmen’s earlier request.
The House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform is the main investigative committee in the House but the minority party requests from lawmakers on the committee are voluntary and can be ignored without legal consequences. Subpoenas can only be authorized by the committee chair or by committee vote. If the balance of power shifts as a result of the midterm elections in November, Democrats would be able to open an official investigation.
After Republicans won the House in 2023, the Oversight Committee, the Judiciary Committee and the Ways and Means Committee opened similar investigations into Hunter Biden’s business dealings overseas and alleged he was profiting from his father’s presidency.
This story was updated with additional details from Garcia’s letter and further context on his holdings.

title: Tropical disturbance in the Gulf could become a storm by Friday. Here’s what forecasters say
text:
BATON ROUGE, La. (WAFB/Gray News) - A tropical disturbance in the Gulf is getting better organized as forecasters say they are watching for possible tropical storm or hurricane development.
Morning satellite imagery Tuesday showed a noticeable increase in thunderstorm activity around the system compared with Monday as it continues organizing over the southwestern Gulf.
The National Hurricane Center said early Tuesday that Invest 92L has an 80% chance of developing within the next 48 hours and an 80% chance of development over the next seven days.
If the system strengthens into a tropical storm, it would be named Isaias.
The system is expected to drift east-northeast through the middle of the week before turning north toward the northern Gulf Coast.
Some early tracks show the storm possibly heading toward Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama and Florida.
The National Hurricane Center said it currently remains too early to determine specific impacts, but people along the northern Gulf Coast should closely monitor the system.
Forecasters in Louisiana said impacts could begin as early as Friday night and continue into Saturday, depending on how quickly the system develops and where it ultimately tracks.
But what those impacts could include remains uncertain.
The risks of rain, wind, storm surge and coastal flooding will become clearer once the system develops and forecasters have a better understanding of its track and strength.

title: It sounds like your bank. That’s what makes it convincing.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
“I’d never fall for that.”
Many of us have had that thought while reading about a scam. From the outside, the warning signs can seem obvious. But in the middle of an ordinary day, a believable story can sound very different.
Imagine this: You’re getting dinner started when a verification code arrives on your phone. You haven’t tried to sign in or requested a code.
Then your phone rings. The caller ID displays your bank’s name. A professional voice says someone may be trying to access your account.
That would explain the unexpected code.
The caller offers to help secure your account and asks you to read the code back or share your screen as you log in, so they can stop unauthorized access.
The timing makes the story convincing. You received something you weren’t expecting, and now someone who appears to be from your bank is calling with an explanation and a solution.
In this example, the caller is a scammer. The unexpected code and the request to share it are the warning signs. You didn’t request the code or initiate the conversation.
October is Cybersecurity Awareness Month, an opportunity to look beyond the obvious scams and recognize the ones that can feel like everyday interactions.
How the scam works
We might picture a scam as an email full of spelling mistakes or a promise of money from a stranger. Those still exist, but a bank impersonation scam can begin with something much more believable: a warning about your account.
Scammers can disguise their phone numbers to make caller ID display a trusted business. They may also know your name or other personal details. Neither confirms who is calling.
In this example, the code itself could be real. Someone attempting to access your account may trigger a legitimate login or password-reset code, then call pretending to be from your bank. Sharing it could help them complete the very action they claim to be stopping.
Some banks use verification codes during calls you make to them at a trusted number. Here, an unexpected caller is asking for a code you didn’t request.
A request to share your screen while banking is another warning sign: it could expose private account information or codes. Giving someone remote control could also allow them to make transactions from your device.
If this happens, keep the code private, decline screen sharing or remote access, and end the conversation. Call your bank directly at a trusted number.
Stop and verify
The caller’s explanation can make a request sound routine. That’s why it helps to pay attention to what someone is asking you to do, even when their story seems to make sense.
An unexpected caller asking for your online banking password, PIN or login code is a reason to stop. So is someone telling you to transfer money to a “safe account” or give them remote access to your phone or computer.
Those requests may come with reassuring language: “We’ll walk you through it.” “This will protect your account.” “We need to take care of this immediately.”
When your money may be at risk, wanting to resolve the problem quickly is understandable. Scammers use that concern to keep the conversation moving before you have time to check their claims.
You don’t have to determine whether the caller is a scammer while you’re still on the phone. You can end the conversation and verify the request yourself.
Call your bank directly using a trusted number from your card, statement or their official website. Avoid calling a number supplied by the person who contacted you or returning the call through your recent call history, since the displayed number may have been faked.
A simple “I’ll call my bank directly to check” is enough.
A text about a locked account or an email warning of suspicious activity can create that same pressure to respond.
Instead of following a link or using contact information in the message, open your banking app yourself or go directly to your bank’s official website.
You can take a warning seriously while still checking where it came from. If there is a real issue, contacting your bank directly allows you to address it through a trusted source.
If you’ve already responded
Maybe you clicked a link before questioning it. Maybe you shared information, read back a code or followed instructions to send money. Or perhaps the conversation seemed fine at the time, but something about it is bothering you now.
Contact your bank promptly and explain what happened. You don’t need to be certain it was a scam before asking for help. Let your bank know what you shared and any steps you took so it can help you determine what to do next.
You can report scams to the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov and internet-related fraud to the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center at IC3.gov. If your account or money may be at risk, contact your bank promptly as well.
Where to find help
Recognizing scams isn’t always as simple as spotting a typo or an unfamiliar number. A believable request can deserve a second look, too.
This Cybersecurity Awareness Month, Franklin Savings Bank encourages everyone, wherever you bank, to make verification part of the routine. For more information on spotting scams and where to report suspicious activity, visit the Franklin Savings Bank blog at franklinsavings.bank and read “Scammers are getting more convincing.”
When an unexpected call or message asks you to share information, grant access or move money, give yourself time to check. End the conversation, contact your bank through a trusted number and confirm the request before taking the next step.
Stop. Verify. Then act.

title: How you can prepare for AI in the workforce
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — From the classrooms to the workplace to nearly every website you visit, artificial intelligence is changing some aspects of how we live.
It has been a dominant topic in the news, with names like Anthropic and Elon Musk frequently mentioned. But how it works can still cause confusion.
We turned to Neil Johnson, a leading researcher on the technology, to break down the basics of AI.
Johnson is a professor of physics and data science at George Washington University in Washington, D.C. He studies artificial intelligence and has written about its impact extensively.
What is AI?
To put it simply, Johnson described AI as “a combination of computer hardware and software.”
“It’s been trained on everything we’ve ever said and put online,” he explained. “It’s been trained on all of that. So suddenly we have a machine that we can ask. How does it work? It has software in it that looks up the answers and extends them - it joins the dots between things it’s seen.”
Why so few AI companies
Johnson said developing AI requires significant financial resources.
“You need a lot of money to have the machinery and the software to be able to train it,” Johnson said. “That’s why we’ve only got a few companies. And so that’s why all of this discussion about policies, dangers are always focused around these companies.”
Will AI replace our jobs?
Johnson said knowing how to use AI tools provides job security.
“Job security - 100% for the person who knows how to use AI tools and can oversee their use in some domain,” Johnson said.
He believes AI will change how people work, but said those who learn to use it, question it and apply its answers will remain important in the workplace.
“There will always be that human element that’s needed alongside AI tools,” Johnson said. “I do think a lot of people are going to lose jobs who don’t then necessarily embrace it.”
Johnson’s advice is to think of AI less as something to compete against and more as a tool that provides a competitive edge.

title: On the same misguided mission, Bernie returns to Maine
text:
I understand why Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders is preparing for a weekend of rallying across Maine beside Senate contender Troy Jackson. I can even allow that it might boost the Democrat’s campaign.
But I wish Sen. Sanders wasn’t coming here.
Sanders has always struck me as a crabby old man who has spent his lifetime griping about nearly every colleague and issue on the national stage — without racking up any serious legislative accomplishments.
Everyone I knew who had spent time around him, mostly staffers on Capitol Hill, had little good to say about him. In person, they told me, he was often a jerk.
Somehow, Sanders became a hero to young people when he began running for president in 2015. They bought his mistaken portrait of former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, the Democratic presidential frontrunner, as a corrupt warmonger.
These idealistic voters wanted change — and believed the crotchety Vermonter could bring it about.
Not me. I worried then, as I still do, that extremists on the left and right will squeeze the political middle into extinction, leaving our leaders unable to compromise and letting major issue linger unsolved.
In the spring of 2016, I was interested to watch Sanders speak to a huge crowd of young people on town green beside Yale University. Those gathered to cheer him on were eager for a more progressive government after two terms with President Barack Obama at the helm.
The lead singer of R.E.M., Michael Stipe, introduced Sanders with a complaint about the “grotesque level of wealth and inequality in America.” He told the crowd, “Brothers and sisters, instead of giving tax breaks to billionaires, we are going to rebuild inner cities.”
Sanders came on and thundered in the same vein, eventually taking a shot at Yale for having such a large endowment while people in neighborhoods next door struggled to survive.
During his address, Sanders told his backers, “Don’t believe what anyone tells you, that we cannot change the status quo.”
While I didn’t really disagree with much of what he had to say, I feared that in knocking Clinton, who was clearly going to be the Democratic nominee, the only thing Sanders was accomplishing was to help elevate Republican Donald Trump.
We know now how it all turned out. And, rest assured, billionaires are doing well while those on the flip side of economic inequality are not. It’s also clear to us now who the real corrupt warmonger in that race was.
The status quo from a decade ago, before the White House became a gilded playhouse for the ultra-rich to stomp on those who are struggling, now seems like something magical.
I know Bernie Sanders isn’t solely responsible for the revolutionary changes of the Trump era. That shame can be traced back to many, including Hillary Clinton and, sadly, to a majority of Americans who bought into the Trumpian agenda of greed and hate.
Sanders will tell Mainers this weekend that it doesn’t have to be this way, that we can throw out Trump’s enablers in Congress, including Sen. Susan Collins, and pursue the America so many have fought to create during the past 250 years.
Maybe so, but I’m tired of big promises and broken government. Castigating the establishment isn’t the way to a better America. Working together is.

title: Dump truck driver praised for action to avoid crash with a loaded school bus in Jonesboro
text:
Maine dump truck driver praised for action to avoid crash with a loaded school bus
The driver of a dump truck is being praised for quick actions to avoid a potentially serious crash involving a school bus.
Washington County Sheriff Barry Curtis told Maine's Total Coverage the incident happened along Route 1 on Monday afternoon when a bus was stopped to let kids off at a home and had its warning lights on and stop sign extended. Curtis said the bus was stopped at the bottom of a hill after a curve in the road and there were several vehicles behind the bus.
Curtis said the truck driver came around the corner when the vehicle in front of him stopped abruptly. The truck, which was fully loaded, didn't have time to stop, but the driver was able to quickly swerve to the right and crash the truck, avoiding any other vehicles.
Curtis said that without the driver's quick reaction, there likely would have been several vehicles involved in a serious crash.
Curtis said he happened upon the crash by chance and arrived just as the driver was climbing out of his wrecked truck. He said the driver was not hurt, but was very shaken up.
Jonesboro Elementary School principal Marjorie Hicks sent a letter to families about the incident.
"We have spoken with an eyewitness to the incident and confirmed that our bus driver, Mrs. Wallace, followed appropriate safety procedures. She remained on the bus with the students and handled the situation calmly and appropriately, contacting emergency services," Hicks wrote. "We understand that students may come home talking about the incident, and we wanted families to have accurate information about what occurred. Most importantly, our students are safe."

title: Group appeals Maine’s decision to give education contracts to AI-powered firm
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Last month, an out-of-state firm backed by private equity and venture capital beat a Maine-based early childhood education organization for a pair of state contracts.
Now, advocates are sounding the alarm over what the decision could mean for Maine children and raising concerns about how the Maine Department of Health and Human Services evaluated the proposals.
Shine Early Learning, a New York organization backed by the private equity behemoth BlackRock, won two multimillion-dollar contracts to provide training and assistance to Maine’s early childhood educators through 2028.
The firm underbid Maine Roads to Quality, a group created in 1999 by the Catherine Cutler Institute at the University of Southern Maine, by about $2 million. Shine Early Learning said it will achieve lower costs by using artificial intelligence to do much of the work Maine Roads’ 30-odd employees currently perform.
Those employees are now bracing for layoffs as Maine Roads might be forced to shut down. The University of Maine System appealed the contract decisions last week.
Ending a decades-long partnership in favor of an out-of-state tech company could have drastic effects on the state’s early childhood education system, said Lauren Stark, an analyst with the progressive Maine Center for Economic Policy.
“There is not necessarily an incentive for the company to improve early learning or to increase access to affordable childcare. There’s not a public good motivation for them as a for-profit venture capitalist company,” Stark said. “The motivation is to have a greater profit.”
“Lower cost is not the same as a better value,” she added.
Maine Roads provides training and assistance to about 10,000 Maine childcare providers each year. It’s cultivated relationships with schools, educators, students and regulators alike over the last 27 years, said University of Maine System spokesperson Samantha Warren.
Work that was historically housed under a single contract was instead split into two earlier this year: One for coaching, credentialing and training educators, and another for providing a DHHS-approved plan “designed to improve (the) quality” of child care services.
Kimberlee Belcher-Badal is the executive director of the National Workforce Registry Alliance, a group that supports early childhood workforce registry systems across the country. The alliance has worked with Maine Roads for decades, Belcher-Badal said.
In a letter to DHHS’ appeals committee, Belcher-Badal said “Maine’s registry and its team are among the strongest in the nation” and questioned whether Shine Early Learning’s plans to implement AI chatbots would really benefit Maine educators.
In Missouri, Montana and many other states where Shine Early Learning operates, established early childcare providers have seen similar outcomes after losing contracts to the firm: Sweeping layoffs, worse services and less person-to-person connection in a field heavily reliant upon it.
DHHS graded Maine Roads’ and Shine Early Learning’s proposals on a scale from 0 to 100, as it does all submissions. Shine Early Learning’s bid for the coaching contract received a 97 and its proposal for the training plan got a perfect 100, public records show. Maine Roads received about 73 points on each.
In a pair of letters sent to the state, the university system questioned how DHHS graded each proposal and asked regulators to invalidate the contract decisions over irregularities in the scoring process. Maine Roads lost points “for no stated reason,” the appeal alleges.
“(DHHS) gave Shine near-perfect technical scores without resolving questions the evaluators themselves raised,” the appeal reads. “The award is arbitrary and capricious, and the evaluation contains irregularities creating fundamental unfairness.”
A DHHS spokesperson said the scores were issued in accordance with the processes laid out in its requests for proposals but did not specify how Shine Early Learning received such high marks.
Shine Early Learning’s website says the company uses “data-driven services and solutions” to “accelerate child and family outcomes.” The company has not responded to requests for comment on its expansion into Maine.
The company’s proposals state they plan to use AI agents and chatbots to screen prospective teachers’ applications, power a “family navigation assistant” and manage the state’s early childcare provider registry.
Stark, with the Maine Center for Economic Policy, is skeptical that AI will be an adequate replacement for Maine Roads’ human staff.
“You need people with expertise to set up the systems, you need mentors who have experience in the field working with early childhood educators. And a chatbot is not a mentor,” she said.
Shine Early Learning is owned by Acelero Inc., a company backed by some of the world’s largest private equity and venture capital companies. The senior portfolio manager for BlackRock, which manages some $11 trillion in assets globally, said the firm was investing in Acelero to widen its reach across the country.
A report published in February by the National Women’s Law Center, a nonprofit advocacy organization, found private equity groups are increasingly acquiring vital community services, from childcare to housing.
“Private equity investors face more structural incentives to prioritize short-term profits than any other form of corporate ownership or investment,” the report states. “This makes them the quickest and most likely to identify and exploit opportunities to extract wealth from any market.”
It is unclear when the appeal will be resolved. The state’s contracts with the firm have not yet been finalized, a DHHS spokesperson said, and won’t be until the appeals process is complete.

title: ‘Why can’t you?’: Woman, 80, hosts her own funeral, celebrates life with her loved ones
text:
MACON, Ga. (WMAZ) - An 80-year-old Georgia woman had a front-row seat to her own funeral.
Shelvy Neal hosted her own funeral Sunday, even though she has a lot more living left to do. She called it a “FOMO funeral” for fear of missing out. It was a celebration of Shelvy’s life, the relationships she’s made and her 80th birthday.
“It’s gonna be about celebrating Christ and my life, 80 years of my life,” Shelvy said before the event. “It’s been a good one.”
The FOMO funeral was held at the Macon property Shelvy and her husband owned for about 25 years before they sold it to a funeral home in 2020. The sale came with a catch: two funerals, one for each of them.
Her husband’s funeral was in March, and it got Shelvy thinking about her own.
“I said, ‘You know, I’d love to be at my own funeral,’” Shelvy said. “My daughter said, ‘Well, why can’t you?’”
So, Shelvy and her family set about planning. Guests were invited to speak at an open microphone, and before the event, Shelvy said she was ready for whatever they might say.
“If they want to, they can say bad things, but I’m gonna be there, and I might cut the mic,” she said. “I’m gonna control my own funeral.”
Around 100 people showed up to Shelvy’s FOMO funeral, which featured a coffin with a cardboard printout of Shelvy lying inside. The real Shelvy wore a sash that read “Back by popular demand,” and her family celebrated with a cake that read, “She refuses to miss anything… especially her own funeral.”
Shelvy herself made the flowers for her funeral, and she was the guest speaker.
“I think it will be easier on my family to do something like this, but also, you know, funeral is F-U-N. And I like fun,” she said.
When the real goodbye comes, Shelvy says it will be a simple graveside service instead of a traditional funeral.

title: Trump expands access to tax-free fuel ahead of midterm elections
text:
Trump expands access to tax-free fuel ahead of midterm elections
President Donald Trump signed an executive order to temporarily expand access to a tax-free fuel called red-dyed diesel.
"I'm announcing another unprecedented step to bring down costs," Trump said during a campaign stop in Nebraska on Monday.
Red-dyed diesel, typically reserved for off-road vehicles, can now be used on highways under the order. The order also defers payment of the applicable federal excise tax for the remainder of the year. While diesel-powered cars and trucks can generally use this fuel, availability may be limited in some areas.
Trump highlighted that the measure is intended to save money for truckers and farmers, especially during harvest season.
Scott Thomsen, a Nebraska farmer, shared his concerns about rising costs despite the president’s efforts.
"President Trump ran on lowering fuel prices, lowering overall expenses, and so far everything's inflated in price," Thomsen said.
Thomsen, who previously supported Trump, said he is now considering sitting out the midterm elections.

title: 'The best dad': 36-year-old who died after collapsing at marathon remembered by family
text:
'The best dad': 36-year-old who died after collapsing at marathon remembered by family
A 36-year-old man died after being taken to a hospital during the Milwaukee Lakefront Half Marathon on Sunday morning.
John Meise, from Waukesha, was later pronounced dead, according to the Milwaukee County Medical Examiner’s Office.
"He was literally the best Dad, and husband and best to everyone in his world," said Stacy Horneck, a spokesperson for the family. "He loved doing everything with his family. To say they're heartbroken is an understatement. He was so funny, and intelligent and talented."
A GoFundMe for the family raised more than $80,000 in less than two days.
Race organizers told 12 News it was the first time in the race's 44-year history that someone has died after participating in the race.
A weather camera from sister station WISN 12 News captured first responders loading Meise onto a stretcher and into an ambulance near the north end of the Hoan Bridge shortly after 10 a.m. A runner told WISN that they saw Meise receiving medical treatment near the 13-mile mark.
Response from Milwaukee Lakefront Marathon
Organizers released a statement after the death was announced:
"The Milwaukee Lakefront Marathon extends its sincere condolences to the family and loved ones of the half marathon participant who passed away following Sunday’s event. We are deeply saddened by this loss and are grateful to the medical personnel, first responders, volunteers and public safety partners who support the safety and well-being of participants throughout race weekend. The Milwaukee Lakefront Marathon maintains established medical and emergency-response protocols, developed in coordination with its medical and public safety partners, including on-course medical support, communications procedures and coordinated response planning. The safety of participants remains a central priority in the planning and operation of the event."

title: Getting Cold Overnight With Frost Likely For Most
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Winds will continue to weaken Tuesday night as high pressure passes south of the region. Skies stay mostly clear, allowing temperatures to drop into the mid 20s to mid 30s. Frost Advisories and Freeze Warnings have been issued for communities where the growing season has not ended. A lingering breeze will make it feel like the 20s for many early Wednesday.
Wednesday: Cold Start, Mostly Sunny
A cold start to Wednesday morning with even colder wind chills. Sunshine will help conditions improve through the morning, but clouds build later in the day. An isolated shower is possible in far northern areas. Highs range from the mid 50s in the north to the upper 50s and low 60s elsewhere. Southwest winds may gust to 25 mph.

A warm front brings milder air, with highs from the upper 50s to low 70s. A cold front then moves slowly across the region, bringing the best chance for scattered showers. Rainfall is expected to be light, offering little relief from drought conditions.

Mostly sunny skies return, with highs in the 50s and low 60s. Northwest winds may gust to 25 mph.

title: ‘Small price to pay’: Trump says Iran can ‘take out’ LA or San Diego during political rally
text:
(Gray News) – President Donald Trump is facing backlash after making a statement Monday night during a political rally suggesting that Iran could take out two cities in the United States.
“It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe. They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego,” Trump said.
Trump was speaking at a political rally in Nebraska when he made the controversial statement.
People at the rally celebrated his suggestion.
“After sending the National Guard and Marines to occupy California, Donald Trump is now saying our foreign enemies should ‘take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego,” Gov. Gavin Newsom wrote on X. “He is deranged and dangerous.”
Los Angeles is the most populous city in California and the second most populous in the United States. It has one of the busiest container ports in the Americas and is home to the U.S. Space Force’s Space Systems Command Headquarters.
LA Mayor Karen Bass reacted to Trump’s statement on X saying, “The role of a president is to protect the country, not to actively threaten it and encourage attacks on American lives.”
“San Diego is not collateral damage. We are not expendable. And we are never a ‘small price to pay.’ Keep our city out of your reckless war talk,” San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria wrote on X.
San Diego is home to Naval Base San Diego, where the Navy SEALs train. There is a large military presence in the city with 70,000 civilians and active-duty service members living and working in the area.
After his shocking statements, Trump claimed the Iran war was close to the end and is “essentially almost over with.”

title: Obituary: Kathleen Alice Donahue Crump
text:
ANDOVER – Kathleen Alice Donahue Crump, 78, went to God on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, at the Rumford Hospital. She resided in Andover, Maine.
Born in Somerville, Mass. on May 6, 1948, she was a daughter to Paula Drew Wixon and Philip Thomas Donahue, Sr. She graduated from Arlington Mass. High School and went on to Boston University and several other schools over the years. She worked as a legal secretary, a medical secretary, and held several positions at a small community hospital in Everett, Mass. where she helped care for her neighbors for 20 years.
She retired to Andover in 1998 with her brother, Kelly Donahue, where she enjoyed the quiet, peaceful nature of the area and being near family. She was active in the Rumford United Methodist Church, and in local quilting groups where she participated in many charitable endeavors. Quilting was her passion and solace over the years, stitching the events of her life into many quilts for family and strangers near and far. Many dear friends in the quilting community enriched her life tremendously.
Special thanks to brother Brad and his wife Corrine for sharing their beautiful land (and their beautiful hearts) with all the family over the years.
She was predeceased by her mother, Paula Wixon, father Philip Donahue, Sr., dear stepmother Sylvia Donahue, and brothers Philip Donahue, Sr., and Walter Downs, Jr.
She is survived by her brother and best friend Kelly Donahue, sister, Darlene Fitzgerald, brother Bradley Downs and wife Corrine; a beloved niece Carla Donahue, and many nieces, nephews grand nieces and nephews who were all a joy to her as she watched them grow and mature.
Friends and family are invited to share memories of Kathleen at http://www.meaderandson.com.
Funeral services will be held 11 a.m. Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026, at the Virgin Memorial Chapel of the Rumford United Methodist Church on Linnell Street in Rumford. Interment will be in the Demeritt Cemetery in Peru.

title: Belfast man charged with manslaughter in crash that killed Old Orchard Beach woman
text:
A Belfast man was arrested on Monday and charged in connection with an April crash in Waldo County that killed an Old Orchard Beach woman.
Adam Sorrentino, 42, has been charged with manslaughter, aggravated criminal OUI resulting in death, OUI, reckless conduct with a dangerous weapon, driving to endanger, and criminal speed, Maine State Police said in a news release Tuesday.
Sorrentino was driving a truck westbound on Route 1 in Stockton Springs on April 13 when he crossed the centerline and collided head-on with a Subaru Forester driven by Anne Pomroy, 77, of Old Orchard Beach, state police said. Pomroy was declared dead at the scene.
Sorrentino is accused of driving at more than 80 mph and having a blood alcohol concentration more than double the legal limit at the time of the crash, police say. He was transported to Waldo County Jail following his arrest.
