title: UMaine football makes a rare move with rare midseason firing. Is it the right one?
text:
ORONO — Jordan Stevens answered the questions, one day after making the most consequential decision of his time as head coach of the University of Maine football team. Stevens was resolute.
Mikahael Waters, Maine’s offensive coordinator and quarterbacks coach since 2024, is out. Sean Green, in his first season on Stevens’ staff as the running backs coach, is now the interim offensive coordinator.
When you fire your offensive coordinator in the middle of the season, you’d better be absolutely sure it’s the right move. It’s not a move you can make emotionally or haphazardly.
“We have a very talented roster, and we’ve done a lot of good things this season. We’ve got to be more consistent. We’ve got to score points,” Stevens said following Tuesday morning’s practice.
The Black Bears are 1-5. Since winning the season opener at Towson, Maine has lost five games in a row. You don’t have to break down the statistics too deeply to see that the team’s offense has been the major contributing factor to the weak start.
Averaging just 270.2 yards per game, Maine ranks 115 of 124 teams in the Football Championship Subdivision, and last in the Coastal Athletic Association. Scoring an average of 14.5 point per game, Maine is 118th nationally and, again, last in the league.
Rushing offense? Ranked 110th at 96 yards per game. Passing offense? Ranked 93th, just over 174 yards per game. Third-down conversions? Ranked 90th with a 33% success rate. The Black Bears’ best national ranking is in first downs, in which they’re tied for 85th.
All that said, firing an assistant coach in the middle of the season is a rare move. It happens, but usually for off-the-field reasons. Conversations with two Maine football alumni whose relationships with the program go back decades said they’ve never heard of a Black Bears coach losing his job midseason.
Stevens noted that the slow start doesn’t all fall on Waters. But he determined that enough of it does to warrant the rare midseason change. Waiting until the end of the season wasn’t going to work.
Stevens sees the situation as one that needs immediate attention, one that can set the tone for the remaining five games.
“When you look at our team, I believe we are a team that can win football games,” Stevens said. “I’m not sitting here just throwing in the towel on the season. I’m not willing to do that.”
Green is no stranger to football fans in Maine. He coached Portland to the Class A state title in 2024. In 2021, Green coached Cape Elizabeth to the Class C championship. Two of the players who were pivotal in those title runs are now among the weapons Green has in the Black Bears’ offense. Running back Nick Laughlin of Cape Elizabeth is a key contributor whose four touchdowns lead the team. Freshman wide receiver Cordell Jones of Portland has yet to see game action.
Green was not made available for comment Tuesday.
College football is a production business, Stevens said. You judge production in wins. Every coach has to do a better job, he said. If players aren’t playing with confidence, coaches need to instill it. If players aren’t executing on the field, coaches need to develop ways to find success. Stevens said he’s not pointing the finger, he’s pointing the thumb, back at himself and the rest of the staff.
“It’s really about us recommitting ourselves to the season,” Stevens said. “I don’t need to make a narrative over scoring more points. You can see that. We need to score more points so we can win football games. … Winning is the expectation, and not winning is never OK. We grow from those experiences, but we do need to compete and win football games. I refuse to hold us to a standard that’s anything less than that. That’s not who I am. That’s not who we’re going to be as a team.”
Since being named head coach prior to the 2022, Stevens’ teams are 16-36, the high point being a 6-6 mark last season. Asked if he felt any other assistant coaches, or even himself, were on the hot seat, Stevens was curt.
“No,” he said.
Is replacing the offensive coordinator exactly what the Black Bears need, or is it a last-ditch effort to keep a season from completely slipping away? Starting with the home game against Bryant on Oct. 17, they’ll have five games to find out.

title: Flock cameras have no business in Lewiston
text:
During the last Supreme Court term, the Court in the case of Chatrie v. United States ruled 6-3 to invalidate a police tactic called a “geofence warrant.”
A geofence warrant is a mass surveillance tool which a law enforcement agency demands from a tech company (like Google) location data from every mobile device within a defined geographic area with a certain timeframe, without specifying a suspect or suspects. It is clear that this constitutes a Fourth Amendment violation; geofencing is a mass, dragnet search of innocent people guilty of no crime.
In June 2025, the Lewiston City Council approved and accepted as part of the U.S. DOJ’s Byrne Community Grant, which was intended for surveillance camera technology. This grant funding then gets us to October 2025, when the Lewiston Police Department entered into a 60-day trial with Flock Safety. Without a City Council vote, the city went on to acquire and implement a 13-camera system.
According to one report, 82 Flock contracts nationwide have been canceled. Unlike Auburn, Lewiston has not decided to end funding. We the people of Lewiston should follow Auburn’s lead in ending Flock’s contract and removing this mass surveillance network. While the Chatrie decision is new, time will show that automated license plate readers are like a geofence warrant, a mass surveillance tactic and a clear violation of the Fourth Amendment.
Matthew Roy
Lewiston

title: Maine’s Beehive Loop Ranks Among the 10 Best Fall Hikes in America
text:
Maine’s Beehive Loop Ranks Among the 10 Best Fall Hikes in America
Fall is the most righteous time of year in Maine. The perfect harvest, beautiful weather, and lack of tourists create an unbeatable vibe, one that practically screams for us to take advantage of it.
That’s why it’s also the perfect time to get outside and enjoy everything that’s wonderful about Maine’s wilderness, especially the iconic Acadia National Park.
While Acadia can be a bit crazy during the summer, the crowds tend to thin out later in the fall, which is great for us natives looking to enjoy everything the park has to offer. And it just so happens to be home to one of the season’s best hikes.
Is Maine's Beehive Trail One of America's Best?
According to the popular outdoor site broadout.com, Acadia’s historic Beehive Trail is one of the best hikes in the entire country to enjoy during the fall.
How good is it? Well, the website claims it’s one of the 10 best, even listing it first. Talk about some serious bragging rights.
Beehive Loop delivers an outsized adventure in a compact distance. The climb rises above Sand Beach on steep granite, iron rungs, ladders, and exposed ledges before opening to views of the Gulf of Maine and Acadia’s autumn-colored hills.
The popular hiking site AllTrails rates the Beehive Trail as “hard” in difficulty. Still, despite its tough reputation, it holds an impressive 4.9 out of 5 rating. The trail offers sweeping views of Maine’s coastline, islands, and Acadia’s iconic Sand Beach, and it's also a favorite for birdwatchers.
How Popular is Acadia National Park's Beehive Trail?
It’s also one of the most popular hikes in the park, and it’s not unusual to encounter long queues at certain points along the trail. Because of its difficulty, it can take time to navigate many of the more technical sections. So if you're planning to tackle it, be sure to plan your time wisely, especially if you are heading during a peak time of year.
It’s pretty great to see the Beehive Loop included on this list. The trail represents everything that’s great about Maine, especially during the fall. Crisp air, autumn leaves, beautiful sunshine, and a challenging coastal mountain trail make for the perfect combination.
READ MORE: Maine’s Acadia National Park Ranks 7th in the Nation with Over 4 Million Visits
One other New England trail made the list: New Hampshire’s Franconia Ridge Loop, which is also exceptional. You can check out the entire list here.

title: On the same misguided mission, Bernie returns to Maine
text:
I understand why Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders is preparing for a weekend of rallying across Maine beside Senate contender Troy Jackson. I can even allow that it might boost the Democrat’s campaign.
But I wish Sen. Sanders wasn’t coming here.
Sanders has always struck me as a crabby old man who has spent his lifetime griping about nearly every colleague and issue on the national stage — without racking up any serious legislative accomplishments.
Everyone I knew who had spent time around him, mostly staffers on Capitol Hill, had little good to say about him. In person, they told me, he was often a jerk.
Somehow, Sanders became a hero to young people when he began running for president in 2015. They bought his mistaken portrait of former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, the Democratic presidential frontrunner, as a corrupt warmonger.
These idealistic voters wanted change — and believed the crotchety Vermonter could bring it about.
Not me. I worried then, as I still do, that extremists on the left and right will squeeze the political middle into extinction, leaving our leaders unable to compromise and letting major issue linger unsolved.
In the spring of 2016, I was interested to watch Sanders speak to a huge crowd of young people on town green beside Yale University. Those gathered to cheer him on were eager for a more progressive government after two terms with President Barack Obama at the helm.
The lead singer of R.E.M., Michael Stipe, introduced Sanders with a complaint about the “grotesque level of wealth and inequality in America.” He told the crowd, “Brothers and sisters, instead of giving tax breaks to billionaires, we are going to rebuild inner cities.”
Sanders came on and thundered in the same vein, eventually taking a shot at Yale for having such a large endowment while people in neighborhoods next door struggled to survive.
During his address, Sanders told his backers, “Don’t believe what anyone tells you, that we cannot change the status quo.”
While I didn’t really disagree with much of what he had to say, I feared that in knocking Clinton, who was clearly going to be the Democratic nominee, the only thing Sanders was accomplishing was to help elevate Republican Donald Trump.
We know now how it all turned out. And, rest assured, billionaires are doing well while those on the flip side of economic inequality are not. It’s also clear to us now who the real corrupt warmonger in that race was.
The status quo from a decade ago, before the White House became a gilded playhouse for the ultra-rich to stomp on those who are struggling, now seems like something magical.
I know Bernie Sanders isn’t solely responsible for the revolutionary changes of the Trump era. That shame can be traced back to many, including Hillary Clinton and, sadly, to a majority of Americans who bought into the Trumpian agenda of greed and hate.
Sanders will tell Mainers this weekend that it doesn’t have to be this way, that we can throw out Trump’s enablers in Congress, including Sen. Susan Collins, and pursue the America so many have fought to create during the past 250 years.
Maybe so, but I’m tired of big promises and broken government. Castigating the establishment isn’t the way to a better America. Working together is.

title: One nurse fired from CMMC has been reinstated, union says
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Central Maine Medical Center disputes union's claim that fired nurse has been reinstated
More than a dozen nurses at the Lewiston hospital were fired last month amid unionization talks
Central Maine Medical Center disputes union's claim that fired nurse has been reinstated
More than a dozen nurses at the Lewiston hospital were fired last month amid unionization talks
One of the 15 nurses recently fired from Central Maine Medical Center in Lewiston has been reinstated and is returning to work this week, according to the National Nurses Organizing Committee, an affiliate of National Nurses United.
The union says the nurse was reinstated on Monday.
A spokesperson for CMMC says that has not happened.
Five other nurses at the hospital were also suspended. The suspensions and terminations happened leading up to a vote by hundreds of nurses at CMMC to join a union.
The nurses voted overwhelmingly on Sept. 24 to join a union.
"Reinstating one nurse is a good first step, but Prime needs to reinstate all nurses who were suspended or fired," said Katie Grinnell, a former RN at CMMC. "Also, Prime must stop challenging our overwhelming victory at the ballot box. We won our union election by a landslide."
Nurses and union leadership have alleged the actions against nurses were retaliation by Prime Healthcare because of the push to unionize. Prime Healthcare owns CMMC.
The hospital previously confirmed the firings, but said the employment actions were based on violations of longstanding policies, not union activity.
In a statement shared with Maine's Total Coverage on Tuesday, a CMMC spokesperson said that no nurses who have been fired or suspended have been reinstated.
"CMMC respects the rights of nurses to lawfully organize and we honor our responsibility to protect patient safety, ensure access to care and maintain a safe environment for patients and staff and all actions involving nurses have been based on documented violations of hospital standards of conduct and established policies designed to uphold those responsibilities," the hospital's spokesperson said in their statement. "No reinstatements from suspension or termination have occurred, and certain matters remain under investigation."
Prime Healthcare also owns Olympia Fields Hospital in Illinois, and the National Nurses Organizing Committee says four nurses who were suspended there have been reinstated.
"Nurses were unlawfully disciplined for our patient advocacy," said Hillary Ferrell, a former RN at Olympia Fields Hospital. "But we will never stop speaking up for our patients. Our patients and our community deserve safe staffing and safe patient care."

title: One of the last surviving stars of Hollywood’s Golden Age dies at age 102
text:
One of the last surviving stars of Hollywood’s Golden Age dies at age 102
Eva Marie Saint had been the oldest living Academy Award winner at the time of her death
One of the last surviving stars of Hollywood’s Golden Age dies at age 102
Eva Marie Saint had been the oldest living Academy Award winner at the time of her death
Eva Marie Saint, the Academy Award-winning actress whose career stretched from the earliest days of live television to the golden era of Hollywood and beyond, has died. She was 102.
A family representative, Jeff Sanderson, confirmed the death.
Born on July 4, 1924, in Newark, New Jersey, to John Merle Saint and Eva Marie Rice Saint, she grew up attending Bethlehem Central High School in Delmar, New York, before studying acting at Bowling Green State University in Ohio, where she graduated in 1946. A theater on the Bowling Green campus bears her name, and she received a lifetime achievement award from her alma mater in 2018.
Saint began her professional life as an NBC page and appeared in early live television broadcasts in the late 1940s. Her stage work brought her to Broadway in the Horton Foote play "The Trip to Bountiful" in 1953. Saint’s film debut came the following year in Elia Kazan’s "On the Waterfront," opposite Marlon Brando. The role of Edie Doyle earned her the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress.
In an interview with "CBS Sunday Morning" in 2014, when asked if she campaigned for an Oscar back then, Saint replied, “I don't think I knew what the word was. Politicians campaigned. No, I mean, it was just different, you know?”
Getty ImagesJohn Springer CollectionMarlon Brando and Eva Marie Saint in On the Waterfront.
In 1959, Alfred Hitchcock chose her over dozens of candidates for the femme fatale role in "North by Northwest," opposite Cary Grant, a film that ranks among the American Film Institute’s 100 Greatest American Movies of All Time. Hitchcock personally selected her wardrobe during a shopping trip to Bergdorf Goodman and worked with her to lower her speaking voice for the part.
"In casting Eva Marie Saint as his romantic vis-à-vis, Mr. Hitchcock has plumbed some talents not shown by the actress heretofore," New York Times critic Abe H. Weiler wrote at the time. "Although she is seemingly a hard, designing type, she also emerges both the sweet heroine and a glamorous charmer."
Getty ImagesArchive PhotosCary Grant and Saint in North by Northwest.
Despite the opportunity for major stardom, Saint chose to limit her film work to spend time with her husband, director Jeffrey Hayden, whom she married in October 1951, and their two children: a son named Darrell, born in 1955, and a daughter named Laurette, born in 1958.
Getty ImagesMichael Ochs ArchivesSaint and husband Jeff Hayden in Los Angeles in 1962.
She later worked extensively in television, winning a Primetime Emmy Award for the 1990 miniseries "People Like Us" after five prior nominations. Saint returned to the silver screen in "Superman Returns" in 2006 as Superman’s adoptive mother, Martha Kent. Her final theatrical film role came in "Winter’s Tale" in 2014.
In 2018, at age 93, she received a standing ovation when she took the stage at the Academy Awards to present the award for Costume Design. Saint received two stars on the Hollywood Walk of Fame: one for movies and one for television.
Getty ImagesFrazer HarrisonSaint on the red carpet at the 2018 Academy Awards.
Hayden died on Christmas Eve in 2016 after a battle with cancer. They were married for 65 years. Saint is survived by her son and daughter, and four grandchildren. On July 4, 2024, she celebrated her 100th birthday with four generations of family in Los Angeles.

title: Frost Advisory for Coastal Maine Tonight
text:
Frost Advisory for Coastal Maine Tonight
Frost Advisory for Coastal Maine Tonight
A Frost Advisory is in effect from midnight Tuesday night until 8 a.m. on Wednesday. Portions of south central and southwest Maine and central and southern New Hampshire will have the advisory in place, but frost is likely for areas inland as well.
Temperatures are expected to be as low as 33 degrees, which will result in frost formation. Areas inland will also be cold, with low temperatures in the low 30s and upper 20s.
The Frost Advisory is limited to the coastline because the growing season is not over in these areas. Other regions across Maine have either already had their first frost or are already past the end of their growing season.
Frost could be harmful to sensitive outdoor plants, so take steps now to protect tender vegetation. Potted plants should be brought inside, and covers may be necessarily for remaining outdoor plants.

title: Belfast man accused of driving drunk in fatal Stockton Springs crash
text:
Maine State Police on Monday arrested Adam Sorrentino, 42, of Belfast, in connection with an April 13 crash in Stockton Springs that killed 77-year-old Anne Pomroy of Old Orchard Beach.
Pomroy was driving a Subaru Forester east on Route 1 at about 6:08 p.m. when she collided with a westbound truck driven by Sorrentino. She succumbed to her injuries at the scene, police said at the time.
Sorrentino was taken to the hospital, where he was treated for injuries that were not considered life-threatening.
On Monday, state police said an investigation found that Sorrentino was driving more than 80 mph and had a blood alcohol concentration of more than twice the legal limit at the time of the crash.
Police allege Sorrentino crossed the centerline and hit Pomroy’s vehicle head-on.
Sorrentino was arrested at his Belfast home on Monday and taken to Waldo County Jail.
He is charged with manslaughter, aggravated criminal OUI-death resulting, reckless conduct with a dangerous weapon, driving to endanger, OUI, and criminal speed.

title: Brewer, Lincoln Academy set the pace at KVAC golf qualifier
text:
VASSALBORO — How do you follow up winning a conference championship despite thunder, lightning and hail that forced delays?
If you’re Bangor’s Jacoby Harvey, you turn around less than 16 hours later and shoot a 79 while dealing with windy conditions.
“You just have to be the most mental (tough),” said Harvey. “Just kind of grind through every shot, take one shot at a time, don’t move past the next one.”
Harvey was one of 33 golfers to shoot a qualifying score for the individual state championship during the Kennebec Valley Athletic Conference qualifier Tuesday at Natanis Golf Course. He tied with Liam Greenlaw of Brewer for the second-best score in Class A behind Greyson Dooley of Messalonskee.
Bangor (349), having already won the KVAC Class A championship Monday, also qualified for the team state championship. Brewer (330), Messalonskee (331) and Camden Hills (336) were the other three Class A teams to qualify.
“I had a good front, shot minus-1, was trying to keep doing what I was doing, obviously,” Harvey said. “Things on the back (nine) didn’t go as planned, but at the end of the day, 79, can’t be complaining.”
Lincoln Academy (343) led the pack in Class B on Tuesday. Leavitt (358), Belfast (362) and Nokomis (364) rounded out the team qualifiers.
“They’re a great bunch of young athletes and they’re a joy to coach,” Lincoln coach Todd Brackett said. “They jell really well. And today, what you don’t know behind the scenes is my No. 3 guy isn’t here. He’s sick. So my No. 7 guy stepped up and actually shot 90, which we used as part of the team score today. So I think that’s the advantage that they have, is we’ve got some depth. One through seven, any given time, they’re going to be competitive.”
Colin Mitchell shot an 80 to anchor Lincoln, tying with Leavitt’s James Brisson for the lowest score in Class B. Caden Chretien (81) of Nokomis placed third.
Mitchell made par on the sixth hole and chipped in for birdie on the seventh after starting the round with a bogey and a double bogey. On the back nine, he started with two double bogeys but was able to string together some pars across the rest of the round.
“I was trying to keep it low under the wind for the most part, just being happy with par, not trying to get too greedy,” Mitchell said.
Like Bangor, Lincoln Academy had already qualified for the state championship. The Eagles won the KVAC Class B championship on Oct. 1, and they excelled again Tuesday on the Tomahawk course.
“I said, ‘You know, guys, let’s treat it more like a practice round,’” Brackett said. “‘Go out. It’s you against the golf course. It doesn’t matter who you’re playing with, just do the best you can. We’re already qualified.’ But they’re like, ‘Geez coach, I want to qualify as an individual.’ So their mindset is to be competitive, I think, anyway. So I’m not sure that (already having qualified) eased their minds as much as I’d hoped it would.”
The Class A team and individual state championships will take place Friday, while the Class B championships are scheduled for Saturday, both on the Tomahawk course at Natanis.

title: Christa Pike is awake and speaking days after failed execution, attorneys say
text:
KNOXVILLE, Tenn. (WVLT/Gray News) -- Christa Pike is awake and speaking days after her failed Tennessee execution, according to her attorneys.
Pike was supposed to be executed via lethal injection in Tennessee last Wednesday.
However, after receiving two doses of what should have been lethal amounts of pentobarbital, she survived.
The failed execution had left her unconscious and on a ventilator at a hospital.
Dr. Paul Allen, a professor of anesthesiology at the University of Tennessee Health Science Center, said the needle never properly made it into her vein; when it came to the reason he believed what may have gone wrong with the execution.
Pike, 50, was 18 when authorities say she and her boyfriend tortured and killed a classmate in a jealous rage in 1995. She became one of the youngest women to be sent to death row.
The head of Tennessee’s prison system has since resigned following the botched execution. Whether the state can proceed with another execution attempt remains to be seen.

title: Food pantries feeling the pinch amid surge in demand
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine food pantries feeling the pinch amid surge in demand
Food pantries in Maine are already seeing a surge in demand with the price of everything else going up. Despite the threat of future funding cuts, local pantries are forging ahead.
Tuesday was distribution day at the South Portland Food Cupboard, and its new location behind the Staples store was packed.
"I believe we had 125 registered with appointments. We had a few walk-ins that didn't have an appointment," said Ellie Gibbs, the distribution manager for the South Portland Food Cupboard. "At the other location a year ago, we might have had maybe 55 or 60."
The South Portland Food Cupboard is right next to the Portland International Jetport runway, a fitting location given food costs are sky-high these days.
Chris Stevens and his fiancée from Buxton are among those who come to the pantry each week to stock up on expensive food that would have broken the budget had they gone to the supermarket.
"We are actually living in our camper right now on family property. It's getting to the point where we'll have to vacate. The next thing is trying to find housing," Stevens said.
Stevens said he is grateful there are food pantries to turn to.
"It's huge, very huge, because without this, there's a lot of people, even if you have EBT," Stevens said.
It's not enough, Stevens said.
Gibbs said the demographic is ever changing.
"We have a good number of our folks who come in and they need an early appointment if possible because they have to get to work," Gibbs said.
With federal cuts threatening future funding for operations like these, the Food Cupboard is digging in and working smarter and harder to keep its system running.
"I think we're going to be fine. We're going to push through, and when we need more food or support, we're going to go out and find it," Gibbs said.
Gibbs said the South Portland Food Cupboard could always use more volunteers to go retrieve extra food from supermarkets and bakeries and bring it to the pantry.

title: Meet Varsity Maine’s 10 unsung heroes of September
text:
Maybe you notice them; maybe you don’t. Either way, there’s something to be said for the “unsung hero” — the player who, while perhaps not putting up the big numbers that catch the headlines, does the little things that are every bit as important in the outcome.
This fall, Varsity Maine is seeking to identify some of those unsung heroes of Maine high school sports. Here are five boys and five girls whose impacts this September were significant, even if they weren’t necessarily measured in goals, assists, touchdowns or yards.
BOYS
Jake Harmon, Monmouth Academy soccer: Bryce Fletcher and Zane Foyt get the plaudits by pouring in goals for Monmouth, but the Mustangs owe just as much of their success to Harmon, who had strong defensive efforts against Mt. Abram on Sept. 16 and against Maranacook on Sept. 29, among others.
Abdirauf Hersi, Lewiston soccer: Hersi’s game-winning assist against Camden Hills on Sept. 8 helped the Blue Devils complete a 3-2 comeback win. On Sept. 19, his well-placed free kick in the dying seconds of the first half against rival Edward Little led to the game’s opening goal.
Wes Pinkham, Bonny Eagle football: Pinkham didn’t record many yards in Bonny Eagle’s season-opening victory over South Portland, but a key catch set up a score that the Scots ultimately needed to win. His strong play in the secondary included a touchdown-saving tackle.
Ethan Reichert, Marshwood football: On a team with just 33 players, each one is asked to do a lot. Reichert has answered the call as a key player on both lines for Marshwood, which went 4-0 in September. He was particularly impactful in the Hawks’ 52-51 thriller over Noble.
Ben Thomas, Winslow football: Winslow’s running backs get the headlines for their gaudy numbers, but that couldn’t happen without strong play from a line that includes a formidable senior in Thomas. He’s also been dominant up front defensively, such as in a 14-6 victory over Freeport.
GIRLS
Addison Barrs, Biddeford field hockey: Mia Mariello’s four goals stole the show in the Tigers’ season-opening win over Sanford/Kennebunk, but Barrs was no less instrumental. The junior was critical to breaking up Spartans possessions, leading to transition play that spurred Biddeford’s offense.
Gracey Copper, Cheverus field hockey: On a defense with no returning starters from 2025, Copper has stepped up for the Stags. Her tenacity while Biddeford launched a barrage of penalty corners at Cheverus in a Sept. 25 showdown was key to the Stags’ 3-2 win in the battle of Class A South powers.
Lauren Jabar, Yarmouth soccer: Jabar helped lead a defense that conceded just two goals all month for a team that was 7-0 in September. A Sept. 3 effort against Cape Elizabeth in which she displayed remarkable 1-on-1 skills and beat the Capers to every ball was particularly noteworthy.
Kristyna Pokorna, Thornton Academy volleyball: Not all stats are created equal; some are the results of plays that change games in key moments. That’s what Pokorna did Sept. 24 against Scarborough with two aces that turned the tide. Oh, and as coach Kayla Arthurs said, don’t let her defense go unnoticed.
Adela Ricker, Gardiner soccer: Goalkeeping is always important, but it’s especially important in one-goal games — exactly where Ricker has thrived. In a Sept. 24 battle with rival Cony, Ricker’s 12 saves were crucial to the Tigers’ 3-2 victory. Gardiner has won five one-goal games this season.

title: Father and son keep guitar-making legacy going together
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
HOLLANDTOWN, Wis. (Aging Untold) — Bruce Petros has been building stringed instruments for 52 years, turning a small woodworking shop into the business Petros Guitars.
“We’re trying to have lasting, lasting beauty in the instrument,” Petros said.
From a $15 kit to a career
Petros got his start while working as a tour guide in Colorado after finding a guitar kit for $15 in a shop and putting it together.
“There was this little tourist town that had, you know, shops,” Petros said. “And I found a guitar kit in this store, and it was like $15. And I took it back to the resort where I was living and put it together. And I looked at it and I went, ‘Wow, this is really cool. I could do this.’”
Petros started building guitars in the basements of rental homes before moving his family to Hollandtown.
“We bought this place and tore down this garage and built the shop, basically,” Petros said.
Building a reputation
Petros Guitars now supplies guitars and ukuleles to musicians around the world, including collectors, working musicians and hobbyists.
“And now this is a little concert ukulele that’s got a curly Koa top and curly bubinga back and sides,” Petros said while displaying one of the company’s string instruments.
Petros said Paul Simon owns one of his instruments, along with other musicians.
Passing down the business
Petros’ son, Matt, is set to take over the business.
“It’s just great to be able to create something with your hands,” Matt Petros said. “There’s never been any pressure. I’ve never been yelled at by my boss or threatened to be fired.”
Bruce Petros said having plans for his son take over the business is the ideal situation.
“A lot of guitar makers when they quit, what are they going to do? You can’t sell a guitar making shop. You can sell the tools and the wood. You can’t sell your reputation,” Bruce Petros said. “So this is kind of the ideal situation where the reputation is built in and it continues on.”
The father and son said each instrument the shop produces is made to have a certain sound.
“They sound better and they play better,” Bruce Petros said. “Figuring out the ways to, you know, eke out every little bit of tone.”
Matt Petros said he looks forward to carrying on the family’s musical legacy.
“Well, you grow up in the shop. That’s all I knew,” Matt Petros said. “And every little boy wants to be like their dad. And I was just lucky enough to be able to do it.”

title: Halloween spending to reach record $13.5 billion nationwide
text:
Halloween spending to reach record $13.5 billion nationwide
The National Retail Federation predicts Halloween spending will hit $13.5 billion this year, with affordability driving creative shopping strategies.
Halloween spending to reach record $13.5 billion nationwide
The National Retail Federation predicts Halloween spending will hit $13.5 billion this year, with affordability driving creative shopping strategies.
Halloween spending is expected to reach a record $13.5 billion this year, with consumers spending an average of $115 per person, according to the National Retail Federation.
The NRF said the increase is driven by a higher number of people celebrating Halloween compared to previous years.
"A lot of it has to do with there are more shoppers this year than in years past. There's more people celebrating," said Allison Zeller, Vice President of Industry and Consumer Insights for the National Retail Federation.
About half of shoppers began their Halloween purchases in September or earlier to spread out costs.
"Affordability is top of mind, and we see a lot of shoppers going to discount stores," Zeller said. "We also see them really spreading their shopping across multiple different channels, multiple different places, and really getting creative with where they're going to get their decorations and their costumes."
On average, shoppers plan to spend $37 on costumes, $37 on decorations, and $35 on candy. To keep costs manageable, the NRF suggests focusing on reusable items.
"To keep the season affordable, consumers are looking for things that they can reuse. So whether that is a decor item that might work into the longer fall season, or items that they can package up and keep and bring about next year," Zeller said.
For additional ways to save on decorations, choose durable pieces and focus on one high-impact area, such as a porch or living room, rather than decorating the entire home.
When it comes to costumes, shoppers are encouraged to look in their closets first. A few accessories and some makeup can transform existing clothing into a creative outfit.
For candy, checking the unit price and buying based on the expected number of trick-or-treaters can help avoid overspending.
Major retailers like Amazon, Target, and Walmart are running sales this week, providing opportunities for Halloween shopping.

title: To tackle nicotine addiction, we need federal resources
text:
I agree with the concern expressed about protecting Maine youth from nicotine addiction (“Susan Collins questions Trump’s FDA nominee about vapes, drugs for rare diseases,” Sept. 24). But if we are going to talk about protecting children, we should also talk about what has happened to the federal infrastructure responsible for tobacco prevention.
On April 1, 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Office on Smoking and Health — the nation’s primary federal tobacco-prevention office — was essentially dismantled. Approximately 200 staff and contractors were terminated. The Tips From Former Smokers campaign was ended, and surveillance systems used to track tobacco use and cessation trends have been degraded.
That matters because the statistics we rely on to understand youth vaping, nicotine-pouch use and other tobacco trends don’t simply appear. They require ongoing federal surveillance and scientific expertise.
Congress ultimately preserved tobacco-control funding for FY2026, yet the Office on Smoking and Health had not been restored.
Sen. Susan Collins deserves credit for questioning a nominee about youth vaping. But as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, she also has an important responsibility to protect the federal tobacco-prevention infrastructure that Maine and other states depend upon.
If we truly want to protect Maine children, we need more than hearings about nicotine. We need the data, science and public health programs to prevent addiction.
Mary Lou Warn
Winslow

title: Suspect, 35, arrested nearly 20 years after 10-year-old boy, stepmother were stabbed to death
text:
FRANKLIN, Ind. (KLTV/Gray News) - Authorities in Indiana believe they have identified a suspect in the deaths of a boy and his stepmother from two decades ago.
A grand jury has returned an indictment against 35-year-old Michael Jerome James in the 2006 murders of Blake and Chynna Dickus.
On July 24, 2006, Blake Dickus, 10 and his stepmother Chynna Dickus, 26, were found stabbed to death.
Newly unsealed indictments suggest the killings may have happened during an attempted burglary.
James would have been about 14 at the time of the killings.
In the years since, the Franklin Police Department has continued to search for their killer, using billboards, a $25,000 reward and “tens of thousands of man-hours” without identifying a suspect until now.
Grand jury members reviewed the evidence for three weeks before delivering the indictment.
James has his first court appearance Thursday morning in Johnson County.

title: Maine’s top court rejects eviction appeal by midcoast farmers
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The couple who managed Harpswell’s last sizable farm have moved themselves and their livestock off the property and lost their latest appeal to Maine’s highest court.
The Maine Supreme Judicial Court rejected the appeal of Joseph and Laura Grady, who ran Two Coves Farm for more than 16 years but were ousted because, according to an arbitrator, they failed to pay roughly $124,000 in rent and grow crops as they had once agreed.
The Aug. 19 ruling capped a protracted legal fight that had the Gradys claiming they were being forced out of their home and stripped of their livelihood in spite of their good-faith efforts and in contravention of Maine’s protections for home renters.
Opposing them was Helen Norton, who — with her late husband — bought the 100-acre tract in hopes of preserving a vestige of Harpswell Neck’s agrarian history. Norton’s lawyers alleged that the Gradys had taken advantage of an ailing 94-year-old woman and were “squatting” on the land while dragging out the process with a series of “11th hour arguments.”
The Supreme Judicial Court ruling rejected the latest of those appeals. It affirmed a longer order dated July 28 in which the court upheld the arbitrator’s decision and rejected the couple’s contention that the arbitrator had exceeded his authority in treating the lease as a strictly commercial contract rather than one that also provided the Gradys with a place to live and raise their children.
Norton said she was pleased by the ruling and is working to make repairs to the property that will allow her to “find a good, responsible farmer and his family and make it a viable working farm” as soon as next spring.
Of the legal fight, she said, “It has cost me a lot of money, it has cost me a lot of time and effort, and it has made us quite unhappy.”
The Gradys declined to participate in an interview for this article. Joe Grady requested questions in writing, then declined to answer them. However, court filings from their legal team lay out their position in detail. In a brief statement emailed to the Anchor, they said they are disappointed but determined.
“The last two years of defending ourselves from the claims made against us have been exhausting; losing our home where we planned to spend the rest of our lives, as well as the business we built from scratch, was devastating and is still fresh for us,” they said in the statement.
Partners in protection
The legal battle brought a bitter close to what began as a pastoral partnership.
Two decades ago, in 2006, Norton and her late husband, Walter, bought a 100-acre saltwater farm near their home on Harpswell Neck. The entity they formed in 2008, Neils Point LLC, granted an agriculture conservation easement to the Maine Farmland Trust, with the Harpswell Heritage Land Trust overseeing the easement.
The purpose of the arrangement was to protect the farm “from encroaching suburban sprawl so that it will always be available for its traditional use as a productive cropland, open fields and forest,” according to the arbitrator’s findings.
In 2009, a young farming couple — the Gradys — signed on as stewards of the property, an agreement renewed in 2017 for an additional 25 years. In exchange for the right to live and farm there, the couple agreed to keep the farm in productive operation and to pay rent equal to 10% of their “annual net proceeds” — their farming revenue minus legitimate operating expenses.
For many years, all seemed to be going smoothly at Two Coves Farm. Drivers passing the property on Harpswell Neck Road saw signs advertising a farm stand along a tree-lined lane that sold, among other things, eggs, lamb, tomatoes, cucumbers, yarn and sheepskins.
Injustice or end of a ‘free ride?’
But trouble arrived last year, when relations between Norton and the Gradys took a sharp downward turn. In July 2025, an arbitrator presided over a hearing to examine Norton’s allegations that the couple had failed to live up to their end of the deal.
After examining evidence and hearing from both sides, arbitrator Timothy J. Bryant, a Portland attorney, concluded that the Gradys had not made rent payments on time and “failed to pay any rent whatsoever for the years of 2023 and 2024.” In a decision dated Oct. 24, 2025, the arbitrator concluded that the Gradys had understated their revenues and “knowingly inflated their operational expenses by treating household and personal expenses as business expenses.”
The arbitrator also agreed with Norton that the Gradys had failed to “use the farm to actively plant and grow productive crops,” as required by the 2017 lease.
He ordered the Gradys to pay Norton’s Neils Point LLC $124,175 and to vacate the farm no later than Dec. 31, 2025.
The Gradys did not move out, instead filing a Dec. 30 appeal asking a Maine Superior Court justice to vacate the decision and allow them to continue working and living at Two Coves. Because the farm was also their home, they argued that state law prohibited them from being evicted without the formal court process guaranteed to residential tenants.
Norton’s legal team countered by saying that the arbitrator’s ruling was sound, and that the Gradys had voluntarily agreed to arbitration as the method for resolving disputes. In a Feb. 4 ruling, Superior Court Justice Darcie N. McElwee sided with Norton and agreed that the Gradys must vacate.
In late February, the Gradys took their appeal to the Supreme Judicial Court.
“This case presents a stark injustice,” wrote the Gradys’ lawyers, Regan A. Sweeney and J. Spencer Hoffman. “A wealthy landowner has utilized commercial arbitration to dispossess a tenant farming family from the property they have called home and worked for over 16 years.”
The lawyers stated that the Gradys had been served a “writ of possession” on Feb. 25, giving them 48 hours to vacate. “The Gradys were afforded no meaningful opportunity to seek appellate relief before the coercive machinery of eviction was set in motion,” they wrote.
The court’s ruling would affect not just the Gradys, their lawyers wrote, but also other farmers.
“Farmers are the backbone of Maine’s communities. They feed their neighbors, steward the land, and embody the independence and self-reliance that define this state’s character,” they said. “Yet the (ruling) treats farmers as something less than every other resident of Maine. The Gradys are people who work the land they live on. They are not commercial tenants operating a warehouse or retail establishment. … Their home is their farm, and their farm is their home. The two are inseparable.”
Norton’s lawyers countered with strong words of their own in a Feb. 27 pleading. Noting that the Gradys had already relocated their livestock and “never grew any crops in the first place,” they said the couple faced no real hardship.
“For the last decade, the (Gradys) have had possession of the farm under false pretenses. For the last two months, they have trespassed on the property unlawfully,” said attorneys Thimi R. Mina and Alfred C. Frawley IV. “Meanwhile, Mrs. Norton is 94 years old and recently suffered a significant injury. Put simply, time is of the essence, and the balance of the equities lies in favor of ending the (Gradys’) decade-long free ride while Mrs. Norton still has the opportunity to put the property to productive use.”
The legal point and counterpoint continued through the spring and summer. Following the adverse July 28 Supreme Judicial Court ruling, the Gradys again appealed and — in August — lost again.
The court rejected the Gradys’ argument that they were entitled to the same channels of legal appeal available to a tenant facing eviction from a rental home. Instead, the Gradys had to abide by the arbitrator’s decision after earlier agreeing on that course of conflict resolution.
As their legal battle wound down, both the Gradys and Norton expressed gratitude for the support they had received from neighbors.
“I am very happy for the support that I’ve received from the community,” said Norton, who, along with her late husband, has invested in conserving a large amount of open land in Harpswell and neighboring communities.
“To all those in Harpswell who have supported us and Two Coves Farm, we want to pass on our thanks and let you all know that we are doing well and have transitioned to a new home,” the Grady family said in their statement emailed to the Anchor.
“We do not know what the future holds at the moment,” they added, “but we will certainly be finding our way back to farming in the months and years ahead.”
