title: Christa Pike is conscious and speaking after Tennessee failed execution, her attorneys say
text:
Christa Pike, a Tennessee inmate who survived Tennessee’s attempt to execute her, is awake and speaking as she receives treatment at a hospital, her attorneys said Tuesday.
“Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care. Despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed. Her recovery is medically unprecedented. Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery,” attorneys for Pike said in a statement.
Her attorneys said they are grateful for the first responders and the medical team at the hospital “who treated Christa like a human and have provided exceptional care to her.”
The statement was the first indication that Pike has improved since an ambulance carried her away from a Nashville prison last Wednesday.
A spokeswoman for the Tennessee Department of Correction said she could provide no information other than that Pike remained hospitalized Tuesday.
Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital as they attempted to put her to death for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. The lethal injection drug didn’t kill her, but her lawyers said her arms were left burned and blistered.
Dr. Joel Zivot, a professor of anesthesiology and surgery in Atlanta who consulted as an expert for Pike’s legal team, said the development “bodes well for a good recovery.” But, he added, it could be weeks or months before anyone knows exactly what her recovery might look like, and whether her competency could be restored to a level that might enable the state to try again to execute her.
“She’s still in the ICU,” he said. “She has recovered to a certain degree that she’s able to be off a ventilator and able to speak, but in no way would I announce her free of further serious risk. There’s still a lot of bad things that can happen here, even when everyone is doing their job well.”
Pike’s attorneys are set to go to court Wednesday as they seek to learn more about what happened in the failed lethal injection.
The attorneys are seeking a court order requiring the Tennessee Department of Correction to preserve evidence, including drug lot numbers, records and other information from the Sept. 30 attempted execution. Chancery Court Judge I’Ashea Myles scheduled a Wednesday morning status conference in the case.
Pike’s attorneys said in their Tuesday statement that they continue to ask Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to commute Pike’s sentence to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
“Christa is a survivor and will take recovery one day at a time,” her attorneys said.

title: Trump doesn't commit to repaying federal funds already spent on controversial ads
text:
Trump doesn't commit to repaying federal funds already spent on controversial ads
A day after President Donald Trump said he would start paying for controversial taxpayer-funded ads with a campaign account, he hasn't committed to refunding the millions of federal dollars already spent on them.
Nearly $12 million worth of ads have already aired, according to AdImpact, as part of the $20 million the Department of Homeland Security tapped for the contract.
But Trump’s plan to pay for the ads with MAGA Inc. doesn’t mean there’s any reimbursement coming, said a White House official who was not authorized to talk publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.
Speaking to reporters Tuesday, Trump said the ads were “really good” and “promotion for the country, done by many presidents before.” Asked whether he'd repay the funds already spent, he said, “We’ll decide.”
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer slammed Trump for not committing to reimbursement and said he believes the president’s plan for covering future costs represents illegal coordination with his super PAC.
“Trump must return this money to the American people and there must be a full investigation into this gross waste and abuse of taxpayer dollars,” Schumer told The Associated Press.
The ads, which began airing in late September, glorify Trump and echo his political messaging going into the midterms. One features a clip of Trump talking about the threat of communism and another is a replay of an ad from his last presidential campaign. The fifth ad in the campaign began airing Tuesday, focusing on the Trump administration's capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro.
Republicans and Democrats alike have said the ads aren't an appropriate use of U.S. government money. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a Republican from South Dakota, said they shouldn't be paid for with taxpayer dollars.
The Trump administration tapped $20 million from the Department of Homeland Security to pay for the campaign-style ads glorifying the president that have drawn widespread criticism. Two top Democratic senators said last week that the money is being drawn from Trump’s so-called “One Big Beautiful Bill” and was supposed to go toward U.S. Customs and Border Protection.
Republican Sen. Katie Britt of Alabama, who chairs the panel that oversees DHS funding, said Tuesday that she had not yet seen Trump’s ads, but she said taxpayer money should be used as intended.
“We’ll take a look at that,” Britt said at the Capitol. “You want to make sure that any use of taxpayer dollars is done judiciously and in accordance with the law.”
Legal experts said the ads might even violate federal statutes, including a law against congressionally appropriated money being used for “publicity or propaganda” and another limiting the partisan political activities of government employees.
The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements similar to what past administrations have done to promote policies. Trump on Monday posted on his Truth Social platform, calling the ads “positive promotion for our Great U.S.A.” while also promising to pay for them with “money I raised for MAGA Inc.”
That is Trump’s political war chest, which had amassed more than $400 million by the end of July. Trump has begun tapping it to boost Republican candidates across the country in the midterm elections.
AP Congressional Correspondent Lisa Mascaro contributed to this report.

title: Susan Collins camp releases new info disputing alleged pay-to-play scheme
text:
Sen. Susan Collins’ reelection campaign released new information on Tuesday that it says absolves the Republican incumbent of the recent pay-to-play allegations currently being seized on by Democrats.
Campaign Manager Steve Abbott took aim at a story published by ProPublica on Sept. 22 that, among other things, reported that former Navatek CEO Martin Kao told the FBI that Collins required political contributions before meeting with donors.
Abbott said the outlet’s reporting failed to acknowledge Collins’ full history with Navatek, the company at the center of the scandal. Collins started working with Navatek only after a local university requested defense funding, Abbott contended.
On a video call with reporters, Abbott showed a 2017 letter from the University of Maine seeking $5 million in federal funding for a project in partnership with Navatek “to launch a collaborative research program to address the U.S. Navy’s pressing need to enhance the mobility of future marine vehicles.” Collins ultimately secured the funding in the fiscal year 2018 budget.
Abbott also showed a photo of Collins meeting with Kao in her office with other officials in February of 2018. Kao later told federal investigators that Collins refused to meet that year with him unless he made a donation to her 2020 reelection campaign.
But Kao did not make his first donation to Collins until June 27, 2018, federal records show.
“ProPublica has the theory that Martin Kao, based on Martin Kao’s word, had to make a donation before he could get in to see Susan Collins,” Abbott said. “As you can see from that picture, it’s not true.”
The photo was taken by a Senate photographer on Feb. 15, 2018, embedded data showed, according to a screenshot released by the campaign.
The campaign’s media call was another example of how Collins is aggressively responding to allegations that could undercut her work as the top senate appropriator. The money she brings home to Maine is a key theme of her reelection campaign against Democrat Troy Jackson, a former logger and state Senate president.
It also comes ahead of Collins’ first televised debate against Troy Jackson, who is likely to raise the issue of ProPublica’s reporting. Jackson has maintained a narrow lead in the Maine’s closely watched Senate race, according to most polls.
Kao pleaded guilty to charges involving money laundering and bank fraud in 2022, and is currently in federal prison. He had been cooperating with federal investigators in an effort to get his sentence reduced.
ProPublica reported that the FBI was gearing up for a widespread corruption probe of Collins and other members of Congress based on statements Kao made to investigators between 2022 and 2024. The outlet reported that the investigation was abandoned when Trump returned to office in 2025 and disbanded anti-corruption units.
After her campaign’s initial response to the ProPublica story, the outlet fact-checked statements made by Collins’ team, finding some of their claims to be false. For example, a Collins spokesperson claimed that the outlet “took the word of” Kao in their story, “someone who pled guilty to five counts of money laundering.”
ProPublica reporters contend that they independently corroborated much of his account, reviewing “a trove of evidence gathered by the FBI,” examining “thousands of pages of legal records” and interviewing “dozens of people familiar with Navatek, its Washington operations and the FBI inquiry.”
The news site reported that Kao gave $150,000 to a super PAC supporting Collins, who in turn promised to steer $32 million in additional contracts to Navatek. Kao made the illegal donation through a shell company because federal contractors are prohibited from donating to political campaigns.
But Abbott said neither Collins, nor anybody else on her staff, would have promised a specific level of funding.
“We would never say that because there is no way we would know that we could get that done,” Abbott said. “No chance that that is true. Absolutely false.”
State and national Democrats are now using the ProPublica report to push an anti-corruption message in the final month of the election.
“The facts are clear — as recently as 2025, the FBI was circling Susan Collins for her involvement in a pay-to-play scheme until the Trump administration killed the unit that was looking into her,” Misha Linnehan, spokesperson for the Maine Democratic Party, said in a statement. “No amount of bluster from Collins’ team can distract Mainers from the fact that she sold them out for campaign cash.”
WinSenate, a super PAC aligned with Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer of New York, launched a $3.4 million ad campaign last week in Maine highlighting the ProPublica story.

title: Russian oligarch says Donald Trump Jr. has paid him back for wedding celebration expenses
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — The Russian oligarch who helped bankroll Donald Trump Jr.’s wedding celebration says the president’s eldest son has paid back the money.
“Yes, he did,” Umar Kremlev told an International Boxing Association press conference in Istanbul on Tuesday. “He did repay the money I spent on the present.” Still, he said he felt the repayment was unnecessary.
“Frankly speaking, I do not understand why he decided to do so,” he went on. “There are all kinds of events organized by all kinds of people. It is as if I invite you to come and visit my country house. Would you expect me to issue an invoice to them afterward?” Speaking through an interpreter, he said that would be “ridiculous.”
ProPublica, a nonprofit investigative website, reported last month that Kremlev, who has close ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin, “footed the bill for hundreds of thousands of dollars of wedding expenses” when Trump Jr. married socialite Bettina Anderson in the Bahamas in May. That included paying to rent one of two private islands where the three-day party was held.
In a subsequent post on her Instagram page signed by the couple, Bettina Trump wrote that they had been married “surrounded ONLY by our family,” but that Kremlev, head of the boxing association, was a “dear friend” who “very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding.”
President Donald Trump, who did not attend the nuptials, previously defended the arrangement but told reporters that the money would be paid back.
“It’s totally allowed,” he said. “But, as I understand it, he paid them back.”
“That’s very common,” he added, “I’ve given wedding parties to numerous people.”
Kremlev, who was recently honored with the Order of Friendship by Putin, also played down the significance, saying the celebration was “a shared event” and “people blew it out of proportion.”
“I mean, why can’t we be friends? We are just friends,” he went on. “We are simply friends and what unites us is love for sports.”
The focus on Kremlev comes as Russia remains at war with Ukraine following its invasion in 2022 and as Trump has failed to broker a promised peace deal between the nations.
Trump Jr. has previously been scrutinized over his ties to Russia. During the 2016 campaign, his meeting with a Russian attorney in Trump Tower to discuss potentially incriminating information about his father’s then-Democratic opponent was a critical element of investigations into whether the Trump campaign coordinated with Russia to meddle in the election to help Trump win.

title: UMaine, Thomas College announce scholarships for Alfond Grant recipients
text:
AUGUSTA — Paige McNef, Samantha Hamilton and Ethan LeHay weren’t fully aware that they were some of the first babies in Maine to receive a $500 Alfond Grant growing up. But when it came time to think about college, those grants came as a big relief.
McNef, Hamilton and LeHay, who grew up in central Maine, all started their first semesters at college this fall, thanks in part to that early investment in their futures.
“I had no clue how I was going to pay for college,” said LeHay, who now goes to Central Maine Community College in Auburn. “Then my grandmother had told me about the Alfond Grant, and that took a huge weight off my shoulders.”
Now LeHay, who is going to come out of his first year of college debt-free, can focus on enjoying the beginning of his college experience.
The Alfond Grant Program, started by Maine businessman and philanthropist Harold Alfond shortly before he died in 2007, has granted $500 to every child born in Maine since 2013, totaling over 184,000 recipients, to use for education after high school. The program was first launched in 2008 and was awarded to 650 children born in Waterville and Augusta before later becoming available to all Maine children.
At an event celebrating this milestone Tuesday on the University of Maine at Augusta campus, the Alfond Scholarship Foundation announced new partnerships with the University of Maine System and Thomas College, which will now offer additional scholarships to eligible Alfond Grant recipients who attend those schools. The scholarships include $250 from the University of Maine system and $500 from Thomas College in Waterville.
“It is our way of saying, ‘Hey, this is one heck of an idea. It is blooming, and we want to make it bloom even bigger,'” Dannel P. Malloy, chancellor of the University of Maine System, said. “And we want to be a part of the effort to make sure that more families, at the birth of a child, are participating in this investment, not just investments in money, investment in the child.”
Eighteen years after the first 650 children received those $500 grants, the value of the grants now total around $2,500 or more depending on additional parental contributions.
The Alfond Scholarship Foundation invests the funds until a child is ready to use them, allowing them to grow over time. Families are also encouraged to open a NextGen 529 account, a state-sponsored investment account for higher education, alongside the grant to add their own contributions and receive matching grants from the Finance Authority of Maine, allowing the accounts to grow even more.
“It (has) that practical benefit of being real money in a real account,” Colleen Quint, president and CEO of the Alfond Scholarship Foundation, said. “It has that aspirational benefit of not just kind of encouraging kids to think about their futures, but also, and we hear this a lot from kids and from parents, is that someone else believes in my child, someone sees my child as having value. And that’s a really powerful thing.”
Early investments in education often have a positive impact on children’s aspirations, development and outcomes in school, Quint said, as well as increasing parents’ aspirations for their children’s futures.
The grant can be used for a wide array of higher education opportunities like college, vocational school, certificate programs, apprenticeships or graduate school and is not limited just to institutions in Maine.
“That’s money all to power the higher education opportunities for Maine kids, and then for those Maine kids to have a better life because of it,” Greg Powell, CEO and president of the Harold Alfond Foundation, said. “I like to think the state is better off too, because it’s really allowed our workforce now to have a leg up, and we will see that in the years ahead.”
Hamilton is using her grant to study civil engineering at University of Maine in Orono, McNef is studying radiology at Kennebec Valley Community College and LeHay is pursuing accounting at Central Maine Community College.
When asked what they would tell younger students preparing for their futures, all three grant recipients said to dream big and invest early.
“Just taking it day by day, going, ‘What can I do today to make my future better?'” Hamilton advised younger students. “And I think the Alfond Grant is incredible in that financially.”

title: Hit or miss, The Biergarten in Skowhegan earns 3 stars
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Biergarten is a casual restaurant, so homey and unpretentious that our server briefly plunked down at the table to chat. I hadn’t experienced this since eating 12 years ago at a place called — not even kidding — It Don’t Matter Family Restaurant, in Highland Home, Alabama. (With a name that nihilistic, you just have to stop in, if only to find out exactly what don’t matter.)
There, as here, the cozy chumminess is all part of the charm.
Located inside a stylishly renovated former wool mill, The Biergarten is an airy, tasteful loft space that applies German aesthetics sparingly. Small deer antlers adorn the communal pine tables; antique beer steins from “mug club” members flank the rough-hewn wood frame of the mirror behind the bar. More Oktoberfest-style tables and benches are available on the back patio alongside the Kennebec River on weekend evenings.
A local brewery had originally planned to open a brewpub in the space before backing out. When Biergarten managing owner Amber Lambke and and her son, general manager Miles Lambke, stepped in, they stuck with the beer theme, since many of the state’s breweries use grains sourced from Skowhegan’s Maine Grains. (Amber Lambke is co-founder and CEO of Maine Grains, and also owns The Miller’s Table, the excellent cafe, bakery and pizzeria in its same building.)
But the Lambkes didn’t want to serve run-of-the-wool-mill pub fare. They’d get a certain amount of out-of-town customers, particularly since The Biergarten is the restaurant for the adjoining boutique hotel, The Skowhegan by Kasa. But they still wanted it to be affordable and family friendly for locals, the bulk of their clientele.
“There’s a void of German food in Central Maine, so it made sense to fill that gap,” Miles said. “And when it comes down to it, German food is basic meat-and-potatoes most of the time. So even though it comes with an unfamiliar name like schnitzel, it’s easy to explain to people and get them on board with fried chicken.”
A pork version is an occasional weekly special, but Chicken Schnitzel ($29) is a staple. Their deep-fried version was well seasoned, with raucously crunchy panko coating, though we found the thin-pounded meat a touch dry. A side of pleasantly soft braised red cabbage offers balanced, straightforward flavors of brown sugar, apples and cider vinegar; a little warm spice might lend fetching depth. Even better were the buttery, squishy squiggles of spaetzle — made from nutty Maine Grains spelt flour, a Biergarten workhorse — with their crisped brown edges.
You have to admire how the Lambkes’ concept provides such a fitting home for Maine-made products like sausage from The Sausage Kitchen in Lisbon Falls, Morse’s sauerkraut and Raye’s Old World brown mustard, all of which are showcased on their Bratwurst ($18). A scrumptious griddled bun from The Good Crust in Canaan cradles the long, juicy link, and might even be the best part of the tasty dish.
The Sausage Kitchen also supplies links for The Wurst Plate ($18), portions of knackwurst, mettwurst and whiskey-peppercorn bratwurst with a trio of mustards. Though fine, the flavor differences among the meats were vanishingly subtle, perhaps defeating the purpose of a sampler.
Our very first taste of The Biergarten was … odd. Their filtered tap water tasted earthy, like fresh-dug beetroot. Miles said while he doesn’t personally notice anything off in the taste, other out-of-town customers have commented about the water. Seems like a new filter is in order.
Then we tried the aptly named Forest Fire ($15), a smoked riff on an Old Fashioned. It looked like a short pour, not quite reaching halfway up its small rocks glass. But the real problem was how the acrid, ashy smoke from dried rosemary (which should be delightfully woodsy) laid waste to an otherwise good cocktail. The cocktail smoker may be also be overdue for maintenance.
We course-corrected with a splendid, malty Ayinger Celebrator Doppelbock ($8.50) and crisp, fruity Raimund Prüm Essence Riesling ($14) from Germany’s Mosel region. The Biergarten stocks 16 beers and ciders on tap, most local, with a few German imports custom-built for the cuisine. They also sell eight wines by the glass ($9-$15), and 16 by the bottle ($32-$78), an approachably priced and unclichéd selection of Old and New World options.
My dining partner grew up in Alsace, France, and flammkuchen (or tarte flambée, as she knew it) is her soul food. She rhapsodizes about thin, cracker-crisp crust smeared with rich crème fraîche and scattered with thin slices of onion and plump lardons. When our Flammkuchen Tavern Pizza ($23) hit the table, she was aghast.
Crunchy bacon bits stand in for lardons, Jackson Pollock-like squirts of crème fraîche are cut with mustard, and — most appalling to her — the crust (from The Good Crust) was far too soft, and actually seemed more like pita bread.
Sure, it’s not authentic, but I won’t fault them for that. It also fails as “tavern pizza,” though. It’s the kind of pizza your mom might try to slip by you on scrounge night.
“Mom, what is this?”
“I told you, it’s pizza. Eat your pizza, dear.”
Our starters and entrées arrived basically at once, though we’d asked for separation. Our server was apologetic, even as she made room on the table for more dishes, glancing helplessly toward the kitchen on that quiet Tuesday night. “They’re just kicking (the dishes) out,” she shrugged.
The Biergarten doesn’t have a head chef, just a kitchen crew that works off recipes and standard operating procedures. Miles explained that the local culinary talent pool has fewer professionally trained cooks than more densely populated areas, so they made sure their menu was uncomplicated and could be pulled off by “people with a variety of skill sets.”
We eventually cleared the decks for dessert, their popular Black Forest Brownie Sundae ($10). The spectacular warm spelt brownie from The Miller’s Table was gooey and intensely fudgy, but buried under too much whipped cream and cherry compote, itself overwhelmed by almond extract.
When I come back to The Biergarten, hopefully to enjoy some lovely fall weather at one of their outdoor tables, I’ll again order the Giant Soft Spelt Pretzel ($13). Its well-calibrated trio of Maine Grains flours make for a tender, chewy belly and crispy inner spindles. Dip a piece into the accompanying Bavarian beer cheese, featuring brie from Haymay Creamery in Farmington, for a touch of funk. I’d like to catch the pork schnitzel special, and I also want to try their Reuben, served on a rye English muffin from Portland chef Ilma Lopez.
The Biertgarten marks its one-year anniversary this month. The missteps in our meal mostly seem like quick and easy fixes, and I’d bet it won’t be long before they’re leveled up. Amber Lambke cares deeply about Maine-made food. She’s helped shape the local and state food economy on a literally granular level. She knows — it all matters.
RATING: ***
WHERE: 7 Island Ave., Skowhegan, skowheganbiergarten.com
SERVING: Noon-8 p.m. Sunday through Thursday; noon-9 p.m. Friday and Saturday; outdoor seating 4-8 p.m. Friday through Sunday
PRICE RANGE: Starters $8-$23, mains $15-$29
NOISE LEVEL: Medium-low on an early weeknight
VEGETARIAN: Some dishes
GLUTEN-FREE: Some dishes
RESERVATIONS: Yes
BAR: Cocktails, wine, beer, cider 
WHEELCHAIR ACCESS: Yes
BOTTOM LINE: When Maine Grains co-founder Amber Lambke and her son Miles launched The Biergarten in The Spinning Mill last October, they aimed to offer family-friendly German beer hall food and beverages at accessible price points. They’ve succeeded in parts, though some dishes and drinks need more attention to detail. Maine Grains spelt flour is the common thread in some of the best items, like a nutty and faintly sweet giant soft pretzel, pillowy buttered spaetzle, and a killer brownie (that gets unfortunately lost in a pile of whipped cream and cherry compote). Sausage, sauerkraut, mustard and buns from Maine partner producers come together in a tasty bratwurst dish, while the flammkuchen was a miss. We had issues with a smoky cocktail, but the local and German beer selection is robust, and the accommodating wine list likely has something that suits both your food and personal preferences. Tables on the back riverside patio seem like a great place to hunker down for fall festivities.
Ratings follow this scale and take into consideration food, atmosphere, service and value and type of restaurant (a casual bistro will be judged as a casual bistro, an expensive upscale restaurant as such):
* Poor 
** Fair
*** Good
**** Excellent
***** Extraordinary
The Maine Sunday Telegram visits each restaurant once; if the first meal was unsatisfactory, the reviewer returns for a second. The reviewer never accepts free food or drink.

title: Maine regulators deny CMP’s $7 rate hike as utility weighs potential layoffs
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine utility regulators denied Central Maine Power Co.’s request for almost $70 million in increased rates on Tuesday, a major win for advocacy groups that means bills will not increase this fall.
The Maine Public Utilities Commission’s unanimous denial of CMP’s bid to increase the average household’s bill by about $7 per month comes with potentially serious financial consequences for the utility, company representatives said in filings before Tuesday’s hearing. A CMP executive told employees last week that the company would reconsider workforce levels if the PUC denied its request.
Current distribution rates are likely to remain in place until the spring, when regulators are expected to decide on the merits of the utility’s full $189 million rate case.
State law allows utilities to recoup “temporary rates” during a longer case, as long as the amount they’re seeking to raise is agreed upon. That’s what CMP was seeking here: the first step of a two-part rate increase, intended to help pay for infrastructure CMP has built in recent years.
The PUC had recommended this approach last year when it dismissed CMP’s five-year plan, which would have raised the average household’s bill by about $35.
But the three members of the Maine Public Utilities Commission agreed Tuesday that intervening groups — from the Office of the Public Advocate to the Department of Energy Resources to consumer advocates — had disputed all $69.3 million of CMP’s ask, and that they therefore could not allow the utility to raise rates.
The commission’s decision aligned with the recommendation of its staff last month.
Much of the dispute was based on return on equity — the return CMP’s shareholders can make on the company’s capital projects. Return on equity is the only way a utility monopoly can make profit under Maine’s regulatory structure, and it’s become a focal point in the rate case.
About two-thirds of CMP’s temporary rate ask was to right-size its return on equity, which the company said was necessary to attract investment and maintain its credit ratings.
“I simply could not pinpoint a number that I would feel comfortable saying was not in dispute in this matter,” PUC Chair Philip Bartlett said during deliberations Tuesday.
Bartlett also said that, since the utility has exceeded its capital spending forecast by about 50% from 2022 to 2025, “to some extent, this is a problem of CMP’s own making.”
In the eight days since PUC staff recommended the commissioners reject CMP’s increase, the utility has removed 70 job postings for line workers and customer service positions, paused plans to improve 19 transformers servicing thousands of customers from York to Rangeley, and halted several other infrastructure projects.
A spokesperson for CMP did not respond Tuesday to a request for comment, but in a filing before the hearing Tuesday, the company said it would be hit hard by a denial.
In addition to deferring upgrades to its grid infrastructure and pausing hiring, CMP said it would be forced to “consider workforce reductions.” The company’s financial outlook was downgraded this summer by S&P Global Ratings to “negative” because of lag in this rate case and a $100 million cash flow deficit.
“Customers do not experience regulatory delay in the abstract,” attorneys for CMP wrote to regulators last week. “They experience it through aging transformers, deferred maintenance, postponed reliability projects, and infrastructure that continues operating long after it should have been replaced.”
Linda Ball, the president and CEO of CMP, said in a Sept. 28 email to employees that it would be irresponsible for the utility not “to carefully evaluate current workforce levels, hiring plans and apprenticeship programs” given the “regulatory challenges we face.”
“I recognize that news like this creates uncertainty and concern,” Ball said in the email. “Please know that our leadership team takes these challenges seriously and remains focused on supporting our employees, maintaining safe and reliable service for our customers, and advocating for the investments necessary to sustain Maine’s electric system for the long term, while balancing the impacts this situation has on the business.”
No decisions about workforce levels have been made, Ball wrote. CMP employs almost 1,000 people, the company’s website says.
Meanwhile, the PUC decision marks a substantial win for advocacy groups, which have fought CMP’s rate increase at each step.
Fight the Hike, a coalition of advocacy groups opposed to CMP’s increase, celebrated the PUC’s decision in a news release and said it would continue to oppose the utility’s efforts to raise rates in the next several months.
“(Delaying grid projects is) an attempt at blackmail,” Seth Berry, the executive director of coalition member Our Power, said in the release. “Unlike any other business, CMP has a monopoly. This is a privilege granted to them by the people of Maine. It’s time for CMP shareholders to start funding grid maintenance from their $160 million in annual profits — not squeezing still more from struggling families.”
Heather Sanborn, the state’s public advocate, said she applauded the PUC’s decision to wait to increase rates until the end of the yearlong proceeding. Any increase should be decided on its merits, she said, and should take into account affordability concerns.
Rebecca Schultz, the clean energy expert for the Natural Resources Council of Maine, one of the intervening parties in the case, applauded the PUC’s decision, especially in the face of rising costs in other areas.
Schultz also criticized CMP’s response.
“In the past few weeks, facing reasonable and completely foreseeable pushback to their request, the company chose to threaten Mainers with cutting union jobs and delaying important safety and reliability upgrades that were already underway,” she said in a statement. “This is unacceptable behavior for any company granted a monopoly business opportunity in Maine.”
The ruling Tuesday is likely to be the final major decision during Bartlett’s tenure as the PUC’s chair. After seven years leading the commission, Bartlett announced last month that he’d be stepping down Friday to move into the private sector.

title: Fryeburg Solar fined $204K for damaging environment
text:
An out-of-state energy developer is facing a civil fine of more than $200,000 after regulators found that heavy runoff generated during the construction of a solar farm in Fryeburg polluted nearby streams and wetlands.
According to its proposed agreement with the state, New Jersey-based Fryeburg Solar jumped the gun in 2021 by starting work at the 45-acre site before it got final approvals and demonstrated that it could afford to decommission the facility if needed.
State inspectors found construction crews exposed more land at one time than allowed, failed to maintain erosion controls and winter construction standards and let sediment and soil runoff pollute wetlands, streams, properties and nearby Lovewell Pond.
The runoff problems began in 2021 and, despite repeated state inspections, violations persisted. The Maine Department of Environmental Protection cited Fryeburg Solar in October 2022 and the underlying landowners in August 2023.
As solar farms spread across rural Maine, the proposed settlement highlights the ecological risks of the burgeoning market. It is also a warning for rural landowners that they may be on the hook if their solar tenants breach environmental laws.
Following legislative changes encouraging community solar, dozens of 5-megawatt arrays were fast-tracked across rural Maine. The land clearing has often collided with the steep topography and long mud seasons, making erosion control a recurring friction point.
Under Maine law, soil discharged into state waters is deemed a pollutant, and inspectors tracked mud plumes flowing toward Lovewell Pond, which is a key recreational, fishing and boating hub in Oxford County.
In late 2022, DEP ordered Fryeburg Solar to implement a state-approved plan to remove the soil and replant wetland vegetation. The developer used a special vacuum system to extract sediment from the 1,717 linear feet of streams and just under an acre of impaired wetlands.
In December 2025, DEP declared the restoration a success and began drawing up a civil penalty of $204,499. Because the amount exceeds $50,000, DEP must report the fine to the IRS, which means Fryeburg Solar won’t be able to write the payment off as a business expense on its taxes.
If approved, the Fryeburg Solar deal will be the sixth consent agreement of 2026, records show.
Fines for the other five range from as low as $1,654 for a homeowner who used driveway gravel to maintain his China Lake boat launch to more than $284,000 for a Milford homeowner who built a driveway over a stream that provided high-value habitat for waterfowl and wading birds.
Procedurally, violators entering a consent agreement must send their penalty payment to DEP before a proposed deal can be considered by the Board of Environmental Protection, said agency spokesman Dave Madore. That won’t happen until after a public comment period ends Nov. 2.
A spokesman for Nautilus Solar, Fryeburg parent company, said a check was mailed on Sept. 26.
“We took those matters seriously and worked closely with the (state), environmental consultants and contractors to address the concerns and implement corrective actions,” the spokesman said in an emailed statement.
The state is not requiring the five individual landowners to pay a civil penalty, but being cited in the settlement can create disclosure requirements during property sales and complicate refinancing.

title: Resident evacuated from Lewiston home after shots fired in backyard
text:
Resident evacuated from Lewiston home after shots fired in backyard, police say
Criminal charges are pending, according to authorities
Resident evacuated from Lewiston home after shots fired in backyard, police say
Criminal charges are pending, according to authorities
The Lewiston Police Department says criminal charges are pending in connection with an incident where shots were fired outside of a home.
Police said that shortly before 9 a.m. Tuesday, officers responded to Baird Avenue after receiving a report of a woman shooting a gun in a backyard.
According to police, the woman was believed to be experiencing a mental health crisis and went back inside her house, which had another person inside.
Officers borrowed a ladder from a local contractor who was working in the area and were able to safely evacuate the other resident from the home.
Police said they then were able to talk with the armed woman, who eventually came out of the house. The woman was taken into custody without incident and taken to a local hospital for evaluation.

title: Public Utilities Commission denies Central Maine Power’s request for temporary rate hike
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
HALLOWELL, Maine - Central Maine Power customers won’t see an immediate temporary rate hike.
State regulators unanimously rejected the company’s request Tuesday morning.
CMP had asked for approval of a $70 million rate increase, which would have temporarily increased the average customer’s bill by about seven dollars.
It’s part of an overall $189 million rate increase request to upgrade equipment that failed or nearly failed this summer.
Several groups objected, including the Public Advocate and AARP Maine.
Public Utilities Commission members say they denied this portion of the proposal over lack of agreement and affordability concerns from public hearings.
CMP’s president warns the decision could impact workforce levels and apprenticeship programs.
PUC Chairman Phil Bartlett said a final decision on CMP’s full rate hike request is expected to be made in April.

title: Woman killed in Hollis single-vehicle crash
text:
Woman killed in single-vehicle crash in Hollis
An SUV rolled over and struck a tree on Bar Mills Road Tuesday afternoon, according to Hollis Fire-Rescue.
Woman killed in single-vehicle crash in Hollis
An SUV rolled over and struck a tree on Bar Mills Road Tuesday afternoon, according to Hollis Fire-Rescue.
A 34-year-old Hollis woman was killed Tuesday afternoon after her SUV went off the road, rolled over and struck a tree, according to Maine State Police.
Police identified the driver as Amber Bowie.
Investigators say Bowie was traveling west on Bar Mills Road around 3:01 p.m. when her vehicle left the road and rolled over before striking a tree. Bowie was pronounced dead at the scene.
Bar Mills Road was closed for about two and a half hours while crews investigated. Traffic was detoured at that time.
The Hollis and Buxton fire departments and Buxton Police Department assisted at the scene.
The crash remains under investigation.

title: Stephen King leads authors with most books banned in schools
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Nearly 12,000 books were pulled off the shelves of schools nationwide in 2025.
The author with the most book bans was Maine’s own Stephen King.
A new study by PEN America says 312 books written by King were pulled including The Shining and The Green Mile.
King also led authors with most book bans for last year’s study.
According to the study, most of the books were banned due to themes of violence, sexuality, and gender identity.
Texas and Florida accounted for most bans.

title: 1,116-pound bluefin tuna caught off NH coast sets state record
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
1,116-pound bluefin tuna caught off New Hampshire coast sets state record
A New Hampshire fisherman broke a state record when he caught a massive bluefin tuna over the weekend.
"We lifted it out of the water and immediately knew it was way bigger than what we thought, and bigger than anything either of us had seen before," said Capt. Jamie Savage, of Savage Charters.
On Saturday night, fisherman Brandon McGirl joined Savage on board the "Out of Line" fishing boat for an overnight charter.
"It was very difficult conditions to try and fish. It was a little bit rougher than we were hoping for," McGirl told WMTW sister station WMUR.
The pair spent hours at sea. Initially, they said it seemed like the fish were finding every line but theirs.
"They never come when you expect them to come," McGirl said.
They were ready to call it a night when the sound they had been waiting for came. The reels started clicking, and they chased the fish for about a mile.
"When it does happen, you almost feel, like, your heart kind of skip a beat just a little bit," McGirl said.
The monster of a fish put up little resistance until it was time to bring it on board. They ended up dragging the fish back at a slow pace, still unaware just how big a catch they were dealing with.
It was bigger than any tuna ever caught in New Hampshire waters, coming in at 1,116 pounds, which is 154 pounds larger than the last record-breaker in 2013.
“If you tuna fish for a long time, to catch a 1,000-pound fish, it's something that you dream of," McGirl said.
A cut taken from the tuna's tail showed that the meat had marbling all over. The fish will now head to market, where it could be sent as far as Japan.
The tuna's tail will stay at the harbor, serving as a trophy and reminder of the record-breaking catch.

title: Meet Varsity Maine’s 10 unsung heroes of September
text:
Maybe you notice them; maybe you don’t. Either way, there’s something to be said for the “unsung hero” — the player who, while perhaps not putting up the big numbers that catch the headlines, does the little things that are every bit as important in the outcome.
This fall, Varsity Maine is seeking to identify some of those unsung heroes of Maine high school sports. Here are five boys and five girls whose impacts this September were significant, even if they weren’t necessarily measured in goals, assists, touchdowns or yards.
BOYS
Jake Harmon, Monmouth Academy soccer: Bryce Fletcher and Zane Foyt get the plaudits by pouring in goals for Monmouth, but the Mustangs owe just as much of their success to Harmon, who had strong defensive efforts against Mt. Abram on Sept. 16 and against Maranacook on Sept. 29, among others.
Abdirauf Hersi, Lewiston soccer: Hersi’s game-winning assist against Camden Hills on Sept. 8 helped the Blue Devils complete a 3-2 comeback win. On Sept. 19, his well-placed free kick in the dying seconds of the first half against rival Edward Little led to the game’s opening goal.
Wes Pinkham, Bonny Eagle football: Pinkham didn’t record many yards in Bonny Eagle’s season-opening victory over South Portland, but a key catch set up a score that the Scots ultimately needed to win. His strong play in the secondary included a touchdown-saving tackle.
Ethan Reichert, Marshwood football: On a team with just 33 players, each one is asked to do a lot. Reichert has answered the call as a key player on both lines for Marshwood, which went 4-0 in September. He was particularly impactful in the Hawks’ 52-51 thriller over Noble.
Ben Thomas, Winslow football: Winslow’s running backs get the headlines for their gaudy numbers, but that couldn’t happen without strong play from a line that includes a formidable senior in Thomas. He’s also been dominant up front defensively, such as in a 14-6 victory over Freeport.
GIRLS
Addison Barrs, Biddeford field hockey: Mia Mariello’s four goals stole the show in the Tigers’ season-opening win over Sanford/Kennebunk, but Barrs was no less instrumental. The junior was critical to breaking up Spartans possessions, leading to transition play that spurred Biddeford’s offense.
Gracey Copper, Cheverus field hockey: On a defense with no returning starters from 2025, Copper has stepped up for the Stags. Her tenacity while Biddeford launched a barrage of penalty corners at Cheverus in a Sept. 25 showdown was key to the Stags’ 3-2 win in the battle of Class A South powers.
Lauren Jabar, Yarmouth soccer: Jabar helped lead a defense that conceded just two goals all month for a team that was 7-0 in September. A Sept. 3 effort against Cape Elizabeth in which she displayed remarkable 1-on-1 skills and beat the Capers to every ball was particularly noteworthy.
Kristyna Pokorna, Thornton Academy volleyball: Not all stats are created equal; some are the results of plays that change games in key moments. That’s what Pokorna did Sept. 24 against Scarborough with two aces that turned the tide. Oh, and as coach Kayla Arthurs said, don’t let her defense go unnoticed.
Adela Ricker, Gardiner soccer: Goalkeeping is always important, but it’s especially important in one-goal games — exactly where Ricker has thrived. In a Sept. 24 battle with rival Cony, Ricker’s 12 saves were crucial to the Tigers’ 3-2 victory. Gardiner has won five one-goal games this season.

title: To thrive, rural educators need more support
text:
Laura Bean is the Mentor Teacher in Residence at the University of Maine College of Education and Human Development, where she leads the Rural THRIVE Foundations program. This column reflects her views and expertise only, not those of the University of Maine or any organization of which she is a member. Timothy Surrette is a professor of education at the University of Maine at Augusta and chair of the Bangor School Committee. This column reflects his views and expertise only, not those of the University of Maine System, Bangor School Department, or any organization of which he is a member.
As the school year begins, many students in Maine are in classrooms taught by educators relatively new to the profession. These teachers, with fewer than five years of experience, bring fresh enthusiasm and represent the future of Maine’s public-school workforce, which is older than the national average.
However, long-standing research findings indicate that early-career teachers experience significant demands, such as learning to manage the classroom environment and student behavior; motivating students and responding to their diverse needs; and taking on workloads heavier than their veteran teacher colleagues.
Early-career rural educators, who often work in schools with limited resources and staffing, report additional and unique challenges, such as professional and social isolation; limited access to professional development; and frequently being asked to teach subjects outside their area of expertise.
These difficult working conditions and persistently uncompetitive wages for new teachers in Maine contribute to a high level of early-teacher attrition and overall teacher shortages. As many as a quarter of Maine’s beginning teachers leave Maine public schools before even reaching year four.
For districts, families, and students, this problem is two-fold: the average cost to replace one teacher ranges from $11,860 to $24,930, meaning that high rates of teacher turnover are expensive. High turnover also has a negative impact on student achievement. When a district has to replace early-career teachers again and again, their students have less access to more experienced teachers who have already grown professionally by navigating the challenges of early-career teaching. Persistent rates of teacher turnover may be one factor to consider when addressing Maine’s historically declining NAEP scores.
According to the U.S. Census Bureau’s 2010 report titled Rural America, Maine and Vermont have the highest proportion of population living in rural areas (about 61%). In fact, 68% of Maine’s schools are classified as rural. Therefore, it’s important that education stakeholders in Maine work collaboratively and creatively to provide specialized and robust support to recruit, retain, and develop rural teachers who are critical to the statewide mission to educate Maine’s children and future workforce.
The good news is that, in addition to salary increases, research indicates that early-career teachers who participate in effective mentoring and induction are far more likely to stay in teaching. 80% of Maine early-career teachers surveyed identified mentoring as an effective support. The challenge for rural schools is finding creative ways to provide this support with their already strained budgets and staffing.
Rural THRIVE Foundations was developed to help districts do just that. Part of the University of Maine College of Education and Human Development, the Rural THRIVE Project, of which Foundations is a part, is funded with $3.3 million in Congressionally Directed Spending awarded to the University of Maine System to promote teacher resilience and retention and student outcomes in Maine’s rural schools. Foundations provides mostly virtual, cross-district mentoring and communities of practice as well as professional learning opportunities that supplement the support early-career teachers receive at their schools. Last year, nearly 30 early-career teachers across Maine received support from nearly 40 experienced educators. They reported that the program helped them feel less isolated and better able to resolve challenges they faced.
As evidenced by the recent passing of LD 470, A Resolve, Directing the Department of Education to Review Teacher Mentoring Programs in Maine Public Schools, there is growing urgency to identify and develop robust and sustainable mechanisms to provide the professional support early-career teachers need and deserve. Rural THRIVE Foundations could serve as an important model for what this support could look like and achieve.

title: Aging Untold: How having babies later alters roles for parents, grandparents
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, explore the realities of having babies later in life and how those pregnancies alter roles for both parents and grandparents.
Plus, find out how reverse mentoring can bridge generational divides on the job to break down workplace stereotypes.
We also meet a father and son in Wisconsin crafting a musical legacy one handmade guitar at a time.
More women over 40 are having children.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said many women now have more wisdom, resources and financial stability by the time they decide to have children.
But pregnancy after 40 is classified as advanced maternal age, and it can carry a higher risk for high blood pressure, preeclampsia, gestational diabetes and chromosomal abnormalities, Rogers said. Physicians who specialize in high-risk pregnancies are available to help manage those risks.
Find the full conversation, including the impact parenthood later in life has on the role of grandparents here.
Reverse mentoring is a strategy that flips the traditional mentor-mentee relationship so every generation in the office has something to teach and something to learn.
Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said these programs are built so older and younger employees can learn from each other.
The Aging Untold experts are providing tips on how different generations can speak to each other and work in collaboration and explaining how longevity in the workforce can be an advantage, not a liability.
Nicole Parmelee is a mom of two and found there was little support for new moms who were dealing with a lack of sleep and breastfeeding challenges while healing after giving birth.
So, she decided to do something about it. She started the New Moms School.
Bruce Petros was working as a tour guide in a town in Colorado when he found the $15 guitar kit that would change his life.
He took the kit he found in a shop back to the resort where he was living and put it together.
“And I looked at it and I went, ‘Wow, this is really cool. I could do this,’” Petros said.
He started building guitars in the basement until he built a shop.
His company, Petros Guitars, now supplies guitars and ukuleles to musicians around the world, including collectors, working musicians and hobbyists. He plans to hand the company down to his son, Matt.

title: How the world is responding to possible case of pneumonic plague after lab worker dies
text:
GENEVA (AP) — The World Health Organization says a possible case of pneumonic plague in Russia presents a “very low” risk outside the country as investigators look into what caused the death of a lab employee there last week.
The U.N. health agency said Tuesday that it has been in contact with Russian authorities following reports of the death last week of a woman who worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East.
The case and the investigation, led by Russian officials, have revived memories of the COVID-19 pandemic and allegations the coronavirus may have emerged at a Chinese lab. WHO has not provided a definitive answer to how the pandemic began.
“There is currently no indication that we are dealing with anything similar to the pandemic,” WHO spokesman Christian Lindmeier told The Associated Press, referring to the woman’s illness.
Here’s what to know about the case and how experts are mobilizing after her death:
Pneumonic plague is a form of the disease that affects the lungs
The incubation period for pneumonic plague — which means lung-based, and is the most virulent form of the disease — can be as short as 24 hours, according to WHO. It’s a less common but severe form that can spread between people through respiratory particles.
If untreated, the illness can be fatal, but recovery rates are high if detected and treated in time, WHO says.
Symptoms include shortness of breath and coughing, often involving the coughing up of blood.
The more common form of plague — bubonic plague — is caused by the bite of an infected flea, and can develop into open sores filled with pus.
Pneumonia is a form of acute respiratory infection that is mostly caused by viruses or bacteria, and is spread generally through contact with infected people or from airborne droplets. WHO says pneumonia is the single largest infectious cause of death in children worldwide.
What Russian officials are saying about the case
Through an international health alert system, Russian health officials on Tuesday said a full range of preventive measures had been carried out — including tracing of the deceased woman’s contacts, medical monitoring and lab tests.
“Test results showed no presence of dangerous infectious disease pathogens in any of the contacts,” said the note from Russian authorities, which was relayed to The Associated Press by WHO.
“Based on available data, laboratory test results, and health status, medical monitoring for 100% of the contacts has now been concluded,” it said. “The epidemiological situation is stable and remains under monitoring.”
The woman died at a hospital in Shelekhov, a town just outside the city of Irkutsk, and its mayor said the hospital was placed under quarantine. The top officials from Russia’s national public health watchdog traveled to the region Friday.
On Monday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov advised the public to follow official statements from the watchdog agency, Rospotrebnadzor, rather than “rumors or speculation.”
WHO has mobilized its own experts to look into the case
Lindmeier, the WHO spokesman, told a U.N. briefing Tuesday that the institute where the woman worked “studies dangerous pathogens,” including plague in a part of Siberia where the disease “occurs naturally in wild animals.”
He said Russian officials have not yet asked for WHO experts to deploy to Russia, where authorities are “looking into whether pneumonic plague caused her death.”
Russian authorities later told WHO that no case of plague has been recorded in Irkutsk, Lindmeier said.
“According to the authorities, the woman’s illness initially presented as a typical acute respiratory viral infection,” he said. “No case of plague or other high threat pathogen has been found.”
Trump and Rubio comment on the case
U.S. President Donald Trump said Monday that he was watching the situation with concern and that the United States would be willing to help, though he said he had not spoken to Russian President Vladimir Putin about the case.
Asked about Trump’s remarks, Kremlin spokesman Peskov said Tuesday that “it is always very good when mutual assistance is offered.” He wouldn’t elaborate further, deferring to Rospotrebnadzor.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged Russian authorities to share more information.
“Maybe there’s nothing there. Maybe it’s bigger than we thought. We don’t know,” he said at a news conference in Iceland.
“We encourage Russia to be more transparent and share more information with the world,” Rubio said, adding this has so far been “quite limited, but hopefully that will change in the next few hours and days.”
Ian Jones, professor of virology at the University of Reading, said that “plague carries a huge history and is still present in many parts of the world, including Russia,” although because of modern living conditions and antibiotics, its potential was limited.
Dr. Glenn Wortmann, at the MedStar Washington Hospital Center, said the bacteria that cause plague don’t “travel very far” and a person would “really need to be face-to-face” with an infected person to get pneumonic plague.
“The chance of this spreading widely in Russia and then extending here to the U.S. will not happen, not with this type of bacteria, because it’s not spread easily and we have antibiotics to stop it from spreading,” he added.
___
Associated Press writers Dasha Litvinova in Tallinn, Estonia, and Matthew Lee in Reykjavik, Iceland, contributed to this report.

title: Father and son keep guitar-making legacy going together
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
HOLLANDTOWN, Wis. (Aging Untold) — Bruce Petros has been building stringed instruments for 52 years, turning a small woodworking shop into the business Petros Guitars.
“We’re trying to have lasting, lasting beauty in the instrument,” Petros said.
From a $15 kit to a career
Petros got his start while working as a tour guide in Colorado after finding a guitar kit for $15 in a shop and putting it together.
“There was this little tourist town that had, you know, shops,” Petros said. “And I found a guitar kit in this store, and it was like $15. And I took it back to the resort where I was living and put it together. And I looked at it and I went, ‘Wow, this is really cool. I could do this.’”
Petros started building guitars in the basements of rental homes before moving his family to Hollandtown.
“We bought this place and tore down this garage and built the shop, basically,” Petros said.
Building a reputation
Petros Guitars now supplies guitars and ukuleles to musicians around the world, including collectors, working musicians and hobbyists.
“And now this is a little concert ukulele that’s got a curly Koa top and curly bubinga back and sides,” Petros said while displaying one of the company’s string instruments.
Petros said Paul Simon owns one of his instruments, along with other musicians.
Passing down the business
Petros’ son, Matt, is set to take over the business.
“It’s just great to be able to create something with your hands,” Matt Petros said. “There’s never been any pressure. I’ve never been yelled at by my boss or threatened to be fired.”
Bruce Petros said having plans for his son take over the business is the ideal situation.
“A lot of guitar makers when they quit, what are they going to do? You can’t sell a guitar making shop. You can sell the tools and the wood. You can’t sell your reputation,” Bruce Petros said. “So this is kind of the ideal situation where the reputation is built in and it continues on.”
The father and son said each instrument the shop produces is made to have a certain sound.
“They sound better and they play better,” Bruce Petros said. “Figuring out the ways to, you know, eke out every little bit of tone.”
Matt Petros said he looks forward to carrying on the family’s musical legacy.
“Well, you grow up in the shop. That’s all I knew,” Matt Petros said. “And every little boy wants to be like their dad. And I was just lucky enough to be able to do it.”

title: Argentina bids Messi farewell in final national team match, ending an era
text:
Lionel Messi caps Argentina farewell with a penalty and 2 assists in a 3-0 win over Benin
Lionel Messi turned his official farewell to Argentina into a gala performance, contributing a penalty and two assists in a 3-0 win over Benin in an international friendly on Tuesday at the Monumental Stadium in Buenos Aires, where the crowd offered a deafening final ovation to the genius who, for over two decades, defined the footballing pulse of a nation.
In front of 85,000 fans, the superstar capped off an international career spanning 21 years, 126 goals, a 2022 World Cup victory, and two Copa América titles.
Orchestrating the win
Following a corner kick taken Messi, defender Nicolás Otamendi connected with a header to open the scoring in the 48th minute. Messi then provided an assist to young talent Nicolás Paz, who paid tribute to the star with an exquisite left-foot finish in the 61st.
Ten minutes later, Messi buried a left-foot penalty into the top corner, adding to his tally as the Albiceleste’s all-time leading scorer.
“Olé, olé, Messi,” the crowd chanted in his honor.
Passing the torch
Despite still playing at a high level at age 39, Messi announced on Aug. 31 that the end of his time with Argentina was set.
Messi played his final match — his 208th for Argentina — amid a spectacular fireworks display. He wore a special edition Albiceleste jersey featuring wider vertical stripes than the standard design, a giant sun, and a golden No. 10 on the back. The back detail featured a goat’s horns in the print — a nod to the “GOAT,” referencing both the animal and his status as the “Greatest of All Time.”
Ten minutes after kickoff, the referee paused the match to honor the Argentine captain. Rivals and teammates approached to greet him while fans rose for a standing ovation. Messi raised his hand in acknowledgment.
“Come, come, sing with me, and a friend you’ll find; hand in hand with Leo Messi, we’ll all celebrate the victory,” the crowd sang to him.
From heartbreak to World Cup glory
A successor to the legendary Diego Maradona, Messi made his debut for the senior national team in 2005. But his journey was fraught with frustration until 2022, when he finally lifted the World Cup — a triumph that secured his place in the pantheon of the sport’s greatest players and cemented his status as a national hero in Argentina.
Accompanied by his sons Thiago, Mateo, and Ciro, Messi was overcome with emotion as the Argentine national anthem played, sung by a veteran of the 1982 Falklands War. Goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez tried to comfort him by placing an arm around his shoulders.
Devoted fans and moving tributes
“It’s not a goodbye, it’s a ‘farewell forever,’ Captain” — that was the message Rebeca Arias and Daniel Lema emblazoned on a hat designed for the occasion. On the brim, they drew various depictions of Messi corresponding to each of the six World Cups he contested. The young couple traveled more than 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) from their native Tucumán to witness his final performance.
“We believe this is a unique moment. It’s all worth it — being here, making the journey we did. Something like this might never happen again with a player,” Arias remarked.
In the last World Cup, Messi went close to another title, falling just short after a 1-0 defeat to Spain in the final. However, the runner-up finish didn't overshadow his remarkable performance in the tournament — featuring eight goals and four assists.
His contribution was so pivotal that Messi has once again entered the conversation for the Ballon d’Or, competing against the two top contenders to succeed him: Spaniard Lamine Yamal and Frenchman Kylian Mbappé.
The Argentine star remains the only footballer to have won the award eight times.
Messi receives honorary doctorate
Before his farewell at the stadium, Messi received an honorary doctorate from the University of Buenos Aires (UBA), a public institution.
The academic institution presented the honor at the national team’s training complex in the suburb of Ezeiza. The star was awarded a diploma and a medal in recognition of his performance with the national team, as well as his influence both on and off the pitch.

title: Fire breaks out at Wilton brewery, deemed accidental
text:
WILTON, Maine (WABI) - A fire broke out Monday afternoon at Ambition Brewing in downtown Wilton.
The fire was contained to one of the two buildings being used by the business, according to the State Fire Marshal’s Office, though the second building did sustain some smoke and water damage. No one was injured.
Officials say the fire was found by the property owner in an area where flooring was in the process of being removed.
Investigators say the underside of the building is partially open to the elements, allowing leaves and other debris to accumulate. They believe that the debris had grown dry and readily combustible, ultimately igniting during the renovation work.
The Fire Marshal’s Office has deemed the fire accidental.
Crews from Wilton, Jay, Farmington, Rumford, Temple and East Dixfield responded. The brewery thanked first responders and neighboring Main Street businesses for their support.
