title: UMaine football fires offensive coordinator Mikahael Waters
text:
The slumping University of Maine football team has fired offensive coordinator Mikahael Waters.
Head coach Jordan Stevens confirmed the move Tuesday. Waters had been offensive coordinator for the Black Bears since 2024.
The move comes as a sputtering Maine offense is ranked 118th out of 124 Football Championship Subdivision teams in points per game (14.5). The Black Bears have lost five consecutive games, most recently a 24-16 home defeat Saturday against Sacred Heart.
Waters was in his eighth season with the Black Bears, having joined the staff in 2019 under then-first-year head coach Nick Charlton. He served as Maine’s tight ends coach from 2019-22 and as special teams coordinator in 2023 prior to his promotion to offensive coordinator.
Maine’s offensive struggles have been a theme all season. In addition to their paltry points-per-game ranking, the Black Bears rank 93rd in passing yards per game and 110th in rushing yards per game. The team has just 66 points in 22 quarters since scoring 21 in the first half of the season opener at Towson.
“We have to coach better, and we have to put our players in a better position to make plays, and that’s from a confidence standpoint and from an execution standpoint,” Stevens told the media Tuesday. “When we talk execution, that’s not on the players; that’s on us to make sure they’re in a position to execute.”
Maine’s output in 2026 is a significant drop-off from the previous two seasons under Waters. The Black Bears averaged 24.2 points per game (67th) last year, and 23.2 points per game (74th) in Waters’ first season as offensive coordinator in 2024.
Sean Green, Maine’s running backs coach and a former state title-winning head coach at Portland and Cape Elizabeth high schools, will take over play-calling duties. Offensive analyst Cooper Heisey will take over for Green as running backs coach.
Maine is on a bye this week. The Black Bears will be back in action at 1 p.m. on Oct. 17 when they host Bryant (4-1 overall, 2-0 Coastal Athletic Association).

title: Christa Pike is conscious and speaking after failed execution, her attorneys say
text:
Christa Pike is conscious and speaking after failed execution, her attorneys say
Christa Pike, a Tennessee inmate who survived Tennessee’s attempt to execute her, is awake and speaking as she receives treatment at a hospital, her attorneys said Tuesday.
“Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care. Despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed. Her recovery is medically unprecedented. Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery,” attorneys for Pike said in a statement.
Related video above | Tennessee House speaker says lawmakers will consider alternative execution methods after Christa Pike’s botched execution
Her attorneys said they are grateful for the first responders and the medical team at the hospital “who treated Christa like a human and have provided exceptional care to her.”
The statement was the first indication that Pike has improved since an ambulance carried her away from a Nashville prison last Wednesday.
A spokeswoman for the Tennessee Department of Correction said she could provide no information other than that Pike remained hospitalized Tuesday.
Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital as they attempted to put her to death for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. The lethal injection drug didn’t kill her, but her lawyers said her arms were left burned and blistered.
Dr. Joel Zivot, a professor of anesthesiology and surgery in Atlanta who consulted as an expert for Pike’s legal team, said the development “bodes well for a good recovery.” But, he added, it could be weeks or months before anyone knows exactly what her recovery might look like, and whether her competency could be restored to a level that might enable the state to try again to execute her.
“She’s still in the ICU,” he said. “She has recovered to a certain degree that she’s able to be off a ventilator and able to speak, but in no way would I announce her free of further serious risk. There’s still a lot of bad things that can happen here, even when everyone is doing their job well.”
Pike’s attorneys are set to go to court Wednesday as they seek to learn more about what happened in the failed lethal injection.
The attorneys are seeking a court order requiring the Tennessee Department of Correction to preserve evidence, including drug lot numbers, records and other information from the Sept. 30 attempted execution. Chancery Court Judge I’Ashea Myles scheduled a Wednesday morning status conference in the case.
Pike’s attorneys said in their Tuesday statement that they continue to ask Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to commute Pike’s sentence to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
“Christa is a survivor and will take recovery one day at a time,” her attorneys said.

title: The flashpoints to look for in Susan Collins and Troy Jackson’s 1st debate
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson finally share a stage Tuesday night in Portland, the first of four televised debates in a race that could decide control of the Senate.
Both are seasoned debaters. Abortion, healthcare, taxes, the Iran war, President Donald Trump, and Jackson’s 20-plus years in Augusta and informal style are all fair game.
Here’s what to watch ahead of the CBS News 13 debate at 7 p.m.
Abortion and Supreme Court
The calendar hands Jackson an opening. Tuesday is exactly eight years since Collins voted to confirm U.S. Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who featured in the court’s 2022 decision to overturn federal abortion rights. Collins, who predicted that wouldn’t happen, criticized the decision but has stood by her vote.
Expect Jackson to remind voters that the Republican also backed Justices Neil Gorsuch and Samuel Alito, whose possible retirement Jackson has seized on as a campaign issue. He held a town hall in Bath on Monday with Planned Parenthood’s Maine fundraising arm.
Collins will return to her standby stance: She weighs judges’ overall qualifications rather than a single issue, and notes she’s the only Republican to vote for all three of the court’s liberal justices. She may also go on offense, as she did in a 2020 debate with Democrat Sara Gideon.
Asked about the court, she called an ad from Gideon claiming she confirmed “181 far right judges” misleading, saying the vast majority of those judges had bipartisan support.
She may also try to tilt the proceedings toward Jackson’s abortion record. Raised Catholic, he now gets perfect ratings from Planned Parenthood, but he once earned perfect marks from an anti-abortion group and backed a 2011 “fetal personhood” bill.
Pressure on ProPublica report
Jackson and allies continue to highlight ProPublica’s report on a defense contractor allegedly engaging in a pay-for-play scheme involving the Collins and other lawmakers.
ProPublica says the FBI was investigating potential corruption as late as 2024 before a Trump administration crackdown on the agency. Collins’ team has said the FBI had not contacted them on the matter since 2021, when they say it was resolved, denying allegations of bribery.
In a video posted Sunday on X, Jackson sits in front of a wall of his own campaign signs, a Diet Coke at his elbow, and reads passages from the article aloud.
Jackson may press another question: What did Collins’ husband, former lobbyist Thomas Daffron, do for Chesapeake Enterprises? The firm, led by Scott Reed, who runs the pro-Collins Pine Tree Results PAC and led the group that took illegal donations from Navatek CEO Martin Kao in 2019, paid him at least $1,000 for consulting last year.
Collins campaign manager Steve Abbott has said he doesn’t know what the consulting work was. Reed told the New York Times that Daffron “never lobbies.” Abbott and the FBI have said Kao’s claims were investigated and nothing implicated Collins, her team or the PAC.
The senator may have a counterpunch: The Washington Post focused this week on Jackson, whose campaign refuses corporate donations, once leading the Maine Senate’s political arm, which was funded in part by the tobacco, gambling and pharmaceutical industries.
Command on national issues
Jackson has spent the campaign tying Collins to Trump on tariffs, immigration enforcement, healthcare and the Iran war, then tying all of it back to Mainers’ wallets.
Tuesday tests whether he can do that on the fly against a five-term incumbent who chairs the Senate Appropriations Committee and rarely misses a chance to say how much money she brings to Maine because of it.
Jackson is likely to swing back at Collins’ signature pitch: the federal money she steers to Maine. He argues that Trump and Republicans have cost the state more than the billions she’s brought home. He points to her vote to advance Trump’s tax bill that cut Medicaid and food aid, though she voted against it in the end, citing future Medicaid cuts.
Foreign policy is Jackson’s thinnest area, by his own admission. Last week, he apologized for remarks on the Israel-Gaza conflict and Maine’s Jewish community, an episode critics say showed he isn’t ready for the Senate. Watch whether Collins brings it up.
Jackson’s last debate
Collins hasn’t debated in six years. Jackson has done several forums and debates this year.
His last face-off with a Republican came in February, during his third-place run in the Democratic gubernatorial primary, against Bobby Charles, now the GOP nominee for governor.
That was a sideshow event during two crowded primaries, but the night previewed a line Collins’ team has since picked up: Jackson is an insider despite running against an incumbent nearing 30 years in office.
Charles pinned energy costs, overdose deaths, housing and property taxes on Democrats, Gov. Janet Mills and Jackson’s two decades in the Legislature. He also amplified past Republican complaints that Jackson had fraudulently obtained a Federal Housing Administration loan, which he denied the Maine Ethics Commission declined to investigate.
Jackson was less polished than the bombastic Charles but didn’t back down, repeatedly pointing at the lawyer and calling him a race-baiter and divisive bully unfit for the Blaine House.
Strategists in both parties expect a more civil night Tuesday, but neither candidate is likely to pull punches. Three more debates follow before voters decide Nov. 3.

title: Televangelist Jim Bakker dead at 86
text:
Jim Bakker, who built ‘PTL Club’ televangelism empire, has died at 86
Jim Bakker, who, along with his first wife Tammy Faye, built an evangelical empire around the hugely successful “The PTL Club” TV show, only to lose it all over a sex scandal and financial crimes, has died. He was 86.
Bakker died Monday, his second wife, Lori Bakker, said in a statement. His cause of death was not immediately clear.
Video above: Remembering those we lost in 2026
The pair lived near the Missouri entertainment town of Branson and filmed their TV show “The Jim Bakker Show” there since it launched in 2003. Bakker suffered a stroke in 2020.
“He was a pioneer of Christian television, but to me, he was my husband, my best friend, and the man I was honored to walk beside through so many seasons of life and ministry,” Lori Bakker said in a statement.
But it was another evangelical program that made Jim and his first wife Tammy Faye Bakker cultural icons — so much so that they were often skewered in the 1980s and 1990s by late-night comedians and parodied on “Saturday Night Live.” A theatrical movie on their lives, “The Eyes of Tammy Faye,” was released in September 2021.
At its peak in the mid-1980s, the Bakkers’ ministry included not only the TV show drawing up to 13 million nightly viewers but also the Christian-based Heritage USA theme park and hotel in Fort Mill, South Carolina.
Bakker was born in Muskegon, Michigan, and attended North Central Bible College in Minneapolis, where he met Tammy Faye. They married in 1961 and dropped out of college to start their own traveling ministry — he preached, she sang and played the accordion as they crossed the country visiting churches and tent revivals.
They caught the attention of televangelist Pat Robertson, and in 1965 launched a children’s show on Robertson’s Christian Broadcasting Network. By 1966, he was hosting “The 700 Club,” a Christian talk show.
Bakker left CBN in 1972 and two years later formed the PTL Satellite Network. “The PTL Club” — PTL stands for “Praise the Lord” — became its signature show.
It hit its heyday in the 1980s; “The PTL Club” was drawing millions of viewers — and bringing in millions of dollars annually from followers.
Sort of a Christian version of “The Tonight Show,” it featured chats with guests and Christian entertainers. Bakker offered upbeat sermons and Tammy Faye — charismatic and always wearing her trademark heavy mascara — sang. Most episodes were taped at their sprawling complex just south of Charlotte, North Carolina.
The couple was so famous that they were often parodied by TV comedians for their lavish lifestyle and Tammy Faye’s abundant makeup.
In March 1987, their empire began to crack when Bakker admitted to a sexual encounter with church clerk Jessica Hahn. Bakker was forced to resign from his own empire, turning over operations to pastor and broadcaster Jerry Falwell.
Tammy Faye stuck by Bakker, often with tears running down her mascara, even as many saw his downfall as a fitting symbol of the greed and hypocrisy of the 1980s.
Things only got worse.
In 1988, Bakker was indicted for mail fraud, wire fraud and conspiracy after an investigation of PTL’s finances. He was convicted and sentenced to 45 years in federal prison, though the sentence was later reduced to eight years.
At a news conference after Bakker was found guilty, Tammy Faye stood in front of the microphones and sang the hymn, “On Christ the Solid Rock I Stand.”
Their marriage crumbled and Tammy Faye divorced Bakker in 1992, just short of their 31st anniversary, while he was still in prison. She later married Roe Messner, a building contractor whose projects included the Heritage USA theme park. Messner was convicted of bankruptcy fraud in 1995 and spent about two years in prison.
Tammy Faye died of colon cancer in 2007.
Bakker was released on parole in 1994. He married his second wife, Lori, in 1998. The couple launched “The Jim Bakker Show” on the PTL Satellite Network five years later.
In June 2021, Bakker and his Morningside Church Productions Inc. settled a lawsuit accusing him of falsely claiming the health supplement Silver Solution could cure COVID-19. The settlement called for $156,000 in refunds to people who paid money or gave contributions to obtain the product in the early days of the pandemic.
The lawsuit said Bakker and a guest made the cure claim during 11 episodes in February and March 2020.
Bakker and Tammy Faye had two children. He and his second wife adopted five children in 2002.

title: Former Bangor Tire Garage On Market Street Becomes Music Studio This December
text:
For over 50 years, the family-run business of Bangor Tire operated out of a garage on Market Street in Bangor. While the business originally started on Franklin Street, it spent a decade on Market Street before ultimately moving to its current location, Coldbrook Road in Hermon, back in 2021.
Following Bangor Tire's exit, Bob Briggs and his family moved their business, Center Line Utility Service, to the location, but it only utilizes a few of the garage bays. Briggs's wife, Jori-Lynn, played with a small group of musicians called the Bangor Ensemble, so he offered to let the group set up in some of the office space to practice.
A little over a year ago, Jori-Lynn passed away suddenly, and the Bangor Ensemble became the Jori-Lynn Ensemble in her honor.
The group wanted to create a musical scholarship to honor her as well, and when they were talking about it, inspiration hit, and the idea to create a musical studio space and name it after her came about.
All of a sudden, this unused space, that was just kind of sitting there, had a new life and purpose.
Read More: After Decades In The City, Bangor Tire Moving To Hermon
Two local musicians have been spearheading the effort, ensuring that the building will soon be filled with tunes instead of tires!
Lisa Cooley and Claude Junkins are working to turn this former automotive garage into a future space for musicians to practice or perform: The Jori-Lynn Studios.
Junkins recently began to spread.
"We are in the process of creating new music instruction, rehearsal, and recital space.
Very reasonable rates, excellent parking, and accessible. Teach instrument or voice?
Looking for a practice location - we may be able to help. Staffed always."
Cooley, who will serve as the organization's Music Director, says the vision is to provide not only the space, but possibly storage down the road for folks to bring in their instruments and gear to make music.
"We are thinking of it as a multi-use studio space. The large space will be available first, and smaller spaces for lessons or practice will be available further on...We will be available for all kinds of rehearsals, but we don't have equipment that other rehearsal studios have. I believe that we will have storage space."
Junkins, a retired project manager from the University of Maine system who also teaches trumpet, says the goal is to make the space feel less like a garage and more like a music space, and that could take a couple of months.
"The family is letting us use the space. I'm doing some work in here...and it's getting there...getting the place softened up and making the place less hollow, from a tire room with a concrete floor to a place with some rugs. We've gotten quite a few people who have responded to the notice...We had one lady who has about 45 piano students, and she wants to be able to move the lessons out of her house, so we hope to be able to accommodate her. "
Read More: October Songs: 35 Songs for Spooky Season
"We have a couple of pianos, one electric and one upright."
Junkins says he hopes to be able to take some donations of instruments, in the future, that could be refurbished and loaned out to students.
"Hopefully students who are not getting the music lessons they want and can't find them will look at this place as a nice place to come, easy parking, wide-open, well lit and secured and monitored, that they would be more apt to spend more time practicing."
He says there's a lot of potential in the space that could be helpful to young musicians and music instructors alike. He sees a future with some great after-school access to musical programs and a space for newly formed bands or groups to gather.
Junkins says the goal is to get things up and running by the New Year, but Cooley says she's hoping to be able to give the public a little sneak peek mid-December.
"This is all very preliminary. However, save the date: December 19th we will have an open house/ holiday celebration at the studio."
Junkins says the Open House will feature some holiday tunes and the Jori-Lynn Ensemble.
If you are interested in helping with the process, in setting up some lessons, or in donating to the cause, you can reach out to Junkins by phone. His phone number is (207) 949-3873.

title: Maine’s Beehive Loop Ranks Among the 10 Best Fall Hikes in America
text:
Maine’s Beehive Loop Ranks Among the 10 Best Fall Hikes in America
Fall is the most righteous time of year in Maine. The perfect harvest, beautiful weather, and lack of tourists create an unbeatable vibe, one that practically screams for us to take advantage of it.
That’s why it’s also the perfect time to get outside and enjoy everything that’s wonderful about Maine’s wilderness, especially the iconic Acadia National Park.
While Acadia can be a bit crazy during the summer, the crowds tend to thin out later in the fall, which is great for us natives looking to enjoy everything the park has to offer. And it just so happens to be home to one of the season’s best hikes.
Is Maine's Beehive Trail One of America's Best?
According to the popular outdoor site broadout.com, Acadia’s historic Beehive Trail is one of the best hikes in the entire country to enjoy during the fall.
How good is it? Well, the website claims it’s one of the 10 best, even listing it first. Talk about some serious bragging rights.
Beehive Loop delivers an outsized adventure in a compact distance. The climb rises above Sand Beach on steep granite, iron rungs, ladders, and exposed ledges before opening to views of the Gulf of Maine and Acadia’s autumn-colored hills.
The popular hiking site AllTrails rates the Beehive Trail as “hard” in difficulty. Still, despite its tough reputation, it holds an impressive 4.9 out of 5 rating. The trail offers sweeping views of Maine’s coastline, islands, and Acadia’s iconic Sand Beach, and it's also a favorite for birdwatchers.
How Popular is Acadia National Park's Beehive Trail?
It’s also one of the most popular hikes in the park, and it’s not unusual to encounter long queues at certain points along the trail. Because of its difficulty, it can take time to navigate many of the more technical sections. So if you're planning to tackle it, be sure to plan your time wisely, especially if you are heading during a peak time of year.
It’s pretty great to see the Beehive Loop included on this list. The trail represents everything that’s great about Maine, especially during the fall. Crisp air, autumn leaves, beautiful sunshine, and a challenging coastal mountain trail make for the perfect combination.

One other New England trail made the list: New Hampshire’s Franconia Ridge Loop, which is also exceptional. You can check out the entire list here.

title: Obituary: Gay P. Maheu
text:
WINSLOW – Gay P. Maheu, 90, of Winslow, Maine, was called to the Lord on Sept. 30, 2026. She was born on August 15, 1936, in Waterville, Maine, the daughter of Wilfred and Gilberte (Roy) Rancourt. Gay was the eldest of four siblings (Ann Gilbert, deceased, Jeanette Leblanc of Florida, and William Rancourt of China, Maine).
Upon graduating with honors from Waterville High School in 1954, Gay entered the work force and worked a wide range of office jobs.
She was married to Donald A. Maheu (deceased) on July 4, 1960. They celebrated 54 years of marriage and five children, Deborah Carr and her husband Michael, Susan Perry and her husband Colonel (Ret) Warren Perry, James Maheu and his wife Kristen, Vera Maheu, and Robert Maheu and his wife Dawn. She is also survived by five grandchildren, Matthew, Erin, Katie, Michael, and Sam; and four great grandchildren, Dalton, Grant, River, and Margot.
Mrs. Maheu was a member of Corpus Christi Parish and served as a volunteer there during coffee hours. As a life member of the Women’s Auxiliary Post 8835 of the Winslow VFW, she worked organizing the children’s Christmas parties. She used her love of sewing to construct quilts for aids babies and to dress teddy bears at Christmas for the Salvation Army. Gay could be found assisting at any school event her children were involved in including sports, band, and religious education. In her free time Gay enjoyed ballet, opera, reading, and coloring.
At the request of the family there will be no visiting hours. A funeral Mass will be celebrated at 10 a.m., Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, at Notre Dame Parish, 116 Silver St., Waterville. A light luncheon will follow the conclusion of mass in the church’s community room. Burial will take place at the Maine Veterans Memorial Cemetery at 143 Blue Star Avenue in Augusta at 2 p.m.
Funeral arrangements are under the care and direction of Veilleux Funeral Home Waterville, Maine.

title: Maine regulators deny CMP’s $7 rate hike as utility weighs potential layoffs
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine utility regulators denied Central Maine Power Co.’s request for almost $70 million in increased rates on Tuesday, a major win for advocacy groups that means bills will not increase this fall.
The Maine Public Utilities Commission’s unanimous denial of CMP’s bid to increase the average household’s bill by about $7 per month comes with potentially serious financial consequences for the utility, company representatives said in filings before Tuesday’s hearing. A CMP executive told employees last week that the company would reconsider workforce levels if the PUC denied its request.
Current distribution rates are likely to remain in place until the spring, when regulators are expected to decide on the merits of the utility’s full $189 million rate case.
State law allows utilities to recoup “temporary rates” during a longer case, as long as the amount they’re seeking to raise is agreed upon. That’s what CMP was seeking here: the first step of a two-part rate increase, intended to help pay for infrastructure CMP has built in recent years.
The PUC had recommended this approach last year when it dismissed CMP’s five-year plan, which would have raised the average household’s bill by about $35.
But the three members of the Maine Public Utilities Commission agreed Tuesday that intervening groups — from the Office of the Public Advocate to the Department of Energy Resources to consumer advocates — had disputed all $69.3 million of CMP’s ask, and that they therefore could not allow the utility to raise rates.
The commission’s decision aligned with the recommendation of its staff last month.
Much of the dispute was based on return on equity — the return CMP’s shareholders can make on the company’s capital projects. Return on equity is the only way a utility monopoly can make profit under Maine’s regulatory structure, and it’s become a focal point in the rate case.
About two-thirds of CMP’s temporary rate ask was to right-size its return on equity, which the company said was necessary to attract investment and maintain its credit ratings.
“I simply could not pinpoint a number that I would feel comfortable saying was not in dispute in this matter,” PUC Chair Philip Bartlett said during deliberations Tuesday.
Bartlett also said that, since the utility has exceeded its capital spending forecast by about 50% from 2022 to 2025, “to some extent, this is a problem of CMP’s own making.”
In the eight days since PUC staff recommended the commissioners reject CMP’s increase, the utility has removed 70 job postings for line workers and customer service positions, paused plans to improve 19 transformers servicing thousands of customers from York to Rangeley, and halted several other infrastructure projects.
A spokesperson for CMP did not respond Tuesday to a request for comment, but in a filing before the hearing Tuesday, the company said it would be hit hard by a denial.
In addition to deferring upgrades to its grid infrastructure and pausing hiring, CMP said it would be forced to “consider workforce reductions.” The company’s financial outlook was downgraded this summer by S&P Global Ratings to “negative” because of lag in this rate case and a $100 million cash flow deficit.
“Customers do not experience regulatory delay in the abstract,” attorneys for CMP wrote to regulators last week. “They experience it through aging transformers, deferred maintenance, postponed reliability projects, and infrastructure that continues operating long after it should have been replaced.”
Linda Ball, the president and CEO of CMP, said in a Sept. 28 email to employees that it would be irresponsible for the utility not “to carefully evaluate current workforce levels, hiring plans and apprenticeship programs” given the “regulatory challenges we face.”
“I recognize that news like this creates uncertainty and concern,” Ball said in the email. “Please know that our leadership team takes these challenges seriously and remains focused on supporting our employees, maintaining safe and reliable service for our customers, and advocating for the investments necessary to sustain Maine’s electric system for the long term, while balancing the impacts this situation has on the business.”
No decisions about workforce levels have been made, Ball wrote. CMP employs almost 1,000 people, the company’s website says.
Meanwhile, the PUC decision marks a substantial win for advocacy groups, which have fought CMP’s rate increase at each step.
Fight the Hike, a coalition of advocacy groups opposed to CMP’s increase, celebrated the PUC’s decision in a news release and said it would continue to oppose the utility’s efforts to raise rates in the next several months.
“(Delaying grid projects is) an attempt at blackmail,” Seth Berry, the executive director of coalition member Our Power, said in the release. “Unlike any other business, CMP has a monopoly. This is a privilege granted to them by the people of Maine. It’s time for CMP shareholders to start funding grid maintenance from their $160 million in annual profits — not squeezing still more from struggling families.”
Heather Sanborn, the state’s public advocate, said she applauded the PUC’s decision to wait to increase rates until the end of the yearlong proceeding. Any increase should be decided on its merits, she said, and should take into account affordability concerns.
Rebecca Schultz, the clean energy expert for the Natural Resources Council of Maine, one of the intervening parties in the case, applauded the PUC’s decision, especially in the face of rising costs in other areas.
Schultz also criticized CMP’s response.
“In the past few weeks, facing reasonable and completely foreseeable pushback to their request, the company chose to threaten Mainers with cutting union jobs and delaying important safety and reliability upgrades that were already underway,” she said in a statement. “This is unacceptable behavior for any company granted a monopoly business opportunity in Maine.”
The ruling Tuesday is likely to be the final major decision during Bartlett’s tenure as the PUC’s chair. After seven years leading the commission, Bartlett announced last month that he’d be stepping down Friday to move into the private sector.

title: Frost and freeze expected across much of the area tonight
text:
Frost and freeze expected across much of the area tonight
The coldest air mass of the season so far is moving into Maine, bringing a sharp change to the weather tonight. Frost is likely tonight, especially across inland and sheltered areas, with some of the colder spots dipping close to freezing.
A big warm-up follows for Wednesday and especially Thursday, when temperatures rebound to well above today’s levels. A cold front will cross the region Thursday and could bring a few showers, but widespread rain is not expected at this point.
High pressure should return for the weekend, bringing generally quiet weather with temperatures closer to seasonal averages. The pattern may turn more unsettled early next week as low pressure develops and moves through the region, bringing another chance for rain.

title: Do National Food Recalls Affect Commons?
text:
This summer, dozens of products were recalled across the U.S. for contamination and disease, with Taylor Farms’ iceberg lettuce and jalepeño products making international headlines. Coming back to Bates this year, I was curious about whether or not the recalls are affecting the college. After all, Commons needs to provide a large group of students, faculty and staff with high-quality food.
Bates DCCE spends approximately $70,000 to $80,000 on groceries each week. According to an article published by Bates News in 2024, one day they recorded as many as 4,789 meals.
In an interview with the Bates Student, Christine Schwartz, Dining Conferences and Campus Events (DCCE) associate vice president, noted that institutional processing uses a different production line than store products. Though they’re buying in bulk, institutional processing usually has fewer contamination issues.
Commons, for example, works with a vendor called North Center, which tracks recalls and immediately notifies Bates should any arise. Schwartz said, “In fact, Commons typically knows before the general public.”
The DCCE team takes additional precautions to ensure food is safe: they sample everything prepped during the day, just in case. They track every food item, date, label and tag in spreadsheets. Menus and purchasing reports are also tracked carefully to quickly narrow down any issues.
Even so, slip-ups occur. Schwartz told me about a time during COVID when around 100 people came down with the same illness. After careful questioning, the DCCE team discovered they all ate a similar meal that day.
The Commons team sprang into action: they traced the issue back to a specific peanut sauce and contacted the Federal Department of Agriculture. The agency took the sauce sample back to its labs for testing. The FDA found traces of Salmonella in the peanuts because they were incorrectly roasted over a fire before arriving at Bates.
For students, the takeaway is simple: if a recall touches Commons, DCCE likely knew before the news did. And if something you ate doesn’t taste tight, telling staff (and the Health Center) helps them trace it.

title: Susan Collins doesn't back down from Brett Kavanaugh vote in 1st debate with Troy Jackson
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
On the eighth anniversary of her vote to confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the U.S. Supreme Court, U.S. Sen. Susan Collins refused to say she regretted it in her first debate with Democrat Troy Jackson. Instead, she turned his own anti-abortion past against him.
The Republican and the former Maine Senate president spent much of Tuesday night’s CBS News 13 debate attacking each other’s records on abortion and ethics. It was the first of four debates in 10 days, four weeks before an election that could decide control of the U.S. Senate.
The two candidates tugged at each other the entire hour. Jackson repeatedly tied Collins to President Donald Trump, whose approval rating in Maine stands at 40% in a Marist poll released Tuesday, while the incumbent looked to distance herself from the president’s tariffs at a time of high costs. The tone matched the similarly divisive 2020 campaign that Collins won despite trailing in nearly every public poll.
Jackson opened before even introducing himself by noting that Maine women begged Collins to vote against Kavanaugh, who later joined the 2022 majority that overturned Roe v. Wade. He pressed further when the candidates got to question each other.
“What will it take for you to admit you’re ever wrong?” Jackson said.
Collins said she judges nominees on their full qualifications, not one issue. She noted she is the only Republican senator to vote for all three justices nominated by recent Democratic presidents.
“I clearly don’t agree with how Brett Kavanaugh voted on Roe v. Wade,” she said.
She then targeted Jackson, a Catholic who has won in conservative northern Maine, including around Collins’ hometown of Caribou. She said there was “only one of us on the stage who’s always been pro-choice, and that’s me,” a reference to his anti-abortion record earlier in his career. He is now endorsed by Planned Parenthood’s Maine chapter and let the attack pass.
The debate also put a spotlight on a ProPublica report that the FBI investigated Collins as late as 2024 over an alleged pay-to-play scheme with Navatek CEO Martin Kao. Kao created a shell company to make an illegal $150,000 donation to a pro-Collins super PAC in 2019. ProPublica reported that the Trump administration shut down the inquiry in 2025, while The New York Times reported that FBI leaders did not find Kao’s claims credible.
Collins said her only link to Navatek was a research partnership with the University of Maine.
“These allegations are completely false,” she said. “The head of Navatek at the time was unfortunately a crook. He is now in jail where he belongs.”
Jackson said his son, a former lobbyist, did nothing wrong when asked about accusations that he used his office to help his family. He quickly pivoted back to the ProPublica report.
“I don’t owe Trump, I don’t owe billionaires nothing,” Jackson said. “But I do owe the people of Maine everything.”
Collins said Jackson “has a lot to answer for” on a Federal Housing Administration loan for an Augusta home that he listed as his primary residence while representing Aroostook County. The Maine Ethics Commission voted unanimously against investigating the matter in 2023. Jackson said his home has always been in Allagash.
The candidates split along the same line on the cost of living. Collins blamed Augusta and Jackson blamed Washington.
Collins said high housing costs, property taxes and electricity rates are “all due to Augusta’s failed policies under the failed leadership of Troy Jackson.” She pointed to the $1.5 billion in earmarks she says she has secured over the past five years as federal help easing the burden.
Jackson put the blame on Collins’ record with Trump. He cited the Iran war and tariffs for soaring fuel and electricity costs, along with the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Collins voted against but helped bring to the Senate floor. Collins said she let the bill advance only so she could write a $50 billion rural health care fund into it.
“It is so frustrating to hear these falsehoods repeated time and time again,” she said.

title: Southern Maine Agency on Aging changes name to AgeMaine
text:
Southern Maine Agency on Aging changes name to AgeMaine, but nonprofit keeps its mission the same
The Southern Maine Agency on Aging now has a new name, but the nonprofit organization says its mission and the services it offers will remain the same.
The nonprofit, now known as AgeMaine, connects adults who are 60 and older with social services and community resources. The organization also provides assistance to older adults who are facing financial hardship and food insecurity, and those who live in rural areas.
Maine is the state with the oldest population, according to U.S. Census data, so AgeMaine is highlighting the importance of tapping into the age-diverse communities for volunteers.
"There are more capable older adults living in Maine than basically anywhere else as a percentage of the population, so how do we tap into this resource? It's an abundant resource here," said Matt Thornhill, founder and CEO of Age Frontier.
"It is a win-win, and it happens so naturally at the community level too," said Megan Walton, president and CEO of AgeMaine. "Folks who are in their 60s or 70s or 80s who have time and ability and resources to give back can do that through a volunteer program."
AgeMaine serves Cumberland and York counties, and is one of five agencies on aging in the state.

title: From childhood drawings to McDonald's cups: Artist takes Chicano art to national brands
text:
From childhood drawings to McDonald's cups: Artist takes Chicano art to national brands
For Cecelia Perez, drawing started at a very young age.
"When I was probably around 4 years old, right before I started elementary school, my mom gave me some markers and a drawing pad," Perez said. "For some reason, I felt like I needed to draw every animal that I could think of off the top of my head."
That childhood hobby eventually became a career.
Perez, a Sacramento native, has built a growing national profile, creating work for brands and organizations including the Sacramento Kings and San Francisco Giants. Her work has also been featured at the Smithsonian Folklife Festival in Washington, D.C.
Now based in the Bay Area, Perez said she still starts her days the same way she did as a child.
"I wake up, and I draw," she said. "Even as a full-blown adult, I still wake up, and I just draw, and it's an absolute dream come true to be able to do this on a daily basis."
Perez's artwork features girls, cars, flowers, and other imagery inspired by Chicano culture.
"I illustrate girls, cars, flowers — anything that really relates to Chicano iconography that people can really recognize," she said.
One of Perez's biggest collaborations began with a mural she designed at a McDonald's on Pacific Avenue in Stockton.
The company liked her work and asked her to design a product.
"Because they liked the work so much, they said, 'Hey, can you also do some product design?'" Perez said. "And I said, 'Yes, of course.'"
The result was a limited-edition McDonald's cup created for Hispanic Heritage Month.
Then came another surprise: McDonald's asked Perez to appear in a commercial promoting the collaboration.
"Then they said, 'We have a little bit of extra in the budget. Do you want to be in the commercial?'" Perez said. "And I said, 'Oh my gosh, that's crazy. Okay, yeah!'"
The McDonald's commercial isn't Perez's first time in front of the camera.
She also appeared in a Modelo campaign highlighting her work as an artist.
"They were just highlighting me as an artist and a drink in between," Perez said.
Perez's "Hey Ruca" brand is sold online and in stores at national retailer Zumiez.
"It's so cool to see the brands that I grew up with, these giants, sitting on the same shelf as me," she said.
Despite her growing list of national collaborations, Perez said Sacramento remains a major source of inspiration.
She credits her parents with introducing her to Chicano art and the Royal Chicano Air Force, the Sacramento-based collective established in the 1970s.
The group used art, murals, and posters as a form of activism, including work connected to the United Farm Workers movement.
"I am most familiar with Chicano art because of my parents introducing me to the RCAF, or the Royal Chicano Air Force, that was established in Sacramento back in the '70s," Perez said. "It was really inspiring to see all those colors and pictures."
Perez's artwork draws on that history while looking toward the future.
"This style of art is important to me because it keeps the concept of nostalgia within the Chicano community alive," she said.
Perez is now working on releasing her first hard copy magazine and is an ambassador for Ford.
This story was produced as part of sister station KCRA's 2026 Project CommUNITY special for Hispanic Heritage Month.

title: Letter: UMaine wasting money on AI that should be spent on faculty and students
text:
Regarding the Sept. 21 BDN article “UMaine goes all-in on AI amid upcoming layoffs and tech fears”: After 20-plus years at the University of Maine teaching and mentoring thousands of students, I am neither shocked nor surprised at past and current states of campus and system dysfunction. More recently, I’ve seen administrators shoving AI down students’ and faculty’s throats while eroding support systems that actually promote thinking, learning, civic responsibility, and humanity.
I believe UMaine is becoming just another institutional wealth pump, supporting a bloated bureaucracy and out-of-touch elite class at the expense of ordinary people and the public good. It is obscene to me that combined salaries of the president and vice chancellor of finance approach $1 million and spending on AI exceeds that, all while workers, support staff, and students struggle to make ends meet. I wonder how much of that AI spending trickles up to enrich our ruling technofascist broligarchy?
If the vice chancellor wants to outsource his own thinking to chatbots on his own dime and time, that’s his business, but surely we can hold administrators to higher standards when they act on behalf of our public university with public funds. And if the job of a vice chancellor is simply coasting from one budget crisis to the next with no accountability, couldn’t a chatbot do that just as effectively and for a fraction of the cost? And I’d bet it could even organize its own emails!
Steve Coghlan
Argyle Township

title: NFL suspends 2 officials after outbursts on a weekend marked by profane flare-ups
text:
NFL suspends 2 officials after outbursts on a weekend marked by profane flare-ups
NFL players have to show sportsmanship, lest they draw flags and/or fines. Now, officiating crews are on notice that they, too, must display appropriate behavior in the heat of the moment.
Related video above: Which states produced the most active NFL players in 2026?
The NFL flagged its officials Monday, suspending line judge Jeff Seeman and referee Adrian Hill, for their actions during a wild Week 4 marked by profane flare-ups that included Aaron Rodgers and Mike McCarthy cursing at each other, and Dre Greenlaw displaying the kind of fiery spirit toward Sean Payton that the Broncos head coach wished had shown up last season in Denver.
Seeman was banned two games for swearing at Trey McBride after Arizona's star tight end argued for a pass interference call when he was hit by a defender before the ball arrived. Hill received a one-game suspension for unprofessional conduct for yelling at Eric Wilson and pointing for him to get away after the Minnesota Vikings linebacker tried to help him to his feet after a collision knocked him over.
Greenlaw, who rejoined the Niners last offseason, forced a fumble and collected a dozen tackles in San Francisco's 24-14 win over the Broncos on Sunday.
After just about every one of his stops, he pointed and hollered at Payton, assuredly still stinging over his departure from Denver in which he said his agent had to inform him the Broncos were moving on just one year into his three-year, $31.5 million deal.
As Payton was walking across the field to shake Mike Shanahan’s hand after the game, Greenlaw approached him and took one more verbal shot at his old coach as fellow linebacker Fred Warner redirected him toward the 49ers' tunnel.
Payton didn't engage with Greenlaw, who told the San Francisco Chronicle, “I told him to get the (expletive) off the field. That’s it: ’Get the (expletive) off the field.”
About the only time Greenlaw showed this much fire in his one season in Denver was when he chased down and berated referee Brad Allen after a wild 33-32 win over the Giants in Week 7. That drew a one-game suspension for Greenlaw just 48 hours after he'd returned from an injured thigh that had bothered him for months.
Greenlaw ended up playing in just eight games and after the season said he preferred Shanahan's liberal use of “vet days” to Payton's hard workouts during the week.
When asked if he had any issue with Greenlaw getting in his face Sunday, Payton said, “No, and I said this to Kyle afterwards, I think the world of him. I really love everything about him and he plays with that emotion. So, it's all good.”
Maybe it's all good in Pittsburgh, too.
McCarthy expressed regret for profanity he used toward Rodgers that was caught on the Thursday night broadcast of Pittsburgh's 27-24 loss to Cleveland.
Midway through the first quarter, a flustered Rodgers was shown looking at Pittsburgh's sideline and yelling, “What the (expletive)? Call it!” The camera then cut to McCarthy, who muttered a profanity in response.
“Communication sometimes is not the best choice of words, but everybody’s competing on the field,” McCarthy said. “I think what’s said on the field, the way I grew up in this game, usually stays on the field. That’s not the case today. I understand that. But any negative communication on my part, I wish I wouldn’t use those words.”
Rodgers said the crowd noise made it difficult to communicate at times, noting, “It was a good crowd. It was loud.”
The hot mic saw to it that Rodgers' message to McCarthy was loud and clear and any amateur lip reader could also clearly decipher the head coach's response to his quarterback who spent 13 seasons with him in Green Bay.
Players yelling at the sidelines — even their own — is nothing new.
Neither are heated exchanges between players and officials.
But these four stood out, especially because they were caught on camera and quickly raced across social media, not the kind of viral moments the NFL prefers. McBride knew Seeman's vulgarity was being broadcast — he pointed toward the camera that caught the line judge's repeated obscenities.
“Obviously, you hate to see it, for obvious reasons,” Arizona coach Mike LaFleur said. “I do want to give the man a little bit of grace, too. I know Jeff. He’s a good man. It’s unfortunate it happened. It can’t happen, obviously, and I’ll leave it at that.”
The incident drew the ire of union leader JC Tretter, a retired offensive lineman who played eight seasons in the NFL: “This kind of behavior from an official towards a player is unacceptable,” Tretter, the NFL Players Association’s executive director, posted on social media along with a video clip of the incident. “Players are consistently held accountable when the roles are reversed. We expect the NFL to hold officials to the same standard.”
Vikings coach Kevin O'Connell lamented the official's out-of-bounds reaction in the Miami-Minnesota game where Wilson was only trying to help Hill to his feet after he got knocked into the referee, who fell down.
“I just think it’s one of those situations in kind of a high-energy moment there,” O’Connell said. “I think stuff like that can happen sometimes, but I don’t have any major concerns, and I think Adrian’s a really good official and does a really good job. I think that was just kind of fast moment that happened, and we can put it behind us, hopefully.”
The league flagged its own officials to make sure that happens.

title: Damariscotta Pumpkinfest Spans Early October With Pumpkin Pancakes, Pie Eating Contests, And Pumpkin Regatta Races
text:
According to Merriam-Webster, a pumpkin is "a large, round, orange-skinned fruit of a trailing vine belonging to the gourd family (Cucurbitaceae)."
While most people use this winter squash as a source of food, with it's flesh and seeds both edible and delicious roasted, pureed or baked into pies or breads, folks in Damariscotta have come to celebrate their pumpkins for all the other things you can do with them.
Read More: Protecting Pumpkins From Wildlife In Your Garden
They revere this glorious gourds to such a degree, they've dedicated an entire weekend's festivities to the giant orange orb, in a way only Mainers could come up with.
How did all of this start?
For almost 20 years (their first big foray into promoting pumpkins was in 2007) the Damariscotta Pumpkinfest and Regatta has been all about educating folks about just how great the pumpkin really is.
"Damariscotta Pumpkinfest & Regatta™ is an innovative program that promotes horticultural education to gardeners of all ages regarding the specific agricultural science required to grow Atlantic Giant Pumpkins."
"This program culminates in a family-oriented festival, held for ten days in early October thorough Indigenous Peoples’ Day weekend each year to showcase the pumpkin growers results in a number of creative ways. "
Read More: 7 Pumpkin Color Meanings You Should Know Before Halloween
What impact has the pumpkin had on this region?
The quiet little community in Lincoln County becomes a hustling and bustling haven for tourists and pumpkin-enthusiast for a short while in fall, as roughly 60,000 visitors make their way to the mid-coast region for the celebrations.
What can visitors expect?
The weekend's festivities include (just to name a few activities) a pumpkin pancake breakfast, pumpkin art, a dessert contest full of pumpkin goodies, a giant pumpkin parade, a kids zone with Mr. Drew and his animals, too!
There's also a pumpkin pie eating contest, a Tour de Gourd 5k & Walk, a pumpkin hunt, a pumpkin drop, a free kids' movie, a pumpkin derby, a whole bunch of pumpkin art and of course the famous Pumpkin Regatta where folks dry to stay afloat in their pumpkin boat!
"The Pumpkinboat Regatta, featuring numerous 400-700 pound, hollowed-out pumpkins with motors attached or paddled, piloted by volunteer captains, racing one another in the Damariscotta Harbor. This event is live-fed into the local theater."
The official Damariscotta Pumpkinfest & Regatta website says the event is completely free to attend and also 100% run by volunteers!
Where do the pumpkins come from?
Well, according to organizers, it all starts in the spring of each year, when "50 third-grade students at local Great Salt Bay School volunteer their time to fill 600 pots with soil and amendments for each year’s seeds."
Those seeds are then distributed to a network of around 400 growers who then, under the advice and tutelage of experts, nurture the plants, to see just how big they can get them to grow.
They take notes and keep logs going, recording what works and what doesn't. Then in October, they bring those pumpkins for an official "weigh off" the weekend before the Pumpkinfest and Regatta, to see who has grown the biggest plant.
How big do these giant pumpkins get?
The pumpkins usually weigh in in the range of 200 lbs to 1,400 lbs. This year's winner was whopping 1847 lbs, grown by a repeat champion grower, Elroy Morgan.
Read More: Maine's Biggest Pumpkin for 2026 Weighs 1847 Pounds
"Seeds from the largest, hardiest pumpkins are dried & planted in the subsequent year, for the purpose of high grading the overall stock."
For a complete list of the weekend's events, you can find that on the Damariscotta Pumpkinfest & Regatta Facebook Page or their website, by clicking here.

title: President Trump approves rare firing squad execution for Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan
text:
President Trump approves rare firing squad execution for Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan
President Donald Trump has approved the execution by firing squad of Army Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan for the 2009 shooting rampage at Fort Hood, Texas.
The U.S. military has not carried out the death penalty since 1961. The Army secretary will decide a time and place for the execution, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell wrote in a post on X.
“Judgement day for Hasan has finally come,” Parnell wrote.
Hasan, an Army psychiatrist, walked into a medical building where soldiers were getting medical checkups, shouted “Allahu akbar” — Arabic for “God is great!” — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun. Thirteen people were killed and more than 30 injured.
He said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims and made almost no effort to defend himself at trial. He told jurors that evidence would show he was the shooter and described himself as a soldier who had “switched sides.”
Trump’s approval triggers a series of procedural steps toward carrying out the execution, but Hasan could put them on hold — potentially for years — with a habeas corpus appeal in the civilian federal court system, according to an article published in May in the magazine Army Lawyer.
Death sentences are extremely rare in the military justice system, and executions even rarer. Four men, including Hasan, are currently on the military's death row at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. President George W. Bush approved the execution Army Spc. Ronald Gray in 2008 but it was put on hold by a judge and he remains at Leavenworth.
The last man executed in the military system was Pvt. John Bennett, hanged in 1961 for raping an 11-year-old girl.
Trump approved the firing squad execution days after a failed attempt to execute Christa Pike by lethal injection pushed Tennessee’s governor to halt further executions this year and order an independent review.
Trump resumed the federal death penalty after an informal moratorium during previous administrations. The federal government executed 13 people between 2020 and early 2021, contributing to making Trump the most prolific execution president in over 130 years.
Asked whether the botched execution in Tennessee would lead him to seek changes to capital punishment, Trump said it was “an interesting situation.”
“It shouldn’t be very difficult,” Trump said of carrying out lethal injections.

title: All fraternities suspended at university amid wave of misconduct reports
text:
TUCSON, Ariz. (KPHO/Gray News) — The University of Arizona has hit pause on all fraternity activities amid a wave of misconduct investigations.
In an internal university memo, Chrissy Lieberman, the dean of students, said her office is investigating multiple reports of misconduct involving nearly half of the 21 fraternities on campus.
The violations range from physical assault, hazing and drug and alcohol violations to creating unsafe environments for students, according to Lieberman.
Effective immediately, all fraternity chapters have been placed on an interim activities suspension until all chapter advisors have met with the dean.
Six fraternities — Zeta Beta Tau, Sigma Phi Epsilon, Phi Delta Theta, Sigma Chi, Theta Xi and Phi Gamma Delta — were suspended immediately.
Swallowing live goldfish, hazing, blackout allegations
Several chapters were deemed responsible for code of conduct violations this spring and remain on disciplinary status, according to the Dean of Students Office.
According to officials, chapters are on active suspension, while others have been banned from working with their new member classes, with severe cases under criminal investigation.
Last month, Sigma Tau Gamma was placed on activities suspension after being accused of forcing members to drink large amounts of alcohol and swallowing live goldfish.
In April, six fraternities were under investigation by the school. Three of them, Sigma Alpha Mu, Sigma Chi and Phi Delta Theta, faced serious allegations.
The allegations against Sigma Alpha Mu include burns from hot liquids, forced alcohol consumption, alcohol poisoning, blackouts and hospitalizations.
Sigma Chi allegedly hosted a party that was alcohol-free, but alcohol was consumed, drugs were knowingly and unknowingly given to members, and multiple people were hospitalized.
Phi Delta Theta was placed on suspension for hazing, where members were allegedly subjected to forced alcohol consumption, degradation, humiliation and other threatening and endangering behaviors.
Another fraternity, Sigma Phi Epsilon, was placed on probation until May 31, 2027, and must pay a fine of nearly $4,000. The accusations against the fraternity included sleep deprivation, forced alcohol consumption, kidnapping and forced calisthenics. Members were also accused of illegal drug use.
The last time the university cut ties with a fraternity was in 2024, when Pi Kappa Phi was found guilty of hazing and violating the school’s code of conduct.
Mandatory meetings with chapter advisers
An activities suspension prohibits the fraternities from hosting, attending, sponsoring and participating in any organizational activities. Only business meetings are allowed during the suspension.
Once a chapter adviser has attended one of the three mandatory meetings, chapters that were in good standing will resume activities as normal.
Chapters with upcoming events must ensure that their adviser attends a mandatory meeting. The chapter must return to good standing before any event can be hosted.
Adviser meetings are said to continue quarterly, and advisers must be in attendance at each meeting. If an adviser doesn’t attend, the chapter will be removed from good standing, and its continuation could be jeopardized.
University president met with fraternities
University President Suresh Garimella met with all fraternity presidents on Aug. 27, where he said that the university would not “tolerate further violations that put our students in harm’s way.”
University leadership told fraternity leadership to “step up and be accountable for the men in their chapters” and stop behaviors that violated the school’s code of conduct.
“It was made clear that if the chapters did not meet this expectation, the university would be forced to act,” Lieberman wrote in the memo, dated Monday.
Cases at capacity
Lieberman said that reports are continuing to pour in about concerns within the fraternities, including from parents, students and the community.
The Dean of Students Office is at capacity for the number of cases its staff can investigate at one time, and every case involved a fraternity chapter, according to Lieberman.
“As you know, the value of the Greek experience is under scrutiny nationwide. It is time for the University of Arizona Greek community to step up and set an example for good. It is time to have difficult conversations with each other and the members of the community,” a portion of the memo stated.
The Dean of Students Office noted it would investigate the allegations alongside the University of Arizona Police Department.

title: How you can prepare for AI in the workforce
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — From the classrooms to the workplace to nearly every website you visit, artificial intelligence is changing some aspects of how we live.
It has been a dominant topic in the news, with names like Anthropic and Elon Musk frequently mentioned. But how it works can still cause confusion.
We turned to Neil Johnson, a leading researcher on the technology, to break down the basics of AI.
Johnson is a professor of physics and data science at George Washington University in Washington, D.C. He studies artificial intelligence and has written about its impact extensively.
What is AI?
To put it simply, Johnson described AI as “a combination of computer hardware and software.”
“It’s been trained on everything we’ve ever said and put online,” he explained. “It’s been trained on all of that. So suddenly we have a machine that we can ask. How does it work? It has software in it that looks up the answers and extends them - it joins the dots between things it’s seen.”
Why so few AI companies
Johnson said developing AI requires significant financial resources.
“You need a lot of money to have the machinery and the software to be able to train it,” Johnson said. “That’s why we’ve only got a few companies. And so that’s why all of this discussion about policies, dangers are always focused around these companies.”
Will AI replace our jobs?
Johnson said knowing how to use AI tools provides job security.
“Job security - 100% for the person who knows how to use AI tools and can oversee their use in some domain,” Johnson said.
He believes AI will change how people work, but said those who learn to use it, question it and apply its answers will remain important in the workplace.
“There will always be that human element that’s needed alongside AI tools,” Johnson said. “I do think a lot of people are going to lose jobs who don’t then necessarily embrace it.”
Johnson’s advice is to think of AI less as something to compete against and more as a tool that provides a competitive edge.
