title: Maine’s top court rejects eviction appeal by midcoast farmers
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The couple who managed Harpswell’s last sizable farm have moved themselves and their livestock off the property and lost their latest appeal to Maine’s highest court.
The Maine Supreme Judicial Court rejected the appeal of Joseph and Laura Grady, who ran Two Coves Farm for more than 16 years but were ousted because, according to an arbitrator, they failed to pay roughly $124,000 in rent and grow crops as they had once agreed.
The Aug. 19 ruling capped a protracted legal fight that had the Gradys claiming they were being forced out of their home and stripped of their livelihood in spite of their good faith efforts and in contravention of Maine’s protections for home renters.
Opposing them was Helen Norton, who — with her late husband — bought the 100-acre tract in hopes of preserving a vestige of Harpswell Neck’s agrarian history. Norton’s lawyers alleged that the Gradys had taken advantage of an ailing 94-year-old woman and were “squatting” on the land while dragging out the process with a series of “11th hour arguments.”
The Supreme Judicial Court ruling rejected the latest of those appeals. It affirmed a longer order dated July 28 in which the court upheld the arbitrator’s decision and spurned the couple’s contention that the arbitrator had exceeded his authority in treating the lease as a strictly commercial contract rather than one that also provided the Gradys with a place to live and raise their children.
Norton said she was pleased by the ruling and is working to make repairs to the property that will allow her to “find a good, responsible farmer and his family and make it a viable working farm” as soon as next spring.
Of the legal fight, she said, “It has cost me a lot of money, it has cost me a lot of time and effort, and it has made us quite unhappy.”
The Gradys declined to participate in an interview for this article. Joe Grady requested questions in writing, then declined to answer them. However, court filings from their legal team lay out their position in detail. In a brief statement emailed to the Anchor, they said they are disappointed but determined.
“The last two years of defending ourselves from the claims made against us have been exhausting; losing our home where we planned to spend the rest of our lives, as well as the business we built from scratch, was devastating and is still fresh for us,” they said in the statement.
Partners in protection
The legal battle brought a bitter closing chapter to what began as a pastoral partnership.
Two decades ago, in 2006, Norton and her late husband, Walter, bought a 100-acre saltwater farm near their home on Harpswell Neck. The entity they formed, Neils Point LLC, in 2008 granted an agriculture conservation easement to the Maine Farmland Trust, with the Harpswell Heritage Land Trust overseeing the easement.
The purpose of the arrangement was to protect the farm “from encroaching suburban sprawl so that it will always be available for its traditional use as a productive cropland, open fields and forest,” according to the arbitrator’s findings.
In 2009, a young farming couple — the Gradys — signed on as stewards of the property, an agreement renewed in 2017 for an additional 25 years. In exchange for the right to live and farm there, the couple agreed to keep the farm in productive operation and to pay rent equal to 10% of their “annual net proceeds” — their farming revenue minus legitimate operating expenses.
For many years, all seemed to be going smoothly at Two Coves Farm. Drivers passing the property on Harpswell Neck Road saw signs advertising a farm stand along a tree-lined lane that sold, among other things, eggs, lamb, tomatoes, cucumbers, yarn and sheepskins.
A ‘stark injustice’ or an end to a ‘free ride’?
But trouble arrived last year, when relations between Norton and the Gradys took a sharp downward turn. In July 2025, an arbitrator presided over a hearing to examine Norton’s allegations that the couple had failed to live up to their end of the deal.
After examining evidence and hearing from both sides, arbitrator and Portland lawyer Timothy J. Bryant concluded that the Gradys had not made rent payments on time and “failed to pay any rent whatsoever for the years of 2023 and 2024.” In a decision dated Oct. 24, 2025, the arbitrator concluded that the Gradys had understated their revenues and “knowingly inflated their operational expenses by treating household and personal expenses as business expenses.”
The arbitrator also agreed with Norton that the Gradys had failed to “use the farm to actively plant and grow productive crops,” as required by the 2017 lease.
He ordered the Gradys to pay Norton’s Neils Point LLC $124,175 and to vacate the farm no later than Dec. 31, 2025.
The Gradys did not move out, instead filing a Dec. 30 appeal asking a Maine Superior Court justice to vacate the decision and allow them to continue working and living at Two Coves. Because the farm was also their home, they argued that state law prohibited them from being evicted without the formal court process guaranteed to residential tenants.
Norton’s legal team countered by saying that the arbitrator’s ruling was sound, and that the Gradys had voluntarily agreed to arbitration as the method for resolving disputes. In a Feb. 4 ruling, Superior Court Justice Darcie N. McElwee sided with Norton and agreed that the Gradys must vacate.
In late February, the Gradys took their appeal to the Supreme Judicial Court.
“This case presents a stark injustice,” wrote the Gradys’ lawyers, Regan A. Sweeney and J. Spencer Hoffman. “A wealthy landowner has utilized commercial arbitration to dispossess a tenant farming family from the property they have called home and worked for over sixteen years.”
The lawyers stated that the Gradys had been served a “writ of possession” on Feb. 25, giving them 48 hours to vacate. “The Gradys were afforded no meaningful opportunity to seek appellate relief before the coercive machinery of eviction was set in motion,” they wrote.
The court’s ruling would affect not just the Gradys, their lawyers wrote, but also other farmers.
“Farmers are the backbone of Maine’s communities. They feed their neighbors, steward the land, and embody the independence and self-reliance that define this State’s character,” they said. “Yet the (ruling) treats farmers as something less than every other resident of Maine. The Gradys are people who work the land they live on. They are not commercial tenants operating a warehouse or retail establishment. … Their home is their farm, and their farm is their home. The two are inseparable.”
Norton’s lawyers countered with strong words of their own in a Feb. 27 pleading. Noting that the Gradys had already relocated their livestock and “never grew any crops in the first place,” they said the couple faced no real hardship.
“For the last decade, the (Gradys) have had possession of the farm under false pretenses. For the last two months, they have trespassed on the property unlawfully,” said attorneys Thimi R. Mina and Alfred C. Frawley IV. “Meanwhile, Mrs. Norton is 94 years old and recently suffered a significant injury. Put simply, time is of the essence, and the balance of the equities lies in favor of ending the (Gradys’) decade-long free ride while Mrs. Norton still has the opportunity to put the property to productive use.”
The legal point and counterpoint continued through the spring and summer. Following the adverse July 28 Supreme Judicial Court ruling, the Gradys again appealed and — in August — lost again.
The court rejected the Gradys’ argument that they were entitled to the same channels of legal appeal available to a tenant facing eviction from a rental home. Instead, the Gradys had to abide by the arbitrator’s decision after earlier agreeing on that course of conflict resolution.
As their legal battle wound down, both the Gradys and Norton expressed gratitude for the support they had received from neighbors.
“I am very happy for the support that I’ve received from the community,” said Norton, who, along with her husband, has invested in conserving a large amount of open land in Harpswell and neighboring communities.
“To all those in Harpswell who have supported us and Two Coves Farm, we want to pass on our thanks and let you all know that we are doing well and have transitioned to a new home,” the Grady family said in their statement emailed to the Anchor.
“We do not know what the future holds at the moment,” they added, “but we will certainly be finding our way back to farming in the months and years ahead.”

title: Maine should vote against Trump
text:
As we cast votes in Maine’s U.S. Senate race this year, we should remember that President Trump has asked voters to pretend that he’s on the ballot.
For once, I agree with him. Trump’s domestic and foreign policies have been disastrous, with tariffs, rising inflation and and war in Iran at the top of a long list. He has indicated that he wants to lead like a dictator, focused on relentless attacks on voting and election results and expressing admiration for Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Kim Jong Un.
Although Sen. Susan Collins holds a position of influence in the Senate, she has not provided a meaningful check on Trump’s power. She voted to advance the “big, beautiful bill” then voted against it. She voted in support of the war in Iran then voted against it. She has also voted for the vast majority of Trump’s dismal administration and judicial nominations.
Donald Trump is on the ballot. Let’s vote against him and Collins, and for Troy Jackson.
Daniel Hildreth
Falmouth

title: Death Notice: Diana M. Markos
Man who allegedly fled from Maine police was found hiding in a pond
text:
A Lebanon man who allegedly fled from police and crashed into three vehicles and a house was found hiding in a pond Monday night.
Zackery Lacourse, 21, was charged with operating under the influence, reckless conduct with a dangerous weapon, failure to stop for a police officer, operating after suspension and leaving the scene of a motor vehicle crash, according to the York County Sheriff’s Office.
Lacrouse was allegedly driving a white 2005 Ford pickup truck erratically with no headlights on Main Street in Waterboro about 10:27 p.m. when a deputy tried to pull him over. He allegedly fled, and the deputy didn’t give chase.
The deputy later found Lacrouse’s truck near the intersection of Main Street and West Road, where he allegedly crashed into a 2017 Subaru Impreza before continuing into the Waterboro House of Pizza’s parking lot, where he hit two parked vehicles and then a home.
The Subaru’s driver, a 30-year-old Shapleigh woman, wasn’t injured.
Lacrouse allegedly fled from the crash. A police dog tracked him down to a nearby pond, where he was trying to hide.
Lacrouse was taken to the York County Jail in Alfred, where he was unable to make bail. He was scheduled to appear in court Wednesday in Biddeford.

title: Whatever method you use, hunting for grouse something to be thankful for
text:
There’s a running quip among Maine hunters regarding the difference between grouse and partridge. When you approach a gallinaceous game bird , if it flies away, it’s a grouse. If it walks away, it’s a partridge.
In truth, our most abundant upland bird is a grouse, a ruffed grouse to be more precise. That’s an important distinction, because in higher elevations and northern areas of Maine, you might also come across a spruce grouse, which is not legal game. The only true partridges in the U.S. have been imported or raised in captivity for hunting preserves.
Still, that tongue-in-cheek distinction has a lot to do with how folks go about hunting the species. In southern and cental Maine, where people are more abundant, the birds are less abundant and considered “wilder” by bird hunters. By that, they mean the birds are more inclined to flush, often long before offering a shot opportunity. Most hunters in these areas employ one of two methods. One is to simply stroll along in hopes of flushing a bird within range. The other is to enlist the aid of dogs.
Dog hunters are a different breed, no pun intended. Regardless of the game, be it birds, bear or hare, the hunt is more about the dogs than the quarry. Watching a well-trained pointer or setter work a scent is a thing of beauty. If they can hold a bird in position until hunters arrive, it’s a win, whether the shot is a hit or a miss.
In the north woods, grouse (or partridge) could be considered a pedestrian bird. One reason is because you’ll often find them walking along the side of the road, or in the middle of it. Another is because their propensity to do so might make them seem a bit dull and uninspiring. Either way, you can’t help but to stop for them.
Some folks are concerned that this method of hunting “easy targets” could be detrimental to grouse populations. One only need look at satellite imagery of the landscape to see the fallacy in that argument. Roads are few and far between, and for every bird you encounter along them, there are just as many where the roads and most hunters don’t go.
Someone once asked me what grouse tastes like. I said, “like turkey, with a hint of cranberry sauce.” Regardless of how they’re harvested, whether randomly, over a stoic setter or on the roadside, we should give thanks for the opportunity.
Bob Humphrey is a freelance writer and Registered Maine Guide who lives in Pownal. He can be reached at: [email protected]

title: Obituary: Diana M. Markos
text:
OLD ORCHARD BEACH – It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of our beloved Mom, Nana, sister, aunt, and friend, who died peacefully on Sept. 28, 2026, surrounded by her loving family, after a brief illness.
The daughter of the late Alson “Ike” and Edna Soule, she was predeceased by her beloved husband, Arthur “Tom” Markos, in 2018.
She leaves behind her daughter, Carol Sinclair, and her husband Robert of Farmingdale, her son, Christopher and his partner Mary Hoffmann of Rockport, and her son, Stephen and his wife Katie of Winchester, Mass. She was the cherished Nana of Nicholas Sinclair and his wife, Lauren, of Boston, Ryan Sinclair and his wife Ellen of Boston, Avery and Arianna Markos of Gardiner, and Quinn and Hayden Markos of Winchester. She is also survived by her sister, Jane Serwacki,, and her husband,, Larry,, of North Berwick, as well as many other family members and dear friends.
She grew up in Auburn, Maine, and graduated from Edward Little High School, Class of 1967. The friendships she made there remained an important part of her life. She especially treasured her longtime group of high school friends, who continued to gather for monthly lunches—a tradition that brought her great joy over the years.
After many years working for the Paper Industry Information Office, she made the decision to retire early and devote herself to what mattered most to her: her family. Family truly was the center of her world, and there was nothing she enjoyed more than having the people she loved gathered together.
She was, quite simply, the strongest person we knew. That strength was matched by an extraordinary capacity to care for others. She lovingly cared for our father through his final days, just as she had cared for her parents and her beloved aunts, whom she looked after with the same unwavering devotion. When someone she loved needed her, she was there—steadfast, selfless, and strong.
Her generosity and devotion to others extended well beyond her family. She was a longtime member of Beta Sigma Phi, a sorority devoted to service, and her church was an important part of her life. For many years, she was a member of Holy Trinity Greek Orthodox Church in Lewiston and, more recently, Holy Trinity Greek Orthodox Church in Portland. She served as Treasurer of Philoptochos and formed many cherished friendships through her years of involvement with the church.
She gave generously of her time and talents to her church community, spending countless hours in the church kitchen baking Greek breads and pastries for functions and celebrations. For her, cooking and baking were acts of love, whether she was doing so for her church community or for the family she adored.
She enjoyed an active lifestyle right up until her illness, rising at the crack of dawn each morning to join her exercise buddies—first at Curves and later at Planet Fitness—often followed by a stop at Panera, where their circle of friends grew to include other regulars who remained in touch throughout her illness. We often joked that she could run circles around all of us.
Her home in Old Orchard Beach became a special gathering place for her extended family and the setting for countless happy memories. She was a phenomenal cook and baker, and the family feasts she lovingly prepared were nothing short of amazing. No gathering was ever small or quiet—they were large, loud, filled with wonderful food, plenty of laughter, and, most of all, love. She delighted in bringing everyone together and creating the traditions and memories her family will carry with them always.
More than anything, she loved being a mother and Nana. Her children and grandchildren were her greatest joy, and she took tremendous pride in each of them. The love she gave so freely will remain at the heart of the family she cherished so deeply.
Our family would like to extend our heartfelt gratitude to the wonderful hospice nurses and caregivers who helped us care for our Mom and made it possible for her to remain peacefully at home, surrounded by the people she loved. We are especially grateful to Betsy, Charlotte, Tabby, and her team for the kindness, compassion, and loving care they provided to her and to our entire family during her final days.
The family will hold a private ceremony at a later date.
In lieu of flowers,
donations in her memory may be made to:
Holy Trinity Greek
Orthodox Church
133 Pleasant St.
Portland, ME 04101 or

title: ‘Small price to pay’: Trump says Iran can ‘take out’ LA or San Diego during political rally
text:
(Gray News) – President Donald Trump is facing backlash after making a statement Monday night during a political rally suggesting that Iran could take out two cities in the United States.
“It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe. They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego,” Trump said.
Trump was speaking at a political rally in Nebraska when he made the controversial statement.
People at the rally celebrated his suggestion.
“After sending the National Guard and Marines to occupy California, Donald Trump is now saying our foreign enemies should ‘take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego,” Gov. Gavin Newsom wrote on X. “He is deranged and dangerous.”
Los Angeles is the most populous city in California and the second most populous in the United States. It has one of the busiest container ports in the Americas and is home to the U.S. Space Force’s Space Systems Command Headquarters.
LA Mayor Karen Bass reacted to Trump’s statement on X saying, “The role of a president is to protect the country, not to actively threaten it and encourage attacks on American lives.”
“San Diego is not collateral damage. We are not expendable. And we are never a ‘small price to pay.’ Keep our city out of your reckless war talk,” San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria wrote on X.
San Diego is home to Naval Base San Diego, where the Navy SEALs train. There is a large military presence in the city with 70,000 civilians and active-duty service members living and working in the area.
After his shocking statements, Trump claimed the Iran war was close to the end and is “essentially almost over with.”

title: What Paramount’s Warner Bros. takeover means for streaming, movies and news
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Tony Soprano, meet Vito Corleone.
In a marriage of two massive Hollywood portfolios, Paramount’s $81 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery closed Tuesday, uniting everything from cartoons featuring Bugs Bunny and SpongeBob Squarepants to news delivered by Anderson Cooper and Gayle King.
The resulting company, a behemoth now known as Skydance, reshapes the media world. Here’s what the deal may mean for streaming, movies, news and more:
Streamers HBO Max and Paramount+ now under same umbrella
Skydance brings Paramount+ together with HBO Max with plans to unify its streaming products “into a single service over time.” What this would be called and how it might affect consumer costs and choices remains unknown. David Ellison, the architect of the deal and the company’s CEO, has suggested HBO could still have some level of independence.
“Our viewpoint is, HBO should stay HBO,” Ellison said earlier this year. “They built a phenomenal brand, they are a leader in this space and we just want them to continue doing more of it. But by bringing the platforms together, all of our content will be able to reach even a broader audience than we can do standalone.”
Paramount also has acquired Warner’s smaller Discovery+ streamer, joining Paramount+, Pluto TV and BET+.
Critics have expressed skepticism about how consumers might benefit, warning that already rising subscription fees could spike as the conglomerate meets payments on the billions of dollars in debt Ellison took on to finance the deal.
What’s not in dispute is the size of the resulting library of content. Paramount+ and HBO Max alone add up to roughly 14% of the U.S. streaming market, comparable to rival Disney+, but still behind Amazon Prime at 17% and Netflix at 19%, according to the streaming guide JustWatch. It pairs movie franchises like “Mission: Impossible” with “Lord of the Rings,” television hits from “I Love Lucy” to “Friends,” and personalities ranging from Guy Fieri to RuPaul.
Don’t expect a “Diners, Drive-Ins and Dives Drag Race” anytime soon, but with so many properties combining forces, there is potential for all kinds of crossover.
Hollywood consolidates even more, shrinking to 4 big studios
Paramount and Warner Bros. are two of Hollywood’s oldest studios. Their merger means fewer companies control legacy film production.
Under a settlement reached last month with 12 states, the combined company has agreed to distribute 30 films in theaters each year for the next two years — and 32 films each year for three years after that. The fine print notes that only 50% of those movies would have to be “produced or jointly produced” by the combined company. Skydance also agreed to increase spending on film production in the U.S. by at least $1.5 billion over the next five years.
Still, many have expressed worry about what further consolidation could mean for jobs and which projects are greenlit down the road. Regulatory filings have indicated that the new ownership will be looking for ways to cut costs — including layoffs and downsizing some overlapping operations.
Hollywood’s big six shrank to five when Disney bought most of 20th Century Fox in a deal finalized in 2019. Now it’s a big four: Skydance, Disney, Universal and Sony.
The deal joins news giants CNN and CBS and some worry about interference
The deal also puts news giants CNN and CBS under the same ownership, a concern among many journalists given the Ellison family’s close relationship with President Donald Trump.
CBS News has taken steps to appeal to more conservative viewers since Ellison installed Free Press founder Bari Weiss as editor-in-chief. At “60 Minutes,” the new management brought heaps of turmoil, with the firings of its executive producer and three veteran correspondents, who have claimed that Weiss sought changes to news reports that appeared to be driven by politics.
Trump, who has attacked the reporting of both networks as “fake news,” said Tuesday that he’s happy the merger closed, and that Skydance is “going to be a great company.”
Foreign investors poised to hold sizable indirect ownership stakes are also in the spotlight. The FCC cleared Paramount’s request for sovereign funds from Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates to indirectly own nearly 50% of the combined company’s equity interests, and potentially up to 100% through future investments, but no voting rights.
Ellison has said editorial independence will be maintained at CNN. The combined company is retaining Mark Thompson as CNN’s editor-in-chief, and has agreed to form a “News Editorial Independence Board.”
Skydance’s corporate board of directors will choose who sits on this new body.
___
Grantham-Philips reported from Chicago.

title: UMaine football fires offensive coordinator Mikahael Waters
text:
The slumping University of Maine football team has fired offensive coordinator Mikahael Waters.
Head coach Jordan Stevens confirmed the move Tuesday. Waters had been offensive coordinator for the Black Bears since 2024.
The move comes as a sputtering Maine offense is ranked 118th out of 124 Football Championship Subdivision teams in points per game (14.5). The Black Bears have lost five consecutive games, most recently a 24-16 home defeat Saturday against Sacred Heart.
Waters was in his eighth season with the Black Bears, having joined the staff in 2019 under then-first-year head coach Nick Charlton. He served as Maine’s tight ends coach from 2019-22 and as special teams coordinator in 2023 prior to his promotion to offensive coordinator.
Maine’s offensive struggles have been a theme all season. In addition to their paltry points-per-game ranking, the Black Bears rank 93rd in passing yards per game and 110th in rushing yards per game. The team has just 66 points in 22 quarters since scoring 21 in the first half of the season opener at Towson.
“We have to coach better, and we have to put our players in a better position to make plays, and that’s from a confidence standpoint and from an execution standpoint,” Stevens told the media Tuesday. “When we talk execution, that’s not on the players; that’s on us to make sure they’re in a position to execute.”
Maine’s output in 2026 is a significant drop-off from the previous two seasons under Waters. The Black Bears averaged 24.2 points per game (67th) last year, and 23.2 points per game (74th) in Waters’ first season as offensive coordinator in 2024.
Sean Green, Maine’s running backs coach and a former state title-winning head coach at Portland and Cape Elizabeth high schools, will take over play-calling duties. Offensive analyst Cooper Heisey will take over for Green as running backs coach.
Maine is on a bye this week. The Black Bears will be back in action at 1 p.m. on Oct. 17 when they host Bryant (4-1 overall, 2-0 Coastal Athletic Association).

title: 4 takeaways from the first debate between Susan Collins and Troy Jackson
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson faced off in a televised debate on Tuesday, sparring over a wide range of topics, including President Donald Trump, high prices and corruption allegations.
It was the first of four debates scheduled for the next two weeks.
Independent polling shows a tight race. Jackson, a 59-year-old former logger and state Senate president, holds a two-point lead over the 73-year-old Collins, according to polling averages from FiftyPlusOne.
But a Marist poll released on Tuesday had Jackson up, 51% to 47%, with only 1% undecided. The Democrat’s four-point lead was just outside of the margin of error of +/- 3.8 percentage points.
Here are a few takeaways from the high-stakes showdown.
1. The candidates blamed each other for the high cost of living
The high cost of living — especially the prices of gasoline and home heating oil — has repeatedly been cited by voters as their top concern leading up to the midterms.
So it’s no surprise that Jackson and Collins tried to blame each other for the situation.
Jackson, perhaps, had the easiest line of attack. Throughout the night, Jackson repeatedly tied Collins to Trump and his unpopular policies and actions, including tariffs, the war with Iran and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025, which cut healthcare and other safety net programs, and gave tax breaks to the wealthy.
Collins, however, pushed back, saying for example that Jackson was cherry-picking one analysis showing she voted with Trump more than 95% of the time. Other analyses showed a much lower rate, she said, noting that she’s not close with the president.
She then raised the issue of high property taxes and electricity rates, saying “those are all due to Augusta’s failed policies under the failed leadership of Troy Jackson,” who served six years as Senate president.
2. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act was in the spotlight.
Jackson repeatedly blamed Collins for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which made permanent tax cuts for the wealthy while making deep cuts to healthcare and safety net programs.
Collins voted to advance the Republican bill to the Senate floor, but voted against enacting it.
Jackson used Collins’ vote advancing the measure to cast her as being on the side of billionaires.
“Senator Collins has had 30 years to show whose side she’s on,” he said. “I don’t owe Donald Trump or the billionaires anything. I don’t fight for billionaires like she does. I owe Mainers everything, and that’s who I’m gonna be fighting for when I’m the next U.S. senator.”
Collins criticized Jackson for distorting her record. She said she only voted to advance the bill so she could help author an amendment inserting a $50 billion fund to help rural hospitals. She said she voted against the final measure’s enactment because of the Medicaid cuts it contained. But the bill passed after Vice President JD Vance cast a tiebreaking vote.
Jackson said that reasoning wasn’t good enough.
“Sen. Collins is like an arsonist who helps set the fire and then she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out,” he said.
3. The candidates accused each other of corruption.
Collins has been under fire for nearly two weeks since ProPublica published a report detailing allegations that she was leveraging her role on the appropriations committee to solicit political donations. The outlet reported the FBI was gearing up for an investigation into Collins’ circle until Trump returned to office in 2025 and disbanded certain anti-corruption units.
Collins defended herself Tuesday, pointing out that she had advocated for a project involving the defense contractor Navatek at the urging of the University of Maine — not at the urging of a donor.
Collins then accused Jackson of corruption, raising questions about a mortgage he signed and reimbursements he got while serving in the Legislature.
Jackson said he signed a mortgage document stating that his second home in Augusta would be his primary residence — which he said he was advised to do since he would spend more than half of the year there.
But a home in Allagash remained his permanent residence as defined by the state law. Jackson said he would travel there every weekend from Augusta, leading to his expense reimbursements.
4. Jackson was aggressive. Collins was knowledgeable.
Throughout the debate, Collins displayed her experience and knowledge of federal policies. She repeatedly called out Jackson for suggesting her committee had authority over things it does not, such as Medicaid rates.
Jackson, meanwhile, was relentless in going after Collins’ record. He criticized her for supporting Brett Kavanaugh’s appointment to the U.S. Supreme Court and for standing behind that vote after the court overturned the federal abortion protections under Roe v. Wade.
And he continued to hammer Collins for voting to advance the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and for supporting Trump’s agenda, despite Collins’ efforts to highlight instances where she has broken with the president — such as her moves to push back against his tariffs and against his administration’s efforts to cut medical research funding.

title: Maine corrections officer indicted for sexual assault
text:
Kennebec County corrections officer indicted for sexual assault over intimate relationship with inmate
A Kennebec County corrections officer has been indicted by a grand jury for sexual assault after investigators said they uncovered an intimate relationship between him and an inmate.
Nicholas Fellows, 37, of Augusta, was indicted for gross sexual assault and unlawful sexual contact.
According to court documents obtained by WMTW media partner WABI, staff members at the Kennebec County Jail contacted investigators in July after discovering the relationship.
An inmate who witnessed the relationship told authorities they saw the female inmate writing explicit notes detailing their relationship and said the inmate had detailed how Fellows was able to get her into a room without cameras to perform sex acts.
Court records state that video evidence from the jail showed the pair entering a room without recording devices as was reported, and that Fellows and the inmate later admitted to the relationship.
Any sexual contact between a corrections officer and an incarcerated person under their authority is a crime under state law.
Kennebec County Sheriff Ken Mason told WABI that Fellows has been removed from his position.
“A report of an alleged violation of our S.O.P. and Maine State law by Officer Nicholas Fellows came to the attention of my command staff who brought it to my attention posthaste,” Mason said. “Mr. Fellows was placed on administrative leave immediately and a criminal investigation was conducted by my Detective Division. After our investigation, we had probable cause for an arrest, and Mr. Fellows was arrested for the offense and terminated from employment with Kennebec County.”
Fellows was released from Two Bridges Regional Jail in Wiscasset on $10,000 bail in August.

title: What Maine’s next generation of farms needs to succeed
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Ryan Douglas is a Maine-based strategic advisor to cultivation businesses and the
author of “Presence is a Strategy: The Competitive Advantage You Can’t Automate.”
Last week, a news report announced that the Lisbon greenhouse facility operated
by Springworks Farm is headed to auction.
Roughly 40 miles away, Vertical Harvest, a high-tech producer of indoor leafy greens in Westbrook, has faced significant delays and has yet to reach the commercial scale it originally envisioned.
If Maine is going to support innovative agriculture with public resources, it should ask one question before a project moves forward: Is the operation ready to run?
Early in my career, I worked for an ornamental flower grower in Mississippi who operated on five acres of patched-up, run-down greenhouses. The facility wasn’t impressive, but the crops were consistently exceptional.
Years later, I consulted for a publicly traded cannabis company in Colombia. It had sophisticated facilities, a ton of cash and a board with impressive credentials. But when I stepped into the company’s greenhouse, I was speechless. Every plant was dead.
How could an operation with every advantage fail at the most basic task, while the unimpressive greenhouse produced exceptional crops?
Those two experiences reinforced a lesson I’ve learned throughout my career: operational readiness is fundamental to success.
As a lifelong Mainer, I’ve spent three decades in commercial horticulture throughout the U.S., Canada and South America. Most of my career has been under glass as a grower, manager and consultant, and I previously served as general manager for Backyard Farms, the 40-acre tomato greenhouse range in Madison.
Operational readiness is having the people, systems and discipline to run a facility reliably from day one. In this business, margins are made or lost in the consistent execution of mundane but essential work.
Skipping a crop walk on Friday could mean missing signs that insect pressure has increased due to warmer weather. By Monday, that small oversight can mean unsaleable product, additional labor and lost revenue.
In a small greenhouse, that mistake may have a limited impact. But at a commercial scale, small mistakes compounded over time can quickly turn into major losses. No amount of money can replace the need for operational experience, seasoned judgment and common sense. Operational readiness must be built into a cultivation project from day one, not treated as a problem to solve once construction is complete.
Springworks Farm received meaningful public support, including a $300,000 Maine Technology Institute award for greenhouse expansion. The Finance Authority of Maine insured a $5 million loan and a $1 million working-capital loan in partnership with Farm
Credit East.
Vertical Harvest received nearly $49 million in USDA-guaranteed loans, approximately $8 million in financing facilitated through Efficiency Maine and $1 million in direct loans from the Finance Authority of Maine.
When public resources support private projects at this scale, Mainers have a legitimate stake in whether those projects are built and managed to succeed. Operational readiness should be scrutinized as closely as technology, job creation, capital investment and economic impact.
I am 100% in favor of continued investment in Maine’s ability to feed itself. Considering our short outdoor growing season, innovative cultivation projects like these will be a key part of the solution. But these latest developments are a reminder that impressive facilities alone aren’t enough.
Public funding shouldn’t just help ambitious agricultural ventures get off the ground. It should increase their chances of actually sticking around.

title: ‘We refuse to close the chapter’: Leaders, Nolan Wells’ parents renew push for federal investigation into his death
text:
INGLEWOOD, Calif. (WLOX/Gray News) — Civil rights attorney Ben Crump and the parents of 18-year-old Nolan Wells, along with other community leaders, held a press conference to call for a federal investigation into Wells’ death.
California Congresswoman Maxine Waters, Florida Congresswoman Frederica Wilson and others sent a letter to Jessica Bowron, acting director of the U.S. National Park Service, asking the agency’s Investigative Services Branch to open a “prompt and exhaustive investigation” into Wells’ death.
The letter read, in part, “Nolan’s family deserves answers, and this matter demands and deserves your immediate attention.”
The letter pointed out that most of Horn Island is federally designated land and asked the park service to “examine every circumstance surrounding Nolan’s death and pursue every available lead.”
“We have not closed our case, and we refuse to close the chapter of Nolan Xavier Wells,” Crump said.
Wells’ body was found in the water just off Horn Island on the morning of July 6. He was reported missing the night of July 4 after he didn’t return from a boating trip with friends.
Two and a half months later, a Jackson County grand jury returned a “no true bill,” meaning no criminal charges or indictments will be issued at this time.
Jackson County District Attorney Angel Meyers McIlrath has repeatedly said that her office has taken the investigation seriously and turned over all available evidence to the grand jury.
Stop AAPI Hate Executive Director Cynthia Choi spoke at the press conference, saying the organization stands with Wells’ family, “for as long as it takes.”
“When a family is denied truth, and when anyone seeking justice is met with closed doors — intimidation instead of answers — this fight belongs to us,” Choi said.
Choi also condemned those attempting to harass or threaten Wells’ family, referencing those who targeted his mother, Christine Wells Wonsley, and her job as a nurse practitioner.
At the National Asian Pacific American Women’s Forum on Saturday, Wonsley was given the organization’s “Voice of Courage” award for “standing in the gap and fighting for the truth of Nolan Wells,” according to Crump.
At Monday’s press conference, Wonsley said she “never thought [she] would be in this position.”
“I never thought I would be someone who was giving a voice to so many who feel like they have none because our justice system told us to take the answer you’ve been given,” Wonsley said. “We have been left with more questions and heartbreak than any answers. As a matter of fact, no one has given us any answers, other than, ‘consistent with accidentally drowning.’ That’s all our Black child, our Black and Asian child, has received, is ‘accidental drowning.’”
Both the state and independent autopsies ruled Wells’ cause and manner of death undetermined. According to the independent autopsy, blunt-force injuries were found on the back of his head and other areas of his back.
The grand jury report noted that accidental drowning is consistent with the evidence and that the evidence does not rule it out.
“Today, I am asking the people whose job it is to serve and protect to keep their word to our family,” Elmore Wonsley, Wells’ dad, said at the press conference. “Our son was found on federal land, and we are asking the FBI to step in and do a full investigation. We’re not asking for special treatment. We’re asking for what any father would do for his child, and that’s to find the truth about what happened to his child.”

title: Portland woman says new rule on prescription drug imports would increase her costs
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND — Maida Uhlig said she’s been purchasing anxiety medication from Canada for about 20 years, and would have to pay thousands more per year if a new U.S. Customs and Border Protection rule goes into effect later this month that would ban people from buying medicines internationally by mail.
Uhlig, 81, of Portland, said she takes Lexapro, which her insurance doesn’t cover because there’s a generic equivalent available. Uhlig said she’s tried the generics, but for her they’re not effective. She said only the brand name medication alleviates her anxiety.
She pays about $675 per year out-of-pocket for the brand name medication, purchasing by mail through Canadian pharmacies. If she had to purchase that same drug in the U.S., Uhlig estimates the cost would be about $6,300.
“I couldn’t do it. I don’t have that money,” said Uhlig, a retired administrative assistant. “It would be debilitating if I couldn’t take this medication.”
The rule is set to go into effect Oct. 22, eliminating an exemption that previously allowed importation of prescription drugs through the international postal system.
U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, D-1st District, said in an interview last week that she signed onto a letter from dozens of House members asking the Trump administration to abandon the rule.
“People have been doing this for a long time, and it shouldn’t be taken away from them,” Pingree said. “We need to make sure people who are getting their prescriptions this way don’t get caught in this trap.”
A 2020 University of Florida study found that about 2 million Americans purchase prescriptions from international pharmacies.
Ken Hunter, executive director of the Campaign for Personal Prescription Importation, a New Jersey-based advocacy group, said in an interview Friday that many countries, including Canada, regulate drug prices more than the U.S., which leads to many prescription medications being cheaper when imported.
Hunter said for decades, the federal government has allowed drugs for individual prescriptions to be imported through the U.S. mail, through the Medicare Modernization Act of 2003. In the era before drugs could be purchased internationally over the internet, the federal government allowed people to drive over the Canadian border to purchase personal prescriptions.
“Drug prices, when buying internationally, are much less than what they are in the U.S., typically half the price to one-fifth the price,” Hunter said. “This is going to price people out of the ability to use these drugs. We are heading toward a significant healthcare crisis.”
Hunter pointed to Eliquis, a blood thinner often prescribed to prevent strokes, as a commonly imported medication. When purchased from Canada, it costs about $550 for a three-month supply, but in the U.S. it’s priced at over $1,000, he said. Hunter said while generic drugs are often inexpensive in the U.S., it can sometimes take years for a new medication to have a generic equivalent. Or, he said, there may be generics available in other countries, but not the United States.
CBP said on Friday that it would respond to questions about the new rule. The agency had not responded by Tuesday.
According to the published rule, CBP cited the potential of “illicit-drug importations” as one of the reasons.
Hunter said banning the importation of personal prescription medications is not going to be effective in reducing the flow of illicit drugs into the U.S., which occur in much larger volumes.
Ann Woloson, executive director of the Maine-based nonprofit Consumers for Affordable Health Care, said in an interview Friday that the impacts of the new rule would be devastating for many who already have difficulty affording their medications.
Many people have high-deductible insurance plans or those where the patient has to pay a certain percentage of drug costs. In those cases, insurance would not protect people from paying thousands in out-of-pocket costs, Woloson said.
“It’s another sad example of how our current administration is going to make it harder for people to afford the healthcare they need,” she said.
Thirty-two percent of Maine residents surveyed this year by Consumers for Affordable Health Care reported that they took fewer pills than prescribed to save money.
Uhlig said she has a supply of anxiety pills that will last about a year, but after that she would have to take a 10-hour, round-trip bus to Montreal to purchase the medications directly from Canadian pharmacies. Hunter said the new rule doesn’t prohibit people from personally crossing the border to buy drugs from Canadian pharmacies, but making people travel long distances to get medications they need would be a hardship for many.
Uhlig said people shouldn’t be forced to pay exorbitant costs for medicine they need.
“It’s so unfair, because people rely on these drugs to live,” she said.

title: French riot police fire tear gas as more than 250,000 rally nationwide for school funding
text:
PARIS (AP) — Police fired tear gas to control crowds in Paris and elsewhere in France on Tuesday as more than a quarter of a million people rallied nationwide to support high school students demanding more education funding, according to government figures. The protests increased pressure on the administration of outgoing President Emmanuel Macron.
As pupils blockaded high schools, large crowds waving flags and placards gathered in Marseille, Strasbourg and other cities. The demonstrations showed how protests that began at a high school in the Paris region in mid-September have grown into a nationwide movement — the latest of many that have marked Macron’s nearly decade-long tenure.
“We need to listen to them,” said Léa Monimart, an adult demonstrator in the northern city of Lille. “They are 17 years old; they are not completely clueless, and they know what they are talking about. It’s important to show that there are adults who support them.”
The Interior Ministry estimated that 266,000 people took part in demonstrations across the country on Tuesday, including 56,000 in Paris, where small groups of protesters clashed with riot officers at a city square at the end of a largely peaceful march.
Nearly 500 people were detained Tuesday, the ministry said. The widespread use of arrests, tear gas and riot-control weapons against teenagers is fueling defiance and angering some parents and teachers. Some student groups called for new protests Thursday.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the police response had been proportionate in “almost all cases” and that the protests had at times turned into riots, requiring police intervention.
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the government and school leaders must listen to students’ concerns and find solutions.
Questioned in parliament on Tuesday about the protest movement, Lecornu denounced “ultra violence” threatening schools. Responding to criticism of police tactics, he pledged that any “accidents” would be investigated and described allegations that the police are racist as a “lie.”
Class boycotts with police making thousands of arrests
More than two weeks of class boycotts and school blockades, and policing that has led to more than 6,500 arrests, mostly of minors, have become a flashpoint in the early days of the presidential election campaign.
Felix Barney, a university student, described the police response as disproportionate, saying it doesn’t make “any sense to hit minors.”
“Riot police, batons, rubber bullets, tear gas,” said Aurélien Le Coq, a lawmaker with the far-left France Unbowed party. Its presidential candidate is strongly backing the protests.
The violence is “absolutely unbearable,” Le Coq said.
Nuñez defended police tactics despite a growing number of severe injuries blamed on officers’ riot-control weapons. In the latest case, a 15-year-old boy lost a hand Monday in an incident involving a police stun grenade. He said 715 officers had been injured.
The teenage protesters have struck a chord amid widespread discontent in France. Frustrations extend beyond immediate difficulties, such as fuel prices that have soared because of the Iran war, to broader concerns about constraints on public spending, rising poverty and wealth inequality under Macron, who can’t run for a third consecutive term.
Against that backdrop, pupils’ complaints that education funding shortfalls are endangering their futures have found a sympathetic audience.
“You say ‘young people are the future,’ so listen to them,” read a handwritten placard attached to a metal barrier outside a Paris school.
Ministry offers online portal for complaints
At the Hélène Boucher lycée, or high school, in Paris’ 20th district, protesters tipped over trash cans and bicycles onto their sides to create a makeshift barricade.
Like hundreds of others around the country, the school was closed. Authorities began shutting schools last week to take some steam out of the demonstrations after widespread damage to schools and mounting injuries among staff, students and police. Classes were totally or partially suspended on Tuesday at 891 schools, according to the Education Ministry.
Facing accusations that it was ignoring protesters, the ministry launched an online portal inviting high school students to anonymously describe the difficulties they face at school and the changes they want to see.
Student protests have drawn attention to rundown classrooms
At Hélène Boucher, parents and other adults positioned themselves on Tuesday between protesters and police keeping watch.
“They are our children. Teachers, parents, federations, we all share the same goal: the protection of children’s rights, and it is a legitimate right to demonstrate and to make demands,” said Emilia Sichili Suriam, who is a member of an association of parents.
Demonstrators have voiced a range of grievances, often centering on a lack of resources and opportunities for students in disadvantaged schools, despite the promise of France’s national motto: “Liberty, Equality, Fraternity.”
Students have drawn attention to rundown classrooms that lack basics such as desks and chairs, become sweltering in summer without air conditioning and, in some cases, are infested with rats. Other common complaints include staff shortages and exhausting workloads. French high school students’ compulsory classroom hours are among the highest in Europe.
Suzanne Nijdam, president of the federation of student associations, vowed that demonstrations would continue until authorities address the complaints.
“So, we really need to act now, and it’s in the government’s hands, to see these demands through to the end,” she said. “It’s a matter of political priority, a matter of prioritizing the youth and the future of our country.”
Neighboring Belgium is also seeing student protests. More than 30 were arrested Tuesday and several police injured in the eastern city of Liege, and smaller protests were held in Brussels and other cities.
___

title: Remembering a beloved family farm dog
text:
In 1948, my maternal grandparents, Florian and Lucille Yeaton, brought home Bonnie, the runt of a border collie litter purchased in Farmington. This scrappy pup caught Grampa’s attention by fearlessly wrestling with littermates twice her size.
They took her to their Mercer farmhouse, where she slept on a horsehair blanket behind the wood cookstove. However, their hopes for a collie to herd sheep and dairy cows dimmed as Bonnie’s weight plummeted.
As a last resort, Grammy Lue wrapped Bonnie in the blanket and, in a gamble, placed her in the pigpen with a 250-pound sow nursing six piglets.
“We’ll know by day’s end whether the sow takes to her,” Grammy said to Grampa.
For 10 days, Bonnie nursed alongside the pink piglets, thriving under her unlikely foster mother’s warmth and care. Her weight — scarcely three pounds — more than doubled. Within two months, she was racing between the farmhouse and the barn.
My grandparents initially wondered if such an unusual start would leave a lasting mark. It did, but not the one they feared. Bonnie matured into an extraordinarily intelligent working dog, consistently proving her capabilities in protecting her family and livestock.
One summer afternoon in 1953, my 5-year-old brother, Robert, came face-to-face with a rabid fox behind the barn. Bonnie didn’t attack. Instead, she steadily nipped at Robert’s heels, driving him back toward the farmhouse while keeping her body between him and the fox. Grampa killed the fox with his shotgun.
A year later, Robert and our cousin, Cheryl, accidentally started a barn fire while playing with matches. Bonnie’s frantic barking alerted the family before anyone smelled smoke. Grampa fought the flames with pails of rainwater from the cistern, Mother smothered them with wet blankets, and Grammy herded the frightened livestock into the pasture. Together, they saved the barn.
But Bonnie’s greatest feat occurred on a sweltering August day in 1958.
While wading in the Sandy River to cool off, my 6-year-old twin brother, Don, was swept into the deep channel. Mother dove in after him but couldn’t dog-paddle fast enough to close the gap as he drifted downstream.
Bonnie understood the river’s currents better than either of them. Instead of immediately jumping in, she sprinted along the high bank, tracking Don as he fought to keep his head above water. Nearly 300 feet downriver, she launched off the bank, entered the current just ahead of the hairpin rapids, clamped onto his shirt collar, and hauled him onto a gravel bar.
The next morning, Don, still shaken, sat beside Grampa in the milking parlor. From his three-legged stool, Grampa squirted warm milk to the waiting barn cats and Bonnie, as he did every morning. Watching Bonnie lick her whiskers, my twin laughed through his tears and pulled her close.
The day before, she had saved his life — that morning, she helped restore his spirit.
Age never dulled her instincts. Shortly after midnight in October 1961, Don and I woke to growls rising from the pumpkin pine floorboards at the foot of our bed.
“Why’s Bonnie growling?” we yelled into the dark.
“Might be a bear in the barnyard,” Grampa answered from the adjacent bedroom. “She found fresh tracks in the orchard yesterday.”
He lit a kerosene lantern and retrieved the 12-gauge from above the kitchen door. Bonnie paced and whined at the latch. The second it lifted, she shot through the doorway and bolted toward the pigpen, her dark silhouette framed by a huge harvest moon.
“You boys go back to bed,” Grammy barked.
We obeyed but opened our bedroom window to listen. The hogs were squealing, Bonnie was barking, and a single shotgun blast cracked across the farm. Then everything went deadly quiet.
The next 10 minutes felt like an hour before Grampa and Bonnie returned to the kitchen.
“She chased a bear clean out of the pigpen,” he said, still catching his breath. “The pen door’s stove to hell, but the hogs are fine.”
Two nights later, a few miles from our farm, Ralph True shot the same bear after it killed one of his sheep. The boar weighed 490 pounds.
“Its front paws,” he told Grampa, “were the size of dinner plates.”
When cancer took Bonnie in April 1962, Grampa wrapped her one last time in the ratty horsehair blanket she’d slept on her entire life and carried her up the knoll to the apple orchard — her favorite spot on the farm. He dug her grave that night by moonlight, working past the frost line with a pickaxe and shovel. The next afternoon, my three siblings and I picked yellow daffodils from the south side of the farmhouse and planted them on her grave.
That evening, my heartbroken 5-year-old sister, Gale, barely ate her supper. When the meal was over, she quietly walked behind the cookstove and scraped her plate into Bonnie’s enamel bowl.
In the morning, her eyes lit up at the sight of an empty bowl.
Years later, E.B. White gave me the words for what Bonnie meant to our family: “A really companionable and indispensable dog is an accident of nature. You can’t get it by breeding for it, and you can’t buy it with money.”
Ron Joseph of Sidney is the author of “Bald Eagles, Bear Cubs, and Hermit Bill: Memories of a Maine Wildlife Biologist,” published by Islandport Press.

title: To tackle nicotine addiction, we need federal resources
text:
I agree with the concern expressed about protecting Maine youth from nicotine addiction (“Susan Collins questions Trump’s FDA nominee about vapes, drugs for rare diseases,” Sept. 24). But if we are going to talk about protecting children, we should also talk about what has happened to the federal infrastructure responsible for tobacco prevention.
On April 1, 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Office on Smoking and Health — the nation’s primary federal tobacco-prevention office — was essentially dismantled. Approximately 200 staff and contractors were terminated. The Tips From Former Smokers campaign was ended, and surveillance systems used to track tobacco use and cessation trends have been degraded.
That matters because the statistics we rely on to understand youth vaping, nicotine-pouch use and other tobacco trends don’t simply appear. They require ongoing federal surveillance and scientific expertise.
Congress ultimately preserved tobacco-control funding for FY2026, yet the Office on Smoking and Health had not been restored.
Sen. Susan Collins deserves credit for questioning a nominee about youth vaping. But as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, she also has an important responsibility to protect the federal tobacco-prevention infrastructure that Maine and other states depend upon.
If we truly want to protect Maine children, we need more than hearings about nicotine. We need the data, science and public health programs to prevent addiction.
Mary Lou Warn
Winslow

title: UK novelist and former politician jailed for lying in libel case, dies at 86
text:
Jeffrey Archer, UK novelist and former politician jailed for lying in libel case, dies at 86
Jeffrey Archer, a British bestselling author who sold more than 300 million book copies in his career and a former politician who was jailed for lying in a high-profile libel case, died Monday.
Reuters reported that Archer died one day before his final novel, "Adam and Eve," was due to be published.
Archer's publisher said the novelist "died suddenly and peacefully at home...between writing seasons." He was 86 years old.
The novelist sold more than 300 million copies of his books, spent over five years on the New York Times bestseller list, and found fans around the world with his pacy thrillers, among them the 1976 debut "Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less" and 1979's mass-selling "Kane & Abel."
According to BBC, Archer was elected MP for the Lincolnshire constituency of Louth in 1969. He served as an MP for five years before becoming the Conservative Party's deputy chairman.
His career in politics, however, was paused in 2001 when he was sentenced to spend four years for perjury and perverting the course of justice.
Archer, BBC reported, was found to have lied in libel action he had brought against The Daily Star newspaper, in which he was awarded £500,000 in damages.
The Star had alleged Archer had slept with a sex worker.
"The peer was found by the court to have perverted the course of justice by asking a former friend to give him a false alibi, and producing fake diary entries to back up his story," BBC reported. "He was also found to have perjured himself on oath during the libel trial."
After only serving two years of his sentence, Archer was released and returned to the House of Lords until he retired in 2024.
Last week, Archer also returned to his former school to promote his last book.
"It's wonderful to come back. What I got a real thrill about when I was walking towards the library is seeing the young boys and girls and thinking, 'that's the next generation'," Archer said at Wellington School.
BBC said Archer, who had celebrated his 60th wedding anniversary with his wife this year, was due to attend the Cheltenham Festival on Saturday to discuss his final novel.

title: Deaf cheer team competes in its first hearing competition
text:
FARIBAULT, Minn. (InvestigateTV) – Minnesota’s only all-deaf high school cheerleading team became the first in its school history to perform in a hearing competition.
In January, the Minnesota State Academy for the Deaf (MSAD) Trojan cheer team competed in their first cheerleading competition of 2026.
MSAD cheerleaders have been tumbling out of Faribault since the 1940’s and have opened the door for 18-year-old Mya Palmer and 16-year-old Sophia Nelson to try something new.
“I like doing the stunts. I’m a base, and I love getting ready and lifting our cheerleader,” Palmer said.
“Cheerleading is kind of random for me, but I like it so far,” Nelson added.
The team is often cheering in the National Deaf Cheer Competition or the Great Plains Schools for the Deaf competitions.
Going into their first hearing competition, coach Marika Ulrich said the Trojans will sign throughout cheer routines.
“We actually rely heavily on visual cues and the drum, which cues us in. It tells us the rhythm of the cheer,” Ulrich said. “We’ll move to the rhythm, like clap our hands, do the jive, that kind of thing, and do our school mascot, the Trojan sign.”
Coach Ulrich is deaf and Coach Miller has a deaf daughter but is hearing. They say having both leading the squad is an advantage.
“It really helps having two coaches because she’s able to instruct, so they’re understanding what I’m saying and then they’re also able to see me do the cheers, so then they can see the visual,” Miller explained.
The Trojans have no doubt they can get the job done together.
The team was the only group registered in their division, therefore they did not place in the competition.
In February 2026, the team earned third place in the Greater Plains Schools for the Deaf cheerleading competition.

title: Bangor police partner with Red Cross for blood drive
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) — The Bangor Police Department teamed up with the American Red Cross to host a blood drive at the donation center on Hammond St. Tuesday.
Local Red Cross leaders said donations have been down since discontinuing mobile blood drives earlier this year.
Partnering with area police departments helps get the word out and bring more volunteers in through the doors.
“Our intent and our hope is that it will encourage people to make an appointment to give blood, and they really have come out in full force today. The police officers themselves are on the docket and community members who support the police are here as well,” said Caroline King, the executive director of the Northern and Eastern Maine Chapter of the Red Cross.
“It’s about helping people and having emergency care services available if something terrible happens. I know that they have shortages throughout the country. Obviously anything that we can do here in our community to help other communities, we should do that,” said Sgt. Jeremy Brock of the Bangor Police Department.
As of 4 p.m. Tuesday, the drive had collected 22 pints of blood and counting.
Those who missed the event can schedule an appointment at RedCrossBlood.org.

John Woodman, 61, was operating the excavator at a job site off Bull Run Road in Gray, where Shaw Brothers and Unitil were working on a petroleum pipeline, according to the Cumberland County Sheriff’s Office.

title: A child rape suspect is expected to become a community’s next police chief. Here’s why
text:
ELIZABETH, La. (KPLC/Gray News) — Leaders in a Louisiana community are responding to the likelihood that a candidate accused of raping two children is set to become their next police chief.
Elizabeth, a village in Allen Parish with around 400 residents, is scheduled to elect its next police chief in November. One of the candidates was recently arrested on rape charges, and now the other has announced that he is stepping down from the race.
Christopher Paul, 48, was arrested in early September after he was accused of raping two 13-year-old girls 20 years ago. He faces two counts of second-degree rape.
Elizabeth Mayor Mandy Green reminded residents in a Facebook post that Paul has not been convicted of a crime, and he is presumed innocent until proven guilty. She also said she and the village’s Board of Aldermen have no authority to change the ballot under state law.
But a big change could also be coming to how Elizabeth chooses its police chief.
During a special-called meeting Friday afternoon, the village’s Board of Aldermen approved an ordinance to put an item on the Dec. 12 ballot that would change the police chief position from an elected position to an appointed position, if voted in.
It is unclear whether the proposition stemmed from the current situation and when it would go into effect. KPLC reached out to village officials, but they declined to comment or did not return our phone calls.
In her post, Green invited residents to attend the village’s next monthly meeting on Oct. 12 to voice their concerns.
“Moving forward, my administration will always act in the best interests of our community. Together with the Board of Aldermen, we remain committed to total transparency, maintaining an open-door policy, and navigating these circumstances together with you,” she wrote.
Paul’s opponent, Zachary LaCaze, said he withdrew after learning that his candidacy violated the Hatch Act because he works for the federal government. LaCaze was running as a nonpartisan candidate, while Paul is running as a Republican. LaCaze said that when asked to choose between his job and the race, he decided to keep his job to continue supporting his family.
The Secretary of State’s Office said Tuesday it has not yet received LaCaze’s withdrawal notice, but when it does, Paul will be elected to the position since he is running unopposed. He is eligible to hold office unless convicted of a felony.
The Youth Peace & Justice Foundation, a national nonprofit that aims to prevent violence against children, called for Paul to voluntarily step aside from the race while the case against him is pending.
The new chief is set to take office on Jan. 1.

title: Michael Bay in ‘Early Talks’ For New ‘Transformers’ Movie
text:
Michael Bay in ‘Early Talks’ to Direct A New ‘Transformers’ Movie
It looks like a new era of Transformers movies is about to begin — and it looks a lot like the old one.
According to Deadline, Paramount (or do we have to call it Skydance now?) is going back to the team that first turned the Hasbro toys into a massive live-action blockbuster franchise to do it again. Per their report, Steven Spielberg — who produced the first Transformers movie, and then remained an executive producer throughout the franchise — is coming back to “lead the creative direction for the eighth live-action installment.”
But that’s not all. They say that Michael Bay is “in early talks to return as director.”
READ MORE: Peter Cullen’s Final Transformers Performance Is a Heartbreaker
Bay directed the first five of the seven previous live-action Transformers films, starting with 2007’s Transformers, and continuing through 2017’s Transformers: The Last Knight. (The two subsequent movies, Bumblebee and Transformers: Rise of the Beasts, were prequels, directed by Travis Knight and Steven Caple Jr., respectively.)
While the Transformers movies under Bay never got great reviews, and their critical reception got worse and worse as time went on, all but his final film were gigantic box office hits, with the franchise peaking with 2011’s Transformers: Dark of the Moon, which earned more than $1.12 billion worldwide.
While Bumblebee and Rise of the Beasts fared a little better with critics, both underperformed in theaters — at least compared to the Bay movies. Bumblebee earned $467 million worldwide, while Rise of the Beasts grossed $441 million, the lowest total for any of the seven Transformers to date.
So if you want to know why Paramount would want to bring back Spielberg and Bay, that’s why.

title: Inspection finds Preble Street is not following parts of Portland shelter management plan
text:
A recent city of Portland inspection found that the Elena’s Way shelter in the Bayside neighborhood is not following elements of its shelter management plan, including its responsibility to monitor safety in the area around the facility.
According to an inspection report produced by the city’s planning department, shelter operator Preble Street failed to meet a requirement that staff conduct hourly walks around the building and only partially met other requirements regarding litter and loitering.
As the city prepares for the building to host a winter warming shelter starting next month, neighbors are questioning how the city plans to mitigate the negative impacts of potentially doubling the number of shelter guests on any given night.
The Elena’s Way inspection report said Preble Street’s management plan includes a commitment to have a staff member, “equipped with a walkie-talkie for safety and emergency use,” walk the perimeter of the building to move along people who may be loitering, and pick up any litter on the sidewalks.
But during the inspection, the organization informed city staff that exterior walks in the evening are not being conducted due to safety concerns. The report states that city staff reminded the shelter that the walks are “intended to support a safe environment for both guests and the surrounding neighborhood.”
Danielle Smaha, senior director of communications at Preble Street, said the organization is looking into how it can appeal the report, “because we don’t feel like it accurately reflects the work that we are doing at Elena’s Way.”
The annual inspection was conducted on the morning of Aug. 28. An inspection at the city-run Homeless Services Center on Riverside Street the same day found that facility to be in compliance with all requirements.
The report on the Elena’s Way shelter said city staff observed “significant loitering around the facility” by non-clients, and staff encouraged Preble Street to work with Portland police on those concerns.
The report said staff have also observed and received complaints regarding significant litter around a designated cleanup zone that is Preble Street’s responsibility.
In response to the inspection results, Smaha said Preble Street is “deeply committed to continuous improvement in all our programs, strengthening our collaborative efforts, and remaining an active, accountable partner in all that we do.”
Smaha said Preble Street works in “close, daily partnership” with the city, Portland police, medical providers, neighborhood stakeholders and “many others to meet the needs of the people we serve, as well as the people who live and work in Portland.”
Kevin Kraft, the city’s director of planning and urban development, said the annual inspections are intended to confirm that a project is operating in accordance with its approved plans.
He said if issues are identified, the operator is notified and given an opportunity and a deadline to correct them. If a site remains out of compliance, the city can pursue enforcement under the code of ordinances. Staff said follow-up inspections will likely be conducted.
Preble Street, based in Portland, operates two low-barrier adult shelters in Portland and one in Bangor. The 40-bed Elena’s Way shelter, at 5 Portland St., opened in 2022. The organization also runs Joe’s Place, a newly redeveloped teen shelter and resource center on Cumberland Avenue.
Last month, city officials announced that the Biddeford nonprofit Seeds of Hope will operate a nightly warming shelter in the basement level of Elena’s Way from November to April. The program was awarded $361,000 in MaineHousing funding last week, but the specific details on the operation are unclear. Officials previously shared a goal of the warming shelter having a capacity of 50-60 people.
City Councilor Sarah Michniewicz, who lives in the neighborhood and serves on the Elena’s Way advisory board, said she has several concerns with the warming shelter proposal and criticized the city’s process in approving the plan.
“The existing shelter is already not meeting the conditions of its approval,” she said. “This is a staff that works with these clients, and if they don’t feel safe going out and walking around, how is the community supposed to feel safe?”
Michniewicz pointed out that the conditional use standards for Elena’s Way stipulate that the sleeping area be limited to the upper level, and that a maximum of 40 shelter guests are allowed at one time. She said while the impact on the neighborhood is a concern, she’s also thinking about how it will impact the existing shelter guests.
Ned Payne, who owns a multiunit building next door on Portland Street, recently sent an email to the Elena’s Way advisory board that said groups of people often congregate on his front stairs and inject or smoke drugs. He said that on Sept. 27, it occurred over a 13-hour span, and that children and families that live in his building have to “sidestep” the activity.
“Not once did someone from Preble Street clear this during a ’round,’ which they are supposed to do hourly as a condition of their license,” he said. “The police also did not intervene, despite knowing this is a problem area and having driven by it multiple times.”
Payne questioned why the city is allowing the winter shelter when it “can’t manage the current environment.”
City spokesperson Jessica Grondin said Tuesday that using the space as a warming shelter does not require council approval because it is a temporary use, but that staff will likely add conditions the shelter operators will need to meet. Michniewicz said she believes changing the conditions at the building should “absolutely” require council action.
Councilor Kate Sykes said the recent inspections show that the city is doing a good job at the Homeless Services Center to meet the requirements set, but she cautioned against using the reports as “a scorecard” between shelters.
As election season moves forward, Sykes said, she believes the political conversation has framed compassion and public safety as “competing values.”
“Safety and justice are things the government has to deliver together,” she said. “People staying in shelters deserve to be safe. Shelter workers deserve to be safe, and neighbors deserve to be safe.”

title: These Winter Storms Could Bury New England This Winter
text:
The staff at The Weather Channel has released their list of names that could be used for severe winter storms over the winter of 2026/2027.
A total of 21 names have been selected for the upcoming winter. They are in alphabetical order, with the exception of the letters that were skipped, of course.
Why Do We Name Winter Storms?
The practice of naming severe winter storms first started in 2012. Believe it or not, the National Weather Service has nothing to do with naming winter storms. While the National Weather Service names tropical storms and hurricanes, it is actually the Weather Channel that started naming winter storms.
Obviously, not every storm gets a name. If they named every storm, we’d go through the list of names in about a month. In order for a storm to get a name, it must bring widespread, high-impact snow or ice that prompts National Weather Service winter storm, blizzard, or ice storm warnings to qualify for a name. Naming lists also avoid current Atlantic and eastern Pacific hurricane names for the next six years, along with retired names tied to especially historic or destructive storms.
According to the Weather Channel there are some good reasons why they do this. You can read more about it on the website.
