title: Arkansas campaign ad sparks conservative backlash for portraying lazy welfare recipient as white
text:
LITTLE ROCK, Ark. (AP) — A new video from Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders was standard issue Republican messaging for promoting her state’s stricter rules for people on Medicaid. No more could able-bodied people lounge around while receiving taxpayer-funded healthcare, she said — they needed to work.
But the decision to portray an unemployed moocher as a young, white, cheeseball-chomping gamer named Brad upset some conservative commentators last week. Five decades after Ronald Reagan popularized the “welfare queen” trope about people living luxuriously while not working, they wanted to know why the video wasn’t featuring a Black woman instead.
“Republicans don’t have the balls to do this ad with ‘Shaniqua’ as the villain,” posted Matt Walsh, a conservative writer. “Even though that would actually be an accurate portrayal of the problem at hand.”
Sean Davis, co-founder of the Federalist website, wrote that “our government has systematically discriminated against white men for decades now, and yet now has the audacity to dishonestly mock young white men as welfare queens.”
Never mind that the video was about Medicaid and not welfare, or that most Medicaid recipients in Arkansas are white. The outrage was a reminder of how old tropes are “chronically accessible” images in some voters’ minds, said Ange-Marie Hancock, author of “The Politics of Disgust and the Public Identity of the ‘Welfare Queen.’”
She thinks the Arkansas video was supposed to appeal to older voters living with unemployed adult children. But conservatives could only focus on race, Hancock said, because the idea of a Black welfare abuser has worked for them for decades.
“The longer race and gendered history really points to ideas that African Americans are lazy, they don’t do the right thing,” she said.
The debate that streaked across social media was the latest example of how conservatives have recently wrestled with racist views. Last month, a Texas political candidate named Bo French posted a picture of nonwhite students cheering at a University of Texas football game, saying “the problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.” Some Republicans denounced French’s post, while it was embraced by those who fear the country’s changing demographics.
Sanders, who is running for reelection this year, “stands by the ad,” said Jordan Powell, her campaign manager.
“We should never confiscate money from hard-working Arkansans to give it away to those who simply choose not to work at all,” Powell told The Associated Press in an emailed statement.
Origins of the ‘welfare queen’ trope in American politics
The “welfare queen” trope is often used to advance restrictions on public assistance programs.
While unsuccessfully running for president in 1976, Reagan complained about a woman in Chicago who was using “80 names, 30 addresses, 12 Social Security cards” to game the system. The story was embellished, but Reagan worked to reshape public assistance programs after winning the White House in 1980.
Allison Butler, author of “The Judgment of Gender: How Women are Centered and Silenced in Pop Culture,” said the debate perpetuated a powerful myth that women of color were siphoning government assistance.
“When you deconstructed that narrative and actually tried to find the source of it … there was no woman of color who wouldn’t get a job and had multiple televisions and a Mercedes-Benz,” Butler said.
Barry Jefferson, president of the NAACP Arkansas State Conference, has condemned the Sanders ad for reducing low-income people to a stereotype where poverty is seen as a flaw. It ignores the complexities that make it harder for low-income people, regardless of race, to support themselves, he said.
“We shouldn’t betray anyone because they are asking for help and they don’t meet your standards,” Jefferson said.
Breaking down the demographics of Medicaid
Created in 1965 as a joint federal and state health insurance program, Medicaid offers free or low-cost medical coverage to people with limited income including the elderly, children or adults with disabilities who cannot work. Nearly 66 million people were enrolled in Medicaid as of June, according to the Medicaid.gov website.
Over 38% of beneficiaries between the ages of 0-64 are white, according to 2024 data from research organization KFF. Nearly 19% are Black.
More work requirements for some Medicaid beneficiaries kicked in across the U.S. this year under President Donald Trump’s big 2025 tax cut and policy law. A handful of Republican-led states, including Arkansas, are going beyond what the law calls for to prevent fraud including demanding more documentation if someone is too medically frail to work.
In July, Sanders soft-launched mandating that healthy people ages 19 to 64 find work, volunteer or attend school at least 80 hours per month to stay in the Arkansas Health and Opportunity for Me Medicaid program, or ARHOME.
Robert Coon, managing partner at Impact Management Group, a political consulting and public-opinion firm with an Arkansas office, said that welfare work requirement policy is generally favored in Arkansas.
But suggestions the person in the ad should be Black are “overtly racist” and “inaccurate,” Coon said.
About 60% of ARHOME recipients are white and around 18% are Black, according to recent data from the state Department of Human Services.
Why Black people often experience need at a higher rate
Right-wing rhetoric about Black Americans and public assistance often ignores how generations of structural racism have produced economic disparities that contribute to their disproportionate participation in these programs.
Fewer Black people than white people overall use social service programs like Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or food stamps. But at roughly 13% of the U.S. population, Black people make up the largest overrepresentation of any racial group. They are 18.5% and 25%, respectively, of Medicaid and SNAP recipients.
Those statistics reflect an extremely difficult road for poor Black communities looking to rise out of poverty and build generational wealth.
Arkansas Democratic congressional candidate Chris Jones, who is Black, grew up in a family relying on food stamps. A welfare recipient is not “looking for a way out of work,” but “for a way forward,” he told AP in a statement.
The bigger question, Jones said, is not race but “why so many people who are working hard still struggle to afford groceries, housing, health care and the basic necessities of life.”
___
Tang reported from Phoenix.

title: Rumford to make changes to solid waste collection
text:
RUMFORD — A public hearing on proposed changes to the weekly curbside solid waste collection rules is set for 6 p.m. Thursday, Oct. 15, at Rumford Falls Auditorium, 145 Congress St.
Town Manager George O’Keefe told the Select Board on Sept. 24 that Archie’s Inc., of Mexico, doing business as J&J Disposal, will provide a 65-gallon container for each residence. No garbage bags or mismatched containers will be allowed at curbside.
The Select Board will present the proposed new regulations when it meets after the hearing, O’Keefe said, and if approved they would be effective sometime in November.
Archie’s will deliver the containers, which are also called toters, O’Keefe said.
“Nobody will have to come down and pick them up. And they won’t be required to pay for their first one. If the container provided is too big for a resident to handle, we’ll have smaller containers that may be provided as well,” the town manager said.
By using toters, which can be grabbed by a hydraulic arm of the waste collecting truck, O’Keefe said the company will save on labor costs that could help hold down future costs to the town for the contracted service.
“The approach is that a 65-gallon container should be sufficient for one household. We are literally limiting that to one container per household per week,” O’Keefe.
The town manager stressed that the proposed regulations are the same as other Maine towns of similar size with municipal curbside collection.
“If trash toters were not already in widespread use elsewhere in other cities and towns in Maine with municipal curbside collection,” he said, “we would not be considering it. The change is for the sake of street cleanliness and to help keep costs under control.”
O’Keefe told the board he was surprised to learn that nearly all buildings with seven or more units in town are already using dumpsters paid for by the landlords. That practice will continue.
The town will send letters to all multifamily building owners to let them know about the proposed new regulations.
There will be no change for the 18-gallon blue recycling bins that are in use.

title: Man dead after excavator overturns in Gray
text:
GRAY, Maine (WABI) - A construction worker is dead after the excavator he was operating overturned in Gray.
According to the Cumberland County Sheriff’s Office, John Woodman, 61, died at a work zone on Bull Run Rd. Monday.
Authorities say Woodman was driving up a steep hill when the excavator overturned.
WABI was told Woodman was a longtime employee of Shaw Brothers Construction.
OSHA was notified and is investigating, along with local authorities.

title: UMaine Augusta to host 45 Maine employers at job fair
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Upwards of 45 employers across more than a dozen industries will be available to meet with prospective hires Wednesday, Oct. 7, at the University of Maine Augusta’s fall job fair.
Employers will include MaineHealth, Northern Light Health, General Dynamics Bath Iron Works, Kennebec Savings Bank, Hannaford, MaineDOT and the Maine Department of Corrections, among others.
This is the first time UMA has held a fall fair; the college typically holds an annual job and resource fair in March.
“We’re adding a fall fair this year to give students and other job seekers more opportunities to connect with employers,” Kristen Eaton, vice president of external affairs, told Mainebiz. “We’re hoping to welcome 75 to 100 job seekers, including UMA students, alumni and community members.”
She noted that Bath Iron Works and MaineHealth are recruiting for full-time positions.
Most participating employers are seeking full-time and part-time workers, and several are also looking for interns, she said.
Eaton added that over one-third of participating employers use “fair chance” or “second chance” hiring practices, giving qualified applicants with criminal records an opportunity to be considered for employment.
Wednesday’s job fair will be held in the Randall Student Center at 46 University Drive in Augusta, from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.
The event is hosted in partnership with Maine CareerCenters and presented through UMA Career Connections and UMS TRANSFORMS Pathways to Careers.
The fair is free and open to the public. The list of participating employers is available at uma.edu/jobfair.

title: Testimony continues in second day of Raymond Brown murder trial
text:
MACHIAS, Maine (WABI) - Jurors heard testimony Tuesday from the medical examiner, DNA analysts, family members and a friend of Linda Maxwell in the murder trial of Raymond Brown.
Brown, 67, of Bangor, is accused of killing Maxwell, 18, of Calais, in 1984.
Body found in river
Prosecutors say Maxwell’s nude body was found at the Robbinston boat landing, floating face-up in the St. Croix River. Investigators say no clothing was ever found.
Jurors heard from first responders, including former Calais patrolman William Cody, and from Maxwell’s brother, Franklin, who said she couldn’t swim and was dating another man at the time.
Boyfriend testifies
That man, Ronald Todd Miller, took the stand and described their relationship as a good relationship.
Miller said he knew Brown through another friend but didn’t have a close relationship with him.
Miller testified about their last outing at Round Pond, saying he, Maxwell and their friends discussed who would drive.
He said Maxwell drove when they left, but Brown took over driving once they got back to Calais. Miller said he went home once they got back.
Defense questions prior statements
The defense questioned Miller about previous statements on the night they were out.
The defense asked Miller to confirm if he was upset with Maxwell for drinking too much and questioned why he let her get behind the wheel anyway.
Miller answered that he didn’t stop her.
The defense also questioned Miller about a statement to police saying he was jealous because Maxwell was speaking to others, but Miller said he did not recall saying that.
When the state questioned Miller again, he clarified he was not jealous but was bothered by the situation at the end of the night, leading him to hop off Brown’s truck and go home.
Miller said he left town in September 1984 after Maxwell’s death.
Testimony in the trial will continue Wednesday.

title: Rumford Hospital celebrates 100 years of healthcare
text:
RUMFORD — More than 200 people gathered under a pair of tents around midday Oct. 2 to celebrate Rumford Hospital’s 100 years of healthcare.
With the hospital in view under cloudy skies and sprinkles, onlookers heard from current and former staff and volunteers who spoke of the history of the hospital and how proud they are to have been part of it.
Among the speakers was retired operating room staff nurse Becky Hall. Her 37 years there included managing the operating room, directing the primary care practices and serving as vice president of Nursing and Patient Care Services. She shared some of the history of Rumford Hospital.
She began by noting that at one point, her office was in the room she was born in.
“I didn’t go far in life,” she joked. “There’s something really special about working in a small community hospital, in a community that you grew up in, taking care of your family, your neighbors, your friends. It truly is rewarding.”
In her research, Hall said that early in the 1900s there were actually two hospitals in Rumford, both in private homes. One was run by Dr. McCarty, the other by Dr. Noyes. They were just down the hill near Strathglass Park, she said.
Then, in June 1924, there was a community movement to actually bring a modern hospital to Rumford. The River Valley was growing. The mill was booming. By September of that year, a fundraising campaign was organized with a goal to raise $200,000. In four days, the committee reported that they had raised half of the money. And six days later, they had surpassed their goal with $267,000.
Groundbreaking took place in May 1925, and 18 months later the hospital construction was complete, a 57-bed hospital with a modern maternity unit. The day after it opened, the first baby, a boy, was born there.
“I’m especially proud of the work that we did for this community and beyond during the pandemic,” Hall said.
Current President Stephany Jacques said Rumford Hospital is already looking ahead to one of the most exciting investments in Rumford Hospital’s future — the renovation and expansion of our emergency department. Sen. Susan Collins secured $6.4 million in federal funding for this project and Prime Healthcare Foundation has committed to at least $1 million more as a match to that grant.
“The renovations will provide additional treatment space for ambulance and walk-in patients and allow our caregivers to work in a more modern and efficient environment. There is something especially meaningful about that investment during our centennial year. One hundred years ago, this community invested in building a hospital because people believed that local healthcare mattered. A century later, we’re continuing that work, investing in Rumford Hospital so it can serve this community for generations to come,” she said.
Barbara Belanger, president of the Rumford Hospital Auxiliary and lead volunteer currently in her 51st year of service to the hospital, said the auxiliary was established in July 1926 to bring goodwill to the Rumford Community Hospital by means of community service and fundraising.
Also present was John Welsh, who served as president and chief executive officer of Rumford Hospital for 23 years, from 1988 until his retirement on July 1, 2011. During his tenure, Welsh oversaw the hospital’s merger with Central Maine Healthcare, the transition to electronic medical records and the construction of the new patient wing, called the John H. Welsh Building.
Conducting the blessing of the hospital and the staff was the Rev. Aaron Damboise, pastor of the Parish of the Holy Savior in Rumford.
Later this month, the hospital will put together a time capsule, donated by the Thibault Remembrance Center in Rumford.

title: In grief, good memories can be comforting
text:
I, like Professor Barbara Held in the case of her sister, don’t deny that my beloved husband died (“Grief is not a problem to be solved,” Opinion, Sept. 29).
We seem to agree there is no one to be angry with — neither one of us believes in God — but, unlike her, I am depressed even though I have accepted my husband’s death. If I am wrong, and my husband is under God’s watch, I appreciate people who are believers praying for him. Yet, I think heaven is not better than being alive and by my side.
Unlike Professor Held, my good memories are comforting. I think of his laughing at my silly jokes; of being able to see his handsome face; of his listening when I needed him to calm or reassure me; and of his undying affection.
I respect Professor Held’s feeling that good memories don’t help. I feel differently. But I was happy that her last memory of her sister was “… a gift from the gods.” I wish my last recollection of my husband was as consoling. He died in agony saying, “Just kill me.”
But as Professor Held states, with a quote from Dr. Colin Murray Parkes: “The pain of grief is just as much a part of life as the joy of love.” I will endure the loneliness because of the loving memories of 51 years of marriage, and I will try to ignore the disturbing remembrances that are painful.
B. Ann Levine, Ph.D.
Kennebunk

title: Eva Marie Saint, star of ‘North by Northwest’ and ‘On the Waterfront,’ dies at 102
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — Eva Marie Saint, the pale, willowy actor who won an Academy Award for her first movie, “On the Waterfront,” and starred opposite Cary Grant in the Alfred Hitchcock thriller “North by Northwest,” has died. She was 102.
Saint, whose acting work lasted well into her 90s, died at her home in Los Angeles on Tuesday, confirmed family representative Jeff Sanderson.
Saint had one of the most spectacular debuts in Hollywood history, as the love interest of Marlon Brando’s tormented Terry Malloy in “On the Waterfront,” and her first trip to the Academy Awards was memorable too. Pregnant with her first child, Saint accepted her Oscar from Frank Sinatra and smilingly murmured a unique winner’s speech: “I think I may have the baby right here.” (Her son, Darrell, was born two days later.)
The award for the 1954 classic made her an instant star, but she soon astonished Hollywood with a firm independence that would mark her career. She refused offers of studio contracts and declined chances to follow up on her great success, explaining that she was taking time off to become acquainted with her new son. (A daughter, Laurette, was born in 1958.)
A curated career
In her first decade in Hollywood, Saint appeared in a mere seven films. She declined such top-level productions as “The Man in the Gray Flannel Suit” with Gregory Peck, “Summer and Smoke” with Laurence Harvey and “The Rainmaker” with Burt Lancaster. She credited her husband, TV and stage director Jeffrey Hayden, with persuading her to star in Hitchcock’s “North by Northwest,” the classic 1959 thriller in which Saint plays a spy who seduces Grant, but ends up falling for him.
“I vividly remember him saying, ‘Honey, I think you should find a quiet spot. I’ll take care of the children and I want you to really think about this and reread this script,’” she told Vanity Fair in 2014. “He was so right. And that’s what husbands are for.”
Instead of being put off by her selectivity, studios continued offering her starring roles in such films as “Exodus” (with Newman), “Raintree County” (Elizabeth Taylor, Montgomery Clift) and “All Fall Down,” with Warren Beatty.
She turned more to television in the 1970s and enjoyed renewed popularity in the 1980s as the mother of Cybill Shepherd in the hit sitcom “Moonlighting” and as Tom Hanks’ mother in the film comedy “Nothing in Common.” She won an Emmy for the 1990 miniseries “People Like Us,” and had roles in such 21st century movies as “Because of Winn-Dixie,” “Superman Returns” and “Winter’s Tale,” adapted from Mark Helprin’s novel of the same name. In 2021, she played Marisa Tomei’s aunt in the brief audio play “The Bus Ride,” part of “The Pack Podcast.”
Saint was married to Hayden for 65 years, until his death in 2016.
That was her real name
When Saint emerged in the public consciousness, many believed her theatrical-sounding name must have been invented. She was born with it on July 4, 1924, in Newark, New Jersey. The family moved to Delmar, a small town near Albany, New York, where her father was a Goodrich Rubber Co. manager. Eva’s goal was to become a third-grade teacher like her mother, but at Bowling Green State University in Ohio she tried out for a play and won the leading role.
After graduation, she lived with her parents and began hunting for acting jobs in Manhattan. After a fruitless year, she landed a two-line role as a telephone operator on a radio drama and soon was working steadily on soap operas and nighttime dramas, appearing for two years as Claudia on “One Man’s Family.” Network television was booming in the early 1950s, and her looks and dramatic sense made her a favorite with casting people and producers.
She credited Lee Strasberg with helping her overcome shyness
A critical turn in Saint’s career came when she auditioned before Elia Kazan and was accepted into the Actors Studio, which shaped a generation of method-actor stars. She credited acting coach Lee Strasberg with helping her overcome her shyness.
“Lee Strasberg, when he got to know me a little bit, gave me a scene to do where I had to cry in front of my peers,” she told The Santa Barbara Independent in 2009. “I worried about it, I worked on it, I tried to use what I was learning at the studio. I finally did the scene, and I cried, and my peers were crying with me. It was just an incredible moment for me.”
Saint was rejected for the single female role in the play “Mister Roberts,” but was hired to understudy the actor chosen, Jocelyn Brando, Marlon’s sister. In six frustrating months Saint never got to substitute for Brando. She finally made it to Broadway in “A Trip to Bountiful,” which she had played on television.
Kazan invited her to try out for the female lead in “On the Waterfront” by improvising a scene with Brando. She was told to try to stop a young man from entering her apartment. She told the Los Angeles Times in 2001: “All I know is that Marlon got in the door and turned on the music. We started dancing. He flicked my skirt. Kazan saw the sparks fly, and that’s how I got the part.”
__
Thomas, a former Associated Press Hollywood correspondent who died in 2014, was the primary writer of this obituary.
__
This story has been corrected to show that Saint and Hayden were married for 65 years, not 55.

title: Chart-topping R&B singer Freddie Jackson dies at 70
text:
(AP) - Grammy-nominated R&B singer Freddie Jackson, known for his smooth ’80s hits “Rock Me Tonight (For Old Times Sake)” and “You Are My Lady,” has died. He was 70.
A statement shared by his family on his official Instagram account confirmed Jackson died Monday, three days after his 70th birthday. No cause of death was provided.
“Freddie was more than a legendary voice. He was a kind, generous soul who loved his fans, his family, his friends, and his music with everything he had. For decades he gave us the songs that became the soundtrack to our love stories, our celebrations, and our most treasured memories. That gift will live on forever,” the statement read.
“To everyone who ever sang along, danced, or felt something when Freddie took the stage: thank you. You were family to him, and he carried your love with him always,” it continued.
Details regarding arrangements will be announced in the coming days.
Jackson was born and raised in Harlem, where he learned all about soul music and sang gospel at White Rock Baptist Church. He started his career in the New York club scene, eventually making his way out West with the band Mystic Merlin in the late ’70s. He soon returned to New York and released his debut album, “Rock Me Tonight,” in 1985. His distinctive voice proved to be his superpower: The album, which was quickly certified platinum by the Recording Industry Association of America, also led to his two career Grammy nominations. Those were for best new artist and best male R&B vocal performance for the single “You Are My Lady.”
“Rock Me Tonight” also created a new R&B superstar: Jackson became a mainstay of those Billboard charts and a fixture of contemporary urban radio play throughout the ’80s and early ’90s.
His sophomore album, 1987’s “Just Like the First Time,” was also certified platinum.
Jackson shared his kidney disease diagnosis in 2024
In 2024, Jackson revealed he had been diagnosed with kidney disease in a video shared to his social media accounts.
“This journey has had its challenges but I’ve decided to face it with openness and resilience,” he said in the clip. “It’s important to me that I share this with you, not just as a part of my personal story, but as a way to make a positive difference.”
At the time, Jackson also revealed he had partnered with the National Kidney Foundation to raise awareness of the disease.
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, more than 1 in 7 American adults has chronic kidney disease. As many as 9 in 10 don’t know they have it.
Chronic kidney disease is a condition where the kidneys are damaged and struggle to filter blood. As a result, excess waste and fluids remain and can lead to other health issues, such as heart disease.

title: Painting bought for $30 at estate sale sells for more than $1.3 million at auction
text:
(CNN) — A $30 find at an estate sale has turned into a million-dollar jackpot.
The small oil painting was discovered in a dark corner of a Michigan home this summer.
The buyer spotted a faint signature reading “Abercrombie, 51” and decided to take a chance.
Experts later confirmed it was Gertrude Abercrombie’s “Alderman Merriam’s Shells,” a 1951 work that had not been seen publicly in nearly 75 years.
The painting was expected to fetch up to $250,000. Instead, it sold at auction for more than $1.35 million, setting a new record for Abercrombie’s work.

title: Get your questions answered at Bangor candidate forum
text:
Bangor voters will have the chance to hear directly from the City Council and School Committee candidates seeking their support at a nonpartisan forum Wednesday evening.
The event will be hosted by the local League of Women Voters chapter in Bangor High School’s Peakes Auditorium.
Candidates taking the stage will include the 12 people vying for three open City Council seats — making up the largest pool in recent memory.

Residents can submit questions before the event by emailing bangor@lwvme.org. Questions at the event will be read by a moderator.
The BDN has profiled all 12 City Council candidates. You can read about them here and hear directly from them about how they’d solve Bangor’s biggest issues here.

title: Augusta Schools proposes closing Hussey Elementary, expanding Farrington
text:
Augusta Schools proposes closing Hussey Elementary, expanding Farrington
The Augusta superintendent's office has formally announced plans to close Hussey Elementary and expand Farrington Elementary, but the decision is ultimately up to voters on Election Day.
Augusta Schools proposes closing Hussey Elementary, expanding Farrington
The Augusta superintendent's office has formally announced plans to close Hussey Elementary and expand Farrington Elementary, but the decision is ultimately up to voters on Election Day.
The Augusta superintendent's office has formally announced plans to close Hussey Elementary and expand Farrington Elementary, but the decision is ultimately up to local voters on Election Day.
The proposal calls for additions to Farrington Elementary and the closure of the Lillian Hussey School. The planned additions to Farrington include a universal pre-K model, 19 new classrooms and a designated STEM space.
The total cost of the project is about $53.5 million, to be reimbursed by the state. Superintendent Mike Tracy, of Augusta Schools, said construction would not be paid for by Augusta taxpayers.
Tracy said the project was approved under the state's prior district funding model, making it the last project in Maine to qualify for full state reimbursement.
"I think it's a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity, especially with the law that just changed where local towns will have to have a local share for any future building projects," Tracy said. "So, the fact that we're on the last project at 100% state-funded is a really big deal."
The new state rule requiring a local contribution started July 1.
The district said that if approved, construction would begin in summer 2028 and finish in summer 2030.

In 2021, she played Marisa Tomei’s aunt in the brief audio play “The Bus Ride,” part of “The Pack Podcast.”
Saint was married to Hayden for 65 years, until his death in 2016.
That was her real name
When Saint emerged in the public consciousness, many believed her theatrical-sounding name must have been invented. She was born with it on July 4, 1924, in Newark, New Jersey. The family moved to Delmar, a small town near Albany, New York, where her father was a Goodrich Rubber Co. manager. Eva’s goal was to become a third-grade teacher like her mother, but at Bowling Green State University in Ohio she tried out for a play and won the leading role.
After graduation, she lived with her parents and began hunting for acting jobs in Manhattan. After a fruitless year, she landed a two-line role as a telephone operator on a radio drama and soon was working steadily on soap operas and nighttime dramas, appearing for two years as Claudia on “One Man’s Family.” Network television was booming in the early 1950s, and her looks and dramatic sense made her a favorite with casting people and producers.
She credited Lee Strasberg with helping her overcome shyness
A critical turn in Saint’s career came when she auditioned before Elia Kazan and was accepted into the Actors Studio, which shaped a generation of method-actor stars. She credited acting coach Lee Strasberg with helping her overcome her shyness.
“Lee Strasberg, when he got to know me a little bit, gave me a scene to do where I had to cry in front of my peers,” she told The Santa Barbara Independent in 2009. “I worried about it, I worked on it, I tried to use what I was learning at the studio. I finally did the scene, and I cried, and my peers were crying with me. It was just an incredible moment for me.”
Saint was rejected for the single female role in the play “Mister Roberts,” but was hired to understudy the actor chosen, Jocelyn Brando, Marlon’s sister. In six frustrating months Saint never got to substitute for Brando. She finally made it to Broadway in “A Trip to Bountiful,” which she had played on television.
Kazan invited her to try out for the female lead in “On the Waterfront” by improvising a scene with Brando. She was told to try to stop a young man from entering her apartment. She told the Los Angeles Times in 2001: “All I know is that Marlon got in the door and turned on the music. We started dancing. He flicked my skirt. Kazan saw the sparks fly, and that’s how I got the part.”
__
Thomas, a former Associated Press Hollywood correspondent who died in 2014, was the primary writer of this obituary.
__
This story has been corrected to show that Saint and Hayden were married for 65 years, not 55.

title: Varsity Maine boys soccer poll has first unanimous No. 1 of 2026
text:
Brunswick won the clash of the top two teams in the Varsity Maine boys soccer poll, so it’s no surprise the Dragons are now the unanimous No. 1. They took over first place last week, but only by one point over Lewiston. But after Brunswick’s 3-2 victory over the Blue Devils last Tuesday, every voter picked the Dragons No. 1 and Lewiston No. 2.
Brunswick is the first unanimous No. 1 in the 2026 boys soccer rankings. In the previous four polls, the first-place votes have been split fairly evenly each week. By the way, Brunswick and Lewiston face off again Thursday in Brunswick.
Thornton Academy, the final unbeaten team in Class A South, jumps from fifth to third. Edward Little moves from seventh to sixth, and Scarborough from 10th to seventh.
Hall-Dale joins the rankings for the first time this fall. The Bulldogs have won seven straight since dropping their season opener to Monmouth Academy.

title: Eligible for a payout? Some Equifax customers could get up to $280 in $100 million settlement
text:
(Gray News) - Equifax has agreed to a proposed $100 million settlement over allegedly incorrect credit scores.
A class action lawsuit alleges the credit bureau reported lower scores for about 4 million people in March and April of 2022, potentially affecting applications for mortgages, car loans and credit cards.
Equifax denies any wrongdoing but did agree to the proposed settlement.
According to the settlement’s website, those eligible to be part of the settlement were sent either an email or physical notice. Those who did receive a notice can file their claim or opt out of the settlement online. Claims can also be mailed to a PO Box.
Settlement class members have until Dec. 28 to file a claim and until Nov. 27 to opt out of the settlement.
Each person who files a claim could receive a payment from $95 to $280, depending on how many claims are submitted. The exact amount each person will receive will not be known until all claims are submitted and validated.
A final hearing on the settlement is scheduled for Jan. 22, 2027.

title: Several injured in Route 1 crash near Hancock-Sullivan bridge
text:
HANCOCK, Maine (WABI) - Several people were injured in a crash on Route 1 near the Hancock-Sullivan bridge Tuesday afternoon.
Maine State Police said the crash happened around 2:30 p.m. when an SUV driven by Amy Houck, 53, of Steuben was traveling east and was rear-ended by a vehicle driven by Nicholas McAfee, 36, of North Little Rock, Arkansas.
The impact caused the SUV to roll over. A passenger in the SUV, Cathy Grant, 66, of Milbridge, was taken to a local hospital with serious injuries.
The other vehicle went off the road, crossed a small field and hit a tree. A passenger in that vehicle was also taken to the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.
Both drivers had minor injuries, according to State Police.
Route 1 was closed for several hours while the crash was investigated and reconstructed.

title: Live updates: Susan Collins and Troy Jackson debate for the first time
text:
Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson are set to debate Tuesday, the first time voters will see them share a stage.
Democrats have long coveted Collins’ seat, which she has held since 1996. But she’s never faced a reelection battle quite like this. The opponent Democratic voters nominated in June, Graham Platner, abruptly withdrew from the race after a woman credibly accused him of sexual assault. (Platner has denied the allegation.) Jackson was nominated to replace Platner at a convention later that month.
Most polls show Jackson ahead of Collins, but the incumbent is outspending him on the airwaves. Tonight’s debate is certain to feature talk about the cost of living, the Iran War, President Donald Trump and Collins’ recent spate of negative national press. Follow along with us live here.
That’s a wrap!
Thanks for following along with us. Until next time.
-Kirby Wilson and Billy Kobin
But I didn’t see anything game changing. Three more debates to go!
-Kirby Wilson
“To be effective in the Senate, you need knowledge, experience, seniority and relationships. That combination has allowed me to pass bipartisan legislation,” Collins said.
Jackson said that “I don’t owe Donald Trump and the billionaires anything. You know, I owe the people of the state everything.” He brought up again how Collins voted with Trump around 96% of the time and that she’s been fighting for “the billionaire class.”
“Tonight, Sen. Collins has told us how powerful she is, but power means nothing if you won’t use it when the people in Maine need it,” Jackson said, adding he passed legislation at the State House to lower prescription drug costs, support childcare and provide universal school meals along with sponsoring abortion access legislation.
“I’m never going to forget where I came from. I’m an everyday person that is so indebted to people who put me in this position to fight for them,” Jackson said.
The two shared a laugh when moderator Gregg Lagerquist of WGME said at the end he was going to ask both of them during the lightning round if the New England Patriots will make the playoffs.
Collins said they absolutely will, and razzed Jackson for being a Steelers fan.
Each candidate left the stage smiling.
-Kirby Wilson
-There should be more restrictions on data centers
-Mifepristone, which is a medication used for abortions, should be available.
But the candidates disagreed over:
-Whether Americans should have to show ID at the polls. (Collins: Yes. Jackson: No.)
-Whether Israel should have the same level of support from the U.S. government, less support, or more support. (Collins: the same. Jackson: less, but there was more nuance to this answer.)
-Kirby Wilson
A note on the style of the candidates
To touch on the optics of the debate or the tone so far, Collins has repeatedly gotten defensive when Jackson has criticized her. It feels safe to say Jackson has been more on offense rather than defense. Not an entirely surprising thing given the incumbent often faces plenty of attacks.
-Billy Kobin
Jackson criticized Collins for voting for Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who Jackson said was clearly going to push for tariffs, long one of Trump’s signature policy aims.
“I’m not going to give her credit for getting one thing back,” Jackson said, when thousands of other items are more expensive under Trump.
-Kirby Wilson
Collins reiterated that “you cannot abolish ICE” while saying it needs reforms. She argued the $70 billion figure that Jackson cited was not really all for ICE but rather split between ICE and Customs and Border Protection.
“You don’t (pour) more money into an agency that is killing people across the country,” Jackson said.
-Billy Kobin
Jackson promises to not be a “blank check” for any president, Republican or Democrat.
-Kirby Wilson
Jackson said he supports Medicare for All and wants to help Mainers get covered.
While Collins points to her 2017 vote to block a Republican attempt to repeal the Affordable Care Act, Jackson noted she and Republicans let ACA tax credits expire at the end of 2025.
-Billy Kobin
Collins responds by noting that she’s always been pro-choice, and that Jackson hasn’t.
“I clearly don’t agree with how Brett Kavanaugh voted on Roe v. Wade,” Collins said.
-Kirby Wilson
Collins referred to Navatek and its former CEO Martin Kao, calling him a “crook.” She mentioned the University of Maine project that Navatek was involved in and a photo of the two of them together, saying that photo was taken months before there was “ever a contribution” from Kao.
Jackson wouldn’t let her get off easy on this, and he brought up how Trump ended the FBI probe that was continuing into Kao and the pro-Collins super PAC. Collins kept criticizing all of this as false.
Collins then brought up Jackson’s past case in which a Republican lawmaker filed an ethics complaint against him for using an Augusta home when serving in the Legislature.
The Maine Ethics Commission voted unanimously against investigating Jackson in 2023, and commissioners noted they could only weigh in on whether Jackson violated any campaign finance rules through the Augusta residence and not on the additional claims that he committed crimes such as mortgage fraud.
-Billy Kobin
In January, Trump said Collins “should never be elected to office again,” though relations between the two seem to have improved since then.
-Billy Kobin and Kirby Wilson
“Whatever,” Jackson said of her rate of voting for the president’s priorities. “It’s far too often.”
-Billy Kobin
“Sen. Collins is like an arsonist who helps set the fire and then she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out,” Jackson said, emphasizing she advanced the bill and that GOP colleagues have “called her a team player.”
-Billy Kobin
Jackson fired back by saying Mainers are struggling because Collins has failed to stand up for Donald Trump as he wages war in Iran.
-Kirby Wilson
It was a more aggressive opening statement than Collins’.
-Kirby Wilson
It will be interesting to see how aggressive Jackson is with his attacks and whether he can land a few blows. He’s not the most gifted speaker, so how he delivers his attacks and responds to Collins’ rebuttals will be important to watch.
Meanwhile, Collins, 73, will have to parry those attacks from Jackson and try to land a few rhetorical punches of her own. Her campaign spoke with reporters earlier today about how they plan to push back on pay-to-play allegations made in a ProPublica story two weeks ago. And she and her Republican allies have been mining Jackson’s legislative record for problematic votes.
This will be Collins’ first televised debate in roughly six years. Her energy and sharpness will likely be scrutinized.
Collins, who has been in office for nearly 30 years, clearly has an advantage when it comes to in-depth knowledge about national policy and international affairs. Jackson has to hold his own without making any gaffes that could live on in social media posts or advertisements.
-Randy Billings

title: Cumberland County low-income transportation funding cut in half
text:
The Regional Transportation Program lost half of its low-income transportation funding, the nonprofit announced Monday.
The Maine Department of Health and Human Services cut 50% of the funding that pays for rides for low-income Mainers in Cumberland County. The state didn’t lose funding for low-income transportation but reallocated funds among providers, Don Libby, executive director of RTP, said. RTP’s reduction is the largest of any transit provider.
For years, DHHS’ Office of Child and Family Services has provided $296,220 so RTP could provide rides for people who need to go to adult daycare programs, the grocery store, medical treatments and other destinations, Libby said.
Because of rising costs of fuel and drivers, RTP was already underfunded, Libby said. Now, it’s losing $148,481.
Located in Westbrook, RTP serves 27 towns in the county. According to the program’s website, it gives about 600 rides daily, serving 2,500 people each year. In 2025-26, it provided 14,000 rides. With its reduced funding, it estimates it will only be able to provide 7,000.
“These riders are dialysis patients, people going to cancer treatments,” Libby said. “Where’s the compassion for the people that need the service the most?”
The funding cuts came as a shock, Libby said, as the Office of Child and Family Services did not discuss the changes ahead of time. Starting in January, RTP will have to cap the number of rides available per rider and reduce service hours.
“If people miss their appointments, they’re going to end up in the emergency room,” Libby said.
DHHS is restructuring federal block grants into one contract, using a poverty-based formula to distribute grant dollars more equitably across the low-income transportation network, DHHS spokesperson Lindsay Hammes said in a statement.
“This formula is used in poverty-based programming in Maine and across the country and is based on published federal poverty data which looks at the percentage of the county population living under 150% federal poverty level,” Hammes said.
There are eight transit providers that receive low-income transportation funding provided through the Social Services Block Grant, according to an email about the funding changes sent to the providers. The Office of Child and Family Services has $1.18 million to budget toward this service.
In 2027-28, five providers will receive more funding, while three will lose funding. RTP is losing the most by far — $148,481 — followed by Kennebec Valley CAP and Penquis CAP, which are losing $35,583 and $9,017, respectively. York County CAC, Western Maine Transportation, Waldo CAP, Ridesource and ARTS will see boosts in funding in 2027-28
RTP has been in business for 50 years, Libby said, and this is by far the most drastic cut it has seen. He encourages people to contact their state representatives and tell them why these services matter.

title: 5 children found alone in boarded-up house without food or power, police say
text:
DAYTON, Ohio (WHIO) - Police in Ohio are investigating after five children were found living inside a boarded-up house without food or electricity.
Dayton Police responded to a boarded-up, abandoned property around 12:30 p.m. last Thursday for a welfare check. Officers found five children, ranging in age from 4 to 12, living inside the house.
Police say it appears there was no food or power in the house, and no adults were present. Body camera footage shows flies in the house, and in one bedroom, there is a mattress on the floor along with piles of clothes and trash.
The children were taken to the hospital for evaluations. They were then placed in the custody of Montgomery County Children’s Services.
The Dayton Police Department’s Care House Unit is investigating the incident.

title: Bath church raising funds to restore rotting 19th-century steeple
text:
BATH — A Bath church is once again seeking funds to restore its clock tower and steeple after uncovering significant rot in the 1850s structure.
First Baptist Church of Bath’s dozen or so congregants worry that the cost of completing the project could force them to close their doors. That’s not an option, though, since many more community members rely on the church for free meals, clothes and necessities.
“We can’t finish this project and leave us with zero money in our treasury, because then we can’t run the building,” said Fred Bogue, a church trustee who is leading the steeple restoration project.
The city of Bath installed the clock at the Washington Street church in 1855. The building dates back to 1853.
“It’s an iconic part of the Bath skyline,” said Sara Bogue, the church’s treasurer and Fred’s wife.
Church members now estimate the project — first expected to cost at least $100,000 — will cost more than $150,000, and there’s no telling what additional expenses they could run into.
The restoration effort was initially triggered when the church’s insurance company said it couldn’t continue to insure the building given the deterioration of the steeple and clock tower.
Sara Bogue recently set up a GoFundMe for the project, which has generated a few hundred dollars so far. Jamie Rines, daughter of Deacon George Snyder and Tammy Snyder, who runs the church’s free clothing closet, has also launched a donation page.
The group also has received some assistance from a Maine Steeples Fund grant.
The contractor, New England Church Restoration, began work on the steeple in August and immediately discovered rotting beams and major structural damage.
“He could literally pull boards off with his fingers, and it just turned into powder,” Fred Bogue said.
Fred Bogue said the fix will include replacing the beams with laminated veneer lumber beams that won’t rot.
“Unfortunately, every step of the way that’s happening as we come down in the building adds to the cost of the project,” he said.
With financial challenges and a shrinking congregation, the church has also struggled to employ a consistent pastor, the Bogues said.
For now, the project is on hold and the bell, which had tolled every hour since 1855, sits silent.
The church feeds dozens of people each Friday and on Thanksgiving at its meal and warming center downstairs. It also offers free clothing at a clothing closet next door, where volunteers recently installed a wheelchair and stroller-accessible ramp.
Church members hope to complete the project so they can focus on serving the community.
“God is at work,” Sara Bogue said.

title: Friends mourn 16-year-old killed after being hit by deputy’s car: ‘She was a great person’
text:
ST. FRANCOIS COUNTY, Mo. (KMOV/Gray News) - An investigation is underway in Missouri as loved ones mourn a 16-year-old girl who died after she was hit by a deputy’s car while lying on the road.
The community held a candlelight vigil Monday night for 16-year-old Persephone Berger, a student at West County High School. She was killed early Saturday after being hit by a St. Francois County Sheriff’s deputy’s car.
“She was just a really lively, understanding person. She never judged a soul. She was just a really sweet person,” said Persephone’s friend, Emma Houser.
Houser, along with Persephone’s friends Riley Skaggs and Isaac Madden, say the 16-year-old’s death weighed on the entire student body Monday as everyone wanted to make sure she was remembered and honored.
“You go to school. You see the photos. You see decorations and talking about it, and you can’t help but cry. It’s very sad,” Madden said.
“Everybody was wearing pink today in honor of her. We hung up pictures, laughed, talked about stories of her, but the halls were extremely quiet. There was a big change,” Skaggs said.
What deputies say happened
St. Francois County Sheriff Jeffrey Crites said deputies responded to a call about 3:43 a.m. Saturday for an unresponsive person lying on the road – later identified as Persephone. The person who made the call stayed at the scene.
As a deputy was approaching the scene, he saw the caller’s car with its hazards on but did not see Persephone on the road and struck her, Crites says. The deputy stayed at the scene and notified their supervisor.
Investigators says it’s unknown why Persephone was on the road.
St. Francois County Coroner Jason Coplin was called to the scene around 4 a.m. He said Persephone had suffered blunt trauma injuries, but an official cause of death cannot be confirmed until further tests are done.
Investigators say a preliminary autopsy conducted Monday did not show any injuries aside from those that involved the crash with the deputy’s car.
The Missouri State Highway Patrol has been asked to conduct an independent crash investigation.
Crites says the crash was not due to a police chase and no deputies left the scene, as some have claimed on social media.
Friends mourn as questions remain
While many questions remain in the community about what happened, Monday night’s vigil was a chance to focus on Persephone.
“She felt kind of like an older sister and like someone you can lean on and talk to about anything,” Houser said. “I relied on her as a person to be there for me, talk to me when I needed to talk to her, just a bunch of stuff.”
Madden said Persephone was one of the first people he met when he moved to the district, and that memory stands out.
“She was very, very kind, cared about everybody, super funny, probably one of the best people that I’ve ever met in my life,” he said. “She was really smart. She had a bright future ahead of her.”
Skaggs said she had known Persephone since middle school, and they became really close in high school.
“Big fan of Harry Potter, brought in some Harry Potter stuff. Her Alanis, her gummy clusters, we brought. But we’ll always remember Persephone as fun-loving, very smart,” she said. “Her loss has made a huge impact on the West County family.”
The three friends are working on a T-shirt fundraiser to support Persephone’s parents and three siblings, so the family knows they’re thinking of them.
“I just want the family to know that she was a great person and made the community come together... She’s very deeply missed,” Madden said.
A GoFundMe has also been set up to support Persephone’s family.

title: Chicago woman sues U.S. government, saying Maine Border Patrol agent shot her
text:
A Chicago woman who says she was shot by a U.S. Customs and Border Protection agent from Maine is now suing the federal government.
Marimar Martinez was driving the morning of Oct. 4, 2025, when she observed three federal agents who appeared to be surveilling a Chicago neighborhood during an immigration enforcement surge last fall, according to her complaint. The lawsuit says she began following the agents through her neighborhood, honking her horn and calling out to alert residents “of the danger she believed the approaching agents posed to them.”
The lawsuit alleges that agent Charles Exum swerved his vehicle into her lane before firing his handgun, shooting Martinez five times. Both the vehicle and gun were government issued, according to the complaint.
Exum never turned on his body camera, according to the complaint, in violation of CBP directive. Martinez alleged that body cameras from two other agents in Exum’s vehicle captured him driving into her lane. Their cameras also recorded an agent saying “do something, (expletive)” as Martinez honked at them, according to the complaint. About four seconds before Exum allegedly drove into Martinez’s lane, the lawsuit says, the videos also recorded an agent saying “it’s time to get aggressive.”
On Tuesday, a spokesperson for CBP said Exum is being investigated for the use of force incident by a board of officials from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice. Exum was placed on administrative leave after the shooting, the spokesperson said. It’s unclear what the agent’s employment status is now.
Exum could not be immediately reached on Tuesday by phone or through either federal agency. He’s not a named defendant in the lawsuit.
Christopher Parente, Martinez’s attorney, said that Chicago police are also conducting a criminal investigation. A spokesperson for Chicago police said that the case remains active and open.
Martinez was charged in October 2025 with assaulting an officer after the other two agents accused her of ramming into their vehicle first. That charge was dismissed in late November.
In Martinez’s complaint, which was filed in the U.S. District Court of Northern Illinois on Monday, she is pursuing claims of negligence, battery, assault, infliction of emotional distress, false imprisonment and false prosecution.
Martinez is a 30-year-old Montessori school teaching aide and a U.S. citizen, according to her complaint. Her lawsuit alleges that during the Department of Homeland Security’s “Operation Midway Blitz” in Chicago last year, agents were “targeting brown people … with little regard for their citizenship.”
Martinez told reporters during a press conference on Monday that she’s suing because “I want to spread awareness because what’s happening is not normal,” according to reporting from ABC7 Chicago.
“We shouldn’t sit here and normalize what’s happening,” Martinez said.
Exum’s name was revealed during Martinez’s criminal case last year, after her defense attorneys complained that he had driven the government vehicle to Maine before they could inspect it. According to documents obtained through a public records request, Exum is certified by the Maine Criminal Justice Academy to enforce Maine law as a federal officer.
Martinez’s attorneys also shared copies of texts that Exum allegedly sent other federal agents after the shooting, in which he appeared to brag about his shooting skills.
“Cool. I’m up for another round of (expletive) around and find out,” Exum allegedly wrote in one text.
Martinez’s attorneys stated in court records that they filed a notice of their claim with the government six months ago.

title: Chart-topping R&B singer Freddie Jackson dies at 70
text:
(AP) - Grammy-nominated R&B singer Freddie Jackson, known for his smooth ’80s hits “Rock Me Tonight (For Old Times Sake)” and “You Are My Lady,” has died. He was 70.
A statement shared by his family on his official Instagram account confirmed Jackson died Monday, three days after his 70th birthday. No cause of death was provided.
“Freddie was more than a legendary voice. He was a kind, generous soul who loved his fans, his family, his friends, and his music with everything he had. For decades he gave us the songs that became the soundtrack to our love stories, our celebrations, and our most treasured memories. That gift will live on forever,” the statement read.
“To everyone who ever sang along, danced, or felt something when Freddie took the stage: thank you. You were family to him, and he carried your love with him always,” it continued.
Details regarding arrangements will be announced in the coming days.
Jackson was born and raised in Harlem, where he learned all about soul music and sang gospel at White Rock Baptist Church. He started his career in the New York club scene, eventually making his way out West with the band Mystic Merlin in the late ’70s. He soon returned to New York and released his debut album, “Rock Me Tonight,” in 1985. His distinctive voice proved to be his superpower: The album, which was quickly certified platinum by the Recording Industry Association of America, also led to his two career Grammy nominations. Those were for best new artist and best male R&B vocal performance for the single “You Are My Lady.”
“Rock Me Tonight” also created a new R&B superstar: Jackson became a mainstay of those Billboard charts and a fixture of contemporary urban radio play throughout the ’80s and early ’90s.
His sophomore album, 1987’s “Just Like the First Time,” was also certified platinum.
Jackson shared his kidney disease diagnosis in 2024
In 2024, Jackson revealed he had been diagnosed with kidney disease in a video shared to his social media accounts.
“This journey has had its challenges but I’ve decided to face it with openness and resilience,” he said in the clip. “It’s important to me that I share this with you, not just as a part of my personal story, but as a way to make a positive difference.”
At the time, Jackson also revealed he had partnered with the National Kidney Foundation to raise awareness of the disease.
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, more than 1 in 7 American adults has chronic kidney disease. As many as 9 in 10 don’t know they have it.
Chronic kidney disease is a condition where the kidneys are damaged and struggle to filter blood. As a result, excess waste and fluids remain and can lead to other health issues, such as heart disease.

title: UMaine, Thomas College announce scholarships for Alfond Grant recipients
text:
AUGUSTA — Paige McNef, Samantha Hamilton and Ethan LeHay weren’t fully aware that they were some of the first babies in Maine to receive a $500 Alfond Grant growing up. But when it came time to think about college, those grants came as a big relief.
McNef, Hamilton and LeHay, who grew up in central Maine, all started their first semesters at college this fall, thanks in part to that early investment in their futures.
“I had no clue how I was going to pay for college,” said LeHay, who now goes to Central Maine Community College in Auburn. “Then my grandmother had told me about the Alfond Grant, and that took a huge weight off my shoulders.”
Now LeHay, who is going to come out of his first year of college debt-free, can focus on enjoying the beginning of his college experience.
The Alfond Grant Program, started by Maine businessman and philanthropist Harold Alfond shortly before he died in 2007, has granted $500 to every child born in Maine since 2013, totaling over 184,000 recipients, to use for education after high school. The program was first launched in 2008 and was awarded to 650 children born in Waterville and Augusta before later becoming available to all Maine children.
At an event celebrating this milestone Tuesday on the University of Maine at Augusta campus, the Alfond Scholarship Foundation announced new partnerships with the University of Maine System and Thomas College, which will now offer additional scholarships to eligible Alfond Grant recipients who attend those schools. The scholarships include $250 from the University of Maine system and $500 from Thomas College in Waterville.
“It is our way of saying, ‘Hey, this is one heck of an idea. It is blooming, and we want to make it bloom even bigger,'” Dannel P. Malloy, chancellor of the University of Maine System, said. “And we want to be a part of the effort to make sure that more families, at the birth of a child, are participating in this investment, not just investments in money, investment in the child.”
Eighteen years after the first 650 children received those $500 grants, the value of the grants now total around $2,500 or more depending on additional parental contributions.
The Alfond Scholarship Foundation invests the funds until a child is ready to use them, allowing them to grow over time. Families are also encouraged to open a NextGen 529 account, a state-sponsored investment account for higher education, alongside the grant to add their own contributions and receive matching grants from the Finance Authority of Maine, allowing the accounts to grow even more.
“It (has) that practical benefit of being real money in a real account,” Colleen Quint, president and CEO of the Alfond Scholarship Foundation, said. “It has that aspirational benefit of not just kind of encouraging kids to think about their futures, but also, and we hear this a lot from kids and from parents, is that someone else believes in my child, someone sees my child as having value. And that’s a really powerful thing.”
Early investments in education often have a positive impact on children’s aspirations, development and outcomes in school, Quint said, as well as increasing parents’ aspirations for their children’s futures.
The grant can be used for a wide array of higher education opportunities like college, vocational school, certificate programs, apprenticeships or graduate school and is not limited just to institutions in Maine.
“That’s money all to power the higher education opportunities for Maine kids, and then for those Maine kids to have a better life because of it,” Greg Powell, CEO and president of the Harold Alfond Foundation, said. “I like to think the state is better off too, because it’s really allowed our workforce now to have a leg up, and we will see that in the years ahead.”
Hamilton is using her grant to study civil engineering at University of Maine in Orono, McNef is studying radiology at Kennebec Valley Community College and LeHay is pursuing accounting at Central Maine Community College.
When asked what they would tell younger students preparing for their futures, all three grant recipients said to dream big and invest early.
“Just taking it day by day, going, ‘What can I do today to make my future better?'” Hamilton advised younger students. “And I think the Alfond Grant is incredible in that financially.”

title: We need Susan Collins’ experience and work ethic more than ever
text:
As a business owner in Maine, I want to express my support for Sen. Susan Collins in the upcoming election. Sen. Collins has served Maine for decades, and during that time she has consistently worked to bring federal resources and opportunities to our state. Her seniority and experience in Washington, D.C. — and particularly her position as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee — give Maine an important voice and critical influence when decisions are made regarding federal funding and priorities, making this position particularly consequential for a state the size of Maine.
That influence has produced tangible results for Maine, which cannot be delivered by an inexperienced U.S. Senate replacement. Her work has supported BIW, UMaine and hundreds of initiatives throughout all 16 Maine counties. According to Sen. Collins’ office, she has helped secure nearly $1.5 billion for 672 projects since 2021. I believe Maine voters need to look carefully at what Sen. Collins’ position in the Senate means for our state and what will be lost if she is no longer representing Maine in Washington.
Timothy Hodgdon
East Boothbay

title: Students turn on Cornell's president over the school's handling of gang rape allegations
text:
ITHACA, N.Y. (AP) — Some of the students outraged by Cornell University’s handling of an alleged fraternity house gang rape are directing their ire at the school’s president, a longtime molecular physiology professor who has faced several crises since taking the top job.
Michael Kotlikoff was Cornell’s longest-serving provost before assuming the presidency on an interim basis in July 2024 and on a permanent basis last year.
In his second month in charge, dining and custodial workers walked off the job in a labor dispute that ended about two weeks later. Last fall, some faculty and students criticized Kotlikoff for agreeing to pay $60 million to end Trump administration civil rights investigations into the Ivy League school. And earlier this year, he defended himself from accusations that he tried to back his car into a group of demonstrators following a debate over Israel and Palestinian rights, saying he was the victim of harassment.
But it was the school’s handling of the investigation into the alleged gang rape at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024, just a few months into his presidency, that threatens his leadership.
The Cornell faculty senate indicated that it plans to vote on a resolution of no confidence in the school’s administrators. And at a Monday protest, students chanted and waved signs calling on Kotlikoff to resign or be fired and for fraternities to be banned.
“Throughout his administration, he’s refused to take accountability for anything that has happened,” said one of the protesters, sophomore Sophia Kong. “He does not represent us.”
Kotlikoff, 75, has come under scrutiny since the woman, identified in court documents only as Jane Doe, filed a lawsuit last month alleging she was sexually assaulted by multiple Chi Phi members two years ago after being pressured into drinking alcohol and taking drugs.
The woman reported the alleged assault to Cornell police in November 2024, three weeks after she said it occurred. Campus police investigated and sent a summary of their findings to the district attorney’s office, which relied on the information in deciding not to bring criminal charges. Separately, Cornell conducted a Title IX investigation.
Amid mounting outrage over the school’s handling of the case, Kotlikoff called the allegations “deeply disturbing” over the weekend. In an apologetic video, he also reaffirmed his commitment to supporting an independent review called for by New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, who has assailed the campus police department for not fully conveying the woman’s story to prosecutors.
No criminal charges have been filed. The Chi Phi chapter was shut down, and the university has said it expelled some students and suspended others. The accused men have all either denied participating or said that the sex that took place was consensual.
Experts are divided on whether it’s fair to criticize Kotlikoff
As some experts see it, Kotlikoff had limited options. Without criminal charges, only Cornell’s Title IX investigation continued. While the federal law is best known as a gamechanger for female college athletes, it also is supposed to protect sexual assault and harassment accusers. But it is packed with protections for the accused, including giving them the right to cross-examine their accuser. Most victims don’t proceed, and when they do, lawsuits from the accuser and accused over the outcome of the proceedings are common.
There are also limits on the punishments schools can mete out, especially for bystanders, said Peter Lake, who directs a center focused on higher education law and policy at Stetson University College of Law in Florida.
If universities act too quickly, they risk a situation like what happened at Duke University two decades ago, when a woman falsely accused three lacrosse players of rape, he said. The players ultimately reached an undisclosed settlement with Duke, which had suspended them, canceled the team’s season and forced their coach to resign after the accusations were first made.
But some point to the role of university leadership in setting campus culture. Critics note that Cornell’s fraternities have a history of problems, including hazing and sexual misconduct, and argue that more should have been done to set a better tone and educate students about consent.
“If you are the leader of that campus and this is part of your portfolio of what happens on your campus, it’s not like ‘Oh well that only affects the members of that fraternity and the women that they’re attempting to sleep with,’” said Jane Stapleton, co-founder of the Prevention Innovations Research Center at the University of New Hampshire. “That impacts the entire fabric of the culture of, ‘How do men respect women? How safe is it to be a woman?’”
Kotlikoff has discussed steps to address the case
Within a few weeks of the alleged assault, Kotlikoff issued a statement detailing the investigation and decrying the alleged behavior as “abhorrent.”
A task force on sexual assault that was launched afterward included recommendations such as improved education on Title IX and what it described as “sexual citizenship.” The report said that a 2025 survey found that 35% of undergraduate women and 8% of undergraduate men report experiencing sexual assault during their time at Cornell.
The extent of Cornell’s investigation has emerged in court records filed after one of the punished students sued the school. According to Cornell’s account, investigators conducted 50 interviews with 32 witnesses and gathered evidence that included witness accounts, electronic communications and social media messages. The process ultimately led to a disciplinary hearing that stretched over 12 days.
Kotlikoff has called for a “serious look” at Greek life, but the end of fraternities on campus is not being considered. Instead, Kotlikoff said Cornell would engage students, alumni and others in examining how to preserve the benefits of Greek life while strengthening accountability and transparency.
Not every president survives such situations
A little over a decade ago, former Baylor University President Ken Starr, best known for the probe that led to Bill Clinton’s presidential impeachment, lost his job amid allegations that the Texas Baptist school mishandled several cases in which football players were accused of attacking women. In 2021, Oregon State trustees accepted the resignation of university president F. King Alexander, concluding he was unable to rebuild trust at the school because of his role in the mishandling of sexual misconduct cases during his previous tenure at Louisiana State University.
More recently, Columbia University President Minouche Shafik was among several U.S. college leaders to resign under pressure for the handling of protests over the war in Gaza.
Soham Bera, a Cornell sophomore, said students have “incredibly low faith” in the university leadership.
“Now, with all this news, with all the attention, we can finally make change,” he said at Monday’s protest.
Lili Rose Mas, a junior who was also calling for Kotlikoff to step down, said she was encouraged by the number of students who joined the protest.
“It makes me have more faith in humanity,” Mas said. “I truly think that Gen Z might be the generation that changes the world, because, like, these old people in the admin are not doing anything, but all the students here care about this.” ___ Hollingsworth reported from Mission, Kansas. title: Yarmouth field hockey takes down Freeport in regional final rematch
text:
YARMOUTH — Graduation wasn’t kind to the Yarmouth field hockey team, which lost nine of 11 starters from last year’s Class B South runner-up.
If there’s any question that the Clippers are still the region’s team to beat, however, they stomped it out Tuesday night.
Vivienne Corriveau had a hat trick, freshman Julie Nasveschuk added two goals, and Yarmouth beat rival Freeport, 5-2, in a showdown between teams who have met in the past three regional finals.
Yarmouth, ranked fifth in the Varsity Maine poll, improves to 10-0 and has won 37 straight regular-season games. Freeport, which nipped the Clippers in last year’s regional final, lost its second straight and falls to 7-2.
“I think everyone was waiting for us to take a step back with losing, more or less, our whole starting lineup,” Clippers coach Bre Page said. “I knew it wasn’t going to be like that. I knew we were going to be just as strong, and we were going to come out and prove we’re still at the top of Class B.”
Quick strikes
• Yarmouth’s ability to quickly move the ball upfield and descend upon the net had Freeport scrambling. The Clippers went up 1-0 when Corriveau poked the ball free and got it to Maya Nasveschuk, who passed back to Corriveau for a goal only 1:42 into the game.
• After Freeport’s Lydia Porter answered another Corriveau goal to make it 2-1 with 12:50 left in the second quarter, Julie Nasveschuk knocked in a loose ball just 43 seconds later.
• Maya Nasveschuk and Corriveau teamed up again for a backbreaker only 14 seconds into the second half, making it 4-1. Goals by Porter and Julie Nasveschuk rounded out the scoring.
“Our main strong suit is moving the ball quickly,” Julie Nasveschuk said. “Our transitions from defense to offense are really fast. That’s what kind of jolts the other team’s defense … and results in them making mistakes.”
Strong chemistry
The heart of Yarmouth’s attack was smooth teamwork between Maya Nasveschuk, one the Clippers’ two returning starters, and Corriveau. Nasveschuk used her elite stickhandling to zip through defenders and send the ball in, and Corriveau was often ready to rap it home.
“I love having Maya in my grade. I’ll never have to play without her,” Corriveau said. “We take the lacrosse (chemistry) into field hockey. … We’re on the same wavelength.”
Unsung hero
While Yarmouth’s attack sizzled, the Clippers dazzled in back, where junior Gianna LaBella provided a formidable barrier in front of goalie Stella Murdoch. She had good checks to derail Freeport possessions, wove around sticks trying to poke the ball loose, and advanced the ball up to start attacks.
“Gianna’s awesome,” Page said. “Gianna’s a brick wall. She can play anywhere. … She knows it’s her moment, and she’s not going to let anyone past her.”
Stat leaders
• Yarmouth: Vivienne Corriveau (three goals, assist), Julie Nasveschuk (two goals), Maya Nasveschuk (two assists), Stella Peck (assist)
• Freeport: Lydia Porter (two goals), Megan Ritz (assist), Lydia Costa (12 saves)
Notable quotes
• “I graduated a bazillion players who have been playing for many years, and when you don’t have a lot of competition at the beginning of the season, you don’t really know what your weaknesses are. Now I know. … You can’t continue to make the same mistake over and over and expect to win a game. Once that has gotten through to everyone, we can move forward.” — Freeport coach Marcia Wood.
• “They’re our rivals. Every game against them, we know it’s going to be tough, we know it’s going to be close. But coming out here and scoring quickly, we had a really great game.” — Maya Nasveschuk.

title: InvestigateTV+: Companies ask for Clean Air Act exemptions
text:
(InvestigateTV) — InvestigateTV+ uncovers an effort by industrial plants to get let off the hook from Clean Air Act regulations.
Plus, one man’s half-century-long quest to trace his ancestry highlights the challenges many Black Americans face.
Then, meet the cheerleading team with a routine you’ve likely never seen.
Permission to Poison?
In March 2025, President Donald Trump’s administration made a tantalizing offer to coal-fired power plants, chemical manufacturing facilities and other factories: Their operations could be exempted from key provisions under the Clean Air Act, the bedrock environmental law estimated to have prevented thousands of premature deaths. All they had to do was ask.
No rigorous application was needed. An email, which they had until the end of the month to send, would suffice.
Finding your family in old documents
Knowing where we come from expands our sense of who we are, according to a 2023 study published in the medical journal “Genealogy.” That study found that learning family history is linked to developing a healthy relationship with one’s identity.
From a bus into a clothing store
A New Orleans teenager has converted a used bus into a traveling clothing boutique, taking his business on the road across the Gulf South.
Deaf cheer team competes in its first-ever hearing competition
Minnesota’s only all-deaf high school cheerleading team became the first in its school history to perform in a hearing competition.
