title: ‘Daughter of Maine’ Erin French talks about how the state shapes the way she cooks
text:
Culinary celebrity Erin French is not a chef, and she wants everyone to know it. She declares as much right from the jump in her brand new cookbook, “Seize the Supper.” To be sure, the owner of The Lost Kitchen restaurant in Freedom is known more for embracing simple, comforting home cooking rather than precious fine dining. And as viewers of her Magnolia Network show, “The Lost Kitchen”— the first of three original TV series — can attest, one of her hallmarks is an ability to turn on a dime and readjust dishes based on the availability and freshness of ingredients on any given day.
That penchant for improvisation is at the heart of “Seize the Supper,” French’s fourth book and third cookbook. On the eve of a national book tour kicking off with a speaking event at the State Theater, she chatted with us about how being a daughter of Maine manifests in her cooking, what hospitality means right now, and where the new book fits into the evolution of her career.
I’ve heard it said that you’re a great ambassador for Maine via your books and shows. You’re also running the restaurant and its adjacent store and café, as well as essentially a mini-media empire. Does that feel like a lot of responsibility?
It continues to be a lot for me to digest. This place [The Lost Kitchen restaurant] keeps us so overwhelmed and busy. But for me, a lot of what happens here is accidental. I was one of those people who didn’t think that I wanted to be in Maine when I was younger and I wanted to get away from here, and then when you get out into the world you start to have an appreciation. This place that really shaped me and the way that I think about food.
How so?
Maine had given me that lens to look at food in a way that the way I took for granted, growing up with a garden or knowing that you could just go out and dig potatoes and boil them and just put some salt and pepper and butter on top and have the best meal of your life. That simplicity was something that was happening organically to my brainwave. So Maine has shaped 100% the way that I am as a cook, And it is pressure. Part of this has been the greatest gift, and sometimes it feels like the greatest burden because the workload is insane and it doesn’t stop, and we don’t have a day off. But I’m constantly grateful to be in this place and have people recognizing what we’re doing. I feel an endless duty being a daughter of this state to keep doing my absolute best for it. I feel like I owe it something because of everything it gave me.
Is there a characteristic of Maine that you identify with most, that shows up in how you run your restaurant — how you cook and serve people?
There’s something very scrappy about Mainers. We use what we have, and [it was] how I opened my restaurant when I started. It was very little and we used what we have in our backyards and was on our shelves, whether it was using mismatched plates and silverware to set the table or foraging for things in the garden or the fields to make arrangements that cost nothing. We have a resourcefulness that is very different than any other place that I’ve been. And that allows you to be a really authentic self. You go other places and you feel like you’re always trying to be like everyone else, but Maine allows you to just be who you are here, and that’s why I think you find so many creative people here, because that’s what this place invites you to do. You feel the permission to be you.
There’s a line in ‘Seize the Supper’ where you write that the book is about ‘being in the moment, eating in the moment, living and embracing right here, right now.’ It strikes me as one of the things that you do regularly on the first show, where you say ‘Okay, we’re out of this ingredient, we need to just completely change tonight’s menu.’
Yes, absolutely. This book is really about a sense of urgency, and answering the call of urgency. It goes back to what we were talking about in Maine, which is always giving us this sense of urgency if the season is changing. It keeps you on your toes…. Living here has taught me about looking around at your surroundings and saying, ‘We’ve got to grab onto what’s happening around us right now or it’s going to slip right past us.’
What compelled you to write another cookbook right now?
I have to say, I really do love writing these books. I am busy all the time, but there’s an arc and the summers are insane and we’re just heads down with the restaurant, and then Maine gives way to fall and things slow down, and then you have winter and that’s time for having more solitude time and for me that’s writing. That’s recipe testing and development and I love that shift. And I have to say, of all the books, it’s my absolute favorite thus far.
Have your books changed from one to the next?
Yeah, this book felt like supremely, confidently me. It is absolutely the way that I live my life. I’ll come home and I’ll be like, it is the perfect night to throw a table out there and we’re gonna have burgers and I’m gonna pick all the things for dinner…. Also, over [the last several years] I realized how precious moments are, and that we do have to grab onto [them] because they won’t be here forever.
You grew up cooking in your family diner. When you were evolving that genre of food — I hate to say elevating or raising it, because great diner food is simply awesome — but evolving it to fine dining (or at least, finer than diner dining), who were your biggest influences? Were there cookbooks that you reached for, or food world leaders that you looked to for influence?
Oh yeah. The huge influencer in my life as a teenager was Martha Stewart, and I used to read her magazines religiously. I got a subscription, which was a lot for me to afford at that time, and I would cut out all the perforated recipes that she used to have in the back. My neighbors around Freedom would call me Little Martha.
There’s that question out there: Are you more of an Ina or a Martha?
I wouldn’t be me without both. They both have influenced me deeply, and I think it was the simplicity and the honesty of their entertaining. To be honest, it was really about the table. I always used to love the table setting so much, and then I figured out quickly [that] I actually had to learn how to cook because you had to serve something at the table. Running restaurants wasn’t something that I ever sought out to do. I just wanted to care for people. I wanted to bring people in and make moments. I didn’t want to be a chef on a line. But I figured out quickly I actually had to learn how to cook, in order to, to create these moods and these feelings around the table. My interest was always setting the table and getting the lighting and music just right. It’s more like being a mood maker than it is a meal maker.
You mentioned above that being an ambassador for Maine, along with the rest of what you do, can be a lot to digest. How much does that include being a public figure? Do public judgments affect you?
It’s rough. It’s rough and it’s not kind. I’ve been Trip Advisor-sober for 10 years now. I could not stand crying in the fetal position at one in the morning after dinner service anymore, and I was like, that’s enough. This relationship is toxic and I’m not going to have this with this online platform anymore.
Apropos of that, what do you say to those who say dinner at The Lost Kitchen is too expensive? (Dinners carry a base price of $295 per person, not including tax, gratuity or alcohol)
Oh, I could write a whole article for you on on that…. We don’t get rich off these dinners. We’re lucky if we break even because of how much goes into them. There’s a reason that things cost what they cost. I believe that you have to pay people well. I believe that you have to buy ingredients that are supporting people well. And if you want to take shortcuts, you’re going to get a shortcut. But if you want to take the long journey with me and you want to come for a five-and-half-hour dinner, I’ll give you every penny’s worth.
Speaking of the dinners, is there a favorite dish in the new cookbook that you feel really embodies how you like to cook — or how you like to seize the supper?
I just love so many of these recipes — more than the others. A lot of the food that I was cooking in the book was everything that I want to eat in that moment, at that time of year. But one that I’m actually crazy about, which you could just buy the book for this one recipe alone, is the tea bars in the ‘Fall’ section. They’re just so goddamn good. Like, so good.
Alexandra Hall is a longtime New England lifestyle writer who lives in Maine.
IF YOU GO
Erin French will talk about her new cookbook “Seize the Supper” at an event co-sponsored by Print: A Bookstore, Oct. 11 at the State Theatre. Tickets to the 7 p.m. event are $50 to $75, available at Ticketmaster.com or fee-free at the State Theatre box office at 609 Congress St., Portland.

title: Paramount and Warner Bros are now one Hollywood giant: Skydance. Here’s how we got here
text:
CHICAGO (AP) — It’s official: Skydance-owned Paramount closed its $81 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery on Tuesday, ushering in a new Hollywood behemoth.
The merger brings two of America’s oldest moviemaking studios together under a new name: Skydance.
HBO Max, titles ranging from “Harry Potter” to “Sinners” and networks such as CNN now also find themselves under the same roof as Paramount+, CBS and the likes of “Top Gun” and “The Godfather.” All are under the helm of billionaire David Ellison and his new co-CEO Ynon Kreiz.
“Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry,” Ellison said. “We couldn’t be more excited to get to work.”
Ellison’s Skydance bought Paramount for $8 billion last year before setting its sights on Warner. What followed erupted into a tumultuous, roughly yearlong fight over the storied Hollywood giant. Including billions of dollars in debt, the acquisition amounts to nearly $111 billion.
The now-combined Skydance marks one of the biggest tie-ups in media and entertainment history, further concentrating power in an industry already run by just a handful of big players. Politics also loomed over much of the process. The Ellison family has notably held a long relationship with Republican President Donald Trump, who said Tuesday that Skydance is “going to be a great company.”
Netflix gets into a bidding war with Paramount for Warner
The early days of Paramount’s quest for Warner turned into a messy bidding war.
Months after disclosing it was open to selling all or part of its business, Warner initially struck a studio and streaming deal with Netflix in December.
But Paramount said it also had made offers that Warner management “never engaged meaningfully” with. It soon launched a hostile counterbid.
The Hollywood giants spent much of early 2026 in a heated back-and-forth over who had a stronger offer, with Warner leadership repeatedly backing Netflix as its preferred suitor. But Netflix bowed out after Paramount eventually upped its offer to buy all of Warner for $31 per share.
Warner and Paramount inked a mutual merger agreement in late February.
Hollywood stars made their thoughts known
Hollywood was closely watching the fight over Warner’s future. From awards shows to online petitions, A-list celebrities and other creatives made their voices known.
In April, thousands of movie stars, writers, directors and other professionals announced their “unequivocal opposition” to the Paramount-Warner merger. An open letter — which was signed by long-outspoken critics of the deal like Jane Fonda and Mark Ruffalo, as well as Hollywood heavyweights from Denis Villeneuve to J.J. Abrams — warned of fewer jobs and “less choice for audiences in the United States and around the world.”
Others lined up to back Paramount as Ellison reiterated his commitments to the movies. At CinemaCon, the company debuted a glossy mini movie about the studio directed by Jon M. Chu and narrated by Tom Cruise — who ended the spot atop the iconic Paramount water tower, with the words “the future is paramount and the future looks pretty great from here.” Director James Cameron also doubled down on his support of Ellison.
The prospect of a new Warner owner also loomed over awards season, from #BlockTheMerger pins to more subtle nods in acceptance speeches. When accepting her Emmy last month, “Remarkably Bright Creatures” actor Sally Field — who also signed the open letter in opposition to the Paramount-Warner deal — stressed that “unique storytelling matters” and “we can’t let those voices be silenced, or compromised or merged.”
Many industry critics were also outspoken when Netflix’s studio and streaming deal was on the table, with a particular focus on the future of movies staying in theaters.
Trump has attacked CNN
Critics are also watching what happens with CNN under Skydance.
Trump has regularly attacked reporting he deems unfavorable at CNN (most recently attempting to bar the outlet from the White House altogether). And over the course of the Warner buyout, his administration also chimed in about hopes for a new owner.
Days after Paramount launched its hostile bid for Warner, Trump said CNN spread “poison and lies” and that it was “imperative” the network be sold. The White House took aim again at CNN in March, over the network’s coverage of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth told reporters that “the sooner David Ellison takes over that network, the better.”
Ellison has said editorial independence will be maintained at CNN. On Tuesday, he told reporters that the company had “not talked to any political leader of any party about news — other than to say that we want to be in the truth business and we want be in the trust business.”
Skydance is retaining Mark Thompson as CNN’s editor-in-chief. And under a settlement finalized last month with states that had sued over the takeover, the company agreed to form a “News Editorial Independence Board.”
Still, critics point to turmoil already seen at CBS under Skydance ownership and aren’t convinced this new body will be able to do much. The company’s corporate board will oversee appointments.
Ellison has maintained a close relationship with Trump overall. He reportedly hosted a dinner in Washington in Trump’s honor in April, on the same day Warner shareholders gave their green light for the merger. In June, just two days after the Justice Department said it wouldn’t intervene in the deal, Ellison attended an Ultimate Fighting Championship match on the White House lawn for Trump’s 80th birthday (streamed by Paramount+).
“We have a good relationship with this administration,” Ellison noted Tuesday. But he said he “also had a really good relationship” with Democratic President Joe Biden, among other politicians.
3 Gulf countries helped back the deal
To help fund its Warner buyout, Paramount racked up billions of dollars in financial backing from three Gulf countries: Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. The Federal Communications Commission approved the company’s request for sizable indirect ownership from those foreign investors.
Paramount previously disclosed it expected those funds to indirectly own nearly 50% of equity interests — but no voting rights — of Skydance. But the company asked for clearance of up to 100% to account for potential future investments, which the FCC granted, citing in part that access to more capital would strengthen the broadcast industry and was therefore “in the public interest.”
The FCC’s sole Democratic commissioner, Anna Gomez, and other critics have called the move alarming and unprecedented. They argue that amount of money opens the door to behind-the-scenes influence.
Legal fights stalled the deal
Paramount cleared antitrust hurdles for its Warner acquisition from the Justice Department and regulators worldwide over the summer.
But in July, Democratic attorneys general from 12 states — led by California’s Rob Bonta — sued to block the merger, alleging the combined company would “extinguish competition” and lead to fewer choices for consumers, particularly movie theatergoers and cable customers.
The Writers Guild of America followed suit.
Settlements emerged in September. The states’ terms, approved by a judge, include pledges from the company to increase film production in the U.S. over the next five years, commit millions of dollars to a fund aimed at supporting workers displaced by the merger and establish new editorial monitoring of CNN and CBS.
Critics said the remedies were too weak, but the settlements cleared the way for the deal to close.

title: President Trump signs order extending tax-free use of red-dyed diesel during Nebraska midterm stop
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
President Trump signs order extending tax-free use of red-dyed diesel during Nebraska midterm stop
President Donald Trump on Monday took his Republican midterm rescue mission to Nebraska, where he signed an executive order to ease limits on the tax-free use of red-dye diesel, a decision he said would save “millions” for farmers and drive down the cost of all goods with just four weeks to go until the elections.
“Pete and Jim, this should absolutely ensure your election, I guarantee you that,” Trump said, addressing GOP Gov. Pete Ricketts, who is running against an independent candidate backed by national Democrats, and Gov. Jim Pillen, who is seeking a second term.
Diesel fuel prices have spiked in the aftermath of the Iran war, rattling voters and putting pressure on Republicans. Diesel fuel that is intended for off-road uses such as agriculture is exempt from federal and state excise taxes, and it is dyed for law enforcement purposes, the White House explained in a fact sheet. Temporarily removing the limits would reduce cost pressures on the businesses that rely on diesel.
“The typical trucker will save more than $100 every time they fill up,” Trump said, signing the executive order onstage before a crowd in Grand Island, Nebraska, located in the solidly conservative south-central part of the state. “Farmers will also save millions and millions of dollars, and this order will also drive down the cost of all goods and to go to grocery prices very substantially.”
Trump's trip is part of what the Republican president says is a 32-day blitz of rallies ahead of Nov. 3 that so far has taken him to ruby-red territory such as Oklahoma and Alabama.
On Wednesday, he'll make his second stop in two weeks in Texas with a rally in San Antonio.
Ricketts, a former governor of the state, was appointed then later elected to fill Sen. Ben Sasse’s seat when he left to run the University of Florida in 2023. Now Ricketts is running for his first full six-year term against independent Dan Osborn — a race that initially was not expected to be competitive but is now being watched by the national parties.
Republicans facing headwinds amid voter discontent
Voters across the country are frustrated with Trump's handling of the economy, including persistently high costs for fuel and groceries. It's a major issue for rural voters who have backed the president and his party in recent elections.
The administration’s plan to allow more imports of foreign beef has particularly roiled the agriculture-rich state of Nebraska. Trump wants to lower beef prices for consumers, but ranchers have rebelled against the import proposal, arguing it would undercut them.
“The plan to import low-quality foreign beef is not helping Nebraska ranchers,” Ricketts told the AP. “I would advise the White House to change that policy and look for longer-term things that will help us build the size of the herd and ultimately bring the price of beef down for consumers.”
In Grand Island, rally-goers said they trusted Trump to solve the high cost of living.
“I feel like if we get our reserves built back up, get this situation in Iran taken care of, our gas prices will go down. The economy as far as groceries and stuff like that, it's going to go down too. It’ll stabilize. I have faith in him. More faith in him than I ever had in any other president," said Marlene Abel from Garfield, Kansas, who traveled to the rally with her sister.
David Kuncl, who grew up on a farm, also urged patience, expressing confidence things would improve in the long run. But the Lincoln, Nebraska, resident insisted Trump wasn't to blame, pointing instead to what he believes is “a coup, a plot to try to hurt Trump" and the Republicans in the midterms.
“It’s hurting us. Gas prices. Diesel prices. Beef prices," he said. “I don’t know why they’re high. But it’s not that Trump’s got anything to do with that. He’ll do what he can. But of course he can’t wave a magic wand and make it go lower.”
There are tentative plans for Trump to travel to other election battlegrounds, including Michigan, North Carolina, Georgia, Ohio, Kansas, Montana, Pennsylvania, Alaska, Nevada and Arizona before November's Election Day. That's according to a person familiar with the plans who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly and cautioned the plans could shift.
There are a few Senate races where independents are the challengers
In the House of Representatives, the Grand Island area is represented by Republican Rep. Adrian Smith, whose race is not expected to be close. But Nebraska has a competitive House race farther east in Omaha, considered the “blue dot” of the state because the area’s electoral vote in presidential elections often goes to Democrats.
Osborn, a former labor union chief, ran against Republican Sen. Deb Fischer in 2024 and lost by 7 percentage points. Though national Democrats support him, he has refused to say what party he would caucus with should he be elected in November.
Other independents in the Senate, including Maine’s Angus King on the moderate end and Vermont’s Bernie Sanders on the left, caucus with Democrats for organizational purposes and committee assignments.
Video below: Here are the Senate races to watch
With the Democratic brand remaining deeply unpopular in conservative states, Osborn isn’t the only declared independent running for the Senate against Republicans this year. In South Dakota, Navy and Air Force veteran Brian Bengs is campaigning as an independent against Republican Sen. Mike Rounds. Bengs ran as a Democrat for the Senate four years ago and was handily defeated by now-Senate Majority Leader John Thune.
It’s a similar dynamic in Idaho, where independent Todd Achilles is challenging GOP Sen. Jim Risch.
Democratic voters in Nebraska chose Cindy Burbank as their party nominee earlier this year, but Burbank specifically campaigned on ensuring that no votes would be siphoned from Osborn in the general election in November, and she has since formally dropped out of the race.
Osborn has been traveling across Nebraska to hold meetings in all 93 counties, and has repeatedly criticized Ricketts for not holding town halls to meet with constituents.
Ricketts, whose family founded TD Ameritrade and owns Major League Baseball’s Chicago Cubs, served as governor from 2015 to 2023.
Vance stumps in Alaska
As Trump traveled to Nebraska, Vice President JD Vance headed to Fairbanks — with his wife and their two youngest kids in tow — to rally with Republican candidates there, including Sen. Dan Sullivan, who is locked in a contest with Democrat Mary Peltola that's one of a handful expected to determine control of the chamber in the November elections.
The two-term senator was in the Oval Office last week as Trump announced that South Korea planned to invest about $54 billion in a natural gas project in Alaska, but South Korean officials were more cautious, saying they needed to assess the project’s commercial viability before committing to the investment.
___
Kim reported from Washington. Associated Press writers Jill Colvin in New York and Meg Kinnard and Michelle L. Price in Washington contributed to this report.

title: Fishing crew reels in record-breaking bluefin tuna: ‘Something that I dream of’
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
RYE, N.H. (WMUR) — A charter fishing trip produced a new state record for the largest bluefin tuna caught in New Hampshire waters.
Captain Jamie Savage and his charter guest, Brandon McGirl, caught a bluefin tuna weighing 1,116 pounds. The previous record, set in 2013, was 962 pounds. The new catch is 154 pounds larger.
Savage and McGirl left for an overnight charter Saturday at 6 a.m. After hours of waiting, they got a bite. Crew members on board worked to get the fish onto the boat, then towed it at a slow pace back to the harbor.
The men said they knew they had a big catch but did not realize how large the fish was until they hoisted it up and saw it in daylight.
“So we lifted it out of the water and immediately knew it was way bigger than what we thought and bigger than anything either of us had seen before,” Savage said.
McGirl said catching a 1,000-pound fish was something he had dreamed of.
“For a long time, catching a 1,000-pound fish, it’s something that I dream of,” McGirl said. “So, I think more than anything, that has always been a goal of mine. Never thought it would actually happen, but to do that and potentially get the record as well is pretty special.”
Tail cut shows meat quality
A cut made to the tuna’s tail showed the quality of its meat.
The tuna is headed to market, where it could be sold as far away as Japan.
The tuna’s tail will remain at the harbor as a trophy to commemorate the record-breaking catch.

title: This database is helping Black families find their enslaved ancestors
text:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. (InvestigateTV) - Knowing where we come from expands our sense of who we are, according to a 2023 study published in the medical journal “Genealogy.” That study found that learning family history is linked to developing a healthy relationship with one’s identity.
But for many Black Americans, the enslavement of their ancestors meant names, records, and history were often erased. Now, a new database in Jackson County, Missouri is trying to put those names back within reach.
Reggie James has long studied the past. His family’s history is no different.
“I knew nothing,” James said.
In 1979, while watching the TV miniseries “Roots: The Next Generation,” the retired schoolteacher felt the pull to discover his own roots.
“It’s not like it is today, where everything has been digitized. You had to go to the archives and use the microfilm, wheeling it by hand to check the census,” James recalled.
Decades of research uncover family lineage
James spent nearly 50 years poring over census records, newspaper clippings and documents from the Jackson County Recorder of Deeds. It was an arduous process, but one that eventually led him to his paternal grandmother, Oletha Brookins, born in 1905.
“When I found her, I saw her mother’s name,” James said. “I never knew her mother’s name.”
James traced the Brookins side of his family in Jackson County back to 1851, mapping the lineage of his enslaved ancestors all the way back to the 17th century, starting in Maine, through Virginia, Kentucky, and ultimately into Clay and Jackson counties, Missouri.
“George is my second great-grandfather, because Oletha is my grandmother, second grandparent, Brookins, he was a slave,” James said, looking at family tree he created.
When asked what goes through his mind about finding so many relatives, James said he’s amazed.
“I’m just in awe of it,” James said. “I have stories on all these people like I knew them.”
The stories give the 75-year-old a place of belonging and a clear identity.
“To know who you really are, to find out what your people went through, what sacrifices they [made] for me to be here,” James said. “The audacity of this whole system, you know.”
Museum creates digital database from historical records
James already did the hard part, decades of page-by-page digging, one record at a time. But now, Jackson County records that were always public are easier to search and understand thanks to staff at the Wornall Majors House Museums.
“The database was a little bit of a happy accident,” said Sarah Bader-King, the museums’ executive director.
Her team was researching property records connected to Alexander Majors, a pioneer freighter who enslaved at least 23 people, when they found a deed of trust.
It listed nine enslaved people not as just property, but by name and age.
“Once I pulled up a couple of these deeds and saw that most of them had names in them, I was like we really have something here,” Bader-King said.
That discovery led them back into the Jackson County Recorder of Deeds, where they found hundreds of deeds, wills, probate records and bills of sale. It’s a trove of legal documents, sometimes difficult to navigate.
“We realized we could provide a service by simply summarizing these documents,” Bader-King said.
The online database, which launched in February 2026, turns 19th-century records into searchable names. Users can search by name, document type, or keywords with results that include document images and plain-language summaries.
“This is not just Black history. It’s American history,” Bader-King said.
Funding project to uncover history
The project received funding support from Kansas City’s Monument Coalition, an organization that works to tell understudied and unknown stories of Kansas City history.
“These are not a mass system of people that we can write as a whole,” said Kevin McPartland, an assistant project manager. “They are individuals, who experienced these things as mothers, fathers, daughters, brothers and sisters.”
McPartland said the Jackson County database is part of a growing national movement.
“Projects like this are popping up across the country,” he said. “So, naming the enslaved, this is a local database but is one database that is joining a growing corpus of databases nationally that are looking at stuff like this.”
The Jackson County database is a digital tool designed to help people piece together their ancestors’ stories. It’s the same work James did by hand for decades, now open to anyone to start.
“I’m happy that they’re doing that,” James said about the new resource tool.
It serves as an invitation to bring lost names back to light.
“You have a lot of people who are interested but they don’t know,” James said. “You never know what you might find.”
Since the interview, the museum has found several hundred more names to add to the database. It is free to use and available online. Click here to access it.
The museum also offers up to two hours of free research help.

title: 3 of Nolan Wells' friends sue NFL Hall of Famer Terrell Owens for defamation
text:
JACKSON, Miss. (AP) — Three friends of Nolan Wells, a Black college student who went missing from a Mississippi island during a Fourth of July celebration and was later found dead, are suing NFL Hall of Famer Terrell Owens for defamation.
Lawyers for the friends said they intend to file several more defamation claims this week against content creators and have previously indicated their intent to sue the Rev. Al Sharpton and “The View” co-host Sunny Hostin for comments they made while discussing Wells’ death.
The fathers of the three friends, who are under 21 and considered minors under Mississippi law, filed the federal lawsuit Monday on their behalf.
The lawsuit alleges Owens defamed the three friends after posting on X: “ARREST THEM IMMEDIATELY!!” Owens’ post also linked to an Instagram video, which theorized the three friends killed Wells and tampered with his phone, according to the lawsuit. The post was made days after a Mississippi grand jury declined to recommend charges in Wells’ death.
Owens has 1.2 million followers on X and had previously pledged $25,000 to a reward fund for information leading to an arrest and conviction in Wells’ death.
“Not only is he defaming them, he’s basically saying to the mob, get your pitchforks, get your torches,” said Edward Paltzik, a defamation and media attorney representing the three friends.
The Associated Press attempted to contact Owens through social media and SMAC Entertainment, which, according to its website, manages Owens, but did not immediately receive a response.
The three were part of a group of 30 friends, including Wells, who rode to Horn Island on three boats on the Fourth of July. Wells’ friends said Wells did not return to the mainland with them, choosing instead to stay behind to talk with a girl, a claim his family has disputed. His body was found two days later off the island’s coast.
Both state and independent autopsies have not determined Wells’ cause of death, though the grand jury found his death was “consistent with drowning.” Wells’ family and their lawyers disputed the grand jury’s findings, pointing to unexplained bruising on the back of his head and noting that his airways and stomach were devoid of water.
Images showing Wells with white friends the day he went missing fueled online speculation that racial dynamics played a role in his death.
Two of the three friends who are suing Owens were singled out online in part because they appear in a photo with Wells and one other friend on a boat, which was circulated on social media after his disappearance. The third called Wells’ mother and the U.S. Coast Guard to report Wells missing.

title: New moms school offers postpartum support
text:
GREENVILLE, S.C. (Aging Untold) — A new program in South Carolina is offering support to women during the postpartum period, connecting them with experts and other mothers navigating early motherhood.
Nicole Parmelee, who has two children, started the New Moms School after her own experience with the fourth trimester, the time after a woman gives birth.
“They prepare you for how to swaddle a baby, how to change a diaper, you know, how to respond to your baby’s cries, but they don’t prepare the mother for how they might feel,” Parmelee said.
A difficult transition
Parmelee said new mothers deal with a lack of sleep, breastfeeding challenges and post-delivery healing.
“It was very isolating,” Parmelee said. “You’re constantly questioning yourself, wondering if you’re doing things the right way, wondering if this is normal.”
Parmelee said she felt there was a lack of support for women during the postpartum period.
“I never knew there was a pelvic floor physical therapist,” Parmelee said. “Everyone tells you when you go to the doctor, if you, ‘Oh, I’m peeing when I sneeze’, or ‘I’m peeing when I laugh or jump’ and they’re like, ‘That’s normal. That happens.’”
Parmelee said she learned that was not normal and that there are ways to help the body heal.
An eight-week program
The New Moms School is an eight-week program that includes support sessions with experts such as a relationship counselor, positive parent coach, therapist, lactation consultant and speech-language pathologist.
“It’s really an investment in the mother because studies have shown that if mom is happy, baby’s happy, family’s happy,” Parmelee said.
The program also connects mothers with each other outside of class through a Facebook group and group chat.
“So not only are we providing them with the experts from the community, but we’re also helping them build their own community,” Parmelee said. “We encourage the moms to get together outside of class. We will put them in a Facebook group so they have contact with each other, we’ll, you know, get a group chat going.”
“That’s just women supporting other women, and we really need more of that,” Parmelee said.

title: 40 miles for 40 acres: Maryland minister walks from Brunswick to Augusta for reparations
text:
RICHMOND —A little more than halfway through his trek in Maine on Tuesday, the Rev. Dr. Robert Turner already knew the walk would be physically and mentally taxing.
“The walks are always long. It’s never a walk where I’m just at the end doing cartwheels. My body is sore. But it’s also a spiritual moment for me. I reflect, I meditate. It’s like a pilgrimage. But it’s also a call to action,” Turner explained.
Turner, who is the pastor at the Empowerment Temple AME Church in Baltimore, was walking about 38 miles from Brunswick to Augusta to advocate for reparations to the descendants of enslaved Africans, a continuation of his previous initiative 40 Miles for 40 Acres, where he walked from Baltimore to Washington, D.C., each month to highlight the broken promise of Union Gen. William T. Sherman’s 40 acres and a mule.
Turner started out at the John Brown Russworm African American Center in Brunswick at 5 a.m., traveling north through Topsham along the Kennebec River, and he expected to reach the State Capitol in Augusta around 5:40 p.m. Outside of Richmond, he walked under a cloudless sky with wind blowing off the river through the rolling roads, holding a sign that read “REPARATIONS NOW” and sporting a reflective orange-and-yellow jacket.
Tuesday’s walk held additional significance. It falls on the 185th anniversary of Maine’s first Colored Convention, the 1841 gathering where African Americans met in Portland to discuss abolition and racial equality across Maine. Turner dedicated his walk to the late Gerald E. Talbot, Maine’s first Black legislator and a civil rights advocate.
“You have so much that has happened here that needs repair from, and the evidence of the suffering is still being felt on Oct. 6, 2026,” Turner said.
Turner cited historical events of oppression and racism in Maine, such as the state’s involvement with the slave trade and the history of Malaga Island. He spoke about continued racial disparities in the state, where Black people are more likely to be incarcerated, underhoused and under the poverty line.
After moving from Tulsa, Oklahoma, to Baltimore in 2021, he decided to walk the 42.9 miles to Washington, D.C., to call for reparations. Since then, he has done that walk 40 times, once every month, and then expanded the cause to a national level with walks in Alabama, North Carolina and Virginia. Maine is his ninth state and he plans to walk in all 50.
“I’ve walked in the ice, the snow, the rain, the thunderstorms, you name it, I’ve walked. I’ve never postponed a walk due to weather,” he said. “So I’ve walked in snowstorms, I’ve walked in weather advisories … I’ve walked when cities were closed down. God has kept me these 49 times. I’ve slipped, but I’ve never fallen.”
Turner’s choice to start his walk in Brunswick holds additional historical significance, being the place where Harriet Beecher Stowe wrote “Uncle Tom’s Cabin,” the anti-slavery novel. John Brown Russwurm was one of the first Black college graduates in the United States, graduating from Bowdoin College in 1826; he eventually helped found the nation’s first Black newspaper.
Walking up Route 24 outside of Richmond, Turner said he’d received both positive and negative reactions. Some responded enthusiastically to the cause. One woman stopped him alongside the road to question why he is not fighting for other groups such as Irish Americans.
“I’m not against anybody who is suffering from getting reparations,” he said.
Turner said his plan, when he reached Augusta, was to lay a wreath of 400 roses down on the state capital to represent 400 years of oppression. He planned to pray at the State Capitol, and read Chapter 61 from the Book of Isaiah in the Bible, which he reads at the end of every walk.
“Then I leave. I leave physically, but spiritually praying and politically advocating through petitions, through emails, through phone calls for repair being done in Maine,” he said.
His next state to walk is South Carolina. He plans to organize his future walks by finding historical dates in the state he will be walking in, hopefully doing the northern states in the summer and the southern states in the winter. He urges each state he walks through to repair the damage that has been done in history.
“I think Maine, by doing reparations, which is the truest form of justice that America has never seen, can help lead the nation. … Maine was one of the first states to abolish slavery,” Turner said. “Maine could also lead the nation as one of the first states to issue reparations.”

title: Live updates: Susan Collins and Troy Jackson debate for the first time
text:
Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson are set to debate Tuesday, the first time voters will see them share a stage.
Democrats have long coveted Collins’ seat, which she has held since 1996. But she’s never faced a reelection battle quite like this. The opponent Democratic voters nominated in June, Graham Platner, abruptly withdrew from the race after a woman credibly accused him of sexual assault. (Platner has denied the allegation.) Jackson was nominated to replace Platner at a convention later that month.
Most polls show Jackson ahead of Collins, but the incumbent is outspending him on the airwaves. Tonight’s debate is certain to feature talk about the cost of living, the Iran War, President Donald Trump and Collins’ recent spate of negative national press. Follow along with us live here.
That’s a wrap!
Thanks for following along with us. Until next time.
-Kirby Wilson and Billy Kobin
But I didn’t see anything game changing. Three more debates to go!
-Kirby Wilson
“To be effective in the Senate, you need knowledge, experience, seniority and relationships. That combination has allowed me to pass bipartisan legislation,” Collins said.
Jackson said that “I don’t owe Donald Trump and the billionaires anything. You know, I owe the people of the state everything.” He brought up again how Collins voted with Trump around 96% of the time and that she’s been fighting for “the billionaire class.”
“Tonight, Sen. Collins has told us how powerful she is, but power means nothing if you won’t use it when the people in Maine need it,” Jackson said, adding he passed legislation at the State House to lower prescription drug costs, support childcare and provide universal school meals along with sponsoring abortion access legislation.
“I’m never going to forget where I came from. I’m an everyday person that is so indebted to people who put me in this position to fight for them,” Jackson said.
The two shared a laugh when moderator Gregg Lagerquist of WGME said at the end he was going to ask both of them during the lightning round if the New England Patriots will make the playoffs.
Collins said they absolutely will, and razzed Jackson for being a Steelers fan.
Each candidate left the stage smiling.
-Kirby Wilson
-There should be more restrictions on data centers
-Mifepristone, which is a medication used for abortions, should be available.
But the candidates disagreed over:
-Whether Americans should have to show ID at the polls. (Collins: Yes. Jackson: No.)
-Whether Israel should have the same level of support from the U.S. government, less support, or more support. (Collins: the same. Jackson: less, but there was more nuance to this answer.)
-Kirby Wilson
A note on the style of the candidates
To touch on the optics of the debate or the tone so far, Collins has repeatedly gotten defensive when Jackson has criticized her. It feels safe to say Jackson has been more on offense rather than defense. Not an entirely surprising thing given the incumbent often faces plenty of attacks.
-Billy Kobin
Jackson criticized Collins for voting for Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who Jackson said was clearly going to push for tariffs, long one of Trump’s signature policy aims.
“I’m not going to give her credit for getting one thing back,” Jackson said, when thousands of other items are more expensive under Trump.
-Kirby Wilson
Collins reiterated that “you cannot abolish ICE” while saying it needs reforms. She argued the $70 billion figure that Jackson cited was not really all for ICE but rather split between ICE and Customs and Border Protection.
“You don’t (pour) more money into an agency that is killing people across the country,” Jackson said.
-Billy Kobin
Jackson promises to not be a “blank check” for any president, Republican or Democrat.
-Kirby Wilson
Jackson said he supports Medicare for All and wants to help Mainers get covered.
While Collins points to her 2017 vote to block a Republican attempt to repeal the Affordable Care Act, Jackson noted she and Republicans let ACA tax credits expire at the end of 2025.
-Billy Kobin
Collins responds by noting that she’s always been pro-choice, and that Jackson hasn’t.
“I clearly don’t agree with how Brett Kavanaugh voted on Roe v. Wade,” Collins said.
-Kirby Wilson
Collins referred to Navatek and its former CEO Martin Kao, calling him a “crook.” She mentioned the University of Maine project that Navatek was involved in and a photo of the two of them together, saying that photo was taken months before there was “ever a contribution” from Kao.
Jackson wouldn’t let her get off easy on this, and he brought up how Trump ended the FBI probe that was continuing into Kao and the pro-Collins super PAC. Collins kept criticizing all of this as false.
Collins then brought up Jackson’s past case in which a Republican lawmaker filed an ethics complaint against him for using an Augusta home when serving in the Legislature.
The Maine Ethics Commission voted unanimously against investigating Jackson in 2023, and commissioners noted they could only weigh in on whether Jackson violated any campaign finance rules through the Augusta residence and not on the additional claims that he committed crimes such as mortgage fraud.
-Billy Kobin
In January, Trump said Collins “should never be elected to office again,” though relations between the two seem to have improved since then.
-Billy Kobin and Kirby Wilson
“Whatever,” Jackson said of her rate of voting for the president’s priorities. “It’s far too often.”
-Billy Kobin
“Sen. Collins is like an arsonist who helps set the fire and then she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out,” Jackson said, emphasizing she advanced the bill and that GOP colleagues have “called her a team player.”
-Billy Kobin
Jackson fired back by saying Mainers are struggling because Collins has failed to stand up for Donald Trump as he wages war in Iran.
-Kirby Wilson
It was a more aggressive opening statement than Collins’.
-Kirby Wilson
It will be interesting to see how aggressive Jackson is with his attacks and whether he can land a few blows. He’s not the most gifted speaker, so how he delivers his attacks and responds to Collins’ rebuttals will be important to watch.
Meanwhile, Collins, 73, will have to parry those attacks from Jackson and try to land a few rhetorical punches of her own. Her campaign spoke with reporters earlier today about how they plan to push back on pay-to-play allegations made in a ProPublica story two weeks ago. And she and her Republican allies have been mining Jackson’s legislative record for problematic votes.
This will be Collins’ first televised debate in roughly six years. Her energy and sharpness will likely be scrutinized.
Collins, who has been in office for nearly 30 years, clearly has an advantage when it comes to in-depth knowledge about national policy and international affairs. Jackson has to hold his own without making any gaffes that could live on in social media posts or advertisements.
-Randy Billings

title: Convicted Massachusetts felon pleads guilty to selling imported plutonium from Russia to dozens
text:
Convicted Massachusetts felon pleads guilty to selling imported plutonium from Russia to dozens
A Massachusetts man pleaded guilty to several charges after the U.S. Attorney's Office said he illegally sold and imported plutonium from Russia.
Jacob D. Miller, 44, of Hadley, was a convicted felon at the time of the illegal importation charges against him.
In 2004, Miller was convicted in state court for possession of child pornography and possession of an explosive device.
After his release, Miller began selling the highly radioactive plutonium and sold the element to 67 people from December 2020 to March 2025, from his home in South Hadley, which is around 15 miles north of Springfield, Massachusetts.
According to the U.S. Attorney's Office, Miller shipped the plutonium to customers in and outside the United States, even as the plutonium was prohibited from being mailed.
Miller's home was searched in April 2025. Police found a box containing bottles of explosive powder, ammunition and rifles, possession of which violated his prior felony convictions.
His laptop and cell phone both contained child sex abuse material, the U.S. Attorney said, which he accessed just one day before the search warrant was carried out.
Miller pleaded guilty to one count of being a felon in possession of ammunition, one count of being a felon in possession of explosive materials, one count of importing nuclear material without lawful authority, one count of mailing hazardous materials and one count of possession of child pornography.
Miller will be sentenced on Jan. 21, 2027, in U.S. District Court.

title: VIDEO: Mountain bikers race to rescue horse submerged neck-deep in mud
text:
VIDEO: Mountain bikers race to rescue horse submerged neck-deep in mud
A horse was rescued by what some would call "unlikely" heroes after being trapped deep in mud for several hours at a New Hampshire park.
The horse, named "Mac," and his owner were riding with two other woman at Bear Brook State Park when the horse made an attempt to turn around on a bridge along part of the trail that was unfamiliar to the group.
"I saw (Mac's) back legs come off the bridge and then (his rider) went off with him," Leighel Webb told Hearst station WMUR. "And then next thing, Shiloh (the horse), same thing, went off the bridge with Betsy (her rider). And then it was me and Scarlett (my horse)."
While the others slowly got up, the largest horse, Mac, was submerged up to his neck in the mud and quickly going into shock. Webb went to find help just as a group of mountain bikers was passing by.
"(Webb) was holding two horses. She was upset and distraught. She had mentioned to our group that there was a horse stuck in the mud," Christopher Harding, one of the mountain bikers in the group, said.
Chris Hill and his wife were also in the group and immediately went over to help.
Watch video of rescue in the play finder above
"I couldn't believe how deep in the water and in the muck this poor horse was and the owner was holding his head up. So, we kind of just ditched our mountain bikes off to the side," Hill said.
Several of the mountain bikers immediately jumped waist-deep into the mud to help free Mac. And hours later, with the help of the first responders, it worked.
"People just tried to do whatever they could to help this horse. They didn't care about their own well-being or safety and just jumped in," Harding said.
Webb calls them heroes.
"He really wanted to live; he was fighting for his life, and there were other people that really wanted him to live too," she said.
Deerfield Fire Department, Pittsfield Fire Department and Deerfield Veterinary Clinic were all on scene to help in Mac's rescue

title: Neighbors helping neighbors: Heat assistance resources on MDI
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MOUNT DESERT ISLAND — As the leaves start to turn and paint the island bright shades of orange, yellow and red, it comes time to think about winter again. For some that means wrapping up the season, pulling traps out of the water, and closing the restaurant down. Heavy on many minds this year will likely be increasing heating bills.
Heating oil prices are up 74% from last winter, an increase that the Department of Energy Resources reports will cost $675 more to fill up a standard 275-gallon oil tank than one year ago.
For some organizations on MDI, that means it’s time to get to work.
Below are various resources to help islanders ease the financial burden of staying warm.
Firewood and fuel assistance
The MDI Community Woodbank held a volunteer day last Sunday, when people showed up to help with splitting and stacking firewood that will go to families who need assistance heating their homes this winter.
The woodbank is available to people who live on MDI, Swans Island, Frenchboro, Great Cranberry and Little Cranberry Islands. Participants are not required to fill out any paperwork and can receive up to half a cord of wood per month.
Now in its second year, the woodbank already has 15 to 20 cords of split, seasoned firewood ready to be picked up or delivered, and founder Andrew Flanagan says they’ve already made 8 deliveries this year.
The MDI Community Woodbank asks that participants apply for aid resources and the neighboring MDI Campfire Coalition, a program co-created by The Neighborhood House and Harbor House in 2008 that’s dedicated to providing heating assistance to residents on MDI.
Residents of any of the municipalities on MDI along with Swans and Cranberry Islands who meet the earnings criteria can apply for a one-time delivery of 150 gallons of heating oil. They will also provide equivalent amounts of other fuels like wood, propane and electric heat.
Neither organization collects administrative fees from the donations that are made to the Coalition, which means “every penny someone gives, buys heating oil,” according to Neighborhood House Executive Director Anne-Marie Hart. “This program is fantastic,” said Hart. “It’s a safety net for so many people.”
Last year, the Campfire Coalition program helped 133 households. The program runs from Oct. 13 to April 30, 2027, and people are encouraged to apply before they run out of fuel as the program is not intended for emergencies.
The MDI Community Woodbank board members understand that completing paperwork to apply for assistance can be overwhelming, so Laura Merrill-Bundy, Resource Coordinator at the YWCA of MDI, attends volunteer days to connect with individuals who may need support. She is available to connect people with aid programs and help them complete applications for assistance free of charge. People in need of assistance can reach out to her at laura@ywcamdi.org to get connected with the YWCA MDI Resource Assistance Program which removes barriers for individuals to access critical resources including heating.
Improving energy efficiency at home
A Climate to Thrive is also stepping in to help educate homeowners on making their homes as energy efficient as possible to save on their heating bill. Their energy coaching program trains volunteers on how to work with their neighbors to identify ways to make their homes more energy efficient.
They are training their next cohort of coaches this fall and have an information session scheduled for 6 p.m. on Oct. 13, at the Community School for Place-Based Education. All are welcome to attend and more information can be found on A Climate to Thrive’s website aclimatetothrive.org/efficiency-coaching.
There are some do-it-yourself projects to prepare houses for the cold winter months, and insulating windows can make a big difference in keeping heat inside.
WindowDressers is an organization dedicated to helping people in Northern New England seal their windows to make their homes more energy efficient in the winter. Their inserts are made of a wooden frame tightly wrapped with a film of plastic that is measured to fit snug in each window. The plastic is clear, so they will still allow light through the window while blocking drafts. Anyone can apply to receive window inserts and is required to attend a community build event to help construct inserts.
There will be a community build at the Bar Harbor Congregational Church from Nov. 7 through Nov. 12 with different shifts and roles for volunteers to sign up for. No experience is required to sign up, and there are different tasks for different levels of ability and mobility.

title: Coast to coast with Ford and Brinkley
text:
It started with an innocent conversation. “I’ve always wanted to drive Route 66,” Brad exclaimed one evening nine months ago.
Me too.
And we were off to the races.
At first, we opted for our respective sports cars but decided that some of the route out west includes old dirt paths that we would hate to overlook but certainly wouldn’t want to take our low-slung, rear-drive cars down rutted dirt roads.
Then we opted for our family crossovers, each of us ensconced in efficient small wagons. Thinking about what we might want to do, how much stuff we might need exploring The Mother Road and then through Utah’s national parks, and a host of other growing wish list stops, maybe renting a Suburban or a minivan might be necessary. And the prices were pretty darned reasonable after making a reservation for one.
And then someone, might have been my navigator, might have been my brother from another mother, but it came out — we should take RVs.
Since neither of us had one, that could prove to be an obstacle.
But only temporarily. Brad and his wife Laurie threw themselves into the quest for a new hotel on wheels, making an acquisition in what seemed mere weeks, finding a mildly used Class A motorhome in great condition. Being a seasoned do-it-all mechanic and been-everywhere-man truck driver, Brad swiftly tackled the upgrades necessary to transform the 20-year-old RV into something more modern.
“Whoa,” we thought. “This is a big leap.” The navigator started to peruse the endless list of RV-ing options, often contrary to what I wanted to be encased in for a lengthy multi-week trip. After weeks of looking (the RV industry could certainly use some more pricing transparency), we agreed that a new unit would be to our liking. And Brinkley, a relatively new RV brand, made the most positive impressions with its Ix 20-foot trailer. Although noone had a completely compromise-free model that suited both of our tastes. Such is the American consumer’s conflicting preferences.
After separate virgin camping experiences, ours a lovely oceanside experience in Belfast, theirs to the wilds outside of Greenville, we locked and loaded our departure dates, lined up a plethora of maps and guidebooks and amassed a huge go-to/wish-for list. All while making countless unexpected purchases to augment our experience of outfitting a rolling box that needed to be our kitchen, bedroom, living room, and bathroom — all in close proximity to each other.
In the meantime, the navigator thought, “Hey, could we leverage our experience to have support from one of the automakers and/or Brinkley?” Long past the time when our Wheels & Waves boating and auto adventures should already be on YouTube, we made a pitch to GM first. After all, it is America’s 250th birthday this year, plus the 100th birthday for the founding of Route 66. Experiencing both and sharing that had to have value, right?
Two proposals to GM got crickets, twice. Not a peep back over two months.
Ford, a long-time member and supporter of the New England Motor Press Association, was next to pursue, and Rhonda, our East Coast press specialist for NEMPA, said, “maybe, let me check.” In three days, we had an answer back that Ford would like to share a Super Duty for our trip, and would enjoy the coverage of how real Americans use their trucks.
And, the Super Duty available was one we had recently sampled — a crew cab, long-bed, big dually Powerstroke Diesel King Ranch model with “only” 500 horsepower and 1,200-pound feet of torque. I think the Ford can pull our small trailer as well as Brad’s RV right over the Continental Divide, if necessary. It didn’t hurt that both the truck and the camper share color schemes.
So, four retired “kids” from Beech Hill Pond are about to travel from the coast of Maine to Santa Monica Pier, absorbing as much of Route 66 as possible, as well as taking the roads less traveled coming back across country. The big city lights will intimidate us, yet the history of this magical road, in fact the majesty of the American west and all of its natural wonders, will amaze us.
And just like Henry Ford’s initial camping adventures with other early 20th century notables, savoring an America that many had never seen, our Super Duty and the Brinkley might be just a tad more comfortable than his Model T and canvas tents.
Next up: East of the Mississippi to Chicago and heading South on Route 66.

title: Authorities investigating fatal excavator accident in Gray
text:
At least one person died in a workplace accident involving an excavator in Gray on Monday, the Cumberland County sheriff says.

title: Bangor leaders address homelessness, winter shelter capacity
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Bangor leaders are addressing homelessness, from winter shelter beds to safety downtown.
Warming shelters took center stage at Monday’s Government Operations Committee meeting.
Shelter funding
MaineHousing awarded funds to expand the Bangor Area Homeless Shelter by five beds and the Brick Church by 65 beds. The Mansion Church and Together Place were not funded.
Officials said an average of 85 people used warming shelter beds each night last winter, topping 100 on 11 nights. They are now planning for the coldest nights ahead.
Police response
Homeless policy was another issue discussed at length. Bangor Chief of Police Mark Hathaway said mental health is just as big of an issue as the addiction crisis in the city.
He said the police department has been overwhelmed, and that it’s hard to keep up with a systemic issue specific to Bangor.
“We have more of a problem here because we literally, and I think everybody understands it, we’re caring for a large chunk of the state’s most vulnerable people. We’re just overwhelmed with it. And I don’t think it’s fair to classify one community as doing a better job, when really, we all know that most communities point their most vulnerable to the community with all the services, and that’s Bangor. We expect the street police officer to solve all of society’s failures, but we don’t give them the tools to do that job,” Hathaway said.
He went on to say that they are doing everything possible to make sure that Bangor’s residents feel comfortable walking around downtown, and that their safety is a top priority.

title: Cumberland County wraps up inventory of untested sexual assault kits
text:
Cumberland County wraps up inventory of untested sexual assault kits
Sexual assault survivors can now check the status of their kits and decide how they want the evidence to be handled
Cumberland County wraps up inventory of untested sexual assault kits
Sexual assault survivors can now check the status of their kits and decide how they want the evidence to be handled
Cumberland County police departments have completed an inventory of old sexual assault kits, wrapping up the latest phase of a countywide effort to improve how sexual assaults are investigated and prosecuted.
During the inventory, law enforcement agencies discovered 620 untested kits.
"I think it's really important for us to be accountable to victims for whatever happened in the past," Cumberland County District Attorney Jacqueline Sartoris said. "This is part of kind of resetting where we are on sex assault cases in general."
The project is funded by a federal grant aimed at addressing the nationwide backlog of untested sexual assault kits. Each kit contains evidence that was collected by a forensic nurse following a sexual assault.
Cumberland County inventoried every kit that was collected before the project began in August 2024. Of the 620 kits, 530 are associated with people who filed police reports. The other 90 kits are anonymous, collected from people who were unsure about whether or not they wanted to report the crime to law enforcement.
"These kits should have been tested a long time ago," Sartoris said. "It's really not the fault of the police departments that that wasn't happening."
Some kits date back to the 1980s, but most are newer. Today, according to Maine law, police departments are required to keep kits for 20 years, but prior to 2018, many kits were kept for only 90 days, meaning much of the older evidence is gone.
"I am sort of devastated on behalf of victims at having to tell them that we don't have a sex assault kit," Sartoris said. "It tells me that our system has been broken for quite some time when it comes to these cases."
During the next phase of the project, the 530 kits associated with police reports will be sent to a private lab for testing.
Under state law, the other 90 kits cannot be tested, despite the fact that prior research showed that many victims assume their kits will be tested whether or not they file a report.
Now that the inventory is complete, survivors can check the status of their kits, and if they choose to do so, people with anonymous kits can file a police report so their kit can be included in testing.
"Each survivor is an individual and a unique person who's going to make choices about how they move forward or not, and I think it's really important for folks to know that they have a choice," said Meg Hatch, executive director of Sexual Assault Services Southern Maine.
Prosecutors like Sartoris say testing is important even if a kit is not used in a court case, because DNA evidence can help catch serial offenders.
"My hope is that this project will demonstrate that there are folks in Cumberland County who are taking these crimes and experiences seriously and who want to hold perpetrators accountable," Hatch said.
People who want to check the status of their kit can email sakit@cumberlandcounty.org or call 207-544-4448. An advocate from Sexual Assault Services Southern Maine will respond within one business day and explain the available options. All communication will be confidential.
To receive general assistance, victims of sexual assault can call a statewide hotline at 1-800-871-7741.
Maine was the last in the nation to start implementing national best practices for the handling of sexual assault evidence. 8 Investigates has been covering the push for reform since February 2024. Click here to view our previous reporting.

title: Cornell brings in ex-Justice official Sally Yates to review school’s handling of sex assault claims
text:
ITHACA, N.Y. (AP) — A former high-ranking Department of Justice official will look at how Cornell handles sexual misconduct complaints, university trustees announced Tuesday as they tried to address an outpouring of anger over allegations of a 2024 gang rape at a fraternity house.
Sally Yates, who was a deputy attorney general in the Obama administration, will spearhead the review, the trustees said in an announcement. The assessment is to include how the Ivy League university investigates reports of sexual assault and sexual harassment, what support students get, how the disciplinary process works, campus police responses and oversight of fraternities, sororities and other student organizations.
The announcement comes after days of outrage and demonstrations over Cornell’s response to a complaint from a woman known publicly only as Jane Doe, who told campus police in November 2024 that she had been sexually assaulted by multiple Chi Phi fraternity brothers the month before after being pressured into drinking and taking drugs.
No criminal charges have been filed. The Chi Phi chapter at Cornell was shut down, and the Ivy League university has said it expelled some students and suspended others.
She sued the university, seven former students, the fraternity and others last month. The suit put a new, nationwide spotlight on the allegations and how the campus police, university and local prosecutor had reacted.
New York’s attorney general is now conducting a criminal investigation, and the state’s governor called for an independent review of Cornell’s handling of the matter — the review that Yates now will lead.
Cornell students, professors and others thronged a campus plaza Monday to protest the university’s response to the matter.

title: Firefighters survive 8-foot fall into burning basement after floor collapses at vacant home
text:
‘Mayday, mayday’: Firefighters survive 8-foot fall into burning basement after floor collapses at vacant home
Rapid intervention and training prevented tragedy during a vacant building search
‘Mayday, mayday’: Firefighters survive 8-foot fall into burning basement after floor collapses at vacant home
Rapid intervention and training prevented tragedy during a vacant building search
Two firefighters in Albuquerque, New Mexico, escaped without injury Wednesday morning after falling eight feet through a floor into a basement fire while responding to a residential structure fire.
Crews were dispatched at 6 a.m. Wednesday to a fire at Alcazar Street and Marquette Avenue, near Louisiana Boulevard. The building was a vacant structure that showed signs of human occupancy.
"There's always a debate about searching vacant buildings. Even though there might be boarded-up structures, there's always that risk and reward. If you take a look in any of those windows, people are staying in there. And so if we have a building that we can search, we're going to do that every time. This is a reminder of what's at stake when we do go inside these structures," said Lt. Jason Fejer, with Albuquerque Fire Rescue.
During the response, crews split up, with Engine 13 working on the first floor and Engine 5 operating in the basement.
"There wasn't much fire involvement here. The roof isn't collapsed. This building is not burned through. It's a small fire in the basement that got into the trusses and our guys fell through it," Fejer said. "We carry thermal imaging cameras, and he could see the heat in the floor, which was about the time that the floor collapsed."
The collapse triggered an immediate call: "Mayday, mayday, mayday, Engine 13 with a mayday, firefighters fell through the floor."
"I almost didn't believe it at first. And then the more I started scrolling through my CAD and seeing that there was not just one firefighter, but two, the reality of it sets in," Fejer said.
The distress call shifted the focus of responding units, including Engine 11, Engine 13, Engine 5, Engine 12, and a Rapid Intervention Team.
"The scene turned from us going into a structure to save a civilian into us trying to save ourselves," Fejer said.
The two firefighters fell eight feet directly into the source of the fire. Both were able to leave the scene without injuries, though they continue to be monitored.
Albuquerque Fire Rescue emphasized that crew training, situational awareness, and teamwork prevented a tragedy, noting that basement fires cause firefighter fatalities annually.
"If we weren't putting water on the fire when those guys went through, this could have been catastrophic," Fejer said. "These guys work so hard, and they take this job so seriously. They are the best that we have. And sometimes we got to be better than luck or make our own luck. And I think that's what today is a testament to."
The department stated it will review the response, including call times, responding units, and scene management, to evaluate if any operational changes are needed.
Albuquerque Fire Rescue noted it has never experienced a line-of-duty death.

title: NTSB preliminary report: Warning horns went off for news helicopter that crashed in Los Angeles
text:
NTSB preliminary report: Warning horns went off for news helicopter that crashed in Los Angeles
Weeks after NBCLA's news helicopter crashed in a Los Angeles suburban neighborhood, the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) released on Tuesday its preliminary findings on the moments before it fell to the ground.
Previous coverage in the video player above
According to NTSB — the lead investigating agency — the AS-350 B2 helicopter was overhead in the Chatsworth neighborhood covering a separate fatal LA Metro bus crash on Sept. 15 when video showed the aircraft began descending rapidly.
The helicopter was flying in the area for about one hour and 24 minutes, NTSB said. The agency cited a four-minute, 21-second-long video that captured unusual noises toward the end.
During most of the recording, NTSB said the helicopter made ambient noise consistent with what a helicopter would normally sound like. But in the last 29 seconds of the video, the aircraft changed frequency, making "intermittent and continuous horns, consistent with the helicopter's main rotor high rpm, low rotor rpm and other aural advisories."
NBCLA reported that its helicopter had warning lights and horns to warn the pilot of danger, including if the rotations per minute began exceeding or going below the safe operating range.
NTSB said during the last minute of its flight, the helicopter was about 800 feet above ground level and began decelerating to about 6 knots (almost 7 mph) ground speed. In the last 29 seconds, it fell by about 38 knots (about 44 mph).
Read the full NTSB preliminary report here. It may take weeks or months before the agency releases a final report.
The crash left the crew on board and a man on the ground dead. Officials have since identified them as NewsChopper4 reporter Eliana Moreno, pilot George Marciniw and pedestrian Edy Gutierrez Mejia.
NBCLA's crew was covering the Metro bus crash, which happened at West Nordhoff Street and De Soto Avenue. Video showed an SUV that rammed through a bus, leaving two people dead and eight more injured.
The SUV driver, Bailee Lynn Rios, is accused of being under the influence of drugs when she swerved into the wrong lane, blew a red light, and she slammed into the bus. She now faces two charges of second-degree murder in the deaths of Daniel Castillo and Gage Weida. Rios has pleaded not guilty in connection with the bus crash.

title: Maine Drivers Enter a Dangerous Time of Year for Crashes With Animals
text:
Maine Drivers Enter a Dangerous Time of Year for Crashes With Animals
While we need to stay alert year-round, this is a particularly important time to be cautious on the road.
👇 KEEP READING: 19 Maine News Stories That Went National in the Last 20 Years 👇
Playcasino.com analyzed federal records of fatal crashes involving vehicles striking live animals on U.S. public roads from 2015 through 2024, counting every death in those crashes regardless of the animal involved.
Using U.S. Census Bureau population estimates, analysts calculated average annual deaths per million residents and ranked states by those rates, excluding Washington, D.C.
Maine ranked 17th in the analysis, with 13 deaths in crashes involving animals from 2015 through 2024, an average annual rate of 0.95 deaths per million residents.
That amounts to an annual risk of about 1 in 1.05 million for Maine residents, compared with about 1 in 1.56 million nationwide.
The Maine Department of Transportation advises drivers to watch roadsides for wildlife, follow posted speed limits and slow down when visibility is poor, especially around dawn, dusk and at night.
Drivers should also pay attention to wildlife crossing signs and be prepared for additional animals to follow, since deer and moose often travel in groups.
And there you have it! Maine’s rate was higher than the national average, offering another reminder to stay alert for wildlife on the road.

title: Obituary: Danal A. Gerrard
text:
WHITEFIELD – Danal A. Gerrard, aka Blondie, Duck Soup, Grampa Dan, July 2, 1965 – Sept. 24, 2026
Danal A. Gerrard, of Whitefield, Maine, has passed away after a one and a half year long courageous battle with cancer in the arms of the ones he loved. He was a comedian until the very end.
He was born in Augusta, Maine to Norma Gerrard. Danny attended the Augusta School System, he had his own rules, which did not coincide with school policies. He left school at the age of 13, and later in life, returned to obtain his GED. At 14, Danny started his journey with the love of his life, Robin, in their first apartment on Mill Street in Augusta. Dan had a new role as a provider, family friends, Gerine Ferris and Jim Martin, provided guidance and opportunity for odd jobs, such as mowing lawns and cemetery maintenance. These experiences gave Dan lifelong knowledge, skills, and abilities which contributed to his growth and career path.
Dan’s longest role was as Foreman of Augusta Parks, Recreation and Cemeteries for over 30 years. In this position, Dan was responsible for maintaining and decorating the city for all festivities. He helped organize the fourth of July parade during his years with the city. He would often joke that his job was to plant trees and people. Later in life, he loved working at the Maragaret Chase Smith House as a maintenance man for the elderly residents; always going above and beyond to put a smile on their faces. His last role, which Dan felt was his most fulfilling throughout his lifelong career of helping others, was as head custodian at Whitefield Elementary School. Where not only his own grandchildren, but teachers and students alike, called him Grampa Dan.
Dan was predeceased by his grandparents; his mother Norma; his sisters Deborah and Diana; his infant son Shawn; and his sister-in-law Candy.
He is survived by his wife of 43 years Robin, their daughter Kellie Coates and her daughters River and Indie and their father Christopher Coates; his daughter Danielle Gerrard and her children Allianna, Kristianna, Jaxson, and Piper and her fiancé Jake Michaud; his brother Darrell Gerrard and fiancé Melanie Bridges, his sister Deana Tardiff, his sister Darcie Verrill and partner Chris Smith, his sister-in-law Tammy Kincaid and husband Brian, his sister-in-law Tracy McKenney and husband Mike.
Duck Soup will be greatly missed by his nieces and nephews, Amanda, Richie, Eric, Josh, Zach, Mitch, Brian, Ashley, Jesse, Jason, Sasha, Kayla, and their families as well as several great nieces, nephews, aunts, uncles, and cousins.
Dan the man had a heart of gold, he was a family man through and through and took pride in carrying on family traditions. He loved to host family holidays and made sure everyone was cared for, especially “The Aunts”, Aunt Joan and Aunt Nancy. Dan enjoyed planning family events and activities from huge camping trips, hikes, beach trips, cliff jumping, to the annual Mother’s Day bash. He was a coach, a certified girl scout, a jack of all trades and master of none. His motto was “the more the merrier”. Although he was a safety-first kind of guy, he liked to push himself and other to the limit. He liked to march to the beat of his own drum. Dan had a zest and passion for life and adventure which often found him in dangerous situations. His main purpose in life was caring for his wife and children. Shhh… don’t tell anyone, but his grandchildren were his pride and joy. He never missed an event for his children or grandchildren and continued to show up even in his last days. Grampa Dan, the man, the myth, the legend.
Dan was an organ donor and when he was diagnosed with cancer, he learned he was no longer eligible. Disheartened by this news, he set out to find an alternative way to give back. Dan learned of the University of New England’s anatomical donation program for orthopedic research. A lifelong educator, he was thrilled by this option. Once the research process is complete, his remains will contribute to the “Ashes to Ash Trees” program bringing his work of planting trees full circle when he becomes one to help oxygenate the planet.
A celebration of life will be held on Saturday, Oct. 10 from 1 p.m. to 3 p.m. at Whitefield Elementary School.
In lieu of flowers, please make donations to:
his daughter Kellie for
final expenses
