title: Meet Varsity Maine’s 10 unsung heroes of September
text:
Maybe you notice them; maybe you don’t. Either way, there’s something to be said for the “unsung hero” — the player who, while perhaps not putting up the big numbers that catch the headlines, does the little things that are every bit as important in the outcome.
This fall, Varsity Maine is seeking to identify some of those unsung heroes of Maine high school sports. Here are five boys and five girls whose impacts this September were significant, even if they weren’t necessarily measured in goals, assists, touchdowns or yards.
BOYS
Jake Harmon, Monmouth Academy soccer: Bryce Fletcher and Zane Foyt get the plaudits by pouring in goals for Monmouth, but the Mustangs owe just as much of their success to Harmon, who had strong defensive efforts against Mt. Abram on Sept. 16 and against Maranacook on Sept. 29, among others.
Abdirauf Hersi, Lewiston soccer: Hersi’s game-winning assist against Camden Hills on Sept. 8 helped the Blue Devils complete a 3-2 comeback win. On Sept. 19, his well-placed free kick in the dying seconds of the first half against rival Edward Little led to the game’s opening goal.
Wes Pinkham, Bonny Eagle football: Pinkham didn’t record many yards in Bonny Eagle’s season-opening victory over South Portland, but a key catch set up a score that the Scots ultimately needed to win. His strong play in the secondary included a touchdown-saving tackle.
Ethan Reichert, Marshwood football: On a team with just 33 players, each one is asked to do a lot. Reichert has answered the call as a key player on both lines for Marshwood, which went 4-0 in September. He was particularly impactful in the Hawks’ 52-51 thriller over Noble.
Ben Thomas, Winslow football: Winslow’s running backs get the headlines for their gaudy numbers, but that couldn’t happen without strong play from a line that includes a formidable senior in Thomas. He’s also been dominant up front defensively, such as in a 14-6 victory over Freeport.
GIRLS
Addison Barrs, Biddeford field hockey: Mia Mariello’s four goals stole the show in the Tigers’ season-opening win over Sanford/Kennebunk, but Barrs was no less instrumental. The junior was critical to breaking up Spartans possessions, leading to transition play that spurred Biddeford’s offense.
Gracey Copper, Cheverus field hockey: On a defense with no returning starters from 2025, Copper has stepped up for the Stags. Her tenacity while Biddeford launched a barrage of penalty corners at Cheverus in a Sept. 25 showdown was key to the Stags’ 3-2 win in the battle of Class A South powers.
Lauren Jabar, Yarmouth soccer: Jabar helped lead a defense that conceded just two goals all month for a team that was 7-0 in September. A Sept. 3 effort against Cape Elizabeth in which she displayed remarkable 1-on-1 skills and beat the Capers to every ball was particularly noteworthy.
Kristyna Pokorna, Thornton Academy volleyball: Not all stats are created equal; some are the results of plays that change games in key moments. That’s what Pokorna did Sept. 24 against Scarborough with two aces that turned the tide. Oh, and as coach Kayla Arthurs said, don’t let her defense go unnoticed.
Adela Ricker, Gardiner soccer: Goalkeeping is always important, but it’s especially important in one-goal games — exactly where Ricker has thrived. In a Sept. 24 battle with rival Cony, Ricker’s 12 saves were crucial to the Tigers’ 3-2 victory. Gardiner has won five one-goal games this season.

title: Arizona welcomes new Taiwan representative office, rejecting warning from China
text:
Arizona welcomes new Taiwan representative office, rejecting warning from China
Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs joined Taiwanese leaders at the opening of an economic and cultural office Monday to aid Taiwanese businesses and citizens in the region, despite pressure from the Chinese government to block it.
Related video: Is US data center opposition a ‘China PR thing,’ as Trump says? Experts say that’s exaggerated
Taiwanese authorities have said the new Phoenix office — their 14th in the United States — will promote collaboration in technology, especially in semiconductor manufacturing, and better serve a growing number of Taiwanese migrants in the city.
After the plans for the office were announced in July, Hobbs received two letters from China’s consulate general in Los Angeles, asking her to object to the proposal, according to documents the governor’s office shared with The Associated Press.
In a July 3 letter, the Chinese authority called the governor to “refute such an attempt by the Taiwan authorities and stop any political gimmicks to harm the friendship and cooperation between China and the State of Arizona.” The stance was reiterated in an Aug. 21 letter.
The letters were first reported by Phoenix radio station KJZZ.
Hobbs highlighted Arizona’s ties with Taiwan at Monday’s opening.
“Every Arizona elected official should show the courage necessary to support the partnership between Arizona and Taiwan,” Hobbs said. “As our economic partnership grows, we are mobilizing every available resource to support Taiwanese companies expanding here in Arizona.”
Beijing claims the island as a breakaway province inseparable from China, while Taiwan considers itself separate from the Chinese mainland and has its own government. Scholars say that local-level collaborations with the Chinese government and Taiwan have become more politicized as U.S.-China relations have deteriorated over the years.
“China firmly opposes official interactions of any form between China’s Taiwan region and the U.S., including its federal and state governments,” Liu Chang, a spokesperson for China’s Embassy in the U.S., said in a statement on Monday.
Taiwan has been increasing its economic footprint in Arizona, with advanced chipmaker Taiwanese Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, or TSMC, pledging $100 billion to expand its operation in northern Phoenix. That brings its total investment in the city to $265 billion, the largest foreign direct investment in U.S. history.
Around 500 Taiwanese engineers are working to ramp up production at TSMC in Arizona, according to Jason Hsu, a former lawmaker in Taiwan and a senior fellow at the public policy think tank Hudson Institute.
Phoenix Mayor Kate Gallego also said the city is seeing a sort of “baby boom” in its Taiwanese communities, with several labor and delivery rooms even launching Mandarin language programs.

title: Windham business leaders sound off on townwide issues
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Windham business leaders discussed topics ranging from a proposed community center, which would be built in the soon-to-be shuttered Windham Middle School, to the North Windham sewer project, which recently began treating wastewater, at a gathering held at Erik’s Church last Wednesday.
The business leader’s gathering, the first of its kind, was organized by the Windham Economic Development Corp., a quasi-governmental organization supporting economic growth. Corporation President Eric Giguere described the event, which included remarks from himself, Town Manager Robert Burns, and Town Council Chair Mark Morrison, as a “meet and greet” to see how the town can work with local businesses to improve the community.
In his address to the business owners, Burns spoke about three major projects in the Windham area. One of these was the North Windham Wastewater Treatment Plant, which has been in development for more than a decade. Burns said the plant, which began functioning and treating wastewater last month, is projected to treat 50,000 gallons of wastewater at startup, which will increase to 160,000 at full buildout. Burns also said work is underway on a conveyance system connecting the plant to Windham High School.
Burns also spoke about the North Windham Moves project, which will reconfigure North Windham to improve accessibility and traffic congestion and add 5 miles of roadway. He has spoken to other executives of cities and towns throughout Maine who would love to have the $28 million in funding the project has received from the federal government.
The business owners expressed mixed opinions on the North Windham Moves project, with some saying the project would give greater visibility to their businesses, while others felt the project was wasteful and unnecessary.
Jennifer White, owner of A Joyful Noise Christian Daycare and Learning Center, asked Burns about health and infrastructure concerns at the middle school, and wondered why the community center wasn’t considered for Manchester School. Burns said the community center went through a significant committee process to utilize the best option, and pointed out the aging public infrastructure in Windham, including a nearly 100-year-old gym at the current town office.
The choice of venue drew controversy from some residents due to the fact that the owner of Erik’s Church, Kenneth Cianchette, is currently running for state Senate as a Republican.
Kate Turpen, president of Windham & Raymond Pride, questioned the neutrality of the venue, saying the decision to hold the business gathering at the bar alienated non-right-leaning and sober residents. Turpen also noted the irony of the Windham Republican Party’s opposition to funding the community center, and said the choice of Erik’s Church as a venue demonstrated Windham’s lack of adequate meeting spaces.
Cianchette said Erik’s Church was not the organizer of the event, and said, “(I’m) not here to talk about politics.”

title: California couple with 21 children arrested on child abuse charges, police say
text:
California couple with 21 children arrested on child abuse charges in surrogacy investigation, police say
A California couple has been arrested on child abuse charges following an investigation into a surrogacy scheme involving at least 21 children, police said Tuesday.
Silvia Zhang and her husband, Guojun Xuan, are expected to face charges of conspiracy to commit child abuse, according to the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department.
Fifteen children were removed from the couple’s opulent home in Arcadia last year after an allegation of abuse, and another six living elsewhere were also located. They ranged in age from 2 months to 13 years, with most between 1 and 3.
Police believe Zhang gave birth to one or two of the children while the rest were born by surrogate.
Video shows nannies abusing children
Zhang and Xuan were first arrested in May 2025 after a hospital reported that their 2-month-old infant had a traumatic head injury, the result of a nanny at the home violently shaking the baby, according to Arcadia police.
Arcadia police did not file charges at the time, in order to finish a full investigation, they said.
The couple told police that they “wanted a large family” and produced what appeared to be legitimate birth certificates, including some from outside California, that list Zhang as the mother of the children. Xuan was listed as the father on at least some of the birth certificates.
During a search of the couple’s home last year, police examined surveillance footage that showed nannies beating the children who were sitting in a classroom-like room. They issued an arrest warrant for the nanny seen hurting the 2-month-old infant, Chunmei Li, but she could not be found.
Surrogates say they were misled
Surrogacy is an agreement between parties to have a woman become pregnant, typically through an embryo transfer, and deliver a baby for another parent.
The practice has no federal regulation, leaving it up to states to set the rules if they choose to allow it.
California is considered a “surrogacy-friendly state” because it has clear laws governing the process. Both sides are required to have lawyers, and there must be a written, notarized contract before an embryo transfer takes place.
Investigators have said they were looking into whether the couple had misled surrogates around the country. At least eight women had come forward to say they were aggressively pursued by the couple to serve as surrogates.
The women, many of whom were first-time surrogates, say they were given misleading or incomplete information about the couple’s family situation and intentions.
At least one, Kayla Elliott, is now trying to get custody of a baby she birthed for the couple.

title: Amazon refund payments are being sent: How to know if you'll be receiving one
text:
Amazon refund payments are being sent out: How to know if you'll be receiving one
Eligible Amazon customers are beginning to receive refunds as part of the company's $2.5 billion settlement with the Federal Trade Commission.
Related video above from 2025: Amazon settlement explained
The settlement, which was originally announced in 2025, was expanded last month to include more customers who could receive bigger refund payments.
Distribution of those expanded, accelerated payments – up to $200 for eligible customers – began on Oct. 1.
"The payments will be made via electronic payment (Venmo or PayPal) or mailed check without requiring consumers to submit claims, respond to notices or complete any forms," the FTC said last month.
The settlement was first announced in September 2025 over federal allegations that the company misled customers over Prime subscriptions. Amazon did not admit liability.
"The revised order will ensure more consumers who were harmed by Amazon's deceptive enrollment and cancellation practices benefit from the FTC's historic settlement," said Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection, in a prepared statement.
What's the settlement for?
Amazon has sent out automatic payments as part of a $2.5 billion settlement over what the FTC described as "dark patterns," or design tricks that made it deceptively easy to enroll in Prime and frustratingly difficult to cancel. In its lawsuit, the FTC said Amazon buried the option to avoid Prime during checkout and required customers to navigate a lengthy unsubscribe path that employees reportedly called the "Iliad," a nod to the long Greek epic you probably read in school, for how many pages and clicks it took to actually cancel your subscription.
Amazon did not admit liability in the settlement but must pay a $1 billion civil penalty and issue $1.5 billion in refunds to customers affected by its enrollment and cancellation practices for Prime subscriptions.
Who is eligible?
Under the revised order, Amazon will be issuing refunds to those who used between 11 and 20 Prime benefits within a 12-month period.
Previously, automatic refunds covered U.S. consumers who signed up for Prime between June 23, 2019, and June 23, 2025, through what the FTC calls a "challenged enrollment flow" who used no more than three Prime benefits within a 12-month period to qualify. Those who used fewer than 10 Prime benefits within a 12-month period were also eligible for a refund in the second phase of the settlement.
What exactly counts as a "benefit?"
The National Consumer Unit previously asked the FTC directly about what qualifies as a "benefit."
The agency clarified that each Prime benefit refers to the total uses of Prime benefits in a year. For example, if you used two-day shipping when you otherwise wouldn't have received two-day shipping, each instance counts as one Prime benefit used.
If you're a Prime user who makes the most of your membership, this settlement probably isn't aimed at you. The FTC says the refund money is intended for consumers who were misled into signing up and then trapped in a cancellation maze they didn't expect.
How much money will eligible customers receive?
According to the FTC, under the revised settlement, eligible Prime customers can receive a refund of their Amazon Prime subscription fees up to $200. This amount was $51 in the original agreement, so those who previously received that amount could still be eligible for $149 more.
"If consumer-accepted payments do not reach the required threshold by February 2027, Amazon will provide additional automatic payments to consumers who previously received refunds under the settlement," according to the FTC. "As part of the revised order, consumers who have accepted payments will be eligible to receive an additional $149, for a total of $200. This last round of supplemental payments will start by April 2027 and will also be distributed automatically."

title: Oprah Winfrey taps a 'riveting' debut novel for her book club
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A debut novel about a 12-year-old girl’s struggles to find herself amid poverty and family strife is Oprah Winfrey’s new book club pick.
On Tuesday, Winfrey announced that she had chosen Amanda Rizkalla’s “Hungered,” which came out in May. Winfrey said in a statement that the 28-year-old Rizkalla had written a “riveting novel” about “families who live outside the margins, living unhoused” and “their hopes, dreams, and the perseverance it takes to face another day.”
Rizkalla, a Los Angeles native who now lives in the Bay Area, was an undergraduate student at Stanford University and received a Master of Fine Arts in creative writing from the University of Wisconsin-Madison. Like so many authors since Winfrey launched her club 30 years ago, she learned she had been selected after receiving a surprise call from Winfrey herself.
“I was so stunned I could hardly believe it was real, and there are still moments where it all feels like one big daydream,” Rizkalla said in a statement.
The Oprah Podcast conversation with Rizkalla can be seen on Winfrey’s YouTube channel and through other outlets.

title: Firefighter catches on fire while responding to burning home
text:
LONDONDERRY, N.H. (WMUR) - A firefighter is recovering after he was engulfed in flames while responding to a house fire.
The incident was captured on video.
The video shows fire bursting from a home as Lt. Mike England rushes out. England thought someone was still inside and was trying to use his thermal imaging camera when a flashover broke out, according to Londonderry Fire Department Battalion Chief Bruce Hallowell.
“So the temperature within the room has risen to a point where the products within the room start to off gas. That off gassing is a combustible gas, and eventually the temperature within the room gets to the point where all of the contents and the gases ignite,” Hallowell said.
The flashover sent England out of the house and off the porch, which is how he fractured his leg.
Other firefighters put out the flames
Hallowell was on the scene Friday night.
“Other firefighters that were there put him out by patting him down to put the fire out, but yeah he was on fire,” Hallowell said.
News Nine spoke to England Sunday morning before he shared the video. He called himself the luckiest unlucky guy when considering his injuries in the context of what happened.
Hallowell pointed to discoloring on England’s gear.
“This discoloring is basically where the thermal assault was taken,” Hallowell said.
Gear credited with saving his life
England’s gear is credited with saving his life. Every member of the Londonderry Fire Department recently received two brand new sets of personal protective equipment, which Hallowell said he is grateful for.
“This is the result. This is the happy result that, you know, the lieutenant was was able to sustain a significant thermal assault, and get out, with very limited injuries,” Hallowell said.
Besides the broken leg, England also suffered minor burns. He was released from the hospital and is recovering at home.

More than 4,800 runners took part in the 2026 Maine Marathon, setting an all-time record for the event, and those participants helped raise more than $850,000 for nearly 100 charities.

title: Video shows school bus crash that killed student on her first day of cheerleading practice
text:
WINTER HAVEN, Fla. (WESH) - A multi-vehicle crash involving a school bus in Winter Haven, Florida, Monday morning left two people dead.
The Polk County Sheriff’s Office said a white Chevy Malibu clipped the back of the school bus, causing it to swerve into another lane.
The bus struck an oncoming Jeep head-on.
WARNING: Some viewers may find this video disturbing.
“You see how quickly death occurs in a vehicle crash, a horrible, horrible, horrible vehicle crash. At that instant, two people lost their life, but there was a lot of emotional pain and injury that occurred in that crash. When this crash happened, it happened in the blink of an eye,” Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said. “So, it was absolutely impossible for that driver to get any kind of control over that bus because it immediately crashed into this Jeep.”
A person in the Jeep was killed. The identity of that person has not been released.
Student identified
A 10th grade student on the bus was also killed. Polk County Public Schools identified her as Adinaluz Guadalupe Prieto Oyola, a student at Winter Haven High School.
“An amazing young lady in every account. Teachers loved her, friends loved her,” Polk County Public Schools Superintendent Frederick Heid said.
Heid said Monday was to be Prieto Oyola’s first day of cheerleading practice.
“As you can imagine, it’s been a very difficult 24 hours,” Heid said.

title: Why you just got a $90 Social Security check, and why 40 million other seniors didn’t
text:
Why you just got a $90 Social Security check, and why 40 million other seniors didn’t
Millions of Americans are receiving $90 from the Social Security Administration this week. But some don't seem to know why.
The checks, which have already hit some seniors' bank accounts, are tied to the Trump administration's announcement that it would send checks to 20 million Medicare enrollees to lower healthcare costs.
But not everyone will get a piece.
Medicare Part B enrollees can expect to receive a one-time payment in October, either through direct deposit or by check, the White House said.
Related video above | Trump’s $5,000 dividend could cost more than $1 trillion. Could it actually happen?
Total monthly costs for the program — which covers costs like doctor's visits, ambulance services and lab tests — start around $200 and vary with income.
To be eligible, seniors must be living in the U.S. and not be already receiving premium assistance from Medicaid or paying adjusted monthly premiums based on income, according to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. Seniors enrolled in Medicare Advantage, a private plan alternative to traditional Medicare coverage, are not eligible for the payment. More than half of eligible Medicare beneficiaries have Medicare Advantage, according to healthcare research nonprofit KFF.
Where is the money coming from?
The White House said the $90 payments for seniors will come from the Medicare Improvement Fund, established by Congress in 2008 as flexible funding to improve program operations and payments to health care providers.
Has the fund been used this way in the past?
Previous administrations have not used the Medicare Improvement Fund in this way, although Congress has periodically taken out money from the fund to pay for other priorities, said Larry Levitt, KFF's executive vice president for health policy. For example, $20.74 billion was used for the creation of the Affordable Care Act in 2010.
“The Medicare Improvement Fund language is quite broad and gives substantial discretion to the administration,” Levitt said.
Why now?
The checks come after the president last month said about 1 million people would get rebate checks of $500 for Affordable Care Act premiums. He has also promised on the campaign trail to send every American adult $5,000 if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections.
That pledge — which would require approval from Congress — would likely cost more than $1 trillion, adding to the deficit and worsening inflation.
Polls show Americans increasingly blame Trump for the high cost of gasoline and groceries with just 17% approving of his handling of inflation. Trump has sought to shrug off concerns about affordability, saying the economy is booming.
The Associated Press contributed to this report

title: Death Notice: Gay P. Maheu
Man arrested months after Stockton Springs crash that killed woman
text:
Maine man arrested months after Stockton Springs crash that killed woman
Suspect charged with manslaughter and OUI, according to state police
Maine man arrested months after Stockton Springs crash that killed woman
Suspect charged with manslaughter and OUI, according to state police
A Maine man is facing multiple charges, including manslaughter and operating under the influence, in connection with a fatal crash that happened nearly six months ago in Stockton Springs.
Adam Sorrentino, 42, of Belfast, was arrested by the Maine State Police in connection with the April 13 crash that killed Anne Pomroy, 77, of Old Orchard Beach.
State police said that on the evening of April 13, Sorrentino was driving a truck west on Route 1 in Stockton Springs when his vehicle crossed the center line and collided head-on with an eastbound Subaru Forester that was being driven by Pomroy.
Pomroy was pronounced dead at the crash scene, while Sorrentino was taken to a local hospital, where he was treated for non-life-threatening injuries.
Investigators determined that Sorrentino was driving faster than 80 mph and had a blood alcohol concentration more than twice the legal limit when the crash happened.
Sorrentino was taken into custody at his Belfast home on Monday and charged with manslaughter, aggravated criminal OUI resulting in death, reckless conduct with a dangerous weapon, driving to endanger, OUI and criminal speeding.
State police said Sorrentino was taken to the Waldo County Jail.
The crash investigation remains ongoing. Authorities are asking anyone who witnessed the crash or has information about the incident to call Maine State Police Trooper Ryan Nadeau at 207-624-7076, ext. 9.

title: Rockland seafood landings plummet to record low
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ROCKLAND, Maine — A once powerhouse port, the city has seen its seafood catch drop dramatically in the past decade.
Landings information from the Maine Department of Marine Resources showed that, in 2025, less than 2.1 million pounds of seafood were landed in Rockland with its value estimated at less than $4.6 million.
This was divided up between 164 licensed harvesters of various seafoods, according to the Department of Marine Resources.
The 2025 catch was down from 7.1 million pounds landed in 2024, which were valued at $6.7 million. In 2016, 33.7 million pounds of seafood were landed in Rockland with a value of nearly $21.1 million. There were 239 licensed harvesters landing seafood in Rockland that year.
In 1983, when Rockland had multiple fish processing plants, 55 million pounds of seafood with a 1983 value of $12 million were landed in docks across the city.
Arthur “Hutch” Hutchinson, the manager of the fish pier, said restrictions on fewer days fishermen are allowed to fish for herring are likely behind the recent decline.
Rockland had long seen much of its volume of landings dominated by herring and menhaden, which have lower per pound values.
The city wants to do something to turn around that decline. The City Council is scheduled to vote on Oct. 14 to apply for a $300,000 Seafood Adaption Fund Grant. The city would be required to match that grant with $15,000, which would come from the fish pier reserve account.
“The Rockland Municipal Fish Pier serves a critical role in the regional seafood supply chain by providing infrastructure that commercial fishing vessels depend on for harbor access, buying bait and selling their catch,” the city stated in its grant proposal.
Economic Development Director Julie Hashem said things like cold storage for seafood and energy efficiency/energy security investments are eligible uses.
The pier supports approximately 85 lobster boats, two herring vessels, five menhaden boats, five scallop boats, two seaweed harvesting operations and a fuel boat serving island communities in Penobscot Bay, the city states in its application. Two commercial bait and buying stations operate on-site. The pier provides berthing, bait supply, fuel access, trap storage and connections to offshore moorings, and serves as a market access point for island fishing vessels.
The first phase of the grant, if received, would look at site use, industry trends and related site planning. Hashem said, for instance, the city could look at anything needed to support existing or emerging fisheries not already on site, and are there uses in the flood plain today that would ideally be on higher ground.
“Despite its critical role in the regional seafood supply chain, the site’s upland area (approximately 1.5 acres) is underutilized and its existing infrastructure is aging and increasingly vulnerable. Cold storage is currently provided by trailers that are both aged and sited at elevations susceptible to storm surge. As climate change drives shifts in species distribution, ocean temperature, and storm frequency, the commercial fishing operations that depend on this pier face compounding pressures: declining traditional fisheries, emerging but underexplored opportunities in aquaculture and new species, and growing physical risk to on-site infrastructure,” the application states.
The second phase, if funded, could fund an improvement such as cold storage.
But it could potentially be any eligible use that comes out of the planning process if folks identify a different need that we aren’t yet aware of, Hashem said.
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.

title: Jim Bakker, who built ‘PTL Club’ televangelism empire, has died at 86
text:
Jim Bakker, who along with his first wife Tammy Faye built an evangelical empire around the hugely successful “The PTL Club” TV show, only to lose it all over a sex scandal and financial crimes, has died. He was 86.
Bakker died Monday, his second wife, Lori Bakker, said in a statement. His cause of death was not immediately clear.
“He was a pioneer of Christian television, but to me, he was my husband, my best friend, and the man I was honored to walk beside through so many seasons of life and ministry,” she said.
The pair lived near the Missouri entertainment town of Branson and filmed their TV show “The Jim Bakker Show” there since it launched in 2003. Bakker suffered a stroke in 2020.
But it was another evangelical program that made Jim and his first wife Tammy Faye Bakker cultural icons — so much so that they were often skewered in the 1980s and 1990s by late-night comedians and parodied on “Saturday Night Live.” A theatrical movie on their lives, “The Eyes of Tammy Faye,” was released in September 2021.
At its peak in the mid-1980s, the Bakkers’ ministry included not only the TV show drawing up to 13 million nightly viewers but also the Christian-based Heritage USA theme park and hotel in Fort Mill, South Carolina.
Bakker got his start as a traveling preacher
Bakker was born in Muskegon, Michigan, and attended North Central Bible College in Minneapolis, where he met Tammy Faye. They married in 1961 and dropped out of college to start their own traveling ministry — he preached, she sang and played the accordion as they crossed the country visiting churches and tent revivals.
They caught the attention of televangelist Pat Robertson, and in 1965 launched a children’s show on Robertson’s Christian Broadcasting Network. By 1966, he was hosting “The 700 Club,” a Christian talk show.
Bakker left CBN in 1972 and two years later formed the PTL Satellite Network. “The PTL Club” — PTL stands for “Praise the Lord” — became its signature show.
When it hit its heyday in the 1980s, “The PTL Club” was drawing millions of viewers — and bringing in millions of dollars annually from followers.
The show featured chats with guests and Christian entertainers. Bakker offered upbeat sermons and Tammy Faye — charismatic and always wearing her trademark heavy mascara — sang. Most episodes were taped at their sprawling complex just south of Charlotte, North Carolina.
The couple was so famous that they were often parodied by TV comedians for their lavish lifestyle and Tammy Faye’s abundant makeup.
Sex scandal and financial crimes damage his empire
In March 1987, their empire began to crack when Bakker admitted to a sexual encounter with church clerk Jessica Hahn. Bakker was forced to resign from his own empire, turning over operations to pastor and broadcaster Jerry Falwell.
Tammy Faye stuck by Bakker, often with tears running down her mascara, even as many saw his downfall as a fitting symbol of the greed and hypocrisy of the 1980s.
Things only got worse.
In 1988, Bakker was indicted for mail fraud, wire fraud and conspiracy after an investigation of PTL’s finances. He was convicted and sentenced to 45 years in federal prison, though the sentence was later reduced to eight years.
At a news conference after Bakker was found guilty, Tammy Faye stood in front of the microphones and sang the hymn, “On Christ the Solid Rock I Stand.”
Their marriage crumbled and Tammy Faye divorced Bakker in 1992, just short of their 31st anniversary, while he was still in prison. She later married Roe Messner, a building contractor whose projects included the Heritage USA theme park. Messner was convicted of bankruptcy fraud in 1995 and spent about two years in prison.
Tammy Faye died of colon cancer in 2007.
Bakker was released on parole in 1994. He married his second wife, Lori, in 1998. The couple launched “The Jim Bakker Show” on the PTL Satellite Network five years later.
In June 2021, Bakker and his Morningside Church Productions Inc. settled a lawsuit accusing him of falsely claiming the health supplement Silver Solution could cure COVID-19. The settlement called for $156,000 in refunds to people who paid money or gave contributions to obtain the product in the early days of the pandemic.
The lawsuit said Bakker and a guest made the cure claim during 11 episodes in February and March of 2020.
Bakker and Tammy Faye had two children. He and his second wife adopted five children in 2002.
___
Salter, a former Associated Press journalist, was the main author of this obituary.

title: Bill Green, who helped Susan Collins win in 2020, is back on TV for her
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
Bill Green, the retired Maine sportscaster whose ads for U.S. Sen. Susan Collins rattled Democrats late in her 2020 race, is back on the air for the Republican with a pitch that echoes his last one.
In the ad, Green speaks as an independent voter and leads with the hostility aimed at the senator who is fighting for a historic sixth term in a toss-up race with former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, a Democrat.
His new ad comes nearly six years to the day that the Collins campaign used him in a crucial series of spots that gave her a trusted and nonpartisan validator when she needed to cut through nationalized attacks and tap into personal goodwill that carried her to a fifth term.
Green’s new ad began running Tuesday. The Collins campaign had aired it 18 times across Maine by 9:30 a.m. according to AdImpact.
“If you’re wondering why more good people don’t run for office, look at the attacks on Susan Collins,” Green says in the 30-second spot. “Her home and office vandalized, her life threatened, and all those outrageous ads repeatedly proven false.”
It was a reference to a long series of campaign developments. Collins’ Bangor home was egged on Sept. 18. Later that month, someone painted a vulgar message linking her to President Donald Trump on her Biddeford office doors. Bangor police have checked on her home hundreds of times since her 2018 vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh.
Jackson condemned the vandalism at her office. While Bangor Daily News fact checks have found that recent Democratic ads overstated claims about a key Medicaid vote and alleged ties to Jeffrey Epstein, the Democrat also has been targeted by false claims on his tax stances.
Green, the brother of longtime Collins aide and ally Julie Green, retired from News Center Maine in 2019. The next fall, Democrats flagged his ads as one of the two late developments that worried them most in the final week of the race. Google searches for Green hit their highest point since his retirement that October.
Collins won by nearly 9 points after trailing in every public poll. Green’s 2020 ad opened with a joke and went after “false attacks” by out-of-staters.
“Did you know that Susan Collins hates dogs? That’s kind of what I’m expecting to hear next from a ridiculous smear campaign,” Green said then.

title: Susan Collins gets more national scrutiny for campaign donations
text:
Donations to Sen. Susan Collins were the subject of another story from a national news outlet Tuesday.
Executives at a company that produces an armored vehicle for the Army donated to political committees supporting Collins, R-Maine, and other appropriators this year after they approved funding for the vehicle — despite Army leaders saying they did not need it, according to a new report from The Intercept.
Monday’s story comes after ProPublica published an investigation in September that focused on how the FBI was probing allegations of a “pay-to-play” scheme involving a convicted former defense contractor and a pro-Collins super PAC before President Donald Trump’s administration ended the investigation in 2025.
The Republican senator and her staff have bashed the recent reporting and have never been charged in connection with any of the allegations. However, the stories have become the source of fresh campaign fodder for former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson and Collins critics amid the high-profile Senate reelection battle between Jackson and Collins.
In February, Congress approved a defense spending bill that included $345 million for the Army to acquire more deliveries of what is known as a Joint Light Tactical Vehicle. Within the next few weeks of that bill’s passage, employees with the vehicle’s maker, AM General, and the company’s PAC gave at least a combined $50,000 to committees supporting Collins, The Intercept reported.
Last year, AM General was ramping up its production line in Indiana when then-Army Secretary Dan Driscoll announced he would cancel its order, saying the additional deliveries of the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle would result in an “excess.” The Intercept noted another appropriator, Rep. Ken Calvert, R-Calif., also received five-figure donations from employees with AM General and the private equity firm that owns it.
Collins’ office said in response to The Intercept’s reporting that Collins did not make the decision to appropriate funds for the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle. It was instead the defense subcommittee chair, Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and vice chair Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del.
Lawmakers in both parties supported the revival of the Army’s order, including the top House Democrat for defense appropriations, Rep. Betty McCollum of Minnesota.
“Sen. Collins was not involved in this decision,” Collins spokesperson Phoebe Keller told The Intercept.
McConnell did not receive donations from employees at AM General or its parent group this election cycle, while the company’s employee PAC gave $2,500 to Coons, The Intercept noted. FEC records show McCollum’s leadership PAC received $5,000 from AM General’s employee PAC last year.
AM General CEO John Chadbourne told the news outlet in an email that the company does not comment on campaign donations, “all of which fully comply with FEC rules and regulations.”
In response to Driscoll’s comment on not needing additional vehicles, a joint statement from the House and Senate, which Collins’ office said was produced by the defense subcommittees, said that the Army had provided “inadequate supporting analysis.”
One concern was that without the efficiencies from a larger order that included the Army, the cost-per-unit price of vehicles that the Marines still wanted would rise, as The Intercept noted.

title: Troy Jackson needs to start running like there’s nothing to lose
text:
Lorenzo Krakowsky of Owls Head is a former teacher and high school principal.
This is a message for Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson.
There is less than a month left to win this election, and it is time for you to make your case urgently and directly to the people of Maine. Enough with the endless fundraising, TV ads, limited community events and outside consultants. Stop listening to the DSCC and the Democratic Party establishment politicos — they’re not Mainers, and they don’t know what we need.
Your personal story and your vision for how to truly serve working Mainers is what will win this thing, and it’s what people will rally around. Folks want to hear from you in person, in their towns and in their counties. They want to be inspired and fired up directly by you. You know Maine and you’ve been fighting for us for years.
Here’s what it will take:
- Use your current funds to go on a 40-day town hall barnstormer through all of Maine, north to south and east to west. Open those town halls to everyone who wants to come. Answer every question that is asked. Stay as long as is needed to hear and connect to everyone.
- Use your volunteers to generate enthusiasm and boost attendance at those town halls. Rally them to phonebank, canvass, go to demonstrations, connect socially and get out the vote now. Get as many folks as possible out to your town halls in October.
- At those town halls, let loose: call Sen. Collins a corrupt politician, call what’s going on in Gaza a genocide, tell your personal story, tell us exactly what you’ve done and what you’re going to do to make life for working Mainers fair and equitable. Run as the fighting progressive that you are. Don’t hold anything back!
- Hold a press conference ASAP to call on Sen. Collins to resign immediately and drop out of the race because of the allegations of corruption against her. Bring this up every single day from now until Election Day.
- Relentlessly pressure Sen. Collins to justify her vote to confirm Brett Kavanaugh and end the right to have abortions, and her votes to fund ICE and support its authoritarian, illegal actions.
- Use the October debates to hammer Sen. Collins about her corruption, her elite insiderism and her incompetence as the Appropriations Committee chair. Label her a corrupt politician, an elitist, a hypocrite, a Trump puppet and an AIPAC tool. Let everyone know she’s in the pocket of special interests and the rich oligarchs outside of Maine who want to crush us. Don’t be deferential.
So many of us are rooting for you, and we are 100% behind you, but we need this campaign to be ferociously urgent, completely open, genuinely grassroots and unrelentingly aggressive.
You need to run like you have nothing to lose — it’s the only way we will win.

title: Maine’s top court rejects eviction appeal by midcoast farmers
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The couple who managed Harpswell’s last sizable farm have moved themselves and their livestock off the property and lost their latest appeal to Maine’s highest court.
The Maine Supreme Judicial Court rejected the appeal of Joseph and Laura Grady, who ran Two Coves Farm for more than 16 years but were ousted because, according to an arbitrator, they failed to pay roughly $124,000 in rent and grow crops as they had once agreed.
The Aug. 19 ruling capped a protracted legal fight that had the Gradys claiming they were being forced out of their home and stripped of their livelihood in spite of their good faith efforts and in contravention of Maine’s protections for home renters.
Opposing them was Helen Norton, who — with her late husband — bought the 100-acre tract in hopes of preserving a vestige of Harpswell Neck’s agrarian history. Norton’s lawyers alleged that the Gradys had taken advantage of an ailing 94-year-old woman and were “squatting” on the land while dragging out the process with a series of “11th hour arguments.”
The Supreme Judicial Court ruling rejected the latest of those appeals. It affirmed a longer order dated July 28 in which the court upheld the arbitrator’s decision and spurned the couple’s contention that the arbitrator had exceeded his authority in treating the lease as a strictly commercial contract rather than one that also provided the Gradys with a place to live and raise their children.
Norton said she was pleased by the ruling and is working to make repairs to the property that will allow her to “find a good, responsible farmer and his family and make it a viable working farm” as soon as next spring.
Of the legal fight, she said, “It has cost me a lot of money, it has cost me a lot of time and effort, and it has made us quite unhappy.”
The Gradys declined to participate in an interview for this article. Joe Grady requested questions in writing, then declined to answer them. However, court filings from their legal team lay out their position in detail. In a brief statement emailed to the Anchor, they said they are disappointed but determined.
“The last two years of defending ourselves from the claims made against us have been exhausting; losing our home where we planned to spend the rest of our lives, as well as the business we built from scratch, was devastating and is still fresh for us,” they said in the statement.
Partners in protection
The legal battle brought a bitter closing chapter to what began as a pastoral partnership.
Two decades ago, in 2006, Norton and her late husband, Walter, bought a 100-acre saltwater farm near their home on Harpswell Neck. The entity they formed, Neils Point LLC, in 2008 granted an agriculture conservation easement to the Maine Farmland Trust, with the Harpswell Heritage Land Trust overseeing the easement.
The purpose of the arrangement was to protect the farm “from encroaching suburban sprawl so that it will always be available for its traditional use as a productive cropland, open fields and forest,” according to the arbitrator’s findings.
In 2009, a young farming couple — the Gradys — signed on as stewards of the property, an agreement renewed in 2017 for an additional 25 years. In exchange for the right to live and farm there, the couple agreed to keep the farm in productive operation and to pay rent equal to 10% of their “annual net proceeds” — their farming revenue minus legitimate operating expenses.
For many years, all seemed to be going smoothly at Two Coves Farm. Drivers passing the property on Harpswell Neck Road saw signs advertising a farm stand along a tree-lined lane that sold, among other things, eggs, lamb, tomatoes, cucumbers, yarn and sheepskins.
A ‘stark injustice’ or an end to a ‘free ride’?
But trouble arrived last year, when relations between Norton and the Gradys took a sharp downward turn. In July 2025, an arbitrator presided over a hearing to examine Norton’s allegations that the couple had failed to live up to their end of the deal.
After examining evidence and hearing from both sides, arbitrator and Portland lawyer Timothy J. Bryant concluded that the Gradys had not made rent payments on time and “failed to pay any rent whatsoever for the years of 2023 and 2024.” In a decision dated Oct. 24, 2025, the arbitrator concluded that the Gradys had understated their revenues and “knowingly inflated their operational expenses by treating household and personal expenses as business expenses.”
The arbitrator also agreed with Norton that the Gradys had failed to “use the farm to actively plant and grow productive crops,” as required by the 2017 lease.
He ordered the Gradys to pay Norton’s Neils Point LLC $124,175 and to vacate the farm no later than Dec. 31, 2025.
The Gradys did not move out, instead filing a Dec. 30 appeal asking a Maine Superior Court justice to vacate the decision and allow them to continue working and living at Two Coves. Because the farm was also their home, they argued that state law prohibited them from being evicted without the formal court process guaranteed to residential tenants.
Norton’s legal team countered by saying that the arbitrator’s ruling was sound, and that the Gradys had voluntarily agreed to arbitration as the method for resolving disputes. In a Feb. 4 ruling, Superior Court Justice Darcie N. McElwee sided with Norton and agreed that the Gradys must vacate.
In late February, the Gradys took their appeal to the Supreme Judicial Court.
“This case presents a stark injustice,” wrote the Gradys’ lawyers, Regan A. Sweeney and J. Spencer Hoffman. “A wealthy landowner has utilized commercial arbitration to dispossess a tenant farming family from the property they have called home and worked for over sixteen years.”
The lawyers stated that the Gradys had been served a “writ of possession” on Feb. 25, giving them 48 hours to vacate. “The Gradys were afforded no meaningful opportunity to seek appellate relief before the coercive machinery of eviction was set in motion,” they wrote.
The court’s ruling would affect not just the Gradys, their lawyers wrote, but also other farmers.
“Farmers are the backbone of Maine’s communities. They feed their neighbors, steward the land, and embody the independence and self-reliance that define this State’s character,” they said. “Yet the (ruling) treats farmers as something less than every other resident of Maine. The Gradys are people who work the land they live on. They are not commercial tenants operating a warehouse or retail establishment. … Their home is their farm, and their farm is their home. The two are inseparable.”
Norton’s lawyers countered with strong words of their own in a Feb. 27 pleading. Noting that the Gradys had already relocated their livestock and “never grew any crops in the first place,” they said the couple faced no real hardship.
“For the last decade, the (Gradys) have had possession of the farm under false pretenses. For the last two months, they have trespassed on the property unlawfully,” said attorneys Thimi R. Mina and Alfred C. Frawley IV. “Meanwhile, Mrs. Norton is 94 years old and recently suffered a significant injury. Put simply, time is of the essence, and the balance of the equities lies in favor of ending the (Gradys’) decade-long free ride while Mrs. Norton still has the opportunity to put the property to productive use.”
The legal point and counterpoint continued through the spring and summer. Following the adverse July 28 Supreme Judicial Court ruling, the Gradys again appealed and — in August — lost again.
The court rejected the Gradys’ argument that they were entitled to the same channels of legal appeal available to a tenant facing eviction from a rental home. Instead, the Gradys had to abide by the arbitrator’s decision after earlier agreeing on that course of conflict resolution.
As their legal battle wound down, both the Gradys and Norton expressed gratitude for the support they had received from neighbors.
“I am very happy for the support that I’ve received from the community,” said Norton, who, along with her husband, has invested in conserving a large amount of open land in Harpswell and neighboring communities.
“To all those in Harpswell who have supported us and Two Coves Farm, we want to pass on our thanks and let you all know that we are doing well and have transitioned to a new home,” the Grady family said in their statement emailed to the Anchor.
“We do not know what the future holds at the moment,” they added, “but we will certainly be finding our way back to farming in the months and years ahead.”

title: Costs will skyrocket for many in Maine if ban on prescription drug imports takes effect
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND — Maida Uhlig said she’s been purchasing anxiety medication from Canada for about 20 years, and would have to pay thousands more per year if a new U.S. Customs and Border Protection rule goes into effect later this month that would ban people from buying medicines internationally by mail.
Uhlig, 81, of Portland, said she takes Lexapro, which her insurance doesn’t cover because there’s a generic equivalent available. Uhlig said she’s tried the generics, but for her they’re not effective. She said only the brand name medication alleviates her anxiety.
She pays about $675 per year out-of-pocket for the brand name medication, purchasing by mail through Canadian pharmacies. If she had to purchase that same drug in the U.S., Uhlig estimates the cost would be about $6,300.
“I couldn’t do it. I don’t have that money,” said Uhlig, a retired administrative assistant. “It would be debilitating if I couldn’t take this medication.”
The rule is set to go into effect Oct. 22, eliminating an exemption that previously allowed importation of prescription drugs through the international postal system.
U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, D-1st District, said in an interview last week that she signed onto a letter from dozens of House members asking the Trump administration to abandon the rule.
“People have been doing this for a long time, and it shouldn’t be taken away from them,” Pingree said. “We need to make sure people who are getting their prescriptions this way don’t get caught in this trap.”
A 2020 University of Florida study found that about 2 million Americans purchase prescriptions from international pharmacies.
Ken Hunter, executive director of the Campaign for Personal Prescription Importation, a New Jersey-based advocacy group, said in an interview Friday that many countries, including Canada, regulate drug prices more than the U.S., which leads to many prescription medications being cheaper when imported.
Hunter said for decades, the federal government has allowed drugs for individual prescriptions to be imported through the U.S. mail, through the Medicare Modernization Act of 2003. In the era before drugs could be purchased internationally over the internet, the federal government allowed people to drive over the Canadian border to purchase personal prescriptions.
“Drug prices, when buying internationally, are much less than what they are in the U.S., typically half the price to one-fifth the price,” Hunter said. “This is going to price people out of the ability to use these drugs. We are heading toward a significant healthcare crisis.”
Hunter pointed to Eliquis, a blood thinner often prescribed to prevent strokes, as a commonly imported medication. When purchased from Canada, it costs about $550 for a three-month supply, but in the U.S. it’s priced at over $1,000, he said. Hunter said while generic drugs are often inexpensive in the U.S., it can sometimes take years for a new medication to have a generic equivalent. Or, he said, there may be generics available in other countries, but not the United States.
CBP said on Friday that it would respond to questions about the new rule. The agency had not responded by Tuesday.
According to the published rule, CBP cited the potential of “illicit-drug importations” as one of the reasons.
Hunter said banning the importation of personal prescription medications is not going to be effective in reducing the flow of illicit drugs into the U.S., which occur in much larger volumes.
Ann Woloson, executive director of the Maine-based nonprofit Consumers for Affordable Health Care, said in an interview Friday that the impacts of the new rule would be devastating for many who already have difficulty affording their medications.
Many people have high-deductible insurance plans or those where the patient has to pay a certain percentage of drug costs. In those cases, insurance would not protect people from paying thousands in out-of-pocket costs, Woloson said.
“It’s another sad example of how our current administration is going to make it harder for people to afford the healthcare they need,” she said.
Thirty-two percent of Maine residents surveyed this year by Consumers for Affordable Health Care reported that they took fewer pills than prescribed to save money.
Uhlig said she has a supply of anxiety pills that will last about a year, but after that she would have to take a 10-hour, round-trip bus to Montreal to purchase the medications directly from Canadian pharmacies. Hunter said the new rule doesn’t prohibit people from personally crossing the border to buy drugs from Canadian pharmacies, but making people travel long distances to get medications they need would be a hardship for many.
Uhlig said people shouldn’t be forced to pay exorbitant costs for medicine they need.
“It’s so unfair, because people rely on these drugs to live,” she said.

title: Obituary: Thomas F. Marx
text:
LIBERTY – Thomas F. Marx, 85, passed away Sept. 30, 2026 at his home in Liberty, Maine after a long illness, surrounded by loved ones and family.
Tom was born in Bronxville, N.Y. to parents Arthur Marx and Marie DeMotte, but soon moved to Alstead, N.H. to live on a farm that he loved. He attended school there and made many friends in the small community, friendships that have lasted for over 50 years. One of his best stories from that time was a cross country trip he made with his friend Dale and a bunch of peanut butter and jelly sandwiches. Tom and his sister, Randee, also enjoyed many adventures together such as the famous mashed potato fight and swimming at Vilas Pool.
Tom attended Columbia University, Harvard University, and the University of Iowa where he obtained his PhD. He began his career as an educator in 1962 as a teacher in New Hampshire. He came to Maine in 1970 to work in the Portland school system and in 1974 he took a position as the Superintendent of Schools in Camden where he remained until his first retirement in 1997.
From 1997 until 2013, Tom served as an Interim Superintendent in Searsport, Appleton, Hope, Lincolnville, Dresden, Monhegan Island, and North Haven. He then began his second retirement!
As an educator, Tom was well known for his negotiating skills, and his ability to solve problems. He was instrumental in the construction of a new high school in Camden, and a new school on North Haven.
But just as important as his career, Tom was a man of many passions. He loved fly-fishing, and made many trips UP NORTH with his friends where they canoed down rivers, fishing as they went. He also loved his Red Sox, even when they were awful! But one of his best days was when the Red Sox FINALLY won a World Series in 2004 and ended the Curse of the Bambino! He also enjoyed coin collecting, gardening, and golf.
Perhaps Tom’s greatest passion was his faithful attendance at AA meetings for over 40 years. Tom went not only for himself but to mentor other attendees. Many of his best friends were found there.
Tom married Lyn Marx (maiden name Lyn Antonson) from Concord, N.H. in 1965. They had two daughters, Sarah and Amy. As a family they had many adventures, such as trips in their VW vans, spending time at the New Hampshire fishing camp, travels abroad, and of course countless cribbage and card games. His daughters remained the joys of his life until he died.
Tom married again in 2009 to Marilyn Stumpff of Liberty. They began another chapter of his life that included travel to many, many places, and a second home in Naples, Fla. Tom fulfilled a life-long dream there by buying a BMW Z3 in baby blue.
Tom really loved all his grandchildren whether by blood or marriage. He enjoyed many activities with them from ballgames, to fishing, to canoeing, and visits to the beach and Santa’s Village. As they grew older, there were spirited discussion of the Red Sox chances that year.
Tom was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s in 2018. It was a long hard journey which ended Sept. 30, 2026 with family around his bedside.
Tom was predeceased by his father, Arthur Marx and his mother, Marie DeMotte Miterko.
Tom is survived by his sister, Randee Barry of Washington Ga.; his first wife, Lyn Marx of Hope; his daughters and their spouses Sarah Marx and Brian McGill, Amy Marx and Chris Koerber; and his wife, Marilyn Stumpff of Liberty. He is also survived by his stepchildren Jenny Tibbetts, Joshua Stumpff and spouse Michelle Holder, and Nathan Stumpff and spouse Yasmeen Hossain. His blended family includes 10 grandchildren, Eli Marx McGill, Hazel Stumpff, Eva Stumpff, Sierra Koerber-Marx, Jasper Marx McGill, Bianca Stumpff, Maya Koerber-Marx, Willow Koerber-Marx, Hank Tibbetts, and Jed Tibbetts.
A memorial service will be held at Riposta Funeral Home in Belfast, on Friday, Oct. 9, from 2 to 4 p.m.

title: Flock cameras have no business in Lewiston
text:
During the last Supreme Court term, the Court in the case of Chatrie v. United States ruled 6-3 to invalidate a police tactic called a “geofence warrant.”
A geofence warrant is a mass surveillance tool which a law enforcement agency demands from a tech company (like Google) location data from every mobile device within a defined geographic area with a certain timeframe, without specifying a suspect or suspects. It is clear that this constitutes a Fourth Amendment violation; geofencing is a mass, dragnet search of innocent people guilty of no crime.
In June 2025, the Lewiston City Council approved and accepted as part of the U.S. DOJ’s Byrne Community Grant, which was intended for surveillance camera technology. This grant funding then gets us to October 2025, when the Lewiston Police Department entered into a 60-day trial with Flock Safety. Without a City Council vote, the city went on to acquire and implement a 13-camera system.
According to one report, 82 Flock contracts nationwide have been canceled. Unlike Auburn, Lewiston has not decided to end funding. We the people of Lewiston should follow Auburn’s lead in ending Flock’s contract and removing this mass surveillance network. While the Chatrie decision is new, time will show that automated license plate readers are like a geofence warrant, a mass surveillance tactic and a clear violation of the Fourth Amendment.
Matthew Roy
Lewiston

title: Frost and freeze advisories issued for coastal Maine; more seasonable conditions expected to end the week
text:
Sub-freezing temperatures Tuesday night into Wednesday are expected to give way to a more seasonable end to the first full week of October in Maine.
The National Weather Service placed all of coastal Maine under a frost advisory from midnight until 8 a.m. Wednesday, with expected lows between 30 and 35 degrees. Meanwhile, interior Cumberland and Androscoggin counties were placed under a freeze warning, with temperatures as low as 25 degrees expected in the same timeframe.
Areas further inland, including Fryeburg, Rumford, Rangeley and Jackman, were also expected to see temperatures fall to between 25 and 30 degrees overnight, according to the weather service.
Despite the equally cold temperatures elsewhere in the state, Hunter Tubbs, a meteorologist at the weather service’s Gray office, explained that the advisories are limited to coastal regions as the growing season remains active there until Oct. 11.
“Some areas are already past the growing season, so we don’t have (advisories) out for those areas,” he said in a phone call Tuesday.
He said this is around the time when meteorologists would expect the region to begin experiencing frosty overnight temperatures. The weather service advises residents to cover or bring inside any sensitive outdoor plants.
Tubbs said Tuesday night into Wednesday would likely see the coldest temperatures of the week, with the remainder of the week looking more seasonable.
“That’s just because we had a strong cold front that came through, and that allowed for strong northwesterly winds to bring down colder air from Canada,” Tubbs explained.
Wednesday’s highs are expected to be in the high 50s and low 60s across southern and central Maine, according to the weather service.
But temperatures are expected to rise Thursday, with some areas, including Portland and Lewiston, slated to be as warm as 70 degrees. Tubbs said the projected uptick in temperatures is thanks to warmer air pushing in from the southwest.
Then, the weather service forecasts high temperatures will dip back down to the low 60s — and even to the low 50s in some western Maine communities — Friday and Saturday. Things are expected to begin warming up again on Sunday, with highs potentially reaching 70 degrees once more on Monday.
Meanwhile, low temperatures are expected to remain fairly steady: Southeastern regions, including Greater Portland, can expect lows in the mid-to-low 40s Thursday through the beginning of next week, while areas farther north and west can expect lows in the mid-to-high 30s.
Some showers could be in the mix across the western mountains late this week, according to the weather service, but Tubbs said it isn’t expected to amount to much.
“As of right now, it doesn’t look like anything significant in terms of rainfall,” he said Tuesday.
On Tuesday morning, the Mount Washington Observatory reported the first measurable snowfall of the season atop New Hampshire’s tallest peak, with just over a half-inch of snow accumulating in a 24-hour period. It noted that a wind gust of 110 miles per hour was recorded.

title: 5-year-old dead, 16-year-old charged after UTV crash
text:
LITTLE COMPTON, R.I. (WJAR) — A 16-year-old is facing charges after a utility terrain vehicle crash that killed a 5-year-old girl, police in Rhode Island said.
Police said the teen was driving a John Deere UTV in a field Sunday afternoon when the driver lost control and the vehicle tipped over. All seven passengers and the driver were ejected from the Gator.
Two children hospitalized
When police arrived, they found two 5-year-old girls seriously hurt, one of whom was unresponsive. Both were taken to the hospital, and one did not survive.
School sends note to parents
The principal of the kindergarten-through-8th grade Wilbur and McMahon School in Little Compton sent a note to parents Sunday night acknowledging the loss in the community. The note said that while the child did not attend WMS, she participated in school activities.
Mental health counselors were available at the school all day Monday.
Charges filed
The teenage driver has been charged with two felonies: driving to endanger resulting in death and driving to endanger resulting in serious bodily injury.
Location
Police said the crash happened at 530 Long Highway. State records show that address is Maurolou Family Farm, a local campground and event venue.

title: Public Utilities Commission denies CMP's request for temporary rate hike
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Public Utilities Commission denies Central Maine Power's request for temporary rate hike
The Maine Public Utilities Commission (PUC) has unanimously denied a portion of Central Maine Power's request for a temporary rate increase.
Central Maine Power (CMP) requested a $189 million increase to help upgrade equipment that failed or got close to failing this summer. According to the company, customers' monthly bills would have increased by an average of $18 per month for a year under the proposal.
A number of groups objected to the proposal, including the Maine Office of the Public Advocate, the Maine Department of Energy Resources, Efficiency Maine Trust, AARP Maine, CMP Ratepayers Unite and the Natural Resources Council of Maine.
The PUC held a deliberations hearing Tuesday morning regarding $69.3 million of CMP's proposal, which all three members of the committee agreed to deny.
The decision from the PUC comes eight days after some of its staff members recommended that the commission deny CMP's request. In the recommended ruling, PUC staff said the commission's policy only allows it to approve rate changes if there are no objections to an amount, which was not the case in this instance.
CMP president and CEO Linda Ball released a statement in response to the recommended ruling, in which she said that the recommendation "carries consequences that extend well beyond the rate case itself."
"Prolonged revenue uncertainty puts pressure on the infrastructure investments, workforce, financing capacity, and grant-funded modernization efforts that customers and communities depend upon. Unfortunately, the consequences of prolonged uncertainty are no longer theoretical," Ball said in her statement. "CMP has already been forced to defer planned capital work, including projects intended to strengthen reliability, improve resilience, and modernize the system, and will continue to do so. CMP will now also be forced to evaluate workforce levels and hiring plans that support current operations and future needs."
Ball also sent a letter to CMP employees on Sept. 28. In the letter, Ball said that the company will need to evaluate current workforce levels, hiring plans and apprenticeship programs as a result of the recommendation from PUC staff members.
"No decisions have been made beyond those already communicated, but it would be irresponsible not to assess all available options given the current circumstances," Ball said in her letter, which was shared with Maine's Total Coverage by a CMP employee.
During Tuesday's deliberations hearing in Hallowell, the PUC's three members said that while they understand concerns raised by CMP, they made the decision to deny the utility's request due to a lack of agreement between parties and affordability concerns that were raised during public hearings.
PUC Chairman Phil Bartlett said a final decision on CMP's full rate hike request is expected to be made in April.

title: Strong effort brings mixed results for UMaine men’s hockey in opening weekend
text:
This past weekend, the University of Maine’s men’s hockey team split a two-game road series against a Holy Cross team that was picked fourth in the preseason poll for Atlantic Hockey America, which is vastly improved but is still considered the worst of the country’s six Division I leagues.
Still, it is difficult to sweep a team on the road and, after an opening-night 4-1 victory, the Black Bears had a dramatic late two-goal rally erased by an overtime game-winner by the Crusaders’ Connor Welsh in a 3-2 setback.
UMaine has 15 newcomers this season, and 12 made their debuts over the weekend, with five registering their first points in a Black Bear uniform. Transfer goalie Petter Wickstrom Stumer made his first start in the loss.
Among the initial observations are that UMaine graduate student left wing and captain Owen Fowler may have been prophetic when he said before the series that the Black Bears are going to be a very good third-period team thanks to their conditioning and the significant upgrade in the size and physicality departments over last season.
UMaine outscored Holy Cross 4-1 in the third period of the two games although one was Fowler’s empty-net goal on Friday night.
UMaine outshot Holy Cross 25-13 in the games’ third periods, including a 13-7 edge on Saturday night despite being assessed five consecutive penalties in the period and having to kill a two-man disadvantage that spanned 1:55 early in the period.
The Black Bears did allow a power play goal on the fourth penalty, which gave Holy Cross a 2-0 lead.
The fact UMaine rallied for two goals 48 seconds apart in the final 3:27 to force overtime is a good sign for the future and highlights the team’s resilience.
The fact the Black Bears took five straight penalties in a game in which they trailed 1-0 entering the period is a concern especially considering it was four veterans who took the penalties. Alternate captain Sully Scholle took two of them. Fowler, Thomas Pichette and Jeremy Langois took the others.
And Welsh’s game-winner in overtime came on a delayed penalty situation.
This team is going to be in a lot of close games so maintaining discipline and staying out of the penalty box will be extremely important.
And goals could be hard to come by because UMaine has only three players who have scored more than seven goals in a college hockey season: Fowler, Tanner Klimpke and Max Scott.
Fowler had 12 last season and 10 in 2024-25 in his first year at UMaine after transferring from UMass Lowell. Transfer Tanner Klimpke had seasons of 15, 10 and 16 goals at Robert Morris and had two power-play goals in Friday’s win.
Max Scott had 12 goals two seasons ago for Brown University before transferring to UMaine.
UMaine had just three even-strength goals vs. Holy Cross. They had two power play goals and an empty-netter.
Winning net-front battles in the offensive zone is going to be a key in order for the Black Bears to score some of those greasy goals via screens, rebounds and deflections.
UMaine head coach Ben Barr said his team needs to be more direct by getting shots on net and attacking rather than trying to make fancy plays like they did on Saturday night.
UMaine has plenty of strong, gritty forwards who are capable of popping 8-10 goals this season and a few others who could surpass the 15-goal plateau. The Black Bears will also get some production from the back end as most of their defensemen have offensive skills.
That was shown over the weekend as two of the three players sharing the team lead in points with three right now are defensemen: sophomore Lukas Peterson (3 assists) and Bemidji State transfer Isa Parekh (1 goal, 2 assists), who is a junior.
Klimpke also has three points on two goals and an assist.
Albin Boija turned in a solid outing on Friday, making 18 saves, and that is a source of encouragement. The 2024-25 second team All-American had a forgettable season a year ago and to get off to a good start is important for him.
Canisius transfer Petter Wickstrom Stumer made 23 saves in his UMaine debut on Saturday.
Barr pointed out that Wickstrom Stumer got beat cleanly to the short side on the first and third goals, which he shouldn’t have, but he expects him to learn from it and continue to get better.
Barr was disappointed with Saturday’s result but not with the effort.
“The effort was awesome all weekend. There were a lot of positives,” said Barr. “The reality of our team is everyone has to be good. If one guy doesn’t show up or is just average, it’s probably not going to be good enough.”
The Black Bears play their home-opening series this weekend against what is likely the best team on their schedule: the sixth-ranked Quinnipiac University Bobcats.
Quinnipiac is one of the nation’s elite programs with 11 NCAA Tournament appearances since 2013 along with three Frozen Fours, two NCAA runner-up finishes and an NCAA title in 2023.
Rand Pecknold’s Bobcats went 27-10-3 a year ago including a win over Providence (5-2) and a loss to North Dakota (5-0) in the Sioux Falls Regional.
The team returns nine of its top 10 scorers including national Rookie of the Year and first team All-American Ethan Wyttenbach, who had 25 goals and 34 assists in 40 games.
He is one of five Bobcats with two goals so far this season after they thumped New Hampshire 10-2 and upended reigning Hockey East tourney champ Merrimack 6-3 this past weekend.
Quinnipiac will expose all of UMaine’s weaknesses while also identifying the Black Bears’ strengths.
“What a great opportunity,” Barr said. “They’re one of the best teams in the country. It’s awesome to go up against them.”
Puck drop will be at 7 p.m. Friday and Saturday nights at Alfond Arena in Orono.

title: Next Jay-to-South Portland ‘superload’ transport to begin Wednesday
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The next “superload” transport is scheduled to depart Jay on Wednesday and reach South Portland next week, according to Maine State Police.
It will depart the former Androscoggin Mill in Jay on Wednesday at about 6 p.m., stay in Turner during the day Thursday, and reach Oxford by early Friday morning for a weekend break, the state police said. It will depart Oxford on Sunday night, stay in Gray on Monday, and hold over the following day in Buxton before completing its route to South Portland by early Wednesday morning, according to the post by state police.
The planned route for the transports is Riley Road to Crash Road in Jay, to Route 4, Route 117, Route 26, Route 202, Route 22, and Route 1 before ending along Broadway and Elm Street in South Portland. Motorists are advised to expect delays and temporary closures along the route as utility crews and law enforcement slowly escort the load.
Barnhart Crane & Rigging completed the first of nine oversize load transports planned for the route Tuesday morning. They carried a heat recovery steam generator from the former mill, which is one of the pieces of equipment that JGT2 Redevelopment, the current owners of the site, are selling to Packaging Corporation of America.
In addition to two more heat recovery steam generators, the remaining planned transports will carry three gas turbines and three gas turbine-driven electric generators, according to JGT2.

title: InvestigateTV+: Companies ask for Clean Air Act exemptions
text:
(InvestigateTV) — InvestigateTV+ uncovers an effort by industrial plants to get let off the hook from Clean Air Act regulations.
Plus, one man’s half-century-long quest to trace his ancestry highlights the challenges many Black Americans face.
Then, meet the cheerleading team with a routine you’ve likely never seen.
Permission to Poison?
In March 2025, President Donald Trump’s administration made a tantalizing offer to coal-fired power plants, chemical manufacturing facilities and other factories: Their operations could be exempted from key provisions under the Clean Air Act, the bedrock environmental law estimated to have prevented thousands of premature deaths. All they had to do was ask.
No rigorous application was needed. An email, which they had until the end of the month to send, would suffice.
Finding your family in old documents
Knowing where we come from expands our sense of who we are, according to a 2023 study published in the medical journal “Genealogy.” That study found that learning family history is linked to developing a healthy relationship with one’s identity.
But for many Black Americans, the enslavement of their ancestors meant names, records, and history were often erased. Now, a new database in Jackson County, Missouri is trying to put those names back within reach.
From a bus into a clothing store
A New Orleans teenager has converted a used bus into a traveling clothing boutique, taking his business on the road across the Gulf South.
Valen Purvis, a student at Rummel High School in New Orleans, operates a mobile clothing store called Transit. The concept began during a family vacation in Point Clear, Alabama.
Deaf cheer team competes in its first-ever hearing competition
Minnesota’s only all-deaf high school cheerleading team became the first in its school history to perform in a hearing competition.
In January, the Minnesota State Academy for the Deaf (MSAD) Trojan cheer team competed in their first cheerleading competition of 2026.
