title: Fishing crew reels in record-breaking bluefin tuna: ‘Something that I dream of’
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
RYE, N.H. (WMUR) — A charter fishing trip produced a new state record for the largest bluefin tuna caught in New Hampshire waters.
Captain Jamie Savage and his charter guest, Brandon McGirl, caught a bluefin tuna weighing 1,116 pounds. The previous record, set in 2013, was 962 pounds. The new catch is 154 pounds larger.
Savage and McGirl left for an overnight charter Saturday at 6 a.m. After hours of waiting, they got a bite. Crew members on board worked to get the fish onto the boat, then towed it at a slow pace back to the harbor.
The men said they knew they had a big catch but did not realize how large the fish was until they hoisted it up and saw it in daylight.
“So we lifted it out of the water and immediately knew it was way bigger than what we thought and bigger than anything either of us had seen before,” Savage said.
McGirl said catching a 1,000-pound fish was something he had dreamed of.
“For a long time, catching a 1,000-pound fish, it’s something that I dream of,” McGirl said. “So, I think more than anything, that has always been a goal of mine. Never thought it would actually happen, but to do that and potentially get the record as well is pretty special.”
Tail cut shows meat quality
A cut made to the tuna’s tail showed the quality of its meat.
The tuna is headed to market, where it could be sold as far away as Japan.
The tuna’s tail will remain at the harbor as a trophy to commemorate the record-breaking catch.

title: Maine Drivers Enter a Dangerous Time of Year for Crashes With Animals
text:
Maine Drivers Enter a Dangerous Time of Year for Crashes With Animals
While we need to stay alert year-round, this is a particularly important time to be cautious on the road.
👇 KEEP READING: 19 Maine News Stories That Went National in the Last 20 Years 👇
Playcasino.com analyzed federal records of fatal crashes involving vehicles striking live animals on U.S. public roads from 2015 through 2024, counting every death in those crashes regardless of the animal involved.
Using U.S. Census Bureau population estimates, analysts calculated average annual deaths per million residents and ranked states by those rates, excluding Washington, D.C.
Maine ranked 17th in the analysis, with 13 deaths in crashes involving animals from 2015 through 2024, an average annual rate of 0.95 deaths per million residents.
That amounts to an annual risk of about 1 in 1.05 million for Maine residents, compared with about 1 in 1.56 million nationwide.
The Maine Department of Transportation advises drivers to watch roadsides for wildlife, follow posted speed limits and slow down when visibility is poor, especially around dawn, dusk and at night.
Drivers should also pay attention to wildlife crossing signs and be prepared for additional animals to follow, since deer and moose often travel in groups.
And there you have it! Maine’s rate was higher than the national average, offering another reminder to stay alert for wildlife on the road.

title: Maine Border Patrol agent accused of shooting woman from behind in federal lawsuit
text:
Maine Border Patrol agent accused of shooting American woman from behind in federal lawsuit
A Maine Border Patrol agent is accused of lying about the shooting of a Chicago woman last year in a new lawsuit filed against the federal government.
Maine Border Patrol agent accused of shooting American woman from behind in federal lawsuit
A Maine Border Patrol agent is accused of lying about the shooting of a Chicago woman last year in a new lawsuit filed against the federal government.
An American citizen shot by a Customs and Border Protection agent one year ago during a sweeping immigration crackdown in Chicago filed a lawsuit against the federal government on Monday, alleging the Maine-based agent lied about the shooting and fired into her vehicle from behind.
Federal prosecutors initially accused Marimar Martinez, then 30, of using her vehicle to strike and box in agent Charles Exum’s SUV on Chicago’s southwest side on Oct. 4, 2025, during “Operation Midway Blitz.” Exum then exited his car and opened fire, leaving Martinez with seven gunshot wounds.
In the month after the shooting, prosecutors filed to dismiss the charges in a dramatic reversal of the closely watched case in the nation's third-largest city.
Agent fired into rear of car, attorneys say
Her lawyers said Monday that they commissioned an expert to analyze bullet trajectories and her injuries and determined Exum wasn't in the path of her car when he opened fire. They said he had walked several feet toward her car, contrary to statements he made to the FBI, and fired off five shots in less than a second, the last from the rear side of her vehicle.
“Charles Exum told the FBI agent on that day, within hours of the shooting, that Marimar was driving her car directly at him, that he shot her five times through the windshield, and that he ceased firing once he was no longer in the path of the vehicle. Those are three objective lies that you’ll see here today,” said one of her attorneys, Chris Parente.
Parente said there were only three bullet holes in Martinez’ windshield on the right passenger side, which indicated Martinez wasn't driving toward the agent. He said the fourth shot was fired through the front passenger side window, adding another bullet hole in the back of Martinez’ car seat showed the agent fired the fifth shot from behind her.
“In what world can a U.S. law enforcement officer stand behind a car and fire his Glock service weapon through the rear passenger window at a young woman who’s crouched over the steering wheel?” Parente said.
He also accused federal authorities of tampering with evidence when Exum was allowed to drive the car, which Parente called “critical evidence,” back to Maine rather than keeping it in Chicago to be examined.
CBP said in a statement to The Associated Press in response to the suit that Exum had been placed on administrative leave. Use-of-force incidents are “thoroughly investigated, reviewed, and presented” to an independent board, it added.
Exum is not a defendant in the lawsuit against the federal government, which was filed under the Federal Tort Claims Act and does not allow for lawsuits against individual agents. It was not known where Exum could be reached.
Body-worn camera footage from another agent in Exum's vehicle before the shooting captured the agents saying it was “time to get aggressive” and making other profanity-laced comments encouraging violence, according to the complaint.
Martinez taken from hospital with bullet holes ‘leaking blood,' suit says
The FBI arrested Martinez, taking her out of the hospital just hours after the shooting when she was “wheelchair bound and her bullet holes were leaking blood through her bandages,” according to the lawsuit. A judge ordered her release two days after her arrest.
Messages released by Martinez’ attorneys in February showed that former head of Border Patrol Greg Bovino had praised Exum, who was on temporary assignment in Chicago, for his “excellent service” after the shooting. Other messages they released showed agents in a group chat congratulating Exum and calling him a “legend.”
Martinez was one several people shot in their cars by federal agents during President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown. An immigration agent shot a Venezuelan delivery driver in his car in Austin, Texas, last month, and another shot a Colombian driver in Biddeford, Maine, in July. The Trump administration has at times justified such shootings as self-defense against people allegedly weaponizing their vehicles.
Martinez appeared with her attorneys at a news conference Monday, saying the various shootings spurred her to file suit.
“If I don’t, then who else, you know? Look at what happened to Renee and all these victims,” she said, referring to Renee Good, a woman shot dead in her vehicle by a federal agent in Minneapolis in January.
“What’s happening is not normal. We shouldn’t stay here and normalize what’s happening,” she said.

title: Ellsworth awards $1.6M contract for new courthouse access road
text:
Ellsworth has awarded a $1.6 million contract to a local construction company for the road connecting High Street to the new Hancock Judicial Center.
The Maine Judicial Branch is building a $55 million judicial complex off High Street behind Merrill Furniture, which will replace the aging, nearly century-old State Street courthouse that state officials say does not meet modern technology and security standards.
Ellsworth is responsible for the extension of Merrill Lane, which now ends just past the furniture store. The Ellsworth City Council awarded the $1,633,545 road project Tuesday evening to RF Jordan and Sons, a three-generation family-owned contracting company that has operated in the city for just over six decades.
The city awarded the contract to the lowest bidder, according to Sara Devlin, deputy city manager. The city passed the proposed contract 4-1. Councilor Steve O’Halloran opposed, councilor Patrick Shea abstained and councilor Carol Patterson-Martineau was absent.
The state began construction on the center, which is expected to be operational by 2028, in July. The road could be completed by October 2027, City Manager Charlie Pearce told the council during Tuesday’s special meeting.
So far, the city has spent $606,462, on the project between consultants, land purchase payments, preliminary road construction materials and staff time, according to a city memo.
The state’s decision to build the modern courthouse off High Street follows a long and winding, multi-year process during which state and city stakeholders first eyed a Surry Road property for the new center.
But after significant pushback from local residents, who argued the Surry Road property would harm the mostly residential neighborhood by bringing more traffic and reducing property values, the state abandoned its plans for the Surry Road location, which it had already purchased in 2024.
Ellsworth, state officials and Alice B. Wardwell, who previously owned the High Street property, entered into a land-swap agreement last year. Wardwell gave the 18-acre parcel off High Street to the state in exchange for 18 acres next to Josie’s Country Store and Cafe.
Had the state opted for the Surry Road option, Ellsworth would not have needed to foot the bill for the new access road, according to Mike Harris, the city’s public works director.
Some city councilors and residents wanted the city-owned road to be built by city employees, though that plan was aborted after estimates for the highway department’s overtime and materials fell to around $2.1 million, according to a city memo.
That estimate didn’t include the cost of outside contractors for certain services the department isn’t licensed or trained to complete, like blasting and electrical work.
Ellsworth city councilors authorized up to $3.8 million in general obligation bonds in early September, about $1.75 million of which will be used on the access road. The bond’s proposed term is 20 years.
In mid-September, the Hancock County commissioners tabled a request from the city for funding assistance for the new access road.
At a mid-October council meeting, staff will propose awarding the engineering services contract to Andrew McCollough, who was involved in the engineering of the Church Street sidewalk and a parking lot and septic system for Surry Elementary School, among other projects, according to his website.
Bowman Constructors, of Newport, is the general contractor on the new 64,200-square-foot, four-courtroom complex.
The city granted a New England based electrical contractor, E.S. Boulos Company, a permit for $2.47 million of electrical services on the courthouse project.
“Change is happening in Ellsworth and change is hard because first what we see is what we lose before we see what we can gain,” councilor Nancy Smith said. “This is a spectacular example of change that can either happen to you or with you. With this two year process, and into the next two years, Ellsworth is choosing to be actively engaged in how the change is happening — it will happen with us, not to us.”

title: UMF to screen Maine mockumentary ‘Canoe Dig It?’
text:
FARMINGTON — The University of Maine at Farmington will host filmmaker and actor Samuel Dunning for a screening of his 2025 mockumentary “Canoe Dig It?” at 7 p.m. Thursday, Oct. 15, at the Emery Community Arts Center.

Dunning, originally from Brunswick, divides his time between the East and West coasts as a filmmaker, actor and model. He graduated from New York University’s Tisch School of the Arts with a bachelor of fine arts degree in film production and direction.
His previous work includes the 2019 horror comedy short “Rick and Ruby,” which won awards at several film festivals, including Sitges Film Festival, Screamfest and Dead by Dawn. Dunning also has received a Best Supporting Actor nomination at the Nevermore Film Festival.

title: Christa Pike is awake and speaking days after failed execution, attorneys say
text:
KNOXVILLE, Tenn. (WVLT/Gray News) -- Christa Pike is awake and speaking days after her failed Tennessee execution, according to her attorneys.
Pike was supposed to be executed via lethal injection in Tennessee last Wednesday.
However, after receiving two doses of what should have been lethal amounts of pentobarbital, she survived.
The failed execution had left her unconscious and on a ventilator at a hospital.
Dr. Paul Allen, a professor of anesthesiology at the University of Tennessee Health Science Center, said the needle never properly made it into her vein; when it came to the reason he believed what may have gone wrong with the execution.
Pike, 50, was 18 when authorities say she and her boyfriend tortured and killed a classmate in a jealous rage in 1995. She became one of the youngest women to be sent to death row.
The head of Tennessee’s prison system has since resigned following the botched execution. Whether the state can proceed with another execution attempt remains to be seen.

title: ‘By God’s grace:’ Lost hiker’s distress call puts emergency crews in the right spot to rescue motorcyclist
text:
LOS ANGELES (KCAL/KCBS) - In California, a lost hiker triggered a series of events that likely saved the life of a motorcycle rider who crashed in a remote area.
“Well, we kind of have a saying around here. We’re not here for this one. We’re here for the next one. We say it all the time,” Mike Leum, a reserve deputy of the Montrose Search and Rescue team, said.
Never has that been more immediately true for the Montrose Search and Rescue team than it was Sunday at about 7:30 p.m. They were headed up here on the Angeles Crest Highway after getting an iPhone SOS from a solo hiker with no idea where he was.
“He was completely lost, like 15 miles away from where he thought he was. He had been hiking for over 12 hours. All, all of it in the wrong direction,” Leum said.
Three units hit the road with the urgency rising as night fell when another call came in. They learned of a motorcycle-car crash about five miles ahead of them.
Leum and fellow reserve deputy Sean Morrisroe got there first.
“It was very dark, very chaotic, debris all over the road,” Morrisroe said. “Right away I saw his left leg, a very traumatic injury, bloody, and we knew right away he needed a tourniquet. So, I applied the tourniquet, twisted it down; it was still bleeding, twisted down some more.”
Time was running out as the motorcyclist’s leg was partially amputated and he had massive blood loss.
“Yeah, it was just by God’s grace that we got that call out for that hiker and we were five minutes away from the accident because he didn’t have 15 minutes, definitely not 20,” Morrisroe said.
Had they not been there, they said a Los Angeles County fire crew would have first responded by car from 35 minutes away.
Instead, Montrose was able to call for the Los Angeles County fire chopper. Jay Balagna and his partner cleared a turnout for the landing:
“That person’s bleeding was so extreme that without that tourniquet being applied as quickly as it was, things could have been a lot different,” Balagna said.
Once the biker was on a four-minute flight to the hospital, the crews continued on the original call. They found the lost hiker off the Rincon Red Box Fire Road, where he told them he’d started hiking that morning in Sierra Madre.
He was dehydrated but otherwise OK.
“There’s a whole lot of issues with his lack of preparedness. And he felt bad. And he was very apologetic,” Leum said. “And I told him, I was like, dude, if you hadn’t hit the SOS, 911, we wouldn’t have been activated. We wouldn’t have been in a place where we were able to save that motorcycle.”
Whether it was luck, fate or divine intervention, the volunteers said one or all of those led them to two people in danger Sunday and reaffirmed that whenever they show up for work they are exactly where they need to be:
“Well, I feel like we were put there for a purpose,” Leum said.
“The fact that we were on our way to that lost hiker and happened to be just short of them on the same road was miraculous, absolutely,” Balanga said.
In another twist, it turned out the motorcycle rider was a co-worker of one of the search team members.
She was able to visit him in the hospital and said he was overwhelmed by the sequence of events that saved him.

title: Tom Cruise's 'Digger' Disaster Has Him Looking for Someone to Blame

Tom Cruise thought Digger would finally deliver the Oscar win that has eluded him.
Instead, sources whisper that the actor is furious, embarrassed and looking for someone to blame after the film's disastrous opening.
The enormously expensive Alejandro González Iñárritu satire stumbled out of the gate with just $1.2 million in Thursday previews following bruising reviews and brutal online reaction.
Tom Cruise Is Reportedly Furious Over 'Digger' Flop
“Tom is furious because Tom hates to lose,” a source tells Naughty But Nice. “He didn’t think he had made another movie. He thought he had made THE movie — the performance that would finally put an Oscar in his hands.”
Now, insiders say Cruise has turned his attention to the people responsible for selling Digger, with the film's marketing and publicity teams facing particularly uncomfortable questions.
He’s blaming the marketing. He’s blaming the PR. He wants to know why audiences weren’t convinced this was an event. There are emergency calls, meetings and a lot of finger-pointing. Tom wants answers.
For Cruise, sources say the embarrassment cuts particularly deep because expectations were so high.
“He was already thinking about awards season,” another source says. “He imagined standing on that stage. Nobody around him was preparing Tom for headlines about empty seats.”
Tom Cruise's 'Digger' Can't Be Saved
And insiders say an uncomfortable realization is setting in behind the scenes: Digger can't be saved.

“That’s what Tom is struggling with,” the source says. “There’s no marketing campaign, PR strategy or famous friend who can fix this now. The audience has spoken.”
The mission now isn't saving Digger. It's containing the damage to Tom Cruise.

title: Authorities investigating fatal excavator accident in Gray
text:
At least one person died in a workplace accident involving an excavator in Gray on Monday, the Cumberland County sheriff says.
Sheriff Kevin Joyce confirmed in a brief email Monday night that the Cumberland County Sheriff’s Office responded to a fatal incident. He did not provide further details about the accident, including how many people were involved, where in Gray it happened or what might have caused it.
The sheriff’s office is assisting the U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration in the investigation, Joyce said.
Sheriff’s office Capt. Kerry Joyce declined to provide further details about the incident Tuesday morning and instead directed a reporter to OSHA.
An OSHA spokesperson confirmed that the agency has begun an investigation but would not be able to share more information until it is completed. OSHA has six months to complete the investigation, the spokesperson added.
This is a developing story.

title: Bangor police partner with Red Cross for blood drive
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) — The Bangor Police Department teamed up with the American Red Cross to host a blood drive at the donation center on Hammond St. Tuesday.
Local Red Cross leaders said donations have been down since discontinuing mobile blood drives earlier this year.
Partnering with area police departments helps get the word out and bring more volunteers in through the doors.
“Our intent and our hope is that it will encourage people to make an appointment to give blood, and they really have come out in full force today. The police officers themselves are on the docket and community members who support the police are here as well,” said Caroline King, the executive director of the Northern and Eastern Maine Chapter of the Red Cross.
“It’s about helping people and having emergency care services available if something terrible happens. I know that they have shortages throughout the country. Obviously anything that we can do here in our community to help other communities, we should do that,” said Sgt. Jeremy Brock of the Bangor Police Department.
As of 4 p.m. Tuesday, the drive had collected 22 pints of blood and counting.
Those who missed the event can schedule an appointment at RedCrossBlood.org.

title: This database is helping Black families find their enslaved ancestors
text:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. (InvestigateTV) - Knowing where we come from expands our sense of who we are, according to a 2023 study published in the medical journal “Genealogy.” That study found that learning family history is linked to developing a healthy relationship with one’s identity.
But for many Black Americans, the enslavement of their ancestors meant names, records, and history were often erased. Now, a new database in Jackson County, Missouri is trying to put those names back within reach.
Reggie James has long studied the past. His family’s history is no different.
“I knew nothing,” James said.
In 1979, while watching the TV miniseries “Roots: The Next Generation,” the retired schoolteacher felt the pull to discover his own roots.
“It’s not like it is today, where everything has been digitized. You had to go to the archives and use the microfilm, wheeling it by hand to check the census,” James recalled.
Decades of research uncover family lineage
James spent nearly 50 years poring over census records, newspaper clippings and documents from the Jackson County Recorder of Deeds. It was an arduous process, but one that eventually led him to his paternal grandmother, Oletha Brookins, born in 1905.
“When I found her, I saw her mother’s name,” James said. “I never knew her mother’s name.”
James traced the Brookins side of his family in Jackson County back to 1851, mapping the lineage of his enslaved ancestors all the way back to the 17th century, starting in Maine, through Virginia, Kentucky, and ultimately into Clay and Jackson counties, Missouri.
“George is my second great-grandfather, because Oletha is my grandmother, second grandparent, Brookins, he was a slave,” James said, looking at family tree he created.
When asked what goes through his mind about finding so many relatives, James said he’s amazed.
“I’m just in awe of it,” James said. “I have stories on all these people like I knew them.”
The stories give the 75-year-old a place of belonging and a clear identity.
“To know who you really are, to find out what your people went through, what sacrifices they [made] for me to be here,” James said. “The audacity of this whole system, you know.”
Museum creates digital database from historical records
James already did the hard part, decades of page-by-page digging, one record at a time. But now, Jackson County records that were always public are easier to search and understand thanks to staff at the Wornall Majors House Museums.
“The database was a little bit of a happy accident,” said Sarah Bader-King, the museums’ executive director.
Her team was researching property records connected to Alexander Majors, a pioneer freighter who enslaved at least 23 people, when they found a deed of trust.
It listed nine enslaved people not as just property, but by name and age.
“Once I pulled up a couple of these deeds and saw that most of them had names in them, I was like we really have something here,” Bader-King said.
That discovery led them back into the Jackson County Recorder of Deeds, where they found hundreds of deeds, wills, probate records and bills of sale. It’s a trove of legal documents, sometimes difficult to navigate.
“We realized we could provide a service by simply summarizing these documents,” Bader-King said.
The online database, which launched in February 2026, turns 19th-century records into searchable names. Users can search by name, document type, or keywords with results that include document images and plain-language summaries.
“This is not just Black history. It’s American history,” Bader-King said.
Funding project to uncover history
The project received funding support from Kansas City’s Monument Coalition, an organization that works to tell understudied and unknown stories of Kansas City history.
“These are not a mass system of people that we can write as a whole,” said Kevin McPartland, an assistant project manager. “They are individuals, who experienced these things as mothers, fathers, daughters, brothers and sisters.”
McPartland said the Jackson County database is part of a growing national movement.
“Projects like this are popping up across the country,” he said. “So, naming the enslaved, this is a local database but is one database that is joining a growing corpus of databases nationally that are looking at stuff like this.”
The Jackson County database is a digital tool designed to help people piece together their ancestors’ stories. It’s the same work James did by hand for decades, now open to anyone to start.
“I’m happy that they’re doing that,” James said about the new resource tool.
It serves as an invitation to bring lost names back to light.
“You have a lot of people who are interested but they don’t know,” James said. “You never know what you might find.”
Since the interview, the museum has found several hundred more names to add to the database. It is free to use and available online. Click here to access it.
The museum also offers up to two hours of free research help.

title: Popular social media star arrested near college bar over the weekend, police say
text:
COLLEGE STATION, Texas. (KBTX/Gray News) - A popular social media star was arrested in Texas near a college bar over the weekend, according to authorities.
Benjamin Beard, 34, known as BenDaDonnn online, was charged Sunday with evading arrest.
Another man, 29-year-old Kenny Carter, was charged with interference with public duties.
Police said they were attempting to clear people from the roadway in front of a bar when a group refused to listen to the officers.
As the incident became physical, police said one of their officers was shoved to the ground by Carter, who identified himself as Beard’s security guard.
Police said an officer used a taser on Beard, who was attempting to get away.
Police said as officers moved the two to a staging area to wait to be taken to jail, a large “entourage” crowded around them before being told several times to move back.
Earlier that evening, Beard appeared on Texas A&M football’s official X account, showing him on the sidelines during the game near the rest of the team.
Another X account showed Beard attempting to enter the locker room during halftime with cameras rolling, only to be kicked out by coach Elko.
Beard is better known on social media platforms as a live streamer and social media influencer who often collaborates with other well-known entertainers, including Drake, and athletes on comedy skits, social media content and music.
He has a combined social media following of over 3.7 million followers across his platforms.

title: Suspect arrested after pregnant woman killed, unborn child removed from her womb
text:
CLARKSVILLE, Tenn. (WYMT/WSMV/Gray News) - Authorities say a man accused of killing a pregnant woman in Kentucky was arrested in Tennessee following a weeklong investigation.
April Barlow Celio, 41, was found dead Sept. 23 at a home in Pineville, Kentucky. The Pineville Police and the Bell County Coroner’s Office determined she was the victim of a homicide.
The next day, investigators learned Celio was pregnant at the time of her death, but the State Medical Examiner’s Office found no fetus in her womb. While processing the crime scene, investigators later found what are believed to be fetal remains.
The investigation identified DeMarcus Kenneth Johnson-Wright as a suspect in the case. He had an extensive violent criminal history and several outstanding violent felony warrants out of Tennessee.
The Bell County District Court issued a warrant for Johnson-Wright on Sep. 25 for first-degree robbery and kidnapping — adult. Additional warrants for him for murder — domestic violence and tampering with physical evidence were issued last Wednesday.
That same day, the U.S. Marshals Service learned Johnson-Wright was living in Clarksville, Tennessee, where he was arrested at a home later that night. A subsequent search warrant was applied for and granted for the home, and marshals say materials relating to the case were recovered.
Johnson-Wright was booked into the Montgomery County Detention Center in Tennessee, where he is awaiting extradition back to Kentucky.
The investigation is ongoing.

title: ‘He had a big heart’: Family mourns 15-year-old killed in downtown Las Vegas shooting
text:
LAS VEGAS (KVVU/Gray News) — A family is mourning the loss of their 15-year-old son who was killed in a shooting in a downtown Las Vegas arts district.
The family of the teen killed in Friday night’s shooting identified him as 15-year-old Carth Onasi Jacobs-Rodgers. The teen’s stepmother said he was a sophomore at Desert Pines High School.
She described him as smart, brave and strong-willed, the oldest of nine siblings, who loved his sisters and little brother, making people laugh, boxing, basketball and video games.
“He had a big heart... He was goofy — when he laughed you couldn’t help but laugh too... He is loved by many and will be missed by all of us,” she said in a statement to KVVU.
The family has set up an online fundraiser to help with funeral costs.
Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department said officers were near South Main Street and West Charleston Boulevard around 10:17 p.m. Friday during a community First Friday event when they heard shots in the area. Officers found two gunshot victims in a crowd, then a third. All three were taken to a hospital. Jacobs-Rodgers later died from his injuries.
Homicide Lt. Robert Price said the two survivors have non-life-threatening injuries.
Detectives determined a fight occurred between several individuals. At some point, an unknown male produced a firearm and began shooting, striking multiple people, police said. The suspect fled prior to officers arriving.
Mayor Pro Tem Olivia Diaz expressed her sympathy with the victims and attendees from the First Friday shooting.
“My heart is with the victims, victims’ families, and First Friday attendees affected by last night’s shooting in the Arts District,” she said. “Thank you to all the LVMPD officers, first responders, First Friday staff, community partners and volunteers who jumped into action to help guide people to safety.”
The First Friday Foundation said it is “heartbroken” and “grateful” for the law enforcement’s swift response. The Arts District Neighborhood Association, which works closely with the foundation, also expressed sadness and pledged to help make First Friday safer moving forward.
“We hold the victims, their loved ones, and all those affected close to our hearts,” the association said.

title: 4 takeaways from the first debate between Susan Collins and Troy Jackson
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson faced off in a televised debate on Tuesday, sparring over a wide range of topics, including President Donald Trump, high prices and corruption allegations.
It was the first of four debates scheduled for the next two weeks.
Independent polling shows a tight race. Jackson, a 59-year-old former logger and state Senate president, holds a two-point lead over the 73-year-old Collins, according to polling averages from FiftyPlusOne.
But a Marist poll released on Tuesday had Jackson up, 51% to 47%, with only 1% undecided. The Democrat’s four-point lead was just outside of the margin of error of +/- 3.8 percentage points.
Here are a few takeaways from the high-stakes showdown.
1. The candidates blamed each other for the high cost of living
The high cost of living — especially the prices of gasoline and home heating oil — has repeatedly been cited by voters as their top concern leading up to the midterms.
So it’s no surprise that Jackson and Collins tried to blame each other for the situation.
Jackson, perhaps, had the easiest line of attack. Throughout the night, Jackson repeatedly tied Collins to Trump and his unpopular policies and actions, including tariffs, the war with Iran and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025, which cut healthcare and other safety net programs, and gave tax breaks to the wealthy.
Collins, however, pushed back, saying for example that Jackson was cherry-picking one analysis showing she voted with Trump more than 95% of the time. Other analyses showed a much lower rate, she said, noting that she’s not close with the president.
She then raised the issue of high property taxes and electricity rates, saying “those are all due to Augusta’s failed policies under the failed leadership of Troy Jackson,” who served six years as Senate president.
2. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act was in the spotlight.
Jackson repeatedly blamed Collins for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which made permanent tax cuts for the wealthy while making deep cuts to healthcare and safety net programs.
Collins voted to advance the Republican bill to the Senate floor, but voted against enacting it.
Jackson used Collins’ vote advancing the measure to cast her as being on the side of billionaires.
“Senator Collins has had 30 years to show whose side she’s on,” he said. “I don’t owe Donald Trump or the billionaires anything. I don’t fight for billionaires like she does. I owe Mainers everything, and that’s who I’m gonna be fighting for when I’m the next U.S. senator.”
Collins criticized Jackson for distorting her record. She said she only voted to advance the bill so she could help author an amendment inserting a $50 billion fund to help rural hospitals. She said she voted against the final measure’s enactment because of the Medicaid cuts it contained. But the bill passed after Vice President JD Vance cast a tiebreaking vote.
Jackson said that reasoning wasn’t good enough.
“Sen. Collins is like an arsonist who helps set the fire and then she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out,” he said.
3. The candidates accused each other of corruption.
Collins has been under fire for nearly two weeks since ProPublica published a report detailing allegations that she was leveraging her role on the appropriations committee to solicit political donations. The outlet reported the FBI was gearing up for an investigation into Collins’ circle until Trump returned to office in 2025 and disbanded certain anti-corruption units.
Collins defended herself Tuesday, pointing out that she had advocated for a project involving the defense contractor Navatek at the urging of the University of Maine — not at the urging of a donor.
Collins then accused Jackson of corruption, raising questions about a mortgage he signed and reimbursements he got while serving in the Legislature.
Jackson said he signed a mortgage document stating that his second home in Augusta would be his primary residence — which he said he was advised to do since he would spend more than half of the year there.
But a home in Allagash remained his permanent residence as defined by the state law. Jackson said he would travel there every weekend from Augusta, leading to his expense reimbursements.
4. Jackson was aggressive. Collins was knowledgeable.
Throughout the debate, Collins displayed her experience and knowledge of federal policies. She repeatedly called out Jackson for suggesting her committee had authority over things it does not, such as Medicaid rates.
Jackson, meanwhile, was relentless in going after Collins’ record. He criticized her for supporting Brett Kavanaugh’s appointment to the U.S. Supreme Court and for standing behind that vote after the court overturned the federal abortion protections under Roe v. Wade.
And he continued to hammer Collins for voting to advance the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and for supporting Trump’s agenda, despite Collins’ efforts to highlight instances where she has broken with the president — such as her moves to push back against his tariffs and against his administration’s efforts to cut medical research funding.

She then raised the issue of high property taxes and electricity rates, saying “those are all due to Augusta’s failed policies under the failed leadership of Troy Jackson,” who served six years as Senate president.
2. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act was in the spotlight.
Jackson repeatedly blamed Collins for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which made permanent tax cuts for the wealthy while making deep cuts to healthcare and safety net programs.
Collins voted to advance the Republican bill to the Senate floor, but voted against enacting it.
Jackson used Collins’ vote advancing the measure to cast her as being on the side of billionaires.
“Senator Collins has had 30 years to show whose side she’s on,” he said. “I don’t owe Donald Trump or the billionaires anything. I don’t fight for billionaires like she does. I owe Mainers everything, and that’s who I’m gonna be fighting for when I’m the next U.S. senator.”
Collins criticized Jackson for distorting her record. She said she only voted to advance the bill so she could help author an amendment inserting a $50 billion fund to help rural hospitals. She said she voted against the final measure’s enactment because of the Medicaid cuts it contained. But the bill passed after Vice President JD Vance cast a tiebreaking vote.
Jackson said that reasoning wasn’t good enough.
“Sen. Collins is like an arsonist who helps set the fire and then she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out,” he said.
3. The candidates accused each other of corruption.
Collins has been under fire for nearly two weeks since ProPublica published a report detailing allegations that she was leveraging her role on the appropriations committee to solicit political donations. The outlet reported the FBI was gearing up for an investigation into Collins’ circle until Trump returned to office in 2025 and disbanded certain anti-corruption units.
Collins defended herself Tuesday, pointing out that she had advocated for a project involving the defense contractor Navatek at the urging of the University of Maine — not at the urging of a donor.
Collins then accused Jackson of corruption, raising questions about a mortgage he signed and reimbursements he got while serving in the Legislature.
Jackson said he signed a mortgage document stating that his second home in Augusta would be his primary residence — which he said he was advised to do since he would spend more than half of the year there.
But a home in Allagash remained his permanent residence as defined by the state law. Jackson said he would travel there every weekend from Augusta, leading to his expense reimbursements.
4. Jackson was aggressive. Collins was knowledgeable.
Throughout the debate, Collins displayed her experience and knowledge of federal policies. She repeatedly called out Jackson for suggesting her committee had authority over things it does not, such as Medicaid rates.
Jackson, meanwhile, was relentless in going after Collins’ record. He criticized her for supporting Brett Kavanaugh’s appointment to the U.S. Supreme Court and for standing behind that vote after the court overturned the federal abortion protections under Roe v. Wade.
And he continued to hammer Collins for voting to advance the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and for supporting Trump’s agenda, despite Collins’ efforts to highlight instances where she has broken with the president — such as her moves to push back against his tariffs and against his administration’s efforts to cut medical research funding.

title: Does Scarborough have town-level limits on where political signs can be posted?
text:
Yes.
Scarborough has local limits on where political signs, which it classifies as temporary signs, can be posted.
The town’s zoning ordinance prohibits temporary signs in rights of way along certain major roadways and near specified intersections to protect scenic views, sensitive areas and traffic safety.
Scarborough repealed a separate political sign ordinance in 2017 and incorporated those rules into its zoning ordinance.
Its rules supplement state law, which allows temporary signs in public rights of way for up to 12 weeks per year and requires identical messages to be at least 30 feet apart.
Other southern Maine communities impose additional restrictions. South Portland prohibits campaign signs in rights of way narrower than 6 feet and in roundabouts and rotaries. Westbrook bars temporary signs from rotary islands, narrow medians, public school grounds, cemeteries and some city parks.
Maine law prohibits unauthorized removal of legally placed political signs.
This fact brief is responsive to conversations such as this one.

title: 'The Blacklist' actor and wife turn car around to adopt unforgettable puppy
text:
'The Blacklist' actor, wife turns car around to adopt New Mexico puppy
Jonathan Holtzman and his wife, Ali Margolies, found their newest family member at Española Humane — but it took a change of heart and a quick U-turn to bring Avocado home
'The Blacklist' actor, wife turns car around to adopt New Mexico puppy
Jonathan Holtzman and his wife, Ali Margolies, found their newest family member at Española Humane — but it took a change of heart and a quick U-turn to bring Avocado home
Jonathan Holtzman, an actor from a popular TV show, and his wife, Ali Margolies, have welcomed a new member into their family: a rescue puppy named Avocado.
But it took a change of heart and a quick U-turn to bring the little dog home.
The couple began looking for a dog after moving to Santa Fe, New Mexico. Although their travel schedule initially kept them from adopting, they continued visiting Española Humane until they had enough time at home to help a puppy adjust.
Holtzman, who played Chuck on NBC's "The Blacklist," said the shelter's staff made an immediate impression.
"As soon as we went there, we were like, ‘OK, no matter what or when, we’re getting our puppy from here,’" he said. "Everyone was professional and caring, and they have incredible resources."
When Holtzman and Margolies first met Avocado, however, the puppy was trembling and reluctant to interact. They believed the shelter environment may have made her anxious, but they were uncertain whether her calm demeanor would fit into their active lifestyle.
Avocado slowly began coming out of her shell, particularly when treats were involved. During a second meeting, she appeared to recognize the couple and showed more of her energetic personality.
Still, Holtzman and Margolies wanted to be certain before adopting Avocado. They left the shelter, planning to sleep on the decision, but they did not get far.
"We were 8 or 10 minutes down the road and just said, ‘If somebody else takes her, we will be devastated,’" Margolies said. "And we turned the car around and got her."
At home, Avocado quickly proved she was anything but shy and calm. The puppy has jumped into her water bowl, learned how to escape her pen and repeatedly tried to eat rocks in the couple's gravel backyard.
Despite this, the couple said Avocado is adjusting well and is becoming more confident every day. They hope to eventually bring her along on hikes and other outdoor adventures.
"It’s just really special to see that personality come out and see her feel so comfortable,” Margolies said, "and just happy to be loved, which we hope to give her a ton of."
For Avocado's first appearance in front of a camera, Holtzman said she knew exactly what to do. She fell asleep right in their arms and was calm throughout the interview.
"She’s playing the role very well," he said. "Perfect doggy."

title: Trump signs order extending tax-free use of red-dyed diesel, saying it will save farmers ‘millions’
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
GRAND ISLAND, Neb. (AP) — President Donald Trump on Monday took his Republican midterm rescue mission to Nebraska, where he signed an executive order to ease limits on the tax-free use of red-dyed diesel, a decision he said would save “millions” for farmers and drive down the cost of all goods with just four weeks to go until the elections.
“Pete and Jim, this should absolutely ensure your election, I guarantee you that,” Trump said, addressing GOP Sen. Pete Ricketts, who is running against an independent candidate backed by national Democrats, and Gov. Jim Pillen, who is seeking a second term.
Diesel fuel prices have spiked in the aftermath of the Iran war, rattling voters and putting pressure on Republicans. Diesel fuel that is intended for off-road uses such as agriculture is exempt from federal and state excise taxes, and it is dyed for law enforcement purposes, the White House explained in a fact sheet. Temporarily removing the limits would reduce cost pressures on the businesses that rely on diesel.
“The typical trucker will save more than $100 every time they fill up,” Trump said, signing the executive order onstage before a crowd in Grand Island, Nebraska, in the solidly conservative south-central part of the state. He said the order will save farmers millions of dollars and drive down the cost of goods.
Patrick De Haan of GasBuddy, a platform that monitors national gasoline and diesel prices, noted last week, when news of the possible action began to surface, that such an order could save money for on-road users but not farmers, who already use red-dyed diesel.
“Taxes aren’t the problem, supply is,” De Haan wrote on X.
Trump’s trip is part of what the Republican president says is a 32-day blitz of rallies ahead of Nov. 3 that so far has taken him to ruby-red territory such as Oklahoma and Alabama. On Wednesday, he’ll make his second stop in two weeks in Texas with a rally in San Antonio.
Ricketts, a former governor of the state, was appointed then later elected to fill Sen. Ben Sasse’s seat when he left to run the University of Florida in 2023. Now Ricketts is running for his first full six-year term against independent Dan Osborn — a race that initially was not expected to be competitive but is now being watched by the national parties.
Republicans facing headwinds amid voter discontent
Voters across the country are frustrated with Trump’s handling of the economy, including persistently high costs for fuel and groceries. It’s a major issue for rural voters who have backed the president and his party in recent elections.
The administration’s plan to allow more imports of foreign beef has particularly roiled the agriculture-rich state of Nebraska. Trump wants to lower beef prices for consumers, but ranchers have rebelled against the import proposal, arguing it would undercut them.
“The plan to import low-quality foreign beef is not helping Nebraska ranchers,” Ricketts told the AP. “I would advise the White House to change that policy and look for longer-term things that will help us build the size of the herd and ultimately bring the price of beef down for consumers.”
In Grand Island, rally-goers said they they trusted Trump to solve the high cost of living.
“I feel like if we get our reserves built back up, get this situation in Iran taken care of, our gas prices will go down. The economy as far as groceries and stuff like that, it’s going to go down too. It’ll stabilize. I have faith in him. More faith in him than I ever had in any other president,” said Marlene Abel from Garfield, Kansas.
David Kuncl, who grew up on a farm, expressed confidence things would improve in the long run. But the Lincoln, Nebraska, resident insisted Trump wasn’t to blame, pointing instead to what he believes is “a coup, a plot to try to hurt Trump” and the Republicans in the midterms.
“It’s hurting us. Gas prices. Diesel prices. Beef prices,” he said. “I don’t know why they’re high. But it’s not that Trump’s got anything to do with that. He’ll do what he can. But of course he can’t wave a magic wand and make it go lower.”
Democrats are aiming to flip a House seat in Nebraska
In the House of Representatives, the Grand Island area is represented by Republican Rep. Adrian Smith, whose race is not expected to be close.
But Nebraska has a competitive House race farther east in Omaha, in the 2nd District — considered the “blue dot” of the state because the area’s electoral vote in presidential elections often goes to Democrats. The district is in the midst of a competitive race between Republican Brinker Harding and Democrat Denise Powell to fill retiring Rep. Don Bacon ’s open seat.
Monday’s rally came as the Congressional Leadership Fund, a super PAC dedicated to electing Republicans to the House, cancelled $1.1 million in planned broadcast spending on behalf of the Republican candidate in the race, according to AdImpact, which tracks campaign media spending. It was a possible sign that GOP leaders feel the money could be put to better use elsewhere. The group did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
There are tentative plans for Trump to travel to other election battlegrounds, including Michigan, North Carolina, Georgia, Ohio, Kansas, Montana, Pennsylvania, Alaska, Nevada and Arizona before November’s Election Day. That’s according to a person familiar with the plans who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly and cautioned the plans could shift.
There are a few Senate races where independents are the challengers
Osborn, a former labor union chief, ran against Republican Sen. Deb Fischer in 2024 and lost by 7 percentage points. Though national Democrats support him, he has refused to say what party he would caucus with should he be elected in November.
Other independents in the Senate, including Maine’s Angus King on the moderate end and Vermont’s Bernie Sanders on the left, caucus with Democrats for organizational purposes and committee assignments.
With the Democratic brand remaining deeply unpopular in conservative states, Osborn isn’t the only declared independent running for the Senate against Republicans this year. In South Dakota, Brian Bengs is campaigning as an independent against Republican Sen. Mike Rounds. Bengs ran as a Democrat for the Senate four years ago and was handily defeated by now-Senate Majority Leader John Thune. It’s a similar dynamic in Idaho, where independent Todd Achilles is challenging GOP Sen. Jim Risch.
Democratic voters in Nebraska chose Cindy Burbank as their party nominee, but Burbank campaigned on ensuring that no votes would be siphoned from Osborn in the general election, and she has since dropped out of the race.
Osborn has been traveling across Nebraska to hold meetings in all 93 counties, and has repeatedly criticized Ricketts for not holding town halls to meet with constituents.
Ricketts, whose family founded TD Ameritrade and owns Major League Baseball’s Chicago Cubs, served as governor from 2015 to 2023.
Vance stumps in Alaska
As Trump traveled to Nebraska, Vice President JD Vance headed to Fairbanks to rally with Republican candidates, including Sen. Dan Sullivan, who is locked in a contest with Democrat Mary Peltola that’s one of a handful expected to determine control of the chamber in the November elections.
Vance praised Sullivan before a crowd gathered at the airport, saying the two-term senator is known for texting Cabinet members in the middle of the night to make the case for Alaska interests.
He cast Peltola, who served in the House from late 2022 and lost reelection in 2024, as ineffective during her time in Congress and called her a “servant of the far left.” Peltola has sought to distance herself from national Democrats and emphasize that she is doing what she thinks is best for the state. Alaska Democrats described Vance’s visit to help Sullivan as an act of desperation.
Sullivan was in the Oval Office last week as Trump announced that South Korea planned to invest about $54 billion in a natural gas project in Alaska, but South Korean officials were more cautious, saying they needed to assess the project’s commercial viability before committing to the investment.
Vance also expressed support for Rep. Nick Begich, whom he called a “machine” and a hard worker. Begich, first elected in 2024, is facing independent Bill Hill, a commercial fisherman and former educator, as his main competitor.
___
This story has been corrected to show that Pete Ricketts is a U.S. senator for Nebraska, not the governor.
___
Kim and Kinnard reported from Washington. Associated Press writers Jill Colvin in New York and Michelle L. Price in Washington and Becky Bohrer in Juneau, Alaska, contributed to this report.

title: ‘By God’s grace:’ Lost hiker’s distress call puts emergency crews in the right spot to rescue motorcyclist
text:
LOS ANGELES (KCAL/KCBS) - In California, a lost hiker triggered a series of events that likely saved the life of a motorcycle rider who crashed in a remote area.
“Well, we kind of have a saying around here. We’re not here for this one. We’re here for the next one. We say it all the time,” Mike Leum, a reserve deputy of the Montrose Search and Rescue team, said.
Never has that been more immediately true for the Montrose Search and Rescue team than it was Sunday at about 7:30 p.m. They were headed up here on the Angeles Crest Highway after getting an iPhone SOS from a solo hiker with no idea where he was.
“He was completely lost, like 15 miles away from where he thought he was. He had been hiking for over 12 hours. All, all of it in the wrong direction,” Leum said.
Three units hit the road with the urgency rising as night fell when another call came in. They learned of a motorcycle-car crash about five miles ahead of them.
Leum and fellow reserve deputy Sean Morrisroe got there first.
“It was very dark, very chaotic, debris all over the road,” Morrisroe said. “Right away I saw his left leg, a very traumatic injury, bloody, and we knew right away he needed a tourniquet. So, I applied the tourniquet, twisted it down; it was still bleeding, twisted down some more.”
Time was running out as the motorcyclist’s leg was partially amputated and he had massive blood loss.
“Yeah, it was just by God’s grace that we got that call out for that hiker and we were five minutes away from the accident because he didn’t have 15 minutes, definitely not 20,” Morrisroe said.
Had they not been there, they said a Los Angeles County fire crew would have first responded by car from 35 minutes away.
Instead, Montrose was able to call for the Los Angeles County fire chopper. Jay Balagna and his partner cleared a turnout for the landing:
“That person’s bleeding was so extreme that without that tourniquet being applied as quickly as it was, things could have been a lot different,” Balagna said.
Once the biker was on a four-minute flight to the hospital, the crews continued on the original call. They found the lost hiker off the Rincon Red Box Fire Road, where he told them he’d started hiking that morning in Sierra Madre.
He was dehydrated but otherwise OK.
“There’s a whole lot of issues with his lack of preparedness. And he felt bad. And he was very apologetic,” Leum said. “And I told him, I was like, dude, if you hadn’t hit the SOS, 911, we wouldn’t have been activated. We wouldn’t have been in a place where we were able to save that motorcycle.”
Whether it was luck, fate or divine intervention, the volunteers said one or all of those led them to two people in danger Sunday and reaffirmed that whenever they show up for work they are exactly where they need to be:
“Well, I feel like we were put there for a purpose,” Leum said.
“The fact that we were on our way to that lost hiker and happened to be just short of them on the same road was miraculous, absolutely,” Balanga said.
In another twist, it turned out the motorcycle rider was a co-worker of one of the search team members.
She was able to visit him in the hospital and said he was overwhelmed by the sequence of events that saved him.

title: Collins campaign pushes back on ProPublica's claims of pay-to-play scheme
text:
Collins campaign pushes back on ProPublica report on claims of pay-to-play scheme
The campaign for Sen. Susan Collins is making a renewed effort to push back against recent reporting and PAC ads that claim she accepted a big campaign donation in 2019 as part of a pay-to-play scheme.
In a report published on Sept. 22, ProPublica said that Collins, R-Maine, steered millions of dollars to defense contractor Martin Kao, the former CEO of Navatek, in return for donations to her 2020 reelection campaign. More specifically, ProPublica reported that the Collins campaign told Kao that he needed to make a campaign donation before meeting Collins, and that Kao was awarded millions in federal contracts after donating to the senator's campaign.
The Collins campaign denied the corruption allegations on the day the ProPublica report was published, and on Tuesday, the campaign again vehemently denied ProPublica's allegations, calling Kao a convicted felon and a liar.
On Tuesday, the Collins campaign presented what it said was proof that the ProPublica report is not true and that the senator did not accept money for favors. The Collins campaign presented a picture of Collins in a meeting with Kao, which was taken by a U.S. Senate photographer and had a timestamp of Feb. 15, 2018. The senator's campaign said that meeting — which was held to discuss a contract Navatek had been granted through the University of Maine — took place months before Kao made any donations to Collins' campaign.
"ProPublica reported that Martin Kao used the Navatek method: get the meeting, make the big initial donation, then have the high-priced lobbyists swoop in. As you can see, we were working with Navatek, through their partnership with the University of Maine, for two years before the big initial donation showed up," said Steve Abbott, Collins' campaign manager.
Abbott also called Kao a liar and pointed out that he is a felon who is serving 87 months in prison on several counts of money laundering and fraud.
"Martin Kao, he tried to sell this story to the FBI. They didn't buy it. He tried to sell it to the Department of Justice, they didn't buy it. Trying to sell it to the federal elections Commission, they didn't buy it. Tried to sell it to the judge, the judge didn't buy it. But ProPublica bought it hook, line and sinker," said Abbott.
On Sept. 23, ProPublica published a follow-up report stating that some of the statements made by Collins and her representatives denying any wrongdoing were not accurate.
